title: Bound within, free without

text: Physical premise (IDWT): There is one infinite-dimensional physical manifold. All sectors form one nested chain of submanifolds within it. Particle depth counts ordinary, literal macroscopic spatial dimensions. “Observed” and “unobserved” describe an observer's access to those dimensions, not different kinds of physical dimension. See spatial meaning and mathematical scope. 1. Claim and status IDWT has one infinite-dimensional physical manifold. Each particle's sector is a nested submanifold, and its depth counts the macroscopic spatial directions in which it has bound structure. A depth-a mode has localized structure in \Xi_a, while the same physical manifold continues beyond it: \Xi_a\hookrightarrow\Xi_b\hookrightarrow M_\infty, \qquad a<b. The founding kinematic statement is: A particle is bound within the dimensions in which it has localized spatial structure and spans every additional dimension in which it has no localized motion. Here spans means coordinate independence: the sector mode has equal support across the additional coordinate and is localized in none of its values. This is the content of bound within, free without. That statement is a premise of the sector ontology. Together with coordinate nesting, it yields the contact theorem below by pullback, pushforward, and Fubini integration. 2. Bound coordinates and free coordinates For nested depths a<b, write the higher coordinate space locally as \Xi_b\simeq\Xi_a\times F_{b/a}, with shared coordinates x\in\Xi_a and additional coordinates y\in F_{b/a}. Globally, the same argument uses a fibre bundle projection \pi_{ba}:\Xi_b\longrightarrow\Xi_a. A depth-a mode has a normalizable bound factor \chi_a(x) on its own sector. Its continuation to depth b is the cylindrical pullback (\pi_{ba}^{*}\chi_a)(x,y)=\chi_a(x). Therefore \partial_{y^j}(\pi_{ba}^{*}\chi_a)=0 \qquad (j=1,\ldots,b-a). The lower-depth particle has no profile that must be aimed at a point of the extra fibre. It spans that fibre because nothing in its spatial mode distinguishes one fibre point from another. The same state is compatible with, but not forced by, a free outer Hamiltonian. In a direction with no binding potential, H_{\mathrm{free}} =-\frac{\hbar^2}{2\mu}\partial_y^2. Its generalized momentum eigenfunctions e^{iky} have uniform magnitude. The zero-momentum member is constant; a nonzero-momentum member has changing phase but still no localized body being carried along the coordinate. A finite wavepacket may have a localized envelope, but it is then a superposition of outer momenta. Thus the translation eigenmode gives the spatial “already-there” sector state, while outer localization represents additional dynamical preparation. More generally, for outer coordinates y=(y^1,\ldots,y^{b-a}), F_K(y)=e^{iK_jy^j}, \qquad |F_K(y)|=1. If the particle has no phase motion in direction y^j, then K_j=0 and \boxed{\partial_{y^j}F_K=0}. It therefore spans every direction with zero phase motion. Nonzero phase motion preserves the same uniform plane-wave magnitude. 3. The cross-depth contact theorem Let \rho_a(x) be a density or current carried by the depth-a mode, and let \rho_b(x,y) be one carried by the depth-b mode. From the higher-depth side, the lower-depth quantity is cylindrical: \rho_a^{\uparrow b}(x,y)=\rho_a(x). For an allowed interaction local on \Xi_b, the overlap is I_{ab} = \int_{\Xi_a}d\mu_a(x) \int_{F_{b/a}}d\mu_F(y)\, \rho_a(x)\rho_b(x,y). Define the pushforward, or marginal, of the higher-depth density: \bar\rho_{b\to a}(x) = (\pi_{ba})_*\rho_b(x) = \int_{F_{b/a}}\rho_b(x,y)\,d\mu_F(y). Fubini's theorem then gives \boxed{ I_{ab} = \int_{\Xi_a} \rho_a(x)\bar\rho_{b\to a}(x)\,d\mu_a(x) }. This is the cross-depth contact theorem. The higher-depth particle contributes through its complete marginal over the extra coordinates, and the cylindrical lower-depth extension covers the entire fibre. The overlap therefore carries the full marginal weight. If \rho_b is a normalized nonnegative density, its whole weight survives the pushforward: \int_{\Xi_a}\bar\rho_{b\to a}\,d\mu_a = \int_{\Xi_b}\rho_b\,d\mu_b =1. This is the precise sense in which contact is full: the interaction integrates the extra coordinates over the complete fibre. For a nonlocal or filtered interaction, replace the pointwise product by a kernel on the shared coordinates: I_{ab}[K] = \int_{\Xi_a\times\Xi_a} \rho_a(x)K_{ab}(x,x')\bar\rho_{b\to a}(x') \,d\mu_a(x)d\mu_a(x'). Unequal depth determines how the modes meet. The kernel, coupling constant, and representation content determine what they do when they meet. 4. Noncompact normalization On an infinite fibre, the cylindrical pullback \pi_{ba}^{*}\chi_a can be used as a translation-invariant generalized state or as a field/observable. These uses need distinct normalizations: a cylindrical field or observable pulled back from \Xi_a; a generalized momentum eigenstate with delta normalization; or a box-normalized approximation, whose density contains an explicit inverse fibre-volume factor. The particle's normalization over its spatial support remains \int_{\Xi_a}|\chi_a(x)|^2d\mu_a(x)=1. The cross-depth interaction of a cylindrical field is finite when the higher-depth density supplies an integrable fibre factor. This does not make it equal to the overlap of two probability-normalized states. In a box of fibre volume V_F, a normalized uniform extension has density \rho_a(x)/V_F; its overlap with a fixed normalized \rho_b is I_{ab}/V_F, tending to zero as the box grows. Cancelling that factor requires a specified flux, source-density, or coupling normalization in the action. It does not follow from Fubini's theorem. The contact formula above uses the cylindrical-field convention, normalized on the physical spatial sector. 5. Reciprocity Let the interaction part of the action be S_{ab}=g_{ab}\int dt\,I_{ab}. For the local form, functional differentiation gives \frac{\delta S_{ab}}{\delta\rho_a(x)} =g_{ab}\bar\rho_{b\to a}(x), and \frac{\delta S_{ab}}{\delta\rho_b(x,y)} =g_{ab}\rho_a(x). The lower-depth mode feels the higher-depth mode through the latter's complete marginal. The higher-depth mode feels the lower-depth mode uniformly across the additional fibre. These are two variations of the same interaction term, so reciprocity follows when the action and kernel have the corresponding exchange symmetry. Both objects remain in their respective sectors. In IDWT's one-field language, \rho_a and \rho_b are sector components of one field \Psi_\infty. A cross-sector term is that field coupling two of its own depth-resolved structures on their shared coordinates. 6. Coupling conditions An interaction requires three ingredients: Coordinate incidence. An embedding or shared-coordinate map must identify the active lower-depth structure inside the higher-depth sector. Coupling filter. The modes must carry compatible charge, representation, chirality, or another interaction handle. The projected current may be zero despite full contact. Dynamics. The action supplies a coupling constant and an interaction kernel or connection. In a fixed nested gauge the inclusion \Xi_a\hookrightarrow\Xi_b is explicit. Rotating spatial frames require the corresponding embedding or projector in the interaction. Coordinate independence supplies complete fibre coverage; the polarization or representation projector on the shared coordinates determines whether the contact channel is nonzero. Numerical coupling ratios come from that projector and the normalized action. 7. Causal evolution Uniform support specifies the mode state. A disturbance evolves through the retarded Green function of the local field equation, whose causal cone governs the propagation of controllable changes. Marginalization specifies the coordinates sampled by the interaction at an event. Thus “already there” supplies coverage while the field equation supplies causal evolution. 8. Photon–electron example For a photon sector of depth 2 and an electron sector of depth 6, use x\in\Xi_2, \qquad y\in F_{6/2}. The photon's spatial current is cylindrical in the electron's four additional coordinates. The electron enters the shared interaction through \bar J_{e\to2}(x) = \int_{F_{6/2}}J_e(x,y)\,d\mu_F(y). An electromagnetic term therefore has the schematic form S_{\gamma e} = e\int dt\int_{\Xi_2} A_\alpha(x)\bar J_e^\alpha(x)\,d\mu_2(x), or its covariant analogue on the full manifold. The photon's coordinate independence across the four additional electron directions supplies the cylindrical extension, and the electron supplies the complete fibre marginal at the shared d=2 interaction. Electric charge and the normalized U(1) connection determine the interaction coefficient e. The same geometry underlies photon transversality. The photon oscillates in its physical spatial two-plane, while outer coordinates carry free phase or zero variation. Higher-depth embedding therefore preserves the spatial polarization plane. 9. Result The defensible chain is \text{spatial localization plus assumed outer translation invariance} \Longrightarrow \text{cylindrical extension across additional coordinates}, followed by \text{cylindrical lower-depth current} + \text{integrable higher-depth current} \Longrightarrow \text{full fibre marginal on the shared depth}. This establishes the marginal overlap formula under the specified cylindrical extension and interaction. Spatial localization alone does not imply outer translation invariance or select that extension. Sector selection, representation filters, coupling constants, masses, and force laws are supplied by the corresponding projected dynamics. 10. Mathematical domain Marginalization also does not by itself make a point particle appear smeared. For an instantaneous point trajectory, \rho_b(x,y,t)=\delta(x-X(t))\delta(y-Y(t)),\qquad \int\rho_b(x,y,t)\,dy=\delta(x-X(t)). An extended visible density instead requires visible extent in the joint state, an ensemble or time average of the trajectory, or detector response. Consequently, observing a spread alone does not distinguish the cylindrical ontology from an unobserved-localized source. Cylindrical extension remains the selected V2 premise here; the claim that smearing uniquely selects it is withdrawn. Coordinate nesting, outer translation invariance, full-coverage coupling, higher-to-lower marginalization, reciprocal response, and coupling filters form one consistent geometric mechanism. On a compact outer fibre, uniform support admits ordinary normalization. On an infinite fibre, it is a cylindrical or generalized state. Coupling magnitudes are computed from the action, kernel, connection, and representation geometry. The companion module Coupling as higher-dimensional polarization supplies the representation-theoretic criterion for full geometric contact to survive the polarization projection as a nonzero interaction.

title: Particle depth as spatial geometry
summary: Literal macroscopic spatial dimensions IDWT has one infinite-dimensional physical manifold, M_\infty. Every particle sector is a nested spatial submanifold of that same manifold: Q_a\hookrightarrow Q_b\hookrightarrow M_\
text:
Literal macroscopic spatial dimensions IDWT has one infinite-dimensional physical manifold, M_\infty. Every particle sector is a nested spatial submanifold of that same manifold: Q_a\hookrightarrow Q_b\hookrightarrow M_\infty,\qquad a<b. This inclusion relates spatial sectors. Individual particles are field structures associated with the sectors; it does not place one particle inside another or make it a constituent of another. In particular, an electron state need not be the restriction of a tau state. A restriction of bundles compares the available field components across sectors; identifying particular particle solutions through that restriction is an additional dynamical assumption. Depth d counts ordinary, literal macroscopic spatial dimensions of Q_d. They are all the same kind of physical dimension. Their coordinates specify position, separation, and motion. A sector is not an internal state space, a compactified auxiliary space, or a configuration-space substitute for physical space. There are no additional physical dimensions outside M_\infty. For the electron and tau, this means Q_6\hookrightarrow Q_{10}: the electron's six spatial dimensions are six of the tau's ten. All ten are the same kind of dimension for the tau. The electron is “flat” relative to it, meaning lower-dimensional, not that the tau has an inherent six-plus-four division. The same relationship holds between three-dimensional nuclei and six-dimensional electrons. “Flat” here describes relative dimensionality, not a claim of zero metric curvature. The photon-transversality construction illustrates this at every containing depth. The photon retains two directions of bound oscillation. There is one perpendicular direction within a three-dimensional sector, four within a six-dimensional sector, and eight within a ten-dimensional sector. These are descriptions relative to the photon; they do not create different kinds of dimensions in the containing sector. IDWT attributes the three-dimensional experience of ordinary matter and observers to the three-dimensional nuclear sector. This general premise does not require a physical division of any higher-depth particle into different kinds of dimensions. The observer map must describe what the observer's interactions register; its dynamics remains to be derived. For example, the electron has six ordinary macroscopic spatial dimensions. In the proposed geometry, Q_6=\mathbb{CP}^3 is its actual spatial submanifold. Three of those dimensions are shared with us. That fact makes none of the six physically different in kind, and does not give the electron an inherent 3+3 split. Grouping coordinates by an observer's access is a choice of description, not a division in the electron. Frame-lock models that use such a grouping have additional assumptions; they do not establish the general origin of three-dimensional experience. This states the physical premise; it does not declare the proposed metric, embedding, lock, or observer response mathematically derived or experimentally established. The following vocabulary applies throughout the research record: Term Physical or mathematical meaning Sector, depth, base Q_d A nested spatial submanifold of M_\infty, with d macroscopic spatial directions. Observed and unobserved directions; formerly “visible” and “hidden” Names relative to an observer or interaction. Directions shared with us are no different in physical kind from any others. These names do not divide the electron into two physical parts. Normal or projection fibre When used for spatial nesting, directions or points of the same physical manifold omitted by a particular restriction or marginal. Spinor, vector-bundle, or mode-space dimension The number of components used to represent fields and modes on that manifold. It introduces no additional physical dimensions or independently postulated internal world. Homogeneous coordinates and coefficient rays Mathematical representations whose meaning must be specified. A homogeneous coordinate for a point of Q_6 represents spatial position; an arbitrary ray of field coefficients does not automatically do so. Multiparticle configuration space A mathematical record of several positions in the same physical manifold, not extra dimensions of physical space. “Intrinsic” in older mathematical passages Defined from a manifold's own metric or tangent bundle. It must never mean that the particle sector is internal or nonspatial. Compact projective geometry A proposed global topology of a spatial submanifold. IDWT has no compactified dimensions. Mathematical compactness sets no physical length scale; conclusions using this topology remain conditional on it and the physical metric scale remains to be derived. Inclusions of nested submanifolds, maps that marginalize spatial coordinates, and projectors acting on field components are different mathematical objects. One cannot establish the first merely by constructing either of the others. See the geometry and nesting audit for the resulting restrictions on existing calculations. The intermediate-depth obstruction sharpens that requirement: the standard \mathrm{CP}^2\subset\mathrm{CP}^3 inclusion cannot factor through a smooth five-dimensional spatial submanifold. A pointwise normal direction exists, but the nonzero normal Euler class prevents the required global line subbundle. Thus assigning candidate topologies at separate depths must be followed by a compatible global embedding construction; local spinor branchings do not supply it. 1. Geometric claim Status: spatial depth and a named geometry are separate hypotheses. The candidate sphere/projective assignments elsewhere in V2 are not proved by the dimension and principal-symbol arguments below. Those arguments also assume the sector embedding and projection stated in their hypotheses; they do not independently select a physical depth. See the geometry premise audit. A particle of depth d lives on a spatial submanifold Q_d of M_\infty with real dimension d. Each spatial coordinate supplies a derivative direction and a conjugate covector component in the principal symbol of the kinetic operator. In IDWT the depth d appears simultaneously in TQ_d, \qquad T^*Q_d, \qquad \gamma^ap_a, \qquad S(n,d), \qquad \pi_{ba}:Q_b	o Q_a, and in the integration measure used for cross-depth contact. These are linked uses of one physical spatial depth. The particle's physical spatial submanifold is Q_d. Its spinor bundle carries the spatial Dirac field. The auxiliary coherent-ray fibre \mathbb{CP}^{d} organizes the phase modes constructed from the d spatial oscillator directions, and embeds by the degree-N Veronese map into the full projective mode space \mathbb P(\mathcal E_{N,d})\cong\mathbb{CP}^{S(N+1,d)-1} at a point (for N>0). These three geometric layers are Q_d, \qquad \Sigma Q_d, \qquad \mathbb P(\mathcal E_{N,d}). Only Q_d names physical spatial dimensions. The other two objects describe the field and its modes on Q_d; their component counts add no dimensions to M_\infty. In particular the auxiliary \mathbb{CP}^{d} here is a space of mode coefficients, distinct from the physical electron submanifold Q_6=\mathbb{CP}^3. 2. Principal symbol on a base manifold Let X be a spatial manifold and F	o X a vector bundle carrying polarization or charge data. A Dirac-type field has kinetic operator \mathcal D_{m int} =i\gamma^\mu
abla_\mu\otimes I_F+A(x), where A(x) acts algebraically on F. Its principal symbol is \sigma_1(\mathcal D_{m int})(x,k) =\gamma^\mu k_\mu\otimes I_F. Additional physical spatial coordinates y^a extend the kinetic operator to \mathcal D_{m spatial} =i\gamma^\mu
abla_\mu+i\Gamma^a
abla_a+A(x,y), and its principal symbol becomes \sigma_1(\mathcal D_{m spatial})(x,y;k,p) =\gamma^\mu k_\mu+\Gamma^ap_a. The covector components p_a are their conjugate momenta. They determine the characteristic set and propagation directions; the short-time heat kernel and spectral dimension; localization and uncertainty relations; the measure over which contact and overlap are calculated; the kinetic response to gradients in those directions. Thus base dimension is read invariantly from the number of independent covector components in the principal symbol. Fibre matrices enter the lower-order algebraic structure and representation content. 3. Application to a particle sector The projected field of a depth-d particle is \psi_d\in\Gamma(\Sigma Q_d\otimes F_d), \qquad \dim_{\mathbb R}Q_d=d. Its kinetic principal symbol is \sigma_1(\mathcal D_d)(q,p) =\gamma_d^ap_a\otimes I_{F_d}, \qquad p\in T_q^*Q_d, with Clifford relation \{\gamma_d^a,\gamma_d^b\}=2g_d^{ab}I. There are exactly d independent local momentum components. They are tied to the d tangent directions of the manifold where the particle lives. The bundle F_d carries spinor polarization, charge, flux, or a finite representation on top of the base geometry: \underbrace{Q_d}_{	ext{physical spatial submanifold}} \quad+\quad \underbrace{\Sigma Q_d}_{	ext{spinor fibre}} \quad+\quad \underbrace{F_d}_{	ext{field representation}}. The plus signs separate mathematical descriptions; they are not a sum of physical dimensions. Any physical role assigned to F_d must come from the one master field and geometry, rather than a separate internal sector. 4. Why the mass count tests the base dimension At each q\in Q_d, the oscillator symbol has d complex amplitudes a_a = rac1{\sqrt2} \left(  rac{x_a}{\ell_d} +i rac{\ell_dp_a}{\hbar} ight), \qquad a=1,\ldots,d. These are the position and momentum quadratures belonging to the tangent and cotangent directions of Q_d. Their shell-k symmetric mode space has rank  inom{k+d-1}{d-1}. The cumulative band through N=n-1 is \mathcal E_{N,d} =  igoplus_{k=0}^{N} \operatorname{Sym}^k(T^*Q_d\otimes\mathbb C), with \operatorname{rank}\mathcal E_{N,d} = inom{N+d}{d} =S(n,d). Thus d enters the mass formula as the rank of the cotangent space whose independent momenta generate the oscillator modes. The homogenized expression \mathcal E_{N,d} \cong \operatorname{Sym}^{N} \left(\mathbf1\oplus T^*Q_d\otimes\mathbb Cight) introduces one slack occupation coordinate. Its ray fibre \mathbb{CP}^{d} compactly organizes the cumulative phase modes. Its real dimension 2d reflects one position and one momentum quadrature for every base direction. 5. Why the coupling construction also uses base geometry Suppose a depth-a sector and a depth-b sector are related by \pi_{ba}:Q_b	o Q_a, \qquad b>a. The lower-depth field reaches the higher sector by pullback: \psi_a^{\uparrow b}=\pi_{ba}^*\psi_a. The higher-depth current reaches the lower sector by pushforward:  ar J_{b	o a}=(\pi_{ba})_*J_b. In local product coordinates (x,y)\in Q_a	imes F_{ba},  ar J_{b	o a}(x) =\int_{F_{ba}}J_b(x,y)\,d\mu_{F_{ba}}(y). The interaction is then an overlap on the common base: I_{ab} =\int_{Q_a} J_a(x) ar J_{b	o a}(x)\,d\mu_{Q_a}(x). This geometric contact uses the additional directions to determine which points can coincide, how a density is marginalized, which polarizations survive the normal-direction contraction, and how the interaction varies with separation and orientation. 6. Normal geometry after lower-depth projection When a higher-depth field is restricted to Q_a\subset Q_b, the tangent bundle splits: TQ_b|_{Q_a}=TQ_a\oplus N_{ba}. A lower-depth observer resolves TQ_a. Rotations of the normal frame N_{ba} act on the projected fields as representation transformations, and the normal connection transforms as a gauge connection. The projection map is therefore 	ext{higher-dimensional geometry} \quad\xrightarrow{	ext{restriction}}\quad 	ext{projected polarization and gauge connection}. The generators descend from the parent Clifford term \Gamma^ap_a and the normal connection. Gauge-like structures are therefore observer restrictions of particle-sector geometry. 7. Combined dimensional evidence The same integer d performs four linked jobs: it is \dim_{\mathbb R}Q_d; it counts the independent momenta in the Dirac principal symbol; it fixes the degree of the simplex mass growth; it fixes the tangent, normal, and fibre dimensions entering cross-depth contact and polarization. The observed mass hierarchies recover d=2,3,4,5,6,10 from scale-free ratios. Those same values organize the coupling projection, its stabilizers, the symmetric-power spectrum, spinor branching, contact marginalization, and mass growth. The projected principal symbol provides the invariant kinetic test joining these structures. 8. Projected-principal-symbol theorem The decisive calculation can be made exactly once the meaning of sector projection is stated. Let i_d:Q_d\hookrightarrow M_\infty be a sector embedding with an orthogonal tangent--normal splitting along Q_d. Let P_d be a smooth zeroth-order orthogonal projector from the restricted master spinor bundle onto a sector bundle \Sigma_d. For a covector p\in T_q^*Q_d, let \iota_dp denote its tangential extension that annihilates the normal bundle. Assume the master operator is Dirac type, so \sigma_1(\mathcal D_\infty)(q,\Xi) =i\,c_\infty(\Xi), and define the sector operator by tangential compression, \mathcal D_d =P_d\mathcal D_\infty^{\parallel}P_d. Because P_d is order zero, symbol composition gives \sigma_1(\mathcal D_d)(q,p) =iP_d c_\infty(\iota_dp)P_d. Derivatives of P_d contribute to the order-zero connection and algebraic mixing terms. The principal momenta remain those in the compressed Clifford symbol. Now impose the essential compatibility condition: \Sigma_d is invariant under tangential Clifford multiplication and its identification with the spin or Spin^c bundle of Q_d obeys P_dc_\infty(\iota_dp)P_d=c_d(p). Choose a local coframe e^1,\ldots,e^d on Q_d and write p=p_ae^a. Then  oxed{ \sigma_1(P_d\mathcal D_\infty^{\parallel}P_d)(q,p) =i\gamma_d^ap_a } with exactly d independent momentum components. The inherited Clifford relation is c_d(p)c_d(r)+c_d(r)c_d(p) =2g_d^{-1}(p,r)I, and hence \sigma_1(\mathcal D_d)(q,p)^2 =-g_d^{-1}(p,p)I for the displayed i\mathcal D convention. Thus the same d-dimensional cotangent metric controls the characteristic kinetic response. For time-dependent dynamics, the same evolution parameter t is used for every sector. The count d here concerns spatial momenta on the nested submanifold; introducing a time parameter does not postulate another spatial manifold or another particle depth. 8.1 Lower-order normal geometry Tangential compression sets normal covectors to zero. The normal connection and normal Clifford products survive in the lower-order part: \mathcal D_d =i\gamma_d^a(\partial_a+\omega_a+A_a^{\perp})+\Phi_d. Here A_a^{\perp} and \Phi_d act algebraically on the lower-depth fibre as the projected gauge polarization, while the principal symbol contains the momenta tangent to Q_d. 8.2 The theorem's hypotheses The result is conditional on three geometric facts: P_d is a smooth zeroth-order bundle projector; sector restriction means tangential compression with normal covectors set to zero; the projected spinor subbundle is invariant under tangential Clifford multiplication. Tangential Clifford invariance gives a full-rank elliptic symbol. Its direct verification for every sector is the diagnostic that the projected geometry retains all d spatial directions. 9. Master-geometry closure Under the hypotheses just stated, the formal calculation is complete: \sigma_1 \left( P_d\mathcal D_\infty^{\parallel}P_d ight)(q,p) =i\gamma_d^ap_a, \qquad p\in T_q^*Q_d. Physical completion constructs the master operator and sector projectors with: exactly d independent momentum components; the Clifford relation for the metric on Q_d; propagation or standing-wave gradients in every one of those directions; the same metric and measure in the self-contact and cross-depth kernels; reduction to the observed lower-depth dispersion after inaccessible momenta are marginalized. The mass and coupling constructions use the same T^*Q_d, metric, and measure. The completed projection therefore joins kinetic propagation, spectral growth, and cross-depth contact in one d-dimensional base geometry.

title: The electron's six-dimensional physical submanifold
summary: 1. Where the electron lives Let \Pi_6:M_\infty\longrightarrow Q_6 be a proposed electron-sector projection within M_\infty. The electron lives on the nested spatial submanifold Q_6, with six literal macroscopic spatial d
text: Physical premise (IDWT): There is one infinite-dimensional physical manifold. All sectors form one nested chain of submanifolds within it. Particle depth counts ordinary, literal macroscopic spatial dimensions. “Observed” and “unobserved” describe an observer's access to those dimensions, not different kinds of physical dimension. See spatial meaning and mathematical scope. 1. Where the electron lives Let \Pi_6:M_\infty\longrightarrow Q_6 be a proposed electron-sector projection within M_\infty. The electron lives on the nested spatial submanifold Q_6, with six literal macroscopic spatial dimensions. The proposed spatial geometry is \boxed{Q_6=\mathbb{CP}^3}. All six are ordinary spatial dimensions of the same physical kind. Three are shared with us; that relationship to our sector creates no inherent division in the electron. This is a physical spatial submanifold of the one infinite manifold. The directions outside the electron's bound sector are further spatial directions of that same manifold and obey bound-within/free-without. A projection with this image must be constructed; writing a projection symbol does not prove the required global nesting or map exists. Three facts must nevertheless remain distinct: a point q\in Q_6, which is the electron's physical spatial position; a homogeneous-coordinate lift Z\in\mathbb C^4\setminus\{0\} with q=[Z]; and the electron Dirac field on Q_6, which is a section of the spatial spinor bundle of \mathbb{CP}^3. Conflating the coordinate lift Z with the value of the Dirac field would turn a useful representation coincidence into a false identity. 2. Two conditional constructions identify the same candidate geometry 2.1 Minimal complex projection A normalized vector in \mathbb C^r has 2r-1 real degrees of freedom. If common phase is redundant, its ray has 2r-2 real degrees of freedom. Requiring this to equal the electron depth gives 2r-2=6 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad r=4. The minimal complex homogeneous ray space is therefore \mathbb P(\mathbb C^4)=\mathbb{CP}^3. This derivation is conditional on complex amplitudes, normalization, and common-phase redundancy. Those premises must ultimately follow from the projected master-field action. 2.2 Six-dimensional pure-spinor geometry Independently, Spin(6)\cong SU(4), and a positive-chirality complex spinor of the model six-dimensional tangent space transforms as S_6^+\cong\mathbb C^4. Every nonzero Weyl spinor in six Euclidean dimensions is pure. Its line determines an orthogonal complex structure J on a model real six-dimensional vector space. The space of those structures is \boxed{ \mathbb P(S_6^+) \cong SO(6)/U(3) \cong \mathbb{CP}^3 }. Thus two independent requirements meet: \text{minimal complex ray of real dimension six} \quad= \text{projective six-dimensional pure-spinor space}. This double derivation is why \mathbb{CP}^3 is presently the strongest sector identification in the theory. 3. Geometry of the physical spatial submanifold Write a sector point as q=[Z], \qquad Z^\dagger Z=1, \qquad Z\sim e^{i\lambda}Z. Let L_q=\mathbb C Z be the selected line and let L_q^\perp be its orthogonal complement. The tangent space is T_q\mathbb{CP}^3 \cong \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb C}(L_q,L_q^\perp). It has complex dimension three and real dimension six. These are the six directions available to the electron inside its sector. The transitive action and stabilizer are \mathbb{CP}^3 \cong SU(4)/U(3). The U(3) stabilizer preserves the electron's selected ray. Its decomposition U(3)\cong[SU(3)\times U(1)]/\mathbb Z_3 makes colour-plus-Abelian coupling a serious stabilizer candidate. The physical identification requires the induced connection to act as colour on quarks, as a singlet on leptons, and with the observed Abelian charges. The natural invariant metric is the Fubini--Study metric, up to an overall length scale R_6: g_6=R_6^2g_{\rm FS}. Under this proposed global geometry, the electron's spatial Laplacian, measure, geodesics, and Dirac operator are those of Q_6=\mathbb{CP}^3. This mathematical manifold is compact. IDWT has no compactified dimensions: none of the six spatial directions is hidden, curled up, or assigned a small compactification scale. The global topology and physical metric scale remain hypotheses to be derived from the master field. 4. Coordinate lift and Dirac field Because c_1(T\mathbb{CP}^3)=4H, the second Stiefel--Whitney class vanishes: w_2(T\mathbb{CP}^3)=0. The electron sector is spin. Let \Sigma Q_6 denote its complex spinor bundle over physical space. The projected electron field has the form \psi_e \in \Gamma(\Sigma Q_6\otimes L_{\rm em}), if it is twisted by an electromagnetic line bundle L_{\rm em}. The homogeneous coordinate Z labels q\in Q_6, while \psi_e(q) is a spinor located at q. A proposed physical bridge may be represented locally by Z=\psi_{e,+}(q) but this is not a global linear identification of the two rank-four bundles. Its precise meaning and derivation belong to the projected electron action. In six real dimensions the spatial Dirac fibre has two chiral halves of complex dimension four. Equal fibre dimensions do not imply equivalent bundles. In the even Kähler chirality convention, \operatorname{ch}(\Sigma^+\mathbb{CP}^3)=4+2H^2-2H^3, whereas the ambient homogeneous-coordinate bundle is trivial. No line twist removes the discrepancy: vanishing first Chern class forces a zero twist, leaving the nonzero second Chern character. A full-rank global linear intertwiner of this proposed kind is therefore excluded, not merely missing. A selected line, a nonlinear construction, or a field-induced scalar potential on the base remains possible, with its own proof obligations. See Spatial spinor bundle obstruction for the characteristic-class calculation and the separate base-selection test. The master-field projection must produce both the sector coordinate and its field: \Pi_6:M_\infty\to Q_6, \qquad \psi_e=P_{6,e}\Psi_\infty. 5. Hopf lift and the canonical U(1) connection The normalized homogeneous coordinates form the Hopf bundle U(1)\longrightarrow S^7 \longrightarrow\mathbb{CP}^3. On a local lift Z, the canonical connection is a=-iZ^\dagger dZ, with curvature f=da. Under a change of local lift, Z\mapsto e^{i\lambda}Z, \qquad a\mapsto a+d\lambda. This is a genuine U(1) connection on the Hopf/tautological bundle over the space where the electron lives. Its cohomology class generates H^2(\mathbb{CP}^3,\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z. Its electromagnetic identification requires A_{\rm em}=\frac{\hbar}{e}a or an equivalent relation to emerge in the covariant Dirac action with the measured electron charge. A geometrically correct U(1) connection can still represent Berry phase, a prequantum line, or another sector phase. 6. A conditional 3+3 coordinate grouping The electron has six ordinary spatial dimensions, with no physical split. The following calculation chooses an observer-adapted grouping in a model vector representation. It separates directions shared with the observer from the others for this calculation only: V_6=V_{\rm obs}\oplus V_{\rm hid} \cong\mathbb R^3\oplus\mathbb R^3. The names are relative to the observer, not properties distinguishing kinds of electron dimension. Under the chosen subgroup Spin(6)\supset Spin(3)_{\rm obs}\times Spin(3)_{\rm hid}, the homogeneous-coordinate/pure-spinor representation branches as \mathbf4=(\mathbf2,\mathbf2). If a diagonal frame lock is additionally assumed, the representation gives (\mathbf2,\mathbf2) \downarrow_{Spin(3)_{\rm diag}} =\mathbf1\oplus\mathbf3. This is the exact representation content of one s-like channel and three p-like channels within that assumed model. It does not establish a physical division of the electron or show that the electron–nucleus interaction supplies this frame constraint. A point q=[Z]\in\mathbb{CP}^3 also determines the orthogonal complex structure J_{AB}(Z)=-iZ^\dagger\Gamma_{AB}Z. Relative to the chosen 3+3 coordinate grouping, J= \begin{pmatrix} A&Q\\ -Q^T&C \end{pmatrix}. The mixed block Q is the candidate composite frame link. When the within-block pieces vanish, J^2=-I forces QQ^T=Q^TQ=I_3, so Q identifies the two three-frames and leaves the diagonal rotation group. The companion frame-lock module tests whether the action actually selects this orbit. 7. The orbit generator and the 1{:}3 harmonic Consider the traceless generator \widetilde G =\frac14\operatorname{diag}(5,-3,-3,1) \in\mathfrak{su}(4). It acts directly on the sector Q_6=\mathbb{CP}^3 through [Z]\longmapsto[e^{-i\theta\widetilde G}Z]. The six-dimensional real vector representation is \Lambda^2\mathbf4. Adding pairs of the four fundamental weights gives three real rotation-plane rates \left(\frac12,\frac12,\frac32\right) \propto 1:1:3. At \theta=2\pi, the projective point closes because the fundamental action is a common phase. The vector representation reaches its antipode. An antipode-even quadratic observer readout therefore has available harmonics 1\quad\text{and}\quad3. This gives a representation-theoretic origin for the slow orbit frequency and the three-times depth frequency used by the six-dimensional visualization. The generator, detector plane, radial response, and angular speed are the remaining dynamical data. 8. Dynamics on the physical spatial submanifold \mathbb{CP}^3 A minimal diagnostic action now has the form S_e = \int dt\int_{Q_6}d\mu_{\rm FS} \left[ \overline\psi_e \left(i\gamma^0D_t+i\slashed D_{Q_6}-m_e\right)\psi_e -V_N(q)\overline\psi_e\psi_e \right] +S_{\rm int}. Here \slashed D_{Q_6} is the spatial Dirac operator for g_6=R_6^2g_{\rm FS}, including every physical line or normal-bundle connection. The nuclear potential V_N and S_{\rm int} must be obtained by projecting the single master-field interaction onto Q_6. The SU(4) isometries supply Killing vector fields K_G for G\in\mathfrak{su}(4). A selected orbit generator enters through the Hamiltonian/Killing flow of K_G. The proposed compact spatial geometry also has a discrete spatial spectrum without adding a flat harmonic oscillator. Compact topology sets no physical length scale: R_6 is still required, and no dimensional compactification is being assumed. Twists of the field bundle on this same sector are described by line bundles \mathcal O(L), with holomorphic section space H^0(\mathbb{CP}^3,\mathcal O(L)) \cong \operatorname{Sym}^L(\mathbb C^4)^*. Its dimension is the genuine combinatorial count \dim H^0(\mathbb{CP}^3,\mathcal O(L)) =\binom{L+3}{3}. All electron-sector measures, radial observables, and Laplacians are defined using g_{\rm FS}, d\mu_{\rm FS}, and the spatial operators on Q_6. A concrete selected-line candidate is now available: since \Sigma=\Lambda^{0,*}\otimes\mathcal O(-2), twisting the spatial spinor by \mathcal O(L+2) places H^0(\mathcal O(L)) in its degree-zero component. This does not trivialize the full spinor bundle. With the compatible Chern connection, those holomorphic sections are spatial Dirac zero modes; the free Dirac term alone does not generate their orbit. A separately supplied Killing drive produces the orbit and, when gauged, contributes a transport current. The distinction between spin twist L+2 and section degree L must be retained in any electromagnetic flux identification. See the selected-line current calculation for the conditional lift, its conserved source, and the unresolved ring sector. 9. The action-level closure target The projected master action must determine: why the electron projection has image Q_6=\mathbb{CP}^3; the scale R_6 of its Fubini--Study metric; the spatial spinor and electromagnetic line bundles; whether the canonical Hopf connection is physical electromagnetism; how the nuclear depth-three sector meets or maps into Q_6; whether that interaction selects the diagonal 3+3 frame lock; the orbit generator, Chern sector, and rate; the observer map from an orbit in Q_6 to three-dimensional detection. The decisive electron equation is the projected spatial equation P_6D_\infty P_6 \equiv \slashed D_{\mathbb{CP}^3} +\text{projected interaction terms}. The cross-depth electron--nucleus block is P_3D_\infty P_6, or its adjoint. Its vertical/normal representation content must produce the frame link and the observed interaction while eliminating forbidden channels. 10. Status Established mathematics the inverse dimension count selecting \mathbb{CP}^3 from minimal complex rays; \mathbb{CP}^3\cong SU(4)/U(3)\cong SO(6)/U(3); the real six-dimensional tangent space of \mathbb{CP}^3; the spin structure of \mathbb{CP}^3; the Hopf U(1) bundle and integral flux classes; (\mathbf2,\mathbf2)\to\mathbf1\oplus\mathbf3 after diagonal locking; the generator's 1{:}1{:}3 vector-plane rates and available quadratic 1{:}3 harmonics; the section count \binom{L+3}{3}. Physical identification still required derivation of the sector projection and metric scale; relation between the master Dirac field and spatial spinors on Q_6; electromagnetic identification of the Hopf connection; dynamical selection of the frame lock and orbit generator; the nuclear interaction and observer map. The conclusion is that \mathbb{CP}^3 is a mathematically coherent candidate for the six-dimensional space where the electron lives. Taking that statement literally makes the construction more unified and also makes the required dynamics much more specific. Sources and companion modules Primary mathematical cross-check: Nathan Berkovits and Sergey A. Cherkis, Higher-Dimensional Twistor Transforms using Pure Spinors — projective pure spinors parameterize SO(2n)/U(n); in six dimensions this space is \mathbb{CP}^3. Companion V2 modules: Coupling as higher-dimensional polarization Conditional electron–nucleus frame model Higher-dimensional magnetism and the projective orbit lock Observer map for the projective electron orbit Tetrahedral bond geometry Bound within, free without

title: Coupling as higher-dimensional polarization
summary: The generalized sector coupling calculation develops reciprocal spatial maps, canonical vertex normalization, common field response, and a neutrino channel control for arbitrary nested sectors. IDWT coupling is direct dy
text: Physical premise (IDWT): There is one infinite-dimensional physical manifold. All sectors form one nested chain of submanifolds within it. Particle depth counts ordinary, literal macroscopic spatial dimensions. “Observed” and “unobserved” describe an observer's access to those dimensions, not different kinds of physical dimension. See spatial meaning and mathematical scope. The generalized sector coupling calculation develops reciprocal spatial maps, canonical vertex normalization, common field response, and a neutrino channel control for arbitrary nested sectors. IDWT coupling is direct dynamics of \Psi_\infty; it assumes no mediator particles. Effective response kernels must be derived from that same field. Both objects carry spatial polarization. The current bilateral calculation retains their relative patterns and reciprocal response. A descending source calculation starts from the higher-dimensional geometry while retaining the lower mode's propagation. The photon's two bound dimensions need not set the source strength. The spatial shape vertices now give an explicit higher-order polarization law, and reciprocal scattering connects it to incoming and outgoing wave flux. A complementary neutral-mode construction derives cancellation between equal spatial rotation planes. Its geometric transport allows a distinct nonzero response within the same neutral modes. These are conditional mechanisms; the physical current and occupied particle solutions must still select and normalize them. The full spatial Dirac calculation now retains the orbital and spin parts of these rotations and the complete scalar source. Its polarized shape response shows how both angular field components respond. A dynamical matching calculation finds shapes with zero static access whose response opens at nonzero frequency, with both objects' polarizations retained. A nested spatial pair solves both profiles from one common interaction energy. Their reciprocal amplitude coupling then follows from the same energy's second derivatives, including both profiles' deformation. These conditional Dirac models provide calculable mechanisms and their limits: scalar binding does not select the occupied polarization, and some bound branches are unstable. Identifying physical photon and neutrino channels still requires the actual particle solution and current. The source-frequency calculation tracks which temporal frequency belongs to the interacting spatial pattern. Exact two-frequency currents provide a bound-frequency clock, while their changing size and full response prevent identifying slow motion alone with weak coupling. Incoming shape modes separates an already formed incident pattern from a force that creates it, retaining both objects' response and the helicity cancellation mechanism. The complete periodic pair response retains both source clocks, both spatial polarizations and scalar-center motion. Its polarization selection test calculates cancelling subspaces for the actual incoming spatial pattern. A checked rest barrier opens linearly in normal momentum, with common physical rotations preserving the result. These are conditional source identities; assigning the occupied photon and neutrino fields and their normalized rates remains a physical derivation. The complete polarization description now tests which spatial tensors retain every amplitude and phase. A reciprocal six-inside-ten example shows why equal mean currents can conceal different responses of the full polarized fields. Spatial textures add the bound-coordinate kinetic terms needed when polarization varies across a particle. These calculations keep both individual fields and their actual spatial equations in view. The complete spatial current now connects translation inertia, magnetic moment and low-frequency polarization response. Retaining the photon phase gives the forward scattering coefficient, while the moving spatial frame fixes the spin-orbit coefficient. The conditional scalar profile does not yet match the electron magnetic moment. Its current and charge normalization remain physical inputs to derive. A separate stationary spatial-wave construction supports exact finite null displacements. Completing its actual spatial profile gives a common interaction and a retarded response with derived outgoing radiation. This is a component-action benchmark, not an identified electromagnetic or weak interaction of the master field. The corresponding polarized pulse collisions have reciprocal energy-dependent delays. The outgoing spatial source depends on both complex polarizations, allowing a radiation zero while conservative coupling survives in this specified component model. 1. Geometric coupling mechanism Full-field controls extend these comparisons to localized encounters. Complete three-dimensional packets show phase-sensitive reciprocal chiral-norm transfer beyond a four-mode truncation. Five-dimensional spatial patterns can increase or decrease a specified subsequent contact comparison; ordered source variations derive its leading change directly from the same local equation. These are unbound-field benchmarks. Their norm transfer is not an assigned particle count or electric charge, and their scalar coefficient has not been identified with measured coupling strengths. The weighted oscillator response also shows why source counts require a physical spectrum and normalization. An exact Hockey-Stick sum alone does not determine a finite effective interaction when additional response modes are included. This module starts from the proposed particle depths, the single Dirac field \Psi_\infty, and bound-within/free-without. A particle's sector is the image of a projection \Pi_d:M_\infty\longrightarrow Q_d, \qquad \dim_{\mathbb R}Q_d=d. The particle lives on Q_d. A successful identification such as Q_6=\mathbb{CP}^3 is therefore its actual six-dimensional spatial submanifold. The sectors are nested through embeddings Q_a\hookrightarrow Q_b. Where a compatible quotient or submersion \pi_{ba}:Q_b\to Q_a also exists, it supplies a further projection map; a quotient alone does not establish the required inclusion. A chosen metric splits the tangent space along the embedded Q_a into tangent and normal directions, and along a submersion into horizontal and vertical directions. This split gives an exact mathematical meaning to higher-dimensional polarization: the local Spin(b) spinor restricts into lower-depth Spin(a) polarization and vertical or normal Spin(b-a) polarization; spatial variation of the projected or normal modes induces a connection over Q_a, whose curvature must be calculated; a frame change alone does not establish a physical interaction; a cross-depth vertex survives only when the extra polarizations contract to a singlet and the tangential representations admit an invariant pairing. Particle depth thereby supplies spinor branchings, normal-bundle gauge candidates, and invariant selection rules. To identify electric charge, colour, weak chirality and coupling constants, the physical holonomy, selected modes and complete current must be derived from the field dynamics. Here d occurs in the base tangent and cotangent spaces, the kinetic principal symbol \gamma^ap_a, and the pushforward measure used for cross-depth contact. The projected-symbol theorem is developed in particle depth as spatial geometry. 2. Structures carried by sector depth A real oriented sector manifold Q_d of depth d supplies at each point: SO(d), \qquad Spin(d), \qquad S^{d-1}\subset\mathbb R^d, together with tensor and spinor representations of those groups. Globally, its topology determines the corresponding spin or Spin^c structure. Complex polarization, a Hermitian form, phase quotient, and connection supply \mathbb{CP}^n, \qquad SU(n), \qquad U(1)_{\rm em}, \qquad SU(2)_L, \qquad SU(3)_{\rm colour}. A complex projective sector is formed from a complex vector space by quotient under common complex scale. A unitary group preserves its Hermitian form, and local frame redundancy supplies the gauge connection. There are accidental low-dimensional isomorphisms, Spin(2)\cong U(1), \qquad Spin(3)\cong SU(2), \qquad Spin(4)\cong SU(2)\times SU(2), \qquad Spin(5)\cong Sp(2), \qquad Spin(6)\cong SU(4). These exact group identities provide the candidate frame symmetries. The Dirac action makes a physical gauge identification by inducing the observed connection, representations, currents, and selection rules. 3. Bound-within/free-without supplies contact A depth-a field is a field on Q_a. Its continuation to the master manifold is the pullback \Psi_a^{\uparrow\infty}=\Pi_a^*\psi_a. It is constant along directions in \ker d\Pi_a. This is the coordinate-free form of spanning every direction in which the particle has no localized motion. When a pair admits a sector projection \pi_{ba}:Q_b\to Q_a, the lower field pulls back to Q_b as \psi_a^{\uparrow b}=\pi_{ba}^*\psi_a. A higher-depth current enters the lower interaction through pushforward over the projection fibre: \bar J_{b\to a}=(\pi_{ba})_*J_b. In local product coordinates this is the full fibre integral. The subsequent invariant projection extracts the component of \bar J_{b\to a} carried by the lower interaction. 4. Clifford factorization At a point where a sector relation supplies a horizontal/vertical or tangent/normal split, let V_b=V_a\oplus N_q, \qquad q=b-a. Over the complex numbers, the Clifford algebra respects an orthogonal direct sum through the graded tensor product: Cl(V_b)_{\mathbb C} \cong Cl(V_a)_{\mathbb C}\,\widehat\otimes\, Cl(N_q)_{\mathbb C}. Accordingly, a higher-depth spinor decomposes under Spin(a)\times Spin(q)\subset Spin(b) into lower-depth spinor factors and normal spinor factors. Schematically, S_b\downarrow_{Spin(a)\times Spin(q)} \sim S_a\,\widehat\otimes\,S_q, with chirality correlated when both factors are even-dimensional. For a=2r and q=2s, S_{a+q}^{+} = (S_a^+\otimes S_q^+) \oplus (S_a^-\otimes S_q^-), S_{a+q}^{-} = (S_a^+\otimes S_q^-) \oplus (S_a^-\otimes S_q^+). This is the first robust coupling result. On their shared directions, a higher-dimensional fermion resolves into a lower spinor and a normal polarization label. The normal label is also what can forbid a coupling. If a lower-depth operator is a scalar under Spin(q), then integration over the normal fibre retains only the Spin(q)-singlet part of the higher current. 5. Vertical and normal geometry produce connections There are two related cases. For a quotient \pi_{ba}:Q_b\to Q_a, the vertical bundle is V_{b/a}=\ker d\pi_{ba}. Choosing a horizontal complement TQ_b=H\oplus V_{b/a} is an Ehresmann connection. When the quotient is a principal G bundle, changing the local fibre frame is a G gauge transformation and the horizontal distribution is a principal gauge connection. The Hopf maps are the special case G=U(1). For an embedding Q_a\hookrightarrow Q_b, the corresponding object is the normal bundle N_{b/a}. Choose a local orthonormal frame adapted to the split: \{e_\alpha\}_{\alpha=1}^{a} \cup \{n_i\}_{i=1}^{q}. Along Q_a, the higher-dimensional spin connection decomposes as \nabla_\mu^{(b)} = \partial_\mu +\frac14\omega_\mu^{\alpha\beta}\Gamma_{\alpha\beta} +\frac12\omega_\mu^{\alpha i}\Gamma_{\alpha i} +\frac14\omega_\mu^{ij}\Gamma_{ij}. The three nontrivial pieces have distinct meanings: \omega_\mu^{\alpha\beta} =\text{the tangential spin connection}, \omega_\mu^{\alpha i} =\text{the mixed or extrinsic coupling}, A_\mu^\perp =\frac14\omega_\mu^{ij}\Gamma_{ij} =\text{the normal-bundle connection}. Under a position-dependent normal-frame rotation h(x)\in Spin(q), the last term transforms as A_\mu^\perp \longmapsto hA_\mu^\perp h^{-1} -(\partial_\mu h)h^{-1}. This is exactly the transformation law of a non-Abelian gauge potential. Its curvature is F^\perp=dA^\perp+A^\perp\wedge A^\perp. The construction uses macroscopic spatial directions of the same M_\infty. Relative to a nested lower sector, rotations among its normal spatial directions preserve the lower tangent frame and act on projected field components as gauge transformations. This is the lower observer's description of spatial geometry, not an independently postulated internal space or a new set of physical dimensions. Together the quotient and embedding cases give the cleanest available realization of coupling as higher-dimensional polarization: \boxed{ \text{vertical or normal rotation of the higher mode} \quad\longrightarrow\quad \text{gauge action induced by spatial rotations seen on the lower sector} }. It remains conditional on the normal connection being dynamical and on its holonomy matching an observed interaction group. 6. The invariant coupling criterion Let a lower carrier transform in F_a, and let two matter sectors restrict to representations R_b and R_c of Spin(a)\times Spin(q). The possible local vertices form the invariant space \boxed{ \mathcal V_{abc} = \operatorname{Inv}_{Spin(a)\times Spin(q)} \left(F_a\otimes R_b^*\otimes R_c\right) }. The dimension of this invariant space counts the allowed geometric vertices. Its zero-dimensional case gives a vanishing interaction; a nonzero space leaves the coupling coefficient to the projected dynamics. For a diagonal current, the tangential test can be written \operatorname{Hom}_{Spin(a)} \left( (R_b^*\otimes R_b)\downarrow_{Spin(a)},F_a^* \right)\ne0, while the normal factors must contract to a singlet. A schematic action is S_{\rm int} =g_{ab}\int_{Q_a} \left\langle A_a,(\pi_{ba})_*J_b \right\rangle. The pushforward implements full cross-depth contact. The invariant brackets implement polarization selection. The constant g_{ab} and the field equations implement dynamics. 7. What the proposed depths actually carry The complex spatial spinors fixed by real depth are: depth spatial spin group irreducible complex spinor derived ray/orientation statement 2 Spin(2)\cong U(1) S_2^\pm\cong\mathbb C a chiral ray is a point; a full Dirac spinor has rays \mathbb{CP}^1 3 Spin(3)\cong SU(2) S_3\cong\mathbb C^2 normalized spinors form S^3; rays form \mathbb{CP}^1 4 Spin(4)\cong SU(2)\times SU(2) S_4^\pm\cong\mathbb C^2 each chiral ray space is \mathbb{CP}^1 5 Spin(5)\cong Sp(2) S_5\cong\mathbb C^4 normalized spinors form S^7 6 Spin(6)\cong SU(4) S_6^\pm\cong\mathbb C^4 \mathbb P(S_6^+)\cong SO(6)/U(3)\cong\mathbb{CP}^3 10 Spin(10) S_{10}^\pm\cong\mathbb C^{16} general chiral rays form \mathbb{CP}^{15}; pure rays form SO(10)/U(5) At depth six, the proposed projective sector and the chiral spinor ray space coincide: Spin(6)\cong SU(4), \qquad \mathbb P(S_6^+)\cong\mathbb{CP}^3. The projected Dirac dynamics selects the relevant chiral component or order parameter for the electron. 8. Exact branchings along the particle-depth chain The adjacent restrictions alternate in a simple way: S_3\downarrow_{Spin(2)} =S_2^+\oplus S_2^-, S_4^+\downarrow_{Spin(3)} \cong S_3, \qquad S_4^-\downarrow_{Spin(3)} \cong S_3, S_5\downarrow_{Spin(4)} =S_4^+\oplus S_4^-, S_6^+\downarrow_{Spin(5)} \cong S_5, \qquad S_6^-\downarrow_{Spin(5)} \cong S_5. Therefore the proposed depths 2,3,4,5,6 form a coherent chain of spatial spinor restrictions. Every step carries the lower-depth spin polarization inside the higher-depth one. The jump from depth six to depth ten also has an exact decomposition. Under Spin(10)\supset Spin(6)\times Spin(4), one chiral spinor branches as S_{10}^+ = (S_6^+\otimes S_4^+) \oplus (S_6^-\otimes S_4^-). Using the low-dimensional isomorphisms, \mathbf{16} =(\mathbf4,\mathbf2,\mathbf1) \oplus (\overline{\mathbf4},\mathbf1,\mathbf2). This makes the 6\leftrightarrow10 relation mathematically substantial: the ten-dimensional polarization contains a six-dimensional chiral spinor together with a two-state normal polarization. The tau projector and electromagnetic generator are the physical closure data. 9. Normal groups implied by selected depth differences For a lower sector embedded in a higher one, the natural normal-frame group is Spin(b-a). Some relevant cases are: shared/higher depths normal depth normal spin group immediate consequence 2\subset3 1 Spin(1)=\mathbb Z_2 a discrete spin factor remains, with no continuous normal rotation connection 3\subset4 1 Spin(1)=\mathbb Z_2 colour requires a non-adjacent normal geometry 4\subset5 1 Spin(1)=\mathbb Z_2 the two spatial chiralities combine 5\subset6 1 Spin(1)=\mathbb Z_2 a six-dimensional Weyl spinor restricts directly to the five-dimensional spinor 2\subset5 3 Spin(3)\cong SU(2) a geometrically natural weak-group candidate exists 3\subset6 3 Spin(3)\cong SU(2) the six-dimensional spinor carries a two-state normal polarization 2\subset6 4 Spin(4)\cong SU(2)\times SU(2) left/right normal factors are available for dynamical selection 6\subset10 4 Spin(4)\cong SU(2)_L\times SU(2)_R exactly the doublet factors in the \mathbf{16} branching 4\subset10 6 Spin(6)\cong SU(4) an SU(4) normal symmetry exists and contains SU(3) subgroups 2\subset10 8 Spin(8) a large triality-bearing normal symmetry exists and would require strong reduction These are structure groups produced by the depth differences. The physical gauge group is the normal holonomy Hol(N_{b/a})\subseteq Spin(b-a), which can be smaller than the full structure group. Its value must follow from the connection and the background state. 10. Interaction audit Electromagnetism Every Dirac spinor admits a vector current of the form J^A=\overline\Psi\Gamma^A\Psi. Its tangential component couples on a shared lower base. Electric charge is the corresponding representation weight. Neutrino neutrality requires the depth-two electromagnetic generator to vanish on the neutrino projector. The electromagnetic identification maps the Spin(2)\cong U(1) frame connection to the phase connection acting with the observed charges. Weak interaction Spin(3)\cong SU(2) appears naturally as the normal group for 2\subset5 and 3\subset6, while Spin(4) supplies two SU(2) factors for 2\subset6 and 6\subset10. Thus the proposed depths contain genuine two-state normal polarizations that could support weak doublets. The weak-sector projector must select the left-chiral component, leave the right component as a singlet, generate hypercharge, and identify one normal SU(2) universally across the fermion sectors. Colour The direct 3\subset4 relation has a one-dimensional normal space. The colour candidate therefore comes from the non-adjacent normal geometry 4\subset10: An SU(3) candidate can sit inside Spin(6)\cong SU(4), which occurs as the normal group for 4\subset10. Reducing SU(4) to an SU(3) subgroup requires a selected normal spinor, vector, or complex direction. The sector projectors must place both quark depths in triplets and the lepton depths in singlets. Gravity Scalar and stress-energy bilinears contain normal singlets, making gravity the least representation-sensitive cross-depth channel. Full marginal contact therefore supports universal gravitational response; the full-manifold dynamics supplies its force law and normalization. Six-to-ten charged-lepton relation The Spin(10)\to Spin(6)\times Spin(4) branching is the strongest direct higher-polarization relation after the six-dimensional electron itself. It naturally adds a two-state left or right normal spinor to a six-dimensional chiral spinor. A projector choosing the appropriate summand could relate the tau to the electron--muon sector. The projector, mass splitting, and universal electromagnetic generator remain open. For the specified linear spatial inclusion \mathbb{CP}^3\subset\mathbb{CP}^5, the global normal-spinor calculation sharpens this statement. The FS normal connection has central U(1) holonomy. Its untwisted chiral factors are \mathcal O(-1)\oplus\mathcal O(1) and a parallel \mathbb C^2. The physical spin twists change which normal component is parallel: matching holomorphic section degrees uses a single normal vacuum line, while the parallel doublet occurs at the stated one-degree shift and odd normal exterior degree. The connection does not itself generate a weak SU(2) interaction or choose a doublet mass splitting. Those results depend on the specified global geometry and leave the full particle source and normalized vertex to be derived. 11. Gauge fields as one-forms Higher-dimensional polarization enlarges the representation and supplies more rotation planes. The gauge connection and curvature remain A\in\Omega^1(Q_a,\mathfrak g), \qquad F=dA+A\wedge A\in\Omega^2(Q_a,\mathfrak g). The higher spatial dimension appears through additional connection components and through the Lie algebra \mathfrak{spin}(q). For any actual p-form coupling, pullback to Q_a retains only tangential components. A component with a normal form index vanishes on the lower base; normal polarization indices carried by the representation are instead contracted through the singlet rule. 12. Inverse derivation of the projective candidates Premise status (2026-09-06): the sphere/projective assignments also occur in V1. The reconstruction below is conditional on the complex-amplitude, normalization, transitivity, and phase assumptions; it does not derive those assumptions from the master dynamics or establish the physical geometry. The assignments remain candidates, including CP3 at depth six and S5 at depth five. See the geometry premise audit. The projective and unitary assignments arise as the solution of an inverse problem. Assume a particle's sector manifold Q_d is the normalized projection of the smallest complex amplitude space \mathbb C^r satisfying the following physical conditions: normalization removes one real radial degree of freedom; for a ray-type state, common complex phase is also redundant; the unitary transformations of the amplitudes act transitively; and the resulting configuration manifold has the prescribed real depth d. For a ray-type state, the normalized vectors form S^{2r-1} and quotienting the common phase gives \mathbb P(\mathbb C^r) =S^{2r-1}/U(1) =\mathbb{CP}^{r-1}. Its real dimension is \dim_{\mathbb R}\mathbb{CP}^{r-1}=2r-2. Therefore an even prescribed depth d=2n uniquely fixes r=n+1, \qquad \mathcal P_{2n}=\mathbb{CP}^{n}, within these assumptions. If common phase remains part of the state, then \dim_{\mathbb R}S^{2r-1}=2r-1, so an odd prescribed depth d=2n+1 uniquely fixes r=n+1, \qquad \widetilde{\mathcal P}_{2n+1}=S^{2n+1}. This reconstructs the complete proposed list: prescribed depth minimal complex amplitude space ray or normalized-vector space homogeneous-space form 2 \mathbb C^2 \mathbb{CP}^1 SU(2)/U(1) 3 \mathbb C^2 S^3 SU(2)/SU(1) 4 \mathbb C^3 \mathbb{CP}^2 SU(3)/U(2) 5 \mathbb C^3 S^5 SU(3)/SU(2) 6 \mathbb C^4 \mathbb{CP}^3 SU(4)/U(3) 10 \mathbb C^6 \mathbb{CP}^5 SU(6)/U(5) Under IDWT's physical premise, this table proposes geometries for actual nested spatial submanifolds of M_\infty: Q_2=\mathbb{CP}^1, \quad Q_3=S^3, \quad Q_4=\mathbb{CP}^2, \quad Q_5=S^5, \quad Q_6=\mathbb{CP}^3, \quad Q_{10}=\mathbb{CP}^5. These assignments must satisfy literal submanifold nesting. The table's dimension count and quotient maps do not establish that condition. In fact, the proposed Q_4=\mathbb{CP}^2 cannot embed smoothly as a hypersurface in Q_5=S^5: its nonzero second Stiefel–Whitney class contradicts the trivial normal-line splitting required in the sphere. Thus the complete named list cannot be accepted as the proposed nested chain. See the nesting audit for the argument. Revising a candidate topology must preserve the physical spatial ontology, rather than reinterpret that candidate as an internal space. The SU(1) entry denotes the trivial stabilizer. More precisely, U(n) in the projective quotient is the subgroup S(U(n)\times U(1))\subset SU(n+1), which is isomorphic to U(n). The reconstruction theorem uses depth plus complex minimal polarization plus the phase rule. The action selects the phase rule in each sector. Spin and Spin^c viability A fermionic sector must support the appropriate Dirac bundle. Complex projective space has c_1(T\mathbb{CP}^n)=(n+1)H, \qquad w_2(T\mathbb{CP}^n)=(n+1)H\pmod2. Therefore \mathbb{CP}^n is spin exactly when n is odd. Every \mathbb{CP}^n is canonically Spin^c, and every sphere in the proposed list is spin. The candidate sectors consequently pass the basic fermion test as follows: sector global Dirac structure consequence Q_3=S^3 spin an ordinary complex spinor bundle exists Q_4=\mathbb{CP}^2 canonically Spin^c a fermion requires a determinant-line connection Q_5=S^5 spin an ordinary complex spinor bundle exists Q_6=\mathbb{CP}^3 spin an ordinary complex spinor bundle exists Q_{10}=\mathbb{CP}^5 spin an ordinary complex spinor bundle exists The exceptional Spin^c requirement at depth four is potentially physical: the proposed inhabitants are electrically charged quarks, and a Spin^c Dirac operator necessarily includes a U(1) line connection. The charge normalization is a coefficient of this connection in the projected action. Physical content of the associated groups The stabilizers of the first three even spaces are \begin{aligned} \mathbb{CP}^1 &: U(1),\\ \mathbb{CP}^2 &: U(2)\cong[SU(2)\times U(1)]/\mathbb Z_2,\\ \mathbb{CP}^3 &: U(3)\cong[SU(3)\times U(1)]/\mathbb Z_3. \end{aligned} This recovers, in dimensions 2, 4, and 6, spaces whose isotropy groups contain precisely the continuous group types associated with electromagnetism, the weak interaction plus an Abelian factor, and colour plus an Abelian factor. That repeated agreement is mathematically nontrivial. It is strong evidence that these spaces are the right sector projections to test. The group acting transitively on \mathbb{CP}^n is PSU(n+1), while U(n) is the stabilizer of a selected ray. The sector vacuum selects that ray, and the induced connection must act on every particle with the observed representation and normalization. The depth-six case is especially strong because two independent routes meet: \text{minimal projective polarization at }d=6 \Longrightarrow\mathbb{CP}^3, and \mathbb P(S_6^+) \cong SO(6)/U(3) \cong\mathbb{CP}^3. The inverse amplitude construction and the spatial pure-spinor construction therefore select the same candidate space on which the electron lives. The odd-to-even projections The adjacent odd and even candidates are related by exact Hopf projections: S^3\longrightarrow\mathbb{CP}^1, \qquad S^5\longrightarrow\mathbb{CP}^2, with U(1) fibre. These are quotient maps, not inclusions of the even manifold as a nested submanifold of the odd one. They supply a conditional coupling construction only after the physical spatial nesting and the role of the phase have been established. Colour identification additionally requires the depth-five projector to be an SU(3) singlet and the two quark projectors to carry the same triplet representation. Limits of uniqueness The uniqueness theorem has the stated domain of minimal complex homogeneous representations. Deriving that class and its transitive unitary structure from the master Dirac action remains a requirement, as does embedding its candidate geometries in the nested physical manifold. At depth ten, the minimal-ray premises select \mathbb{CP}^5, while the chiral spatial spinor is \mathbb C^{16}. The tau calculation must select an six-component representation of the same master field or a specific intertwiner between these two descriptions. Neither introduces dimensions outside M_\infty. 13. The decisive calculation Begin with a Dirac action on the full manifold, S_\Psi = \int_{M_\infty} \overline\Psi_\infty \left(i\Gamma^A\nabla_A-\mathcal M\right) \Psi_\infty\,d\mu. Let P_d denote the dynamically defined projection onto fields living on Q_d. The spatial sector operator and a cross-sector block are D_d=P_dD_\infty P_d, \qquad D_{de}=P_dD_\infty P_e. The diagonal operator must be the appropriate spin or Spin^c Dirac operator on the actual manifold Q_d. For each quotient or embedding relation, decompose the cross-sector operator into tangential, mixed, and vertical or normal pieces and calculate P_d\Gamma^A\nabla_A P_e. The calculation must answer four questions: Which vertical- or normal-bundle holonomy groups actually occur? Which sector spinors form singlets, doublets, or higher multiplets under those groups? Which diagonal and transition blocks survive? Are their normalizations universal where observation requires them to be? The most informative first tests are Hol(N_{5/2})\subseteq Spin(3)\cong SU(2), for a possible weak doublet structure, Hol(N_{10/4})\subseteq Spin(6)\cong SU(4), for a possible SU(3) colour reduction, and S_{10}^+\downarrow_{Spin(6)\times Spin(4)}, for the charged-lepton relation. Success requires more than recovering familiar group names. The same calculation must prove that the neutrino electromagnetic generator and lepton colour generators vanish, that both quark depths receive the same colour representation, and that unwanted off-diagonal transitions are absent or massively suppressed. 14. Status Derived from dimensionality and spin geometry the sector-projection ontology and horizontal/vertical or tangent/normal splits for related particle sectors; complex Clifford factorization and every displayed spinor branching; the vertical/normal-frame connection and its gauge transformation law; the invariant/singlet criterion for a cross-depth vertex; the exceptional six-dimensional projective spinor orientation; the Spin(10)\to Spin(6)\times Spin(4) chiral decomposition; conditional uniqueness of the \mathbb{CP}^n/S^{2n+1} sector list from depth, minimal complex amplitudes, normalization, and the phase rule; the spin/Spin^c viability test for every candidate sector manifold. Physically promising but conditional observed forces as vertical- or normal-bundle holonomies; the reconstructed homogeneous spaces as the actual particle-sector projections Q_d; weak SU(2) from a three-dimensional normal bundle; colour SU(3) as a reduced subgroup of a six-dimensional normal spin group; the tau’s ten-dimensional spatial field described relative to the electron’s six-dimensional submanifold through the corresponding Spin(6)\times Spin(4) representation; this does not divide the tau’s spatial directions into different physical kinds. Open physical derivations any Standard Model gauge identification; electric charge or hypercharge assignments; colour triplet and singlet assignments; parity violation; coupling constants; the particle-depth spectrum itself; the dynamical choice of complex-minimal polarization and phase quotient in each sector. The concise result is: \boxed{ \text{higher-dimensional polarization supplies candidate geometric channels;} \quad \text{the projected holonomies must reproduce the observed gauge theory.} } A specified reciprocal spatial benchmark The local scalar Dirac response provides an exact causal response at a specified uniform background. The instantaneous scalar causality test and spatial harmonic comparison constrain the interpretation of the proposed smooth kernel: its local master-field derivation remains open. Local polarized Dirac pulses also give a direct autonomous encounter under the written local scalar term. The nonlinear pulse comparison shows both stronger and weaker normalized pattern match after reciprocal response. Transverse binding, particle identification and different-depth source maps remain required before this control describes observed coupling. A single projective moment action now supplies both complete scalar Dirac responses on the assumed nested projective geometries. The spatial pair calculation retains complex profiles and their phases in an exact symmetry class; both patterns deform and their interaction overlap can increase or decrease. This provides a test of changing spatial compatibility. The geometry, instantaneous nonlocal interaction and retained current decomposition remain inputs, so observed vertices and causal master-field dynamics are still separate derivation requirements.
