title: Photon transversality at every coordinate depth
summary: 1. The claim to explain The photon is an excitation bound in two macroscopic spatial dimensions of the nested manifold: \Xi_2\subset\Xi_3\subset\Xi_4\subset\cdots\subset\Xi_\infty. The single time coordinate is shared at
text: Physical premise (IDWT): There is one infinite-dimensional physical manifold. All sectors form one nested chain of submanifolds within it. Particle depth counts ordinary, literal macroscopic spatial dimensions. “Observed” and “unobserved” describe an observer's access to those dimensions, not different kinds of physical dimension. See spatial meaning and mathematical scope. 1. The claim to explain The photon is an excitation bound in two macroscopic spatial dimensions of the nested manifold: \Xi_2\subset\Xi_3\subset\Xi_4\subset\cdots\subset\Xi_\infty. The single time coordinate is shared at every depth. Ordinary observers occupy the r=3 level of this nesting. The photon's two dimensions are ordinary spatial dimensions shared with every containing sector. For an electron there are six ordinary spatial dimensions, two of which contain the photon plane; for a tau there are ten. This comparison makes none of the containing particle's dimensions different in kind. Likewise, the electron's six are six of the tau's ten: the electron is lower-dimensional, or “flat,” relative to the tau. These are nested submanifolds, not particles made of separate dimensional compartments. The transversality problem is therefore: Why must the ambient momentum of a photon bound in two spatial dimensions be perpendicular to its two directions of oscillation at every depth that contains it? Photon masslessness and the complete electromagnetic field equations are the neighbouring dynamical problems. 2. The physical spatial plane and its normal bundle Let x be the photon's centre and let E_{\gamma,x}\subset T_x\Xi_\infty be its oriented physical spatial two-plane. This is the local physical content of the d=2 assignment: \dim E_{\gamma,x}=2. Its orientation is a dynamical variable. At a containing depth r\geq3, write its image as E_{\gamma,x}^{(r)}\subset T_x\Xi_r. With the spatial metric restricted to that depth, there is an orthogonal decomposition T_x\Xi_r = E_{\gamma,x}^{(r)} \oplus N_{\gamma,x}^{(r)}, where N_{\gamma,x}^{(r)} = \left(E_{\gamma,x}^{(r)}\right)^\perp, \qquad \dim N_{\gamma,x}^{(r)}=r-2. The second summand is the normal space available for propagation relative to the photon plane. At observer depth its dimension is \dim N_{\gamma}^{(3)}=1. At deeper levels the photon plane is still two-dimensional while its normal space has more possible directions. Here “normal” is the geometric word for perpendicular to the chosen photon plane. It is a relationship to that plane, not a different kind of spatial dimension. There are four such directions within the electron's six and eight within the tau's ten. Neither containing sector acquires an inherent physical split from this description of the photon. 3. The depth-independent transversality theorem This is a conditional geometric theorem: assigning polarization to the physical spatial plane and propagation momentum to its normal space already enforces their orthogonality. The depth-two assignment alone does not derive those assignments, select the separated mode below, or establish the electromagnetic constraint equations. Free outer dynamics also allow wavepackets; constant outer intensity describes the chosen momentum eigenmode, not every photon. Choose coordinates u on the physical spatial plane and y on its normal space: u\in E_{\gamma,x}^{(r)}, \qquad y\in N_{\gamma,x}^{(r)}. Bound within, free without gives the two coordinate sets different jobs. The photon's physical oscillation is the spatially bound mode \chi_0(u) in its two bound spatial directions. Those same directions belong to the containing sectors. In the outer directions it has no localized envelope: a free momentum eigenmode has constant magnitude and a changing phase. The separated photon mode is \Psi_\gamma(u,y,t) = \chi_0(u)\,\boldsymbol\varepsilon\, e^{i(\mathbf K\cdot y-\omega t)}, where \boldsymbol\varepsilon \in E_{\gamma,x}^{(r)}\otimes\mathbb C, \qquad \mathbf K\in N_{\gamma,x}^{(r)}. Its intensity is independent of the free coordinate: |\Psi_\gamma(u,y,t)|^2 = |\chi_0(u)|^2|\boldsymbol\varepsilon|^2. This is the precise meaning of “the photon is already there.” Its support is uniform in the free direction, while its phase gradient carries energy, momentum, and the sequence of possible interactions. The polarization belongs to the physical spatial plane, \boldsymbol\varepsilon\in E_\gamma, while the phase gradient belongs to the outer free coordinates, \mathbf K\in N_\gamma. By orthogonality, \boxed{\mathbf K\cdot\boldsymbol\varepsilon=0.} This conclusion holds for every r containing the photon plane. At depth r=3, the normal space is one-dimensional, producing the familiar picture of one propagation axis and a two-dimensional transverse plane. At depth r>3, the photon may propagate along any direction in an (r-2)-dimensional normal space, but every such direction remains perpendicular to both spatial photon directions. Including the shared time coordinate, define K^A=(\omega,\mathbf K), \qquad \varepsilon^A=(0,\boldsymbol\varepsilon). Then K_A\varepsilon^A=0. If the photon is massless, its dispersion relation additionally gives K_AK^A=0, \qquad \omega^2=\|\mathbf K\|^2. Masslessness makes K null. Transversality follows from the allocation of phase propagation and physical oscillation to orthogonal parts of the nested manifold. 4. Momentum without rest mass Energy, momentum, and invariant rest mass obey E^2=p^2c^2+m^2c^4. For m=0 and E>0, \boxed{p=\frac{E}{c}>0.} The same result follows directly from the field stress tensor. Let u be the wave's energy density and \mathbf S its energy-flux vector. The field momentum density is \mathbf g=\frac{\mathbf S}{c^2}. For freely propagating radiation, |\mathbf S|=cu, \qquad |\mathbf g|=\frac{u}{c}. Integrating a finite pulse gives \mathbf p = \frac{E}{c}\,\widehat{\mathbf K}. Uniform support and nonzero Noether momentum coexist because the plane-wave factor has unit magnitude and a nonzero phase gradient: \left|e^{i(\mathbf K\cdot y-\omega t)}\right|=1, \qquad -i\nabla_y e^{i(\mathbf K\cdot y-\omega t)} = \mathbf K e^{i(\mathbf K\cdot y-\omega t)}. If the one-quantum normalization is used, the same statement is E=\hbar\omega, \qquad \mathbf p=\hbar\mathbf K, \qquad \omega=c|\mathbf K|. The ratio p/E=1/c is classical wave kinematics and is independent of the absolute value of \hbar. It is the wave's Noether momentum and energy flux. Finally, n=0 labels the unexcited spatial mass mode. External frequency \omega, wave vector \mathbf K, energy E, and momentum \mathbf p remain the freely specifiable wave data, allowing a zero-rest-mass sector mode to carry arbitrary photon energy. 5. Why there are two polarization modes Choose an oriented orthonormal basis \{\mathbf e_1,\mathbf e_2\} of the physical spatial plane. Any photon oscillation is \boldsymbol\varepsilon = a_1\mathbf e_1+a_2\mathbf e_2. The polarization vector has component count \dim_{\mathbb C}\left(E_\gamma\otimes\mathbb C\right)=2, at every containing depth. Increasing r enlarges the possible normal propagation directions while preserving these two polarization modes. The circular basis is \mathbf e_\pm = \frac{\mathbf e_1\pm i\mathbf e_2}{\sqrt2}. Under a rotation of the photon plane through angle \alpha, \mathbf e_\pm \longmapsto e^{\mp i\alpha}\mathbf e_\pm. These are the two orientation weights \pm1 of the physical spatial SO(2)\simeq U(1) geometry. At depth r=3, where the plane is the complete spatial complement of the propagation direction, these weights are precisely the usual photon helicities \pm1. At higher depths the full massless little group is larger, and the same two circular polarization modes form the d=2 sector representation. A real or parity-complete electromagnetic field contains both circular modes, providing the two observed helicities at observer depth. 6. Orientation at an arbitrary depth The space of possible orientations of the photon plane at depth r is the oriented Grassmannian \operatorname{Gr}^{+}_2(T_x\Xi_r). A photon configuration at that depth consists geometrically of a pair (E_\gamma,\mathbf K), \qquad E_\gamma\in\operatorname{Gr}^{+}_2(T_x\Xi_r), \qquad \mathbf K\in E_\gamma^\perp. This is the depth-independent state geometry. It reduces at r=3 to the familiar coincidence \operatorname{Gr}^{+}_2(\mathbb R^3) \simeq S^2 \simeq \mathbb{CP}^1, because an oriented plane in three dimensions is determined by its oriented unit normal. This realizes the physical photon plane in observer geometry. For the r=3 realization, the right- and left-circular polarization line bundles over the direction sphere have c_1(\mathcal L_\pm)=\pm2, and can be written, up to orientation convention, as \mathcal L_\pm\simeq\mathcal O(\pm2). This is the spin-one topology visible at that depth. The helicity bundles are \mathcal O(\pm2), while the basic amplitude Hopf line is \mathcal O(1). Thus the physical spatial plane has the required observer-level realization. 7. Relation to a gauge field The geometric condition \mathbf K\cdot\boldsymbol\varepsilon=0 removes a longitudinal spatial oscillation once normal propagation has been established. A full account of electromagnetism must additionally explain the gauge connection and its dynamics. A phase-gradient proposal would write A_A=\partial_A\theta, \qquad F_{AB}=\partial_AA_B-\partial_BA_A. For a globally smooth single-valued phase this gives F=d^2\theta=0. This is a pure-gauge configuration. A propagating photon uses a genuine U(1) connection, defined independently or patchwise, whose physical components are restricted to the rank-two photon bundle E_\gamma. The projected electromagnetic action must derive: the connection's propagating sector is restricted to E_\gamma; its momentum lies in E_\gamma^\perp. With an effective curvature action S_{\rm EM} = -\frac14\int F_{AB}F^{AB}\,d\mu, a plane wave obeys K^2\varepsilon^B-K^B(K\cdot\varepsilon)=0. For a nonzero null mode this is consistent with K\cdot\varepsilon=0, while gauge equivalence \varepsilon^A\sim\varepsilon^A+\alpha K^A removes the pure-gauge direction. The sector projector restricts the physical polarization and bound oscillation to the spatial d=2 photon plane. The phase momentum remains in the perpendicular directions described above; restricting polarization is not restricting that momentum to the photon plane. 8. The Hopf sector connection and its extension The physical \mathbb{CP}^1 sector geometry offers a nontrivial local connection. For a normalized representative z\in\mathbb C^2, with z^\dagger z=1 and z\sim e^{i\alpha}z, define A_A=-iz^\dagger\partial_Az. Then A_A\longmapsto A_A+\partial_A\alpha and F_{AB} = -i\left( \partial_Az^\dagger\partial_Bz - \partial_Bz^\dagger\partial_Az \right), which can be nonzero. This is a genuine improvement over A=d\theta. This sector curvature is the pullback of the Fubini--Study area form \omega on the two-real-dimensional target \mathbb{CP}^1. Since \omega\wedge\omega=0 there, F\wedge F=0. A single such map captures the polarization geometry of an individual radiation mode. The full-manifold connection extends this geometry with curvature components in every supported coordinate two-plane. That construction is developed in Higher-dimensional magnetism and the projective orbit lock. 9. The dynamical masslessness condition The convention S(0,2)=0 labels the photon zero mode. Exact masslessness requires the projected action to possess a gauge symmetry or dynamical identity forbidding a scalar mass endomorphism on this mode: \boxed{P_{\gamma}\mathcal M P_{\gamma}=0}, where \mathcal M is the full radiatively corrected mass operator. 10. Exact result and open bridge For every containing depth r\geq3, the IDWT premises are: the photon has an oriented rank-two spatial plane E_\gamma^{(r)}\subset T\Xi_r; the nesting metric supplies the orthogonal normal bundle N_\gamma^{(r)}=(E_\gamma^{(r)})^\perp; photon oscillations lie in E_\gamma^{(r)}; bound-within/free-without factorizes the mode into spatial u dependence and a constant-magnitude free phase in the outer coordinates y; the real or parity-complete field contains both SO(2) orientation weights. The phase gradient then lies in N_\gamma^{(r)}, and \boxed{ \boldsymbol\varepsilon\in E_\gamma^{(r)}, \qquad \mathbf K\in N_\gamma^{(r)}, \qquad \mathbf K\cdot\boldsymbol\varepsilon=0, \qquad \dim E_\gamma^{(r)}=2.} Thus transversality and the two polarization modes are invariant with observer depth. At r=3, the normal space has dimension one and the two spatial rotation weights are the familiar helicities \pm1. The projector equation follows from this factorization: \boxed{P_{E_\gamma}\mathbf K=0.} The action-level closure targets are the separated solution, the dynamics and source of the full-manifold U(1) connection, its relation to the sector Hopf curvatures, and protection of the n=0 mode's exact masslessness. Observer-level cross-checks E. Palmerduca and H. Qin, Photon topology: the two photon helicity line bundles over nonzero three-momentum have first Chern numbers \mp2. P. Caban and J. Rembieliński, Photon polarization and Wigner's little group: the massless little group and helicity phase at observer depth r=3.

title: Higher-dimensional magnetism and the projective orbit lock
summary: 1. Claim and status Electromagnetism is a connection on the full manifold, with magnetic curvature on its supported coordinate two-planes. A depth-six electron can therefore carry orbital magnetic motion across its full
text: Physical premise (IDWT): There is one infinite-dimensional physical manifold. All sectors form one nested chain of submanifolds within it. Particle depth counts ordinary, literal macroscopic spatial dimensions. “Observed” and “unobserved” describe an observer's access to those dimensions, not different kinds of physical dimension. See spatial meaning and mathematical scope. 1. Claim and status Electromagnetism is a connection on the full manifold, with magnetic curvature on its supported coordinate two-planes. A depth-six electron can therefore carry orbital magnetic motion across its full sector geometry. For every angular level L\geq1, the Hopf geometry of the electron's local Q_6=\mathbb{CP}^3 electron sector admits an exact construction with three linked properties: the magnetic flux is the integer first Chern number L; the state space is the degree-L symmetric representation, whose dimension is \binom{L+3}{3}; one shell-independent U(1) isometry induces the complete generator used by the corrected orbital visualization, including its exact frequency lock. The topology and representation theorem are exact. What remains open is the dynamical selection law: why an electron bound to a nucleus selects flux sector L and the required orientation of the magnetic two-form. The L=0 case is separate because its bundle has zero flux and only one constant section. 2. A magnetic field is a two-form Let x^A denote coordinates on the full spatial manifold. A U(1) connection acts through D_A=\partial_A-i\frac{q}{\hbar}A_A, with gauge-invariant curvature F_{AB}=\partial_AA_B-\partial_BA_A. The antisymmetric tensor F_{AB} assigns magnetic curvature to coordinate two-planes. Its observer-space components have the three-dimensional dual \mathbf B. For approximately constant curvature, choose symmetric gauge A_A=-\frac12F_{AB}x^B. Expanding (p-qA)^2/(2m) to first order in F gives \boxed{ H_{\rm mag} =-\frac{q}{2m}\sum_{A<B}F_{AB}L^{AB} }, \qquad L^{AB}=x^Ap^B-x^Bp^A. Thus a spatially varying connection acts on orbital orientation through the generators L^{AB} as well as through its scalar charge phase. This is compatible with bound-within/free-without. The photon has a spatial two-dimensional transverse mode and spans the additional dimensions in which it has no localized motion. Consequently its connection makes full contact with a depth-six electron while the photon retains two spatial oscillation directions. 3. The Hopf connection on the electron sector Represent the local electron orientation by a normalized vector Z=(z_1,z_2,z_3,z_4)\in S^7\subset\mathbb C^4, \qquad Z^\dagger Z=1, with projective identification Z\sim e^{i\chi}Z. The canonical Hopf connection is \mathcal A=-iZ^\dagger dZ. Under a change of local phase, Z\longmapsto e^{i\chi}Z, \qquad \mathcal A\longmapsto\mathcal A+d\chi. Its curvature is \mathcal F=d\mathcal A, which is the Fubini--Study Kähler form up to normalization and sign convention. On a projective line, \frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{\mathbb{CP}^1}\mathcal F=1. The degree-L bundle therefore has \boxed{c_1(\mathcal O(L))=L.} In physical units one may take A^{\rm phys}=\frac{\hbar}{e}\mathcal A, \qquad F^{\rm phys}=\frac{\hbar}{e}\mathcal F, so that \frac{e}{2\pi\hbar} \int_{\mathbb{CP}^1}F_L^{\rm phys}=L. The electron has electric charge -e, while the independent integer L labels the magnetic flux sector of the background line bundle. 4. Combinatorics is the representation The holomorphic sections of the degree-L bundle are homogeneous degree-L polynomials in four coordinates: H^0(\mathbb{CP}^3,\mathcal O(L)) \cong\operatorname{Sym}^L(\mathbb C^4)^*. The dual depends on whether coordinates or linear functionals carry the fundamental action. It reverses all weights together, leaving the projective orbit invariant. A monomial is labelled by four nonnegative exponents with total L: z_1^{a_1}z_2^{a_2}z_3^{a_3}z_4^{a_4}, \qquad a_1+a_2+a_3+a_4=L. Stars-and-bars counting gives \boxed{ \dim H^0(\mathbb{CP}^3,\mathcal O(L)) =\binom{L+3}{3} }. Combinatorics counts the basis states of the geometrically specified representation and fixes the lobe sequence through those state weights. 5. The exact generator theorem Consider the single U(1) isometry acting on the fundamental coordinates with generator G=\operatorname{diag}(1,-1,-1,0). Its action is Hamiltonian on \mathbb{CP}^3. The moment map is \mu_G([Z]) =\frac{Z^\dagger GZ}{Z^\dagger Z}, and the classical Hamiltonian flow is [Z]\longmapsto[e^{-i\theta G}Z]. Normalize the Fubini--Study form by \frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{\mathbb{CP}^1}\omega_{\rm FS}=1. The prequantum connection on \mathcal O(L) then has curvature F_{\nabla_L}=-iL\omega_{\rm FS}, and the moment map at that level is \mu_G^{(L)}([Z]) =L\frac{Z^\dagger GZ}{Z^\dagger Z}. In holomorphic polarization, the lifted infinitesimal action is, up to the single overall sign fixed by the flow convention, \widehat G_L =\sum_{j=1}^4g_jz_j\frac{\partial}{\partial z_j}. It acts on a monomial z^a by \widehat G_Lz^a =\left(\sum_{j=1}^4a_jg_j\right)z^a. This is the canonical first-order prequantum-to-representation bridge. A central change G\mapsto G+cI adds the same eigenvalue cL to every degree-L section and therefore contributes only a common projective phase. For L\geq1, choose the four sections z_1^L, \qquad z_2^L, \qquad z_3z_4^{L-1}, \qquad z_4^L. Their weights under G are respectively L, \qquad -L, \qquad -1, \qquad 0. For the first pair define u=\frac{z_1^L+z_2^L}{\sqrt2}, \qquad v=\frac{z_1^L-z_2^L}{\sqrt2}. Changing from (z_1^L,z_2^L) to (u,v) gives \begin{pmatrix} L&0\\0&-L \end{pmatrix} \longmapsto \begin{pmatrix} 0&L\\L&0 \end{pmatrix} =L\sigma_x. Therefore the induced generator on this four-state subspace is \boxed{ G_L\big|_{\mathcal V_L} =L\sigma_x\oplus\operatorname{diag}(-1,0) }. Choosing the scalar I/4, which is invisible on projective space, gives \boxed{ M_L =\omega\left(G_L\big|_{\mathcal V_L}+\frac14I\right) =\omega \begin{pmatrix} \tfrac14&L&0&0\\ L&\tfrac14&0&0\\ 0&0&-\tfrac34&0\\ 0&0&0&\tfrac14 \end{pmatrix} }. This is an identity for every L\geq1. Here I/4 fixes the displayed energy zero on each four-state subspace. The coefficient L and the unit clock are weights of one U(1) action and evolve with the same group parameter \theta=\omega t. 5.1 Uniqueness theorem The generator follows from five premises: the homogeneous coordinates split into a two-coordinate amplitude plane (z_1,z_2) and a disjoint two-coordinate clock plane (z_3,z_4); one diagonal generator \operatorname{diag}(g_1,g_2,g_3,g_4) acts at every L; the amplitude uses the extremal pure powers z_1^L,z_2^L; the clock reference is z_4^L and its primitive adjacent state is z_3z_4^{L-1}; the clock gap sets the unit of the group parameter. Subtracting the reference weight Lg_4, the required four weights give L(g_1-g_4)=L, \qquad L(g_2-g_4)=-L, \qquad g_3-g_4=-1. Hence g_1-g_4=1, \qquad g_2-g_4=-1, \qquad g_3-g_4=-1, and therefore \boxed{ G=cI+\operatorname{diag}(1,-1,-1,0) }. The constraint matrix has rank three, with nullspace spanned by (1,1,1,1). Thus its continuous freedom is the central shift cI, which is projectively invisible. Reversing the overall sign reverses field orientation, and permutations relabel the chosen coordinates. The clock state is also forced within its plane. Every degree-L clock monomial is z_3^kz_4^{L-k} and has relative weight -k. Primitive unit winding requires k=1; k>1 produces a higher clock harmonic. Consequently the generator and the clock monomial are unique within the stated diagonal, amplitude/clock decomposition. 6. Consequence for the orbital projection For z(0)=\left(A,0,\frac{B}{\sqrt2},\frac{B}{\sqrt2}\right), \qquad A^2+B^2=1, the flow of M_L is z_1=Ae^{-i\theta/4}\cos(L\theta), \qquad z_2=-iAe^{-i\theta/4}\sin(L\theta), z_3=\frac{B}{\sqrt2}e^{3i\theta/4}, \qquad z_4=\frac{B}{\sqrt2}e^{-i\theta/4}. The projectively invariant radius and clock are r([z]) =\frac{|z_1|}{\sqrt{|z_1|^2+|z_2|^2}} =|\cos(L\theta)|, e^{i\phi([z])} =\frac{z_3\bar z_4}{|z_3z_4|} =e^{i\theta}. Hence the aligned observer map is X+iY =Rr([z])e^{i\phi([z])} =R|\cos(L\theta)|e^{i\theta}. It has exactly 2L separated radial maxima for L>0. The sequence L=1,2,3 consequently gives two, four, and six aligned lobes. The complete three-dimensional detector map is supplied by the observer-response module. 7. Observer-space magnetic scale The usual angular-momentum generator already explains the L scaling. On the extremal pair, \frac{L_z}{\hbar}|L,\pm L\rangle =\pm L|L,\pm L\rangle, and its even/odd basis again gives L\sigma_x. In the proton rest frame the ordinary magnetic contribution begins with the motional scale B_{\rm mot}\simeq vE/c^2, yielding \frac{\omega_{\rm mot}}{\omega_{\rm orb}} =\frac{\alpha^2}{2n^2}. This observer-space contribution is a fine-structure correction of relative size \alpha^2/(2n^2) under the stated circular-orbit assumptions. It cannot supply an order-one lock in that estimate. Additional curvature planes of the depth-six sector are a proposed source, not a conclusion proved by the smallness of this one contribution. 8. A conditional flux-through-disk corollary Suppose, as an additional observer-map hypothesis, that all L flux quanta thread an observed orbit disk of radius r uniformly. Then \frac{eB\pi r^2}{2\pi\hbar}=L \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \frac{eB}{2m} =\frac{L\hbar}{mr^2}. If the same circular state satisfies mvr=L\hbar, the right side is v/r, so \omega_B=\omega_{\rm orb}. This confirms that flux quantization is dimensionally and algebraically compatible with the lock. Identification of the projective Chern cycle with a uniformly threaded observer-space disk is the additional hypothesis of this corollary. 8.1 The L=0 dimension theorem and minimal ring At L=0, H^0(\mathbb{CP}^3,\mathcal O(0))=\mathbb C. Its projectivization is \mathbb{CP}^0, a single point. Any Hamiltonian acts there only by a common phase. Therefore \boxed{ \dim H^0(\mathbb{CP}^3,\mathcal O(0))=1 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad N_{\rm relative\ phase}=0. } The one-dimensional section space carries a common phase and zero relative phase coordinates. The displayed M_0 trajectory nevertheless has z_2(t)=0 identically, so it already lies in a three-state subspace. Remove that unused coordinate and write M_0^{\rm min}=\omega\operatorname{diag}(0,-1,0), \qquad z_0^{\rm min}(0) =\left(A,\frac{B}{\sqrt2},\frac{B}{\sqrt2}\right). The first entry is a constant amplitude state. The last two form a clock doublet, giving \frac{z_2(t)\overline{z_3(t)}}{|z_2(t)z_3(t)|} =e^{i\omega t}, \qquad r(t)=1, and hence the exact ring X+iY=Re^{i\omega t}. This is the minimal completion: one state fixes a nonzero amplitude and two states provide the minimum gauge-invariant relative-phase clock. The L=0 sector therefore consists of its Chern-zero magnetic state together with a universal clock doublet whose physical origin is a closure condition. 9. What is proved and what remains The defensible chain for L\geq1 is c_1(\mathcal O(L))=L \Longrightarrow H^0(\mathbb{CP}^3,\mathcal O(L)) =\operatorname{Sym}^L(\mathbb C^4)^* \Longrightarrow G_L\big|_{\mathcal V_L} =L\sigma_x\oplus\operatorname{diag}(-1,0) \Longrightarrow M_L. This establishes mathematical sufficiency: higher-dimensional U(1) magnetism, Hopf flux, and degree-L combinatorics can produce the corrected projective orbital flow with its exact orbital frequency lock. The remaining physical work is specific: derive from the projected master-field action why a bound electron occupies the flux sector whose Chern number equals its atomic angular label L; derive how the nucleus or bound-state geometry selects the isometry orientation G=\operatorname{diag}(1,-1,-1,0), up to projective conjugacy; derive the relevant Hopf/Kähler curvature as the electromagnetic connection on the full manifold; derive the complete three-dimensional observer map and its finite transverse intensity profile; derive the physical origin of the minimal universal clock required at L=0; the trajectory and the obstruction inside \mathcal O(0) are now mathematically settled. These are the dynamical and observational closure conditions attached to the exact topology, representation, and generator identities. 10. Physical synthesis The electron geometry combines degree-L symmetric-power combinatorics, Hopf Chern quantization, higher-dimensional coordinate contact, and the projective orbit theorem. The electromagnetic connection has curvature F=d\mathcal A, while an exact phase gradient has vanishing local curvature. The full-dimensional tensor F_{AB} generates a Hamiltonian isometry acting on the electron's projective orientation. The interactive projection is visualizations/6d-orbit-slice.html. The representation-theoretic identification of the same SU(4) generator with an actual six-dimensional rotation is developed in Pure-spinor bridge for the six-dimensional electron. The action-level test of whether the nucleus selects its mixed spinor frame is Conditional electron–nucleus frame model.

title: Observer map for the projective electron orbit
summary: 1. The observer-response problem The physical target is an electron trajectory in the six macroscopic spatial dimensions of its nested Q_6=\mathbb{CP}^3 submanifold. Three are shared with us, but all six are ordinary spa
text: Physical premise (IDWT): There is one infinite-dimensional physical manifold. All sectors form one nested chain of submanifolds within it. Particle depth counts ordinary, literal macroscopic spatial dimensions. “Observed” and “unobserved” describe an observer's access to those dimensions, not different kinds of physical dimension. See spatial meaning and mathematical scope. 1. The observer-response problem The physical target is an electron trajectory in the six macroscopic spatial dimensions of its nested Q_6=\mathbb{CP}^3 submanifold. Three are shared with us, but all six are ordinary spatial dimensions of the same kind. An observer map describes the three-dimensional response to that physical motion; it does not divide the electron into different kinds of dimensions. The general role of the three-dimensional nuclear sector in constraining ordinary matter and observers must be distinguished from a particular 3+3 frame-lock model. The latter does not by itself derive the former. The magnetic construction currently determines a Hamiltonian trajectory of coefficients in a selected field-mode space. Its map to the displayed curve is conditional: it must be connected to motion on the physical Q_6 and to the nuclear-constrained detector. It is not a replacement of physical space by an internal orientation space. This missing connection limits what the calculation proves; it does not change the theory's spatial premise. This module classifies the data fixed by projective symmetry, the amplitude/clock splitting, and rotational covariance, together with the remaining response functions: the primitive angular clock is unique up to orientation; the general rotationally covariant plane map has a fixed form; the count of 2L lobes is robust under a whole class of radial detector responses; the Born-intensity premise selects the displayed radius within that class; uniform Hamiltonian time gives a canonical occupation measure on the curve; the apparatus coupling selects the third displayed coordinate and transverse detector width. 2. Projective data available to an observer Let z=(z_1,z_2,z_3,z_4)\in\mathbb C^4\setminus\{0\}, \qquad [z]=[cz],\quad c\in\mathbb C^*. Every physical readout must be unchanged by this common complex rescaling. The normalized coordinate occupations are p_j([z]) =\frac{|z_j|^2}{z^\dagger z}, \qquad \sum_{j=1}^4p_j=1. Whenever z_i and z_j are nonzero, their relative phase is represented by \chi_{ij}([z]) =\frac{z_i\bar z_j}{|z_iz_j|} =e^{i(\arg z_i-\arg z_j)}. Both objects are projectively invariant. They are the occupation and relative-angle data available after the common scale and phase have been removed. Split the chosen four-state orbit into amplitude and clock planes, \mathcal V=\mathcal V_A\oplus\mathcal V_C, \qquad \mathcal V_A=\operatorname{span}(z_1,z_2), \qquad \mathcal V_C=\operatorname{span}(z_3,z_4). Conditioning on the amplitude plane gives q([z]) =\frac{p_1}{p_1+p_2} =\frac{|z_1|^2}{|z_1|^2+|z_2|^2}. The primitive clock phase is e^{i\phi([z])} =\chi_{34}([z]) =\frac{z_3\bar z_4}{|z_3z_4|}. Along the magnetic orbit, q(\theta)=\cos^2(L\theta), \qquad e^{i\phi(\theta)}=e^{i\theta}. 3. Uniqueness of the primitive clock A phase character constructed only from the two clock coordinates and unchanged by their common phase has the form \chi_m =e^{im(\arg z_3-\arg z_4)}, \qquad m\in\mathbb Z. Along the orbit it winds m times: \chi_m(\theta)=e^{im\theta}. A primitive clock closes once per turn, which forces |m|=1. Thus \boxed{ e^{i\phi}=\frac{z_3\bar z_4}{|z_3z_4|} } is unique up to complex conjugation, which reverses orientation, and an overall constant phase, which rotates the apparatus axes. 4. Classification of covariant plane maps Restrict the readout to the two arguments q and \phi. This is an additional measurement ansatz: projective invariance alone permits other occupations and relative phases. The classification below is complete only within this restricted class. Let W=X+iY be a complex coordinate in an observer-aligned plane. Rotating the clock by \alpha must rotate the apparatus coordinate by the same angle: W(q,\phi+\alpha)=e^{i\alpha}W(q,\phi). Set \alpha=-\phi. The covariance equation immediately gives W(q,\phi)=e^{i\phi}W(q,0). Therefore every orientation-preserving covariant plane map is \boxed{ W=R h(q)e^{i\phi} }, where R>0 is the spatial scale and h may be complex. An occupation-dependent argument of h(q) is an angular shear: points at different radii are rotated by different extra angles. If the aligned apparatus also respects reflection across its chosen axis, W(q,-\phi)=\overline{W(q,\phi)}, then h(q) is real. Write this real response as f(q). Nonnegativity is an additional radial-response condition, used below with monotonicity, rather than a consequence of reflection alone. The reflection-aligned maps are \boxed{ W=Rf(q)e^{i\phi}. } Orientation reversal replaces e^{i\phi} by e^{-i\phi}. The readout ansatz selects the arguments q and \phi; rotation covariance fixes the equivariant form. Reflection alignment removes the possible angular shear. The detector response supplies the radial function f. 5. Radial-response invariance of the lobe count Suppose the detector response satisfies f(0)=0 and is strictly increasing on [0,1]. Along the orbit, |W(\theta)| =R f\!\left(\cos^2(L\theta)\right). The occupation q(\theta) has maxima at \theta=\frac{k\pi}{L} and zeros at \theta=\frac{(k+\tfrac12)\pi}{L}. A strictly increasing f preserves those extrema. Hence every map in this class has exactly \boxed{2L\text{ separated radial lobes per primitive clock turn}.} The lobe count is therefore a topological/order property of the locked amplitude and clock, invariant across the stated class of f. The theorem's response class is continuous, strictly increasing, and satisfies f(0)=0. Those conditions preserve the extrema and separate adjacent lobes at the origin. 6. What selects the displayed radius The displayed visualization uses r=\sqrt q. This follows if the detector obeys the intensity premise \frac{X^2+Y^2}{R^2}=q. That premise is an amplitude-to-intensity-style relation: squared observed radius equals normalized occupation of the selected amplitude component. It then forces \boxed{ W =R\sqrt q\,e^{i\phi} =R\frac{|z_1|}{\sqrt{|z_1|^2+|z_2|^2}} \frac{z_3\bar z_4}{|z_3z_4|} }. Along the orbit, W(\theta)=R|\cos(L\theta)|e^{i\theta}. Thus the current plane map is unique under five explicit requirements: projective invariance; dependence only on the selected amplitude occupation and primitive clock; rotational covariance; reflection alignment and a nonnegative radial response, excluding angular shear and fixing the radial sign; the intensity readout (X^2+Y^2)/R^2=q. Requirements 1--3 give the family Rh(q)e^{i\phi}, reflection alignment makes h=f real, and the intensity readout with nonnegativity fixes f(q)=\sqrt q. 7. Canonical occupation measure on the orbit The Hamiltonian flow uses the compact group parameter \theta\in[0,2\pi). Its invariant probability measure is normalized Haar measure d\nu(\theta)=\frac{d\theta}{2\pi}. The plane curve W_L therefore carries the pushforward measure \boxed{ \mu_L(B) =\frac{1}{2\pi} \int_0^{2\pi} \mathbf1_B\!\left(W_L(\theta)\right)d\theta } for every measurable detector region B. Identifying the group parameter with uniform physical time selects this measure directly. The amplitude occupation Q=\cos^2(L\Theta), \qquad \Theta\sim\operatorname{Uniform}[0,2\pi), has the arcsine density \boxed{ f_Q(q)=\frac{1}{\pi\sqrt{q(1-q)}} }, \qquad 0<q<1, independently of nonzero integer L. For the Born radius \rho=R\sqrt Q, the radial density is \boxed{ f_\rho(\rho) =\frac{2}{\pi\sqrt{R^2-\rho^2}} }, \qquad 0<\rho<R. The distribution is singular near the turning radius because the radial velocity vanishes there. Different L values share the same one-dimensional radial marginal; their distinction is the angular arrangement of the lobes. 8. From a curve measure to detector intensity The exact pushforward \mu_L is supported on a one-dimensional curve. A finite detector profile requires a normalized response kernel K_\sigma(x): K_\sigma(x)\geq0, \qquad \int K_\sigma(x)d^3x=1. If detections sample the trajectory uniformly in physical time and the apparatus response is spatially translation invariant, the registered density for a three-dimensional trajectory \Gamma_L(\theta) is \boxed{ \rho_{\rm obs}(x) =\frac{1}{2\pi} \int_0^{2\pi} K_\sigma\!\left(x-\Gamma_L(\theta)\right)d\theta }. It is automatically normalized. The Hamiltonian gives the time-occupation measure; identifying that with detection probability is an additional interaction assumption. The apparatus model must justify the sampling law, kernel shape, and width \sigma. Neither this convolution nor a spread in detection positions is a direct observation of the electron's physical shape. 9. The depth observable The current visualization supplements the plane theorem with Z_{\rm display} =\eta R\sqrt{1-q}\cos(3\phi). This is projectively invariant and leaves the exact plane lobe count intact. The apparatus coupling selects a scalar depth coordinate from the admissible real functions Z=D(q,\phi) consistent with the apparatus symmetries. Fourier harmonics \sqrt{1-q}\cos(m\phi) for different integers m are inequivalent examples with the same plane projection. The pure-spinor bridge sharpens this result. In the six-vector representation, the same generator has plane rates 1{:}1{:}3. An antipode-invariant quadratic readout of a slow plane and the fast plane therefore carries e^{\pm i\phi} and \cos(3\phi) respectively. The integer three is thus representation-natural once an even vector detector map is assumed. The apparatus coupling selects the spatial vector/frame datum, the slow and fast readout planes, and the radial factor. A physical depth coordinate follows from an embedding of the apparatus's three resolved axes into the electron's six-dimensional tangent space and the coupling by which the apparatus samples the orbit. 10. The L=0 observer map For the minimal three-state L=0 completion, the amplitude occupation is constant: q=1, while the clock remains primitive: e^{i\phi}=e^{i\theta}. Every normalized covariant response has constant radius, so W(\theta)=Rf(1)e^{i\theta}. Choosing the normalization f(1)=1 gives a ring. Thus the ring follows once the universal clock doublet is supplied. The degree-zero line representation is one-dimensional, so this relative-phase doublet is an additional dynamical ingredient. For an atomic L=0 state, the projected clock must have zero ordinary angular-momentum expectation. This can occur through unobserved-sector motion or through an aligned display of the occupation measure; the observer coupling must select one realization. 11. Defensible conclusion The observer-plane mathematics is now complete at the following scope: \text{projective invariants} + \text{primitive clock} + \text{readout restricted to }(q,\phi) + \text{rotation and reflection covariance} \Longrightarrow W=Rf(q)e^{\pm i\phi}. Strict monotonicity and f(0)=0 imply exactly 2L lobes. The additional Born-intensity premise selects f(q)=\sqrt q. Uniform group time supplies a canonical probability measure on the curve and an exact arcsine radial distribution. The unresolved pieces belong to detector physics: selection and weighting of the representation-allowed 1{:}3 vector harmonics, the embedding into three apparatus axes, the finite response kernel, and the L=0 unobserved-motion or angular-momentum cancellation. These are the input and closure layers of the observer map. Sources and provenance Canonical calculation: files/idwt.py STEP 130. title: Selection of the electron's magnetic flux sector
summary: 1. The flux-sector and rate problem Under the amplitude/clock premises, the projective orbit has a unique U(1) generator up to physically expected equivalences. Its dynamical completion asks: Why does a bound electron oc
text: Physical premise (IDWT): There is one infinite-dimensional physical manifold. All sectors form one nested chain of submanifolds within it. Particle depth counts ordinary, literal macroscopic spatial dimensions. “Observed” and “unobserved” describe an observer's access to those dimensions, not different kinds of physical dimension. See spatial meaning and mathematical scope. 1. The flux-sector and rate problem Under the amplitude/clock premises, the projective orbit has a unique U(1) generator up to physically expected equivalences. Its dynamical completion asks: Why does a bound electron occupy a particular integral magnetic sector, and what fixes the dimensional rate multiplying its unique generator? The companion generator theorem establishes the compatible projective flow. This module reduces its physical selection to a flux functional, a line-bundle identification, and a dimensional rate. 2. The integer match is forced once the representations are identified Let k\geq0 be the first Chern number of the electron's magnetic line bundle: \frac{e}{2\pi\hbar} \int_{\mathbb{CP}^1}F_k=k. In the locked extremal construction, the degree-k representation has generator weights \pm k. With a primitive unit clock, its projective amplitude consequently has r(\theta)=|\cos(k\theta)| and therefore exactly 2k separated radial lobes. The angular family conventionally labelled by nonnegative integer L has 2L lobes in the aligned extremal readout. Identifying these as the same angular representation gives 2k=2L \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \boxed{k=L}. If signed Chern sectors are retained, the result is |k|=L; the sign reverses orientation. Thus representation matching fixes the equality of the flux integer and angular label. The bound-state dynamics selects one member of these angular representations, expressing the ordinary angular quantum number as a topological-sector choice. 3. The atomic conjugacy class The representative used in the aligned calculation is G=\operatorname{diag}(1,-1,-1,0). For any U\in U(4), G_U=UGU^\dagger has the same eigenvalues, induced weights, closure, and lobe theorem after the observer frame is transformed with it. The eigenvalue multiplicities are (-1,-1,0,1):\qquad(2,1,1). Its stabilizer is therefore U(2)\times U(1)\times U(1), and the full unitary-equivalence family is the ten-real-dimensional conjugacy orbit \mathcal O_G =\frac{U(4)}{U(2)\times U(1)\times U(1)}. Subtracting the trace gives an element of \mathfrak{su}(4) without changing the conjugacy orbit. Since SU(4)\simeq\operatorname{Spin}(6), the double cover of SO(6), this same ten-dimensional family is the orbit under six-dimensional spatial rotations, provided the four complex coordinates carry the corresponding spinor representation assumed by the \mathbb{CP}^3 construction. An isolated central potential preserves that orbit. Preparation, neighbouring nuclei, an external field, or the apparatus may select an aligned representative. Spatial isotropy follows when the four coordinates carry the physical \operatorname{Spin}(6) spinor action; the algebraic result by itself is unitary equivalence. The physical closure condition is support of the generator's conjugacy class by the atomic action. Coordinate alignment belongs to state preparation and observation. 4. When Hopf curvature becomes physical electromagnetism The canonical Hopf connection lives on the electron's configuration manifold Q_6=\mathbb{CP}^3. Let \mathcal A be the canonical connection on the Hopf/tautological line bundle over Q_6, and let \mathcal F be its curvature. The proposed physical normalization is locally A^{\rm phys} =\frac{\hbar}{e}\mathcal A, \qquad F^{\rm phys} =\frac{\hbar}{e}\mathcal F. Then dF^{\rm phys}=0 follows automatically, and the integral flux is evaluated directly on the generating \mathbb{CP}^1\subset Q_6. Physical electromagnetism is the case in which this same line connection enters the projected spatial Dirac operator: \boxed{ \text{the connection in }P_6D_\infty P_6 \text{ has curvature }F^{\rm phys}=(\hbar/e)\mathcal F. } A nontrivial Hopf line on the generating two-cycle uses patchwise normalized lifts. The electron field lives in \Sigma Q_6\otimes L_{\rm em}. The projected action must identify L_{\rm em} with a specified power and orientation of the tautological line and derive its field equation. 5. The harmonic representative in each flux sector The second cohomology of complex projective space is one-dimensional: H^2(\mathbb{CP}^3,\mathbb R) =\mathbb R[\omega_{\rm FS}]. Therefore the harmonic curvature representing Chern sector k is F_k^{\rm harm} =\frac{\hbar}{e}k\omega_{\rm FS} with the normalization \frac{1}{2\pi} \int_{\mathbb{CP}^1}\omega_{\rm FS}=1. For any curvature in the same cohomology class, F=F_k^{\rm harm}+d\alpha, orthogonality of harmonic and exact forms gives \|F\|^2 =\|F_k^{\rm harm}\|^2+\|d\alpha\|^2 \geq\|F_k^{\rm harm}\|^2. Thus the uniform Kähler curvature is the unique minimum-norm curvature in its flux sector. Since H^1(\mathbb{CP}^3)=0, connections producing that curvature are gauge-equivalent. This supplies a variational reason for the uniform-flux premise on the spatial projective cycle. The observer map supplies the corresponding Euclidean disk. 6. What a flux-selection functional must accomplish A curvature-energy term by itself penalizes nonzero flux. Schematically, E_{\rm curv}[F] =\frac{1}{2g^2}\|F\|^2 gives, on the harmonic representative, E_{\rm curv}(k)\propto k^2. Its isolated minimum is k=0. Selection of a nonzero atomic angular sector therefore comes from the electron's bound-state orientation: either as a topological constraint or through an interaction energy depending jointly on the matter angular state and k. The required selection statement has the form E_{\rm bound}(k;L) >E_{\rm bound}(L;L) \qquad \text{for every }k\ne L. For an orbit carrying angular label L, representation matching locates the minimum at |k|=L. The bound-state part of the projected master-field action must supply the displayed inequality; Chern topology supplies the discrete sectors and their representations. 7. The dynamical rate The quantum Hamiltonian has the form \widehat H_L =\hbar\omega\widehat G_L. The Chern number and weight lattice fix the dimensionless eigenvalue ratios of \widehat G_L, while \omega is a dimensional coefficient supplied by the bound-state dynamics. For any positive \lambda, \widehat H_L \longmapsto \lambda\widehat H_L leaves the bundle, Chern number, state multiplicities, projective curve, closure, and lobe count unchanged while rescaling \theta=\omega t \quad\longmapsto\quad \theta=\lambda\omega t. Hence the topology leaves one positive dimensional parameter: \boxed{ \omega\text{ is supplied by the bound-state dynamics.} } It must come from a dimensional coefficient in the bound-state dynamics. The flux-through-disk relation \frac{eB}{2m} =\frac{L\hbar}{mr^2} equals the orbital rate when mvr=L\hbar, using the additional map from projective flux to the observed orbit area. This is a dynamical closure target for the bound-state action. 8. The reduced open problem The completed mathematics removes three apparent freedoms: matching the angular representation forces |k|=L; the amplitude/clock premises force the generator modulo projective and orientation equivalences; fixed flux selects the uniform harmonic curvature as the minimum-norm representative. The projected master-field action still has to provide: the projective spinor section \Phi\in\Gamma(\mathbb P(S_6^+)) and the identification F^{\rm phys}=(\hbar/e)\Phi^*\mathcal F; the bound-state term or constraint that makes sector k=L dynamically dynamically occupied; the dimensional coefficient \omega; the connection between projective flux area and the spatial area sampled by an observer; the origin of the universal relative-phase clock needed by L=0. These are the explicit closure equations for the projected electromagnetic sector. Sources and provenance Canonical calculation: files/idwt.py STEP 130. title: A conditional frame model of electron–nucleus binding
summary: 1. Binding within the one physical manifold The electron has six ordinary macroscopic spatial dimensions. The nucleus's three are shared with it through nesting in the same M_\infty. This makes none of the electron's dim
text: Physical premise (IDWT): There is one infinite-dimensional physical manifold. All sectors form one nested chain of submanifolds within it. Particle depth counts ordinary, literal macroscopic spatial dimensions. “Observed” and “unobserved” describe an observer's access to those dimensions, not different kinds of physical dimension. See spatial meaning and mathematical scope. 1. Binding within the one physical manifold The electron has six ordinary macroscopic spatial dimensions. The nucleus's three are shared with it through nesting in the same M_\infty. This makes none of the electron's dimensions different in kind and gives the electron no inherent 3+3 split. The module studies an additional, conditional frame model using observer-adapted coordinates on the physical spatial geometry Q_6=\mathbb{CP}^3 \cong SO(6)/U(3). The geometry is a premise of the binding calculation, not selected by this module itself. The chiral selection calculation now gives an effective mechanism producing a CP3 collective minimum family, while its identification with the spatial base and its master-field origin remain explicit derivation targets. This distinction does not reopen the electron's assigned depth. A point q=[Z]\in Q_6 is equivalently an orthogonal complex structure J(q) on a model real six-dimensional vector space V_6. The calculation chooses a three-dimensional observer frame associated with the nucleus and groups the model coordinates relative to it: V_6=O\oplus H \cong\mathbb R^3\oplus\mathbb R^3. This grouping is mathematical bookkeeping relative to the chosen frame, not a physical division within the electron. It does not establish the general reason ordinary matter and observers experience three dimensions. The conditional model asks: Does the projected electron–nucleus interaction define an energy function on Q_6 whose minimum makes the electron's complex structure exchange the two nuclear-relative three-planes? The required geometry can be characterized exactly. The projected cross-sector kernel on Q_3\times Q_6 determines the sign and magnitude of the binding potential. 2. One field, two sector projections The fundamental field is the Dirac field on the full manifold, \Psi_\infty\in\Gamma(\Sigma M_\infty). The electron and nucleus are modes of this one field, bound on nested spatial submanifolds. The proposed sector maps refer to those physical submanifolds: \Pi_6:M_\infty\to Q_6, \qquad \Pi_N:M_\infty\to Q_N. The electron field is a spatial spinor on its sector, \psi_e=P_{6,e}\Psi_\infty \in\Gamma(\Sigma Q_6\otimes L_{\rm em}), while the electron's sector coordinate is independently q=[Z]\in Q_6. Both arise from the master theory. Here Z is a homogeneous coordinate for the electron's position in Q_6, while \psi_{e,+}(q) is the value of its chiral Dirac section. 3. The chosen observer-relative coordinates Here O groups directions shared with the chosen observer, and H groups the remaining directions. All six are ordinary spatial dimensions of the same kind. The model vector space V_6 represents these directions; its use in a homogeneous-space formula does not create another physical space or establish a global tangent-frame identification. Let P be the orthogonal projector onto the nuclear-relative three-plane O\subset V_6, and let 1-P project onto H=O^\perp. These projectors implement the chosen coordinate grouping; they do not establish two physically distinct kinds of electron dimension. Selecting O reduces the model rotation symmetry as SO(6)\longrightarrow SO(3)_O\times SO(3)_H. This gives two coordinate three-planes within the model. An additionally assumed frame lock reduces their product symmetry to a diagonal subgroup. 4. Every electron-sector point supplies the candidate link Choose a normalized homogeneous lift Z\in\mathbb C^4. The corresponding orthogonal complex structure is J_{AB}(q) =-iZ^\dagger\Gamma_{AB}Z, \qquad J^T=-J, \qquad J^2=-I_6. The formula is independent of the common phase of Z. Relative to V_6=O\oplus H, write J= \begin{pmatrix} A&Q\\ -Q^T&C \end{pmatrix}, where A and C are antisymmetric 3\times3 matrices. The mixed block Q=PJ(1-P) maps the unobserved three-plane to the nuclear-relative three-plane. It is a coordinate function on Q_6. Under independent frame rotations, (R_O,R_H)\in SO(3)_O\times SO(3)_H, it transforms as Q\longmapsto R_OQR_H^T. A full-rank selected value of Q can therefore identify the two frames. 5. Exact block algebra The equation J^2=-I_6 gives A^2-QQ^T=-I_3, C^2-Q^TQ=-I_3, and AQ+QC=0. Define the invariant \boxed{ s(q;P)=\frac12\lVert A\rVert_F^2 =\frac12\lVert PJP\rVert_F^2 }. For an antisymmetric 3\times3 matrix, A=[a]_\times for a vector a\in\mathbb R^3, and \frac12\lVert A\rVert_F^2=|a|^2. The complex-structure identities imply 0\le s\le1 and fix the singular values of Q: \boxed{ \sigma(Q)= \left\{1,\sqrt{1-s},\sqrt{1-s}\right\}. } They also give \frac12\lVert C\rVert_F^2=s. Thus one scalar labels the SO(3)_O\times SO(3)_H orbit relevant to locking. 6. The locked orbit At s=0, the antisymmetric blocks vanish: A=C=0. The block identities then force QQ^T=Q^TQ=I_3. After choosing orientation, Q\in SO(3). A selected value Q_0 is preserved by pairs satisfying R_OQ_0R_H^T=Q_0, which form a diagonal SO(3). Hence \boxed{ s=0 \Longrightarrow SO(3)_O\times SO(3)_H \longrightarrow SO(3)_{\rm diag}. } Under the spin double cover, the homogeneous-coordinate representation obeys \mathbf4=(\mathbf2,\mathbf2) \longrightarrow \mathbf1\oplus\mathbf3. This is the exact s\oplus p branching used in the chemistry construction. 7. Entanglement interpretation Under Spin(3)_O\times Spin(3)_H, the normalized homogeneous coordinate Z\in\mathbb C^4 may be treated as a pure state in \mathbb C^2_O\otimes\mathbb C^2_H. By local rotations it has Schmidt form Z_\lambda = \sqrt\lambda\,|00\rangle +\sqrt{1-\lambda}\,|11\rangle, \qquad \frac12\le\lambda\le1. The locking invariant is s=(2\lambda-1)^2, while the concurrence satisfies \mathcal C=2\sqrt{\lambda(1-\lambda)}, \qquad \boxed{\mathcal C^2=1-s}. The assumed frame lock is therefore the maximally entangled orbit in this two-frame representation. The representation does not divide the physical electron into two parts. 8. A canonical one-parameter family Let K= \begin{pmatrix} 0&-1&0\\ 1&0&0\\ 0&0&0 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad D_s=\operatorname{diag} \left(\sqrt{1-s},\sqrt{1-s},1\right). Then J(s)= \begin{pmatrix} \sqrt s\,K&D_s\\ -D_s&-\sqrt s\,K \end{pmatrix} obeys J(s)^T=-J(s), \qquad J(s)^2=-I_6. This family crosses every value of the locking invariant and provides the shortest variational test of a proposed electron--nucleus interaction. 9. The projected binding energy Project the master interaction onto the actual sector manifolds: K_{N6}:Q_N\times Q_6\longrightarrow\mathbb R. For a fixed nuclear bound state with density \rho_N(u), the electron sees V_N(q) = \int_{Q_N} \rho_N(u)K_{N6}(u,q)\,d\mu_N(u). If the nuclear configuration is invariant under SO(3)_O\times SO(3)_H, then V_N may depend on the electron coordinate only through s at lowest orbit level: V_N(q)=V_0+\kappa s(q;P)+O(s^2). The decisive coefficient is \boxed{ \kappa = \left.\frac{dV_N(J(s))}{ds}\right|_{s=0}. } Its sign has an immediate meaning: \begin{array}{c|c} \kappa>0& s=0\text{ is locally selected},\\ \kappa=0& \text{the interaction does not select the lock at this order},\\ \kappa<0& s=0\text{ is locally disfavoured}. \end{array} Because q=[Z] is the electron's sector coordinate, a scalar interaction on Q_6 may depend on s(q;P). The projected kernel determines that dependence and hence the sign of \kappa. Here “selected” means locally preferred in energy, not automatic dynamical capture. A fixed-nucleus reduction with the invariant Hamiltonian structure on SO(6)/U(3) gives the explicit conditional flow \dot J=\frac{2V'(s)}{\mathcal I}[PJP,J],\qquad \dot A=\dot C=0,\qquad Q(t)=\exp\!\left(\frac{2V'(s_0)}{\mathcal I}A_0t\right)Q_0. The positive action scale \mathcal I fixes the symplectic normalization; it is not a derived nuclear inertia. This reduced contribution generates precession for 0<s_0<1 and nonzero V'(s_0), but conserves s rather than attracting the electron to s=0. At s=0 the contribution vanishes. The derivation, endpoint qualifications, and independent numerical checks are recorded in Flat nucleus precession. This is a trajectory on the proposed electron-sector manifold, not a stationary-orbital calculation. The nuclear kernel, the connection to the relative orbital clock, and the physical three-coordinate readout remain to be supplied before it yields the existing petal construction. An explicit inverse candidate for the orientation channel is now available: K_{N6}^{\rm orient}(u,J) =\frac{\gamma(u)}2\|P(u)JP(u)\|_F^2. For a common nuclear plane and normalized density this gives V_N=\bar\gamma s, with \bar\gamma=\int\rho_N\gamma\,d\mu_N. This reconstructs the reduced precession energy but does not derive \gamma, radial binding, or a unique microscopic interaction. The inverse-kernel calculation also gives the reciprocal projector variation and distinguishes this quadratic channel from the oriented linear source needed to produce the visualization's particular fixed rotation generator. A forward effective-source construction now produces this inverse channel: a positive-cost mixed-plane response with energy \|X\|^2/(2\chi)-g\operatorname{tr}(X^TQ) gives \kappa=\chi g^2 after minimizing over X. Its reciprocal dynamics admit checked collective precession branches; see Induced cross-plane response. A gapped contact source also gives a saturating kernel and a self-consistent rotation without the harmonic-response approximation. The existence of that contact channel, its gap and coupling remain hypotheses, not derived nuclear properties. These constructions generate an orientation interaction; they do not replace the outstanding spatial binding and physical current calculations. 10. Electron equation on physical space The bound-state problem is \left( i\gamma^0D_t +i\slashed D_{\mathbb{CP}^3} -m_e -V_N(q) \right)\psi_e(q)=0, with all required electromagnetic and normal/vertical connections included in \slashed D_{\mathbb{CP}^3}. Equivalently, it is the projected master operator P_6D_\infty P_6 in the nuclear background supplied through P_ND_\infty P_6. The calculation of \kappa uses the spatial Fubini--Study metric and measure on \mathbb{CP}^3. Any local approximation is derived from that operator. 11. What a positive result would unify If \kappa>0, the chain is \Psi_\infty \longrightarrow q_e=[Z]\in Q_6 \longrightarrow J(q_e) \longrightarrow Q\in SO(3) \longrightarrow Spin(3)_{\rm diag} \longrightarrow \mathbf1\oplus\mathbf3. It would place in one sector coordinate: the six-dimensional electron position; the projective orbit; the complex-structure frame link; the chemical s\oplus p decomposition; and the tetrahedral occupation simplex. The magnetic generator, Chern sector, rate, radial detector response, and molecular bond-angle distortion remain the subsequent selection problems. 12. Status Established mathematics every point of Q_6=\mathbb{CP}^3 determines J; the exact block identities and one-parameter orbit invariant s; the singular values of the mixed frame link; s=0 gives an orthogonal link and diagonal stabilizer; \mathcal C^2=1-s in the two-spin-frame representation; the canonical family J(s). Open physics derivation of the nuclear-to-electron kernel on Q_N\times Q_6; the sign of \kappa; the relation of the sector coordinate to the electron spinor field on physical space; the metric scale and full spatial Dirac operator; the molecular and detector couplings. The assumed frame model defines a potential-minimization problem. Its algebra is exact within the chosen grouping; its physical application and dynamical selection remain open. It does not establish an inherent division of the electron's six dimensions or the origin of three-dimensional experience. title: Tetrahedral bond geometry from the projective electron sector
summary: 1. Claim and status This module is a conditional occupation-simplex and hybrid-state construction. It is not a calculation of actual multi-nucleus electron trajectories. The four-state bonding-space identification and mo
text: Physical premise (IDWT): There is one infinite-dimensional physical manifold. All sectors form one nested chain of submanifolds within it. Particle depth counts ordinary, literal macroscopic spatial dimensions. “Observed” and “unobserved” describe an observer's access to those dimensions, not different kinds of physical dimension. See spatial meaning and mathematical scope. 1. Claim and status This module is a conditional occupation-simplex and hybrid-state construction. It is not a calculation of actual multi-nucleus electron trajectories. The four-state bonding-space identification and molecular energy are additional premises; its tetrahedral angle is not independent evidence of electron depth or a solution of the reciprocal orbit problem. The ideal tetrahedral bond angle is the angle of the centred occupation simplex of \mathbb{CP}^3. The same result appears in the observable bonding subspace \mathcal V_{sp} =\operatorname{span}\{|s\rangle,|p_x\rangle,|p_y\rangle,|p_z\rangle\} \cong\mathbb C^4. Four equivalent orthogonal hybrids in this space point toward the vertices of a regular tetrahedron, giving \boxed{\theta_{\rm tet}=\arccos(-1/3)=109.4712206\ldots^\circ.} This angle follows exactly from equivalence, orthogonality, and the stated observer-space identification. Ammonia and water are less symmetric because one or two of the four occupied states are lone-pair states. Orthogonality then proves how an unequal s-occupation changes the bond angle and proves that greater lone-pair s-occupation compresses it. A molecular energy minimization determines the amount of redistribution and therefore the numerical angles. 2. Why chemistry belongs to the same physics The single-electron orbit module uses four homogeneous coordinates for the electron's projective orientation: [z_1:z_2:z_3:z_4]\in\mathbb{CP}^3. At a molecular centre, the lowest observable sigma-bonding space also has four complex components: one s state and three p states. Together they form one four-dimensional state space, and a molecule chooses an orthogonal basis adapted to its surrounding nuclei. Axial symmetry about a neighbouring nucleus produces the bond-directed form, while fermionic occupancy permits an orthonormal basis of the occupied subspace. The projective construction adds a geometric statement: the four equivalent directions are the vertices of the same simplex that is the moment polytope of \mathbb{CP}^3. Both derivations express the geometry of one copy of \mathbb C^4. The pure-spinor bridge makes the proposed physical identification precise: under \operatorname{Spin}(3)_{\rm obs}\times\operatorname{Spin}(3)_{\rm hid} the chiral four is (\mathbf2,\mathbf2), and diagonal frame locking gives \mathbf2\otimes\mathbf2=\mathbf1\oplus\mathbf3=s\oplus p. Until the bound-state action derives that diagonal locking, equality of the two copies of \mathbb C^4 is the conditional intertwiner used in this module. The two-factor representation in this comparison is a model assumption. It does not physically divide the electron's six spatial dimensions: all six are the same kind, including the three shared with the observer. A coordinate grouping alone cannot establish a physical frame lock. 3. The centred-simplex theorem The toric occupation map of \mathbb{CP}^3 is p_i([z])=\frac{|z_i|^2}{\sum_{j=1}^4|z_j|^2}, \qquad p_i\geq0, \qquad \sum_{i=1}^4p_i=1. Its image is the standard three-simplex \Delta_3. Let e_i be its four coordinate vertices and subtract the barycentre: v_i=e_i-\frac14(1,1,1,1). All v_i lie in the three-real-dimensional hyperplane \mathcal H=\left\{x\in\mathbb R^4:\sum_i x_i=0\right\}. Their inner products are v_i\cdot v_i=1-\frac12+\frac14=\frac34, and, for i\neq j, v_i\cdot v_j=0-\frac14-\frac14+\frac14=-\frac14. After normalization, n_i=\frac{2}{\sqrt3}v_i, the four directions obey n_i\cdot n_j=-\frac13 \qquad(i\neq j). Therefore \boxed{ \cos\theta_{ij}=-\frac13 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \theta_{ij}=109.4712206\ldots^\circ }. Any isometry from \mathcal H to the observer's three spatial axes rotates the tetrahedron while preserving this angle. Projective geometry supplies the three-dimensional affine occupation simplex. The observer/binding map identifies that hyperplane with molecular bond directions. The hybrid-state calculation below supplies this map under the sigma-bonding premises. 4. The equivalent hybrid-state theorem Write a normalized real sigma hybrid directed along \mathbf n_i\in\mathbb R^3 as |h_i\rangle =a_i|s\rangle +\sqrt{1-a_i^2}\, \mathbf n_i\cdot|\mathbf p\rangle. For four occupied orthonormal states spanning \mathcal V_{sp}, completeness gives \sum_{i=1}^4|\langle s|h_i\rangle|^2 =\sum_{i=1}^4a_i^2 =1. If the four environments are equivalent, all s-shares are equal, so a_i^2=\frac14. Pairwise orthogonality then gives 0=\langle h_i|h_j\rangle =\frac14+\frac34\,\mathbf n_i\cdot\mathbf n_j, and hence \mathbf n_i\cdot\mathbf n_j=-\frac13. The hybrid directions are therefore isometric to the normalized centred simplex vertices of the preceding section. Methane is the leading physical example: four equivalent C--H bonding environments approximately realize the regular solution. The derivation uses: the four-state s+3p space; bond-directed sigma states; orthogonality of the occupied one-electron states; equivalence of the four ligand environments; identification of their direction vectors with observer-space bond axes. The fifth condition is the explicit molecular observer map. 5. Unequal occupations: ammonia and water For non-equivalent hybrids, orthogonality gives the exact relation \boxed{ \mathbf n_i\cdot\mathbf n_j =-\frac{a_i a_j} {\sqrt{(1-a_i^2)(1-a_j^2)}} }. Let there be n_b equivalent bond states and n_{\rm lp}=4-n_b equivalent lone-pair states. Parameterize their s-shares by s_b=a_b^2=\frac14-\delta, s_{\rm lp}=a_{\rm lp}^2 =\frac14+\frac{n_b}{n_{\rm lp}}\delta. Then n_b s_b+n_{\rm lp}s_{\rm lp}=1, so completeness is automatic. The bond--bond angle obeys \boxed{ \cos\theta_{bb} =-\frac{s_b}{1-s_b} =-\frac{\tfrac14-\delta}{\tfrac34+\delta} }. Moreover, \frac{d}{d\delta}\cos\theta_{bb} =\frac{1}{(\tfrac34+\delta)^2}>0. Since \arccos is decreasing, positive \delta compresses the visible bond angle below the tetrahedral value. Thus the qualitative ordering follows conditionally: s_{\rm lp}>s_b \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \theta_{bb}<\theta_{\rm tet}. Using gas-phase reference angles gives the occupation parameters Molecule Reference angle s_b s_{\rm lp} \delta CH_4 109.471^\circ ideal 0.2500 -- 0 NH_3 106.67^\circ 0.2229 0.3313 0.0271 H_2O 104.5^\circ 0.2002 0.2998 0.0498 These values invert the measured angles to infer the corresponding occupations. They show the required direction of redistribution and a larger effect in water. The energy calculation in Section 7 is the selection equation for those shares. 6. The continuous occupation family Completeness and orthogonality admit a continuous family of \delta values. Let a=(a_1,a_2,a_3,a_4) be any positive vector satisfying \sum_i a_i^2=1. The Gram matrix of the remaining p components of four orthonormal hybrids is G_p=I-aa^T. It is positive semidefinite and has rank three. Consequently it always admits a realization by four vectors in \mathbb R^3. Dividing the ith vector by \sqrt{1-a_i^2} produces unit bond/lone-pair directions satisfying the exact overlap formula of the previous section. Therefore a continuous family of s-share assignments, including a continuous family of \delta values, is compatible with completeness and orthogonality. The geometry determines the angle once \delta is known. Selection of \delta belongs to the molecular energy functional: \boxed{ \text{four equivalent projective channels} \longrightarrow109.47^\circ, \qquad \delta=\arg\min_\delta E_{\rm molecule}. } The statement that lone pairs repel more becomes quantitative when the electron interaction energy yields the corresponding occupation inequality. 7. What must select the distortion The physical angle is a minimum of the Born--Oppenheimer energy surface. In the one-parameter reduction it has the form E(\delta,R) =E_{\rm one\ centre}(\delta) +E_{\rm two\ centre}(\delta,R) +V_{NN}(\delta,R). The complete occupied s+3p space makes the trace of every one-electron operator on that space basis-independent. Selection of \delta therefore comes from geometry-dependent multi-centre terms. A Slater-orbital estimate finds that the one-centre electron--electron contribution changes by less than 0.004 atomic units over the tested interval. The hydrogen--hydrogen nuclear repulsion increases as the bond angle closes, so that term resists positive \delta. The selecting contribution is the geometry-dependent two-centre electronic energy: nuclear attraction, Coulomb repulsion, exchange, and correlation of orbitals extending between the heavy atom and the hydrogen nuclei. A quantitative derivation must minimize these terms simultaneously in \delta and the bond lengths. In the marginal-exactness regime, this is the ordinary three-dimensional molecular Hamiltonian expressed in the projective-orbit basis. The closure target is \frac{\partial E}{\partial\delta}=0, \qquad \frac{\partial E}{\partial R}=0, with measured angles excluded from both equations. The current result derives the tetrahedral value and the angle--occupation map. Numerical molecular angles await this minimization. 8. What this says about a six-dimensional electron The result gives the chain \mathbb{CP}^3 \longrightarrow \text{four-state occupation simplex} \longrightarrow \text{centred tetrahedron} \longrightarrow 109.471^\circ. It explains why four equivalent bonding channels of a depth-six electron can present themselves as four tetrahedral directions to a three-dimensional observer. It also joins the orbital-lobe construction and molecular geometry to the same projective state space. The model identifies this four-state structure as the observable bonding face of the electron's underlying \mathbb{CP}^3 sector. A specific empirical discriminator for the larger identification remains an open target. text:
