Physical norms and density units must be fixed before applying this test; rescaling each candidate afterward changes the argument of F. Different depths additionally need their common master-field reduction and normalization. If (3)–(5) hold with a smooth law on the required current range, put U(J)=\int_0^J F(s)\,ds. The real action is  egin{aligned} \mathcal S[\psi]&=\int d	au\left[  rac i2 igl(\langle\psi,\dot\psiangle- \langle\dot\psi,\psiangle igr)-E[\psi]ight],\ E[\psi]&=\langle\psi,\mathscr D\psiangle+\int U(J)\,dV. \end{aligned} 	ag{8} Its full complex variation gives exactly (1). The same scalar law fixes the complete local response:  oxed{ \delta\!\left(F(J) eta\psiight) =F(J) eta h+ 2F'(J)\operatorname{Re}(\psi^\dagger eta h)\, eta\psi. } 	ag{9} This includes both ordinary and conjugate variations, as in the complete scalar source linearization. Coupling is therefore a constraint on the inverse law itself. The inverse spectral response comparison likewise distinguishes shared frequencies from a complete interaction. There is no independent coefficient for each particle pair. The total current of an encounter includes its spatial interference before U(J) is evaluated. The inferred law need not be unique outside the sampled current ranges. A background with constant current determines F at one value but generally leaves F' undetermined there. Thus mass frequencies alone do not determine every coupling response or the complete master dynamics. The excited spatial response calculation tests this constraint on nonlinearly deformed assigned modes. The same local interaction produces a calculable resonance in their full complex response, showing why stationary source compatibility and spatial stability must be assessed together. Apply the test to unchanged spatial Dirac pairs Let \phi_n be a normalized zero-form eigenfield and let \eta_n=\mathscr D\phi_n/\lambda_n be its normalized exact one-form partner: \mathscr D\phi_n=\lambda_n\eta_n,\qquad \mathscr D\eta_n=\lambda_n\phi_n,\qquad \lambda_n= rac{2\sqrt{n(n+5)}}R. 	ag{10} Consider the unchanged paired spatial profile \chi_n=c_n\phi_n+s_n\eta_n, with real constant weights, c_n^2+s_n^2=1, and both nonzero. The common overall phase is arbitrary. The two form equations require  egin{aligned} \lambda_ns_n+M(x)c_n&=\omega_nc_n,\ \lambda_nc_n-M(x)s_n&=\omega_ns_n. \end{aligned} 	ag{11} Where the respective spatial components are nonzero, these give M=\omega_n-\lambda_n rac{s_n}{c_n} =\lambda_n rac{c_n}{s_n}-\omega_n. 	ag{12} Continuity extends this one constant coefficient over the remaining points of the explicit Jacobi profile. In particular,  oxed{\omega_n^2=\lambda_n^2+M_n^2.} 	ag{13} Changing F does not alter this fixed-profile requirement. It follows from the full spatial equation, before taking any expectation or dropping a complementary source. For the pole-centered physical CP3 field at line degree two, write p_n(t)=P_n^{(2,2)}(2t-1). Up to its positive common normalization, the two local densities are |\phi_n|^2\propto t^2p_n^2,\qquad |\eta_n|^2\propto  rac{t^3(1-t)(p_n')^2}{n(n+5)}. 	ag{14} For every n\ge1, the polynomial has simple interior zeros. At such a zero the scalar current of \chi_n is negative, because the odd component is nonzero. At t=1 the odd component vanishes and the scalar current is positive. Between the last polynomial zero and that pole, the current therefore crosses zero while the complete spinor is nonzero. Every such unchanged pure pair consequently requires  oxed{F(0)=M_n.} 	ag{15} Its complete current image is an interval containing zero. The same field forces F to be constant on that interval, so F'=0 in its interior. Multiplying the physical norm by a positive factor preserves the zero-current argument. The written massless scalar law F(J)=gJ has F(0)=0 and therefore cannot support these unchanged profiles with M_n
e0. A nonzero bare value F(0) would instead give the same constant coefficient to every such pair. Neither option supplies distinct simplex coefficients on the unchanged spatial profiles. The assigned two-frequency target fails this pure-profile test Keep the common six-dimensional geometry and its one fixed radius. The assigned target is \omega_n=\mu S(n,6) at n=13,35. Equations (13) and (15) would require one real constant M. For x_n=n(n+5), this gives  rac{\omega_{35}}{\omega_{13}} =\sqrt{ rac{x_{35}+(MR/2)^2}{x_{13}+(MR/2)^2}} \le\sqrt{ rac{x_{35}}{x_{13}}}. 	ag{16} The actual numbers are: Quantity Value Largest ratio from a shared real gap on this fixed geometry \sqrt{ rac{1400}{234}}\approx2.445998 Assigned simplex frequency ratio  rac{ inom{40}{6}}{ inom{18}{6}}= rac{3515}{17}\approx206.764706 No smooth scalar function of J can resolve this discrepancy while retaining those unchanged pure spatial pairs and the same fixed geometry. This extends the earlier holomorphic source-preservation condition to an explicit nonzero-kinetic paired family. The result does not cover nonlinear spatial dressing, other polarization textures or a self-consistently changing geometry. The round-space scalar branch, for example, has constant nonzero current and does not satisfy the current-crossing hypothesis used in (15). These distinctions are part of the theorem's scope, rather than reasons to reassign the particle depths or mass indices. A dressed field can pass the same inverse test The local curved scalar construction already supplies nonlinear branches whose even and odd spatial profiles change together. They provide a positive control for the reconstruction, independently of the desired particle masses. Use the radius-one, unit-volume convention and fix one local law F(J)=\kappa J with \kappa=0.15. Take physical norms Q=1 and Q=3. The normalized branch solver then uses g=\kappa Q: Physical norm Q Normalized solver coefficient g Stationary frequency 1 0.15 0.417382662446 3 0.45 1.106712764874 At successively larger paired cutoffs 8,14,22, independent uncompressed spatial derivatives reduce the full residual below 6	imes10^{-15} in this numerical control. Both profiles retain nonzero odd spatial dressing. At equal physical currents J=0.25,1,3, the inverse formula recovers the same M=\kappa J from both fields. Their spatial derivatives also recover the same F'(J)=0.15. This validates both parts of the inverse procedure on solutions of a common local action. It is not a mass prediction, a quantization of Q or a stability proof for those branches. It demonstrates why solving the changed spatial field can succeed where the unchanged-profile test fails. Frequency and rest energy still need separate identification For a stationary solution of (1), (8) gives  oxed{\omega Q-E =\int\left[J F(J)-U(J)ight]\,dV.} 	ag{17} Along a smooth family of constrained stationary solutions, dE/dQ=\omega. Neither identity makes E/Q equal to \omega for a general nonlinear interaction. This agrees with the local scalar normalization calculation. Thus the inverse frequency target, the total energy of a localized particle and an observed rest mass must be connected by the same physical normalization and dynamics. The current calculation reconstructs and tests a candidate scalar law; it does not establish that final physical identification. Verification inverse_scalar_law_checks.py checks the real scalar minimization and its complete complex residual at spinor ranks two, eight and thirty-two. General complex basis changes, imaginary-source controls and full action variations retain the ordinary and conjugate responses. Actual curved derivatives verify the constant coefficient of the paired Jacobi fields and locate their nonvanishing-spinor current zeros. Exact integer comparisons check (16) at the unchanged assigned indices. Independent spatial derivatives, quadrature and increasing paired cutoffs reconstruct the common law and its coupling derivative on the dressed controls.

title: Causal constraint on reconstructed simplex dynamics
summary: An exact commutator on the actual curved spatial geometry proves that the reconstructed all-band polynomial dynamics have no finite propagation speed, while leaving open causal nonlinear dynamics with selected simplex particle frequencies.
text: Summary: An exact commutator on the actual curved spatial geometry proves that the reconstructed all-band polynomial dynamics have no finite propagation speed, while leaving open causal nonlinear dynamics with selected simplex particle frequencies. What the inverse frequency match does not settle The inverse construction gives local Hermitian equations with exact frequencies \pm\mu S(n,2m) on their complete first Dirac pair. Their full canonical norm is conserved. However, every member of that polynomial class fails a finite-propagation test when used as a fixed equation for all spatial modes. This conclusion follows directly on the specified physical \mathbb{CP}^m geometry with line connection \mathcal O(m-1). It does not require a flat approximation, a positive-frequency projection or a group-velocity interpretation. The physical radius R is arbitrary and finite. These remain ordinary macroscopic spatial directions; no direction is compactified. The result constrains an inverse dynamical ansatz. A nonlinear particle mass is not required to equal the frequency of every small disturbance of one fixed quadratic background. Causal dynamics that select several nonlinear particle states remain a different problem. No particle depth or assigned mass index is changed by this test. Finite propagation requires a bounded local commutator Let H be self-adjoint on the complete spatial field and U(\tau)=e^{-i\tau H} its unitary evolution. A finite propagation speed c means that every initial field supported in K satisfies \operatorname{supp}U(\tau)\psi \subseteq\{x:\operatorname{dist}(x,K)\le c|\tau|\}. \tag{1} For an ordinary first-order Dirac operator, its bounded commutator with a Lipschitz scalar function expresses its local spatial speed. See McIntosh and Morris, Section 1 for the first-order propagation theorem. The necessary estimate used here can be proved without assuming that H is first order. Let f be a bounded real function with Lipschitz constant L_f. For \tau\ne0, put r=c|\tau| and \delta=L_fr, and partition the field space using the multiplication projections E_j=\mathbf1_{\{j\delta\le f<(j+1)\delta\}},\qquad f_\delta=\sum_j j\delta E_j. \tag{2} Zero values of c or L_f follow by using an arbitrarily larger positive bound or by observing that a constant function commutes. Two bins whose indices differ by at least three are separated by more than r. Equation (1) therefore gives E_jU(\tau)E_k=0 when |j-k|\ge3. For each remaining index difference \ell, the operator \sum_jE_{j+\ell}U(\tau)E_j has norm at most one: its domain blocks are orthogonal, its range blocks are orthogonal and \|U(\tau)\|=1. It follows that \begin{aligned} \|[f_\delta,U(\tau)]\| &\le\delta\sum_{\ell=-2}^{2}|\ell|=6\delta,\\ \|[f-f_\delta,U(\tau)]\|&\le2\delta. \end{aligned} \tag{3} The deliberately nonoptimal constant is sufficient: \boxed{\|[f,U(\tau)]\|\le8c|\tau|L_f.} \tag{4} For a smooth field \psi such that \psi and f\psi lie in the domain of H, differentiate at \tau=0. Equation (4) implies \boxed{\|[H,f]\psi\|\le8cL_f\|\psi\|.} \tag{5} Thus an unbounded commutator with one bounded smooth spatial function excludes a finite propagation speed for the full unitary equation. The argument applies on a compact spatial manifold as well: a finite diameter does not remove the small-time requirement. Evaluate that commutator on the actual spatial field Retain the complete inverse operator H_{a,b}=\mathscr D_c+ \mu\left[a(X_0)T_0+\beta b(X_0)\right],\qquad X_0=T_0^2,\quad T_0=\frac R2\mathscr D_0. \tag{6} The other spinor families still have their operator \mathscr D_c. All inverse candidates have Xa(X)^2+b(X)^2=P_m(X)^2,\qquad b(X)=\frac{X^m}{(2m)!}+O(X^{m-1}). \tag{7} The overall negative sign allowed in the classification changes the sign of the following commutator but not its norm. Use the global spatial function t=|Z_0|^2/|Z|^2. For the specified physical FS metric, |\nabla t|^2=\frac{4t(1-t)}{R^2},\qquad L_t=\frac1R. \tag{8} Let \phi_n be the normalized zero-form Jacobi field from the curved Dirac construction, at L=m-1. It is a legitimate smooth state of the complete field. It need not be a positive-frequency eigenstate of (6). Multiplication by t has the exact recurrence \begin{aligned} t\phi_n&=\gamma_n\phi_{n+1}+\frac12\phi_n+ \gamma_{n-1}\phi_{n-1},\\ \gamma_n&=\frac12 \sqrt{\frac{(n+1)(n+2m-1)} {(2n+2m-1)(2n+2m+1)}}. \end{aligned} \tag{9} The last term is absent at n=0. The coordinate is an actual function on physical space; the index n is a mathematical spatial mode label. On zero forms, \beta=1 and X_0\phi_n=x_n\phi_n, with x_n=n(n+2m-1). The term a(X_0)T_0 changes form degree and \mathscr D_c annihilates both \phi_n and t\phi_n. Consequently the zero-form component of the full commutator is \begin{aligned} \Pi_0[H_{a,b},t]\phi_n =\mu\bigl\{& \gamma_n[b(x_{n+1})-b(x_n)]\phi_{n+1}\\ &+\gamma_{n-1}[b(x_{n-1})-b(x_n)]\phi_{n-1}\bigr\}. \end{aligned} \tag{10} This projection only supplies a lower bound on the complete response. It is the local form-degree projection, not a projection onto one frequency sign. The odd component and all complementary equations remain present and cannot cancel an orthogonal zero-form component. Define \begin{aligned} C_n^2={}&\gamma_n^2[b(x_{n+1})-b(x_n)]^2\\ &+\gamma_{n-1}^2[b(x_{n-1})-b(x_n)]^2. \end{aligned} \tag{11} Equations (9)–(10) imply \|[H_{a,b},t]\phi_n\|\ge\mu C_n. \tag{12} For every root allocation in the inverse class, \gamma_n\longrightarrow\frac14,\qquad b(x_{n+1})-b(x_n)= \frac{n^{2m-1}}{(2m-1)!}+O(n^{2m-2}). \tag{13} The other difference has the opposite leading sign. Hence \boxed{C_n\sim \frac{n^{2m-1}}{\sqrt8\,(2m-1)!}\longrightarrow\infty.} \tag{14} But a finite propagation speed would require, by (5) and (8), \mu C_n\le\frac{8c}{R} \quad\text{for every }n. \tag{15} This is impossible for any fixed nonzero \mu and finite positive R,c. It proves the failure of finite propagation on the full curved equation, including all nine coefficient pairs at depth six and all eighty-one at depth ten. Real spatial depth Common growth of the lower bound C_n Six \frac{n^5}{120\sqrt8} Ten \frac{n^9}{362\,880\sqrt8} The asymptotic indices in this proof are test fields allowed by the proposed equation. They are not alternative particle assignments. What can and cannot change this conclusion The original first-order operator has [\mathscr D,t] equal to local Clifford multiplication by dt, up to the convention for i. Its norm is bounded by 1/R. This provides a direct curved-space control for the test above. The same obstruction also applies to the direct insertion H=\mathscr D+\mu\beta P_m(X_0), even though that insertion keeps the original first-order kinetic term. On the test field \phi_n, its zero-form commutator is still (10) with b=P_m; the ordinary Dirac commutator contributes only to the odd form. Thus promoting the polynomial mass coefficient to an operator on every spatial disturbance needs a causal completion as well. A coefficient obtained only on selected nonlinear stationary particle states is not covered by that promotion. A fixed smooth multiplication potential cannot cancel (10); it commutes with t. In particular, adding the specified local scalar term g(\psi^\dagger\beta\psi)\beta\psi has vanishing linearization at the zero field. Its small-amplitude equation still has the same obstruction. For a smooth local nonlinearity F(\psi^\dagger\beta\psi)\beta\psi, a nonzero F(0) adds only a multiplication term to that linearization. Likewise, a fixed positive commuting kinetic metric in the inverse action gives iZ\dot f=ZH_{a,b}f and the same evolution i\dot f=H_{a,b}f. That normalization does not repair (15). A different same-field dynamical completion would need to change the propagation equation itself. The scalar response calculation remains valid mathematics for its specified action. Its reciprocal coefficients and spatial residuals are useful inverse constraints, but this action cannot yet represent a fundamental causal particle interaction at unrestricted spatial frequencies. A controlled effective reduction may retain the polynomial over a limited regime, provided its causal parent, retained modes, frequency range and approximation error are derived. A cutoff alone is not a proof of causal support. The local Dirac retarded response already illustrates how causal propagation can survive a same-field reduction when its full frequency dependence is kept. The instantaneous interaction test addresses a different source of acausality: an explicitly nonlocal instantaneous spatial potential. Most importantly, (14) does not exclude a universal causal nonlinear equation whose distinct self-consistent particle solutions have selected simplex masses. That equation would have to generate the particle spectrum through its nonlinear spatial states and normalization, without imposing this unrestricted high-order dispersion on every disturbance. The inverse scalar-law construction develops that alternative with the original Dirac kinetics. It tests the full spatial residual and the requirement that all particle candidates obey one function of the scalar current. Verification inverse_simplex_causality_checks.py checks exact finite differences for every root allocation at depths six and ten. Independent Jacobi polynomials and repeated application of the actual curved differential operator verify the full formula (10). Physical curved quadrature and its refinement independently check the normalized recurrence. The paired matrix equation retains both frequency branches and verifies the complete norm lower bound. The original Dirac operator supplies the bounded local commutator control. Finite block contractions also check the range-partition estimate; the continuum proof is (2)–(5), not a conclusion drawn from those finite numerical examples.

title: Scalar response of reconstructed simplex dynamics
summary: Reconstructed actions with identical simplex frequencies redistribute a fixed total scalar response between frequency branches, while their common local scalar interaction gives distinct spatial self-sources and reciprocal phase-sensitive mode transfer.
text:
Summary: Reconstructed actions with identical simplex frequencies redistribute a fixed total scalar response between frequency branches, while their common local scalar interaction gives distinct spatial self-sources and reciprocal phase-sensitive mode transfer. Compare the same interaction on the inverse actions The inverse dynamics construction gives a family of local Hermitian Hamiltonians with the same complete simplex frequencies, using the geometric simplex polynomial. Coupling can test more than that spectrum. Here every candidate is given the same specified scalar interaction of the one physical field:  oxed{ E[\psi]=\langle\psi,H_{a,b}\psiangle+  rac g2\int J(x)^2\,d
u(x),\qquad J=\psi^\dagger eta\psi. } 	ag{1} Use the canonically normalized physical spinor, with time-kinetic metric equal to the identity, and unit-volume spatial measure d
u. The general normalization rule applies if a different physical lift is specified. Equation (1) uses one real coefficient g, not an independent coefficient for every pair of occupied modes. Its relation to the frequency scale \mu is not derived by the inverse construction. The scalar current in (1) is a test of the written scalar interaction. It is not identified with electric charge. Both frequency branches and every form component of the field remain available; neither frequency sign is assigned an antiparticle interpretation. The calculations use the specified actual spatial CP3 geometry with line connection \mathcal O(2). Its physical radius remains unknown, and no dimensions are compactified. The two-mode example below is a common-center spatial symmetry control, not a complete encounter of separated particles. Sector nesting does not imply particle containment. The complete curved causality test excludes finite propagation for these fixed polynomial actions at unrestricted spatial frequencies. Their coupling calculations below remain conditional inverse constraints. A causal completion or a controlled effective regime has not been derived for them. The full eigenspace fixes the uniform scalar response On a paired spatial family at x_n=n(n+5), write P(x)= rac{x(x+4)(x+6)}{720},\qquad u_n= rac{\sqrt{x_n}\,a(x_n)}{P(x_n)},\qquad v_n= rac{b(x_n)}{P(x_n)}. 	ag{2} The exact inverse identity is u_n^2+v_n^2=1. Using the isometric Dirac map between zero forms and their exact one-form partners, the normalized paired Hamiltonian is  rac{H_n}{\mu P(x_n)} = egin{pmatrix}v_nI&u_nI\u_nI&-v_nI\end{pmatrix}. 	ag{3} Each identity matrix acts on the entire spatial multiplicity of the family. Changing the basis of either component inserts the corresponding unitary partner map and leaves the following identities unchanged. No single complex polarization is assumed. Let \mathsf P_n^\pm be the two complete frequency projectors. For the uniform scalar operator  eta,  oxed{ \mathsf P_n^+ eta\mathsf P_n^+ =v_n\mathsf P_n^+, } 	ag{4} and  oxed{ \mathsf P_n^+ eta\mathsf P_n^- eta\mathsf P_n^+ =(1-v_n^2)\mathsf P_n^+. } 	ag{5} For every normalized positive-frequency polarization, the squared response within that frequency branch is v_n^2, while the squared response in its opposite-frequency partner is 1-v_n^2. The inclusive response is exactly  oxed{v_n^2+(1-v_n^2)=1.} 	ag{6} Thus the inverse actions redistribute scalar response without changing the total norm of  eta\psi. Actual transition rates also require the temporal source, accessible outgoing frequencies and the physical spatial matrix element. A small value in (4) does not establish weak coupling to all channels. This is consistent with the need to retain the complete scalar response. Separate a local field equivalence from different responses The nine polynomial pairs at depth six include pairs with a replaced by -a and the same b. Define the local form-degree unitary U=I-2\Pi_0. 	ag{7} It reverses the zero-form phase. title: Reconstructing dynamics with exact simplex frequencies
summary: An inverse polynomial classification gives nine local Hermitian dynamics with exact simplex frequencies on the specified six-dimensional Dirac pair, while canonical normalization fixes their action and the original unchanged kinetic term cannot realize that spectrum through a scalar polynomial alone.
text: Summary: An inverse polynomial classification gives nine local Hermitian dynamics with exact simplex frequencies on the specified six-dimensional Dirac pair, while canonical normalization fixes their action and the original unchanged kinetic term cannot realize that spectrum through a scalar polynomial alone. Reconstruct the full frequency rather than only its coefficient The geometric derivative construction supplies the dimensionless operator P(X)=\frac{X(X+4)(X+6)}{720},\qquad P\bigl(n(n+5)\bigr)=S(n,6). \tag{1} It acts on a specified family of spatial spinors on physical CP3 with line connection \mathcal O(2). The inverse problem here is stronger than asking for this scalar coefficient: require the complete positive frequency on that family to be \mu S(n,6), with one fixed \mu>0. There are explicit local Hermitian dynamics that satisfy that target. Within the two-polynomial class defined below, there are nine solutions at depth six up to a simultaneous sign of the two polynomials. The corresponding number at depth ten is eighty-one. They give the same frequencies while acting differently on the paired form components. These are reconstructed quadratic actions. The calculation does not derive them from the algebraic master scalar current, select occupied particle modes or prove causal propagation. The positive field norm and the full complementary spinor kinetics are retained explicitly. CP3 and CP5 remain conditional actual macroscopic spatial geometries with unknown physical radii and no compactification. The constructions at the two depths are independent sector calculations. They do not require an electron state to be a restriction of a tau state; only the sectors belong to the nested spatial chain. Preserve every form component of the spatial field On physical \mathbb{CP}^m, use the specified bundle \Lambda^{0,*}\otimes\mathcal O(m-1) and the spatial Dirac operator \mathscr D=\sqrt2(\bar\partial+\bar\partial^\dagger). The dagger includes the physical FS metric and measure. Let \Pi_q project onto exterior degree q, and let \beta be exterior parity. Define \begin{aligned} \mathscr D_0&=\sqrt2\left(\bar\partial^\dagger\Pi_1+ \bar\partial\Pi_0\right),\\ \mathscr D_c&=\mathscr D-\mathscr D_0,\qquad T_0=\frac R2\mathscr D_0,\qquad X_0=T_0^2. \end{aligned} \tag{2} The local Hodge decomposition and \bar\partial^2=0 give \mathscr D_0\mathscr D_c=\mathscr D_c\mathscr D_0=0, \qquad \{\beta,\mathscr D_0\}=\{\beta,\mathscr D_c\}=0. \tag{3} On the complete zero/exact-one-form family, X_0 has values x_n=n(n+2m-1). On the other form families it vanishes, while \mathscr D_c retains their original kinetic equation. Harmonic components remain in the full field space. The dimensionless target polynomial at real depth 2m is P_m(X)=\frac{1}{(2m)!} \prod_{j=0}^{m-1}\left[X+j(2m-1-j)\right],\qquad P_m(x_n)=S(n,2m). \tag{4} It has one zero at X=0 and distinct negative zeros at -c_j, where c_j=j(2m-1-j)>0 for 1\le j\le m-1. No particle mode or dimensionality is reassigned. What keeping the original kinetic term would require First retain \mathscr D_0 and change only a real scalar polynomial B(X_0). On its paired family, H=\mathscr D_0+\beta B(X_0) \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \omega^2=\frac{4X}{R^2}+B(X)^2. \tag{5} Exact target frequencies at every x_n would require the polynomial identity \boxed{B(X)^2=\mu^2P_m(X)^2-\frac{4X}{R^2}.} \tag{6} Equality on infinitely many distinct x_n forces equality as polynomials. At X=0, (6) gives B(0)=0. Its left side therefore has no linear term, while the right side has coefficient -4/R^2. No polynomial B satisfies (6) at a finite physical radius. A specified spectral square root can instead be defined on the positive paired spectrum: B(x_n)=\sqrt{\mu^2P_m(x_n)^2-\frac{4x_n}{R^2}},\qquad B(0)=0. \tag{7} For (7) to be real on every positive level, its first level imposes \mu R\ge2\sqrt{2m}. This condition is sufficient because P_m(X)/\sqrt X increases for X>0. The resulting spectral operator is not a finite differential polynomial. Defining it supplies neither a local master interaction nor a causal reduction. Equation (6) identifies the constraint that a scalar-only inverse construction has to address. A local polynomial class that meets the target exactly Allow both coefficients on the paired family to change: \boxed{ H_{a,b}=\mathscr D_c+ \mu\left[a(X_0)T_0+\beta b(X_0)\right], } \tag{8} where a,b are real dimensionless polynomials with b(0)=0. The identity b(0)=0 prevents an extra scalar term on the complementary form families. Using (3) gives H_{a,b}^2=\mathscr D_c^2+ \mu^2\left[X_0a(X_0)^2+b(X_0)^2\right]. \tag{9} Thus the exact inverse condition is \boxed{Xa(X)^2+b(X)^2=P_m(X)^2.} \tag{10} Every solution gives both frequencies \pm\mu P_m(x_n) on the complete paired family. The other spinor families retain their original kinetic spectrum. Neither frequency sign is identified with an antiparticle or electric charge. Both terms in (10) are nonnegative for X\ge0. Their leading coefficients cannot cancel. Consequently \deg b=m and \deg a\le m-1. The constant and linear coefficients of (10) give, respectively, b(0)=0,\qquad a(0)=0. \tag{11} In particular none of these solutions retains the original constant coefficient a=2/(\mu R) of \mathscr D_0 while changing only the scalar polynomial. The change to the kinetic operator is part of the reconstructed dynamics, rather than a normalization convention. Classify all real polynomial solutions in this class Introduce a mathematical polynomial variable y and write C(y)=b(y^2)+iy\,a(y^2). \tag{12} For real coefficients, C(-y) is the coefficient conjugate of C(y). Equation (10) becomes C(y)C(-y) =\frac{y^4}{[(2m)!]^2} \prod_{j=1}^{m-1}(y^2+c_j)^2. \tag{13} The root at zero has multiplicity two in C. For each distinct pair \pm i\sqrt{c_j}, its two copies can be allocated in three ways: one to each root, or both to either root. Fixing the positive leading coefficient of b, all solutions are therefore \boxed{ C(y)=\frac{y^2}{(2m)!}\prod_{j=1}^{m-1}F_{j,\epsilon_j}(y), \qquad \epsilon_j\in\{-1,0,1\}, } \tag{14} with F_{j,0}=y^2+c_j,\qquad F_{j,\pm1}=(y\pm i\sqrt{c_j})^2. \tag{15} Every choice has the conjugation property in (12), so its even part is a real b(y^2) and its odd part is iy times a real a(y^2). Conversely, the roots and leading coefficient in (13) leave no additional polynomial choices. A simultaneous sign change of a,b gives the remaining solutions. The count up to that sign is \boxed{3^{m-1}:\qquad 9\text{ at depth six},\quad 81\text{ at depth ten}.} \tag{16} This classification is restricted to the class (8). It does not classify all matrix-valued, nonpolynomial or nonlinear dynamics. At depth six, three illustrative members are: Choice a(X) b(X) Both factors balanced 0 \frac{X(X+4)(X+6)}{720} Rotate the factor X+4 \frac{4X(X+6)}{720} \frac{X(X-4)(X+6)}{720} Rotate the factor X+6 \frac{2\sqrt6X(X+4)}{720} \frac{X(X+4)(X-6)}{720} For the second row, for example, (10) follows from 16X+(X-4)^2=(X+4)^2. The two mixed examples have a nonzero odd-component coupling and an exact simplex frequency. The remaining members follow directly from (14), including opposite signs for each rotation. Reconstruct the action with the correct field norm Let f be the full field coordinates in a fixed Hilbert space, and let Z>0 be a specified, time-independent kinetic metric. For a target self-adjoint Hamiltonian H, the real quadratic action \mathcal S[f]=\int dt\left\{ \frac i2\left(\langle f,Z\dot f\rangle- \langle\dot f,Zf\rangle\right) -\langle f,Kf\rangle\right\}, \qquad K=Z^{1/2}HZ^{1/2}, \tag{17} gives iZ\dot f=Kf,\qquad u=Z^{1/2}f\quad\Longrightarrow\quad i\dot u=Hu. \tag{18} All spatial adjoints and every complex variation are included. The conserved norm is \langle f,Zf\rangle=\|u\|^2. This construction works also for noncommuting Z,H; that general formula alone does not guarantee spatial locality of K. If Z and H commute, K=ZH. Polynomial commuting data in the present construction then give a local quadratic action. The natural zero-form jet metric at depth six is Z(X)=(X^2+12X+40)/40. To obtain P(X) after canonical normalization, its energy numerator must therefore be \boxed{ Z(X)P(X)= \frac{X^5+22X^4+184X^3+688X^2+960X}{28\,800}. } \tag{19} Using Z(X_0) on the complete paired field, with value one on the complement, is a specified extension of that metric. Multiplying the complete target (8) by this Z gives the corresponding local inverse action. Its scalar energy term has spatial order ten. The earlier P/Z result used energy numerator P; (19) deliberately changes that energy to meet the inverse target. The algebraic master current has not thereby been shown to contain the additional derivatives. A field-dependent or time-dependent Z needs its complete variation and kinetic connection. Equations (17)–(18) assume fixed data; they cannot be used to omit the response of a moving geometric background. The canonical coupling calculation likewise normalizes each interaction leg using the same field metric. Physical scope of the reconstruction Each operator (8) is Hermitian on smooth spatial fields and has a self-adjoint realization defined by the complete harmonic decomposition. Its unitary linear evolution preserves the full canonical norm. Finite linear superpositions do not develop exponentially growing amplitudes under this fixed quadratic action. The complete scalar-response comparison adds the same local interaction to each reconstructed action. Equal frequencies allow different spatial responses; both frequency branches retain a fixed inclusive scalar strength. The complete nonlinear source also drives spatial components beyond a chosen pure occupied mode. That statement is not nonlinear particle stability. These equations permit every spectral level and do not select the assigned occupied states. They do not by themselves specify a nonlinear interaction between two particle structures. Locality as a differential expression also does not establish a finite propagation cone for a higher-order spatial equation. The complete curved causality test now proves that every member of (8), used on all spatial modes, lacks a finite propagation speed. The test uses a local spatial commutator and retains both frequency branches. These actions therefore need a controlled effective interpretation or a different causal completion. The inverse calculation supplies explicit actions that meet the target frequency identity and a complete classification within (8). Their physical coupling and state selection remain additional constraints. This approach is consistent with the distinction between an effective action and its deeper origin in Burgess, Section 3.3. No scale hierarchy or effective cutoff has been derived here. Verification inverse_simplex_dynamics_checks.py independently compares the real polynomial recurrence with all complex root allocations, exact coefficient identities and Hermitian matrix diagonalization. The six-dimensional and ten-dimensional spectra are checked at the unchanged assigned indices. Repeated application of the actual curved zero-form and one-form differential operators checks the reconstructed action on spatial Jacobi fields. Independent curved quadrature retains their complete kinetic norms. Full complex Dolbeault complexes verify preservation of the complementary spinor equation. Noncommuting positive kinetic metrics, direct energy variations and norm conservation independently check the inverse action.

title: Simplex counts in a physical projective spectral band
summary: A fixed-line cumulative spatial band on CP3 has exactly twenty times the simplex rank and a corresponding polarized point eigenvalue, while its full Dirac pair and smooth scalar self-source retain additional components and nonconstant coefficients.
text:
Summary: A fixed-line cumulative spatial band on CP3 has exactly twenty times the simplex rank and a corresponding polarized point eigenvalue, while its full Dirac pair and smooth scalar self-source retain additional components and nonconstant coefficients. An actual spatial band has the simplex count On physical \mathbb{CP}^3 with the specified line connection \mathcal O(3), retain every zero-form spatial spectral shell from 0 through N=n-1. The complete band has dimension  oxed{ \mathscr D_N= inom{N+3}{3} inom{N+6}{3} =20 inom{n+5}{6}=20S(n,6). } 	ag{1} Its physical point evaluation in the zero-form polarization is rank one and has nonzero eigenvalue \mathscr D_N/\mathcal V, where \mathcal V is the physical volume. Thus a specified point contact has an exact simplex coefficient with a single factor of twenty independent of the band. This is a different space of spatial fields from the holomorphic tangent-mode band: the line degree here stays fixed while nonholomorphic spatial harmonics are added. It also uses a different connection from the \mathcal O(2) derivative polynomial. The two calculations should not be combined without a map between their bundles and actions. The count and evaluation operator can be derived. A smooth local scalar current has not thereby become a point insertion. The explicit reproducing state below has a different self-contact expectation and drives complementary components. The geometry is conditional actual CP3 with ordinary macroscopic spatial directions, no compactification and unknown FS scale R. The calculations at CP5 below use a separately specified actual ten-dimensional geometry. Line and spectral labels are field data, not additional physical dimensions or charge assignments. Sum all fixed-line spatial shells For complex dimension m and L\ge0, consider the zero-form sections in the full bundle \Lambda^{0,*}\otimes\mathcal O(L). Their spatial squared-Dirac eigenvalues are X_k=k(k+L+m),\qquad X= rac{R^2\mathscr D_L^2}{4},\qquad k=0,1,\ldots. 	ag{2} The complete projective spectrum includes this family and all the other spinor families. Here the cumulative zero-form subspace is \mathcal K_N= igoplus_{k=0}^N\mathcal H_k. There is a direct polynomial count. A shell can be represented by a trace-free homogeneous polynomial of holomorphic and antiholomorphic degrees (k+L,k), with its line homogeneity retained. Taking a trace lowers both degrees by one. The harmonic decomposition of the complete polynomial space gives d_k=\dim\mathcal H_k = inom{k+m}{m} inom{k+L+m}{m} - inom{k+m-1}{m} inom{k+L+m-1}{m}. 	ag{3} The subtracted product is zero at k=0. The same dimensions follow from the SU(m+1) Weyl formula. Summing the differences in (3) yields  oxed{ \mathscr D_N=\dim\mathcal K_N = inom{N+m}{m} inom{N+L+m}{m}. } 	ag{4} Multiplication by |Z|^2 in the homogeneous polynomial description realizes the nested cumulative inclusions. On unit homogeneous coordinates it preserves the existing spatial section. The band therefore has one fixed connection and compatible spatial inclusions. At L=m the two factorial products join:  oxed{ \mathscr D_N = inom{2m}{m} inom{N+2m}{2m} = inom{2m}{m}S(n,2m),\qquad N=n-1. } 	ag{5} The constant factor is 20 at depth six and 252 at depth ten. For example: Spatial depth Fixed line degree Mass-band label n Spatial band rank 6 3 13 371\,280=20(18\,564) 6 3 35 76\,767\,600=20(3\,838\,380) 10 5 23 252(64\,512\,240) These are complete band dimensions, not observed particle counts. The original cumulative convention N=n-1 is retained. The identity does not establish a competing assignment of physical particle dimensionalities. Derive the polarized point operator Use the unit-volume spatial measure d
u first. At a physical point x, evaluation maps \mathcal K_N	o\mathcal O(L)_x, a one-dimensional fibre. Its point form is T_{N,x}=\operatorname{ev}_x^\dagger\operatorname{ev}_x. 	ag{6} Spatial homogeneity makes the diagonal reproducing kernel constant. Its trace integral is \mathscr D_N, so  oxed{ T_{N,x}	ext{ has rank one},\qquad T_{N,x}^2=\mathscr D_NT_{N,x}. } 	ag{7} With the physical measure d\mathrm{vol}=\mathcal Vd
u, the nonzero eigenvalue is instead \mathscr D_N/\mathcal V, where \mathcal V=\pi^mR^{2m}/m!. Equation (5) therefore fixes the band dependence of a specified polarized point form. The point x is a position in the actual spatial manifold. It is not the auxiliary occupied tangent-mode ray in the mass-contact construction. Matching their ranks up to a constant does not identify their representations, evaluation maps or physical sources. Keep the entire associated Dirac pair For every k\ge1, the zero-form family has an exact one-form Dirac partner of the same dimension d_k. The cumulative paired band therefore has total rank 2\mathscr D_N-d_0,\qquad d_0= inom{L+m}{m}. 	ag{8} It includes both Dirac signs and all its zero modes. The remaining spinor families belong to the complementary space of the full field equation. The full point evaluation of this paired band is not rank one. The zero-form fibre has evaluation eigenvalue \mathscr D_N. The one-form fibre has rank m; its isotropy representation is irreducible and its trace is \mathscr D_N-d_0. Thus, for N\ge1, the positive point form has eigenvalues  oxed{ \mathscr D_N\quad	ext{once},\qquad  rac{\mathscr D_N-d_0}{m}\quad	ext{$m$ times}. } 	ag{9} For the scalar  eta point form the second eigenvalue has a minus sign. At N=0 only the zero-form contribution remains. All values in (9) acquire 1/\mathcal V with the physical measure. No Dirac sign or exterior parity is identified with an antiparticle. The one-form value also follows by actual spatial differentiation. In local holomorphic line frames, the kernel of one zero-form shell is K_k(z,w)= d_k(1+z\cdot ar w)^L  rac{P_k^{(m-1,L)}(2t_{zw}-1)} {P_k^{(m-1,L)}(1)},\qquad t_{zw}=  rac{|1+z\cdot ar w|^2}{(1+|z|^2)(1+|w|^2)}. 	ag{10} At z=w=0, \partial_{ ar z_a}\partial_{w_b}K_k = rac{d_kX_k}{m}\delta_{ab}. 	ag{11} The normalized Dirac partner map and the physical one-form metric divide this by X_k, giving d_k/m in every one-form direction. This retains the angular polarizations that a single radial one-form at the pole would miss. The reproducing state is a smooth field Choose x=[1,0,\ldots,0] and let t=|Z_0|^2/|Z|^2. Define A_N= inom{N+L+m}{m},\qquad B_N= inom{N+m}{m},\qquad \mathscr D_N=A_NB_N. With unit homogeneous coordinates for y, summing the shell kernels gives the exact cumulative kernel K_N(y,x)=A_N Z_0^L P_N^{(m,L)}(2t-1). 	ag{12} Its squared spatial norm is \mathscr D_N. The unit-norm reproducing state \psi_{N,x}=K_N(\cdot,x)/\sqrt{\mathscr D_N} therefore has density  oxed{ ho_N(t)= rac{A_N}{B_N}\, t^L igl[P_N^{(m,L)}(2t-1) igr]^2, \qquad \intho_Nd
u=1. } 	ag{13} It reaches ho_N(x)=\mathscr D_N at the pole, but has a finite spatial profile. Its scalar self-current is that smooth profile, not a delta distribution. Evaluate the actual local scalar self-source For this unit-norm zero-form state, the local scalar interaction has occupied expectation  oxed{ \mathcal A_N=\intho_N^2d
u =m\left( rac{A_N}{B_N}ight)^2 \int_0^1t^{2L}(1-t)^{m-1}  igl[P_N^{(m,L)}(2t-1) igr]^4dt. } 	ag{14} This integral follows from the same physical norm used for (7). It can be evaluated exactly by finite beta integrals. At m=L=3: Cumulative cutoff N Point eigenvalue \mathscr D_N Local quartic \mathcal A_N \mathcal A_N/\mathscr D_N 0 20  rac{100}{21}  rac5{21} 1 140 23.170163 0.165501 12 371\,280 46\,113.932673 0.124203 34 76\,767\,600 9\,372\,719.126622 0.122092 The ratios at the unchanged electron and muon cutoffs differ. The smooth self-current of these reproducing states therefore does not reproduce the point coefficient with one exact common factor. There is also a field-equation residual. Let \mathsf P_N be the zero-form band projector and define r_N=\mathsf P_N(ho_N\psi_{N,x})-\mathcal A_N\psi_{N,x}. 	ag{15} Exact projection onto every retained Jacobi shell gives r_N
e0 at N=1,2,12,34. The scalar source also has a nonzero component outside the band at every tested cutoff, including N=0. Its full norm and both residual norms are calculated from the same polynomial source; the test does not stop at its occupied expectation. Independently, the free Dirac term satisfies  oxed{ \|\mathscr D_L\psi_{N,x}\|^2 = rac4{R^2\mathscr D_N} \sum_{k=1}^{N}X_kd_k>0 \qquad(N\ge1). } 	ag{16} A purely zero-form reproducing state consequently requires its odd Dirac component to solve a stationary scalar equation. The point-form eigenvector alone is not a complete stationary particle field. For physical norm Q, the profile is scaled by \sqrt{Q/\mathcal V}. Its occupied scalar coefficient acquires gQ/\mathcal V times \mathcal A_N. This is still an expectation of the source, rather than an exact stationary frequency in the presence of (15)–(16). Consequence for the contact derivation There is now a fixed-connection band of actual spatial functions with the exact simplex dimension up to one sector constant. Its polarized physical point operator has the matching eigenvalue. These are conditional mathematical constructions with a canonical spatial norm. The remaining step is to derive that particular point interaction and its occupied full spinor field from the master action. The tested smooth local scalar source does not supply it directly. A different self-consistent spatial state remains possible and must be solved with its complementary components. The consistent-band analysis explains why prescribing a point form and deriving a local self-interaction are separate operations. The spatial scalar Dirac equation provides the full variational setting for continuing the occupied field. Verification projective_spectral_contact_checks.py compares harmonic trace subtraction, independent Weyl dimensions and actual normalized pole evaluation. Exact polynomial summation verifies the cumulative kernel. Independent mixed derivatives of the two-point kernel check all one-form point polarizations. Exact beta integration gives the quartic and complete projected source norms. Independent curved quadrature retains every radial Dirac partner through the assigned cutoffs. Complex variations of the complete zero/one-form spatial action check the reciprocal Hessian, with neither relative phases nor the conjugate response omitted.

title: Canonical norm of the projective derivative lift
summary: The complete projective holomorphic jet lift has a calculable kinetic norm that changes its reduced simplex coefficient, while canonical compression keeps the local scalar response bounded on any fixed smooth background.
text: Summary: The complete projective holomorphic jet lift has a calculable kinetic norm that changes its reduced simplex coefficient, while canonical compression keeps the local scalar response bounded on any fixed smooth background. The geometric polynomial needs its parent-field norm The projective covariant derivative has an exact simplex adjoint square on the specified CP3 line bundle: P(X)=\frac{X(X+4)(X+6)}{720}, \qquad X=\left.\frac{R^2\mathscr D_2^2}{4}\right|_{\text{zero forms}}. \tag{1} One possible route to a master-field origin is to represent the lower field and its derivatives by components of a larger field. For the natural projective holomorphic jet lift, that route has an explicitly nonconstant kinetic metric: \boxed{Z(X)=\frac{X^2+12X+40}{40}.} \tag{2} If this lifted field carries the canonical time derivative, the reduced coefficient of the derivative energy is P(X)/Z(X). The metric cannot be omitted while retaining that physical lift. The following calculation derives it without discarding any component or adjusting the occupied indices. The geometry remains conditional physical CP3 with unknown radius R, ordinary macroscopic spatial directions and no compactification. The finite jet carrier describes derivatives of the same spatial field. Its mathematical rank adds no physical spatial directions, and its realization as components of the master spinor is a further hypothesis. The full osculating polynomial Work first on \mathbb{CP}^m with L\ge0. Let \mathcal H_L=H^0(\mathbb{CP}^m,\mathcal O(L)), \qquad D_L=\dim\mathcal H_L=\binom{L+m}{m}. \tag{3} Give \mathcal H_L its invariant norm from unit-volume spatial integration. For a smooth section f and a point x, there is a unique polynomial section whose holomorphic derivatives through order L at x agree with those of f. Define \mathcal J_Lf(x) to be its complete coefficient vector in \mathcal H_L. This is the osculating polynomial: it matches the entire holomorphic jet, not just the value or one coherent direction. In an affine chart, the monomials of degree at most L form a basis of the same number of jets. Their derivative matrix is invertible. Projective coordinate covariance makes the construction global. For a holomorphic section, the same polynomial works at every point, so its coefficient vector is constant over the base. The degree L here is the line degree of the physical spatial section. For CP3 and L=2, D_L=10. It is not the auxiliary mass-band rank S(n,6) and does not relabel the electron or muon mode. Derive the pointwise metric on all derivatives At the origin of an affine chart, write f(z)=\sum_{|\alpha|\le L}f_\alpha z^\alpha +\text{terms of higher holomorphic order}. An orthonormal basis of the polynomial carrier is e_\alpha(Z)= \sqrt{\frac{D_LL!}{(L-|\alpha|)!\,\alpha!}}\, Z_0^{L-|\alpha|}Z^\alpha. \tag{4} The coefficient of e_\alpha in the osculating polynomial is f_\alpha\sqrt{(L-|\alpha|)!\alpha!/(D_LL!)}. At this point the holomorphic connection coefficients vanish. Contracting every tensor index and grouping by j=|\alpha| gives \boxed{ |\mathcal J_Lf(x)|^2 =\frac1{D_L}\sum_{j=0}^{L} \frac{(L-j)!}{L!\,j!} \left(\frac{R^2}{2}\right)^j |\mathcal B_jf(x)|^2. } \tag{5} Here \mathcal B_j is the complete symmetric covariant derivative defined in the derivative note. Both norms use the physical Hermitian metric. Physical SU(m+1) isometries move any point to this origin and act unitarily on \mathcal H_L. Thus (5) holds globally. The factors in (5) are fixed by polynomial interpolation and the actual section norm. They are not optional weights for independent derivative coordinates. A field of jets still obeys the derivative compatibility conditions. Integrate the induced kinetic operator The derivative norm identity gives, on the degree-n zero-form family, \frac{\|\mathcal B_jf_n\|^2}{\|f_n\|^2} =\left(\frac2{R^2}\right)^j (n+L)_{\underline j}(n+m)_j. \tag{6} Since X=n(n+L+m) on that family, integrating (5) yields \boxed{ \mathcal J_L^\dagger\mathcal J_L=Z_{m,L}(X) =\frac1{D_L} \sum_{j=0}^{L}\frac{(L-j)!}{L!\,j!} \prod_{k=0}^{j-1}[X+(L-k)(m+k)]. } \tag{7} The empty product is one. Every coefficient of this polynomial is positive, and Z_{m,L}(X)\ge1 for X\ge0. The identity holds on the full section space because each irreducible spatial family has the eigenvalue obtained in (6). There is an exact use of the Hockey-Stick Identity here. At n=0 the derivative factors in (6) reduce (7) to Z_{m,L}(0) =\frac1{D_L}\sum_{j=0}^{L}\frac{(m)_j}{j!} =\frac{\displaystyle\sum_{j=0}^{L}\binom{m+j-1}{j}} {\displaystyle\binom{m+L}{m}} =1. \tag{8} The combinatorial sum verifies the correct norm of a holomorphic section and its constant polynomial lift. It does not supply a mass enhancement. For m=3,L=2, (7) is Z(X)=\frac1{10} \left[1+\frac{X+6}{2}+\frac{(X+6)(X+4)}4\right] =\frac{X^2+12X+40}{40}, \tag{9} which proves (2). Vary the action with the same time-kinetic norm Suppose the physical reduction uses Y=\mathcal J_Lf and gives that complete field its ordinary positive kinetic norm. The time-kinetic term for f is then \operatorname{Re}\langle f,iZ\partial_tf\rangle. If its specified derivative energy is \mu\langle f,P(X)f\rangle, variation gives iZ(X)\partial_tf=\mu P(X)f. \tag{10} Defining the canonically normalized amplitude u=Z^{1/2}f gives \boxed{i\partial_tu=\mu\,\frac{P(X)}{Z(X)}u.} \tag{11} This is the contribution of the stated derivative energy to this specified reduced component. It is not a complete spatial Dirac dispersion relation or an observed rest mass. The full spinor construction separately retains the first-order kinetic operator and both signs. At the unchanged assigned indices: Spatial index n S(n,6) Derived norm Z_n Canonical coefficient P/Z 13 18\,564 \frac{14\,401}{10} \frac{185\,640}{14\,401}\approx12.891 35 3\,838\,380 49\,421 \frac{3\,838\,380}{49\,421}\approx77.667 Their coefficient ratio is approximately 6.025, rather than the simplex ratio. Rescaling the whole carrier by a constant does not remove its dependence on n. More generally, at L=m-1 the leading terms in (7) and in the normalized derivative polynomial give \boxed{\frac{P(X)}{Z_{m,m-1}(X)} \sim\frac{X}{2m^2}\qquad(X\longrightarrow\infty).} \tag{12} For CP3 this is X/18. The complete derivative lift accounts for four of the six powers of the high spectral degree in its kinetic norm. This conclusion depends on using the lifted field as the canonical parent. If f itself is the canonical field of a separately specified action, its kinetic norm is the one in that action. Equation (7) is a constraint on this concrete lift, not a change to the valid geometric identity (1). Compress the actual algebraic scalar current The same norm issue applies directly to the written local scalar interaction, without introducing the derivative energy. Let T be the specified linear field lift, Z=T^\dagger T its positive kinetic operator and U=TZ^{-1/2},\qquad U^\dagger U=I. \tag{13} For the projective jet lift, (7) computes Z explicitly. Equation (13) is its isometric form on the canonical retained field. Retain the full parent spinor and its scalar matrix \beta^\dagger=\beta, \beta^2=I. At a fixed smooth background Y_0, set J_0=Y_0^\dagger\beta Y_0. The complete real-linear derivative of the cubic scalar source is \mathcal V_{Y_0}h =g\left[J_0\beta h +2\operatorname{Re}(Y_0^\dagger\beta h)\,\beta Y_0\right]. \tag{14} All complex amplitudes and their conjugate response are present. Since |J_0|\le|Y_0|^2, its pointwise operator norm obeys \|\mathcal V_{Y_0}\| \le3|g|\,|Y_0|^2. \tag{15} On a fixed bounded smooth spatial background, multiplication by this response is a bounded real-linear operator. Canonical compression gives \boxed{ \|U^\dagger\mathcal V_{Y_0}U\| \le3|g|\,\|Y_0\|_\infty^2. } \tag{16} The derivatives in T do not invalidate the bound: the same derivatives occur in Z, and their canonical combination U is an isometry. A constant scalar contribution M\|\mathcal J_Lf\|^2 in the selected component similarly becomes M\|u\|^2. Thus this canonical compression of the algebraic scalar source cannot equal a nonzero constant times the unbounded polynomial P(X) on all degrees of one fixed smooth background. This is a statement about the specified linear lift and fixed-background response. It does not impose a uniform bound across different self-consistent particle backgrounds, whose densities may differ. It also does not replace a nonlinear, frequency-dependent elimination of other spatial components. Those require the full complementary variation. The geometric simplex operator remains a concrete candidate. The natural osculating-polynomial lift, by itself, does not derive it as a canonically normalized physical mass interaction. Verification projective_jet_norm_checks.py constructs and inverts the complete polynomial interpolation matrix. Arbitrary complex spatial jets verify (5) against independent full tensor contractions at nonzero projective coordinates. Exact arithmetic checks the norm polynomial, the Hockey-Stick normalization and the unchanged assigned indices. Independent curved quadrature verifies the full Gram matrix through degree 35; complex action variations verify the canonical coefficient. Complete real-linear scalar variations with every spinor polarization check the compression bound (16).

title: Deriving the simplex polynomial from spatial covariant derivatives
summary: The first purely holomorphic differential annihilator on the specified CP3 line bundle has an adjoint square with the exact simplex spectrum, giving a geometric construction of the polynomial and a local extension to its complete Dirac pair.

A differential construction fixes the polynomial On the specified line bundle \mathcal O(2) over physical \mathbb{CP}^3, take the full symmetric third holomorphic covariant derivative \mathcal B_3s=

They are not independently chosen polynomial coefficients. The overall normalization sets the first nonzero eigenvalue to one. Define the complete derivative and its tensor norm For a nonnegative line degree L, let \mathcal B_k: \Gamma(\mathcal O(L)) \longrightarrow \Gamma igl(\operatorname{Sym}^k T^{*1,0}\otimes\mathcal O(L) igr) 	ag{4} be the symmetric k-fold covariant derivative. The tensor norm in (4) is inherited from the full tensor product. In particular, all ordered index contractions are retained, with no extra factor of 1/k! in the norm. On the affine chart [1,z_1,\ldots,z_m], put t=(1+|z|^2)^{-1},\qquad h_L=t^L,\qquad \Gamma^k_{ij}=-t(\delta_i^k ar z_j+\delta_j^k ar z_i). 	ag{5} The line connection has holomorphic coefficient -Lt ar z_i. For any constant complex direction v, define u=t\sum_i ar z_iv_i. Then \partial_vu=-u^2. Contracting every tensor index with v gives the exact recurrence \mathcal B_{k+1}s(v^{k+1}) = igl(\partial_v+(2k-L)u igr)\mathcal B_ks(v^k). 	ag{6} The coefficient 2k includes the connection on all k tensor indices; omitting it would give a different operator. Induction in (6) gives \mathcal B_ks(v^k)= \sum_{j=0}^{k} (-1)^{k-j} inom kj (L-j)_{\underline{k-j}}\, u^{k-j}\partial_v^js, 	ag{7} where a_{\underline r}=a(a-1)\cdots(a-r+1), with a_{\underline0}=1. At k=L+1, every coefficient with j<k vanishes. Therefore  oxed{\mathcal B_{L+1}s=\partial^{L+1}s} 	ag{8} in this affine holomorphic line frame. Polarization of (6)–(7) recovers the complete mixed tensor, not merely its value in one chosen direction. Why the affine expression is globally geometric A smooth section of \mathcal O(L) can be represented in homogeneous coordinates by a function F satisfying F(\lambda Z, ar\lambda ar Z)=\lambda^L F(Z, ar Z). 	ag{9} Its holomorphic Euler identity is Z^A\partial_AF=LF. Differentiating it L times shows that Z^{A_0}\partial_{A_0}\partial_{A_1}\cdots\partial_{A_L}F=0. 	ag{10} Thus \partial^{L+1}F is horizontal in every tensor slot. Its homogeneity makes it descend precisely to the bundle in (4). This gives the coordinate-independent projective operator (8). The argument applies to smooth sections; it does not assume that the field itself is holomorphic. On a holomorphic section, F is a homogeneous polynomial of degree L, so (8) vanishes. Conversely, the holomorphic sections supply every holomorphic jet through order L at each point. A nonzero purely holomorphic differential operator of smaller order cannot annihilate all those jets. This construction belongs to the projective differential setting described by Eastwood and Gover. Equations (5)–(10) give the particular operator used here directly. The differential operator is projectively defined; its positive adjoint square additionally uses the specified FS metric and measure. No general conformal invariance of the spinor mass action is assumed. Derive its spectrum using physical spatial fields Use the spatial Jacobi construction on \mathbb{CP}^m with line degree L. In the coherent chart frame, a representative of its zero-form spectral family is s_n=\chi p_n(t),\qquad p_n(t)=P_n^{(m-1,L)}(2t-1),\qquad X s_n=n(n+L+m)s_n. 	ag{11} The normalization of the coherent holomorphic section \chi cancels from the following norm ratio. The original radial weight is t^L(1-t)^{m-1}dt. Direct use of (5) on all tensor indices gives \mathcal B_ks_n =\chi\,t^kQ_k(t)\, ar z^{\otimes k},\qquad Q_{k+1}=(k-L)Q_k-tQ_k',\qquad Q_0=p_n. 	ag{12} The physical inverse metric contracts each copy of  ar z with squared norm 2|z|^2/(R^2t^2). Hence  rac{\|\mathcal B_ks_n\|^2}{\|s_n\|^2} = \left( rac2{R^2}ight)^k  rac{\displaystyle\int_0^1 t^{L-k}(1-t)^{m-1+k}|Q_k(t)|^2dt} {\displaystyle\int_0^1 t^L(1-t)^{m-1}|p_n(t)|^2dt}. 	ag{13} The recurrence also has the exact Jacobi form Q_k=(-1)^kt^{k-L} rac{d^k}{dt^k}(t^Lp_n) =(-1)^k(n+L)_{\underline k} P_n^{(m-1+k,L-k)}(2t-1). 	ag{14} It follows by differentiating the finite Jacobi polynomial, or its hypergeometric expression. With \alpha, eta>-1, the shifted Jacobi norm is I_n(\alpha, eta)=  rac{\Gamma(n+\alpha+1)\Gamma(n+ eta+1)} {(2n+\alpha+ eta+1)n!\,\Gamma(n+\alpha+ eta+1)}. 	ag{15} This is DLMF Table 18.3.1 after changing variables from [-1,1] to [0,1]. For 0\le k\le L, substitution in (13) immediately gives  oxed{  rac{\|\mathcal B_ks_n\|^2}{\|s_n\|^2} =\left( rac2{R^2}ight)^k (n+L)_{\underline k}(n+m)_k. } 	ag{16} Here (a)_k=a(a+1)\cdots(a+k-1) is the rising factorial. For n\ge1, P_n^{(\alpha,-1)}(2t-1) = rac{n+\alpha}{n}\, tP_{n-1}^{(\alpha,1)}(2t-1). 	ag{17} Its factor t makes (13) finite and reduces it to the ordinary positive weight t(1-t)^\alpha. Using (15) on that polynomial proves (16) also for k=L+1. The n=0 field is annihilated separately, as required by (8). The operator and metric commute with physical SU(m+1) isometries. The zero-form section spectrum is a multiplicity-free sum of irreducible families, and an isometry orbit of the representative (11) spans its family. The adjoint square acts as a scalar on each one. Thus (16) determines its eigenvalue on every complex spatial polarization in that family, beyond the radial representative. The balanced degree gives the consecutive simplex factors Set L=m-1 and take its first annihilator, of order k=m. Equation (16) becomes  oxed{ \mathcal B_m^\dagger\mathcal B_m ig|_n = rac{2^m}{R^{2m}}\, (n)_m(n+m)_m = rac{2^m}{R^{2m}}\,(n)_{2m}. } 	ag{18} The two rising products are adjacent. Normalizing at n=1 therefore gives exactly S(n,2m) for every n\ge1. For a general L, the first annihilator instead gives (n)_{L+1}(n+m)_{L+1}. In particular, \mathcal M_6(13)=18\,564,\qquad \mathcal M_6(35)=3\,838\,380,\qquad \mathcal M_{10}(23)=64\,512\,240. 	ag{19} The ten-dimensional construction has its own specified line connection. No particle mode or dimensionality is reassigned in (19). Extend to the complete Dirac pair The geometric derivative above acts on zero-form sections. A mass insertion must also treat their one-form Dirac partners. Let \Pi_0,\Pi_1 be the local exterior-degree projectors, and put X_0= rac{R^2}{2} \left( ar\partial^\dagger\Pi_1 ar\partial + ar\partial\Pi_0 ar\partial^\daggeright). 	ag{20} The local Hodge calculation in the spectral note proves [X_0,\mathscr D_L]=[X_0, eta]=0. It equals X on the complete zero/exact-one-form pair and vanishes on the other form families and on harmonic fields. The resulting specified local extension is  oxed{\mathcal M_{m pair} = rac{X_0(X_0+4)(X_0+6)}{720}.} 	ag{21} It has the geometric value (3) on both Dirac signs. All remaining spinor polarizations stay in the field equation with their full kinetic action. Giving this additional interaction zero action on those families is an extension choice, not a dynamical proof that they are unoccupied. For real \mu, the specified quadratic energy E_\mu(\psi)=\langle\psi,\mathscr D_2\psiangle +\mu\langle\psi, eta\mathcal M_{m pair}\psiangle 	ag{22} is real and varies into a Hermitian scalar insertion. On a populated first-family mode the complete frequencies are still \omega_\pm=\pm\sqrt{ rac{4n(n+5)}{R^2}+\mu^2S(n,6)^2}. 	ag{23} Deriving the polynomial from a covariant derivative does not remove this kinetic contribution. What has and has not been supplied by the construction The inverse dynamics calculation now gives explicit local actions whose complete paired frequencies equal the simplex values. Those actions modify both kinetic and scalar terms and compensate the field norm consistently. They are reconstructed candidates, with physical coupling and causal propagation still to be tested. The calculation supplies an explicit global geometric differential operator, its physical adjoint, its complete zero-form spectrum and a local Hermitian extension to the associated Dirac pair. The relative polynomial coefficients and the all-degree simplex identity follow from those data. The remaining physical step is to obtain the derivative energy from the one-field master action, together with its common normalization, connection and occupied spatial states. Neither these operator identities nor their numerical verification establish the physical projective geometry or experimental particle masses.
