Stability under arbitrary omitted spatial interactions or changes to the kernel remains a separate problem. For an occupied ray, let a_j=x_j+iy_j describe the normalized perturbation into its opposite eigenspinor. Choose that eigenspinor's sign so that the scalar transition matrix element is b_j=\epsilon_j/E_j. The quadratic energy at fixed q_j is \delta^2\mathcal E =-2\sum_j q_jE_j|a_j|^2 +2\kappa\left(\sum_j q_jb_jx_j\right)^2. \tag{9} Cauchy--Schwarz and (5) give \kappa\sum_j\frac{q_j\epsilon_j^2}{E_j^3} =1-\kappa M^2\sum_j\frac{q_j}{E_j^3}<1, \tag{10} so (9) is strictly negative on these ray directions. The phase and positive-band polarization directions remain flat. Opposite-band polarizations orthogonal to z_j are also retained: they have frequency 2E_j and do not drive the scalar source to first order. The coupled ray equations are \dot x_j=-2E_jy_j,\qquad \dot y_j=2E_jx_j-2\kappa b_j\sum_kq_kb_kx_k. \tag{11} After a positive diagonal change of coordinates, their squared-frequency matrix is the symmetric matrix \mathcal K=4\left[\operatorname{diag}(E_j^2)-\kappa ww^T\right], \qquad w_j=\frac{\sqrt{q_j}\epsilon_j}{\sqrt{E_j}}. \tag{12} Subtract 4M^2I and use (5). The remaining rank-one perturbation of 4\operatorname{diag}(\epsilon_j^2) is nonnegative and has a one-dimensional null space, since \kappa\sum w_j^2/\epsilon_j^2=1. Therefore \boxed{\Omega_{\mathrm{scalar}}=2M} \tag{13} is an exact lowest ray response frequency, with all other ray frequencies larger. In the original coordinates its eigenvector has x_j\propto 1/\epsilon_j, so its integrated scalar variation is nonzero. The complete field linearization verifies that no polarization was lost. In the rotating frame of (4), set v=\beta\phi and W=\bigoplus_j E_j I_{2r_j}. For arbitrary complex perturbations, i\dot\eta=A\eta+B\bar\eta,\qquad A=\mathscr D+M\beta-W+\kappa vv^\dagger,\qquad B=\kappa vv^T. \tag{14} This retains changes of each pair norm as well as all phase and polarization directions. Such norm changes can produce zero-frequency Jordan motion in the rotating frame. The fixed-norm orbital-stability statement does not mistake these for a strictly positive full Hessian. The scalar pole, its residue and the field energy An applied scalar coefficient f(t)\beta gives \delta M=\kappa\delta S+f. Solving (11) with time convention e^{-i\Omega t} yields \delta S=\chi(\Omega)f,\qquad \chi(\Omega)=\frac{\chi_0(\Omega)}{1-\kappa\chi_0(\Omega)},\qquad \chi_0(\Omega)=4\sum_j \frac{q_j\epsilon_j^2}{E_j(4E_j^2-\Omega^2)}. \tag{15} At \Omega=2M, (5) makes \chi_0=1/\kappa. The pole is simple, with \chi(\Omega)=\frac{\mathcal R}{4M^2-\Omega^2}+O(1),\qquad \mathcal R=\frac{4}{\kappa^2\displaystyle\sum_jq_j/(E_j\epsilon_j^2)}>0. \tag{16} The diagnostic obtains the same response by solving the complete real linearization (14), independently of the ray reduction. For a purely zero-kinetic field the scalar source is conserved and its driven response vanishes; a formal opposite-chirality frequency 2M is then invisible to this scalar probe. Equation (16) explicitly assumes every \epsilon_j>0. The total energy of (4) is \boxed{\mathcal E_*= \sum_j q_jE_j-\frac{M^2}{2\kappa},\qquad \frac{\partial\mathcal E_*}{\partial q_j}=E_j.} \tag{17} The derivative follows by stationary elimination of M in (8). Thus M, the phase frequencies E_j, the collective frequency 2M, and the full energy \mathcal E_* have distinct meanings within this same model. The local scalar normalization gives the corresponding energy-frequency distinction for a spatially local action. None of these quantities has been identified here as the observed rest mass of an isolated particle. What the cumulative count does at fixed canonical norm Let Q=\sum q_j, \Lambda=\kappa Q, and a_r=\sum q_j\epsilon_j^r/Q. For a fixed finite spectrum and \Lambda large compared with its kinetic frequencies, (5) gives M=\Lambda-\frac{a_2}{2\Lambda} +\frac{3a_4-4a_2^2}{8\Lambda^3} +O(\Lambda^{-5}). \tag{18} The omitted coefficient contains sixth-order spectral moments. Convexity of (x+M^2)^{-1/2} also gives the exact bounds, on an existing branch, \sqrt{\max(0,\Lambda^2-a_2)}\le M \le\sqrt{\Lambda^2-\epsilon_{\min}^2}<\Lambda. \tag{19} If every counted mode carries one unit of canonical norm, Q equals the number of modes. The leading coefficient M\simeq\kappa Q then contains that count without inserting it into \kappa. This is a result about an extensive field norm. Its leading total energy is \mathcal E_*\simeq\kappa Q^2/2, rather than \kappa Q. If the total canonical norm is one, the occupation weights instead sum to one and M\le\kappa for every band. In the strong-response limit M\simeq\kappa, independently of the mode count. Both the scalar coefficient and its collective frequency inherit this normalization. More sharply, suppose shell energies increase with their label and occupation is uniform per counted mode at fixed total norm. Adding the next shell decreases the weighted average of (\epsilon^2+M^2)^{-1/2} at every trial M. Its intersection with 1/\kappa therefore moves to a smaller M, or the positive branch ceases to exist. This is an exact comparison at unchanged \kappa. It does not change the committed particle mode selections. A field-coordinate rescaling cannot turn the extensive case into the normalized case while preserving their apparent coefficients. Substituting \psi=\sqrt D\,\varphi multiplies the original kinetic term by D and its quartic by D^2. Restoring the canonical field restores the original physical norm. Dividing the entire action by a band-dependent D would be an additional physical prescription. Hockey-Stick moments and a specified spatial spectrum For cumulative oscillator shell weights w_k=\binom{k+d-1}{d-1},\qquad D_N=\sum_{k=0}^Nw_k=\binom{N+d}{d}, \tag{20} Hockey-Stick also supplies all factorial moments: \frac1{D_N}\sum_{k=0}^Nw_k(k)_{\underline r} =\frac{d}{d+r}(N)_{\underline r}. \tag{21} Indeed, multiplying w_k by the falling factorial gives d(d+1)\cdots(d+r-1)\binom{k+d-1}{d+r-1}; summing and dividing by D_N proves (21). Consequently \langle k\rangle=dN/(d+1) and \langle k^2\rangle=dN(N-1)/(d+2)+dN/(d+1). These identities calculate the kinetic moments in (18) once a kinetic spectrum has actually been specified. The count alone does not specify it. One geometric comparison is the round even-dimensional spatial sphere of physical radius R. Its Dirac frequencies and positive multiplicities are \epsilon_k=\frac{k+d/2}{R},\qquad r_k=2^{d/2}\binom{k+d-1}{d-1},\qquad \sum_{k=0}^Nr_k=2^{d/2}D_N. \tag{22} These are the standard spherical Dirac eigenvalues and degeneracies; see Camporesi and Higuchi, equations (3.41)–(3.44). Here the sphere is an explicitly different candidate global spatial geometry, not an identification of the proposed CP3 space. Its directions remain ordinary macroscopic spatial directions, with no compactification or chosen small radius. Equation (22) supplies a conditional spectral comparison, not a selection of physical topology or a complete nested geometry. The spin factor is eight at depth six and thirty-two at depth ten, and cannot silently be discarded in a comparison of extensive norms. The diagnostic uses the assigned cumulative bands N=12,34 at depth six and N=22 at depth ten, retaining those spin factors. It solves (5) for both extensive and unit total norms with the same stated coefficients, measured in units of R^{-1}. No radius or coefficient is fitted to observed masses. The fixed-norm bound and decreasing-gap result survive. Verification and physical consequence scalar_gap_normalization_checks.py checks the exact shell sums and six factorial moments, gap thresholds, bounds and asymptotic orders. Complex controls retain one to four kinetic pairs, up to three degenerate polarizations per pair, all conjugate variations, and common coordinate covariance. Independent energy derivatives, the complete field spectrum, driven scalar response and nonlinear time evolution verify the finite model's equations. The calculation provides a self-consistent scalar coefficient and a collective response pole from one specified interaction. It also locates the normalization needed for a count enhancement. A physical simplex mass law still requires a master-derived kernel, a justified occupation and canonical norm, viable spatial particle states, and a rest-mass identification. This comparison neither establishes nor overturns the assigned particle dimensionalities.

title: Nonlinear mass reduction with spatial response
summary: Eliminating complementary spatial Dirac modes gives a nonlinear effective action, its exact induced norm, and a positive source-leakage criterion for departures from a common linear contact scale.
text: Summary: Eliminating complementary spatial Dirac modes gives a nonlinear effective action, its exact induced norm, and a positive source-leakage criterion for departures from a common linear contact scale. The interaction coefficient and the occupied field The occupied-graph action retains the simplex count as a nonlinear coefficient. Determining its physical consequence requires solving the spatial field and its normalization. The calculation below eliminates complementary modes of that same field while retaining their contribution to both quantities. It does not derive the graph action from the master interaction. Let the spatial Hilbert space have a fixed physical measure and canonical time-kinetic norm. Its self-adjoint spatial Dirac operator and chirality obey \mathscr D^\dagger=\mathscr D,\qquad \beta^\dagger=\beta,\qquad \beta^2=I,\qquad \{\mathscr D,\beta\}=0. \tag{1} These are operators on actual spatial fields, not a replacement of spatial coordinates by coefficient rays. The calculation applies at any spatial depth for which the following spectral and regularity hypotheses hold; six dimensions alone do not establish them. Let P project onto the entire zero space in the problem being reduced, assume \beta P=P, and write Q=I-P. Require an invertible complementary operator \mathscr D_Q=Q\mathscr DQ. If a restricted spatial symmetry class is used, it must be invariant under the full equation, and every zero mode in that class must be retained. A negative-chirality zero mode cannot silently be inverted or omitted. For finite Galerkin systems these are finite matrix assumptions. On a smooth closed spatial manifold, an elliptic Dirac operator with a spectral gap on Q supplies the complementary inverse between the appropriate Sobolev spaces. One sufficient framework uses H^s, s>d/2, so products are controlled, and a scalar kernel bounded on that space. The local kernel is the identity. The resulting real-analytic implicit-function argument is local near zero coupling and zero frequency. It is not a claim about arbitrary coupling or continuous spectra without a gap. Use a fixed real reciprocal scalar kernel K, with \begin{aligned} \sigma_\psi&=\psi^\dagger\beta\psi,& V_\psi&=K\sigma_\psi,\\ U(\psi)&=\langle\sigma_\psi,K\sigma_\psi\rangle,& E_g(\psi)&=\langle\psi,\mathscr D\psi\rangle+\frac g2U(\psi). \end{aligned} \tag{2} The scalar potential acts by multiplication and commutes with \beta. Its complete gradient is \nabla_{\bar\psi}E_g=\mathscr D\psi+g\beta V_\psi\psi. \tag{3} Both ordinary and conjugate variations of the scalar source are part of (3). A fixed potential evaluated on an unchanging target would give a different reduction. Exact stationary elimination and the norm At a real trial frequency \omega, form \mathcal R(\psi;g,\omega)=E_g(\psi)-\omega\|\psi\|^2, \qquad \psi=u+y,\quad u=Pu,\quad y=Qy. \tag{4} Solve the full complementary equation Q[\mathscr D(u+y)+g\beta V_{u+y}(u+y)-\omega(u+y)]=0. \tag{5} The invertibility in (1) gives a unique small local solution y=y(u,g,\omega). Substitute this solution into (4), defining \mathcal R_{\rm eff}. Stationarity in y removes its implicit derivatives from every first variation. In particular, \boxed{-\partial_\omega\mathcal R_{\rm eff} =\|u+y(u,g,\omega)\|^2.} \tag{6} The reduced field's norm is therefore not generally \|u\|^2. Equation (6) is exact on the local complementary branch. This norm is the phase-symmetry norm of the written action; no ordinary electric charge or particle-number interpretation has been assigned to it. The stationary second variation has an equally exact expression. In real coordinates retaining both quadratures, let H be the full Hessian of (4). Where H_{QQ} is invertible, \boxed{H_{\rm eff}=H_{PP}-H_{PQ}H_{QQ}^{-1}H_{QP}.} \tag{7} This nonlinear stationary reduction uses the same elimination principle as the linear Feshbach--Schur method. The band-consistency calculation explains why eliminating modes and bare compression obey different consistency rules. Neither (7) nor a positive curvature in a restricted subspace establishes dynamical stability of the full Dirac field. Leading effective action, including complementary normalization For u in the positive-chirality zero space define \rho_u=u^\dagger u,\qquad V_u=K\rho_u,\qquad t_u=\mathscr D_Q^{-1}Q(V_uu). \tag{8} The vector t_u has opposite chirality. With \epsilon=|g|+|\omega|, expansion of (5) gives y=-g t_u -g\mathscr D_Q^{-1}Q[(\omega+gV_u)t_u] +O(\epsilon^3). \tag{9} The first displayed term is negative-chirality and the second is positive-chirality. Their pointwise scalar cross term and their norm cross term vanish. Substitution into the complete functional yields \boxed{ \begin{aligned} \mathcal R_{\rm eff}(u;g,\omega) ={}&\frac g2U(u)-\omega\|u\|^2\\ &-g^2\omega\|t_u\|^2-g^3\langle t_u,V_ut_u\rangle +O(\epsilon^5). \end{aligned}} \tag{10} One can check the cubic terms directly. Write the first two terms of y as y_1,y_2. The kinetic cross term is 2\operatorname{Re}\langle y_1,\mathscr Dy_2\rangle. The scalar energy contributes 2g\operatorname{Re}\langle V_uu,y_2\rangle -g\langle y_1,V_uy_1\rangle. Because \mathscr Dy_1=-gQ(V_uu), the two terms containing y_2 cancel. The norm term contributes -\omega\|y_1\|^2. These are exactly the two cubic contributions in (10). There is no term of total degree four: the symmetry y(u,-g,-\omega)=\beta y(u,g,\omega),\qquad \mathcal R_{\rm eff}(u;-g,-\omega) =-\mathcal R_{\rm eff}(u;g,\omega) \tag{11} follows from uniqueness of the local complementary solution and (1). The analytic remainder in (10) can also be differentiated. Equation (6) therefore gives \boxed{Q_{\rm eff}=\|u\|^2+g^2\|t_u\|^2+O(\epsilon^4).} \tag{12} The reduced equation must be varied together with this norm. Keeping only the last scalar-potential term of (10) would miss a contribution of the same order to the normalized frequency. A normalized branch and a criterion for an exact linear scale Let \chi be a unit vector in the retained zero space satisfying P(V_\chi\chi)=A\chi,\qquad A=U(\chi). \tag{13} This is stationarity of the restricted scalar quartic on its unit sphere. Assume a smooth parity-compatible normalized branch through \chi. For a one-dimensional complex zero space its local existence follows after fixing the phase; in a larger space the retained stationary problem must also be solved, with its symmetries and degeneracies accounted for. Define \eta=-\mathscr D_Q^{-1}Q(V_\chi\chi),\quad a=\|\eta\|^2,\quad b=\langle\eta,V_\chi\eta\rangle, \quad C=Aa+b. \tag{14} The full field is \phi_g=\chi+g\eta+g^2\zeta+O(g^3), where \operatorname{Re}\langle\chi,\zeta\rangle=-a/2 fixes the total norm. Its complementary equation at second order gives \mathscr D\zeta=(A+V_\chi)\eta. Reciprocity of K then gives \boxed{\omega(g)=gA-4g^3C+O(g^5),\qquad E_g(\phi_g)=\frac{gA}{2}-g^3C+O(g^5).} \tag{15} For example, \operatorname{Re}\langle V_\chi\chi,\zeta\rangle =-Aa/2-Aa-b. The scalar expansion is consequently U(\phi_g)=A-6g^2C+O(g^4). Together with the exact identity E_g=\omega-gU(\phi_g)/2, this proves both expressions in (15). The local scalar normalization explains why nonlinear frequency and total energy must be distinguished before a physical rest mass is identified. If A>0 and the multiplication operator V_\chi\ge0, then \boxed{C\ge A\|\eta\|^2,\qquad C=0\ \Longleftrightarrow\ Q(V_\chi\chi)=0.} \tag{16} Here positivity of the potential is an explicit hypothesis; a positive quadratic kernel form alone need not imply a pointwise positive potential. Under (13), vanishing source in the complement means V_\chi\chi=A\chi. Thus the unchanged field \phi_g=\chi is an exact branch with \omega=gA for every g for which the stated equation is defined. Its total energy is gA/2. Equation (16) gives a concrete route to exact linearity: the selected spatial field must make its scalar source preserve its zero-mode line. It also gives a necessary condition for exact linearity of the analytic branch under these positivity hypotheses. Existence of such a line does not establish its stability, occupied mode index or observed mass. What a common simplex coefficient would have to preserve Suppose, conditionally, that an independently derived graph interaction has supplied g_N=\kappa D_N, D_N=\binom{N+d}{d}. Applying (15) to its normalized spatial branches gives \begin{aligned} \omega_N&=\kappa D_NA_N-4\kappa^3D_N^3C_N+O(\kappa^5),\\ E_N&=\frac{\kappa D_NA_N}{2}-\kappa^3D_N^3C_N+O(\kappa^5). \end{aligned} \tag{17} The remainder here is at each fixed band; uniform control across growing bands needs its own estimates. Even if A_N is common, the next term requires control of D_N^2C_N. A common bare \kappa is insufficient to establish a common physical mass coefficient after spatial response. As a strictly specified control, take the same spatial branch family at two coefficients g_i=\kappa D_i, so A,C are identical. Then \begin{aligned} \frac{\omega_2/\omega_1}{D_2/D_1} &=1-4\frac CA\kappa^2(D_2^2-D_1^2)+O(\kappa^4),\\ \frac{E_2/E_1}{D_2/D_1} &=1-2\frac CA\kappa^2(D_2^2-D_1^2)+O(\kappa^4). \end{aligned} \tag{18} For the committed six-dimensional counts D_1=S(13,6)=18564 and D_2=S(35,6)=3838380, the coefficient ratio is 3515/17. The diagnostic holds the control action fixed and verifies both corrections in (18) without adjusting either coefficient separately. This control does not identify its fields with the physical electron and muon. Their actual band-dependent profiles, normalization and master interaction remain to be obtained. It neither changes the committed mode selections nor tests alternative particle dimensionalities. An independent six-dimensional spatial comparison The specified spatial CP3 branch provides an independent differential-equation test of the reduction. CP3 here is the candidate actual six-dimensional spatial topology with an undetermined metric radius, not compactified auxiliary dimensions. Its section degree L is not the cumulative mass-band label N. For local contact at L=1, the exact spatial coefficients are A=\frac85,\qquad a=\frac4{125},\qquad b=\frac{48}{875}, \qquad C=\frac{464}{4375}. \tag{19} Equation (15) recovers the existing cubic frequency -1856g^3/4375. The new calculation also reproduces the reduced action, the induced norm and the normalized energy. Direct complex complementary solves agree with the independent real spatial continuation, and increased Jacobi cutoffs preserve the coefficients. At L=0 the constant source has \eta=0 and gives the exact linear branch, as (16) predicts. The known local-contact instability at positive L remains present. Correctly deriving its effective frequency does not turn that branch into a viable electron. The spatial source-preservation theorem classifies the vanishing condition (16) for the specified holomorphic CP3 zero modes. It requires a constant scalar potential; a covariant kernel satisfying it also loses shape selection within that band. The theorem includes a full nonlinear stability result for the mean kernel and bounds on a finite screened-response correction. The scalar gap comparison examines a different mechanism: generating a scalar coefficient by summing occupied kinetic modes of the same field. It derives the complete collective response and tests whether the cumulative count survives at a fixed canonical norm. Its global kernel is specified independently of the occupied-graph prescription used in (17). Verification nonlinear_mass_reduction_checks.py independently solves the nonlinear complementary and normalized equations. It checks complex source derivatives, the complete real Schur Hessian, retained spaces with one to three complex modes, common-frame covariance, the exact frequency derivative (6), fourth- and fifth-order remainders, the independent norm identity dE/dQ=\omega, and the common-coefficient comparison (18). Physical six-dimensional checks use both chiral radial components at section degrees 0,1,3,6, three specified scalar kernels, and two spatial cutoffs. These finite checks support the displayed conditional derivation; they do not supply the missing master kernel.

title: Frequency accounting for scalar Born response
summary: Complete scalar vertices remove the negative-frequency resonant Born channel for positive incoming waves, while a finite-time positive preparation can retain a nonresonant response; the distinction follows from spatial momentum, frequency and both angular contractions.
text:
Summary: Complete scalar vertices remove the negative-frequency resonant Born channel for positive incoming waves, while a finite-time positive preparation can retain a nonresonant response; the distinction follows from spatial momentum, frequency and both angular contractions. Positive incoming bands and the complete cubic source Consider the specified local scalar equation on \mathbb R^D, D\ge2, i\partial_t\Psi=H(-i
abla)\Psi +g(\Psi^\dagger eta\Psi) eta\Psi, \quad H(p)=\alpha\cdot p+m eta, \quad E_p=\sqrt{|p|^2+m^2},\quad m\ge0. 	ag{1} The matrices retain the complete spatial Clifford module, as in the positive-frequency scalar vertex. Its minimal complex size is n=2^{\lfloor(D+1)/2floor}. The spatial directions are ordinary physical coordinates. A specified free mass coefficient m is an input to this comparison. The signed projectors are P_\pm(p)= rac12\left(I\pm rac{H(p)}{E_p}ight). 	ag{2} For m=0, the single point p=0 has no defined signed band and is excluded where a projector is used. It has zero continuum measure. Let the complete incoming Fourier spinor satisfy A(p)=P_+(p)A(p), so the free field is \Psi_0(x,t)=\int rac{d^Dp}{(2\pi)^{D/2}} A(p)e^{ip\cdot x-iE_pt}. 	ag{3} The negative-frequency projection is a spectral component of this classical field. Its physical particle interpretation remains open; it is not assigned an antiparticle meaning or a sign of electric charge. The full negative-output Born coefficient Build the local scalar before projecting the cubic source. At output momentum k, put p=q+r-k,\qquad V(k;q,r)=P_-(k) eta A(r) \left[A(p)^\dagger eta A(q)ight], \qquad \delta=E_q+E_r+E_k-E_p. 	ag{4} The first Born term in the interaction picture over a time interval I is  oxed{\mathcal B^-_I(k) =- rac{ig}{(2\pi)^D} \int d^Dq\,d^Dr\,V(k;q,r) \int_I e^{-i\delta t}\,dt.} 	ag{5} The conjugated slot contributes e^{-ip\cdot x+iE_pt}; the two unconjugated slots contribute e^{i(q+r)\cdot x-i(E_q+E_r)t}. Integration over both q,r retains both coherent permutations. Treating only one selected scalar contraction as the whole source would omit terms. Formula (5) is an explicitly computed cubic response of the same field. It introduces no independent response particle or interaction coefficient. It is not a quantum-fermion scattering matrix. The massive resonance cannot close Write w=-k, so p=q+r+w. For m>0, convexity of the relativistic energy gives E_q+E_r+E_w\ge 3\sqrt{|p/3|^2+m^2}=\sqrt{|p|^2+9m^2}. 	ag{6} Equality occurs at q=r=w=p/3. Therefore  oxed{\delta\ge \sqrt{|p|^2+9m^2}-\sqrt{|p|^2+m^2}>0.} 	ag{7} There is no negative-output on-shell cubic resonance among three positive incoming free-frequency factors with this common mass. This is a kinematic statement about the signed source equation, not a statement that its finite-time forcing is zero. The massless resonance has two vanishing scalar contractions For m=0, let a=|q|, b=|r|, c=|w|, A_0=a+b+c, and P=|p|. Then \delta=A_0-P\ge0 by the triangle inequality. For nonzero q,r,w, equality requires all three to point in the same direction as p. The complete scalar projector norms are  egin{aligned} \|P_+(p) eta P_+(q)\|_{m op} &=\sin rac{	heta_{pq}}2,\ \|P_-(k) eta P_+(r)\|_{m op} &=\sin rac{	heta_{wr}}2. \end{aligned} 	ag{8} The first is the established positive-band half-angle identity. For the second, conjugating P_-(k) by  eta and compressing to P_+(r) gives squared singular strength (1+\widehat k\cdot\widehat r)/2 =(1-\widehat w\cdot\widehat r)/2. Both contractions vanish on the massless resonant geometry. The statement retains every polarization and is independent of a special depth-five assignment. A bound through the collinear limit A zero of the numerator alone is insufficient to handle a small frequency denominator. Here its cancellation is quantitative. For p,q,r,w
e0,  egin{aligned} \delta&=\sum_{j=q,r,w}|j| \left(1-\widehat p\cdot\widehat jight),\ (A_0+P)\delta&=4\left[ ab\sin^2 rac{	heta_{qr}}2 +ac\sin^2 rac{	heta_{qw}}2 +bc\sin^2 rac{	heta_{rw}}2ight]. \end{aligned} 	ag{9} The first identity follows by taking the scalar product of p=q+r+w with \widehat p; the second follows by expanding A_0^2-|q+r+w|^2. All terms on their right are nonnegative. Thus \sin rac{	heta_{pq}}2\le\sqrt{ rac{\delta}{2a}}, \qquad \sin rac{	heta_{wr}}2\le \sqrt{ rac{(A_0+P)\delta}{4bc}}. 	ag{10} Combining both complete vertices yields  oxed{ rac{\|V(k;q,r)\|}{\delta} \le\sqrt{ rac{A_0+P}{8abc}} \|A(p)\|\,\|A(q)\|\,\|A(r)\|.} 	ag{11} This bound holds off resonance and remains bounded as the nonzero momenta become collinear. It does not discard the output infrared dependence c^{-1/2}. For a finite time window, |\int_0^T e^{-i\delta t}dt|\le2/\delta; (11) consequently controls the full nonresonant source contribution without a secular collinear pole. A localized Born scattering limit For a precise continuum statement, assume A\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^D\setminus\{0\};\mathbb C^n), A=P_+A, with momentum support 0<\kappa\le|p|\le\Lambda. This describes smooth spatially decaying free fields, rather than isolated plane waves or a finite periodic regulator. For the symmetric interval I=[-T,T], (5) contains 2\sin(T\delta)/\delta. In the massless case, (11) makes V/\delta integrable over the compact q,r support for every fixed k
e0. Values on its measure-zero resonant set can be assigned arbitrarily for this integral. The phase gradient is 
abla_{q,r}\delta= (\widehat q-\widehat p,\widehat r-\widehat p). 	ag{12} Its critical set requires q,r,p to be collinear with the fixed w=-k, a measure-zero set when D\ge2. Away from that set, a local change to the phase as one coordinate gives an integrable phase density. The Riemann–Lebesgue lemma then makes its oscillatory integral tend to zero for every nonzero output k. The output is supported in |k|\le3\Lambda, and (11) also supplies a uniform bound proportional to |k|^{-1/2}. Its square is locally integrable at zero for D\ge2, since the radial integral is proportional to \int_0^{3\Lambda}ho^{D-2}dho. Dominated convergence therefore gives  oxed{\lim_{T	o\infty}\|\mathcal B^-_{[-T,T]}\|_{L^2_k}=0.} 	ag{13} For m>0, the uniform gap (7) on the bounded incoming support makes the quotient bounded. The phase gradient is (q/E_q-p/E_p,r/E_r-p/E_p); its critical set at fixed k is the single possible point p=q=r=k. The same argument gives (13). This proof uses the integrable oscillatory coefficient directly; it does not treat a delta function of the degenerate massless resonance as an ordinary regular hypersurface measure. Equation (13) concerns the explicit Born term. Interpreting it as the derivative of a complete nonlinear incoming-to-outgoing map additionally requires that map and its differentiability. A finite-time positive preparation is different For I=[0,T], \int_0^T e^{-i\delta t}dt = rac{1-e^{-i\delta T}}{i\delta}. 	ag{14} Under the same localized assumptions, the oscillatory part vanishes after momentum integration as T	o\infty, but the constant part can leave  oxed{\mathcal B^-_{[0,\infty)}(k) =- rac{g}{(2\pi)^D} \int d^Dq\,d^Dr\, rac{V(k;q,r)}{\delta}.} 	ag{15} For a concrete nonzero source, in two dimensions take \alpha=(\sigma_x,\sigma_y),  eta=\sigma_z and unit positive spinors \xi_j=(1,e^{i	heta_j})^T/\sqrt2 along the momenta p=(0,2), q=(2,1), r=(-1,2). At k=(1,1) the two coherent permutations have a combined negative-output norm approximately 0.199709, with \delta=2\sqrt5+\sqrt2-2. Narrow smooth momentum bumps around these separated carriers preserve a nonzero contribution to (15) by continuity; the other generated momenta are distinct. The isolated plane waves themselves are only source controls and do not have the localized scattering limit (13). This is a nonresonant correction associated with the finite initial preparation. Its existence is compatible with (13). The localized encounter simulations prepare positive free-frequency packets at a finite time; their tails already overlap. Positive preparation therefore does not justify deleting subsequently generated negative-frequency components or assigning their norm a higher perturbative order without further work. The initial-data prescription also matters for the retarded local response about its specified background; that separate spectrum is not the free spectrum used above. Verification and mathematical context scalar_born_response.py implements the full projectors, cubic vertex, stable angular detuning and both time-window kernels. scalar_born_checks.py runs 1,205 checks of full Clifford modules at every spatial dimension from two through ten, including nearly collinear bands and both massive and massless detuning identities. An independent spatial Fourier extraction retains both coherent permutations. Direct forced evolution of the complete signed Dirac mode verifies its nonzero finite-time response and its normalization. Common physical rotations preserve the full vector source. The broader nonlinear theory already exploits related scalar null structure. Bournaveas and Candy, Theorem 1.1 prove small-data global existence and scattering for the massless cubic Soler and Thirring equations at the critical homogeneous Sobolev regularity in two and three spatial dimensions. Their Remark 1.4 explains the inhomogeneous version using conserved L^2 norm. That theorem is not a global-existence claim for the higher-dimensional finite-amplitude preparations considered here. These frequency restrictions constrain a specified classical scalar term. They supply no charge assignment, bound-particle identification, or observed coupling rate. The conserved spatial charge question remains a separate physical requirement.

title: Time ordering of spatial compatibility
summary: The leading change of the prescribed spatial contact is a Poisson bracket with the second time-ordered source generator, identifying a reciprocal feedback contribution that a single integrated overlap omits.
text:
Summary: The leading change of the prescribed spatial contact is a Poisson bracket with the second time-ordered source generator, identifying a reciprocal feedback contribution that a single integrated overlap omits. Keep the full spatial Hamiltonian at each stage The localized compatibility functional compares the same free encounter for the incoming field and the fully evolved outgoing field after removing known free propagation. Its leading scattering variation preserves that functional. The next term can be derived from the same scalar source without adding an alignment rule. Use the local scalar Dirac equation, i\partial_t\Psi=D\Psi+g(\Psi^\dagger eta\Psi) eta\Psi, \qquad U(t)=e^{-iDt},\qquad \psi_I(t)=U(-t)\Psi(t). 	ag{1} For a canonical field argument \psi, define \chi_t=U(t)\psi,\quad \sigma_t=\chi_t^\dagger eta\chi_t, \qquad h_t[\psi]= rac12\int\sigma_t^2\,d^Dx. 	ag{2} These are full spatial functionals; both complex patterns enter the same local scalar. The interaction-picture equation is Hamiltonian with g h_t. Its explicit time dependence comes from the free spatial operator, even though (1) is autonomous. Use the positive spatial inner product and gradient convention \delta F=2\operatorname{Re}\langle
abla_*F,\delta\psiangle. The canonical Poisson bracket is  oxed{\{F,G\}=2\operatorname{Im} \langle
abla_*F,
abla_*Gangle,\qquad \dot F=\{F,G\}\quad\hbox{when }\dot\psi=-i
abla_*G.} 	ag{3} All formulas below are finite-order, fixed-duration expansions where regular solutions depend smoothly on g. They hold directly in a finite canonical spatial regulator. A continuum use additionally needs sufficient regularity and control of the displayed derivatives and integrals; no convergence of an infinite Magnus series is asserted. The first two source generators Let T>0 be fixed. Define  oxed{ K_1=\int_0^T h_t\,dt= rac12\mathcal C_T, \qquad K_2= rac12\int_0^Tdt\int_0^t ds\,\{h_t,h_s\}. } 	ag{4} For any sufficiently differentiable real functional F, the complete interaction-picture map gives  egin{aligned} F[\psi_I(T)]={}&F[\psi_I(0)]+g\{F,K_1\}\ &+g^2\left(\{F,K_2\} + rac12\{\{F,K_1\},K_1\}ight)+O(g^3), \end{aligned} 	ag{5} with the brackets on the right evaluated at the incoming field. For the sign convention, write L_G F=\{F,G\}. Two stages, h_s first and h_t second, pull back observables in the order e^{gL_{h_s}}e^{gL_{h_t}}. The Jacobi identity gives [L_{h_s},L_{h_t}]=L_{\{h_t,h_s\}}. Expanding that ordered product through second order yields (4)–(5). Integrating over all ordered pairs gives the displayed time triangle. This is the Hamiltonian form of the standard chronological expansion; see Blanes, Casas, Oteo and Ros, section 3.4.1. Taking F=\mathcal C_T=2K_1 eliminates both the first-order term and the repeated first-generator bracket:  oxed{\Delta\mathcal C_T =g^2\{\mathcal C_T,K_2\}[\psi_{m in}]+O(g^3).} 	ag{6} Thus the first contact change is controlled by how the full spatial Hamiltonians at different encounter stages fail to commute. The integral of their separate contact strengths is insufficient to determine it. The sign of (6) is not fixed by the nonnegativity of \mathcal C_T. If \{h_t,h_s\}=0 as functionals for every pair of stages on the relevant domain, then \{\mathcal C_T,h_t\}=0 and the full interaction-picture evolution conserves \mathcal C_T exactly. By contrast, a zero numerical value of K_2 at one incoming field does not ensure a zero gradient or a zero bracket in (6). The coefficient retains both complete complex variations The full source gradient and its real-linear derivative are  egin{aligned} f_t=
abla_*h_t &=U(-t)[\sigma_t eta\chi_t],\ H_t\eta=(\mathrm d f_t)_\psi[\eta] &=U(-t)\left[ 2\operatorname{Re}(\chi_t^\dagger eta U(t)\eta)\, eta\chi_t +\sigma_t eta U(t)\etaight]. \end{aligned} 	ag{7} The inner product inside the real part in (7) is pointwise; the outer source remains a complete spatial field. In a Galerkin implementation, the local product is followed by the same orthogonal spatial projection as the original energy variation. Since H_t is symmetric for the real canonical inner product,  egin{aligned} K_2&=\int_0^Tdt\int_0^t ds\, \operatorname{Im}\langle f_t,f_sangle,\ 
abla_*K_2 &= rac12\int_0^Tdt\int_0^t ds\, \left[H_t(-if_s)+H_s(if_t)ight]. \end{aligned} 	ag{8} For example, varying the integrand of \{h_t,h_s\} gives 2\operatorname{Im}(\langle H_t\eta,f_sangle+ \langle f_t,H_s\etaangle); moving the two real-symmetric Hessians to the other slot gives (8). With F_1=\int_0^T f_tdt, the coefficient in (6) is  oxed{\{\mathcal C_T,K_2\} =4\operatorname{Im}\langle F_1,
abla_*K_2angle.} 	ag{9} Dropping the conjugate-dependent part of (7), holding one pattern fixed, or replacing its local scalar by an average would change (8)–(9). No independent coefficient has been introduced: g is still the single scalar coefficient of (1). An independent full-field expansion Iterating the interaction-picture differential equation directly gives \psi_I(T)=\psi_{m in}-igF_1+g^2 B_2+O(g^3), \quad B_2=-i\int_0^Tdt\int_0^t ds\,H_t(-if_s). 	ag{10} The generator formula instead gives B_2=-i
abla_*K_2- rac{i}{2} \int_0^T H_t(-iF_1)dt. 	ag{11} Splitting the square time integral in (11) into its two triangles and using (8) reproduces (10). This provides a check on the source ordering and the factors of two, without interpreting the generator as a new physical field. Reversing the prescribed sequence h_t\mapsto h_{T-t} leaves K_1 unchanged and sends K_2\mapsto-K_2. It therefore reverses the coefficient (6). This is a control on a sequence of Hamiltonians, not a claim that freely departing spatial packets reverse themselves or naturally repeat an encounter. Compute the coefficient by direct coupling variations The same coefficient can be calculated without the double time integral. Expand the physical field at fixed preparation as \Psi_g=\chi+g a+g^2 b+O(g^3), with \chi=U(t)\psi_{m in}. Writing N(\chi)=(\chi^\dagger eta\chi) eta\chi, direct variation of the complete spatial equation gives  egin{aligned} i\partial_t a&=Da+N(\chi),&a(0)&=0,\ i\partial_t b&=Db+(\mathrm dN)_\chi[a],&b(0)&=0. \end{aligned} 	ag{12} The source derivative is the full real-linear expression in (7), before conjugation by the free propagators. It includes the response of both spatial patterns. In the interaction picture, a_I(T)=-iF_1 and b_I(T)=B_2. Let \mathcal H_C=2\int_0^T H_tdt be the real Hessian of the prescribed contact. Taylor expansion of that same functional gives  oxed{c_2=2\operatorname{Re}\langle
abla_*\mathcal C_T,b_I(T)angle +\operatorname{Re}\langle a_I(T),\mathcal H_C a_I(T)angle, \qquad \Delta\mathcal C_T=g^2 c_2+O(g^3).} 	ag{13} Equations (6) and (13) give the same coefficient using different calculations. The direct method integrates two inhomogeneous spatial variations and one single time quadrature. It does not fit a coefficient to completed nonlinear collisions. spatial_packet_variations.py implements (12)–(13), with timestamped results and optional variation fields. Its local Hessian differentiates every quadrature component of the original scalar energy. spatial_packet_variation_checks.py runs 28 checks, including independent cubic polarization, scalar energy variation, both norm coefficients, comparison with the ordered generator and full nonlinear evolution. The same checks include positive renormalization of both complete outgoing patterns. Verification and physical scope packet_time_order.py evaluates the two generators and both full-field expressions using the normalized axial spatial equation. For its homogeneous cubic source, the Hessian also has the exact polarization identity H_t\eta= rac{f_t(\psi+\eta)-f_t(\psi-\eta)}2-f_t(\eta). 	ag{14} packet_time_order_checks.py runs 50 checks. It checks (14) by independent directional differentiation, verifies real Hessian symmetry and the scalar variation of K_2, refines the time quadrature and checks source-order reversal. Complete nonlinear spatial evolution at dimensions three and five approaches (10) with cubic field error and approaches the contact coefficient (9) under small-coupling refinement. A frozen-transport control conserves the same contact under its full spatial nonlinear source. The result explains a conditional feedback contribution in the stated comparison protocol. It does not select occupied bound-particle patterns, fix their physical sizes, assign observed interaction channels, or imply a universal tendency toward improved compatibility.

title: Localized scalar wave encounters
summary: Complete three-dimensional packet evolution retains phase-sensitive reciprocal transfer beyond a plane-wave truncation, with a continuum reflection law and independent spatial, temporal and boundary refinements.
text: Summary: Complete three-dimensional packet evolution retains phase-sensitive reciprocal transfer beyond a plane-wave truncation, with a continuum reflection law and independent spatial, temporal and boundary refinements. From a resonant contraction to the full spatial equation The resonant quartet calculation identifies a coherent channel through which two complex spatial patterns can exchange positive canonical norm. The full local scalar equation also generates momenta outside that quartet. A localized preparation further contains a continuum of directions and frequencies. Here evolve all four complex components on all three ordinary coordinates: i\partial_t\Psi=-i\alpha\cdot\nabla\Psi +g(\Psi^\dagger\beta\Psi)\beta\Psi, \quad \alpha_j=\operatorname{diag}(\sigma_j,-\sigma_j), \quad \beta=\begin{pmatrix}0&I_2\\I_2&0\end{pmatrix}. \tag{1} The \sigma_j in the matrix definition are Pauli matrices. Write \Psi=(u,v)^T and c=u^\dagger v. The scalar current is \sigma=2\operatorname{Re}c. The full positive-frequency vertex gives Q_u=\int u^\dagger u\,d^3x,\qquad Q_v=\int v^\dagger v\,d^3x,\qquad \dot Q_u=2g\operatorname{Im}\int c^2d^3x=-\dot Q_v. \tag{2} The two blocks are components of the same classical field. Their norms are not electric charges or identified particle counts. These are unbound spatial wave controls; no bound elementary pair has been selected. A precise four-packet preparation For a center x_0, carrier p, width w and constant four-component seed \xi, define a canonically normalized packet by \widehat R(k;p,x_0,w,\xi)=\mathcal N P_+(k)\xi\, e^{-w^2|k-p|^2/2-ik\cdot x_0}, \qquad P_+(k)=\frac12\left(I+\frac{\alpha\cdot k}{|k|}\right). \tag{3} Choose \mathcal N>0 so its full spatial norm is one. The continuum zero-momentum point has measure zero; the numerical preparation sets that grid coefficient to zero. Positive-frequency projection is applied once at preparation. Evolution under (1) retains every subsequently generated component. Frequency sign is not assigned an antiparticle interpretation. Put e_p=e_z, e_q=(\sin\theta,0,\cos\theta), and s=\sin(\theta/2), c_\theta=\cos(\theta/2). The incident seeds are u_+=(1,0,0,0)^T,\quad u_-=(0,1,0,0)^T, \quad v_+=(0,0,-s,c_\theta)^T, \quad v_-=(0,0,c_\theta,s)^T. \tag{4} With w=2 and carrier magnitude 2, define \begin{aligned} u_0&=\frac{R(2e_p,-4e_p,2,u_+)+R(-2e_p,4e_p,2,u_-)}{\sqrt2},\\ v_0&=\frac{e^{i\varphi}}{\sqrt2} \left[R(2e_q,-4e_q,2,v_+)+R(-2e_q,4e_q,2,v_-)\right],\\ \Psi(0)&=u_0/\|u_0\|+v_0/\|v_0\|. \end{aligned} \tag{5} There are four localized incoming packets organized into two complete complex chiral patterns, each of norm one. Both patterns propagate, diffract and respond. Here \varphi is a global phase of the entire second pattern. This differs from the main-mode phase in the textured five-dimensional compatibility preparation. Why opposite phases reverse the transfer There is an exact continuum symmetry of (1) and (5). Let n=\frac{e_p-e_q}{|e_p-e_q|}=(-c_\theta,0,s),\qquad O=I_3-2nn^T,\qquad U=-i\,\sigma\cdot n,\qquad S=\beta\operatorname{diag}(U,U). \tag{6} The ordinary spatial reflection O exchanges e_p and e_q. Its spinor lift satisfies S\alpha_jS^\dagger=\sum_kO_{kj}\alpha_k, \qquad S\beta S^\dagger=\beta. \tag{7} Thus \Psi(x,t)\mapsto S\Psi(O^{-1}x,t) preserves the entire kinetic operator and the nonlinear scalar source, while exchanging the two chiral blocks. The isotropic Gaussian and complete projector in (3) transform covariantly. Directly, Su_\pm=i v_\pm,\qquad Sv_\pm=i u_\pm, \qquad S\Psi_\varphi(O^{-1}x,0)=i e^{i\varphi}\Psi_{-\varphi}(x,0). \tag{8} Uniqueness on any interval of regular evolution and the constant phase symmetry of (1) therefore imply \boxed{Q_u(-\varphi,t)=Q_v(\varphi,t),\qquad \Delta Q_u(-\varphi,t)=-\Delta Q_u(\varphi,t).} \tag{9} The second identity uses initial norms one and total norm two. It holds for the full continuum evolution, including generated modes. It is not limited to the four-mode resonant approximation. An oblique reflection does not preserve a finite periodic cube; exact finite-grid oddness is consequently not the numerical requirement. Refinement must recover the continuum comparison. Localized transfer and its numerical scale At fixed g=2, T=10 and \cos\theta=0.6, full evolution gives \Delta Q_u\simeq+0.01770 for \varphi=+\pi/4 and the opposite sign for -\pi/4. Thus about 1.77\% of the initial first-block norm is transferred, with equal and opposite change of the second. These are specified model units, not a measured conversion probability. The two nonzero traces use the same N=80, \delta t=0.04 grid. The right-angle trace uses N=64 at the same step. Recorded numerical data, the vector figure and plotting code retain the preparations and numerical quantities used in the display. The numerical operator uses an exact free Fourier propagator and an exact local reaction, \Psi\longmapsto \cos(g\sigma\,\delta t)\Psi -i\sin(g\sigma\,\delta t)\beta\Psi, \tag{10} in symmetric Strang splitting. The reaction keeps its own pointwise scalar and positive density fixed; the spatial step changes the pattern. The box [-L,L]^3 is storage for a localized-field approximation, not physical compactification. Positive-frequency packets have tails, so exact compact support or a strictly zero boundary signal is not assumed. Points per axis N L Step \delta t \Delta Q_u, phase +\pi/4 Maximum energy drift 64 16 0.04 0.01769528052 7.95\times10^{-7} 80 16 0.04 0.01770118605 8.04\times10^{-7} 96 16 0.04 0.01770118604 8.04\times10^{-7} 80 16 0.02 0.01770168036 2.01\times10^{-7} 100 20 0.04 0.01770118606 8.04\times10^{-7} Time-step halving reduces the energy error by approximately four, as expected for this splitting. Spatial refinement from 80 to 96 changes the transfer by about 10^{-11}; the remaining time error is larger. Reporting many numerical digits here exposes convergence, not physical precision. The full complex fields also converge. Fourier interpolation from 80 to 96 points changes the final field by 1.83\times10^{-7} in positive L^2 norm. Halving the time step changes it by 2.28\times10^{-6}. At the same spacing, increasing L from 16 to 20 changes the nonlinear response in the common central cube by 2.84\times10^{-6}; the larger total-field difference, about 3.84\times10^{-5}, includes the changed initial and free tails. At N=80, changing only the phase gives \Delta Q_u=-0.01770118590, within 1.6\times10^{-10} of the opposite-phase magnitude. At N=64 and right angles, the transfer stays below 3.2\times10^{-10} over the encounter, while the full field still differs from its free control by about 0.0369 in positive L^2 norm. This is a numerical control for the one-polarization transfer node. It does not establish an exact right-angle theorem for all localized continuum data, and it is not zero interaction. Independent spatial control A simpler head-on preparation contains one packet in each chiral pattern, with carriers \pm2e_z, centers \mp4e_z, width two and unit norms. At the same g=2, T=10, its full field differs from free evolution by approximately 0.05013, with only about 7\times10^{-10} chiral norm transfer in the stated refinement. There is phase and spatial deformation without a large norm exchange. The independently derived axial spatial equation reconstructs this same three-dimensional field using radial Laguerre modes and axial Fourier modes. Its refined nonlinear response agrees with the Cartesian N=96, \delta t=0.04 response to about 3.2\times10^{-6} in full positive L^2 norm. Comparing the response means comparing \Psi_g(T)-U(T)\Psi(0); the total fields have larger differences from their initial and freely propagated tails. This cross-check uses two different spatial discretizations of the same complete equation. Reproduction and scope scalar_packet_collision_checks.py constructs (5), evolves all spatial components through scalar_wave_packets.py, and records both chiral norms, full field changes, energy and momentum. For the positive-phase preparation: OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS=1 OMP_NUM_THREADS=1 MKL_NUM_THREADS=1 \ python experiments/scalar_packet_collision_checks.py \ --packet-size 80 --quartet-cosine .6 --phase .7853981633974483 \ --step .04 --output-dir experiments/results --save-fields Change the phase sign for the reciprocal comparison, or set --quartet-cosine 0 for the right-angle control. Without --packet-size, the diagnostic runs 101 checks, including independent full spatial ODE integration, energy variation, time convergence and the complete reflection identities (7)–(8). Reports and optional field archives have timestamped filenames. The calculation confirms a permitted spatial mechanism of the specified scalar term beyond plane-wave truncation. Bound particle shapes, their common physical normalization, their nested-sector channel maps and their measured interaction rates remain to be derived.

title: Changing compatibility of localized spatial packets
summary: A prescribed free-encounter functional separates reciprocal spatial deformation from free motion; the same local scalar dynamics can increase or decrease it for fully localized complex preparations, with its first change beginning beyond the leading scattering variation.

title: Resonant scalar wave quartets
summary: Four positive-frequency spatial waves permit reciprocal scalar norm transfer; the exact coherent contraction and its sharp bound depend on complete polarization vectors, with a right-angle cancellation restricted to one polarization per chiral band.
text: Summary: Four positive-frequency spatial waves permit reciprocal scalar norm transfer; the exact coherent contraction and its sharp bound depend on complete polarization vectors, with a right-angle cancellation restricted to one polarization per chiral band. Positive incoming frequencies do not forbid all reciprocal transfer The local scalar equation is i\partial_t\Psi=-i\alpha\cdot\nabla\Psi+g(\Psi^\dagger\beta\Psi)\beta\Psi. \tag{1} For two opposite complete kinetic chiralities, write \Psi=(\Psi_u,\Psi_v)^T and \zeta=\Psi_u^\dagger\Psi_v in the block convention \beta=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&I\\I&0\end{smallmatrix}\right). The full scalar vertex gives \sigma=2\operatorname{Re}\zeta, \qquad \dot Q_u=2g\operatorname{Im}\int\zeta^2dx, \qquad \dot Q_v=-\dot Q_u. \tag{2} Strictly positive free frequency removes a particular conjugate contribution for the one-axis traveling pulse class. That argument uses its momentum support. It does not establish a universal prohibition for several incoming directions. Here all four incoming waves have the same positive free frequency k_0>0. Their momenta are p,-p in one chiral block and q,-q in the other, with |p|=|q|=k_0,\qquad p=k_0 e_z,\qquad q=k_0(\sin\theta\,e_x+\cos\theta\,e_z), \quad 0<\theta<\pi. \tag{3} Thus the opposite pairs have equal total momentum and frequency. The physical coordinates are ordinary spatial directions of the same containing space. These plane waves are unbound controls; their amplitudes below are densities per spatial volume. A finite box can regulate a commensurate example without assigning physical compactification. The amplitudes are classical complex field coefficients. This calculation is not an antisymmetrized quantum-fermion scattering matrix or an observed particle reaction rate. Retain every polarization in each occupied chiral band Let the total spatial dimension be odd, D\ge3, and use \alpha_j=\operatorname{diag}(\Gamma_j,-\Gamma_j). Choose a complete basis W_+ of the +1 eigenspace of \Gamma_z, and set W_-=\Gamma_xW_+. Each has P=2^{(D-3)/2} \tag{4} columns. Both are actual spinor frames, not additional spatial coordinates. Put s=\sin(\theta/2) and c=\cos(\theta/2). The two fields are \begin{aligned} \Psi_u&=e^{-ik_0t} \left(W_+A_+e^{ip\cdot x}+W_-A_-e^{-ip\cdot x}\right),\\ \Psi_v&=e^{-ik_0t} \left[(-sW_++cW_-)B_+e^{iq\cdot x} +(cW_++sW_-)B_-e^{-iq\cdot x}\right], \end{aligned} \tag{5} where all four A_\pm,B_\pm\in\mathbb C^P are unrestricted complex polarization vectors. The lower block's minus sign in its kinetic operator is essential: the displayed frames at q and -q are its positive-frequency states. No negative-frequency incident wave has been inserted. Define the complete overlap matrix G_{st}=A_s^\dagger B_t,\qquad s,t\in\{+,-\}. \tag{6} The cross scalar retains four spatial phases, with coefficients -sG_{++},cG_{+-},cG_{-+},sG_{--} at momenta q-p,-q-p,q+p,-q+p, respectively. Under a common physical rotation, both momenta and all frames rotate together and leave this contraction unchanged. The exact spatial quartic mean Let brackets denote the spatial mean over these noncollinear plane phases, or over a compatible Fourier regulator. Put a=s^2, b=c^2. Orthogonality of distinct spatial Fourier phases gives \begin{aligned} \langle|\zeta|^2\rangle &=a(|G_{++}|^2+|G_{--}|^2) +b(|G_{+-}|^2+|G_{-+}|^2),\\ \boxed{\langle\zeta^2\rangle=2\mathcal T,\qquad \mathcal T=-aG_{++}G_{--}+bG_{+-}G_{-+}.} \end{aligned} \tag{7} The second line survives because opposite incoming pairs have the same total momentum and frequency. It is a coherent product, not a sum of squared channel counts. The full interaction energy density is \boxed{\mathcal H= \frac g2\langle\sigma^2\rangle =g\left[a(|G_{++}|^2+|G_{--}|^2) +b(|G_{+-}|^2+|G_{-+}|^2)+2\operatorname{Re}\mathcal T\right].} \tag{8} For g\ge0 this is nonnegative, as is clear from its original local square. The scalar mean itself vanishes at distinct p,q, but the local interaction and its quartic mean need not vanish. Replacing the current by its spatial mean before varying (1) would miss them. Both complete amplitude systems follow from one energy Use the canonical mean kinetic term and subtract the common carrier k_0. Define real matrices w=\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\b&a\end{pmatrix}, \qquad \kappa=\begin{pmatrix}-a&b\\b&-a\end{pmatrix}. \tag{9} The reciprocal gradients of (8) are \boxed{ \begin{aligned} i\dot A_s&=g\sum_t\left[ w_{st}B_tG_{st}^*+\kappa_{st}B_tG_{-s,-t}\right],\\ i\dot B_t&=g\sum_s\left[ w_{st}A_sG_{st}+\kappa_{st}A_sG_{-s,-t}^*\right]. \end{aligned}} \tag{10} In particular, with Q_u=\|A_+\|^2+\|A_-\|^2 and similarly Q_v, \boxed{\dot Q_u=4g\operatorname{Im}\mathcal T, \qquad \dot Q_v=-4g\operatorname{Im}\mathcal T.} \tag{11} These are norm densities for the plane-wave preparation. The imbalance \|A_+\|^2-\|A_-\|^2 is conserved, as is its B counterpart; the exchanged pairs carry zero net spatial momentum. The canonical total norm and the same energy (8) are conserved. Full complex polarization vectors continue evolving in (10). The exact local equation also generates spatial momenta \pm p\pm2q and \pm q\pm2p. At the initial common source frequency k_0, they are off the positive free-frequency shell for noncollinear p,q. Thus (10) is the first-order resonant projection, or the corresponding weak-interaction amplitude system after excluding those detuned modes. It is not an exact four-mode invariant subspace of (1). The smallest positive detuning is \Delta=k_0[\sqrt{5-4|\cos\theta|}-1]; the weak-mode separation requires |g|(Q_u+Q_v)\ll\Delta. As \theta approaches a collinear endpoint, the detuning can vanish; the distinct-mode reduction then needs reconsideration. A one-polarization cancellation and its precise limit For P=1 the two products in \mathcal T contain the same four scalar amplitudes. Therefore \mathcal T=\cos\theta\,A_+^*A_-^*B_+B_-. \tag{12} The transfer contribution vanishes at \theta=\pi/2 for all phases. The ordinary terms in (8) remain present. This is a zero in the pair norm-transfer channel, not zero interaction. For P\ge2, the products in (7) are independent. At right angles, \boxed{\langle\zeta^2\rangle=-\det G.} \tag{13} For example, at Q_u=Q_v=1, take A_+=\frac{e_1}{\sqrt2},\quad A_-=\frac{e_2}{\sqrt2},\quad B_+=e^{i\phi}\frac{e_1}{\sqrt2},\quad B_-=e^{i\phi}\frac{e_2}{\sqrt2}. \tag{14} Equations (11) and (13) give \boxed{\dot Q_u=-\frac g2\sin(2\phi).} \tag{15} Changing only \phi from \pi/4 to -\pi/4 reverses the transfer at the same positive coupling. The complete massless chiral band at D=5 already permits (14), as do higher odd dimensions. The cancellation at D=3 here uses its single positive-frequency polarization within each selected kinetic chirality; it is not a statement that physical three-dimensional particles have only one polarization. A sharp normalized bound For arbitrary complex vectors in the stated preparation, \boxed{ |\dot Q_u|\le |g|Q_uQ_v \begin{cases} |\cos\theta|,&P=1,\\[2pt] \dfrac{1+|\cos\theta|}{2},&P\ge2. \end{cases}} \tag{16} Both bounds are attained. For P=1, use |A_+A_-|\le Q_u/2 and |B_+B_-|\le Q_v/2 in (12), then choose the product's phase to be imaginary. For P\ge2, factor out the four vector norms. For unit vectors u,v in the B slots, the remaining bilinear contraction is governed by M=b\,vu^T-a\,uv^T. \tag{17} Its largest singular value is at most \max(a,b). To see this, a common unitary change of basis and a phase put u=e_1, v=re_1+\sqrt{1-r^2}e_2, 0\le r\le1. The nonzero block is M=\begin{pmatrix}(b-a)r&-a\sqrt{1-r^2}\\ b\sqrt{1-r^2}&0\end{pmatrix}. \tag{18} Assume b\ge a; the other case exchanges them. For M^\dagger M, its trace is a^2+b^2-2ab r^2\le2b^2, and \det(b^2I-M^\dagger M) =b^2a r^2[2(b-a)+a r^2]\ge0. \tag{19} Both eigenvalues are therefore at most b^2. It follows that |\mathcal T|\le\max(a,b)Q_uQ_v/4, giving (16). Orthogonal B polarizations and appropriately matched or swapped A polarizations attain the largest singular value; balanced norms and the appropriate overall phase attain the transfer bound. The maximum stops increasing once two polarization directions are available. Additional component counts do not multiply (16). Which bound a physical spatial pattern approaches depends on its occupied vectors, phases and geometry. Verification and physical scope scalar_quartet_checks.py runs 2,158 checks. It constructs the full Clifford waves at D=3,5,7,9, builds every Fourier coefficient of the local scalar and its nonlinear source, and compares the resulting energy and both resonant gradients with (7)–(10). It retains the other generated spatial modes and checks their detuning. Independent energy variations, complete vector evolution, norm transfer and preparations attaining both bounds check scalar_wave_quartets.py. This result demonstrates a permitted phase-sensitive channel of the specified scalar term. It does not assign electric charge, select bound particle geometries or derive observed weak rates. In particular, the neutrino control cannot be satisfied by asserting that five-dimensional polarization necessarily suppresses all interaction: the same full space permits the nonzero example (15). Localized scalar wave encounters evolve spatially finite preparations with the complete nonlinear equation, including the momenta omitted by the resonant projection. They retain phase-sensitive reciprocal transfer and an exact continuum reflection law.

title: Axial spatial Dirac packets
summary: An exact angular family retains complete complex polarization vectors and transverse localization in odd-dimensional scalar Dirac dynamics, with a variational radial and axial regulator for reciprocal packet encounters.
text:
Summary: An exact angular family retains complete complex polarization vectors and transverse localization in odd-dimensional scalar Dirac dynamics, with a variational radial and axial regulator for reciprocal packet encounters. An ordinary spatial family with explicit angular dependence Consider the same local scalar equation used by the positive-frequency vertices, now in odd ordinary spatial dimension D\ge3: i\partial_t\Psi=-i\alpha\cdot
abla\Psi+g\sigma eta\Psi, \qquad \sigma=\Psi^\dagger eta\Psi. 	ag{1} This is a specified flat-space scalar term. The following packets are unbound fields, not identified photons, neutrinos or leptons. Choosing a spatial symmetry of their preparation does not introduce compactified or internal dimensions. Write x=(x_\perp,z)\in\mathbb R^{D-1}	imes\mathbb R, r=|x_\perp|, and s=D-1. Let \Gamma_j be a minimal complex Clifford representation for the D spatial directions. Choose \alpha_j= egin{pmatrix}\Gamma_j&0\0&-\Gamma_j\end{pmatrix}, \qquad  eta= egin{pmatrix}0&I\I&0\end{pmatrix}, \qquad \Gamma_r=\sum_{j=1}^{s}\Gamma_j rac{x_j}{r}. 	ag{2} The two blocks are the opposite complete kinetic chiralities. Let W contain an entire orthonormal basis of the +1 eigenspace of \Gamma_z. Its dimension is P=2^{(D-3)/2}. Since \{\Gamma_z,\Gamma_r\}=0, W^\dagger W=I_P, \qquad W^\dagger\Gamma_r W=0, \qquad (\Gamma_r W)^\dagger\Gamma_r W=I_P. 	ag{3} At each nonzero transverse position, (W,\Gamma_r W) spans the complete chiral spinor space. Take the full spatial field  oxed{ \Psi_u=W F_u(t,r,z)+\Gamma_r W G_u(t,r,z),\qquad \Psi_v=W F_v(t,r,z)+\Gamma_r W G_v(t,r,z), } 	ag{4} where every F_b,G_b is a complex P-component vector. Their polarization can vary with radius and axial position. The retained angular dependence is the actual matrix \Gamma_r. This is a restricted angular family, not a representation of arbitrary angular textures. Its pointwise completeness does not remove that restriction on how different positions are related. For D=3, choose W=(1,0)^T. Equation (4) reads \Psi=(F_u,e^{i\varphi}G_u,F_v,e^{i\varphi}G_v)^T. 	ag{5} The axial angular structure is familiar from the three-dimensional Dirac separation described by Fillion-Gourdeau, Lorin and Bandrauk, section 2, after a constant change of spinor basis. The nonlinear closure and higher-dimensional formulas below follow directly from (1)–(4). For smooth Cartesian fields at the axis, F_b is smooth in r^2, and G_b=r times a function smooth in r^2. The full local equation closes exactly The scalar is independent of transverse angle, but retains the complete complex interference:  oxed{\sigma=2\operatorname{Re}(F_u^\dagger F_v+G_u^\dagger G_v).} 	ag{6} This expression follows from the complete field before any spatial integration. It is not a density average replacing its polarization. The Clifford derivative gives \Gamma_\perp\cdot
abla_\perp(WF)=\Gamma_r W\partial_rF, \qquad \Gamma_\perp\cdot
abla_\perp(\Gamma_r WG) =W\left(\partial_r+ rac{s-1}{r}ight)G. 	ag{7} Indeed, \sum_j\Gamma_j\partial_j\Gamma_r=(s-1)I/r. Together with \Gamma_zW=W and \Gamma_z\Gamma_rW=-\Gamma_rW, this yields  oxed{  egin{aligned} i\partial_tF_u&=-i\partial_zF_u -i\left(\partial_r+ rac{D-2}{r}ight)G_u+g\sigma F_v,\ i\partial_tG_u&=+i\partial_zG_u-i\partial_rF_u+g\sigma G_v,\ i\partial_tF_v&=+i\partial_zF_v +i\left(\partial_r+ rac{D-2}{r}ight)G_v+g\sigma F_u,\ i\partial_tG_v&=-i\partial_zG_v+i\partial_rF_v+g\sigma G_u. \end{aligned}} 	ag{8} Every source and derivative stays in (4). Thus any sufficiently regular solution of (8) reconstructs a solution of (1), with its full angular spinor factor. Both incoming patterns evolve. A common rotation of the physical coordinates, axis and spinor frame transports the same solution. Physical norm, source and conserved polarization Let S_{s-1}=2\pi^{s/2}/\Gamma(s/2) be the area of the unit transverse sphere. The physical volume element and positive norm are dV=S_{s-1}r^{s-1}dr\,dz, \qquad Q=\int dV\sum_{b=u,v}(F_b^\dagger F_b+G_b^\dagger G_b). 	ag{9} The energy is the full Dirac kinetic energy plus g\int\sigma^2dV/2. In particular, the radial derivative's adjoint in this norm is (\partial_r)^\dagger=-\partial_r- rac{s-1}{r}, 	ag{10} with the stated regularity and sufficient decay. Dropping the divergence term would change both the dynamics and norm. The reduced action is invariant under the same constant unitary transformation of all four polarization vectors. Consequently the entire Hermitian matrix  oxed{\mathcal P=\int dV\sum_{b=u,v} (F_bF_b^\dagger+G_bG_b^\dagger)} 	ag{11} is conserved. Its trace is Q. This is a symmetry of the specified angular family. It does not state that a local spatial overlap or either object's individual polarization matrix is fixed. Writing c=F_u^\dagger F_v+G_u^\dagger G_v gives the reciprocal law \dot Q_u=2g\operatorname{Im}\int c^2dV, \qquad \dot Q_v=-\dot Q_u. 	ag{12} A complete single-chirality field has \sigma=0 and evolves freely. Another exact control occurs when all F_u,G_u lie in a fixed polarization subspace orthogonal to the subspace containing F_v,G_v. Then c=0 pointwise and the free evolution preserves the mismatch. At P\ge2 this admits nonzero localized fields on both sides. It neither forces the occupied patterns into those subspaces nor makes five dimensions uniquely noninteracting. Spatially varying textures can span the whole polarization space. A finite regulator derived from the same local energy For numerical work, choose a radial scale w and retain N functions in each of the two radial families. Put x=r^2/w^2 and \alpha=s/2-1. Define  egin{aligned} \phi_n^0(r)&=A_n e^{-x/2}L_n^\alpha(x),& A_n^2&= rac{2n!}{S_{s-1}w^s\Gamma(n+s/2)},\ \phi_n^1(r)&=B_n\sqrt{x}e^{-x/2}L_n^{\alpha+1}(x),& B_n^2&= rac{2n!}{S_{s-1}w^s\Gamma(n+s/2+1)}. \end{aligned} 	ag{13} Each family is orthonormal in S_{s-1}r^{s-1}dr. This extends the independently normalized radial spatial Dirac basis. The exact derivative identity is \partial_r\phi_n^0=- rac1w \left[\sqrt{n+s/2}\,\phi_n^1+\sqrt n\,\phi_{n-1}^1ight]. 	ag{14} Let D_{mn} be that derivative matrix, with G rows and F columns. For axial Fourier momentum k, the upper chiral Galerkin operator is H_u(k)= egin{pmatrix}kI&iD^\dagger\-iD&-kI\end{pmatrix}, \qquad H_v(k)=-H_u(k). 	ag{15} It is self-adjoint in the canonical coefficient norm. The reverse derivative has a complementary radial component at the finite cutoff; convergence in N is required. The finite regulator is not an assertion that the continuum field occupies only these modes. If D=U\Lambda V^\dagger, transform F by V^\dagger and G by U^\dagger. Each free block has frequencies \pm\sqrt{k^2+\lambda_j^2}, supplying its exact propagator and positive-frequency projector. Applying that projector prepares an incoming field. The nonlinear evolution retains both free-frequency signs thereafter; neither is assigned an antiparticle interpretation. The local quartic has exact finite-basis radial quadrature. Write the polynomial parts of F,G as f,g, including \sqrt x in the G basis, so \sigma=e^{-x}\sigma_{m pol}. Changing variable to u=2x gives  oxed{ E_{m int}= rac g2 rac{S_{s-1}w^s}{2^{s/2+1}} \int dz\int_0^\infty du\,u^{s/2-1}e^{-u} \sigma_{m pol}(u/2,z)^2. } 	ag{16} Every quartic product contains an even number of G factors. The remaining integrand is polynomial in u, of degree at most 4N-2. A generalized Gauss–Laguerre rule of order 2N or higher therefore integrates (16) exactly in this retained radial space. The nonlinear coefficient source is its full complex derivative. The axis uses a finite Fourier interval as numerical storage for localized fields. For an even number N_z of retained complex modes, zero-padding to 2N_z before evaluating (16), followed by orthogonal projection of the source, integrates the quartic without Fourier aliasing. This preserves the finite action's axial translation symmetry and corresponding momentum. The interval and radial scale are numerical choices requiring convergence checks; they do not specify a physical compactification or the geometry of the observed three-dimensional space. Verification and limits axial_scalar_checks.py reconstructs the complete Cartesian spinor and differentiates it in every ordinary direction at D=3,5,7,9. It checks (6)–(8), physical rotation covariance, the normalized radial basis and its independent derivatives, full complex source variation, exact quartic quadrature, conserved norm, axial momentum and the matrix (11). Independent full matrix exponentials verify the free propagator and complete positive-frequency projection implemented by axial_scalar_packets.py. The diagnostic runs 192 checks, including full nonlinear evolution of complex spatial textures and a five-dimensional localized comparison with both zero and nonzero scalar sources. Spatial, radial and temporal refinement remain necessary for any particular collision result. The family provides transverse localization and several spatial polarizations with a tractable full-source equation. It supplies no bound-particle depth assignment or electric and weak channel embedding. With dimensionless Q and \hbar=c=1, [g]=\mathrm{length}^{D-1}. Choosing equal numerical g values at different D does not by itself define one physically normalized interaction across nested sectors. Changing compatibility of localized spatial packets uses this full angular family to compare both outgoing complex patterns after removing their known free evolution. A precisely specified future encounter has either increased or decreased scalar contact for different five-dimensional preparations under the same local dynamics. A separate spherical vector family works in both odd and even dimensions, including six and ten. Its full radial polarization vectors retain tangential current while scalar density is radial. It has one radial center and does not extend the present axial encounter ansatz to a general even-dimensional collision.

title: Positive-frequency scalar vertices
summary: The full positive-frequency scalar Dirac vertex has an exact canonical singular strength, with a massless half-angle law, chirality-dependent zeros and reciprocal spatial interference that must be retained before channel counting.
text: Summary: The full positive-frequency scalar Dirac vertex has an exact canonical singular strength, with a massless half-angle law, chirality-dependent zeros and reciprocal spatial interference that must be retained before channel counting. Normalize the complete incoming bands Use the scalar matrix \beta appearing in the written Dirac source, on one flat containing spatial chart with d\ge2 ordinary directions and \hbar=c=1. Let H(p)=\alpha\cdot p+m\beta,\qquad E_p=\sqrt{|p|^2+m^2},\qquad P_p=\frac{I+H(p)/E_p}{2}, \tag{1} where m\ge0 is a specified mass coefficient of this free-band comparison. At m=0, exclude the single zero-momentum point when defining the positive band. The minimal full complex module has dimension n=2^{\lfloor(d+1)/2\rfloor}. Choose any isometric positive-frequency frame U_p, U_p^\dagger U_p=I_{n/2} and U_pU_p^\dagger=P_p. The complete scalar vertex between momenta q and p is \boxed{C(p,q)=U_p^\dagger\beta U_q.} \tag{2} This is the canonical positive-norm convention used by the massive current projection. Changing to a different external-wave normalization would change its factors and the associated kinetic metric together. The input and output spaces retain every positive-frequency polarization, not a single selected spin direction. Exact singular strength The Clifford relations give \beta P_p\beta= \frac12\left[I+\frac{-\alpha\cdot p+m\beta}{E_p}\right]. \tag{3} For A=-\alpha\cdot p+m\beta, its anticommutator with H(q) is \{A,H(q)\}=2(m^2-p\cdot q)I. Compressing this identity to the +E_q eigenspace yields P_q A P_q=\frac{m^2-p\cdot q}{E_q}P_q. \tag{4} Consequently \boxed{C(p,q)^\dagger C(p,q)=\tau(p,q)I_{n/2},\qquad \tau(p,q)=\frac12\left[1+\frac{m^2-p\cdot q}{E_pE_q}\right].} \tag{5} The reciprocal identity is CC^\dagger=\tau I_{n/2}, and C(q,p)=C(p,q)^\dagger. Every singular value is exactly \sqrt{\tau}. For \tau>0 the full vertex is a scaled unitary map between the two canonical bands. Its unitary part still contains polarization and phase information. For m>0 and finite momenta, \tau>0. At p=q, (2) reduces to (m/E_p)I, recovering \tau=m^2/E_p^2. The forward scalar-density factor is a particular momentum configuration, not a general nonforward interaction strength. The massless angular law For m=0, let \theta be the angle between the two nonzero spatial momenta. Then \boxed{\tau(p,q)=\frac{1-\widehat p\cdot\widehat q}{2} =\sin^2\frac\theta2.} \tag{6} Exactly co-propagating bands have C=0, even for different momentum magnitudes. Opposite directions have unit singular strength. At every nonzero angle, a nonzero input polarization has a nonzero response somewhere in the complete output band. This does not make every individual vertex nonzero. For unit polarizations a,b, |a^\dagger C(p,q)b|^2\le\tau(p,q), \tag{7} and the chosen two patterns can be orthogonal under that map. A particular observed channel also involves its actual spatial inclusion and readout. Equation (6) alone neither identifies an electromagnetic channel nor predicts a scattering rate. Under a common physical rotation, transform both momenta and spinor frames by the covering spin rotation. The scalar vertex is unchanged in the transported frames because the spin rotation commutes with \beta. Independent changes of polarization bases instead give C\mapsto V_p^\dagger C V_q and preserve (5). Chirality gives a channel zero, not a depth-five exception At odd total spatial dimension, the kinetic involution commutes with every massless P_p and anticommutes with \beta. Its positive-frequency eigenspaces each have dimension n/4. Writing the restricted involutions as C_p^{\rm kin} and C_q^{\rm kin} gives C_p^{\rm kin}C(p,q)=-C(p,q)C_q^{\rm kin}. \tag{8} Thus the scalar vertex vanishes between two equal kinetic chiralities for every pair of momenta. Between opposite chiralities, its singular strength is still \sqrt\tau. The complete vertex remains consistent with (5): its nonzero response is in the opposite output block. This occurs at every odd total spatial dimension, including three, five, seven and nine. It supplies no unique depth-five selection and no electric-charge assignment. The neutrino control continues to require a derived neutral electromagnetic channel and surviving weak vertices. Both kinetic signs refer to components of the same field; their particle-antiparticle meaning remains open. If a field also propagates through containing spatial directions, use the complete containing kinetic operator. A lower odd-dimensional involution anticommutes with every additional normal \alpha_j. The lower class can therefore mix under normal motion. The corresponding protection question is treated explicitly in spatially invariant scalar-null fields. Assemble the actual spatial current before projecting A positive-frequency free packet has the form \Psi(x,t)=\int\frac{d^dp}{(2\pi)^{d/2}}\, U_p a(p)e^{ip\cdot x-iE_pt},\qquad \|\Psi\|_{L^2}^2=\int\|a(p)\|^2d^dp. \tag{9} Its scalar current is the full coherent contraction \boxed{\sigma(x,t)= \iint\frac{d^dp\,d^dq}{(2\pi)^d}\, a(p)^\dagger C(p,q)a(q) e^{i(q-p)\cdot x-i(E_q-E_p)t}.} \tag{10} At m=0 every monochromatic forward scalar is zero, but the off-diagonal momentum pairs in (10) can remain nonzero. A spatial packet cannot generally be replaced by an incoherent sum of those forward scalars. A packet confined to one complete odd-dimensional kinetic chirality does have zero scalar, because every matrix element in (10) then vanishes. For two such packets of opposite kinetic chirality, denote them by \psi_+ and \psi_- and put c(x,t)=\psi_+^\dagger\beta\psi_-. Their individual scalar self-currents vanish, while the total scalar is \sigma=2\operatorname{Re}c. \tag{11} For the local equation i\partial_t\Psi=D\Psi+g\sigma\beta\Psi, the exact two rows are \boxed{ i\partial_t\psi_+=D\psi_++g\sigma\beta\psi_-, \qquad i\partial_t\psi_-=D\psi_-+g\sigma\beta\psi_+. } \tag{12} Both patterns respond to the same local scalar. For sufficiently decaying fields, their positive norms satisfy \boxed{\frac{dQ_+}{dt}=2g\operatorname{Im}\int c^2dx,\qquad \frac{dQ_-}{dt}=-\frac{dQ_+}{dt}.} \tag{13} The derivative follows from 2\operatorname{Re}\langle\psi_+,-ig\sigma\beta\psi_-\rangle. Its sign depends on the full complex cross pattern. Individual norms need not be conserved even though their sum is. Equation (12) retains all generated frequency components; positive frequency is an initial preparation, not a projection imposed at every nonlinear time step. These full spatial equations generalize the local cross-source structure of polarized traveling pulses. They do not assume automatic alignment, a fixed target or a mediator particle. What counting can and cannot multiply For a fixed unit incoming polarization b, summing over a complete orthonormal output band gives \sum_{j=1}^{n/2}|e_j^\dagger Cb|^2=\tau. \tag{14} Summing additionally over all orthonormal inputs gives \operatorname{Tr}(C^\dagger C)=(n/2)\tau, while averaging over those inputs gives \tau again. The number of available components is not an extra enhancement of one normalized incident field. Similarly, a cumulative spatial-mode count can organize the available channels, but their actual current contraction, kinetic metric and spectral weights remain necessary. The oscillator source marginals show how Hockey-Stick sums enter a specified projection after those ingredients are supplied. They do not replace (10) by a depth-only coupling coefficient. Verification positive_scalar_vertex_checks.py checks full positive-frequency eigenspaces, all singular values, reciprocity, projector identities and physical rotations in every spatial dimension from two through ten. Independent spatial superpositions verify the complete current, including diagonal massive terms and complex interference. General angular superpositions check the exact chiral source zeros and both reciprocal nonlinear source rows. Containing-direction tests retain every additional Clifford matrix and distinguish lower-class leakage from a scalar zero protected by a complete containing symmetry. These results verify the specified scalar operator and incoming preparations; a physical particle-channel embedding, flux normalization and observed rate remain separate calculations. scalar_wave_packets.py implements (12) on a full three-dimensional Cartesian grid with all four complex components. Its incoming Fourier Gaussian is projected onto the complete positive-frequency band once, then evolved with the exact local reaction and exact free Fourier propagator in a symmetric time splitting. The numerical periodic box is a regulator for localized ordinary spatial fields, not a physical compactification. scalar_packet_collision_checks.py checks that solver against an independently assembled four-component nonlinear differential equation. The default 101 checks include energy variation, reciprocal norm transfer, positive-frequency preparation and second-order time convergence. Its optional larger packet runs record spatial and temporal refinement data; a finite-grid collision is a conditional unbound-field benchmark, not an identified particle pair. Axial spatial Dirac packets retain transverse localization and complete complex polarization vectors in an exact angular family at odd total spatial dimension. Their radial and axial equation comes from the same local scalar, with both patterns evolving and the full angular spinor dependence reconstructed explicitly. Resonant scalar wave quartets provide a multi-directional positive-frequency preparation with reciprocal chiral norm transfer. The exact coherent contraction has a sharp normalized bound. A right-angle cancellation for one polarization per selected chiral band is removed by allowed complete higher-dimensional vectors; counting the components cannot determine that contraction. Frequency accounting for scalar Born response uses both complete vertices to control the negative-output source. A resonant cancellation for positive incoming scattering data coexists with nonzero finite-time forcing from a positive initial preparation.

title: Projective nesting and intermediate spatial depths
summary: Normal characteristic classes obstruct odd intermediate depths in standard projective nesting and obstruct a full sequence of one-dimensional depth increments between any embedded CP spaces whose lower complex dimension is at least two.
