Summary: Normal characteristic classes obstruct odd intermediate depths in standard projective nesting and obstruct a full sequence of one-dimensional depth increments between any embedded CP spaces whose lower complex dimension is at least two. A partial inclusion is not a complete spatial chain IDWT requires its physical sectors to be nested submanifolds of one ordinary spatial manifold. The geometry premise audit already distinguishes that requirement from assigning a name to each spatial depth. Here a normal-bundle calculation determines when the standard projective inclusions can contain intermediate spatial depths. The calculation concerns actual spatial embeddings, not projectors on field coefficients. It assumes the stated global projective topologies. It introduces no compactification or small spatial scale. Changing the metric radius, interaction strength or occupied spinor does not change the characteristic classes used below. Consider the standard inclusion \mathrm{CP}^a\hookrightarrow\mathrm{CP}^{a+q},\qquad [Z]\longmapsto[Z,0],\qquad a,q\ge1. 	ag{1} Its spatial depths are 2a and 2(a+q). The normal-bundle derivation gives N=\mathcal O(1)\otimes\mathbb C^q,\qquad H^*(\mathrm{CP}^a;\mathbb Z)=\mathbb Z[h]/(h^{a+1}), 	ag{2} where h=c_1(\mathcal O(1)). Writing N_{\mathbb R} for the real rank-2q normal bundle,  oxed{c(N)=(1+h)^q,\qquad e(N_{\mathbb R})=h^q,\qquad p(N_{\mathbb R})=(1+h^2)^q.} 	ag{3} All expressions are truncated in the cohomology of the lower base. In particular e(N_{\mathbb R})

An ambient Riemannian metric supplies an orthogonal splitting N_{\mathbb R}=A_r\oplus B_{2q-r}. 	ag{5} Here A is the normal of the lower space in Y, and B is the normal of Y in the higher space, restricted to the lower space. Every real bundle over \mathrm{CP}^a is orientable because H^1(\mathrm{CP}^a;\mathbb Z_2)=0. If r is odd, both ranks in (5) are odd. Their Euler classes lie in odd-degree cohomology of \mathrm{CP}^a, which vanishes. The Euler product formula therefore requires e(N_{\mathbb R})=e(A)e(B)=0. 	ag{6} This contradicts (3) whenever q\le a. Consequently  oxed{q\le a\quad\Longrightarrow\quad 	ext{no odd-dimensional intermediate }Y	ext{ in (4)}.} 	ag{7} The Euler product and odd-rank facts follow from Thom classes; see Cohen, The Topology of Fiber Bundles, Corollary 3.12 and Proposition 3.13. Equations (5)–(7) apply those standard results to the actual spatial inclusion. The intermediate space need not itself be projective or have a prescribed metric. A one-dimensional intermediate normal direction would be a real line subbundle of \mathcal O(1)_{\mathbb R}. Over the simply connected lower base that line would be trivial and would give a nowhere-zero normal vector. Its nonzero Euler class prevents such a vector. A normal direction exists in every coordinate chart, but these directions cannot be chosen consistently over the entire lower space. Every one-dimensional increment requires a real normal frame There is a stronger condition if every intermediate depth is required: M^d=Y_d\subset Y_{d+1}\subset\cdots\subset Y_D=X^D. 	ag{8} Restrict each successive normal line to M. Their sum is N_MX. If H^1(M;\mathbb Z_2)=0, each line is trivial, so  oxed{	ext{A full chain (8) implies }N_MX\cong \mathbf1^{D-d}	ext{ as a real bundle}.} 	ag{9} Conversely, a real normal frame and a tubular neighborhood give intermediate images of M times coordinate balls of every dimension. This supplies smooth intermediate submanifolds near M; it does not require them to be closed or geodesically complete, or turn the whole ambient space into a product. The criterion concerns existence of the stated embeddings, not their dynamics or physical selection. For the standard projective inclusion with a\ge2, p_1(N_{\mathbb R})=qh^2 already contradicts (9), including when q>a and the top Euler class vanishes for dimensional reasons. Vanishing of the Euler obstruction alone is not sufficient. Changing the projective embedding does not restore a full chain The full-chain obstruction extends to any smooth embedding i:\mathrm{CP}^a\hookrightarrow\mathrm{CP}^b, with b>a\ge2. No holomorphic assumption is needed for this part. Let H be the ambient hyperplane class and write i^*H=u h for some integer u. For the real tangent bundle of \mathrm{CP}^m, the Euler sequence gives p_1(T\mathrm{CP}^m)=(m+1)H^2: equivalently use p_1=c_1^2-2c_2 with c_1=(m+1)H and c_2= inom{m+1}{2}H^2. The real tangent-normal splitting therefore gives  oxed{p_1(N_i)=\left[(b+1)u^2-(a+1)ight]h^2.} 	ag{10} The characteristic-class rules and real complexification convention are detailed in Cohen, chapter 3, section 5. There is no torsion ambiguity on the cohomology of \mathrm{CP}^a. The coefficient in (10) cannot vanish: for u=0 it is -(a+1), while for |u|\ge1 it is at least b-a>0. Since h^2
e0 for a\ge2, no such smooth embedding has a trivial real normal bundle. Hence  oxed{b>a\ge2\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \mathrm{CP}^a\hookrightarrow\mathrm{CP}^b 	ext{ cannot be refined through every intermediate spatial depth}.} 	ag{11} For example, an arbitrary smooth CP3-to-CP5 embedding would have p_1(N_i)=(6u^2-4)h^2. Changing the embedding cannot supply a full 6,7,8,9,10 sequence of smooth nested spatial submanifolds. This statement is stronger than, and distinct from, the obstruction to a complex tangent splitting over all of CP5 in the CP5 tangent audit. A constructive control where intermediate spaces do exist The lower-dimensional exception is useful. For \mathrm{CP}^1\subset\mathrm{CP}^3, the real normal bundle underlying \mathcal O(1)\oplus\mathcal O(1) has an explicit global orthonormal frame, despite being nontrivial as a complex bundle. Let z\in\mathbb C^2 be a unit representative of [z]\in\mathrm{CP}^1, let \sigma_j be the Pauli matrices, and set A_0=I,\qquad A_j=i\sigma_j\quad(1\le j\le3),\qquad W(z)=(A_0z,A_1z,A_2z,A_3z). 	ag{12} These four normal columns obey \operatorname{Re}[W(z)^\dagger W(z)]=I_4,\qquad W(e^{i	heta}z)=e^{i	heta}W(z). 	ag{13} The second identity makes them well-defined sections of \operatorname{Hom}(\mathbb Cz,\mathbb C^2). The first follows because A_i^\dagger A_j is anti-Hermitian for i
e j. They are a real frame, not four independent complex columns. The normal connection can still have curvature; a topological frame is not a frame of parallel vectors. For actual physical metric radius R, the normal exponential is explicit. For real y\in\mathbb R^4, r=|y|<\pi R/2, put \Phi([z],y)= \left[\cos(r/R)z,\  rac{\sin(r/R)}r W(z)yight], 	ag{14} using its continuous value at r=0. The projective representative has unit norm and (13) makes (14) independent of the phase choice of z. For a sufficiently small tubular radius, restricting y successively to \mathbb R^1,\mathbb R^2,\mathbb R^3 gives compatible smooth submanifolds of real dimensions three, four and five containing the same CP1 inside CP3. These intermediate spaces are tubular constructions, not CP2 or an assigned nuclear geometry. No measured length or small extra-dimensional scale is attached to the tube parameter. The example shows precisely why (7) and (11) retain their hypotheses; it does not select physical sectors or their global completeness. Consequences for the coupling construction The complete CP1 normal-frame criterion The same construction classifies the standard inclusions with lower space \mathrm{CP}^1. Their normal bundle is \mathcal O(1)\otimes\mathbb C^q: here q is complex codimension, and the ordinary real normal dimension is 2q. For q=2m, group its complex lines into m pairs. Each pair has the real frame (12)–(13), so their direct sum gives a global real frame of rank 2q: N_{\mathbb R}\cong  igoplus_{j=1}^{m} \left(\mathcal O(1)\oplus\mathcal O(1)ight)_{\mathbb R} \cong\mathbf1^{2q}. 	ag{15} For odd q, triviality is obstructed. The equatorial transition of \mathcal O(1) over \mathrm{CP}^1\cong S^2 is one full rotation of its real two-plane. For q copies, the lift of this transition loop to \operatorname{Spin}(2q) ends at (-1)^q=-1: each plane contributes its spin half-angle sign. It is therefore not a contractible loop in SO(2q), whereas a trivial real bundle has a contractible clutching loop. Equivalently its second Stiefel–Whitney class is w_2(N_{\mathbb R})=qh mod2
e0. Together with (15), this proves  oxed{\mathrm{CP}^1\subset\mathrm{CP}^{1+q} 	ext{ has a trivial real normal bundle exactly when }q	ext{ is even}.} 	ag{16} Equation (9) and the tubular construction then give the corresponding criterion for a full sequence of intermediate depths near CP1. In particular, CP1 inside CP5 permits such tubular intermediate spaces; it does not make its depth-six intermediate a global CP3. The full CP3-to-CP5 obstruction above remains unchanged. These existence statements neither select physical sectors nor establish completeness of the tubular intermediate spaces. Keep the actual nesting hypotheses The standard CP3-to-CP5 pair remains a valid partial inclusion with its computed normal connection and reciprocal specified kernel. It cannot simultaneously be declared the complete spatial chain through all the intervening depths. If only selected depths are retained in a calculation, its scope must say so. The obstruction at 2	o3	o4 and at 4	o5	o6 directly affects the alternating sphere/projective candidate list. Merely replacing the odd-dimensional sphere by another smooth odd-dimensional manifold does not fix a standard projective inclusion on either side. Compatible geometries and embeddings need a new construction. The parallel two-state normal spinor factor in the six-to-ten branching also does not provide a real normal frame. For that inclusion, \Sigma^-N is a trivial complex doublet while e(N_{\mathbb R})=h^2
e0. Spinor components and ordinary spatial normal directions are different bundles. On a contractible spatial chart these global obstructions disappear. Using such a chart is a different domain from the entire projective space and needs its own field domain, boundary conditions and normalization. Local mode counting by itself supplies neither the missing global embeddings nor a physical geometry. Verification projective_nesting_checks.py runs 1,385 checks. Exact tangent-bundle quotients and real complexification recover the characteristic classes independently. Finite differences of the actual normal connection and improper spatial curvature integrals verify the primitive characteristic numbers and their independence of R. The code also checks the global phase covariance, real orthonormality, explicit inverse and induced metric of the constructive tube. The topological conclusions rely on the proofs above and the cited bundle theorems. A finite scan of dimensions or integer degrees is a consistency check, not a substitute for the all-degree argument. No empirical geometry or particle coupling is identified by this result.

title: Spatially invariant scalar-null fields
summary: The minimal massless spatial Dirac module admits complete kinetic scalar-null classes at every odd spatial depth, while even depths have no such constant linear class; this parity result does not select a particle or a physical charge.
text: Summary: The minimal massless spatial Dirac module admits complete kinetic scalar-null classes at every odd spatial depth, while even depths have no such constant linear class; this parity result does not select a particle or a physical charge. State the dynamical question The complete source derivative distinguishes a zero background scalar from a zero response to every perturbation. A further question is whether spatial motion preserves a proposed family of zero-source fields. Consider the specified local equation in d ordinary flat spatial directions, with \hbar=c=1: i\partial_t\Psi=-i\sum_{j=1}^d\alpha_j\partial_j\Psi +g(\Psi^\dagger\beta\Psi)\beta\Psi. \tag{1} The Hermitian matrices \alpha_j,\beta square to one and anticommute pairwise. Use one minimal irreducible complex module of their full Clifford algebra, of dimension n=2^{\lfloor(d+1)/2\rfloor}. Components of this module are field amplitudes over ordinary space. The calculation introduces neither compactification nor a choice of global physical topology. We classify constant complex-linear subspaces E\subset\mathbb C^n with two properties: all spatial derivatives preserve fields valued in E, and every such field has zero scalar source. For the orthogonal projector P_E, these conditions are precisely [P_E,\alpha_j]=0\quad(1\le j\le d),\qquad P_E\beta P_E=0. \tag{2} Hermiticity makes an invariant subspace reducing, giving the commutator condition. The scalar condition follows from complex polarization of u^\dagger\beta u=0 for all u\in E. It retains every relative phase; testing just a few real vectors would be insufficient. Odd spatial depth For odd d, define C=i^{(d-1)/2}\alpha_1\cdots\alpha_d,\qquad P_\pm=\frac{I\pm C}{2}. \tag{3} Moving a matrix through the product gives C^\dagger=C,\quad C^2=I,\quad [C,\alpha_j]=0,\quad \{C,\beta\}=0. \tag{4} Thus \beta exchanges the two eigenspaces, each of complex dimension n/2, and \boxed{P_\pm\beta P_\pm=0.} \tag{5} For any sufficiently regular initial field with P_\pm\Psi=\Psi, the free massless Dirac evolution stays in that same space. Equation (5) makes its nonlinear scalar term vanish pointwise for the entire evolution. It is therefore also an exact solution of (1). Spatially varying complex polarization and all momentum directions are allowed. The positive-frequency spectral projection of \alpha\cdot p commutes with C, so positive-frequency wavepackets can be prepared in these classes as well. If two full fields belong to the same class, their sum does too: (\Psi_1+\Psi_2)^\dagger\beta(\Psi_1+\Psi_2)=0. \tag{6} Their local scalar interaction vanishes even where their spatial profiles overlap. Opposite classes have a possible cross scalar 2\operatorname{Re}(\Psi_+^\dagger\beta\Psi_-), determined by their actual profiles and phases. This is a dynamical sufficient condition for a source zero, complementing the traveling-pulse conditions in local polarized coupling. Completeness and the even-depth result The usual complex Clifford classification states that an even number of generators gives one full matrix algebra, while an odd number gives two simple blocks. See the complex case in Etingof's Mathematical Ideas and Notions of Quantum Field Theory, section 11.3. Here its application concerns the kinetic generators alone, inside the larger module that also contains \beta. For even d, the 2^d=n^2 products of distinct \alpha_j form a basis of \operatorname{Mat}_n(\mathbb C). Consequently a projector commuting with them is either 0 or I. The latter fails P\beta P=0. There is no nonzero class satisfying (2). For odd d, the kinetic algebra acts irreducibly on each C eigenspace, with commutant exactly \operatorname{span}_{\mathbb C}\{I,C\}. Its orthogonal projectors are 0,I,P_+,P_-; only P_+ and P_- are nonzero and scalar-null. Thus (3) supplies the complete answer under the stated module and constant-subspace assumptions. An explicit matrix check of the commutant avoids choosing a polarization basis. The commuting conjugation projections give \mathcal E(X)= \prod_{j=1}^d\frac{I+\operatorname{Ad}_{\alpha_j}}2(X) = \begin{cases} \dfrac{\operatorname{Tr}X}{n}I,&d\ {\rm even},\\[6pt] \dfrac{\operatorname{Tr}X}{n}I+ \dfrac{\operatorname{Tr}(CX)}n C,&d\ {\rm odd}. \end{cases} \tag{7} Ordinary spatial depth d Full complex module n Dimension of each nonzero class 1 2 1 2 2 none 3 4 2 4 4 none 5 8 4 6 8 none 7 16 8 8 16 none 9 32 16 10 32 none Multiple module copies or additional independent action terms change the problem and can enlarge or break these invariant spaces. A position-dependent projector requires its own connection terms. Equation (7) does not classify those extensions, nonlinear families, or all individual zero-source solutions at even depth. Propagation through containing spatial directions The dimension d in (1) counts all derivatives retained in that equation. Applying it to a lower particle while omitting its permitted normal propagation is a further restriction. Use the containing Clifford module when that propagation is present, as in normal Dirac propagation. For an odd set of lower directions, form C_d from their \alpha_j. Every additional normal kinetic matrix \alpha_a anticommutes with it: \{C_d,\alpha_a\}=0,\qquad P_\pm\alpha_aP_\pm=0. \tag{8} The extra derivative maps the lower class into its complementary class. For a normal momentum k, its full symbol obeys A_N(k)=\sum_a k_a\alpha_a,\qquad A_N(k)^2=|k|^2I. \tag{9} If an initial field lies in P_+ and evolves under this normal kinetic term alone, the fraction in P_- is \sin^2(|k|t). Projecting back onto P_+ at every step would delete the actual propagation. More generally, a smooth ambient field constrained to the fixed lower class for all times would have to satisfy D_N\Psi=0. For flat normal \mathbb R^q, (9) shows that a square-integrable normal profile satisfying this condition is zero: its Fourier transform vanishes at every nonzero k, and an L^2 function cannot be supported at the single point k=0. This concerns the stated smooth ambient extension and fixed projector. It does not exclude a field defined on a lower spatial submanifold, other confinement dynamics, or a complete containing-space symmetry. In particular, an odd-dimensional containing space has its own kinetic involution. That complete class can preserve scalar nullity while the lower class mixes. A full positive-frequency plane also has zero scalar at every spatial depth. Lower-class mixing alone is therefore not a proof of nonzero scalar interaction. The positive-frequency vertex calculation tests both the complete angular current and these containing-direction qualifications. Physical scope This is a parity result; depths three, five, seven and nine share it. It does not single out the depth-five assignment. Within either class the written scalar term supplies no self-binding, so the theorem does not construct a localized particle. Exact invariance also differs from stability against perturbations outside the class. The complete null-plane response has a density-dependent instability even though its background scalar vanishes identically. The operator C anticommutes with \beta. It therefore fails the general scalar-potential charge condition in conserved spatial charge. Its sign has not been identified with electric charge or an observed weak representation. The neutrino control still requires electric neutrality and nonzero weak vertices. The two signs are not assigned particle and antiparticle meanings. This kinetic involution also differs from the even-bound-depth \Xi=\beta\Gamma_b in collective translation waves, which commutes with \beta, and from the rest Spin(6) polarization in the massive current projection. They solve different spatial representation problems. Verification scalar_plane_response_checks.py checks the involution, every kinetic commutator, scalar-null complex superpositions, arbitrary spatial derivatives, and the full commutant projection for every depth from one through ten. scalar_plane_response.py provides the shared Clifford involution and complete plane-response operators. The results test the specified equation and representation, not the physical realization of a particle sector.

u<p). 	ag{13} In contrast, a nonzero purely transverse static momentum has \chi_{m null}(0,q)=0. General static poles satisfy |q|^2=2a|q_\parallel|: two elastic-scattering spheres centered at \pm ae, each of radius a. These directional limits and resonances exclude treating this background's response as one universal positive elliptic overlap coefficient. Nonlinear comparison and scope The nonnull moving branches emerge at the same threshold and have a continuously connecting scalar response. Neither family is a localized particle or a discrete mass selection. scalar_plane_response_checks.py compares (4) with the complete spinor symbol in spatial dimensions two through six and ten, with complex polarizations and general momenta. u=0.3,1,1.4. Halving the initial perturbation from 10^{-5} to 5	imes10^{-6} approximately halves the error divided by that perturbation amplitude, as required for a first variation. Over 0\le t\le4, the selected linear perturbations amplify by approximately 1.016, 8.062 and 157.53, respectively. Positive norm and the complete kinetic-plus-scalar energy remain conserved. These are dynamical checks of the stated controls; they do not measure a physical particle coupling.

title: Moving nonlinear scalar planes and their response
summary: The local scalar Dirac equation has continuous nonnull traveling-plane branches whose complete self-consistent response has a covariant closed form, with proper density, conjugate modes and the conserved norm treated explicitly.
text:
Summary: The local scalar Dirac equation has continuous nonnull traveling-plane branches whose complete self-consistent response has a covariant closed form, with proper density, conjugate modes and the conserved norm treated explicitly. Continuous branches of the written equation Use the local scalar equation in ordinary flat spatial \mathbb R^d, d\ge2, with one time, \hbar=c=1 and the full minimal complex Dirac module: i\partial_t\Psi=-i\alpha\cdot
abla\Psi+ g(\Psi^\dagger eta\Psi) eta\Psi+J eta\Psi. 	ag{1} The real scalar probe J tests this same field. The plane backgrounds below are unbound controls with density per unit volume. Their effective scalar mass coefficient is not an identified particle mass, and no physical vacuum or global spatial topology has been selected. At J=0 put \Psi=e^{i oldsymbol p\cdot x-i\Omega t}\phi, ho=\phi^\dagger\phi>0, \sigma=\phi^\dagger eta\phi and M=g\sigma. The stationary equation and its anticommutator with  eta imply (\alpha\cdot oldsymbol p+M eta)\phi=\Omega\phi, \quad \Omega^2=| oldsymbol p|^2+M^2, \quad \Omega\sigma=Mho. 	ag{2} For M
e0, self-consistency therefore requires  oxed{\Omega=gho,\qquad M=\pm\sqrt{g^2ho^2-| oldsymbol p|^2}.} 	ag{3} For g>0 these positive-frequency branches begin at gho=| oldsymbol p|, the threshold of the scalar-null plane. The signs in (3) refer to the scalar density. No particle-antiparticle interpretation is assigned. For example, let p=| oldsymbol p|>0 and \alpha( oldsymbol p/p)w=w. In the two-dimensional span of w, eta w, write \phi=\sqrtho\left(\cos rac	heta2\,w+ \sin rac	heta2\, eta wight),\quad \cos	heta= rac p{gho},\quad \sin	heta= rac M{gho}. 	ag{4} The fixed-norm energy density is \mathcal E=\phi^\dagger\alpha\cdot oldsymbol p\,\phi+g\sigma^2/2. Writing 
u=gho gives  rac{\mathcal E_{m nonnull}}ho=  rac
u2+ rac{p^2}{2
u},\qquad  rac{\mathcal E_{m nonnull}-\mathcal E_{m null}}ho = rac{(
u-p)^2}{2
u}. 	ag{5} This is a continuous density-dependent branch, with no discrete depth or mass selection. Proper scalar density and the moving frame Select M>0, g>0, and an arbitrary unit rest polarization w_0 with  eta w_0=w_0. Put \Omega=\sqrt{M^2+| oldsymbol p|^2} and ho=\Omega/g. The explicit field is  oxed{\phi= \sqrt{ rac{ho(\Omega+M)}{2\Omega}} \left(I+ rac{\alpha\cdot oldsymbol p}{\Omega+M}ight)w_0.} 	ag{6} This is the full positive-energy Dirac frame, with its mass coefficient now fixed by the same nonlinear source. Direct calculation gives \phi^\dagger\phi= rac\Omega g,\qquad \phi^\dagger eta\phi= rac M g,\qquad \phi^\dagger\alpha_j\phi= rac{p_j}g. 	ag{7} Thus \sigma=M/g is the proper rest density, whereas ho=\Omega/g is the positive density in the moving frame. Confusing the two changes the response coefficient. The spin boost S( oldsymbol p)=\sqrt{ rac{\Omega+M}{2M}} \left(I+ rac{\alpha\cdot oldsymbol p}{\Omega+M}ight) 	ag{8} satisfies S^\dagger eta S= eta and \phi=S\sqrt{M/g}\,w_0. Its current velocity is  oldsymbol p/\Omega. It is a change of spacetime frame, not a new spatial dimension or a compactification. Derive the full feedback response In the carrier frame let v= eta\phi, and retain \zeta_q=(\eta_q,\overline{\eta_{-q}})^{\mathsf T}. Define  egin{aligned} H_{m f}(q)&= \operatorname{diag}\!\left( \alpha\cdot( oldsymbol p+q)+M eta-\Omega,\, -\overline{\alpha\cdot( oldsymbol p-q)+M eta-\Omega}ight),\ f&= inom v{- ar v},\qquad r=(v^\dagger,v^{\mathsf T}),\qquad \mathcal H(q)=H_{m f}(q)+gfr. \end{aligned} 	ag{9} Here fJ is the probe force and r\zeta=\delta\sigma its scalar readout. The rank-one update in doubled variables contains both ordinary and conjugate variations; it is not a prescribed occupied-ray mass contact. For frequency z, introduce the Minkowski notation K=(z,q),\quad K^2=z^2-|q|^2,\qquad P=(\Omega, oldsymbol p),\quad P\cdot K=\Omega z- oldsymbol p\cdot q,\quad P^2=M^2. 	ag{10} Inverting the two free Dirac blocks, using (7), gives  egin{aligned} \chi_{m f} &=r(z-H_{m f})^{-1}f\ &= rac1g\left[  rac{P\cdot K+2M^2}{K^2+2P\cdot K} - rac{P\cdot K-2M^2}{K^2-2P\cdot K}ight]\ &=- rac4g  rac{(P\cdot K)^2-M^2K^2}{(K^2)^2-4(P\cdot K)^2}. \end{aligned} 	ag{11} For example, the upper numerator follows from v^\dagger v=\Omega/g, v^\dagger\alpha_jv=-p_j/g, and v^\dagger eta v=M/g. Self-consistency says \delta\sigma=\chi_{m f}(J+g\delta\sigma). The exact response of the full linearized equation is therefore  oxed{\chi(z,q)= rac{\chi_{m f}}{1-g\chi_{m f}} =- rac4g\,  rac{(P\cdot K)^2-M^2K^2}{K^2(K^2-4M^2)}.} 	ag{12} Equivalently, for u=P/M, \chi=-4M\sigma[(u\cdot K)^2-K^2]/[K^2(K^2-4M^2)]. The formula is independent of the chosen constant rest polarization for this scalar-to-scalar probe. The full spinor response, other channel projections and nonuniform polarization textures retain additional information. Complete spectrum and the zero-mode qualification The matrix determinant lemma applied to (9) gives  oxed{\det(z-\mathcal H)= (K^2+2P\cdot K)^{n/2-1} (K^2-2P\cdot K)^{n/2-1} K^2(K^2-4M^2).} 	ag{13} Thus the four scalar-sector frequencies are \pm|q|,\qquad \pm\sqrt{|q|^2+4M^2}, 	ag{14} and the remaining frequencies are -\Omega\pm\sqrt{| oldsymbol p+q|^2+M^2},\qquad \Omega\pm\sqrt{| oldsymbol p-q|^2+M^2}, 	ag{15} each with multiplicity n/2-1. All are real. Their algebraic multiplicities and possible degeneracies are retained in (13). This is a spectral result, not a proof of bounded linear evolution. At q=0 the phase vector and fixed-momentum norm derivative satisfy \zeta_{m ph}= inom{i\phi}{-i ar\phi},\qquad \zeta_ho= rac g{2M} inom{ eta\phi}{\overline{ eta\phi}}, \qquad \mathcal H(0)\zeta_{m ph}=0,\quad \mathcal H(0)\zeta_ho=-ig\zeta_{m ph}. 	ag{16} This is the norm-frequency Jordan pair. Its secular phase change must be treated before making any stability claim, and real eigenvalues alone do not establish nonlinear stability. Tiny numerical splittings of this exact zero block are checked against (16), rather than interpreted as a measured growth rate. Retarded and static meanings The stable spectral poles in (12) use the retarded boundary value z=\omega+i0. Their two wave factors are the same ones in the uniform rest response. The numerator is a local differential operator, so the response preserves the causal support of those wave propagators. The first-order Dirac system fixes the compatible initial data; rewriting (12) as a fourth-order scalar equation does not add independent initial data. Both response channels are modes of the original field, not mediator particles. At nonzero static momentum,  oxed{\chi(0,q)= - rac4g\,  rac{M^2+( oldsymbol p\cdot q)^2/|q|^2}{|q|^2+4M^2}.} 	ag{17} At exactly zero momentum the continuous frequency expression is \chi(z,0)=- rac{4| oldsymbol p|^2}{g(z^2-4M^2)},\qquad \chi(0,0)= rac{| oldsymbol p|^2}{gM^2}. 	ag{18} At rest, a spatially constant scalar probe changes only phase and this response is zero. Equation (17) has a different small-momentum limit. The frequency and momentum limits do not commute. An undamped initial-value experiment can also retain oscillatory transients; its late-time field need not settle to a static branch. There is an independent nonlinear check of (18). Hold ho and  oldsymbol p fixed and add a constant small J. The total mass coefficient  ar M of a nearby positive-frequency stationary plane satisfies  ar M=gho rac{ ar M} {\sqrt{| oldsymbol p|^2+ ar M^2}}+J,\qquad \sigma(J)= rac{ ar M-J}g. 	ag{19} Differentiate at the unforced solution  ar M=M, \Omega=gho:  rac{d ar M}{dJ}= rac{\Omega^2}{M^2},\qquad  oxed{ rac{d\sigma}{dJ}= rac{| oldsymbol p|^2}{gM^2}.} 	ag{20} This fixes the norm throughout, instead of changing the background density to keep an arbitrarily fixed carrier. Connection to the null threshold For fixed p=| oldsymbol p|>0 and g>0, let M	o0^+. Then \Omega	o p, ho	o p/g, and (12) tends to \chi(z,q)\longrightarrow - rac{4p^2}{g}\,  rac{(z-q_\parallel)^2}{(z^2-|q|^2)^2}. 	ag{21} This is exactly the scalar-null response at 
u=p. The branch connection follows from one local equation with one coefficient. It does not turn the continuous control family into a mass quantization or an empirical coupling law. Verification scalar_plane_response.py implements the complete Fourier symbol and exact responses. scalar_plane_response_checks.py runs 2,594 checks across the linked plane and kinetic-null calculations. For (6)–(21) it checks arbitrary complex rest polarizations in spatial dimensions two, three, five, six and ten, diverse momenta, the full nonlinear source, current and spin boost. Direct full-spinor resolvents and determinant ratios check the feedback derivation independently of its scalar formula. Both field and momentum are rotated together to test physical rotation covariance. The exact zero-mode vectors are checked separately from the nonzero spectrum. Independently solved nonlinear stationary equations with positive and negative probes verify (20) at fixed norm. The approach to (21) has quadratic error in M away from its poles.

title: Complete scalar response and null directions
summary: The complete local scalar-source derivative is invertible at nonzero scalar density, while a scalar-null field retains one real response direction whose kinetic protection and projected channel meaning must be tested separately.
text: Summary: The complete local scalar-source derivative is invertible at nonzero scalar density, while a scalar-null field retains one real response direction whose kinetic protection and projected channel meaning must be tested separately. Source response is distinct from a projected vertex At a physical spatial point, consider the written scalar contribution \mathcal N(\phi)=g s\beta\phi,\qquad s=\phi^\dagger\beta\phi,\qquad \rho=\phi^\dagger\phi, \tag{1} with real g, Hermitian \beta^2=I, and the full spinor fiber retained. The invariants obey |s|\le\rho. They are scalar and positive densities over ordinary physical space; spinor components do not introduce more spatial dimensions. The complete derivative is \boxed{J_\phi\eta=D\mathcal N(\phi)\eta =g\left[s\beta\eta+2\beta\phi\, \operatorname{Re}(\phi^\dagger\beta\eta)\right].} \tag{2} This note determines its entire pointwise response spectrum. It does not assert that every projected particle vertex is nonzero. A vertex includes spatial wavefunctions, an output projection, kinetic normalization and the appropriate current channel. Also, J_\phi is only the nonlinear source derivative: the complete rotating-frame operator includes D-\mu. Its symmetry zero modes or cancellations are not excluded by an invertible J_\phi alone. Exact real response spectrum Let \beta have p\ge1 positive and q\ge1 negative complex directions, with n=p+q. Regard the complex fiber as a real 2n-dimensional Hilbert space with inner product \operatorname{Re}(\eta^\dagger\xi). Writing v=\beta\phi, equation (2) is the real symmetric operator \boxed{J_\phi=g\left(s\beta+2v\otimes_{\mathbb R}v\right).} \tag{3} The real Hessian of the energy density g s^2/2 is 2J_\phi; the factor two follows from \delta E=2\operatorname{Re} (\mathcal N^\dagger\delta\phi). The rank-one term in (3) is real-linear, not a complex-linear rank-one operator acting alone. Diagonalize \beta and use unitary changes within its two eigenspaces to put \phi=(a,b) in one real direction of each, where a^2=\frac{\rho+s}{2},\qquad b^2=\frac{\rho-s}{2}. The remaining real directions give g s with multiplicity 2p-1 and -g s with multiplicity 2q-1. On the two displayed real directions, J_\phi/g is \begin{pmatrix} 3a^2-b^2&-2ab\\-2ab&-a^2+3b^2 \end{pmatrix}. \tag{4} Its trace is 2\rho and determinant is -3s^2. Thus the full spectrum is \boxed{g s\ (2p-1),\quad -g s\ (2q-1),\quad g\left(\rho+\sqrt{\rho^2+3s^2}\right),\quad g\left(\rho-\sqrt{\rho^2+3s^2}\right).} \tag{5} The multiplicities in parentheses count real directions. Formula (5) also has the correct pure-chirality limits |s|=\rho. No spatial-depth counting identity changes this pointwise spectrum. Nonzero scalar density leaves no full source kernel If g\ne0 and s\ne0, every eigenvalue in (5) is nonzero. In particular, \boxed{\det_{\mathbb R}J_\phi=3g^{2n}s^{2n},} \tag{6} and the exact real-linear inverse is \boxed{J_\phi^{-1}\xi=\frac1{g s} \left[\beta\xi-\frac{2\phi}{3s} \operatorname{Re}(\phi^\dagger\xi)\right].} \tag{7} Substitution in (2) verifies (7). Equivalently, apply the rank-one inverse identity to sI+2\phi\operatorname{Re}(\phi^\dagger\beta\,\cdot), whose rank-one functional takes value 2s on \phi. For example, suppose \phi^\dagger\beta\eta=0. The scalar itself has zero first variation in that direction, but the full source still changes by g s\beta\eta. Freezing the final field factor would erase this term and create an artificial nullspace. The nonlinear map has a related exact invariant: \omega=\mathcal N(\phi)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \omega^\dagger\beta\omega=g^2s^3. \tag{8} For nonzero output scalar t=\omega^\dagger\beta\omega, take the real cube root s=(t/g^2)^{1/3} and recover \phi=\beta\omega/(g s). The scalar-null input cone maps to zero. A nonzero scalar-null output does not occur in the image of this local cubic map. A small scalar does not suppress every response The exact smallest singular value in the canonical real metric is \boxed{s_{\min}(J_\phi)=|g| \left(\sqrt{\rho^2+3s^2}-\rho\right) =\frac{3|g|s^2}{\sqrt{\rho^2+3s^2}+\rho}.} \tag{9} The second expression avoids subtractive numerical cancellation. It is no greater than |g s|, because |s|\le\rho. For 0<|s|\ll\rho, the weakest response is approximately 3|g|s^2/(2\rho), but the largest is approximately 2|g|\rho. |s|/\rho, with g=\rho=1 Smallest singular value Largest singular value 1 1 3 0.1 0.0148892 2.0148892 0.01 0.000149989 2.000149989 0 0 2 Near cancellation of the background scalar can therefore leave a very weak direction and a strong direction simultaneously. It is insufficient to explain universal rare interaction without specifying the actual incident and observed spatial channels. If a spatial perturbation is supported where |s(x)|\ge s_*>0 and \rho(x)\le\rho_{\max}, integrating (9) gives \|J_\phi\eta\|_{L^2}\ge |g|\left(\sqrt{\rho_{\max}^2+3s_*^2}-\rho_{\max}\right) \|\eta\|_{L^2}. \tag{10} This is a full-source estimate on the stated support. A localized field generally has s\to0 in its tails, so (10) must not be promoted to a uniform gap over all space. For a complete orthonormal output family f_a, Parseval gives \sum_a|\langle f_a,J_\phi\eta\rangle|^2=\|J_\phi\eta\|^2. A selected channel can still vanish, and a finite output band can miss the response altogether. Counting that band is not a substitute for evaluating its spatial projection. What the rank-one null response actually means At s=0 and \rho>0, \boxed{\mathcal N(\phi)=0,\qquad J_\phi=2g(\beta\phi)\otimes_{\mathbb R}(\beta\phi).} \tag{11} The complete source derivative has one real responsive direction and 2n-1 real null directions. In particular, J_\phi(\beta\phi)=2g\rho\beta\phi. A zero background self-source therefore does not mean an absence of interaction with a probe. This rank-one operator also does not provide an occupied-ray self-contact. Let P_\phi=\phi\phi^\dagger/\rho. At scalar nullity, \phi^\dagger\beta\phi=0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad P_\phi J_\phi=0. \tag{12} Its responsive direction is orthogonal to the occupied complex ray. Projecting onto that ray removes the response. The rank-one source derivative cannot be identified with a nonzero mass operator on the occupied ray. The graph-contact variation likewise distinguishes an occupied coefficient from the complete field-dependent response; its graph kernel and normalization are separate specified ingredients. Spatial kinetics can activate an initially null scalar The exact zero crossings of local polarized pulses use their actual traveling solutions and full spatial compatibility. Nullity of the scalar at one time alone does not impose that dynamics. A simple control uses two ordinary spatial directions x,y, with anticommuting \alpha_x,\alpha_y,\beta. Choose a unit initial spinor \phi_0 satisfying \alpha_x\phi_0=\phi_0,\qquad \alpha_y\phi_0=-i\beta\phi_0. \tag{13} The full plane field \Psi(t,y)=e^{iky}\phi(t) obeys i\dot\phi=(k\alpha_y+g s\beta)\phi,\qquad s=\phi^\dagger\beta\phi, \tag{14} and begins with s(0)=0, \rho=1. Direct differentiation gives \dot s(0)=-2k, independently of g. The actual transverse kinetic term immediately produces a scalar source. This is an unbound plane control per unit volume. The preparation in (13) mixes both signs of the free energy associated with its actual momentum along y; it is not proposed as a positive-energy particle state. An eigenplane with \alpha_y\phi_0=\phi_0 instead has an invariant scalar zero and solves the full equation as a free positive-frequency wave. The difference is the occupied kinetic mode, not scalar nullity alone. For completeness, the nonlinear scalar evolution in (14) closes exactly. On the invariant two-component plane use \alpha_x=\sigma_z, \alpha_y=-\sigma_y, \beta=\sigma_x. Writing v=\langle\sigma_y\rangle, w=\langle\sigma_z\rangle, the conserved energy is -kv+g s^2/2=0 and \dot s=-2kw. The Bloch equations therefore imply \boxed{\ddot s+4k^2s+2g^2s^3=0,\qquad s(0)=0,\quad\dot s(0)=-2k,} \tag{15} \dot s^2+4k^2s^2+g^2s^4=4k^2. \tag{16} For k>0, its amplitude is \boxed{|s|_{\max}=\sqrt{\frac{2k}{\sqrt{k^2+g^2}+k}}.} \tag{17} At g=0, s(t)=-\sin(2kt). This exact source activation occurs with conserved positive norm and conserved total energy; the scalar term has not introduced an external driving field or a mediator particle. Consequence for physical coupling tests The classification of scalar-null fields identifies constant linear preparations whose zero source survives every spatial derivative. The full null-plane response separately determines whether perturbations outside an exact zero-source background stay bounded. Its stability threshold shows why invariance alone is insufficient. The local scalar term admits real source nullspaces at particular fields and exact mismatched traveling solutions. Its nonzero-scalar response is nevertheless full rank before projection, and its null cone is not invariant under arbitrary spatial motion. A protected physical suppression therefore requires the actual occupied solution, its full kinetic evolution and the derived channel map. These statements do not establish electric neutrality or eliminate weak vertices. The neutrino channel control keeps those physical requirements separate. No special depth-five zero, band-independent mass coefficient or observed rate follows from (5) or (11). Verification local_scalar_response_rank_checks.py runs 2,116 checks. Independent finite differences of the cubic source test the derivative; full real spectra, singular values, multiplicities, determinants and inverse maps are checked in complex rotated Clifford frames. Null-source and occupied-ray projections are tested separately from selected output channels. Full complex spatial-plane evolution in dimensions three, six and ten is compared with the independently integrated scalar equation (15), its first integral and the exact free limit. These tests concern the specified local equation and its source geometry, not measured particle interactions.

title: Local polarized Dirac pulse coupling
summary: The local scalar Dirac term gives exact polarized pulse equations, a complete spatial mismatch criterion and reciprocal weak-scattering maps with both ordinary and phase-conjugate contributions.
text: Summary: The local scalar Dirac term gives exact polarized pulse equations, a complete spatial mismatch criterion and reciprocal weak-scattering maps with both ordinary and phase-conjugate contributions. A direct local same-field calculation Consider the written scalar Dirac contribution on a specified flat ordinary spatial region, with zero bare mass: i\partial_t\Psi=-i\alpha_j\partial_j\Psi +g(\Psi^\dagger\beta\Psi)\beta\Psi. \tag{1} The Hermitian matrices satisfy \{\alpha_i,\alpha_j\}=2\delta_{ij}I, \{\alpha_i,\beta\}=0, \beta^2=I. The coefficient g is the one scalar coefficient in this equation; no separate one-way or pair coefficient is inserted. Other contributions to a completed master action are not supplied by (1). Choose a physical unit direction e and let x=e\cdot\mathbf x. Fields homogeneous in all transverse ordinary directions form an exact class of (1). This is a plane pulse control with finite norm per unit transverse volume, not a transversely bound particle. It introduces no compactification and does not fix the global geometry of any IDWT sector. The bound-profile polarization waves have different profile and mass assumptions. Let E_+ be an orthonormal frame of the complete +1 eigenspace of \alpha(e), of complex dimension s, and set E_-=\beta E_+. Every spinor in the chosen Clifford module can be written \Psi=E_+R+E_-L,\qquad R,L\in\mathbb C^s. \tag{2} The vectors R(t,x) and L(t,x) retain every traveling polarization and its spatial phase. They are two parts of the same field, not mediator particles or extra spatial dimensions. Their positive kinetic norm is additive because the two frames are orthogonal. Their scalar current is the cross term \boxed{\sigma=\Psi^\dagger\beta\Psi =R^\dagger L+L^\dagger R=2\operatorname{Re}(R^\dagger L).} \tag{3} It is not the sum of two nonzero individual scalar sources. Substitution in the full equation gives exactly \boxed{i(\partial_t+\partial_x)R=g\sigma L,\qquad i(\partial_t-\partial_x)L=g\sigma R.} \tag{4} Both responses follow from the same local interaction. A common physical rotation acts on the direction, coordinates, Clifford frame and field together and preserves (3)–(4). Causal support and conserved quantities Pure one-way pulses R=A(x-t),L=0, or R=0,L=B(x+t), solve (4) for arbitrary smooth complex vector profiles. No fixed polarization or carrier frequency is required for that statement. In the coupled equation, R=0 makes its source zero on that characteristic, and similarly for L. While a regular solution exists, each pulse therefore stays within the characteristic support of its own incoming profile. The interaction acts only where those supports cross. This domain of dependence follows from a local equation, addressing the issue exposed by the instantaneous scalar test. There is a matrix continuity identity: \boxed{\partial_t(RR^\dagger+LL^\dagger) +\partial_x(RR^\dagger-LL^\dagger)=0.} \tag{5} The two nonlinear matrix sources cancel. Thus M_R+M_L=\int(RR^\dagger+LL^\dagger)dx \tag{6} is conserved, including its trace, the total positive norm. This matrix identity reflects the common U(s) symmetry of the transversely homogeneous class. It is not a derived physical gauge group; general transverse derivatives do not have that entire symmetry. The directional norms N_R=\operatorname{Tr}M_R and N_L can change oppositely. They have not been assigned electric charges. The local action also conserves energy and momentum: E=\int\left[-iR^\dagger R_x+iL^\dagger L_x+ \frac g2\sigma^2\right]dx,\qquad P=\int-i(R^\dagger R_x+L^\dagger L_x)dx. \tag{7} Boundary terms vanish for decaying or supported profiles. For separated incoming and outgoing pulses the scalar term vanishes. Their directional kinetic energies then satisfy E_R=(E+P)/2 and E_L=(E-P)/2, so each agrees before and after the complete encounter. The classical Dirac kinetic energy has both signs; this observation does not turn arbitrary real pulses into positive-energy particle states. Exact mismatch of complete spatial patterns The free crossing R=A(\xi), L=B(\eta), \xi=x-t, \eta=x+t, is an exact nonlinear solution if and only if \boxed{\operatorname{Re}\big[A(\xi)^\dagger B(\eta)\big]=0} \tag{8} for every pair of occupied characteristics that meets, apart from the trivial case g=0. This criterion follows directly from both equations in (4). Realifying the complex vectors makes it an ordinary orthogonality condition between their full real spatial spans in \mathbb R^{2s}. For A=a f, B=b h with a^\dagger b=0, the interaction vanishes for every pair of complex envelopes f,h. Both pulses can occupy the same spatial region while the scalar source remains zero. If a^\dagger b is purely imaginary and both envelopes are real, (8) also holds. That latter cancellation can be opened by spatial phase variation even when the intensity profiles are unchanged. A fixed target vector does not represent a general texture. An incoming polarization must obey (8) against every direction and phase occupied by the target profile, not merely against its spatial average. Complete scalar response shows why an instantaneously vanishing scalar is insufficient on its own: the source still has a responsive direction, and general spatial kinetics can activate it. Equation (8) uses actual traveling solutions and their full encounter. A complete geometric scattering functional For finite incoming profiles define both kinds of moments: M_A=\int AA^\dagger d\xi,\quad C_A=\int AA^{\mathsf T}d\xi, \qquad M_B=\int BB^\dagger d\eta,\quad C_B=\int BB^{\mathsf T}d\eta. \tag{9} M is Hermitian and positive semidefinite. The complex symmetric C retains phase information that M omits. These are integrals of spatial profiles of the same field, not new dynamical fields. For the complete free encounter, dx\,dt=\tfrac12d\xi\,d\eta. Expanding (2\operatorname{Re}A^\dagger B)^2 gives \boxed{\mathcal C[A,B]=\int\sigma_{\rm free}^2dx\,dt =\operatorname{Tr}(M_AM_B) +\operatorname{Re}\operatorname{Tr}(C_A^\dagger C_B)\ge0.} \tag{10} For profiles initially separated, integrate over their full future crossing; for decaying scattering profiles, use the complete time axis. The right-hand side is zero precisely for (8), subject to the stated support conditions. Discarding C_A,C_B would misclassify some complete scalar-source zeros. Reciprocal weak-scattering map Integrate (4) along the right-moving characteristic, evaluating its source on the free profiles at first order in g. Since d\eta=2dt, \boxed{A_{\rm out}=A-\frac{ig}{2} \left(M_BA+C_B\bar A\right)+O(g^2).} \tag{11} Integration along the left-moving characteristic similarly gives \boxed{B_{\rm out}=B-\frac{ig}{2} \left(M_AB+C_A\bar B\right)+O(g^2).} \tag{12} For example, the term (A^\dagger B)B integrates to C_B\bar A, whereas (B^\dagger A)B integrates to M_BA. The first correction is therefore real-linear in the incident pattern; it cannot generally be replaced by a single complex-linear overlap. The integrated interaction functional is g\mathcal C/2. Its derivatives with respect to \bar A and \bar B are exactly the two brackets in (11)–(12), multiplied by g/2. Thus one scalar action generates both scattering responses with the canonical kinetic normalization. Small g here means the corresponding dimensionless products |g|N_A,|g|N_B are small in the chosen units. For smooth finite profiles on a regular finite encounter, the Duhamel expansion supplies the displayed O(g^2) remainder. Taking the norm derivative yields \boxed{\Delta N_A =g\operatorname{Im}\operatorname{Tr}(C_BC_A^\dagger)+O(g^2), \qquad \Delta N_B=-\Delta N_A+O(g^2).} \tag{13} The ordinary Hermitian term alone does not transfer directional norm at this order. Phase-sensitive spatial coherence can do so. This is not a particle–antiparticle conversion claim. Positive free frequencies sharpen the selection rule On the full line, suppose the incoming profiles have strictly positive free kinetic frequencies: A(\xi)=\frac1{\sqrt{2\pi}}\int_0^\infty a(k)e^{ik\xi}dk, \qquad B(\eta)=\frac1{\sqrt{2\pi}}\int_0^\infty b(q)e^{-iq\eta}dq. \tag{14} Assume sufficiently decaying profiles and no zero-frequency distribution. Parseval's identity pairs opposite Fourier frequencies in \int AA^T, so C_A=C_B=0. Consequently \mathcal C=\operatorname{Tr}(M_AM_B),\qquad \Delta A=-\frac{ig}{2}M_BA+O(g^2),\quad \Delta B=-\frac{ig}{2}M_AB+O(g^2). \tag{15} Each leading correction is a unitary polarization rotation to first order. No independent coefficient or phase average was used to remove the conjugate term; its absence follows from the occupied spectrum. The exact zero (8) also strengthens. The two-variable Fourier transform of A^\dagger B has support in the negative-negative frequency quadrant; its conjugate has support in the positive-positive quadrant. These supports are disjoint. Their sum can vanish only if \boxed{a(k)^\dagger b(q)=0\quad\text{for almost every }k,q>0.} \tag{16} Equivalently, the complete complex polarization spans of the two spectra are orthogonal. A quarter-turn phase with real envelopes is not an additional strictly positive-frequency escape from (16). Exactly supported spatial pulses cannot also be strictly one-sided in Fourier frequency; these two controlled assumptions must remain distinct. In particular, \ker M_B=\{v:\ B(\eta)^\dagger v=0\text{ for almost every }\eta\}. \tag{17} A target whose polarization texture spans the complete traveling space has positive definite M_B and no constant dark polarization. Extra polarization dimensions allow possible orthogonal patterns; they do not ensure that the dynamics select them. Scope and verification local_polarized_collision.py implements the complete local equations, both moments and both weak maps. local_polarized_collision_checks.py verifies the full Clifford reconstruction and physical rotation covariance at several spatial dimensions, exact nonlinear source zeros, independent spacetime source integrals, complete complex action derivatives and quadratic convergence to the weak map. The same checks test continuous Fourier integrals of positive-frequency packets and full nonlinear collisions. Their changing spatial compatibility is measured after both patterns have responded, including spatial textures in all four traveling polarizations of an eight-component module. The result establishes local polarization-sensitive coupling in this specified term and spatial class. It does not identify photons, neutrinos or bound leptons, select different particle depths, supply transverse localization, or derive a common coefficient after distinct-depth reduction. Every tested depth admits nonzero scalar coupling as well as permitted mismatches; no special depth-five zero follows from component counting.

title: Changing compatibility in a local Dirac collision
summary: Independent full spatial evolutions of the local scalar Dirac equation show reciprocal pulse deformations that increase or decrease normalized scalar-pattern compatibility while preserving the combined polarization matrix.
text: Summary: Independent full spatial evolutions of the local scalar Dirac equation show reciprocal pulse deformations that increase or decrease normalized scalar-pattern compatibility while preserving the combined polarization matrix. An autonomous local encounter Use the exact plane pulse equations derived from the local scalar Dirac term: i(\partial_t+\partial_x)R=g\sigma L,\qquad i(\partial_t-\partial_x)L=g\sigma R, \qquad\sigma=2\operatorname{Re}R^\dagger L. \tag{1} Both complex spatial patterns evolve; there is no prescribed target, externally forced probe or instantaneous spatial convolution. The scalar cross term of the one field is retained at each spatial point. This control uses zero bare mass and fields homogeneous in transverse ordinary spatial directions. It is not a transversely bound particle pair or a derived relation between different depths. The projective spatial pair tests a different, specified nonlocal action. The present calculation tests changing compatibility in a local equation, while retaining its more restricted flat plane pulse geometry. The uniform-background response instead uses a prescribed probe and a different background. Prepare both spatial polarization textures Let b(s)=\begin{cases}\exp[1-(1-s^2)^{-1}],&|s|<1,\\0,&|s|\ge1, \end{cases} \quad F(s)=\frac{b(s/1.5)}{\sqrt{\int b(u/1.5)^2du}}, \tag{2} and define a real unitary rotation in a selected two-polarization plane, U(\theta)=\begin{pmatrix}\cos\theta&\sin\theta\\ -\sin\theta&\cos\theta\end{pmatrix}. \tag{3} The initial pulses are \begin{aligned} R(0,x)&=F(x+3)e^{3i(x+3)}U(\theta_R(x+3))a,\\ L(0,x)&=F(x-3)e^{-3i(x-3)}U(\theta_L(x-3))b_\phi, \end{aligned} \tag{4} a=\binom10,\quad b_\phi=\binom{0.7e^{i\phi}}{\sqrt{0.51}e^{-0.4i}}, \quad\theta_R(s)=0.35\sin(1.3s),\quad \theta_L(s)=0.25\cos(0.8s). \tag{5} Each initial positive norm is one. The two pulses start on disjoint intervals centered at -3 and 3. Their characteristic supports cross only during 1.5<t<4.5 and are separated again at t=6. The coefficient is fixed at g=1 for both preparations below. These supported pulses have nonzero carriers but are not strictly positive-frequency states: exact spatial support and exact one-sided Fourier support cannot both hold. The positive-frequency selection theorem in the analytic pulse note is established separately. The pulses in (4) have not been identified with physical incoming particles. Measure the changed patterns after both responses At a given time, form M_R=\int RR^\dagger dx,\quad C_R=\int RR^{\mathsf T}dx, \qquad M_L=\int LL^\dagger dx,\quad C_L=\int LL^{\mathsf T}dx. The scalar-pattern measure is \boxed{\mathcal C=\operatorname{Tr}(M_RM_L) +\operatorname{Re}\operatorname{Tr}(C_R^\dagger C_L), \qquad \widehat{\mathcal C}=\frac{\mathcal C}{N_RN_L}.} \tag{6} For a free crossing of the specified two profiles, \mathcal C equals the complete spacetime integral of \sigma^2. Evaluating it on outgoing profiles asks how those changed patterns would engage in another complete crossing. It is not their instantaneous local contact after they have separated, and it is not a measured scattering rate. Independent translations of the profiles leave (6) unchanged. The normalized quantity removes changes of their two positive norms. Both are relevant because (1) permits directional norm transfer, while preserving the total. Pointwise Cauchy–Schwarz gives 0\le\widehat{\mathcal C}\le2. The first weak-scattering map is generated by g\mathcal C/2 itself. Its Hamiltonian variation therefore gives \mathcal C_{\rm out}=\mathcal C_{\rm in}+O(g^2). That leading approximation alone cannot establish the changing-match effect. The following results come from the complete nonlinear equations. Both strengthening and weakening survive independent checks The refined spatial solution gives: Initial phase \phi Initial \mathcal C Outgoing \mathcal C Outgoing N_R 0.8 0.566257932 0.578943909 1.001204974 2.0 0.340034978 0.336433051 1.000323340 The other norm is N_L=2-N_R. Dividing by N_RN_L preserves both conclusions: normalized compatibility increases by more than 0.012 in the first preparation and decreases by more than 0.003 in the second. The difference is not an imposed alignment rule or merely the change in the amount of field in either outgoing pulse. The full combined polarization matrix M_R+M_L remains conserved. This stronger identity checks all complex polarization components, not only their summed norm. The local interaction source is zero before the supports meet and after they separate. The comparison uses exact characteristic transport and exact local nonlinear reaction. For a reaction step of duration h, \sigma is constant during that substep and \boxed{R'=\cos(g\sigma h)R-i\sin(g\sigma h)L,\qquad L'=\cos(g\sigma h)L-i\sin(g\sigma h)R.} \tag{7} Half a reaction, one characteristic shift, and half a reaction give a second-order spatial and temporal scheme with \Delta t=\Delta x. The numerical interval [-16,16) has an unreached buffer throughout the run. Circular array indexing is a storage method, not an assumption that a physical direction is compactified. An independent solver uses Fourier spatial derivatives and adaptive continuous-time DOP853 integration of the full complex first-order equation. It does not use (7), the weak-scattering map or the compatibility formula to evolve the fields. Its outgoing values are 0.578944463 and 0.336433102 respectively. Spatial step Outgoing \mathcal C, \phi=0.8 Outgoing \mathcal C, \phi=2.0 1/64 0.578935603 0.336432288 1/128 0.578942248 0.336432899 1/256 0.578943909 0.336433051 The values approach the independent solution at the expected second order. The maximum intermediate energy errors decrease from 1.65\times10^{-4} to 1.06\times10^{-5} in the first case, and from 1.03\times10^{-4} to 6.43\times10^{-6} in the second. The combined norm and matrix identities remain accurate to numerical roundoff. Once the fields are separated, both directional kinetic energies agree with their incoming values, as required by total energy and momentum. Full traveling multiplet and exact controls The two-plane data in (4) provide transparent comparison parameters; they are not asserted to represent every polarization of a six-dimensional field. A further calculation occupies all four traveling polarizations of a chosen eight-component spatial Clifford module. Both profiles have complex, spatially varying polarization and the combined matrix has four strictly positive eigenvalues, (0.00087970,\ 0.02007333,\ 0.54629695,\ 1.43275002). \tag{8} The complete four-component evolution conserves that matrix and is covariant under a common change of traveling polarization basis. Its scalar-pattern measure changes from 0.211053195 to 0.210230023. The full physical rotation test separately rotates the propagation direction and Clifford matrices; the larger basis symmetry of the transversely homogeneous class is not labeled a physical gauge symmetry. Exact mismatched crossings provide another control. Orthogonal complex polarizations with arbitrary carriers evolve as the two free pulses through their entire overlap, with zero scalar source. Real-envelope quarter-turn phase preparations also give the exact zero predicted by the local equation; adding a spatial phase opens that latter cancellation. The same spatial depths permit a nonzero source when their polarizations are changed. The weak-scattering test independently reduces g from 0.04 to 0.02 to 0.01. Its combined full-field error against the first-order map is 5.61\times10^{-4}, 1.39\times10^{-4}, and 3.47\times10^{-5}, respectively, confirming the predicted quadratic remainder. Interpretation This calculation supplies a concrete mechanism for reciprocal change of spatial compatibility within the written local scalar equation. It also supplies exact polarization-sensitive noninteractions under that same rule. Both results retain the complete scalar cross term, physical propagation, complex phases and the response of both patterns. Its limits remain substantial: the pulses are unbound in transverse space, their geometry is flat, their physical particle identity is unspecified, and distinct-depth embeddings and observed electric and weak vertices have not been derived. Successful conservation and convergence establish the conditional field calculation, not experimental support for IDWT. Verification local_polarized_collision.py contains the complete local evolution and moment functions. local_polarized_collision_checks.py contains the independent full spatial solver, refinement comparisons, complete Clifford and polarization tests, exact mismatch controls, continuous positive-frequency integrals and both complex weak-scattering responses. All checks remain active under Python optimization.

title: Causal limit of an instantaneous scalar moment interaction
summary: Smooth spatially separated initial data show that the instantaneous scalar moment equation changes a local current before causal contact, so its physical use requires a controlled retarded reduction.
text:
Summary: Smooth spatially separated initial data show that the instantaneous scalar moment equation changes a local current before causal contact, so its physical use requires a controlled retarded reduction. A local observable tests the domain of dependence The common projective moment action gives i\partial_t\Psi=(D+V[\Psi] eta)\Psi, \qquad V_\Psi(X)=\kappa\int K(X,Y)\sigma(Y)\,d
u(Y), \quad \sigma=\Psi^\dagger eta\Psi, 	ag{1} where K(X,Y)=\operatorname{Tr}(P_XP_Y) and d

A state with both chirality components can therefore have a different local current derivative immediately, even though all its initial data near the target are identical. title: Spatial harmonics of the moment kernel and local response
summary: The projective moment kernel is exactly a screened inverse truncated to two scalar harmonic levels, while the derived local Dirac response retains higher harmonics, its induced sign and the direct contact term.
text:
Summary: The projective moment kernel is exactly a screened inverse truncated to two scalar harmonic levels, while the derived local Dirac response retains higher harmonics, its induced sign and the direct contact term. Then A\Pi_\ell=\lambda_\ell^2\Pi_\ell,\qquad \lambda_\ell^2= rac{4\ell(\ell+m)}{R^2}, 	ag{1} \dim\Pi_\ell=  inom{\ell+m}{m}^2- inom{\ell+m-1}{m}^2, \qquad \dim\Pi_0=1. 	ag{2} One construction uses bihomogeneous polynomials of degree (\ell,\ell) on \mathbb C^{m+1} restricted to the unit sphere and invariant under its common phase. title: Reciprocal spatial Dirac pair
summary: The same spatial moment interaction drives reciprocal deformation of complete complex Dirac profiles in an exact CP3–CP5 symmetry class, including a generated two-form component and phase-dependent changes in interaction overlap.
text: Summary: The same spatial moment interaction drives reciprocal deformation of complete complex Dirac profiles in an exact CP3–CP5 symmetry class, including a generated two-form component and phase-dependent changes in interaction overlap. The physical comparison and its scope Use the single spatial moment kernel on the specified linear inclusion \mathbb{CP}^a\subset\mathbb{CP}^{a+q}. The six-to-ten comparison has a=3,q=2. All spatial directions remain ordinary macroscopic dimensions of the same manifold. The projective topology, common metric scale, spin twists and current-family decomposition are explicit assumptions; no compactification is introduced. Take the lower spinor bundle to be \Lambda^{0,*}\otimes\mathcal O(L) and the higher one \Lambda^{0,*}\otimes\mathcal O(K), with their FS/Chern Dirac operators. The integer section degrees are independent of the auxiliary mass-band labels. Their normal bundle relation does not supply an occupied-state assignment. This calculation tests an aligned-center spatial symmetry class while retaining its complete complex field profiles. It is not a generic relative-orientation calculation or a replacement for the evolving electron–nucleus orbit. Its purpose is to determine whether the stated common kernel can actually change both spatial patterns under one action. A larger exact higher-dimensional spatial class Choose homogeneous coordinate blocks \mathbb C^{a+q+1}=\mathbb C\oplus\mathbb C^a\oplus\mathbb C^q. The first coordinate fixes the common profile center, the next a belong to the rest of the lower projective subspace, and the final q are normal to that chosen subspace. These are coordinate descriptions relative to the pair. A common physical isometry rotates all three blocks, both fields and the embedding together. Define the global intensity functions x=\frac{|Z_0|^2}{|Z|^2},\qquad z=\frac{\|Z_{\rm normal}\|^2}{|Z|^2},\qquad y=1-x-z, \tag{1} and the normalized holomorphic section \chi=\sqrt{\binom{K+a+q}{a+q}}Z_0^K. The higher field class is \boxed{\varphi_b=\chi\left[F+A\bar\partial x+C\bar\partial z +B\bar\partial x\wedge\bar\partial z\right],} \tag{2} with all four profiles arbitrary complex functions of (x,z). The exterior degrees are zero, one, one and two; their chirality signs are +,-,-,+. These are spinor components, not additional spatial dimensions. Smooth profiles define global sections, including where \chi or a displayed differential vanishes. The lower field retains the complete complex radial zero-form/one-form class in the spatial scalar branch. The higher field needs both variables: the lower source distinguishes shared directions from normal directions in the higher field equation. Measure, scalar current and the full Dirac derivative After angular integration, the norm of (2) uses the Dirichlet probability measure with parameters (K+1,a,q): w(x,z)\,dx\,dz =\frac{\Gamma(K+a+q+1)}{\Gamma(K+1)\Gamma(a)\Gamma(q)} x^K y^{a-1}z^{q-1}\,dx\,dz. \tag{3} The one-form metric and two-form squared norm are \boxed{G=2\begin{pmatrix}x(1-x)&-xz\\-xz&z(1-z)\end{pmatrix}, \qquad \Delta=\det G=4xyz.} \tag{4} Thus the positive norm density relative to w is |F|^2+(A,C)^\dagger G(A,C)+\Delta|B|^2, while the scalar current has the one-form term with a minus sign. No polarization component is discarded from this specified class. Write \mathscr S=K+a+q+1 and let d denote the restriction of \bar\partial to the displayed forms. Then dF=(F_x,F_z),\qquad d(A,C)=C_x-A_z,\qquad dB=0. \tag{5} Its weighted adjoints, computed with (3)–(4), are \boxed{d^\dagger(A,C)=-\frac1w\operatorname{div}\!\left[wG \begin{pmatrix}A\\C\end{pmatrix}\right],} \tag{6} \boxed{d^\dagger B=2\begin{pmatrix} z(1-z)B_z-xzB_x+(q-\mathscr S z)B\\ xzB_z-x(1-x)B_x+(\mathscr S x-K-1)B \end{pmatrix}.} \tag{7} The complete spatial Dirac operator in this class is D=\sqrt2(d+d^\dagger). These formulas can also be derived directly in all a+q complex chart coordinates using the FS inverse metric and the line connection. The three-form derivative vanishes identically; the other omitted form components are not generated. A scalar potential depending on x,z preserves the class. Equations (2) and (5)–(7) therefore define an exact invariant class of the spatial PDE. Local phase current Let \eta=(A,C)^{\mathsf T}. The positive norm obeys a local continuity equation after angular integration: \partial_t\left[w(|F|^2+\eta^\dagger G\eta+\Delta|B|^2)\right] +\partial_x(wj^x)+\partial_z(wj^z)=0, \tag{8} where \boxed{\begin{pmatrix}j^x\\j^z\end{pmatrix} =2\sqrt2\operatorname{Im}\left[ \bar F G\eta-\bar B\Delta\begin{pmatrix}C\\-A\end{pmatrix} \right].} \tag{9} The real scalar potential adds no source to (8). It changes the relative phases and thereby changes these spatial currents. Equation (9) retains the two-form contribution as well as the zero-form/one-form one. The positive phase norm is not an assigned electric charge. One interaction and both evolving moment matrices Let the lower scalar block moments be (u_a,v_a) and the higher ones be (u_b,v_b,w_b), obtained by integrating the signed scalar current against the three coordinate intensities. The lower field has no normal block. Their ambient matrices are M_a=\operatorname{diag}\left(u_a,\frac{v_a}{a}I_a,0_q\right), \qquad M_b=\operatorname{diag}\left(u_b,\frac{v_b}{a}I_a, \frac{w_b}{q}I_q\right). \tag{10} Put U=u_a+u_b, V=v_a+v_b, W=w_b. The same interaction energy is \boxed{E_{\rm int}=\frac\kappa2 \left[U^2+\frac{V^2}{a}+\frac{W^2}{q}\right], \qquad I_{ab}=\operatorname{Tr}(M_aM_b) =u_au_b+\frac{v_av_b}{a}.} \tag{11} Its full higher potential is \kappa[Ux+Vy/a+Wz/q]. The lower potential is its restriction to the lower space, \kappa[Ut+V(1-t)/a]. Every moment varies with its own complete complex field. The coefficients 1/a,1/q are the normalized block multiplicities of the same ambient trace, not separate pair couplings. A canonical approximation with a spatial residual Use polynomial degrees at most N for F, N-1 for each of A,C, and N-2 for B. This entire polynomial form complex is invariant under the linear operator (5)–(7). It has \boxed{2N^2+2N+1} \tag{12} complex modes, with both Dirac signs and one zero mode. No nonlinear invariance is claimed for a finite cutoff; the moment potential can generate higher polynomial degree. The zero-form basis uses the normalized polynomials (1-x)^jP_i^{(a+q+2j-1,K)}(2x-1) P_j^{(a-1,q-1)}\!\left(\frac{2z}{1-x}-1\right), \qquad i+j\le N. Their norms follow from the two beta measures in the coordinates x and z/(1-x). The one-form and two-form Gram matrices include G and \Delta; positive Cholesky transformations make all coefficient kinetic norms canonical. The nonlinear energy remains (11), so its ordinary and conjugate Hessians follow from the same three moment matrices. Refinement checks the time derivative against the uncompressed differential expressions (5)–(7) on a separate spatial grid. Agreement of a few moment values alone is not the convergence criterion. Reciprocal changing overlap in a specified preparation For a=3,q=2,L=K=1, set both phase norms to one and use \kappa=2 in common radius units. Prepare each field in its own stationary branch of the same smooth kernel, then evolve their autonomous complete pair action. No target is held fixed and no time-dependent alignment force is imposed. Over the sampled interval 0\le t\le20: Scalar interaction overlap Value Initial I_{ab} 0.199482310985 Sampled minimum, at t=6.1 0.194893252070 Sampled maximum, at t=6.7 0.200660187556 The overlap becomes both smaller and larger than its initial value. It is not monotone. The initially absent higher two-form component acquires a squared norm of about 1.049\times10^{-7} by the sampled time t=18.8. This component belongs to the actual spatial spinor equation; freezing the original one-variable profile removes it. Cutoffs N=5 and N=7 agree on these overlap values to better than 10^{-10}. At the listed times and two additional checks, the maximum uncompressed spatial residual drops from about 1.2\times10^{-9} to 2.4\times10^{-13}. These are deterministic numerical checks of the stated model, not measured particle interaction strengths. The phase dependence is separately observable in the equations. Starting from the same two self profiles, multiply all lower odd components by e^{0.6i} and all higher odd components by e^{-0.4i}. The entire initial positive and scalar densities remain unchanged, as does I_{ab}. Its initial derivative becomes approximately -0.000820812710. Conjugating both preparations gives the same instantaneous densities and +0.000820812710 instead. This is a mathematical phase/reversal comparison, with no antiparticle assignment. What has been established The common kernel can drive reciprocal changes in complete spatial profiles within this exact symmetry class, with conserved norms and energy. Both signs of changing scalar overlap occur without an imposed steering rule. This is a spatial Dirac counterpart to the finite coherent-mode deformation example, with its own action and different constraints. The aligned embedding and profile symmetry remain restrictions. Stable occupied particles, arbitrary relative orientations, phase-sensitive cross-current terms from the master field, the actual electron orbit, and observed electromagnetic and weak vertices have not been derived. The calculation supplies a reproducible full-equation test for a common kernel, rather than a depth-only interaction coefficient. Verification projective_spatial_pair_checks.py checks the actual coordinate Dirac operator through two-form degree, three-form closure, local continuity, complete canonical mode metrics, both nonlinear Hessian blocks, same-kernel self-branch normalization, reciprocal trajectories, phase preparations and refined spatial residuals.
