title: One spatial kernel on a projective chain
summary: A single bounded spatial moment kernel gives reciprocal full-spinor Dirac equations on specified nested projective sectors, with conserved norms, global evolution and no independent interaction coefficient for each pair.
text: Summary: A single bounded spatial moment kernel gives reciprocal full-spinor Dirac equations on specified nested projective sectors, with conserved norms, global evolution and no independent interaction coefficient for each pair. A declared common spatial action Consider any finite nested family of linear projective spatial submanifolds inside one specified containing projective space. Their metric, embeddings and spin or Spin^c connections are fixed. These are ordinary physical spatial directions within the same manifold; no dimension is compactified. The projective geometry and its physical scale remain conditional inputs. This finite family is a partial chain of even-dimensional submanifolds. The intermediate-depth calculation shows why it cannot automatically be filled in at every ordinary spatial depth: for example, the standard CP3-to-CP5 inclusion admits no seven- or nine-dimensional intermediate submanifold. The pair action below remains conditional on its specified partial family; it does not complete the geometry of the full hierarchy. For each family d, let \psi_d be its complete spatial spinor and D_d its self-adjoint Dirac operator, with chirality involution \beta_d. Use canonical positive kinetic norms. This specifies an orthogonal decomposition of retained mode families of the one field and the additive scalar source below. If another decomposition has cross kinetic or cross-current terms, those terms must be retained rather than inferred away from spatial nesting; see canonical normalization. Let i_d embed the spatial sector in the common projective space and put P_X=XX^\dagger/(X^\dagger X). Specify the same kernel everywhere: \boxed{K(X,Y)=\operatorname{Tr}(P_XP_Y) =\frac{|X^\dagger Y|^2}{|X|^2|Y|^2}.} \tag{1} There is no dimension-dependent multiplier in (1). Its unit-FS integral on CPm is 1/(m+1), which follows from the geometry. Normalizing it separately to one at every depth would change the common kernel. Using each sector's physical spatial measure, define \sigma_d=\psi_d^\dagger\beta_d\psi_d,\qquad M_d=\int P_{i_d(x)}\sigma_d(x)\,d\mathrm{vol}_d(x),\qquad M=\sum_dM_d. \tag{2} The matrices M_d are moments of the same field's scalar currents. They are not extra spatial dimensions, independent dynamical fields or mediator particles. The complete energy is \boxed{E=\sum_d\langle\psi_d,D_d\psi_d\rangle +\frac\kappa2\operatorname{Tr}M^2.} \tag{3} Writing Q_d=\|\psi_d\|^2, the single coefficient has units [\kappa]=[E]/[Q_d]^2. A common radius can be used to express time and \kappa dimensionlessly. No separate self or pair coefficient is fitted. This is a specified reduction to test, not a derivation of (1)–(3) from the master action. Scalar bilinears make the interaction globally defined without a spinor-to-spinor bundle identification between different sectors. It describes scalar-current interaction, not a particle-changing vertex. The normal spinor factors remain relevant when such a vertex or a nonscalar current is proposed. The interaction in (3) is spatially nonlocal and instantaneous: every potential uses the other sources at the same time. Its mathematical well-posedness below does not establish relativistic causal propagation. A physical use as an effective interaction requires a controlled reduction of local master-field dynamics, with the omitted propagation times and response frequencies specified. The local-current causality test now gives smooth, norm-preserving separated initial data for which this instantaneous equation changes the target's current derivative immediately. The spatial harmonic comparison identifies the kernel as a specific low-harmonic truncation, and shows why the direct term and signed induced response of local Dirac dynamics do not yet derive it. Both complete spatial responses Varying (3), including the dependence of every moment on its field, gives \boxed{i\partial_t\psi_d =\left[D_d+\kappa\operatorname{Tr}(P_{i_d(x)}M)\beta_d\right]\psi_d.} \tag{4} For two families, the cross energy is \kappa\operatorname{Tr}(M_aM_b). The response of either family uses the other one's same moment matrix. In particular, the lower response and the higher response contain the weighted marginal and its adjoint; the higher-dimensional potential is a smooth function on its full space. Every spinor component and relative phase within each field remains in (4). This particular additive scalar-current action has an independent overall phase symmetry for each family. Consequently Q_d=\|\psi_d\|^2 is separately conserved, while energy can move between the families. These phase norms have not been assigned physical electric charges. For static geometry, (3) is conserved on sufficiently regular solutions. The entire construction is covariant under a common projective isometry of the fields and all embeddings: P\mapsto UPU^\dagger and M\mapsto UMU^\dagger. Rotating one source while holding its physical embedding fixed is a different configuration, not this covariance test. Global evolution follows from the conserved norms The signed scalar current satisfies |\sigma_d|\le|\psi_d|^2. Hence, with Q_{\rm tot}=\sum_dQ_d, \boxed{\|M\|_{\rm op}\le Q_{\rm tot},\qquad |\kappa\operatorname{Tr}(P_XM)|\le|\kappa|Q_{\rm tot}.} \tag{5} On the direct sum of the sector L^2 spaces, write the nonlinear part of (4) as F(\psi). For two fields in the ball of squared norm at most Q_*, the moment difference obeys \|M(\psi)-M(\phi)\|_{\rm op} \le(\|\psi\|+\|\phi\|)\|\psi-\phi\|. Adding and subtracting the potential of \psi acting on \phi gives \boxed{\|F(\psi)-F(\phi)\| \le3|\kappa|Q_*\|\psi-\phi\|.} \tag{6} The free Dirac group is unitary. Its Duhamel equation with the locally Lipschitz nonlinearity (6) therefore has a unique local mild L^2 solution. Conservation of the positive norms keeps it in the same ball, so it extends for all finite times. The norm identity can first be proved for smooth approximations and then passed to their L^2 limit. Smooth initial fields remain smooth. All spatial derivatives of the potential are bounded by a geometry-dependent constant times |\kappa|Q_{\rm tot}, because it is a finite linear combination of smooth projective moment functions. Standard differentiated energy estimates bound every fixed Sobolev norm on finite time intervals. This argument concerns the complete spinor equations, independently of a finite-mode approximation or a profile symmetry. Global existence is not stability of a particular particle. The spatial Dirac energy has both signs; (5) does not supply an orbital stability theorem or a preferred occupied mode. Spatial phase information changes subsequent interaction For a fixed scalar test function f, the scalar moment is m_f=\langle\psi,f\beta\psi\rangle. On a regular solution, \boxed{\dot m_f=i\langle\psi,[D,f\beta]\psi\rangle.} \tag{7} The nonlinear term cancels from this first derivative because two scalar multiplication operators times \beta commute. It changes the field and therefore changes later values of (7). A holomorphic or other finite projection can alter this commutator, so its moment flow must not be substituted for the uncompressed spatial equation. The spatially varying relative phase between even and odd form components is consequential. Multiplying all odd components by e^{i\theta} leaves the instantaneous scalar density unchanged, but generally changes (7). Opposite phase preparations can therefore have identical initial scalar interaction overlap and different subsequent responses. The full spatial pair calculation supplies an explicit example and checks its coordinate residuals. Relation to the single-sector kernel and mass question On a single CP3 sector, (1) is one quarter of the normalized kernel in the smooth moment-contact calculation. That conversion must be included when using its stationary solver. For general complex dimension m, its normalized-kernel strength is \kappa Q/(m+1) in common radius units. A normalized coherent holomorphic section of degree L on a projective subspace with projector P_A has M=Q\frac{P_A+LP_z}{L+m+1},\qquad \boxed{\frac{\operatorname{Tr}M^2}{Q^2} =\frac{(L+1)^2+m}{(L+m+1)^2}\le1.} \tag{8} Thus this fixed bounded kernel does not itself produce an unbounded simplex mass multiplier. Its constructive role is a common, reciprocal, well-defined spatial interaction whose field response can be tested. Its derivation, physical scale, occupied patterns and observed electric and weak channels remain separate requirements. Verification projective_spatial_pair.py implements the same action and both full complex source derivatives in an exact spatial symmetry class. projective_spatial_pair_checks.py checks the ordinary and conjugate response, canonical kinetic forms, independent coordinate equations, conserved norms and energy, and refined spatial pair trajectories. The global existence argument above is analytic and does not follow merely from successful finite evolution.

Conditional integration therefore gives R_{p,c	o a}=R_{p,b	o a}R_{p,c	o b}, with the reverse order for adjoints. This is source reduction, not propagation through another particle. title: Normal spinors in projective nesting
summary: The standard physical CP3 inclusion in CP5 has an explicit global normal-spinor decomposition and Abelian normal holonomy, with twist-dependent parallel factors that sharpen the six-to-ten coupling test.
text:
Summary: The standard physical CP3 inclusion in CP5 has an explicit global normal-spinor decomposition and Abelian normal holonomy, with twist-dependent parallel factors that sharpen the six-to-ten coupling test. The specified spatial embedding Consider the candidate physical inclusion \mathbb{CP}^a\hookrightarrow\mathbb{CP}^{a+q},\qquad [Z]\longmapsto[Z,0], 	ag{1} with the same FS metric scale and its induced connections. Here a,q are complex dimensions: the lower spatial depth is 2a, the higher depth is 2(a+q) and the normal spatial depth is 2q. The electron–tau comparison is a=3,q=2. These are ordinary spatial submanifolds of the same physical manifold. The split is relative to the chosen lower submanifold, not a division into different kinds of dimensions in the higher particle. No dimension is compactified. The global projective geometries, embedding and metric are explicit hypotheses, rather than consequences of depth alone. The pointwise branching S_{10}^+=(S_6^+\otimes S_4^+)\oplus(S_6^-\otimes S_4^-) does not yet specify the bundles or their connection. Equation (1) allows those data to be computed. Normal bundle and actual holonomy Write A=\mathbb C^{a+1}, W=\mathbb C^q and let \ell\subset A denote the tautological line at a spatial point. The tangent space of the ambient projective manifold restricts as \operatorname{Hom}(\ell,(A\oplus W)/\ell) =\operatorname{Hom}(\ell,A/\ell) \oplus\operatorname{Hom}(\ell,W). Thus the complex normal bundle is  oxed{N=\mathcal O(1)\otimes W.} 	ag{2} The linear projective subspace is totally geodesic. Its normal connection is the Chern connection on \mathcal O(1) tensored with the constant identity on W. This can be verified directly from the ambient spatial metric. In the chart [1,z,w], put t=(1+|z|^2)^{-1} on w=0. The normal Hermitian metric is tI_q, so its connection in a holomorphic frame is  oxed{
abla^N=d+\alpha I_q,\qquad \alpha=\partial\log t=-t\sum_i ar z_i\,dz_i.} 	ag{3} The ambient Christoffel symbols satisfy \Gamma^\mu_{i
u}=-t ar z_i\delta^\mu_
u and \Gamma^\mu_{ij}=0 for normal indices \mu,
u and tangent indices i,j. The latter equality is the vanishing second fundamental form. In the curvature-four convention, F^N=-2i\omega_{m FS}I_q. 	ag{4} For radius R, write the same formula as F^N=-2i\omega_R I_q/R^2. All curvature endomorphisms lie on one central line. Since they are nonzero and the base is simply connected, the normal vector holonomy is exactly the central U(1). The available normal-frame group SO(2q) is much larger than this particular connection's holonomy. The complete normal spinor factors For even q, c_1(N)=qH is even and the normal bundle is spin. Using the complex structure and its unique spin structure gives \Sigma N=\Lambda^*N\otimes(\det N)^{-1/2} = igoplus_{k=0}^{q} \mathcal O(k-q/2)\otimes\Lambda^kW. 	ag{5} Here the Hermitian metric identifies the usual antiholomorphic cotangent description of spinors with \Lambda^*N. Exterior parity specifies chirality. Formula (5) is a unitary, connection-preserving decomposition; the normal-bundle identification and parallel splitting also appear in Ginoux and Habib, Lemma 4.2 and Corollary 4.4. The normal holonomy weight is k-q/2 and its multiplicity is  inom qk. The curvature on that summand is (k-q/2)F_{\mathcal O(1)}. Therefore its covariantly constant sections vanish unless k=q/2. Precisely  oxed{\dim\ker
abla^{\Sigma N}= inom q{q/2}.} 	ag{6} This is a count of parallel normal polarizations on the specified lower space, not the number of particles or the kernel of the full ambient Dirac operator. If q is odd, the normal bundle in (2) is not spin; a Spin^c construction and its determinant line must be retained. For a=3,q=2, the two chiral normal bundles are  oxed{\Sigma^+N=\mathcal O(-1)\oplus\mathcal O(1), \qquad \Sigma^-N=\mathbf1\otimes\mathbb C^2.} 	ag{7} The second doublet is globally parallel; the first consists of two curved line bundles. In these chirality conventions the global version of the sixteen-dimensional branching is  oxed{ \left.\Sigma^+\mathbb{CP}^5ight|_{\mathbb{CP}^3} =\Sigma^+\mathbb{CP}^3\otimes [\mathcal O(-1)\oplus\mathcal O(1)] \ \oplus\ \Sigma^-\mathbb{CP}^3\otimes\mathbb C^2.} 	ag{8} It is a splitting along the lower spatial submanifold. It does not split T\mathbb{CP}^5 into rank three and rank two over all of CP5, which the global tangent obstruction excludes. Retain the physical line twists The selected electron construction uses \Sigma\mathbb{CP}^3\otimes\mathcal O(L+2), rather than the untwisted spinor bundle. More generally, on odd complex dimension a, write \mathcal S_a(L)=\Sigma\mathbb{CP}^a \otimes\mathcal O igl(L+(a+1)/2 igr) =\Lambda^{0,*}T^*\mathbb{CP}^a\otimes\mathcal O(L). Restrict the corresponding higher bundle \mathcal S_{a+q}(K). Combining its relative line twist with (5) yields  oxed{ \left.\mathcal S_{a+q}(K)ight|_{\mathbb{CP}^a} = igoplus_{k=0}^{q} \mathcal S_a(L)\,\widehat\otimes\,  igl[\mathcal O(K-L+k)\otimes\Lambda^kW igr].} 	ag{9} The hat retains normal exterior parity. This formula also has the canonical Spin^c interpretation when an ordinary spin splitting is unavailable. Its relative factor is parallel exactly when k=L-K. Consequently the number of parallel normal factors is  oxed{  egin{cases}  inom q{L-K},&0\le L-K\le q,\ 0,&	ext{otherwise}. \end{cases}} 	ag{10} For the six-to-ten comparison this becomes: Relative section degree Parallel normal factor Normal exterior parity L=K 1 even, k=0 L=K+1 2 odd, k=1 L=K+2 1 even, k=2 Other L-K 0 none In particular, matching two holomorphic degree-zero spinor components with the same section degree uses k=0. It does not automatically occupy the two-state normal factor. A full projected field can contain other form components, but their dynamics and occupation must be computed. The section degrees here are not the auxiliary cumulative mass-band labels. These line weights are geometric connection weights, with no electric charge or particle–antiparticle assignment made here. The projective mass inheritance test applies this connection formula to the new simplex polynomial. Canonical CP5 contains its required lower line degree at top normal degree. Full normal Clifford derivatives mix that component, and complete form-degree matching constrains a shared construction at both depths. Global intermediate spatial depths The normal characteristic obstruction adds a constraint to (2): its real normal Euler class is H^q. When q\le a, the specified inclusion cannot factor through a smooth odd-dimensional intermediate space. For CP3 inside CP5, this excludes intermediate depths seven and nine. A parallel normal spinor doublet is compatible with that obstruction: it is not a frame of ordinary normal vectors. The direct six-to-ten inclusion and its branching remain valid; the missing intermediate embeddings cannot be inferred from them. What the geometry permits and what it selects Parallel normal endomorphisms may mix equal holonomy weights. Their complex dimension in (5) is \dim\operatorname{End}_{m Hol}(\Sigma N) =\sum_{k=0}^{q} inom qk^2= inom{2q}q. 	ag{11} For q=2, this is six: two scalar blocks on \Sigma^+N and the four-dimensional matrix algebra on the parallel doublet \Sigma^-N. Thus parallel transport alone permits a full two-by-two matrix there; it does not determine that matrix or its eigenvalues. There is a second symmetry constraint. Normal rotations of W are ambient isometries fixing the entire embedded lower subspace. Their SU(2) action on the parallel doublet is irreducible. An interaction invariant under all those rotations acts as a scalar on the doublet. It cannot choose a unique line or split its two eigenvalues. Selecting a normal pattern can break that symmetry, but then the pattern and its response are additional dynamical data of the same field. The standard FS normal connection itself remains Abelian. A non-Abelian normal response needs a changed geometry or a derived field-dependent connection; the existence of an SU(2) frame action does not supply it. The separate gauge-carrier construction makes the same structure-group/holonomy distinction on a different bundle. Equations (8)–(10) sharpen the charged-lepton test: the proposed pair's twists, form components and normal current must match a global factor. The resulting vertex still needs its spatial matrix element and canonical kinetic normalization. Neither the parallel multiplicity nor the invariant-endomorphism count fixes a mass ratio, an observed weak coupling or neutrino neutrality. Verification projective_normal_bundle_checks.py checks the ambient coordinate connection and vanishing mixed second fundamental form, normal curvature and loop transport, full Clifford holonomy weights and chiral restrictions, twist-dependent parallel multiplicities, Chern-character compatibility and invariant matrix spaces.

title: Scalar Dirac branch on proposed CP3

Summary: The specified twisted Dirac field on physical CP3 admits an exact spatial symmetry reduction and a small scalar-contact branch, with opposite chirality and an explicit cubic frequency correction. Physical geometry, bundle and normalization The proposed electron \mathbb{CP}^3 is an actual six-dimensional physical spatial manifold. This calculation tests a stationary scalar contact field on that geometry. It does not replace the electron–nucleus orbit construction with a stationary orbital. IDWT has no compactified dimensions. Its six electron directions are ordinary macroscopic spatial dimensions of the same kind as the three shared with an ordinary observer. The global CP3 topology and FS metric used here are explicit geometric hypotheses. Mathematical compactness of that candidate does not make any direction hidden, curled up, or small; the physical scale remains undetermined. Results using its finite volume or discrete spatial spectrum are conditional on those geometric hypotheses. Use the specified spinor-line lift: the spin twist \mathcal O(L+2) gives the full bundle \Lambda^{0,*}\otimes\mathcal O(L) and the spatial Dirac operator \mathscr D_L=\sqrt2( ar\partial_L+ ar\partial_L^\dagger). The integer L\ge0 and its Chern connection remain inputs. This selected construction preserves the full spinor-bundle obstruction. For the derivation, write m for complex dimension, with m=3 in the physical comparison. On \mathbb{CP}^m, the same formulas use the specified canonical Spin^c bundle \Lambda^{0,*}\otimes\mathcal O(L). Let the FS metric have holomorphic sectional curvature 4/R^2 and physical volume \mathcal V=\pi^mR^{2m}/m!. Its unit-volume measure is d

u.} 	ag{1} This is a specified spatial reduction of the scalar contact action. Its geometry and connection change the hypotheses of the flat radial theorem. An exact spatial symmetry class Choose a projective center and normalized coherent holomorphic section \chi=\sqrt{D_L}Z_0^L, with D_L= inom{L+m}{m},\qquad t= rac{|Z_0|^2}{|Z|^2},\qquad ho_0=|\chi|^2=D_Lt^L. The radial measure weighted by this section is w(t)dt=ho_0\,m(1-t)^{m-1}dt = rac{t^L(1-t)^{m-1}}{\mathrm B(L+1,m)}dt. 	ag{2} Retain the complete complex functions in the spinor class  oxed{\varphi=\chi\,[F(t)+G(t) ar\partial t].} 	ag{3} The two terms have exterior degrees zero and one. They are spatial spinor components, not two extra dimensions. Smooth F,G give global sections, including at the zeros of \chi. Since  ar\partial\chi=0 and  ar\partial(G ar\partial t)=0, the two-form part of the Dirac derivative vanishes identically. The scalar source in (1) also preserves (3). The norm and scalar are \|\varphi\|^2=\int_0^1w(|F|^2+a|G|^2)dt, \qquad \sigma=ho_0(|F|^2-a|G|^2). 	ag{4} Adjointness in this weighted measure gives the full Dirac action:  oxed{\mathscr D_L(F\chi)=\sqrt2F'\chi ar\partial t, \qquad \mathscr D_L(G\chi ar\partial t) =- rac{\sqrt2}{w}(waG)'\chi.} 	ag{5} It can also be checked in physical complex coordinates on the chart Z_0
e0. There t=(1+|z|^2)^{-1}, the line metric is t^L, and g^{i ar j}=t^{-1}(\delta_{ij}+z_i ar z_j). For a line-valued one-form \eta, the adjoint is  ar\partial_L^\dagger\eta=-2g^{i ar j} (\partial_i\eta_{ ar j}-Lt ar z_i\eta_{ ar j}). Substituting \eta=G ar\partial t\chi gives \mathscr D_L(G\chi ar\partial t) =-2\sqrt2\,[t(1-t)G'+(L+1-(L+m+1)t)G]\chi. 	ag{6} This independent coordinate formula fixes the metric factors and keeps all components of the spatial derivative. Complete Jacobi modes and the complementary gap On the zero-form part, (5) squares to \mathscr D_L^2(F\chi) =-4[t(1-t)F''+(L+1-(L+m+1)t)F']\chi. 	ag{7} Let p_n be P_n^{(m-1,L)}(2t-1) normalized in w(t)dt, so p_0=1. Jacobi's differential equation gives \mathscr D_L^2(\chi p_n)=\lambda_n^2\chi p_n, \qquad \lambda_n=2\sqrt{n(n+L+m)}. 	ag{8} This agrees with the corresponding twisted Dirac spectral family in Ginoux and Habib, Theorem 4.5, using tautological twist exponent -L-(m+1)/2 when m is odd. Equation (7) derives the needed family directly; no other spectral family is removed from the physical theory by this calculation. For n\ge1, define the normalized one-forms q_n=\mathscr D_L(\chi p_n)/\lambda_n. Then \mathscr D_Lq_n=\lambda_n\chi p_n. The complete basis in (3) consists of \chi, these zero-form modes and their one-form partners. Their energies are zero and \pm\lambda_n. The zero mode is simple in this fixed symmetry class, and the complement has gap \lambda_1=2\sqrt{L+m+1}. Its complex extension supplies the allowed time-dependent perturbations. Common physical FS isometries rotate the center and the entire spinor construction together, giving the corresponding family of branches. u= rac{D_L^2}{D_{2L}},\qquad q=(ho_0-A)\chi,\qquad \eta=-\mathscr D_{L,\perp}^{-1}q. 	ag{9} The projected source has zero component along \chi. The full branch has the expansion \varphi=\chi+\varepsilon\eta+\varepsilon^2\xi+O(\varepsilon^3), \qquad \langle\chi,\xiangle=-	frac12\|\eta\|^2. 	ag{10} The symmetry \varphi(-\varepsilon)= eta\varphi(\varepsilon) makes the frequency odd in \varepsilon. Expanding (1) gives \mathscr D_L\xi=(A+ho_0)\eta. Hence \langleho_0\chi,\xiangle =- rac{3A}{2}\|\eta\|^2-\intho_0|\eta|^2d
u. Projection of the next order onto \chi yields  oxed{\Omega=\varepsilon A-4\varepsilon^3J+O(\varepsilon^5), \qquad \mathcal E= rac{\varepsilon A}{2}-\varepsilon^3J +O(\varepsilon^5), \quad J=A\|\eta\|^2+\intho_0|\eta|^2d
u.} 	ag{11} J>0 for L>0. The vanishing second-order massless correction in the orbit-drive analysis therefore does not imply all-order protection for this nonlinear source. For m=3,L=1, p_1=5t-2 and direct beta integrals give A= rac85,\quad \|\eta\|^2= rac4{125},\quad \intho_0|\eta|^2d
u= rac{48}{875},\quad  oxed{\Omega= rac85\varepsilon- rac{1856}{4375}\varepsilon^3 +O(\varepsilon^5).} 	ag{12} For L=0, the constant section instead solves the full equation exactly with \Omega=\varepsilon. The finite volume of this proposed global geometry supplies the normalization absent from the flat infinite-space comparison. That conclusion is conditional on the global CP3 model and does not invoke compactification. Interpretation and verification The physical frequency is \omega=\Omega/R, with \varepsilon=gQR/\mathcal V. It depends on the specified spatial geometry, norm and complete profile, as in local scalar normalization. The count D_L= inom{L+3}{3} belongs to physical CP3 sections; it is distinct from the auxiliary six-direction cumulative mass count  inom{N+6}{6}. Neither L=N nor a particle mass assignment follows. Existence also does not imply stability. The local-contact instability detects an unstable Dirac complement for every L>0 at sufficiently small nonzero coupling. A smooth physical moment kernel gives a different controlled stability comparison. cp3_scalar_dirac.py retains all complex coefficients in successive finite approximations to (3), with exact quartic quadrature and normalized branch continuation. cp3_scalar_dirac_checks.py checks independent coordinate derivatives, complete component closure, Jacobi normalization, the frequency expansion, conjugate response and uncompressed spatial residuals on refined grids.

title: Local contact instability on proposed CP3
summary: Every positive-degree coherent branch of the specified massless local scalar Dirac action on physical CP3 has a small-coupling oscillatory instability in its complete radial Dirac complement.
text: Summary: Every positive-degree coherent branch of the specified massless local scalar Dirac action on physical CP3 has a small-coupling oscillatory instability in its complete radial Dirac complement. Precise statement Use the metric, twist, normalization and full spatial equation of the specified CP3 scalar branch. The physical space is CP3, the bare mass is zero, and the interaction is local \varepsilon(\varphi^\dagger\beta\varphi)\beta\varphi. For each fixed integer L\ge1, its branch through the coherent holomorphic section is spectrally unstable for every sufficiently small nonzero \varepsilon. The proof retains both Dirac signs and conjugate variations. The unstable mode belongs to an exact invariant class of spatial spinors, so it is also an instability of the full specified field equation. The statement does not extend automatically to other kernels, additional field terms, other branches or arbitrary coupling strengths. It does not make a particle–antiparticle identification from Dirac signs. Full complex linearization Expand both chirality components in the complete Jacobi modes and write their complex coefficients as c. At a real stationary profile, the linearized gradient in its rotating frame has the form i\dot\eta=(A-\Omega I)\eta+B\bar\eta, \qquad A=A^\dagger,\quad B=B^{\mathsf T}. \tag{1} The bar denotes conjugation of the mode coefficients in this linearization. Setting \eta=x+iy gives \dot x=L_-y,\qquad \dot y=-L_+x, \qquad L_\pm=A\pm B-\Omega I. \tag{2} For a real spatial background with components F and H=\sqrt aG, the nonlinear part of L_+ has pointwise blocks \varepsilon\rho_0 \begin{pmatrix}3F^2-H^2&-2FH\\-2FH&3H^2-F^2\end{pmatrix}, \tag{3} integrated with the respective zero-form and one-form basis functions. The nonlinear part of L_- is \varepsilon\rho_0(F^2-H^2)\operatorname{diag}(1,-1). Both include the full Dirac off-diagonal operator and subtract \Omega. In particular L_-c=0 is the exact phase-symmetry zero mode. Opposite-energy modes form a resonant pair At zero coupling, let u_n=\chi p_n and v_n=\mathscr D_Lu_n/\lambda_n. The complete Dirac modes are (u_n\pm v_n)/\sqrt2 with energies \pm\lambda_n. In (1), a positive-energy coefficient and the conjugate of a negative-energy coefficient have the same unperturbed frequency +\lambda_n. Dropping either removes this resonance. Let A_0=\int\rho_0^2d\nu,\qquad U_n=\int_0^1w\rho_0p_n^2dt,\qquad V_n=\int_0^1w\rho_0Q_n^2dt. The first-order matrix on this two-dimensional frequency subspace is \boxed{\lambda_n I+\varepsilon \begin{pmatrix}a_n&b_n\\-b_n&-a_n\end{pmatrix}, \qquad a_n=U_n-\frac{V_n}{2}-A_0, \quad b_n=\frac{U_n}{2}.} \tag{4} Thus its frequencies are \nu_{n,\pm}=\lambda_n\pm\varepsilon \sqrt{a_n^2-b_n^2}+O(\varepsilon^2). \tag{5} The actual stationary profile differs from \chi at order \varepsilon. Since it enters the nonlinear Hessian multiplied by \varepsilon, that correction changes (4) only at the next order. The first level is unstable at every positive degree For n=1, put s=L+m+1. The normalized Jacobi mode is p_1(t)=\sqrt{\frac{s+1}{(L+1)m}}[st-(L+1)], \qquad Q_1(t)=\sqrt{\frac{s(s+1)}{(L+1)m}}\sqrt{t(1-t)}. \tag{6} The measure w\rho_0/A_0 is the beta distribution with parameters (2L+1,m). Its first two moments evaluate (4). At m=3 this gives \frac{U_1}{A_0}=\frac{2(L+1)(L+5)}{(L+2)(2L+5)},\qquad \frac{V_1}{A_0}= \frac{(L+4)(L+5)(2L+1)}{2(L+1)(L+2)(2L+5)}. \tag{7} Substitution and factorization produce the exact sign: \boxed{\frac{a_1^2-b_1^2}{A_0^2} =-\frac{L(2L^2+21L+7)(6L^3+35L^2+81L+40)} {16(L+1)^2(L+2)^2(2L+5)^2}<0\quad(L\ge1).} \tag{8} Every factor other than the displayed minus sign is positive. The physical exponential growth rate is consequently \Gamma=\frac{|\varepsilon|}{R}\sqrt{b_1^2-a_1^2} +O(\varepsilon^2/R), \tag{9} while the mode oscillates at frequency close to \lambda_1/R. This is an oscillatory instability, not the phase zero mode. For L=1, the coefficients reduce to A_0=\frac85,\quad U_1=\frac{64}{35},\quad V_1=\frac{12}{7}, \quad a_1=-\frac{22}{35},\quad b_1=\frac{32}{35}, \quad \boxed{\Gamma R=\sqrt{\frac{108}{245}}|\varepsilon| +O(\varepsilon^2).} \tag{10} At \varepsilon=10^{-3}, the leading growth is 0.0006639400022/R. Independent finite approximations to the corrected branch give the first growth pair near 0.0006639375673/R, with oscillation frequency near 4.4721371142/R. Why this is not an artifact of a finite cutoff In the complete radial class, the unperturbed frequencies \lambda_n=2\sqrt{n(n+L+3)} are discrete and separated. The cluster at +\lambda_1 has dimension two in the doubled equation (1). The smooth background on the specified global CP3 geometry makes the perturbation a bounded analytic operator on the same Dirac domain. Its Riesz projection is therefore an analytic finite-dimensional cluster, with first-order matrix exactly (4). The two nonreal eigenvalues supplied by (8) are distinct at first order. They persist for sufficiently small nonzero coupling; higher orders cannot cancel their leading imaginary parts. This proves the spectral statement for the complete symmetry class. The class is invariant under the full spatial equation, so these eigenmodes are valid spatial perturbations even when all other angular and spinor components are admitted. No convergence of the largest growth rate over all modes is needed for this proof. One unstable isolated pair is sufficient. Numerical near-zero roots associated with the phase Jordan block are also not the modes used in (8)–(10). Relation to the projected coherent calculation Restricting the action to holomorphic zero forms gives the smooth quartic with coefficient D_L^2/D_{2L}. Its finite holomorphic coherent set is orbitally stable within that finite action, taking its projective complex dimension to be three here. The missing radial one-form partners create the instability just proved. The comparison therefore distinguishes a stable projected pattern from a stable solution of the spatial Dirac equation. The smooth moment-kernel calculation changes the actual scalar interaction and tests which part of this resonance survives; it does not reinterpret the local-contact result. Verification cp3_scalar_dirac_checks.py checks the real and conjugate Hessian by independent differences, the exact beta moments and factorization, the first resonant pair at successively refined mode cutoffs, and the uncompressed spatial equation for each background. Its nonlinear evolutions retain both complex chirality profiles and the conserved norm and energy.

text:

This positive matrix fixes the full ordinary and conjugate response; holding S,T fixed would omit it. Corrected spatial branches At the coherent zero mode, the potential and first frequency are V_0(t)= rac{(m+1)(1+Lt)}{L+m+1},\qquad  oxed{A_1=\int wV_0dt = rac{(m+1)[(L+1)^2+m]}{(L+m+1)^2}.} 	ag{5} The same normalized implicit-function argument gives a small-coupling branch. Its odd first correction is \eta=-\mathscr D_{L,\perp}^{-1}(V_0-A_1)\chi and contains only the first Jacobi level. Kernel reciprocity gives the frequency \Omega=\varepsilon A_1-4\varepsilon^3 \left[A_1\|\eta\|^2+\int V_0|\eta|^2d
uight] +O(\varepsilon^5). 	ag{6} For m=3,L=1, A_1=28/25. This differs from the local value 8/5 because the physical action has changed. It is not a rescaling of an unchanged field profile. The complete radial resonance changes For each radial Dirac level, use U_n=\int wV_0p_n^2dt,\qquad V_n=\int wV_0Q_n^2dt, \qquad R_n=\iintho_0(Z)p_n(Z)K_1(Z,W)ho_0(W)p_n(W)d
u(Z)d
u(W). The first resonant matrix has the form already derived for local contact, but now  oxed{a_n= rac{U_n-V_n+R_n}{2}-A_1,\qquad b_n= rac{R_n}{2}.} 	ag{7} The finite-rank moment kernel and Jacobi orthogonality give  oxed{R_1= rac{(m+1)^2(L+1)}{(L+m+1)^2(L+m+2)}, \qquad R_n=0\quad(n\ge2).} 	ag{8} Indeed, the first variation of S pairs p_n with the constant, while the first variation of T pairs it with t. Only p_1 survives. Its contribution is C_{TT}\operatorname{Var}_w(t), which evaluates to (8). Counting modes cannot replace this source selection calculation. For m=3, \operatorname{osc}V_0=4L/(L+4) and |U_n-V_n|\le\operatorname{osc}V_0, because both modes are normalized. The following strictly positive margin controls every radial level:  oxed{A_1- rac12\operatorname{osc}V_0-R_1 = rac{2(L^3+5L^2+32)}{(L+4)^2(L+5)}>0.} 	ag{9} Since 0\le R_n\le R_1, (9) gives both a_n+b_n<0 and a_n-b_n<0, uniformly in n. Thus a_n^2-b_n^2>0 and every first-order radial frequency splitting is real, with a nonzero uniform separation at fixed L. There is a corresponding small-coupling spectral statement within this complete symmetry class. The free radial gaps satisfy \lambda_{n+1}-\lambda_n>2. The smooth branch produces a bounded analytic perturbation with a uniform O(\varepsilon^2) remainder. Separated Riesz clusters therefore have uniform first-order approximations (7). The two distinct real frequencies in each nonzero cluster remain in disjoint neighborhoods for sufficiently small nonzero coupling. The frequency matrix is real, so a single eigenvalue in each such neighborhood must remain real; a nonreal one would bring its conjugate into the same neighborhood. The two-dimensional zero cluster remains the phase mode and its norm-frequency generalized partner: varying the norm continues the nearby stationary family and its frequency, whose leading derivative is nonzero. These facts exclude exponential radial modes at sufficiently small coupling. This establishes spectral stability in the full complex radial class (3), not nonlinear orbital stability or stability against every angular and polarization perturbation of a particle. An exact resolution comparison Consider the declared positive mixture K_	heta=(1-	heta)K_1+	heta\delta, 0\le	heta\le1, where the delta uses the same unit FS measure. At equality the first-order test is degenerate and higher orders are required. This is a threshold in a specified family of kernels, not an observed coupling or a fitted IDWT parameter. What this comparison supplies The calculation changes a concrete feature of one scalar kernel and recomputes the stationary spatial field and its reciprocal response. It does not derive that kernel, select L, determine the physical radius, identify ordinary electric charge, or establish observed interactions between particles associated with the nested spatial sectors. title: Consistent band contacts
summary: A fixed bare kernel must have compatible cumulative compressions, while coherent projective contact changes under the standard band inclusion and effective kernels obey a different Schur consistency law.
text: Summary: A fixed bare kernel must have compatible cumulative compressions, while coherent projective contact changes under the standard band inclusion and effective kernels obey a different Schur consistency law. What a common bare operator requires At fixed spatial depth d, let \mathcal B_N=\bigoplus_{k=0}^N\operatorname{Sym}^k\mathbb C^d with normalized oscillator occupations |\alpha\rangle, |\alpha|\le N. Let I_N:\mathcal B_N\hookrightarrow\mathcal B_{N+1} preserve each existing occupation. These are mode labels on the same specified spatial sector, not additional physical dimensions. If a fixed bare operator or quadratic form A is defined on the union of these spaces, its compressions A_N=P_NAP_N satisfy \boxed{I_N^\dagger A_{N+1}I_N=A_N.} \tag{1} This follows by testing the two forms on any pair of vectors already in \mathcal B_N. Conversely, a Hermitian family satisfying (1) defines a unique form on finite occupation sums. Boundedness, closability and an infinite-space operator domain require additional control; finite consistency alone does not establish them. The spatial point form at a fixed position and width satisfies (1): its matrix entries \overline{h_\alpha(X)}h_\beta(X) remain the same when more modes are admitted. Its growing nonzero eigenvalue is consistent with an unchanged lower matrix block. Test the normalized homogenized coherent family Identify \mathcal B_N with \operatorname{Sym}^N(\mathbb C\oplus\mathbb C^d) using normalized occupation states. For a fixed unit vector z=(z_0,z_1,\ldots,z_d), the coherent coefficients are (v_N(z))_\alpha= \sqrt{\frac{N!}{(N-k)!\,\alpha!}}\, z_0^{N-k}z_1^{\alpha_1}\cdots z_d^{\alpha_d}, \qquad k=|\alpha|\le N. \tag{2} The standard cumulative inclusion adds one unused, or zeroth, occupation. Direct comparison of (2) at two consecutive bands gives I_N^\dagger v_{N+1}(z)=z_0 C_Nv_N(z), \qquad (C_N)_\alpha=\sqrt{\frac{N+1}{N+1-k}}. \tag{3} For \Lambda_N(z)=D_N|v_N(z)\rangle\langle v_N(z)| and D_N=\binom{N+d}{d}, the resulting compression is \boxed{I_N^\dagger\Lambda_{N+1}(z)I_N =D_{N+1}|z_0|^2C_N|v_N(z)\rangle\langle v_N(z)|C_N.} \tag{4} It is generally different from \Lambda_N(z). At z=e_0, the same ground matrix entry is D_{N+1} on the left and D_N on the right. For N\ge1 and a ray with nonzero z_0 and a nonzero transverse coordinate, C_N changes the relative ground and degree-one amplitudes, so even the compressed rank-one direction changes. A scalar rescaling alone cannot repair that directional difference. At z_0=0, the left side vanishes completely. Consequently, the projective point-contact family is not the sequence of compressions of one fixed linear form under this fixed-ray, normalized cumulative identification. Each individual projective contact theorem remains exact. The family uses a different homogeneous line bundle and evaluation map at each N. This is a test of a particular proposed operator bridge. If N labels different physical branches rather than a common cutoff, if the master operator depends on the full field, or if the spatial embedding and kinetic metric depend on N, their actual relations must replace (1). Such data cannot be inferred from equality of dimensions alone. Effective operators have Schur consistency Compression and effective reduction are different operations. Let D(\zeta)=A-\zeta I in a finite complete mode space, and split retained modes P_N from the complement Q_N. When the indicated inverses exist, eliminating the complement gives F_N(\zeta)=D_{NN}-D_{NQ}D_{QQ}^{-1}D_{QN}, \qquad \boxed{F_N(\zeta)^{-1}=P_ND(\zeta)^{-1}P_N.} \tag{5} The identity follows by solving the complementary block equation and substituting it into the retained equation. Hence it is the inverse effective operator that has the compression relation I_N^\dagger F_{N+1}(\zeta)^{-1}I_N=F_N(\zeta)^{-1}. \tag{6} Equivalently, taking a Schur complement through an intermediate band gives the same result as direct elimination. For a positive static Hessian, the eliminated block also fixes the sign of the correction: F_N=D_{NN}-B D_{QQ}^{-1}B^\dagger\le D_{NN}. Thus failure of (1) is not by itself a failure of an effective master reduction. A proposed effective family must instead supply the complementary modes, its frequency dependence and the consistency in (5)–(6). These are modes of the same field \Psi_\infty; no mediator particles have been introduced. The common field response also tracks its kinetic normalization and retarded boundary conditions. A controlled local limit of the coherent evaluation map There is a useful mathematical connection to an ordinary bosonic coherent coefficient sequence. In the affine chart set z=\frac{(1,a/\sqrt N)}{\sqrt{1+|a|^2/N}},\qquad a\in\mathbb C^d. For fixed occupation \alpha of degree k, (2) becomes (v_N)_\alpha= \sqrt{\frac{N(N-1)\cdots(N-k+1)}{N^k}} \left(1+\frac{|a|^2}{N}\right)^{-N/2} \frac{a^\alpha}{\sqrt{\alpha!}} \longrightarrow e^{-|a|^2/2}\frac{a^\alpha}{\sqrt{\alpha!}}. \tag{7} The measure must transform as well. Unit-volume FS measure in this chart is d\nu_{\rm FS}= \frac{d!}{\pi^dN^d}\left(1+\frac{|a|^2}{N}\right)^{-d-1} d^{2d}a. Since D_Nd!/N^d=\prod_{j=1}^d(1+j/N), its contact measure satisfies \boxed{D_Nd\nu_{\rm FS}\longrightarrow\pi^{-d}d^{2d}a} \tag{8} at fixed a. The coherent operator density then has a finite limit per unit a volume. Equations (7)–(8) are a local large-band limit, not an exact finite-band identification. The coordinates a describe mode amplitudes; they do not replace any physical spatial dimensions. Changing the measure in an action also transforms its delta functions and source coefficients. A normalization factor cannot simply be discarded while holding those other ingredients fixed. Finite ray resolution separately quantifies how a specified smooth symbol approaches point contact at fixed N. Verification coherent_kernel_consistency_checks.py checks (3)–(4) in every retained occupation, fixed spatial point compression, direct and staged complex Schur elimination, compressed resolvents and the coefficient/measure limits in (7)–(8).

title: Finite ray resolution
summary: A normalized coherent symbol of specified finite width has an exact full Toeplitz spectrum and a controlled point-contact error, with distinct fixed-width and fixed-band limits.
text: Summary: A normalized coherent symbol of specified finite width has an exact full Toeplitz spectrum and a controlled point-contact error, with distinct fixed-width and fixed-band limits. Specify a width independently of the retained band On the auxiliary mode-ray space \mathbb{CP}^d, use unit FS measure, \mathcal H_N=H^0(\mathbb{CP}^d,\mathcal O(N)) and D_N=\binom{N+d}{d}. These are the mode fibres of the projective contact comparison, not additional physical spatial dimensions. For a specified ray z and integer p\ge0, define the positive symbol f_{p,z}(u)=D_p|u^\dagger z|^{2p},\qquad \int f_{p,z}d\nu=1, \qquad T_{N,p}=P_N f_{p,z}P_N. \tag{1} Here p fixes the source width independently of the band N. p=0 is uniform; increasing p concentrates the source about z. It is a prescribed comparison symbol. Its width and source variation would need to follow from the master action in a physical application. Exact full spectrum Choose z=e_0. Phase integration makes T_{N,p} diagonal on normalized monomials. If their zeroth occupation is k, the FS moments are \int\prod_{r=0}^{d}|u_r|^{2m_r}d\nu =\frac{d!\prod_r m_r!}{(d+\sum_r m_r)!}. These follow from iterated Euler beta integrals on the unit simplex. Substitution into (1) gives \boxed{\lambda_k(N,p) =D_p\frac{(N+d)!}{(N+p+d)!}\frac{(p+k)!}{k!}, \qquad m_k=\binom{N-k+d-1}{d-1}.} \tag{2} For p>0 these eigenvalues increase with k. In particular, \boxed{\lambda_{\rm top}(N,p)=\frac{D_ND_p}{D_{N+p}}, \qquad \frac{\lambda_{N-j}}{\lambda_{\rm top}} =\frac{N(N-1)\cdots(N-j+1)} {(N+p)(N+p-1)\cdots(N+p-j+1)}.} \tag{3} Every eigenvalue is positive at finite p, and \sum_k m_k\lambda_k=D_N. At p=0, (2) gives the identity operator. At p=N, (3) reproduces the smooth coherent-density coefficient D_N^2/D_{2N} used in the complete quartic action. Exact distance from point contact At fixed N\ge1, p\to\infty gives T_{N,p}\to D_N|z;N\rangle\langle z;N|. The coherent line is its top eigenvector for every p. The sum of all complementary eigenvalues is D_N-\lambda_{\rm top}, so no complementary eigenvalue exceeds that deficit. Therefore \boxed{\frac{\|T_{N,p}-D_N|z;N\rangle\langle z;N|\|}{D_N} =\varepsilon_{N,p} =1-\frac{D_p}{D_{N+p}} =1-\prod_{i=1}^d\frac{p+i}{p+N+i}.} \tag{4} Writing each factor as 1-N/(p+N+i), the product bound \prod(1-a_i)\ge1-\sum a_i and 1-a_i\le e^{-a_i} give \boxed{1-\exp\left[-\frac{dN}{p+N+d}\right] \le\varepsilon_{N,p}\le\frac{dN}{p+N+1}.} \tag{5} The upper bound may exceed one; (4) gives the exact value. These formulas state quantitatively how narrow a specified symbol must be for the point operator to be a useful approximation. For two bands N_2>N_1 with the same p, \frac{\lambda_{\rm top}(N_2,p)}{\lambda_{\rm top}(N_1,p)} =\frac{D_{N_2}}{D_{N_1}} \prod_{i=1}^d\frac{p+N_1+i}{p+N_2+i}. \tag{6} Its relative correction to the point-contact ratio is independent of an overall common scale and remains nonzero at every finite p. This is an operator comparison; extracting particle frequencies still requires the complete normalized spatial field equation. Limits with different physical inputs At fixed p and N\to\infty, \lambda_{\rm top}(N,p)\to D_p=\|f_{p,z}\|_\infty. It stays bounded while D_N grows. More generally, \|P_N fP_N\|\le\|f\|_\infty for any fixed bounded multiplier. A bounded symbol of fixed amplitude and width cannot produce an unbounded simplex eigenvalue merely by increasing the cutoff. If instead p/N\to a>0, then \frac{\lambda_{\rm top}(N,p)}{D_N} \longrightarrow\left(\frac a{1+a}\right)^d. \tag{7} The leading simplex power can therefore coexist with a shrinking source width, but (7) is asymptotic. It does not make the finite-band coefficient exactly independent of N. A prescribed N-dependent width must be explained by the same action and normalization as the other field data. There is also an exact extremal statement. For any positive unit measure \mu on the ray space, define T_\mu=D_N\int|u;N\rangle\langle u;N|\,d\mu(u). Then \|T_\mu\|\le D_N. Equality for a normalized vector v requires |\langle v,u;N\rangle|=1 for \mu-almost every u. For N\ge1, distinct projective rays give distinct coherent lines; thus equality holds exactly when \mu is a point measure. This statement uses the positive unit-measure convention. Signed symbols, different total source strength or additional operator terms change its hypotheses. Consistent band contacts addresses the separate requirement that a proposed family arise from one common bare operator or a specified effective reduction. Verification coherent_kernel_consistency_checks.py checks (2) by independent beta quadrature and complete CP1 matrices, the exact trace and full error spectrum, both bounds in (5), finite band ratios, and the distinct limits in (3) and (7).

title: Oscillator source marginals
summary: Spatial oscillator marginals have exact weighted Hockey-Stick singular strengths, while physical bilinear currents require their full coefficient contractions before projection.
text: Summary: Spatial oscillator marginals have exact weighted Hockey-Stick singular strengths, while physical bilinear currents require their full coefficient contractions before projection. A specified spatial projection In a flat product comparison, let a containing physical spatial sector be \mathbb R^{d+q} and a lower sector be \mathbb R^d. Write coordinates (x,y) relative to this inclusion, with q perpendicular directions. Every coordinate is an ordinary macroscopic spatial coordinate of the same kind. This calculation choice does not give the containing particle an inherent division into two spaces. Curved geometry, transport of spinor indices and the actual particle profiles require their own reduction. At a common width w>0, use the normalized functions h_n^w(y)=\left(\frac w\pi\right)^{1/4} \frac{H_n(\sqrt w y)e^{-wy^2/2}}{\sqrt{2^n n!}}, \qquad h_\alpha^w(x)=\prod_i h_{\alpha_i}^w(x_i). \tag{1} Their cumulative band \mathcal B_{N,d} contains |\alpha|\le N and has dimension D_d(N)=\binom{N+d}{d}. The normalized oscillator construction fixes this spatial measure and basis. Splitting occupations proves the exact decomposition \mathcal B_{N,d+q} =\bigoplus_{j=0}^N \mathcal B_{N-j,d}\otimes \operatorname{Sym}^{j}\mathbb C^q, \qquad D_{d+q}(N)=\sum_{j=0}^N \binom{j+q-1}{q-1}D_d(N-j). \tag{2} For q=1 this is the ordinary Hockey-Stick identity. It counts the available spatial modes. To obtain a coupling map one must also calculate their amplitudes in the specified source pairing. Marginal of a linear scalar source First regard the higher band as a space of linear scalar sources j, with arbitrary complex coefficients. Define (Rj)(x)=\int_{\mathbb R^q}j(x,y)\,dy. \tag{3} Integrating the Hermite generating function against e^{-y^2/2} gives c_{2m+1}=0,\qquad c_{2m}=\int h_{2m}^w(y)dy =c_0\sqrt{\frac{\binom{2m}{m}}{4^m}}, \qquad c_0=\sqrt2\,\pi^{1/4}w^{-1/4}. \tag{4} Thus the complete matrix, before squaring any amplitude, is \boxed{R_{\alpha;\alpha',\beta} =\delta_{\alpha\alpha'}\prod_{i=1}^q c_{\beta_i}, \qquad |\alpha'|+|\beta|\le N.} \tag{5} Every even normal occupation contributes. A normal ground-state bra would give a different operator. The constant cylindrical dual in (3) need not belong to the untruncated L^2 space. On these finite source bands, R^\dagger is well defined and represents its projection back into the band, consistently with nested reciprocity. Divide R by c_0^q only to express its entries in ground-integral units. For a shared occupation of degree k=|\alpha|, put M=\lfloor(N-k)/2\rfloor. Different rows have disjoint support, and \frac{(RR^\dagger)_{\alpha\alpha}}{c_0^{2q}} =\sum_{|m|\le M}\prod_{i=1}^q\frac{\binom{2m_i}{m_i}}{4^{m_i}}. \tag{6} The one-coordinate generating function is (1-t)^{-1/2}. Its qth power shows that the shell of paired degree r has weight w_q(r)=(q/2)_r/r!, where (a)_r is the rising factorial. A final cumulative sum multiplies the generating function by (1-t)^{-1}: \boxed{\sum_{r=0}^{M}\binom{r+q/2-1}{r} =\binom{M+q/2}{M}.} \tag{7} Generalized binomials here mean the rising-factorial expressions; all weights are positive. Equation (7) is the squared singular strength of R/c_0^q, with multiplicity \binom{k+d-1}{d-1} at shared degree k. For even q it is an ordinary integer binomial sum. Normal directions q Squared strength at M=2, in the stated units 1 15/8 2 3 3 35/8 4 6 5 63/8 6 10 For q=4, the sum is 1+2+\cdots+(M+1)=\binom{M+2}{2}. A ten-to-six spatial inclusion has this codimension. Identifying these particular scalar source bands with occupied tau and electron patterns would require their actual field and bundle construction. Both responses and spectral weights For the declared scalar pairing U=g\operatorname{Re}\langle a,KRb\rangle, real differentials give the reciprocal source forces gKRb and gR^\dagger K^\dagger a. The convention is \delta U=\operatorname{Re}\langle\delta a,F_a\rangle +\operatorname{Re}\langle\delta b,F_b\rangle; a complex Hamiltonian using Wirtinger derivatives must retain its corresponding factor of two. Field-dependent sources or geometry require additional derivatives. In a positive same-field response with diagonal stiffness \ell_{k+2r}>0, the particular matrix RL^{-1}R^\dagger has entries G_k=c_0^{2q}\sum_{r=0}^{\lfloor(N-k)/2\rfloor} \frac{\binom{r+q/2-1}{r}}{\ell_{k+2r}}. \tag{8} Only constant stiffness on these channels permits the denominator to leave the sum. The full common field response also retains direct terms and the actual source maps. Its retarded version needs the physical frequencies and boundary conditions. Canonical normalization acts on the field's kinetic metric; dividing by c_0^q does not perform that step. The \beta=0 columns prove that R has full row rank D_d(N) and nullity D_{d+q}(N)-D_d(N). The map admits both visible and invisible source combinations at every codimension. There is no special depth-five zero in (7). Phases can change a source cancellation. In one normal direction, (h_0-\sqrt2e^{-i\varphi}h_2)/\sqrt3 has squared integral c_0^2(4/3)\sin^2(\varphi/2). Free oscillator evolution changes \varphi at the gap 4w. This is source beating, not a reciprocal encounter calculation or a conserved electric-neutral sector. Construct a bilinear current before using the sum For an actual spatial wave, let each c_{\alpha\beta} be a spinor coefficient and write \Psi(x,y)=\sum_{|\alpha|+|\beta|\le N} c_{\alpha\beta}h_\alpha^w(x)h_\beta^w(y), \qquad j=\Psi^\dagger\Gamma\Psi, \tag{9} with a specified constant Hermitian vertex \Gamma. The positive density has \Gamma=I; the Dirac scalar has \Gamma=\beta_{\rm D}. Spatially varying vertices and frame transport must remain inside the integral. Orthonormality in the normal coordinates gives the exact result \boxed{(Rj)(x)=\sum_{\alpha,\alpha',\beta} c_{\alpha'\beta}^{\dagger}\Gamma c_{\alpha\beta} h_{\alpha'}^w(x)h_\alpha^w(x).} \tag{10} The sums obey both cumulative bounds. In particular, the normal occupation is contracted with the same normal occupation, rather than multiplied by the one-field integral c_\beta in (4). For \Gamma=I this is the partial trace of the full mode density matrix. It keeps shared-coordinate coherence and all spinor components. There is no contradiction with (5). The bilinear in (9) is a Gaussian times a polynomial of degree at most 2N, so it lies in the scalar source band \mathcal B_{2N,d+q} at width 2w. First forming its coefficients there, and then applying (5) at that width and cutoff, reproduces (10). Applying R to \Psi and squaring would instead introduce interference between orthogonal normal modes. For a normalized separated positive density |\psi(x)|^2|f(y)|^2, (10) simply gives |\psi(x)|^2 because \int|f|^2dy=1. A normal wave whose linear integral vanishes still has a positive unit density integral. Thus the source singular strengths are not universal multipliers of normalized particle charge or contact strength. For the declared density interaction U=g\int \rho_a(x)(R\rho_b)(x)dx, variation gives V_a=gR\rho_b and V_b(x,y)=g\rho_a(x), followed by the respective band compressions. Both reciprocal responses follow from the same energy. This particular cylindrical response does not by itself transfer normal oscillator occupation: its higher operator is block diagonal in \beta. More general transported vertices and spatial kernels can change that property. Covariance and verification The isotropic oscillator band is preserved by common rotations of the physical coordinates. Rotate the containing field, lower inclusion and normal frame together in (3); a change of integration variables gives the same marginal in the rotated lower coordinates. The result does not assign a preferred physical split. Holding the inclusion fixed while rotating only one pattern describes a different preparation. spatial_oscillator_projection_checks.py verifies exact occupation sums, independent Hermite quadrature, full finite singular spectra, complex reciprocal variation, chain composition, rotated inclusions, nonuniform response weights and the independent bilinear-current construction (9)–(10). The same paired-occupation weights also appear in spatial point contact. Spectral weights in oscillator response derives the cutoff convergence criterion for (8), with exact affine-spectrum limits and the remaining shared-mode dependence in codimension four. The criterion retains the source map and response spectrum together.

title: Spatial oscillator point contact
summary: A point contact on actual flat spatial oscillator waves has a position-dependent reproducing strength, whose central value is a weighted Hockey-Stick count rather than the projective simplex dimension.
text: Summary: A point contact on actual flat spatial oscillator waves has a position-dependent reproducing strength, whose central value is a weighted Hockey-Stick count rather than the projective simplex dimension. The physical spatial evaluation operator Fix ordinary spatial coordinates x\in\mathbb R^d, Lebesgue measure, oscillator width w>0, and the cumulative normalized Hermite band \mathcal B_{N,d} of oscillator modes. Let P_N be its orthogonal projector. Point evaluation at X defines a finite positive quadratic form \langle f,A_N(X)f\rangle=|f(X)|^2, \qquad A_N(X)=P_N\delta_XP_N. \tag{1} No untruncated bounded delta multiplication operator is assumed. In the real normalized Hermite basis, the finite matrix is A_{\alpha\beta}=h_\alpha^w(X)h_\beta^w(X). It has rank one and its sole nonzero eigenvalue is \boxed{K_{N,d}^w(X,X)=\sum_{|\alpha|\le N}|h_\alpha^w(X)|^2.} \tag{2} This strength has physical units of inverse spatial volume and depends on position and width. Integrating (2) over X gives the dimension D_d(N)=\binom{N+d}{d}, because each basis mode is normalized. The dimension is therefore the integrated trace density, not its value at an arbitrary spatial point. Mehler's formula and the central count Apply Mehler's formula to each spatial coordinate, including the Gaussian factors in the normalized modes. The shell generating function is \sum_{\alpha\ge0}|h_\alpha^w(X)|^2t^{|\alpha|} =\left(\frac w\pi\right)^{d/2}(1-t^2)^{-d/2} \exp\left[-w|X|^2\frac{1-t}{1+t}\right]. \tag{3} Multiplication by (1-t)^{-1} sums all shells through N: \boxed{\sum_{N=0}^{\infty}K_{N,d}^w(X,X)t^N =\frac{(w/\pi)^{d/2}}{(1-t)(1-t^2)^{d/2}} \exp\left[-w|X|^2\frac{1-t}{1+t}\right],\quad |t|<1.} \tag{4} This depends on X only through |X|, as required by physical rotation covariance of the complete isotropic band. The evaluation vector itself retains all spatial mode amplitudes. At the oscillator center, odd occupations vanish. For M=\lfloor N/2\rfloor, the coefficient in (4) becomes \boxed{K_{N,d}^w(0,0)=\left(\frac w\pi\right)^{d/2} \sum_{r=0}^{M}\frac{(d/2)_r}{r!} =\left(\frac w\pi\right)^{d/2}\binom{M+d/2}{M}.} \tag{5} This is the weighted Hockey-Stick identity derived in oscillator source marginals. At fixed d,w and large N, the gamma-function ratio gives K_{N,d}^w(0,0)\sim \frac{(w/\pi)^{d/2}}{\Gamma(d/2+1)} \left(\frac N2\right)^{d/2}, \qquad D_d(N)\sim\frac{N^d}{d!}. \tag{6} For example, at d=6 and the same width, \frac{K_{34,6}^w(0,0)}{K_{12,6}^w(0,0)} =\frac{\binom{20}{17}}{\binom{9}{6}} =\frac{95}{7}\simeq13.5714, \qquad \frac{D_6(34)}{D_6(12)}\simeq206.7647. \tag{7} These are operator comparisons, not predicted particle mass ratios. An independently derived width w_N changes (5); choosing it to fit a desired power is additional structure. Even restoring a leading power would not prove the exact finite-band simplex law. Fourier duality with the normal marginal For q normal coordinates, define the restriction (Ef)(x)=f(x,0) and the scaled unitary Fourier transform (\mathcal F_w f)(y)=\left(\frac w{2\pi}\right)^{q/2} \int e^{-iw y\cdot y'}f(y')dy'. Direct Fourier transformation of the Hermite generating function gives \mathcal F_w h_\beta^w=(-i)^{|\beta|}h_\beta^w. At zero normal position, h_{2m}^w(0)=\left(\frac w\pi\right)^{1/4} (-1)^m\sqrt{\frac{\binom{2m}{m}}{4^m}}, \qquad h_{2m+1}^w(0)=0. Evaluation of the Fourier integral at zero therefore proves, on the finite band, \boxed{R=\left(\frac{2\pi}{w}\right)^{q/2}E\mathcal F_w.} \tag{8} The Fourier transform preserves total oscillator degree. Consequently, the restriction and marginal have the same singular spectrum after their displayed dimensional factors are removed. Their even-mode phases differ. Equality of singular strengths does not make them the same response to a fixed complex spatial preparation. Relation to projective ray contact The projective contact calculation uses H^0(\mathbb{CP}^d,\mathcal O(N)) with a homogeneous unit-volume Fubini–Study measure. Its point contact has constant strength D_d(N). The point in that construction is a mode ray; the point X in (1) is a position in an actual flat spatial chart. An equality of finite dimensions does not identify the two evaluation operators or measures. There is an elementary vector test. Under the usual normalized homogenization of occupations, the spatial vector at X=0 has a nonzero ground coefficient, zero degree-one coefficients and nonzero degree-two coefficients whenever N\ge2. A Veronese coherent vector z^{\otimes N} with nonzero ground coefficient and vanishing all degree-one coefficients must have z_1=\cdots=z_d=0, which also eliminates every degree-two coefficient. Thus central spatial evaluation is not a projective coherent ray in that identification. The unfinished coordinate-to-ray kernel bridge must specify the actual transform, measure, field-dependent data and kinetic normalization. Equations (1)–(8) give a fully specified spatial comparison against which such a bridge can be tested. They do not replace the proposed compact physical geometry of an IDWT particle. Verification spatial_oscillator_projection_checks.py checks direct Hermite evaluation against (3)–(5), integrates the trace density, verifies physical rotation covariance and Fourier phases, and constructs the full marginal and restriction matrices independently.

title: Local scalar contact normalization
summary: Spatial normalization turns a scalar contact coefficient into a profile-dependent frequency, with exact virial, scaling and massive one-dimensional benchmarks.
text:
Summary: Spatial normalization turns a scalar contact coefficient into a profile-dependent frequency, with exact virial, scaling and massive one-dimensional benchmarks. A spatial action after the graph pairing The defined graph pairing reduces its single-source interaction to g_N( ar\Psi\Psi)^2/2, with g_N=\kappa D_N and D_N= inom{N+d}{d}. This identifies a scalar nonlinear coefficient. Extracting a frequency still requires the spatial field equation. Consider a specified flat comparison on the physical spatial space \mathbb R^d, with Hermitian Clifford matrices \alpha_j, eta, \hbar=c=1, and fixed bare scalar coefficient m\ge0: \mathcal E_g[\Psi]=\int\left[ \Psi^\dagger(-i\alpha\cdot
abla+m eta)\Psi + rac g2(\Psi^\dagger eta\Psi)^2ight]dx, \qquad i\partial_t\Psi= \left[-i\alpha\cdot
abla+(m+g\sigma) etaight]\Psi, 	ag{1} where \sigma=\Psi^\dagger eta\Psi and g is real. The spatial measure and time-kinetic norm are fixed. The spinor components do not add physical dimensions or independent fields. The complete nonlinear source and its conjugate response are given in Dirac source linearization. The present comparison supplies no confining background or additional interaction. It must not replace the proposed global spatial geometry of a particle. In particular, the electron's proposed \mathbb{CP}^3 is an actual six-dimensional spatial manifold, with geometric and bundle data absent from (1). Frequency, scalar overlap and total energy Suppose \Psi=e^{-i\omega t}\phi is an admissible stationary solution, with finite integrals and sufficient decay for the variations below. Define Q=\int\phi^\dagger\phi,\qquad S=\int\phi^\dagger eta\phi,\qquad I=\int(\phi^\dagger eta\phi)^2,\qquad T=\int\phi^\dagger(-i\alpha\cdot
abla)\phi. Q is the positive phase-symmetry norm, not an assigned ordinary electric charge. S is signed; I is nonnegative. Multiplying the stationary equation by \phi^\dagger and integrating gives  oxed{\omega Q=T+mS+gI, \qquad \mathcal E=T+mS+ rac g2I =\omega Q- rac g2I.} 	ag{2} Thus the nonlinear spectral frequency and the total energy per norm are different quantities. A physical rest-energy identification must specify which quantity and normalization it uses. The norm-preserving dilation \phi_\lambda(x)=\lambda^{d/2}\phi(\lambda x) leaves Q,S fixed, while T\mapsto\lambda T and I\mapsto\lambda^dI. Stationarity of \mathcal E-\omega Q gives  oxed{T+ rac{dg}{2}I=0,\qquad \omega Q=mS+\left(1- rac d2ight)gI.} 	ag{3} This is the local quartic instance of the nonlinear Dirac virial identity; see Comech, Lemma 3.2. It uses an admissible dilation on flat infinite space. A boundary, curvature, a nonlocal kernel or a spatially varying background adds terms or changes the allowed variation. At m=0 and d>2, (3) implies \omega Q=- rac{d-2}{2}gI,\qquad \mathcal E=- rac{d-1}{2}gI = rac{d-1}{d-2}\omega Q. 	ag{4} For example, the positive-g branch cannot have positive frequency and positive norm under these hypotheses. This sign condition is only necessary; it does not prove that the other sign supports a bound state. Removing the coupling changes the normalization Write g=\varepsilon h, where h=|g|>0 and \varepsilon=\operatorname{sgn}g. For any fixed spatial operator, the substitution \phi=h^{-1/2}\varphi turns (1) into the same equation at unit coupling \varepsilon. The frequency is unchanged by this amplitude rescaling, but Q_g(\omega)= rac{Q_\varepsilon(\omega)}h. 	ag{5} Consequently, a fixed physical norm Q_* requires  oxed{Q_\varepsilon(\omega)=hQ_*.} 	ag{6} The frequency is obtained from the branch's norm-frequency curve; it is not the bare coupling multiplied by an unchanged normalized profile. Several branches or turning points require their own selection. For the massless flat equation there is an additional homogeneity. If a unit-coupling solution \phi_0 of frequency \omega_0 and norm Q_0 exists, then \phi_{h,s}(x)=h^{-1/2}s^{1/2}\phi_0(sx),\qquad \omega_{h,s}=s\omega_0,\qquad Q_{h,s}= rac{Q_0}{h}s^{1-d}. 	ag{7} The Dirac derivative and the cubic source both acquire the factor h^{-1/2}s^{3/2}, proving the field equation directly. For d>1, fixed norm therefore selects  oxed{\omega_h=\omega_0 \left( rac{Q_0}{hQ_*}ight)^{1/(d-1)}.} 	ag{8} This is a conditional scaling relation, not an existence theorem. The massless radial analysis shows that the standard regular radial ansatz has no such finite-norm solution in this particular flat local model. If the only band dependence in a proposed massless spatial reduction were g_N=\kappa D_N, (8) would give \omega_N\propto D_N^{-1/(d-1)} on the same scaling branch. The linear simplex frequency would require additional structure beyond that reduction. A band-dependent spatial operator, changing branch, physical geometric scale or other action term changes the hypotheses; none is silently excluded from IDWT. An exact massive benchmark with fixed norm A constructive check is available on one ordinary spatial dimension. Take m>0, g=-h<0,  eta=\operatorname{diag}(1,-1) and -i\alpha\partial_x=\left( egin{smallmatrix}0&\partial_x\ -\partial_x&0\end{smallmatrix}ight). A real stationary profile \phi=(f,u)^{\mathsf T} satisfies f'=-(\omega+m-h\sigma)u, \qquad u'=(\omega-m+h\sigma)f, \qquad \sigma=f^2-u^2. 	ag{9} For 0<\omega<m, set k=\sqrt{m^2-\omega^2} and A(x)=m+\omega\cosh(2kx). The exact solution is  oxed{ f(x)=\sqrt{ rac{2(m+\omega)}h}\,  rac{k\cosh(kx)}{A(x)},\qquad u(x)=\sqrt{ rac{2(m-\omega)}h}\,  rac{k\sinh(kx)}{A(x)}.} 	ag{10} The unit-coupling formula and its power-law extension are presented by Cuevas-Maraver and collaborators, Section 3.1. Direct differentiation checks both equations (9), including the sign and the factor h. Both components are retained. Here \sigma(x)= rac{2k^2}{hA(x)},\qquad ho(x)= rac{2k^2[m\cosh(2kx)+\omega]}{hA(x)^2}. Substitute t=	anh(kx) into the norm integral. Its integrand becomes ho(x)dx= rac{2k}h\,  rac{(m+\omega)+(m-\omega)t^2} {[(m+\omega)-(m-\omega)t^2]^2}dt = rac{2k}h\,d\left[  rac{t}{(m+\omega)-(m-\omega)t^2}ight]. Evaluation from t=-1 to t=1, and the corresponding scalar integral, give  oxed{Q= rac{2k}{h\omega},\qquad S= rac2h\operatorname{arcosh} rac m\omega,\qquad I= rac4{h^2}\left[m\operatorname{arcosh} rac m\omega-kight].} 	ag{11} The virial and total energy become T=hI/2 and \mathcal E=mS, in agreement with (2)–(3). At the same fixed norm Q_* for every coupling, (11) gives the explicit frequency  oxed{\omega(h;Q_*)=  rac{m}{\sqrt{1+(hQ_*/2)^2}}.} 	ag{12} Increasing the nonlinear coefficient changes the normalized profile and lowers this branch's frequency. Equation (12) supplies a complete counterexample to inferring a linear frequency law from the absence of a band index in a bare coupling. It is a one-dimensional comparison, not an electron or neutrino model. Relation to the spatial moment model The existing scalar Dirac moment branch uses a nonlocal centered quadratic spatial moment. Its interaction scales as \lambda^{-4} under norm-preserving dilation, giving a different virial and a massless frequency proportional to g_0^{1/5}. Equations (3) and (8) instead follow from local scalar contact. The physical kernel determines which normalization law applies. Canonical coupling normalization must also precede comparison of different retained mode families or spatial sectors. An oscillator dimension count cannot replace these profile and kinetic calculations. The specified CP3 scalar branch gives a curved spatial comparison with its own physical volume and metric scale. It restores the full radial Dirac components and computes the normalized frequency through cubic order. Its different global hypotheses are explicit; the flat scaling and tail arguments cannot be transferred to it. The nonlinear spatial reduction eliminates the complementary Dirac modes together with their norm. It derives the effective stationary action, distinguishes its normalized frequency and energy corrections, and gives a source-preservation condition for an exact linear contact branch under explicit positivity hypotheses. Verification local_scalar_profile_checks.py checks the exact massive equations by independent spatial differences, integrates all quantities in (11), verifies the virial and fixed-norm frequency, and checks massless scaling directly in the complete spatial Dirac operator with arbitrary complex rest polarizations.

title: Massless radial scalar contact
summary: The flat massless cubic scalar Dirac equation has no nonzero finite-norm stationary wave in its standard regular radial ansatz, by a zero-frequency identity and an exact tail argument.
text:
Summary: The flat massless cubic scalar Dirac equation has no nonzero finite-norm stationary wave in its standard regular radial ansatz, by a zero-frequency identity and an exact tail argument. Equation and exact scope Consider only the flat local scalar Dirac equation i\partial_t\Psi= \left[-i\alpha\cdot
abla+g(\Psi^\dagger eta\Psi) etaight]\Psi, \qquad x\in\mathbb R^d,\quad d\ge1,\quad g\in\mathbb R. 	ag{1} There is no bare mass, prescribed background or additional kernel. The coordinates are ordinary physical spatial coordinates. This comparison does not replace the proposed curved spatial geometry of an IDWT particle. Choose a constant unit spinor \chi with  eta\chi=\chi and the standard stationary radial ansatz \Psi(t,x)=e^{-i\omega t}\left[ f(r)\chi+i u(r)\alpha(\widehat x)\chiight], \qquad r=|x|,\quad \omega\in\mathbb R. 	ag{2} The profiles may be complex. Assume they are classical away from zero, regular at the origin with finite f(0) and u(0)=0, and have finite positive norm Q=|S^{d-1}|\int_0^\infty r^{d-1}  igl(|f(r)|^2+|u(r)|^2 igr)dr<\infty. 	ag{3} For d=1, the spherical factor accounts for the two half-lines in the even/odd extension of (2). All allowed constant rest polarizations \chi are retained. Higher angular sectors and spatially varying polarization textures are outside this ansatz. The Clifford relations give \sigma=\Psi^\dagger eta\Psi=|f|^2-|u|^2 and reduce (1) to  oxed{f'=-(\omega+V)u,\qquad u'=(\omega-V)f- rac{d-1}{r}u, \qquad V=g(|f|^2-|u|^2).} 	ag{4} This radial representation follows the spatial Dirac construction; it does not turn the physical manifold into a one-dimensional space. The angular dependence is contained explicitly in (2). Under precisely these assumptions, the only solution is zero. The proof separates zero and nonzero frequency. Zero frequency: a monotone scalar density At \omega=0, differentiate the scalar using both equations (4):  oxed{\sigma' =2\operatorname{Re}( ar f f'- ar u u') = rac{2(d-1)}r|u|^2\ge0.} 	ag{5} The nonlinear terms cancel for either sign of g and for complex profiles. Regularity gives \sigma(0)=|f(0)|^2\ge0. If \sigma were positive at any radius, it would remain bounded below by a positive constant thereafter. Since |f|^2+|u|^2\ge\sigma, (3) would diverge. Hence \sigma\equiv0 and V\equiv0. For d>1, (5) also gives u\equiv0, and then f\equiv0. For d=1, (4) at zero frequency and V=0 makes both profiles constant, and finite norm again makes both zero. Nonzero frequency: the free radial fundamental matrix Let \omega
e0 and remove the radial measure by defining U(r)=r^{(d-1)/2} egin{pmatrix}f(r)\u(r)\end{pmatrix}. Then Q/|S^{d-1}|=\int\|U(r)\|^2dr, and (4) becomes U'=\left[  egin{pmatrix}(d-1)/(2r)&-\omega\ \omega&-(d-1)/(2r)\end{pmatrix} + egin{pmatrix}0&-V\-V&0\end{pmatrix} ight]U. 	ag{6} Set k=|\omega| and 
u=(d-2)/2. A fundamental matrix for the free part is  oxed{F(r)=\sqrt r egin{pmatrix} J_
u(kr)&Y_
u(kr)\ \operatorname{sgn}(\omega)J_{
u+1}(kr) &\operatorname{sgn}(\omega)Y_{
u+1}(kr) \end{pmatrix},\qquad \det F=- rac2{\pi\omega}.} 	ag{7} The Bessel recurrence verifies the differential equation. The Wronskian identity gives the determinant, and the large-argument expansions show that both F and F^{-1} are bounded on every sufficiently far tail. Its columns have oscillatory, nondecaying amplitudes in the measure-normalized coordinate U. Finite norm would make the self-potential integrable For any fixed R>0, the assumed finite norm implies \int_R^\infty |V(r)|dr \le |g|\int_R^\infty(|f|^2+|u|^2)dr \le rac{|g|}{R^{d-1}} \int_R^\infty r^{d-1}(|f|^2+|u|^2)dr<\infty. 	ag{8} Along a hypothetical solution, regard its actual real V(r) as a fixed coefficient and put W=F^{-1}U. Equation (6) gives W'=C(r)W,\qquad C(r)=F(r)^{-1} egin{pmatrix}0&-V(r)\-V(r)&0\end{pmatrix}F(r), \qquad \int_R^\infty\|C(r)\|dr<\infty. 	ag{9} For completeness, let Y(R)=I and Y'=CY. Gronwall's inequality bounds Y and its inverse by the exponential of the integral in (9). Their derivatives are integrable, so both have limits at infinity. Since Y^{-1}Y=I, the limiting matrix Y_\infty is invertible. Thus every nonzero initial W(R) has a nonzero limit W_\infty=Y_\infty W(R). The bound on F^{-1} now implies that \|U(r)\| is bounded below by a positive constant on a sufficiently far tail. Consequently \int\|U(r)\|^2dr diverges, contradicting (3). A solution that vanishes at one positive radius is identically zero by the ordinary uniqueness theorem for (4). This proves the nonzero-frequency case. Consequence for the contact construction Replacing g by the graph coefficient \kappa D_N cannot change this radial existence result. The graph pairing alone therefore does not supply a normalized stationary profile of form (2) when reduced to (1) on flat infinite space. This conclusion identifies the limits of a specific spatial reduction. The proof uses the flat infinite tail, zero bare mass, local cubic scalar source and the stated radial form. It does not apply to the proposed global \mathbb{CP}^3 electron geometry, nonradial polarization patterns, additional same-field interactions or different asymptotic backgrounds. It also does not apply to the nonlocal scalar moment model, whose self-generated quadratic mass profile grows at infinity. The exact massive one-dimensional solution in local scalar normalization provides a positive control: adding m>0 creates a frequency gap and admits decaying profiles. Its fixed-norm frequency is nevertheless a nonlinear function of the contact coefficient. title: Coherent pair deformation

text:
Summary: A common positive-density quartic drives two coherent mode patterns into shape deformations, with reciprocal changes in contact fixed by conserved energy and rotation moments. The action is S=\int dt\left[  rac i2(a^\dagger\dot a-\dot a^\dagger a +b^\dagger\dot b-\dot b^\dagger b) - rac\kappa2\intho^2d
u_{m FS}ight]. 	ag{1} The line bundles of degrees N and M need not be identified to add their Hermitian densities. Orthogonality and the kinetic metric are assumptions of this component action; spatial nesting alone supplies neither. A coherent scalar sum with interference is a different current. The positive density here is also different from the indefinite scalar Dirac bilinear  ar\Psi\Psi. This calculation retains all complex coefficients of its two families. It tests mode-pattern deformation in a specified action, rather than claiming a full particle-pair interaction on the physical base. The projective fibre adds no physical spatial dimensions. Different physical depths additionally require actual normal-bundle maps and spatial kinetic normalization. No independent field or mediator particle is introduced. A single symmetric product gives both reciprocal forces Let T_{NM}:\mathcal H_N\otimes\mathcal H_M	o\mathcal H_{N+M} orthogonally symmetrize every tensor index. In normalized occupations, T_{NM}(|\alphaangle\otimes| etaangle) =\sqrt{ rac{ inom N\alpha inom M eta} { inom{N+M}{\alpha+ eta}}}\,|\alpha+ etaangle. 	ag{2} The multi-index Vandermonde identity gives T_{NM}T_{NM}^\dagger=I. Define C_{NM}= rac{D_ND_M}{D_{N+M}},\qquad q=T_{NM}(a\otimes b),\qquad A_bh=T_{NM}(h\otimes b),\qquad B_ak=T_{NM}(a\otimes k). The cross-density overlap is exactly  oxed{I(a,b)=\int|s_a|^2|s_b|^2d
u_{m FS} =C_{NM}\|q\|^2.} 	ag{3} Its two derivatives are C_{NM}A_b^\dagger q and C_{NM}B_a^\dagger q. If F_N is the complete unit-coupling single-family quartic gradient, (1) gives  oxed{ i\dot a=\kappa igl(F_N(a)+C_{NM}A_b^\dagger q igr),\qquad i\dot b=\kappa igl(F_M(b)+C_{NM}B_a^\dagger q igr).} 	ag{4} Both responses, their relative coefficient and their self-interactions come from the same \kappa. Coherent overlap and the missing shape directions For unit coherent preparations a=z^{\otimes N}, b=w^{\otimes M}, let 	au=|z^\dagger w|^2. Symmetrizing the two products gives the finite polynomial  oxed{I(z^{\otimes N},w^{\otimes M}) = rac{C_{NM}}{ inom{N+M}{N}} \sum_{j=0}^{\min(N,M)} inom Nj inom Mj	au^j.} 	ag{5} One derivation groups permutations by the number j of indices exchanged between the two tensor blocks. Those terms have overlap 	au^j and multiplicity  inom Nj inom Mj; their total number at 	au=1 is  inom{N+M}{N} by Vandermonde.
