To test invariance, use common mode-frame covariance and component phases to set z=e_0 and w=ce_0+se_1, where c,s>0 and c^2+s^2=1. The component of the cross-gradient on |N-j,jangle is  egin{aligned} G_j={}& rac{D_ND_M\sqrt{ inom Nj}\,d!}{(N+M+d)!} \sum_{r=0}^{M-j} inom Mr inom M{r+j} c^{2M-2r-j}s^{2r+j}\ &\hspace{27mm}\cdot(N+M-r-j)!\,(r+j)!, \qquad 0\le j\le\min(N,M). \end{aligned} 	ag{6} Components with j>M vanish. Expanding the two powers of w in the projected current and using the FS monomial integral proves (6). Every summand is positive in the stated nonaligned preparation. In particular, G_2>0 whenever N,M\ge2. At a coherent tensor, its phase and norm occupy j=0, and its coherent ray tangents occupy j=1. Therefore the j=2 force lies outside that tangent space. The self-gradient contributes only the carrier direction, so it cannot cancel this force. The reciprocal calculation gives the same conclusion for the other pattern. Thus the coherent product manifold is not invariant for a generic nonaligned pair with N,M\ge2. A calculation that varies only the two rays discards genuine solutions of the retained coefficient equations. When \min(N,M)=1, the cross-force has only j=0,1 in either adapted frame. Changing contact follows from conservation Write A(a)=\int|s_a|^4, B(b)=\int|s_b|^4, and \lambda_R=D_R^2/D_{2R}. For the same coherent initial preparation, conservation of \operatorname{tr}S^2 gives  oxed{ \operatorname{tr}(ho_a(t)ho_b(t))-J_aJ_b	au_0 = rac{N^2[J_a^2-\operatorname{tr}ho_a(t)^2] +M^2[J_b^2-\operatorname{tr}ho_b(t)^2]}{2NM}\ge0.} 	ag{10} The inequality uses positivity and the fixed traces. This one-index compatibility is distinct from the full density overlap I; both obey preparation-dependent balances. If both patterns remain coherent, (10) forces their relative ray overlap to remain 	au_0. Full shape changes are precisely what allow this restricted conclusion to change. Exact active-subspace reduction for this preparation Initially, S in (9) has support on V=\operatorname{span}\{z,w\}, of complex dimension at most two. For x\perp V, conservation gives 0=x^\dagger Sx=Nx^\daggerho_ax+Mx^\daggerho_bx. Both terms are nonnegative, hence both vanish. The tensors therefore remain in \operatorname{Sym}^N(V)\oplus\operatorname{Sym}^M(V). 	ag{11} This is an invariant consequence of the complete equations for the stated preparation. title: Aligned coherent pair
summary: The complete positive-density pair action has an aligned coherent stationary set with an explicit ambient Hessian and finite-mode nonlinear orbital stability.
text: Summary: The complete positive-density pair action has an aligned coherent stationary set with an explicit ambient Hessian and finite-mode nonlinear orbital stability. Stationary branch of the common action Use the complete canonical component action and notation of coherent pair deformation: E=\frac\kappa2\int(|s_a|^2+|s_b|^2)^2d\nu_{\rm FS}, \quad \lambda_R=\frac{D_R^2}{D_{2R}}, \quad C=\frac{D_ND_M}{D_{N+M}}. This is a declared positive-density action in a mode fibre, with orthogonal bundle components and a specified kinetic metric. It is not the full scalar Dirac action or a physical spatial bound-state theorem. Coefficient indices add no physical spatial dimensions. For fixed positive norms J_a,J_b, choose the same unit ray z in both families. The complete equations admit \begin{aligned} a(t)&=\sqrt{J_a}e^{-i\omega_at}z^{\otimes N}, &\omega_a&=\kappa(\lambda_NJ_a+CJ_b),\\ b(t)&=\sqrt{J_b}e^{-i\omega_bt}z^{\otimes M}, &\omega_b&=\kappa(\lambda_MJ_b+CJ_a). \end{aligned} \tag{1} The self and cross gradients each point along the occupied tensor. Their independent carrier phases are allowed by the two norm symmetries. All transverse mode blocks Choose z=e_0 and rotate out the two frequencies in (1). Label an occupation by its transverse degree j. Define r_{N,j}=\frac{(N)_{\underline j}}{(2N)_{\underline j}}, \qquad p_j=\frac{(N)_{\underline j}}{(N+M)_{\underline j}}, \qquad q_j=\frac{(M)_{\underline j}}{(N+M)_{\underline j}}. For 1\le j\le\min(N,M), each transverse occupation carries the two-by-two complex-linear equation i\frac d{dt} \begin{pmatrix}\eta_{a,j}\\\eta_{b,j}\end{pmatrix} =\kappa\begin{pmatrix} J_a\lambda_N(2r_{N,j}-1)+J_bC(p_j-1) &C\sqrt{J_aJ_bp_jq_j}\\ C\sqrt{J_aJ_bp_jq_j} &J_b\lambda_M(2r_{M,j}-1)+J_aC(q_j-1) \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix}\eta_{a,j}\\\eta_{b,j}\end{pmatrix}. \tag{2} For j present in only one family, keep its diagonal entry. The multiplicity of each transverse occupation block is \binom{j+d-1}{d-1}. Summing these multiplicities over each family recovers its entire band dimension. To derive (2), differentiate both factors of the density and retain both components' variations. The self blocks are the single-family Hessian. In the cross term, multiplication by the other coherent density gives the ratios p_j and q_j. The mixed derivative gives their geometric mean. Projected phase selection permits anomalous, conjugate-linear terms only in the two j=0 carrier components. No such terms are discarded in the transverse equation. At j=1, (2) reduces to \frac{\kappa C}{N+M} \begin{pmatrix} -J_bM&\sqrt{J_aJ_bNM}\\ \sqrt{J_aJ_bNM}&-J_aN \end{pmatrix}. \tag{3} Its eigenvalues are 0,\qquad -\frac{\kappa C(J_bM+J_aN)}{N+M}. \tag{4} The zero eigenvector (\sqrt{J_aN},\sqrt{J_bM}) rotates both coherent rays together. The other mode changes their relative orientation. For j\ge2, p_j+q_j<1. Thus the cross part of (2), divided by \kappa C, has negative trace and determinant J_aJ_b(1-p_j-q_j)>0. The self diagonal terms also have negative sign because r_{R,j}<1/2. All nonzero transverse frequencies are therefore real and have sign opposite to \kappa. The only transverse zero modes are the d common coherent rotations. The j=0 sector contains the two phase zero modes and carrier drifts caused by varying the conserved norms; fixed norms remove those radial changes. Nonlinear orbital stability in the full finite space Orthogonal symmetrization obeys I(a,b)=C\|T_{NM}(a\otimes b)\|^2\le CJ_aJ_b. \tag{5} Equality requires the product tensor to be fully symmetric. Swapping one index between the two normalized factors then gives \operatorname{tr}(\widehat\rho_a\widehat\rho_b)=1, where both contractions are positive with trace one. Equality forces both to be the same rank-one projector, hence a and b are coherent tensors on the same ray. The converse is immediate. Together with the sharp self bounds, this shows that the aligned set is exactly the global energy maximum at fixed norms for \kappa>0, and the global minimum for \kappa<0. The nonnegative deficit \mathcal D= \frac{\lambda_NJ_a^2+\lambda_MJ_b^2}{2}+CJ_aJ_b -\left[\frac{A(a)+B(b)}2+I(a,b)\right] \tag{6} vanishes precisely on that set. The product of the two fixed-norm spheres is compact. On any closed subset separated from the aligned set, (6) has a positive minimum. Conservation of both norms and the energy therefore proves nonlinear orbital stability of the entire aligned set for either nonzero sign of \kappa. This argument retains all ambient coefficients, including perturbations outside a prepared two-dimensional generating subspace. It supplies a finite-mode result stronger than the absence of growing linear modes. It remains separate from stability of physical spatial profiles, omitted bands and complete Dirac polarizations. Stability does not imply capture into alignment The conserved rotation moment is S=N\rho_a+M\rho_b. A pair of nonparallel coherent rays has a rank-two S, whereas an exactly aligned coherent pair has rank one. The former cannot evolve into the latter under these equations while preserving all its moments. The deformation calculation shows how contact can nevertheless increase: the patterns can depart from the coherent subset and retain their conserved moments in shape modes. An energy extremum alone does not justify an alignment or relaxation law. Physical time scales require the actual kinetic normalization, and a physical capture process requires its own allowed outgoing modes. Verification coherent_pair_variation_checks.py compares (2) against the complete differentiated action in all ambient occupation sectors, including the anomalous blocks and both stationary equations. Exact rational inequalities and combinatorial multiplicities cover large degrees without allocating their enormous matrices.

title: Graph contact variation
summary: A defined graph-measure pairing retains the simplex coefficient, but its full self-variation cancels ray stiffness and does not select a coherent pattern.
text: Summary: A defined graph-measure pairing retains the simplex coefficient, but its full self-variation cancels ray stiffness and does not select a coherent pattern. A well-defined graph pairing At a point of the physical spatial manifold Q_d, use the homogenized mode carrier \mathcal H_N=\operatorname{Sym}^N(\mathbb C^{d+1}), D_N=\binom{N+d}{d}, with normalized coherent vectors |z;N\rangle. The projective mode fibre describes oscillator-symbol data; it adds no physical spatial dimensions. The physical base and fibre are distinguished in the self-contact module. Write P_z=|z;N\rangle\langle z;N| and define the single pairing kernel B_N(z,w)=D_N\operatorname{tr}(P_zP_w) =D_N|z^\dagger w|^{2N},\qquad \int B_N(z,w)d\nu_{\rm FS}(w)=1. \tag{1} For a real scalar current J(q) and a specified field-dependent ray z_\Psi(q), the finite signed measure \mu_q=J(q)\delta_{[z_\Psi(q)]} is well defined. A candidate interaction is E_{\rm graph} =\frac\kappa2\int_{Q_d} \int\!\int B_N(u,v)d\mu_q(u)d\mu_q(v)\,d\mu_{Q_d}(q). \tag{2} Equation (2) pairs two measures against a smooth finite-band kernel. It never multiplies two delta distributions at the same integration variable. The kernel family, its normalization and this pairing are specified additions to the action; ordinary locality of J^2 does not derive them. This supplies a precise candidate completion of the graph-contact construction. Exact total variation of one occupied graph The coincident value B_N(z,z)=D_N is constant. Therefore (2) is exactly \boxed{E_{\rm graph} =\frac{\kappa D_N}{2}\int_{Q_d}J(q)^2d\mu_{Q_d}(q).} \tag{3} Every variation of the ray cancels before any field equation is imposed. This remains true if z_\Psi depends on derivatives of the physical field, provided it is a well-defined differentiable ray along the variation. The residual variation comes from J, the physical measure and any additional action terms. On a fixed physical geometry, \delta E_{\rm graph}=\kappa D_N\int J\,\delta J\,d\mu_{Q_d}. \tag{4} For J=\bar\Psi\Psi, an interaction Lagrangian equal to minus (3) contributes -\kappa D_NJ\Psi to the Euler--Lagrange equation obtained by varying \bar\Psi. In Hamiltonian form its contribution is \kappa D_N(\Psi^\dagger\beta\Psi)\beta\Psi. The simplex factor survives as a nonlinear scalar coupling coefficient. A normalized stationary spatial profile, its kinetic contribution and its frequency must still be solved; (3) does not identify that frequency with a rest mass proportional to D_N. Why the apparent self-orientation stiffness cancels Hold J fixed and let P(\theta) be a moving coherent projector. At one physical point, (2) is \kappa D_NJ^2\operatorname{tr}(P^2)/2. Its second derivative is \frac{d^2E}{d\theta^2} =\kappa D_NJ^2\left[ \operatorname{tr}\bigl((P')^2\bigr) +\operatorname{tr}(PP'')\right]=0. \tag{5} For the unit generating curve z(\theta)=(\cos\theta,\sin\theta,0,\ldots), at zero, \begin{aligned} |z;N\rangle'&=\sqrt N\,|N-1,1\rangle,\\ |z;N\rangle''&=-N|N,0\rangle +\sqrt{2N(N-1)}\,|N-2,2\rangle. \end{aligned} The last term is absent for N=1. Substitution gives \operatorname{tr}((P')^2)=2N, \qquad \operatorname{tr}(PP'')=-2N. \tag{6} The positive source-Gram contribution and the curvature of the moving source cancel exactly. Keeping only the first term in (5) would supply an artificial self-orientation stiffness. The weaker identity P(\delta P)P=0 already removes a diagonal first variation; (5) accounts for both terms at second order. Occupied frequency does not determine the response operator For a finite coefficient illustration only, choose J=c^\dagger c and the canonical time-kinetic term. Equation (3) becomes E(c)=\frac{\kappa D_N}{2}(c^\dagger c)^2, \qquad i\dot c=\kappa D_N(c^\dagger c)c. \tag{7} Every coefficient pattern rotates by the same phase at a fixed norm. Every projective direction is stationary. In particular, this action does not distinguish the coherent tensors from other vectors in \mathcal H_N. The complete derivative of the right-hand side is \delta F=A\eta+B\bar\eta,\qquad A=\kappa D_N(JI+cc^\dagger),\qquad B=\kappa D_Ncc^{\mathsf T}. \tag{8} After subtracting the carrier frequency \Omega=\kappa D_NJ, all directions orthogonal to c have zero frequency. By contrast, freezing the rank-one matrix \kappa D_Ncc^\dagger would give the same occupied frequency but a transverse rotating-frame frequency -\Omega. When that matrix depends on the evolving c, its derivative restores exactly (8). Its instantaneous rank does not determine the nonlinear response spectrum. Here the arbitrary coefficient ray [c]\in\mathbb P(\mathcal H_N) must not be confused with the smaller coherent subset [z^{\otimes N}]. Nor is the positive coefficient norm in (7) a replacement for the scalar Dirac current used in (4). For another distinct prescription, fix z and vary E=\kappa|s_c(z)|^4/2, where s_c(z)=\sqrt{D_N}\langle z;N|c\rangle. On c=\sqrt J|z;N\rangle, its frequency is \kappa D_N^2J. This quartic evaluated density is different from the graph current J\delta_z in (2). The number of evaluations matters. The smooth quartic action, in contrast, has nonzero restoring frequencies for departures from the coherent set. Its occupied multiplier is D_N^2/D_{2N}. Matching one occupied eigenvalue is therefore insufficient to identify either action's complete response or its pattern-selection properties. Two graph rays retain a reciprocal orientation interaction At one common mode fibre, replace the single measure by \mu=J_a\delta_{z_a}+J_b\delta_{z_b}. For fixed positive coefficient norms J_a,J_b, (2) gives E=\frac{\kappa D_N}{2} \left[J_a^2+J_b^2+2J_aJ_b\tau^N\right], \qquad \tau=|z_a^\dagger z_b|^2. \tag{9} There is a cross-ray force although the isolated self-ray force vanishes. To make its time evolution explicit, restrict both degree-N coefficient patterns to coherent tensors and pull back their canonical kinetic form. The two ray symplectic weights are NJ_a and NJ_b. In a horizontal phase gauge, with s=z_a^\dagger z_b, the equations are \begin{aligned} i\dot z_a&=\kappa D_NJ_b\tau^{N-1}\bar s\,(z_b-sz_a),\\ i\dot z_b&=\kappa D_NJ_a\tau^{N-1}s\,(z_a-\bar s z_b). \end{aligned} \tag{10} Both objects respond to the same energy. Direct differentiation gives \dot\tau=0,\qquad \frac d{dt}\left(J_a z_az_a^\dagger+J_bz_bz_b^\dagger\right)=0. \tag{11} Indeed, put S=J_a z_az_a^\dagger+J_bz_bz_b^\dagger and \omega=\kappa D_N\tau^{N-1}. The ray projectors obey \dot P_a=-i\omega[S,P_a] and the same equation for P_b; their exact solution is common conjugation by e^{-i\omega St}. These P_a,P_b act on the generating vectors, rather than on \mathcal H_N. A common unitary change of mode frame preserves all equations. Its physical rotation subgroup also preserves them. Thus this specified first-order two-ray reduction produces reciprocal precession, with constant relative overlap. It does not by itself implement changing compatibility of complete physical spatial patterns. The bilateral orientation benchmark has a related conservation law. Full coefficient deformations, spatial transport, spinor structure and kinetic normalization remain separate parts of a particle-pair calculation in the one field \Psi_\infty. Physical spatial profile Complete local scalar response also separates rank from occupied-ray self-contact at an actual physical point. Its scalar-null source derivative has one real responsive direction, but that direction is orthogonal to the occupied complex ray and gives zero after projection onto it. This does not derive the graph kernel or its simplex normalization. Local scalar normalization tracks the remaining spatial equation: virial and fixed-norm constraints make the nonlinear coefficient and its frequency distinct. In the flat massless local reduction, the standard regular radial ansatz has no nonzero finite-norm stationary solution. The actual physical geometric and bundle terms must be retained when testing a particle profile. The direct derivative calculation gives the local scalar term before adding the graph pairing. Its coefficient count repeats local source eigenvalues; it does not generate the factor in (3). This makes the extra interaction premise explicit even when the graph ray is described by field derivatives. Verification graph_contact_variation_checks.py checks kernel normalization, complete moving-projector curvature, both coefficient Hessian blocks, fixed and varying rank-one matrices, reciprocal ray derivatives and the exact pair trajectory. It includes depths six and ten without constructing their large occupied-band matrices. Canonical normalization explains the additional physical metric needed to interpret the finite coefficient frequencies.

title: Coherent quartic variation
summary: A smooth quartic action has exactly coherent extrema, an explicit complete mode Hessian and finite-mode orbital stability, with the smooth-contact frequency multiplier.
text:
Summary: A smooth quartic action has exactly coherent extrema, an explicit complete mode Hessian and finite-mode orbital stability, with the smooth-contact frequency multiplier. A specified action on the complete mode band The cumulative tangent-mode carrier at physical depth d is \mathcal H_N=\operatorname{Sym}^N(\mathbb C^{d+1}), \qquad D_N= inom{N+d}{d},\qquad N\ge1. Its generating space consists of d complexified spatial tangent directions and one homogenizing coefficient. Its projective ray space is an auxiliary mode fibre. It does not add physical spatial dimensions, or replace the actual electron spatial manifold by \mathbb{CP}^6. The self-contact module defines the physical base and mode fibre separately. At a fixed spatial base point, or after a separately specified spatial profile reduction, retain every coefficient c\in\mathcal H_N. For a unit generating vector u, write |u;Nangle=u^{\otimes N} and define the normalized coherent transform s_c([u])=\sqrt{D_N}\langle u;N|cangle, \qquad \int |s_c|^2\,d
u_{m FS}=\|c\|^2=J, 	ag{1} where the Fubini--Study measure has total volume one. The phase of this transform depends on the lift of [u]; its absolute square is well defined. Specify the canonical finite-mode action S_N[c]=\int dt\left[  rac i2(c^\dagger\dot c-\dot c^\dagger c)-E_N(c)ight], \qquad E_N(c)= rac{\kappa}{2}\int |s_c|^4\,d
u_{m FS}, \qquad \kappa\in\mathbb R. 	ag{2} The coefficient kinetic metric in (2) is part of this declared action. Equation (1) alone does not prove that a physical spatial Dirac reduction has this metric; its canonical normalization must be derived separately. No omitted spatial kinetic term or spinor component is silently identified with (2). Exact symmetric product formula Let T:\mathcal H_N\otimes\mathcal H_N	o\mathcal H_{2N} be orthogonal symmetrization of all 2N tensor indices, with the target identified with its symmetric subspace. It satisfies TT^\dagger=I and T^\dagger T=\Pi_{2N}, the projector onto that subspace. Put \lambda_N= rac{D_N^2}{D_{2N}},\qquad Q(c)=T(c\otimes c),\qquad A_c h=T(h\otimes c). Applying the coherent resolution of identity at degree 2N gives  oxed{\int |s_c|^4\,d
u_{m FS} =\lambda_N\|Q(c)\|^2,\qquad i\dot c=\kappa\lambda_N A_c^\dagger Q(c).} 	ag{3} Indeed, the product of the two degree-N coherent transforms is (D_N/\sqrt{D_{2N}})s_{Q(c)}, and \delta Q=2A_c\delta c. Varying (2) with respect to \overline c produces the second identity, including its coefficient. It is the complete cubic vector field on \mathcal H_N, not its evaluation on a frozen ray. For an orthonormal occupation basis |\alphaangle, |\alpha|=N, the map can be computed without a tensor of four mode indices: T(|\alphaangle\otimes| etaangle) =t_{\alpha eta}|\alpha+ etaangle, \qquad t_{\alpha eta} =\sqrt{ rac{ inom N\alpha inom N eta} { inom{2N}{\alpha+ eta}}}. 	ag{4} The multi-index Vandermonde identity makes the sum of t_{\alpha eta}^2 at any fixed \alpha+ eta equal to one. This checks the coisometry normalization independently. Coherent states are precisely the sharp extrema Orthogonal projection cannot increase a norm. Consequently  oxed{\int|s_c|^4\,d
u_{m FS} \le\lambda_N\|c\|^4.} 	ag{5} For nonzero c, equality holds exactly when c is a coherent tensor, c=\sqrt J e^{i\phi}z^{\otimes N} with \|z\|=1. Here is a direct proof of the equality condition. Normalize c and suppose c\otimes c lies in the fully symmetric 2N-index subspace. Exchanging one index between the two copies then has expectation one. That expectation is \operatorname{tr}(ho_1^2), where ho_1 is the one-index contraction of |cangle\langle c|. Since ho_1 is positive with trace one, it must have rank one. A tensor with a pure one-index contraction factors across that index; symmetry forces all remaining indices to carry the same vector. The converse follows immediately from z^{\otimes N}\otimes z^{\otimes N}=z^{\otimes2N}. For N=1 every vector is already coherent. This is the fourth-moment instance of coherent-state concentration. The broader convex-function inequality is due to Lieb and Solovej, with equality and quantitative results developed by Nicola, Riccardi and Tilli. The elementary projector proof above supplies the particular result needed for the action without an entropy argument. At fixed J, the coherent orbit is therefore the complete set of global energy maxima for \kappa>0, and global minima for \kappa<0. This is variational selection in the specified finite coefficient space; it does not establish the preferred sign of a physical scalar interaction. Exact coherent branch and nonlinear frequency For c_0=\sqrt J z^{\otimes N}, (3) gives  oxed{c(t)=e^{-i\Omega_N t}c_0,\qquad \Omega_N=\kappa J\lambda_N =\kappa J rac{D_N^2}{D_{2N}}.} 	ag{6} Every coefficient equation is satisfied. The ray [z] is stationary and only its common phase evolves. Coherence therefore supplies an exact stationary branch of the smooth action, without replacing its spectrum by that of a point insertion. The norm J is conserved by the phase symmetry. All mode-frame rotation moments are also conserved. In tensor notation, ho_1= rac1N igl(\langle c,a_j^\dagger a_i cangle igr)_{ij}, \qquad \operatorname{tr}ho_1=J, \qquad \dotho_1=0. 	ag{7} The operators a_j^\dagger a_i act on the symmetric occupation indices. Equation (7) follows from the U(d+1) invariance of (2). This mode-fibre symmetry is an assumption of the isotropic completion, not an additional set of physical spatial rotations. In particular, conservative evolution does not generally capture an arbitrary pattern into a coherent minimum: its energy and the one-index contraction are fixed. Complete perturbation equation Choose z=e_0 by mode-frame covariance and use a frame rotating with \Omega_N. For c=e^{-i\Omega_Nt}(c_0+\eta), define the normalized Toeplitz eigenvalue ratio r_j= rac{N(N-1)\cdots(N-j+1)} {2N(2N-1)\cdots(2N-j+1)},\qquad r_0=1, \qquad 0\le j\le N. 	ag{8} Here j counts occupations outside coordinate zero. Its complex multiplicity is  inom{j+d-1}{d-1}. The full linearized equation is  oxed{  egin{aligned} i\dot\eta_0&=\kappa J\lambda_N(\eta_0+\overline\eta_0),\ i\dot\eta_j&=\kappa J\lambda_N(2r_j-1)\eta_j, \qquad 1\le j\le N. \end{aligned}} 	ag{9} To obtain it directly, write V for multiplication by |s_{c_0}|^2 followed by projection. Its eigenvalue in sector j is J\lambda_Nr_j, as follows from the exact FS monomial integral. The variation of |s|^2s has both terms \delta(|s|^2s)=2|s|^2\delta s+s^2\delta\overline s. The second term has a nonzero projected matrix entry only when the two occupation multi-indices sum to 2Ne_0, so only the radial entry survives. Subtracting the rotating-frame frequency gives (9). Dropping this conjugate term would give an incorrect radial equation. Since r_1=1/2, the d complex tangent directions to the coherent ray are zero modes. For j\ge2, 0<r_j<1/2, and all remaining frequencies are real and have the same sign opposite to \kappa. When N\ge2, the smallest nonzero absolute frequency is |\Omega_{m transverse,min}| =|\kappa|J\lambda_N rac{N}{2N-1}. 	ag{10} The radial equation contains the phase zero mode and the phase drift caused by changing the conserved norm. On a fixed-norm space modulo phase this does not supply an exponentially growing perturbation. Finite-mode nonlinear orbital stability At fixed nonzero J, the state sphere is compact. For N\ge2 the nonnegative deficit \mathcal D(c)=\lambda_NJ^2-\int|s_c|^4\,d
u_{m FS} vanishes exactly on the compact coherent orbit. It has a strictly positive minimum on every closed subset a positive distance from that orbit. Norm and energy conservation therefore imply nonlinear orbital stability of the coherent set under (3), for either nonzero sign of \kappa. The polynomial vector field exists globally because the norm remains bounded. This argument supplies finite-mode nonlinear stability, rather than inferring it solely from real linearized frequencies. The conclusion concerns the whole coherent set, including phase and ray rotations. It is not attraction to one prepared ray. Physical spatial variation, omitted bands, Dirac components, nuclear sources and additional interaction terms require their own stability analysis. Consequence for the mass construction For unit coefficient norm and a band-independent \kappa, the derived frequency multiplier is D_N^2/D_{2N}. The occupied point-contact multiplier is D_N. Their ratio is  rac{\lambda_N}{D_N} = rac{D_N}{D_{2N}} =\prod_{r=1}^d rac{N+r}{2N+r}, which depends on N and tends to 2^{-d} for large N at fixed d. At the specified electron and muon bands (12,34) in depth six, (6) gives the smooth-action ratio 137.029686760779, while the point count gives 206.764705882353. These are the distinct prescriptions compared in the contact-kernel audit. Thus coherent extrema and finite-mode stability can be established for a specific action while its mass-sequence multiplier remains different. Converting (6) into a physical rest mass additionally requires the spatial Dirac equation, its normalized profile and the identification of its pole. Reciprocal extension The complete pair action retains both full mode families. A generic pair leaves the coherent subset, and conservation relates its shape deformation to changing density contact. The aligned stationary set has a separate complete stability calculation. Verification and related coherent_contact_variation_checks.py checks independent FS quadrature, the full nonlinear gradient and both Hessian blocks, symmetric-product normalization, the coherent stationary equation, all perturbation sectors and complete finite-mode evolution. Exact rational formulas also cover large bands without allocating their matrices. The supporting algebra is in coherent_mode_algebra.py. Contact-kernel audit — distinguishes the point and smooth spectral prescriptions used here. Canonical coupling normalization — specifies the physical kinetic metric needed before interpreting the coefficient frequency. Bilateral polarization coupling — separates conservative orientation evolution from encounter-driven changes in compatibility.

title: Contact-kernel audit
summary: Point-contact and smooth-density spectra are compared without identifying their operators.
text:
Physical premise (IDWT): There is one infinite-dimensional physical manifold. All sectors form one nested chain of submanifolds within it. Particle depth counts ordinary, literal macroscopic spatial dimensions. “Observed” and “unobserved” describe an observer's access to those dimensions, not different kinds of physical dimension. See spatial meaning and mathematical scope. Summary: Point-contact and smooth-density spectra are compared without identifying their operators. NOT A PHYSICS MODULE. These are exact finite-band comparison calculations and an action-level audit. The graph-supported point-contact construction remains a live hypothesis; no alternative tested here is silently substituted for it. 1. The source distinction that motivated the test The self-contact source, Section 6.2, explicitly lifts the scalar current onto the graph of a chosen projective ray: \mathcal J_d(q,[u])=J_d(q)\delta_{m FS}([u],[z_{\Psi_d}(q)]), \qquad J_d= ar\Psi_d\Psi_d. It then writes the scalar interaction \mathcal L_{m sc}=-(\kappa_d/2)J_d^2, whose scalar Euler--Lagrange term is -\kappa_dJ_d\Psi_d. Its diagonal kernel is local multiplication. Later in the same subsection, the self-field insertion is identified with a delta concentrated at the selected ray. Section 6.3 proves the finite-band projection theorem for that point insertion, and Section 6.4 applies it to the proposed nonlinear Dirac term. The distinction is important: a kernel f(u)\delta(u,u') specifies multiplication by f, whereas a coefficient f(u)=\delta(u,z) specifies a point-supported multiplier. Locality of the diagonal kernel alone does not choose that coefficient. The graph lift is explicitly an additional part of the written construction; it must neither be ignored nor mistaken for an already completed derivation of the action's projected dynamics. Merely integrating J(q)^2 against the normalized graph delta returns J(q)^2. It does not automatically insert a new finite-band pairing kernel into the action. Establishing that pairing is the remaining dynamical step identified by this audit, not a request for an amplitude measurement. 2. The exact point-contact theorem survives For \mathcal H_N=H^0(\mathbb{CP}^d,\mathcal O(N)), \qquad D_N= inom{N+d}{d}, use unit Fubini-Study measure and the specified homogeneous Hermitian normalization. The reproducing kernel has constant diagonal K_N(z,z)=D_N. Its normalized coherent line is |z;Nangle=K_{N,z}/\sqrt{D_N}. The point-symbol quadratic form is \langle s,T_{\delta_z}tangle=\overline{s(z)}t(z). It gives T_{\delta_z}=P_N\delta_zP_N =|K_{N,z}angle\langle K_{N,z}| =D_N|z;Nangle\langle z;N|. Its nonzero eigenvalue is exactly D_N. This result depends on the stated ray, finite band, measure, and covariance assumptions. It is not the claim that every algebraic scalar interaction has this spectrum. The source itself makes isotropic projective completion a necessary premise and separately requires a band-blind normalized coefficient; see Sections 6.3--6.4 and 9. 3. Three different local multiplier prescriptions In the same finite Hilbert space, compare the following unit-normalized symbols: Symbol on the ray space Projected operator spectrum Constant 1 Eigenvalue 1 with multiplicity D_N Point source \delta_z Eigenvalue D_N once, otherwise zero Smooth coherent density j_z(u)=D_N|\langle u,zangle|^{2N} Full positive spectrum below, with largest eigenvalue D_N^2/D_{2N} All three have projected trace D_N. Equal trace therefore does not imply equal spectrum. The smooth case has rank D_N, whereas the point case has rank one. These are different operators, not alternative normalizations of the same eigenvector. The smooth symbol is normalized because \int_{\mathbb{CP}^d}|\langle u,zangle|^{2N}d
u(u)= rac{1}{D_N}. It is a comparison prescription: the source graph lift selects a point symbol, not automatically this smooth density. 4. Full smooth-symbol spectrum Choose z along coordinate zero. On normalized degree-N monomials, let k be the occupation of that coordinate. The remaining d occupations sum to N-k. Unit-FS monomial moments obey \int \prod_{r=0}^{d}|u_r|^{2m_r}d
u(u) = rac{d!\prod_rm_r!}{(d+\sum_rm_r)!}. The normalized monomial of multi-index \alpha, |\alpha|=N, has squared normalization (N+d)!/(d!\prod_r\alpha_r!). Multiplication by D_N|u_0|^{2N} therefore gives the diagonal eigenvalue  oxed{\lambda_k =D_N rac{(N+d)!}{(2N+d)!} rac{(N+k)!}{k!}}, \qquad 0\le k\le N, with multiplicity  oxed{m_k= inom{N-k+d-1}{d-1}}. Phase invariance makes the off-diagonal monomial integrals vanish. The largest eigenvalue occurs at k=N and simplifies to  oxed{\lambda_{\max}= rac{D_N^2}{D_{2N}}}. The checks verify positivity, \sum_km_k=D_N, and \sum_km_k\lambda_k=D_N for the tested bands, using exact rational arithmetic. They do not require constructing the largest matrices explicitly. N,d D_N Smooth largest eigenvalue Smooth largest eigenvalue divided by D_N 1,1 2 4/3 2/3 2,2 6 12/5 2/5 3,3 20 100/21 5/21 2,4 15 45/14 3/14 12,6 18564 580.391724138 0.0312643678161 34,6 3838380 79530.8961572 0.0207199120872 For example, at (N,d)=(3,3) the complete spectrum is 5/21, 20/21, 50/21, 100/21, with multiplicities 10,6,3,1, respectively. 5. A same-sector shape test, not a scale fit Using the already specified electron and muon bands, N_e=12, N_\mu=34, d=6, a common band-independent coefficient cancels in either prescription. The point prescription gives  rac{D_{34}}{D_{12}}= rac{3515}{17} \approx206.764705882353. The smooth-symbol occupied-line prescription gives  rac{D_{34}^2/D_{68}}{D_{12}^2/D_{24}} = rac{9441729375}{68902802} \approx137.029686760779. These are calculated spectral ratios under two different prescriptions, not new experimental measurements. An overall electron unit conversion cannot make the prescriptions identical. This demonstrates the importance of the operator choice. It does not disprove the graph-supported point construction by imposing the smooth construction in its place. No experimental precision or significance claim is made in this note. 6. Single contact evaluation versus double smearing The finite-band coherent pairing kernel is B_N(z,w)=\langle z;N|T_{\delta_w}|z;Nangle =D_N|\langle z,wangle|^{2N}. It satisfies \int B_N(z,w)d
u(w)=1, \qquad B_N(z,z)=D_N. A point source evaluated at its own ray uses the coincident value of this one kernel. Replacing the source by its smooth coherent density and averaging the test coherent density against it instead gives \int B_N(z,w)^2d
u(w)= rac{D_N^2}{D_{2N}}. This is the previously undocumented explanation of the two eigenvalues. A graph-source interaction with one such finite-band pairing can retain the linear simplex count; two smoothings yield a different quantity. Neither operation may be silently substituted for the other. What remains open is the action-level origin and ordering of the pairing: the proposed graph current, the nonlinear variation, and the finite-band projection have to be joined in one specified construction. The test establishes a consistent mathematical distinction, not that the full master action has already supplied this joining. 7. Moving self-consistent ray: the limited cancellation that is exact Differentiate P^2=P for a differentiable orthogonal projector: (\delta P)P+P(\delta P)=\delta P. Multiplying by P on both sides gives  oxed{P(\delta P)P=0.} For a normalized u on the occupied line, \langle u,\delta P\,uangle=0. This was checked with a complex ray u=(3/5,4i/5)^T and a Hermitian generator of projector motion. It removes the automatic objection that every change of the self-consistent ray must shift the occupied eigenvalue at first order. It does not imply (\delta P)u=0, erase off-diagonal variations, or prove the full nonlinear Euler--Lagrange equation. In particular, derivative dependence of the ray, variation of the contact coefficient, kinetic contributions, and stability of the coherent branch remain separate questions. No claim of complete variational closure follows from the diagonal projector identity. 8. Findings to carry forward Graph contact variation supplies a defined measure-pairing action with one finite-band kernel. Its self-contraction retains D_N, while its full ray-dependent variation cancels self-orientation stiffness. The remaining scalar coefficient still needs a normalized spatial solution before it can be interpreted as a rest mass. Coherent quartic variation gives the complete action-level calculation for the smooth prescription. Coherent tensors are its sharp fourth-moment extrema, and its full conjugate-linear Hessian and finite-mode orbital stability can be derived. Its nonlinear frequency still contains D_N^2/D_{2N}. Thus the existence of a coherent stationary branch does not by itself select the point-contact mass sequence. Checked: the point-contact identity; the constant, point, and smooth comparison spectra; the exact smooth-symbol family ratio; normalization and coincidence of the single pairing kernel; its squared-kernel integral; and the diagonal moving-projector cancellation. Not established: that ordinary diagonal locality alone forces the graph symbol; that the graph lift by itself supplies the required action pairing; that double smearing is the correct V2 prescription; that the chosen coherent branch solves and is selected by the full projected dynamics; or that these calculations determine a baryon frequency. No current magnitude, field amplitude, or profile parameter was fitted. The unknowns are operator identification and the derivation or cancellation of their physical coefficients. The regression script reproduces the finite tests; the source passages are self-contact Sections 6.1--6.4 and 9. Related Research status — current proof boundaries and correction guidance. Band consistency and finite resolution Consistent band contacts tests how the coherent family changes under the specified cumulative oscillator inclusion. A fixed bare kernel has one compatibility law; an effective kernel obtained by eliminating same-field modes has a different Schur consistency law. Finite ray resolution independently varies the symbol width and retained band, giving the complete spectrum and an exact operator-norm error relative to the point contact.

title: When a two-frequency spatial symmetry exists
summary: A constant antilinear reduction requires a specific involution of the complete spatial Dirac matrices, and its existence, scalar interference and compatibility with nested field projections can be checked directly.
text: Summary: A constant antilinear reduction requires a specific involution of the complete spatial Dirac matrices, and its existence, scalar interference and compatibility with nested field projections can be checked directly. A special solution family need not be a symmetry of arbitrary fields The radial two-frequency map constructs full solutions from arbitrary complex radial profiles. Extending that map to arbitrary spatial perturbations requires an additional matrix identity. The number of field components alone does not supply it. Here r counts the ordinary macroscopic spatial derivatives actually retained in the equation. A bound depth d has r=d when normal motion is suppressed, and r=d+1 when one existing normal direction is included. These coordinates belong to the one nested manifold. Matrix ranks and conjugation operations describe its field components; they do not introduce new physical dimensions. Consider H=-i\sum_{j=1}^r\alpha_j\partial_j+\beta\mathfrak m, \qquad \mathfrak m\in\mathbb R. \tag{1} Use constant Clifford matrices in the stated flat spatial model, on a common domain preserved by the proposed conjugation and boundary conditions. A matrix identity alone does not establish a symmetry of a different operator domain or of a curved spatial bundle. A coordinate-preserving antilinear partner C=B\mathsf K, where \mathsf K conjugates the field components, must obey \boxed{B\alpha_j^*=\alpha_jB,\qquad B\beta^*=-\beta B,\qquad B^\dagger B=I.} \tag{2} These identities give CH=-HC, including every retained derivative. They also give (C\psi)^\dagger\beta(C\psi)=-\psi^\dagger\beta\psi. To mix \psi and C\psi while preserving the scalar source for arbitrary complex fields, their cross bilinear must vanish. This requires \boxed{(\beta B)^T=-\beta B, \qquad C^2=BB^*=I.} \tag{3} Under (2), the two conditions in (3) are equivalent. For example, BB^*=I makes the unitary B symmetric, and then (\beta B)^T=B\beta^*=-\beta B. The related nonlinear Dirac symmetry and its matrix requirements are discussed by Boussaïd and Comech. The calculations below check the actual spatial matrices and the centered moment source used here, rather than assuming a symmetry from a smaller field representation. Check the complete Clifford representation The standard complex Clifford representation can be constructed from Pauli matrices: \gamma_{2j-1}=Z^{\otimes(j-1)}\otimes X\otimes I^{\otimes(k-j)}, \qquad \gamma_{2j}=Z^{\otimes(j-1)}\otimes Y\otimes I^{\otimes(k-j)}. \tag{4} For an odd number 2k+1 of generators, append \gamma_{2k+1}=Z^{\otimes k}. Use the first r generators as \alpha_j and the last as \beta. This is an irreducible complex representation of the full indicated Clifford algebra. Each generator has \gamma_j^*=\epsilon_j\gamma_j, with \epsilon_j=\pm1. For a product B=\prod_{j\in S}\gamma_j of m=|S| distinct generators, B\gamma_jB^{-1}=(-1)^{m-\mathbf1_{j\in S}}\gamma_j, \qquad BB^*=(-1)^{N_{\rm imag}+m(m-1)/2}I. \tag{5} Here N_{\rm imag} counts imaginary generators in the product. The required signs are \epsilon_j on spatial generators and -\epsilon_\beta on the scalar generator. Equations (4)–(5) provide explicit intertwiners and their squares. For r=4 and r=8, the product of all r+1 generators is a nonzero real scalar times I. Equations (2) would make antilinear conjugation change its sign, but a real scalar cannot change under such conjugation. No B satisfying (2) exists in those stated representations. When a solution exists, any two invertible solutions of (2) differ by a matrix commuting with every generator. Irreducibility makes that matrix a scalar. A phase change of B cannot change BB^*, so a computed negative square cannot be replaced by a positive square in the same irreducible representation. retained spatial derivatives r complex field components result for C^2 1 2 +I 2 2 +I 3 4 +I 4 4 no intertwiner satisfying (2) 5 8 -I 6 8 -I 7 16 -I 8 16 no intertwiner satisfying (2) 9 32 +I 10 32 +I 11 64 +I Thus the minimal five- and six-dimensional bound equations do not have the involution (3). Including one normal derivative gives r=6 or r=7 and still has a negative square. The corresponding ten-dimensional examples have a positive square. These are matrix statements about the specified operators, not assignments of particle charge, stability or interaction strength. A positive square gives a controlled nonlinear map When (2)–(3) hold, define \mathcal T\psi=a\psi+bC\psi, \qquad s=|a|^2-|b|^2>0. \tag{6} Pointwise scalar interference vanishes, giving \sigma[\mathcal T\psi]=s\sigma[\psi]. In the centered moment source, the scalar center is unchanged and its second moment is multiplied by s, provided its scalar normalization is nonzero. Consequently, if \psi solves the complete spatial source equation at coefficient g_0s, then \mathcal T\psi solves it at g_0 with the same bare scalar term. This follows directly by applying (2) to each derivative and using the transformed scalar moment. The real-linear map has \boxed{\mathcal T^{-1}=\frac{\bar a-bC}{s},\qquad \operatorname{Im}\langle\mathcal T u,\mathcal T v\rangle =s\operatorname{Im}\langle u,v\rangle.} \tag{7} At fixed nonzero s it is invertible and transfers the growth exponents of the corresponding full real field linearizations. The map becomes poorly conditioned when its two weights approach equality: \operatorname{cond}_{\mathbb R}\mathcal T =\frac{|a|+|b|}{|a|-|b|}. \tag{8} The number norm is generally different from the radial isometry: \boxed{\|\mathcal T\psi\|^2 =(|a|^2+|b|^2)\|\psi\|^2 +2\operatorname{Re}\big[\bar a b\langle\psi,C\psi\rangle\big].} \tag{9} The cross term need not vanish on arbitrary fields. A stationary nonzero-frequency eigenfunction is orthogonal to its opposite-frequency partner, but that fact must not be applied to every perturbation. For C^2=-I, equation (2) instead makes \beta B symmetric. Generic complex fields then have nonzero \psi^\dagger\beta C\psi, so the single scalar scaling used in (6) fails. Exact radial and real anisotropic two-frequency families can still exist through their own spatial identities. They do not require a global transformation of every field perturbation. Include the existing normal direction before using the symmetry A symmetry of the bound equation must also satisfy BY^*=YB to include its normal derivative. In the tested three-dimensional bound representation, the involution instead has BY^*=-YB. At normal momentum q, it therefore obeys B H_{-q}^*+H_qB=2qYB, \qquad H_q=H_b+qY. \tag{10} Its bound-space reduction fails as soon as that normal propagation is retained. In the tested five-dimensional case, the negative-square partner respects the normal derivative but still fails the arbitrary-field scalar-interference condition. These are distinct requirements, checked separately in the full spatial source. The occupied polarizations also matter. A background generated by (6) must have Y\phi_2=C\phi_1, or \phi_2=YC\phi_1. That is a specific correlation between the two occupied profiles. It cannot be presumed for independent polarizations. For the deformed three-dimensional profile in a 2\subset3 pair, this correlated preparation cancels all scalar rest sidebands. The full normal response still opens them. The analogous orthogonal preparation in the deformed five-dimensional profile of a 3\subset5 pair has nonzero scalar sidebands even at rest. Orthogonality alone therefore does not substitute for the full spatial symmetry calculation. The reciprocal periodic response retains these channels directly. A containing-space involution need not preserve a projected sector Suppose a higher representation has C^2=I, and P selects a lower field copy while retaining its lower spatial Clifford operators and \beta. If CP=PC, restricting C to that copy would give a positive-square solution of (2) there. That is impossible when the selected minimal lower representation requires C^2=-I. The containing involution must then leave that selected copy. This can be checked explicitly in the 64-component representation with ten bound derivatives and one common normal derivative. Commuting rotation projectors on the other containing directions select a lower minimal copy of rank 8 for bound depth five or rank 16 for bound depth six. For the checked projectors, \boxed{PBP^*=0,\qquad \|(I-P)BP^*\|_F^2=\operatorname{rank}P.} \tag{11} The transformation's full norm goes into complementary field components. Those components still describe the same nested physical manifold. This is a compatibility condition on a symmetry and a chosen field projection, not an obstruction to the nesting of the spatial sectors. The spatial reflection analysis provides related constraints on their polarization multiplicities. Verification and scope antilinear_dirac_checks.py constructs (4)–(5), checks every spatial matrix relation, and independently solves the complete complex linear intertwiner equations at the smaller ranks. It checks scalar interference, the real kinetic form, the inverse and number norm on arbitrary complex field vectors. Complete centered nonlinear source evaluations test the map beyond a stationary ansatz. Independent prepared spatial resolvents test the correlated-polarization sidebands. Explicit containing-space projectors verify (11). Reports are timestamped and checks remain active with Python optimization. The obstruction concerns constant coordinate-preserving antilinear maps in the specified representations. Additional field multiplicities, spatial reflections, nonlocal transformations and special solution families require their own analysis. The full periodic source equation remains available without assuming this reduction.

title: Two-frequency spatial Dirac currents
summary: Opposite-frequency components of the same spatial Dirac field give exact current oscillations at twice the bound frequency, with a common scalar source and explicit normalization, size and response constraints.
text: Summary: Opposite-frequency components of the same spatial Dirac field give exact current oscillations at twice the bound frequency, with a common scalar source and explicit normalization, size and response constraints. Construct a spatial clock from the bound field itself A stationary field's common phase cancels from its bilinear observables. Nevertheless, the scalar Dirac model admits exact fields whose spatial currents oscillate at a frequency fixed by their bound profile. This provides a concrete construction to examine when asking whether slow particle oscillations can weaken coupling. Use ordinary bound coordinates x\in\mathbb R^d and one existing normal coordinate y in a containing sector of the same nested physical manifold. The two components below belong to one field. No interaction particle or extra internal spatial direction is introduced. The specific source model used here is local in time and y, with a centered spatial moment over the bound coordinates: \begin{gathered} \sigma=\Psi^\dagger\beta\Psi,\qquad Q_\sigma=\int\sigma\,dx\ne0,\qquad X_\sigma=Q_\sigma^{-1}\int x\sigma\,dx,\\ M_\sigma=\int(x-X_\sigma)(x-X_\sigma)^T\sigma\,dx,\\ i\partial_t\Psi=\left[-i\alpha_i\partial_i-i\alpha_y\partial_y +\beta\left(m_0+g_0(x-X_\sigma)^TM_\sigma(x-X_\sigma)\right)\right]\Psi. \end{gathered} The Hermitian matrices obey the ordinary spatial Clifford relations; \beta anticommutes with each \alpha. With X_\sigma=0 and a radial source, the bound operator is H_b=-i\alpha_i\partial_i+\beta(m_0+a_{\rm source}r^2). Only boosts in the (t,y) plane are used below; full spacetime Lorentz covariance of this bound-coordinate kernel is not assumed. For a real radial bound profile, the normal-partner construction supplies H_b\phi=M\phi,\qquad H_b(\alpha_y\phi)=-M\alpha_y\phi, \qquad \int\phi^\dagger\phi\,dx=1. \tag{1} The two fields are orthogonal. The stronger pointwise scalar identity is \phi^\dagger\beta\alpha_y\phi=0, \qquad (\alpha_y\phi)^\dagger\beta(\alpha_y\phi) =-\phi^\dagger\beta\phi. \tag{2} It follows from the full upper and lower radial components, as established for all selected rest polarizations in Spatial Dirac polarization waves. An exact nonlinear two-frequency family Choose complex constants a,b and define \boxed{\Psi(t,x)=a\phi(x)e^{-iMt} +b\alpha_y\phi(x)e^{iMt}.} \tag{3} Set n=|a|^2+|b|^2 and s=|a|^2-|b|^2. Equation (2) gives \boxed{\Psi^\dagger\beta\Psi=s\,\phi^\dagger\beta\phi, \qquad \int\Psi^\dagger\Psi\,dx=n.} \tag{4} Solve the bound profile with this same scalar weight s. Its scalar center and every scalar binding moment are then constant. Each frequency component solves the same frozen bound equation, and their sum preserves exactly the source which defined that equation. Thus (3) solves the full nonlinear scalar moment equation, uniformly in y. Two-frequency solitary waves also occur in nonlinear Dirac models with local scalar interaction; see Boussaïd and Comech. Equations (1)–(4) prove the present construction directly for the specified spatial moment source. Stability results for a different source model are not being assumed here. The current and number-density pattern really move Write the reference bilinears as \rho_0=\phi^\dagger\phi, j_{i0}=\phi^\dagger\alpha_i\phi and j_{y0}=\phi^\dagger\alpha_y\phi. Define z(t)=\bar a b e^{2iMt},\qquad v_i(x)=\phi^\dagger(-i\alpha_i\alpha_y)\phi\in\mathbb R. Direct multiplication of the complete spatial field gives \boxed{ \begin{aligned} \rho(t,x)&=n\rho_0(x)+2\operatorname{Re}z(t)\,j_{y0}(x),\\ j_y(t,x)&=n j_{y0}(x)+2\operatorname{Re}z(t)\,\rho_0(x),\\ j_i(t,x)&=s j_{i0}(x)-2\operatorname{Im}z(t)\,v_i(x). \end{aligned}} \tag{5} These are currents over literal spatial coordinates. Their identification with a particular electromagnetic source still requires the physical current map. The scalar binding density in (4) does not move with them. For n=1, the integrated normal current has oscillation amplitude 2|ab|=\sqrt{1-s^2}. It can remain large when the bound frequency is small. The bound number-density centroid provides another check. For a radial rest polarization w, put J_{iy}=w^\dagger(-i\alpha_i\alpha_y)w,\qquad F_0=\frac{1-2G/d}{2M}, \quad G=\int g(r)^2r^{d-1}dr. \tag{6} Then \boxed{X_{\rho,i}(t)=2\operatorname{Re}z(t)F_0J_{iy}, \qquad \dot X_{\rho,i}=-4M\operatorname{Im}z(t)F_0J_{iy}.} \tag{7} Independent integration of j_i yields precisely the second expression, checking spatial continuity. The scalar center stays fixed. For the tested pure odd-dimensional preparations, \sum_iJ_{iy}^2=1; the selected six-dimensional rest chirality instead has J_{iy}=0. A slower clock increases the excursion scale F_0\propto1/M at fixed radial shape. The corresponding speed amplitude is \sqrt{1-s^2}(1-2G/d) for the unit odd-dimensional circulation. It stays finite: low frequency alone does not imply a small moving current. The five-dimensional field still occupies all five bound spatial directions. Keep the canonical norm and the common coefficient fixed Set n=1, 0<s\le1, and choose |a|^2=\frac{1+s}{2},\qquad |b|^2=\frac{1-s}{2}. \tag{8} For the zero-bare-mass scalar moment branch, let M_* and \phi_* denote the profile at s=1 with a fixed coefficient g_0. The exact self-consistent scaling is \boxed{\lambda=s^{1/5},\qquad \phi_s(x)=\lambda^{d/2}\phi_*(\lambda x),\qquad M(s)=\lambda M_*,\qquad a_{\rm source}(s)=\lambda^3a_{\rm source}(1).} \tag{9} Both frequency components use this readjusted profile. The full field's source satisfies a_{\rm source}=g_0sT/d, where T=\int r^2\phi_s^\dagger\beta\phi_s\,dx. Under dilation, T\mapsto\lambda^{-2}T, so self-consistency gives \lambda^3=s\lambda^{-2} and hence \lambda=s^{1/5}. The full field's canonical norm remains one; s measures their signed scalar balance. The total scalar second moment scales as s\lambda^{-2}=s^{3/5}, while the squared number-density radius scales as s^{-2/5}. Reducing the scalar balance therefore makes the current clock slower and the bound field broader using the same g_0. For d=5, g_0=6.5 and zero bare mass, independent spatial solves give: scalar balance s bound frequency M current frequency 2M bound centroid excursion amplitude centroid speed amplitude 1 2.472753 4.945506 0 0 0.5 2.152656 4.305313 0.185593 0.799034 0.05 1.358234 2.716469 0.339224 0.921491 0.001 0.621127 1.242255 0.742718 0.922645 These are model units and a continuous family, not a neutrino mass table. The same construction works at the tested depths three and six. The action has not selected a particular s or a uniquely five-dimensional preparation. As s\to0, the bound profile spreads without limit, so the endpoint is not a finite localized zero-frequency particle. The conserved full field energy per chosen normal normalization interval is the bound kinetic expectation plus \mathcal E_{\rm int}=g_0\operatorname{tr}(M_\sigma^2)/2. For the zero-bare-mass family it is \boxed{\mathcal E(s) =sM(s)-\mathcal E_{\rm int}(s) =\frac56sM(s)=\frac56M_*s^{6/5}.} \tag{10} The first equality retains the opposite signs of the two frequencies; the last uses the spatial dilation law. A periodic field containing both signs is not a single stationary energy eigenmode. Neither M nor (10) can be assigned a measured neutrino mass without deriving that particle identification and its propagation normalization. A small mean scalar source does not fix its response The shrinking scalar moment in (9) reduces its diagonal scalar cross energy against a fixed partner in the specified moment kernel. The other partner must readjust at finite coupling, and the full variation still includes changes of s, shape and polarization. For example, parametrize (8) by a=\cos\theta, |b|=\sin\theta, with 0\le\theta<\pi/4, so s=\cos2\theta. Differentiating the readjusted energy gives \frac{d\mathcal E}{d\theta} =-2M(s)\sqrt{1-s^2},\qquad \boxed{\frac{d^2\mathcal E}{d\theta^2} =\frac{4M(s)}{5s}(1-6s^2).} \tag{11} For small positive s, the second derivative grows as s^{-4/5}. Thus a small mean binding source can coexist with a large response to changing the relative components. This curvature is not a stability proof for the periodic field. Its linearized source also has explicit time dependence. If the spatial moment columns are C(t)=aC_+e^{-iMt}+bC_-e^{iMt}, the ordinary and conjugate feedback blocks contain respectively C(t)\kappa C(t)^\dagger, \qquad C(t)\kappa C(t)^T. \tag{12} Here \kappa is the constant moment curvature at the unchanged scalar source, including the scalar-center response where required. The blocks in (12) contain frequencies 0,\pm2M. A perturbation can therefore drive sidebands separated by 2M. Its response requires a calculation with periodic coefficients, or an equivalent Floquet expansion; substituting 2M into a stationary single-frequency susceptibility does not supply it. Periodic spatial source response derives that complete equation. Some scalar readouts satisfy an exact finite spectral cancellation at rest, while normal propagation reopens their sidebands. The full shape response provides the relevant spatial source columns, with the time dependence retained here. Motion changes the source phase seen by the partner The normal boost symmetry gives another exact solution: \Psi_\eta(t,x,y) =e^{\eta\alpha_y/2}\Psi_0(\tau,x),\qquad \tau=\cosh\eta\,t-\sinh\eta\,y. \tag{13} Its scalar source remains the same pointwise. The current's oscillating phase is 2M\tau, with frequency 2M\cosh\eta and normal wavenumber 2M\sinh\eta in these coordinates. Along a comoving trajectory it accumulates at 2M per proper time. At a fixed position the uniform boosted pattern instead oscillates at 2M\cosh\eta. A finite encounter also includes the spatial envelope and overlap of both objects. Their motion cannot be represented by inserting the rest clock alone into a target response. The general source-frequency accounting is in Source frequencies in spatial coupling. Radial dynamics of two-frequency fields extends this stationary construction to arbitrary complex radial motion. It proves the distinct number and kinetic weights and transfers an existing radial instability into the full two-frequency field. Verification source_frequency_checks.py recomputes the scalar profile at fixed common coefficient and unit total norm for several scalar balances and depths. Full spatial quadrature checks the density, moments, currents, centroid and conserved energy. Independent finite derivatives in every bound coordinate, time and the normal direction verify both unboosted and boosted nonlinear solutions. Independent temporal Fourier transforms recover the twice-frequency current and the periodic source-feedback blocks. Energy differences verify (11). The construction supplies an exact spatial clock and its limitations; full stability, the occupied neutrino geometry and physical photon coupling remain to be established. Related Normal propagation of spatial Dirac modes — supplies the partner, boost and current-moment identities. Spatial Dirac polarization waves — supplies the complete spatial polarization frame. Source frequencies in spatial coupling — explains the clock sampled by a physical output map.

title: Bilateral polarization coupling
summary: Keeping both objects polarized gives covariant tensor pairings, distinct source and response zeros, and a reciprocal orientation model with exactly conserved relative overlap.
text: Summary: Keeping both objects polarized gives covariant tensor pairings, distinct source and response zeros, and a reciprocal orientation model with exactly conserved relative overlap. Both objects carry spatial polarization Let the two particle patterns carry spatial tensors J_a(x;\alpha) and J_b(y;\beta), where \alpha,\beta label their respective preparations. These parameters describe fields on actual nested macroscopic spatial submanifolds of one infinite manifold. They are not additional physical dimensions. Each object has its own polarization and can change in response to the other; a fixed-target calculation is a conditional snapshot. The working physical hypothesis is that this reciprocal motion can improve or worsen the match between the spatial patterns. An encounter may therefore strengthen its subsequent coupling or move the patterns toward incompatibility. Changing compatibility is a proposed part of the mechanism, to be tested from the same field equations. The calculation must follow both patterns during the encounter and determine which responses initiate and sustain that change. Initial overlap alone does not determine the outcome. Neither automatic alignment nor conserved relative overlap is a general requirement; the exactly conserved overlap in the benchmark below is a property of its specified restricted dynamics. A specified reciprocal two-form term can be written U[\alpha,\beta] =-g\operatorname{Re}\int\!\int \left\langle J_a(x;\alpha), \mathcal K_{ab}(x,y)J_b(y;\beta)\right\rangle d\mu_a(x)d\mu_b(y). \tag{1} The kernel includes the actual spatial maps, frame transport, and any derivatives prescribed by the action. All tensors must be paired in compatible frames. Reciprocity uses the adjoint kernel for the reverse variation. Equation (1) is a conditional term of the one field's energy; the kernel and tensor observables must come from its action. Under a common rotation of all physical geometric data, J\mapsto RJR^T and \mathcal K transforms correspondingly, leaving (1) unchanged. Rotating only the particles while keeping an anisotropic environment fixed is a different physical preparation and need not preserve the energy. For a local isotropic benchmark, with two real tensors at one common point, the expression reduces to U=-g\langle A,B\rangle, \qquad\langle A,B\rangle=-\frac12\operatorname{tr}(AB). \tag{2} If A=R_aA_0R_a^T and B=R_bB_0R_b^T, this depends on the relative rotation R_a^TR_b. Either tensor can be the lower or higher pattern. The formula does not privilege one as the only polarized object. Plane alignment includes both principal directions For oriented orthonormal pairs u_1,u_2 and v_1,v_2, put A=u_1\wedge u_2 and B=v_1\wedge v_2, with u\wedge v=uv^T-vu^T. Direct expansion gives \boxed{ \langle A,B\rangle =(u_1\cdot v_1)(u_2\cdot v_2) -(u_1\cdot v_2)(u_2\cdot v_1) =\det(U^TV),} \tag{3} where U=(u_1,u_2) and V=(v_1,v_2). The singular values of U^TV are \cos\theta_1,\cos\theta_2, the two principal-angle cosines. Hence the squared pairing is |\langle A,B\rangle|^2 =\cos^2\theta_1\cos^2\theta_2. \tag{4} The sign of (3) also retains relative orientation. For several rotational planes, expand A=\sum_i a_i A_i and B=\sum_j b_j B_j: \langle A,B\rangle =\sum_{i,j}a_i b_j\det(U_i^TV_j). \tag{5} Contributions to this same scalar pairing add before it is squared. Opposite orientations can cancel despite nonzero overlap of individual planes. Complex oscillating tensors additionally retain their relative phases through the Hermitian pairing. A temporal or ensemble average must be justified by the specified preparation. A zero static source need not be a zero response Let a photon amplitude a couple to a target preparation \beta through U(a,\beta)=-g\,a\,s(\beta), \qquad s(\beta)=\langle B_\gamma,J_b(\beta)\rangle \tag{6} for one real wave quadrature. The background can satisfy s(\beta_0)=0 while the mixed derivative is nonzero: \boxed{\frac{\partial^2U}{\partial a\,\partial\beta} =-g\left\langle B_\gamma, \frac{\partial J_b}{\partial\beta}\right\rangle.} \tag{7} For an exact example in three ordinary spatial directions, choose B_\gamma=e_1\wedge e_2 and J_b(\theta) =\cos\theta\,(e_2\wedge e_3) +\sin\theta\,(e_1\wedge e_2). This is a unit simple two-form for every \theta. Its static pairing at zero is zero, but s'(0)=1. An incoming wave can therefore drive the target's angular variation even when the target's unperturbed projection supplies no source in that wave direction. For two varying target patterns and a fixed kernel, the mixed variation of (1) contains \delta_a\delta_b U =-g\operatorname{Re}\int\!\int \langle\delta J_a,\mathcal K_{ab}\delta J_b\rangle d\mu_a d\mu_b. \tag{8} When the kernel, embeddings, or measures also change, include those derivatives. A claim of no linear coupling must test all allowed response tangents and the other action terms. The value of (1) at one preparation, by itself, is insufficient. A complete mode-fibre pair action provides a conditional deformation benchmark: two initially coherent patterns leave the coherent subset, and their changing density contact is constrained by energy and rotation moments. This positive-density component model retains shape responses beyond two ray angles; its auxiliary mode-space dynamics still require a physical spatial and Dirac-current reduction. A solvable reciprocal orientation benchmark For the finite isotropic energy (2), give A and B fixed coadjoint orbits of SO(D) and positive symplectic weights \ell_a,\ell_b. Specify the Lie–Poisson convention \ell_a\dot A=[A,\nabla_AU], \qquad \ell_b\dot B=[B,\nabla_BU]. The equations are \ell_a\dot A=-g[A,B], \qquad \ell_b\dot B=g[A,B]. \tag{9} Both polarizations respond. Their weighted sum S=\ell_aA+\ell_bB is constant, as are their individual spectra, the overlap \langle A,B\rangle, and the energy. Since \dot A=\frac{g}{\ell_a\ell_b}[S,A], \qquad \dot B=\frac{g}{\ell_a\ell_b}[S,B], the exact solution is \boxed{ R(t)=\exp\left(\frac{gt}{\ell_a\ell_b}S\right), \qquad A(t)=R(t)A(0)R(t)^T, \qquad B(t)=R(t)B(0)R(t)^T.} \tag{10} The weights are coefficients of a specified first-order orientation action, not values inferred from spatial depth. These orbit dynamics preserve tensor spectra and rotate both objects together. They produce precession, with no attraction toward a better matched relative angle. Testing the proposed improvement or loss of compatibility during an encounter therefore requires derived spatial motion, anisotropy, or response structure beyond this benchmark. The direction of that change must follow from the equations, rather than a rule that always favors alignment. Equation (9) assumes the displayed orbit variations are admissible. Fixed sector embeddings or geometric constraints can restrict the allowed generators and require reaction terms. The benchmark does not establish that arbitrary rotations preserve every global nested embedding. Following the full field beyond its mean rotation tensor The coadjoint benchmark follows the two-form observables. They need not specify the complete polarized field at a higher spatial depth. Equal-current spatial polarizations derives a reciprocal six-inside-ten example from a rotation-moment energy and both full spatial kinetic terms. Its mean tensors remain fixed while the higher field can rotate into an orthogonal polarization. Thus even a two-form interaction can require more field information to describe its response than the mean two-forms alone retain. Relation to the photon and higher-sector calculations The tensor J_d in photon plane coupling already specifies one target polarization, while E,k,c specify the photon's polarization and propagation. Its projector calculation freezes the target at that preparation. Equations (7)–(8) supply the additional test when both can respond. The descending source starts from the higher pattern; its derivative gives the reverse response. The Dirac source derivative computes that derivative explicitly for one written nonlinear term. These descriptions can coexist: the higher geometry may determine the source while the two objects' relative polarizations determine which response is engaged. Verification polarization_coupling_checks.py checks the displayed identities with independent spatial quadrature, energy variations, or full finite-system evolution as appropriate. These checks verify the declared mathematics and benchmarks, not empirical couplings. Related Descending photon source — separates the source value from its reciprocal derivative. Photon plane coupling — fixes both spatial preparations for one instantaneous overlap. Dirac source linearization — retains the changes of the higher field and its nonlinear source. Canonical free-pair operator — gives an earlier two-electron example whose invariants depend on both complex structures. Polarized response spectrum weights the spatially allowed responses by their frequencies and finite exposure time. Coherent spatial overlap evaluates both objects' shapes and phases in exact Gaussian and opposing-lobe examples.

title: Canonical coupling normalization
summary: Kinetic Gram matrices fix normalized transition vertices and conserved generators, separating charge universality from profile-dependent interaction strength.
text: Summary: Kinetic Gram matrices fix normalized transition vertices and conserved generators, separating charge universality from profile-dependent interaction strength. Modes and the kinetic metric Use finite sets of linearly independent, admissible mode sections in arbitrary nested physical sectors. Their coefficient labels are not additional spatial dimensions. Let S_d map coefficients c_d to the spatial field, and let the positive time-kinetic form induce Z_d=S_d^\dagger S_d>0,\qquad L_{\rm kin}=\sum_d i c_d^\dagger Z_d\dot c_d. The dagger includes the specified spatial measure and bundle inner product. The block form assumes kinetic orthogonality between the retained families. Spatial nesting alone does not imply it. If cross terms occur, use the full positive Gram matrix for the independent combined basis and normalize that matrix. Redundant sections must first be removed; a singular Gram matrix cannot be normalized with an inverse. With \hbar=1, define z_d=Z_d^{1/2}c_d. The kinetic term becomes i z_d^\dagger\dot z_d. For a coherent cross-sector vertex with a single real perturbation amplitude A of the same field, U_{\rm tr}=A\,c_a^\dagger K_{ab}c_b+\text{complex conjugate}, Here A is a retained variation of \Psi_\infty, and the trilinear term is conditional on its expansion from that field's action. It does not introduce a separate interaction field or a mediator particle. The matter-normalized vertex is \widehat K_{ab}=Z_a^{-1/2}K_{ab}Z_b^{-1/2}. \tag{1} If A has time-kinetic coefficient Z_A>0, its canonical amplitude is A_c=\sqrt{Z_A}A, and the fully normalized vertex is \widehat K_{ab}/\sqrt{Z_A}. Matrix-valued response metrics require the corresponding transformation on their own index. For a density source j_d=c_d^\dagger T_dc_d, the transformation instead is j_d=z_d^\dagger\widehat T_dz_d,\qquad \widehat T_d=Z_d^{-1/2}T_dZ_d^{-1/2}. \tag{2} Each current has two matter legs. A current-current interaction therefore cannot be normalized by applying (1) just once to its matrix of scalar coefficients. Measures and spatial maps must be transformed consistently. Independence of coefficient conventions Under any invertible basis change c_d=T_d'\widetilde c_d, \widetilde Z_d=T_d'^\dagger Z_dT_d',\qquad \widetilde K_{ab}=T_a'^\dagger K_{ab}T_b'. The matrix U_d=Z_d^{1/2}T_d'\widetilde Z_d^{-1/2} is unitary, because U_d^\dagger U_d=I. Substitution proves \widetilde{\widehat K}_{ab}=U_a^\dagger\widehat K_{ab}U_b. \tag{3} Thus rank and singular values of the normalized vertex are independent of the arbitrary normalization of its basis sections. Its entries still depend on which physical states are used; mass eigenbases and their relative phases have to be determined to predict particular transitions. The existing CKM calculation is a concrete application. For a single mode per family, |K_{ab}|/\sqrt{Z_aZ_bZ_A} is invariant. The pair energy g_{ab}j_aj_b, a transition vertex, and a mass-operator coefficient remain different objects even if all are called couplings. Generators, charge, and selection Let a self-adjoint generator \mathsf Q preserve each retained mode subspace, so \mathsf Q S_d=S_d q_d,\qquad q_d^\dagger Z_d=Z_dq_d. The normalized generator is Hermitian: \widehat q_d=Z_d^{1/2}q_dZ_d^{-1/2}. If the underlying generator is the same scalar q on two families, \mathsf Q S_a=qS_a and \mathsf Q S_b=qS_b, then their unnormalized charge matrices are qZ_a,qZ_b. After normalization both become qI, regardless of spatial depth, profile width, or the number of retained modes. This proves preservation of a common charge under projection and normalization. It does not derive which master generator is electric charge, its eigenvalues, or why both physical sectors carry the same one. A neutral field perturbation preserves this charge when \widehat q_a\widehat K_{ab}=\widehat K_{ab}\widehat q_b. \tag{4} For charge eigenvectors with eigenvalues q_i,q_j, (4) reads (q_i-q_j)\widehat K_{ij}=0. A charged complex field amplitude transforming as A\mapsto e^{i q_A\theta}A, with matter transforming as z_d\mapsto e^{i\widehat q_d\theta}z_d, changes the criterion to \widehat q_a\widehat K_{ab}-\widehat K_{ab}\widehat q_b =q_A\widehat K_{ab}. \tag{5} This is the infinitesimal invariance of A z_a^\dagger\widehat K_{ab}z_b. It is a selection rule, not a numerical prediction of an allowed entry. For non-Abelian generators the perturbation index transforms too, giving an invariant tensor rather than a single charge-difference equation. Universal charge and resolved spatial structure For a normalized positive density \rho_d carrying the same charge q, the projected spatial form factor is F_d(k)=q\int_{Q_d}e^{ik\cdot r(x)}\rho_d(x)\,d\mu_d(x), \qquad F_d(0)=q. Here r is the specified readout onto shared spatial coordinates. The zero-momentum identity uses the complete conserved marginal. It does not require all the F_d(k) to agree at nonzero momentum. For a centered Gaussian shared marginal with covariance C_d, F_d(k)=q\,e^{-k^{\mathsf T}C_dk/2}. Thus equal charge is consistent with unequal spatial response and contact integrals. A mode count or spatial width need not multiply a normalized particle's charge. This statement concerns an assumed conserved charge; neutral composite distributions or other electromagnetic operators need their own form factors. The quantum-field benchmark is charge universality in the Thomson limit, described in PDG, Electroweak Model, §10.3.1. The calculation above is an action-level projection identity, not an all-orders proof of that benchmark for V2. A common gauge-field kinetic normalization and a gauge-consistent elimination of omitted modes remain necessary. The projected current note gives the exact local conservation defect when a truncation drops such modes. Related and verification Generalized sector coupling — the theory-wide calculation and its physical inputs. Nested sector reciprocity — fixes the spatial pairing used in the raw vertex. Common field response — applies response factorization only after the source convention is specified. Neutrino channel control — applies charge selection without suppressing every interaction. generalized_coupling_checks.py tests nonorthogonal bases, nonunitary basis changes, conserved generators, charged transition selection, and independently integrated form factors.

title: Canonical spatial spin response
summary: The full moving spatial frame fixes the canonical particle center and relates its electric spin-orbit response to the magnetic moment without an independent coefficient.
text: Summary: The full moving spatial frame fixes the canonical particle center and relates its electric spin-orbit response to the magnetic moment without an independent coefficient. Retain the entire occupied polarization The conditional spatial current calculation supplies a normalized radial Dirac profile on d ordinary spatial coordinates. Its centered scalar binding determines the translation inertia \mathcal I and current moment F_0. With a normalized complex vector z in the complete occupied multiplet, write J_{ij}=z^\dagger B_{ij}z,\qquad B_{ij}=W_{\rm rest}^\dagger(-i\alpha_i\alpha_j)W_{\rm rest}, \qquad g_{\rm mag}=4\mathcal I F_0. \tag{1} Here W_{\rm rest} embeds the upper radial polarization at rest. The full spatial field includes its lower radial component. These matrices describe spatial rotations and add no physical dimensions. The complete polarization description keeps the whole vector z even when its bivector J does not determine every higher-dimensional polarization observable. The soft current derivation gives the velocity tangent \zeta_i=iMx_i\phi+\alpha_i\phi/2 and the number centroid R_\rho=X+F_0Jv. The charge q and minimal connection of that same field remain conditional inputs. Work to first order in a weak electric field and to the leading nontrivial order in the particle velocity. Normalize the moving spatial frame Let W(x) contain every normalized rest profile as columns, and let Z_i(x)=iMx_iW+\alpha_iW/2. Full spatial integration gives matrix identities \int W^\dagger W=I,\qquad \int W^\dagger Z_i=0,\qquad K_{ij}-K_{ji}=-\frac i2B_{ij},\qquad K_{ij}=\int Z_i^\dagger Z_j. \tag{2} The first mixed integral vanishes by parity. The last identity is the matrix version of the velocity symplectic curvature; it holds before choosing the occupied ray. Normalize W_v=W+v_iZ_i by its integrated Gram matrix: \widetilde W_v=W_v(\int W_v^\dagger W_v)^{-1/2}. For the field \widetilde W_vz, the term containing dz remains the canonical \tfrac i2(z^\dagger dz-dz^\dagger z). Equation (2) fixes the leading velocity connection as i\int\widetilde W_v^\dagger d\widetilde W_v =\tfrac14v_iB_{ij}dv_j+\cdots. A local frame gauge can absorb the symmetric connection terms of a higher-order profile completion; the curvature at rest is fixed by its actual first tangents. Together with the translation momentum, the retained action one-form is \theta=\frac i2(z^\dagger dz-dz^\dagger z) +\mathcal I v\cdot dX+\frac14v_iJ_{ij}dv_j. \tag{3} This states the orders needed below, not an all-velocity canonical description of the scalar-bound particle. Find the canonical spatial center Define \boxed{ P=\mathcal I v,\qquad r=X+\frac{Jv}{4\mathcal I}.} \tag{4} Then P\cdot dr=\mathcal I v\cdot dX+\tfrac14v\cdot J\,dv. This remains true when z changes: the extra term is \tfrac14v_i(dJ_{ij})v_j=0 because dJ is antisymmetric. Thus (3) becomes the usual P\cdot dr plus the full polarization one-form. No frozen-spin assumption is needed for this coordinate identity. The physical number centroid is consequently \boxed{ R_\rho=r+\frac{g_{\rm mag}-1}{4\mathcal I^2}JP.} \tag{5} The scalar center, canonical center and number centroid describe different moments of the same moving spatial field. They are not separate physical spaces or a division of the six-dimensional electron. Obtain the electric spin-orbit coefficient For a uniform electric field, the actual charge energy is -qE\cdot R_\rho. Its velocity-dependent part in canonical coordinates is \boxed{ H_{\rm SO} =-\frac{q(g_{\rm mag}-1)}{4\mathcal I^2} \sum_{i<j}J_{ij}(E_iP_j-E_jP_i).} \tag{6} For a chosen three-dimensional measurement plane, J_{ij}=2\epsilon_{ijk}S_k, so H_{\rm SO} =-\frac{q(g_{\rm mag}-1)}{2\mathcal I^2} \,S\cdot(E\times P). \tag{7} The same current gives the rest magnetic term H_B=-qg_{\rm mag}S\cdot B/(2\mathcal I) in that plane. With the conventional coefficient names c_F=g_{\rm mag}/2 and c_S=g_{\rm mag}-1, \boxed{c_S=2c_F-1.} \tag{8} This agrees with the low-velocity spin-half electromagnetic coefficient relation derived from Lorentz invariance; see the explicit Lagrangian and matching discussion in Paz, An Introduction to NRQED, equation (3). The comparison concerns the response coefficients of an individual particle. It imports no mediator-particle interpretation and does not model an atom. There is a direct consistency check. Put c=(g_{\rm mag}-1)/(4\mathcal I^2) and keep J fixed at linear order in the applied field. Equations (5)–(6) give \dot P=qE, \dot r=P/\mathcal I+qcJE and therefore \dot R_\rho=v+2qcJE.
