This is exactly the full spatial current derived independently from the complete source resolvent. The result fixes the leading uniform-field spin-orbit response. Spatial field gradients, the Darwin term, finite-frequency deformation and an all-velocity spin-precession law require further calculation. The scalar six-dimensional ground profile still gives g_{\rm mag}\simeq2.07691916, so this coefficient relation does not repair its mismatch with the electron magnetic moment. The same parameters also control the soft forward scattering term; these related tests must be satisfied together. Verification soft_photon_response_checks.py integrates (2) as full spatial matrices at depths three and six, normalizes the moving frame, and independently differentiates its overlap to recover the Berry connection. Halving the velocity tests the omitted order. Arbitrary complex polarization variations check (4), while the canonical equations are compared with the independently derived spatial current. All checks remain active under Python optimization.

title: Coherent spatial overlap
summary: Exact complex Gaussian overlaps retain both objects' shapes, polarizations, and spatial phases, while normalized opposing lobes give a concrete low-momentum source cancellation.
text: Summary: Exact complex Gaussian overlaps retain both objects' shapes, polarizations, and spatial phases, while normalized opposing lobes give a concrete low-momentum source cancellation. Spatial source patterns, before averaging After deriving a source or response operator, a local overlap may take the form \mathcal A(k)=\int \langle F_a(x),F_b(x)\rangle e^{-ik\cdot x}\,d^Dx. \tag{1} Both F_a and F_b are polarized spatial patterns. Their components must be expressed in compatible frames and normalized according to the action. Equation (1) adopts a local identity pairing; a derivative or nonlocal kernel must be retained when the action supplies one. The coordinates belong to one common physical chart of the nested manifold. This benchmark uses finite test functions or wavepackets after the spatial mode maps have been specified. It does not replace a lower field's cylindrical continuation by a thin sheet, or identify wavepacket localization in a free direction with a new bound dimension. For an actual nonlinear source, first calculate F_b from the higher field as in descending photon source. Substituting a bare wavefunction or a positive density for a different source would change (1). Exact overlap of two Gaussian amplitude profiles Let A,B be real positive-definite D\times D matrices. Choose \psi_a(x)=\left(\frac{\det A}{\pi^D}\right)^{1/4} \exp\left[-\frac12(x-X_a)^TA(x-X_a)+ip_a\cdot x+i\phi_a\right], and the analogous \psi_b using B,X_b,p_b,\phi_b. Both have unit L^2 norm. If F_a=\psi_a T_a and F_b=\psi_b T_b with constant normalized tensors, the result is \mathcal A(k)=\langle T_a,T_b\rangle\,I_{ab}(k). \tag{2} Put S=A+B,\qquad m=S^{-1}(AX_a+BX_b), \qquad q=p_b-p_a-k,\qquad \Delta X=X_a-X_b. Completing the real square gives (x-X_a)^TA(x-X_a)+(x-X_b)^TB(x-X_b) =(x-m)^TS(x-m)+D_0, where D_0=X_a^TAX_a+X_b^TBX_b-m^TSm =\Delta X^T(A^{-1}+B^{-1})^{-1}\Delta X. The last identity holds without assuming that A and B commute. Diagonalizing S and taking the characteristic function of the centered Gaussian now yields \boxed{ I_{ab}(k)= \frac{2^{D/2}(\det A\det B)^{1/4}}{\sqrt{\det S}} \exp\left[-\frac12D_0-\frac12q^TS^{-1}q +iq\cdot m+i(\phi_b-\phi_a)\right].} \tag{3} Thus spatial separation, shape covariance, phase-gradient mismatch, and tensor polarization all remain visible. At equal profiles and k=0, I_{aa}=1. Cauchy–Schwarz gives |I_{ab}(k)|\leq1 for every k, since the Fourier phase has unit magnitude. The positive density overlap in Gaussian contact profiles is a different quantity: it has different normalization and no relative wave phase. It cannot stand in for (3) when interference is relevant. Two structured objects For finite patterns F_a=\sum_i a_i\psi_{ai}T_{ai}, \qquad F_b=\sum_j b_j\psi_{bj}T_{bj}, linearity gives the exact amplitude \boxed{\mathcal A(k)= \sum_{i,j}\overline a_i b_j \langle T_{ai},T_{bj}\rangle I_{ai,bj}(k).} \tag{4} Both objects' orientations and phases occur in every term. Individual nonzero overlaps can cancel in the sum. The full Gram matrix of the component profiles determines the normalization of a and b; the lobes are not assumed orthogonal merely because their centers differ. If physical dynamics makes some outputs distinguishable, sum their intensities only after separating those outputs. A normalized shape with a vanishing long-wavelength source For an explicit finite source use the real normalized amplitude \psi_\sigma(x)=(\pi\sigma^2)^{-D/4} e^{-|x|^2/(2\sigma^2)},\qquad \sigma>0. For a fixed nonzero displacement L, define opposing lobes f_-(x)= \frac{\psi_\sigma(x-L/2)-\psi_\sigma(x+L/2)} {\sqrt{2\left(1-e^{-|L|^2/(4\sigma^2)}\right)}}. \tag{5} Their overlap is e^{-|L|^2/(4\sigma^2)}, so \|f_-\|_2=1. With Fourier convention \widetilde f(k)=\int f(x)e^{-ik\cdot x}d^Dx, \boxed{ \widetilde f_-(k)= \frac{-2i\sin(k\cdot L/2)} {\sqrt{2\left(1-e^{-|L|^2/(4\sigma^2)}\right)}} \widetilde\psi_\sigma(k),} \tag{6} where \widetilde\psi_\sigma(k) =2^{D/2}\pi^{D/4}\sigma^{D/2} e^{-\sigma^2|k|^2/2}. The zero at k=0 comes from spatial cancellation while the source has unit norm. For fixed L,\sigma and |k\cdot L|\ll1, its squared Fourier amplitude begins at order (k\cdot L)^2. Directions with k\cdot L=0 remain exactly dark for this source. This is a shape-induced selection within the declared linear source map, not a small coefficient inserted into that map. For a tensor source f_-(x)T_b, additionally contract its tensor with the other object's polarized test pattern. The node in (6) and the tensor pairing are separate factors only for this separated preparation. General moment cancellation Suppose an integrable scalar or tensor source s(x) has finite absolute moment of order m and \int x^\alpha s(x)d^Dx=0 \quad\text{for every multi-index }|\alpha|<m. Subtract the degree-m-1 Taylor polynomial of e^{-ik\cdot x} under the integral. Its real-variable integral remainder is bounded by |k\cdot x|^m/m!, which proves \boxed{ \|\widetilde s(k)\| \leq\frac{|k|^m}{m!} \int |x|^m\|s(x)\|d^Dx.} \tag{7} This gives a calculable low-momentum suppression from vanishing source moments. The moments must vanish for the source produced by the actual field equation. Squaring an odd field can remove its odd parity, so an odd bare shape alone does not establish the moment conditions. The same construction is available at many depths. A distinctive particle prediction requires the field dynamics to select the relevant shape, scale, and source symmetry, and requires the coupling to allowed response tangents to be checked as well. A zero source does not by itself exclude a nonzero susceptibility. Verification polarization_coupling_checks.py checks the displayed identities with independent spatial quadrature, energy variations, or full finite-system evolution as appropriate. These checks verify the declared mathematics and benchmarks, not empirical couplings. Related Bilateral polarization coupling — retains both tensor states and distinguishes source values from mixed response derivatives. Descending photon source — defines which higher-field source is projected. Polarized response spectrum — combines spatial matrix elements with frequency and exposure. Gaussian contact profiles — contrasts density contact with the complex amplitude overlap derived here.

title: Collective translation waves
summary: Full source feedback gives the normal propagation of spatial translation modes, with exact inertia and stiffness identities and a subluminal two-polarization branch at bound depth two.
text: Summary: Full source feedback gives the normal propagation of spatial translation modes, with exact inertia and stiffness identities and a subluminal two-polarization branch at bound depth two. Translate a complete bound field A field bound in two spatial directions has two independent displacement directions. If those displacements vary along a perpendicular propagation coordinate, they provide a concrete candidate for a two-polarization wave. The propagation speed must follow from the complete field equation. Use the scalar Dirac moment branch, with actual bound coordinates x\in\mathbb R^d and an existing perpendicular coordinate y in a containing sector. All coordinates are ordinary macroscopic directions in the one nested physical manifold. Set the underlying Dirac wave speed to one. The normalized resting profile satisfies H_b\phi=M\phi,\qquad H_b=-i\alpha_i\partial_i+\beta(m+a|x|^2),\qquad \int\phi^\dagger\phi\,dx=1. \tag{1} Here M is the profile's stationary frequency and m its bare scalar coefficient. The full centered moment energy determines a: Q_\sigma=\int\phi^\dagger\beta\phi\,dx,\qquad T_\sigma=\int |x|^2\phi^\dagger\beta\phi\,dx,\qquad a=\frac{g_0T_\sigma}{d}. \tag{2} Q_\sigma denotes scalar normalization, not electric charge. The source is local in (t,y) and uses the centered scalar moments in the bound coordinates, as specified in Normal propagation of spatial Dirac modes. A small displacement has spatial tangent \eta_i=-\partial_i\phi,\qquad \Psi=e^{-iMt}\big[\phi+X_i(t,y)\eta_i+\cdots\big]. \tag{3} The omitted terms include the velocity and normal-gradient response of the full spatial profile. Retaining only the displaced density would miss them, just as a general polarization texture can omit a nonzero Dirac complement. Identify when the dipole source closes Let Y=\alpha_y anticommute with every bound \alpha_i and with \beta. For even d, define the Hermitian involutions \Gamma_b=i^{d/2}\alpha_1\cdots\alpha_d,\qquad \Xi=\beta\Gamma_b. \tag{4} They obey [\Xi,H_b]=0,\qquad [\Xi,\beta f(x)]=0,\qquad \{\Xi,Y\}=0. \tag{5} Choose one complete spatial chirality, \Xi\phi=\phi. Every scalar source column \beta f(x)\phi then has that same chirality, while its normal partner has the opposite chirality. This is a decomposition of spatial field components, with no additional physical dimensions. Consequently the term linear in qY between scalar source columns vanishes in the exact normal resolvent. The remaining terms are even in the normal wavenumber q. The parity \beta\mathcal R, where \mathcal R\phi(x)=\phi(-x), further separates odd dipole sources from even second-moment sources. Thus all scalar shape sources can be retained while the dipole block closes. This proof uses the selected even-dimensional chirality. At odd bound depth, normal propagation can mix dipole and shape sources through the field's mixed circulation. An isolated odd-dimensional dipole formula must not be substituted for that full coupled problem. Keep the complete normal and conjugate response The dipole source columns and their curvature are b_i=\beta x_i\phi,\qquad \kappa=-\frac{2a}{Q_\sigma}. \tag{6} The curvature comes from varying the scalar center, as derived in Translational Dirac response. For a circular eigenpolarization \lambda of the radial circulation, let w_{\lambda n}\ge0 be the squared source projections on the complete bound eigenfields with energies E_n. Both angular Dirac families belong in this spectral sum. The full bare dipole response is \boxed{ \begin{aligned} \chi_\lambda(\omega,q) ={}&\sum_n w_{\lambda n} \frac{\omega+M+E_n}{(\omega+M)^2-E_n^2-q^2}\\ &+\sum_n w_{-\lambda n} \frac{-\omega+M+E_n}{(-\omega+M)^2-E_n^2-q^2}. \end{aligned}} \tag{7} The second line retains the conjugate fluctuation. At q=0 this reduces to the usual two signed frequency resolvents. Equation (7) follows from the exact Clifford inverse, not a fixed-profile envelope dispersion. The source-carrying modes solve 1-\kappa\chi_\lambda(\omega,q)=0. \tag{8} Source-free modes and any canceled frozen poles remain part of the full field spectrum. For example, the normal partner of a degenerate stationary polarization can have zero dipole residue; it must not be counted as a dipole pole merely because it appears in the frozen denominator. Translation invariance and commuting momentum generators give \kappa\chi_\lambda(0,0)=1,\qquad \partial_\omega\chi_\lambda(0,0)=0. \tag{9} Expand the dipole response at the origin as \chi_\lambda=\frac1\kappa+ \frac12\chi_{\omega\omega}\omega^2+ \chi_{q^2}q^2+ O(\omega^3,\omega q^2,q^4). \tag{10} The inverse force response then has leading coefficients \boxed{ \mathcal I=-2a^2\chi_{\omega\omega},\qquad \mathcal K=4a^2\chi_{q^2},\qquad c_{\rm tr}^2=\frac{\mathcal K}{\mathcal I}.} \tag{11} Indeed, a scalar force coefficient f_i adds energy f_i\delta P_i=Q_\sigma f_iX_i. The full dipole response becomes \delta P_i=Q_\sigma^2f_i/(\mathcal I\omega^2-\mathcal Kq^2) to this order. This fixes the normalization of both coefficients. Derive the coefficients directly in physical space Put L=H_b-M. The spatial Dirac identities [H_b,x_i]=-i\alpha_i,\qquad \{H_b,\alpha_i\}=-2i\partial_i \tag{12} give explicit inhomogeneous solutions: \boxed{ L^{-1}\eta_i=Mx_i\phi-\frac i2\alpha_i\phi,\qquad (H_b+M)^{-1}\eta_i=-\frac i2\alpha_i\phi.} \tag{13} These inverses are taken on the relevant complementary subspaces. Equivalently, apply the displayed operators to the right sides to verify the equations directly. Kernel components have zero dipole residue and do not contribute to the coefficients. The velocity correction is iL^{-1}\eta_i. Its first scalar-density variation is zero pointwise: the iMx_i\phi term is a phase variation, and \beta\alpha_i is anti-Hermitian. The full source therefore permits this generalized translation partner. The normal correction lies in the opposite \Xi sector and has no first-order scalar-source feedback by (5). The complete ordinary/conjugate response gives \mathcal I=2\operatorname{Re}\langle\eta_i,L^{-1}\eta_i\rangle, \qquad \mathcal K=2\operatorname{Re} \langle\eta_i,(H_b+M)^{-1}\eta_i\rangle. \tag{14} Define the actual bound kinetic contribution in direction i: T_i=\langle\phi,\alpha_i(-i\partial_i)\phi\rangle. \tag{15} Localization and unit normalization imply 2\operatorname{Re}\langle-\partial_i\phi,x_i\phi\rangle=1. Integration by parts in the other term gives -i\langle-\partial_i\phi,\alpha_i\phi\rangle=T_i. Substitution into (13)–(14) proves \boxed{\mathcal I=M+T_i,\qquad \mathcal K=T_i,\qquad c_{\rm tr}^2=\frac{T_i}{M+T_i}.} \tag{16} For a radial field, T_i=T/d with T=\langle\phi,-i\alpha_i\partial_i\phi\rangle. The quadratic scalar virial identity is T=2aT_\sigma, while M=T+mQ_\sigma+aT_\sigma. Thus \boxed{ T_i=\frac{2(M-mQ_\sigma)}{3d},\qquad m=0\ \Longrightarrow\ c_{\rm tr}^2=\frac{2}{3d+2}.} \tag{17} This also explains the previously computed translation inertias without fitting their numerical values. Two transverse polarizations do not fix the speed For the zero-bare-mass branch, the small-wavenumber speeds are: bound spatial depth number of displacement directions speed in Dirac units 2 2 \frac12 6 6 \frac1{\sqrt{10}} 10 10 \frac14 The depth-two modes are genuine source-carrying, gapless spatial displacements with two transverse polarizations. Within this specified scalar moment model they propagate at half the underlying wave speed. Changing the common scalar coupling only rescales the zero-bare-mass profile; it does not change (17). This is distinct from the lightlike propagation required by the photon construction. The action's covariance in (t,y) does not make every collective excitation lightlike about a finite-frequency, finite-density background. Likewise, covariance under rotations within the bound space does not complete the kernel's dynamics under rotations mixing bound and free directions. At higher orders the circular branches can differ. Positivity of \mathcal I and \mathcal K describes this low-frequency displacement sector; it does not remove separate radial instabilities or establish a stable physical particle. The same full velocity partner determines the low-frequency current and magnetic moment in Soft spatial current response. Null spatial pulses supplies a constructive stationary-background comparison with equal time and propagation norms, while keeping its component action distinct from this scalar Dirac branch. Verification collective_translation_wave_checks.py evaluates both full angular radial families and their normal partners. It compares the exact coefficients with independent spatial derivatives and radial/angular quadrature, and verifies the source equation against the full normal and conjugate matrices. A separate Cartesian Hermite construction retains every scalar second moment and both scalar-center sources at bound depth two. Independent nonlinear source variations verify its curvature. Increasing its total degree from 24 through 30 to 36 brings the displacement frequency toward the independently calculated radial result. Reports are timestamped and all checks remain active under Python optimization.

title: Common field response
summary: Eliminating stable response modes of the same field gives a Gram correction to the direct coupling, with exact reciprocity and a proportional-profile criterion for rank one.
text: Summary: Eliminating stable response modes of the same field gives a Gram correction to the direct coupling, with exact reciprocity and a proportional-profile criterion for rank one. Direct coupling and reduction of one field IDWT has one field \Psi_\infty and no mediator particles. Its cross-sector interactions belong to that field's own action. Start with a specified background and independent real coordinates for its admissible variations in a finite region: \delta\Psi_\infty=S_{\rm r}j+S_{\rm s}X. Here j describes retained variations and X describes other variations of the same field. The maps must respect the actual spatial embeddings, constraints, and normalization. Real coordinates may describe a complex classical field or a specified mean-field energy; they add no physical dimensions. Independent variations do not imply separate physical fields. At a stationary background, the energy's second variation has blocks E^{(2)}=\frac12\langle j,H_{\rm rr}j\rangle +\langle X,H_{\rm sr}j\rangle+\frac12\langle X,LX\rangle, \qquad H_{\rm rs}=H_{\rm sr}^{*}. Set B=-H_{\rm sr}. Thus both the direct block H_{\rm rr} and the response source Bj are derived from the same Hessian. A physical application must calculate these blocks; specifying them as a benchmark does not derive them from IDWT. Constraints and any zero modes must be handled before an inverse is taken. For retained source currents j_d on a finite collection of nested sectors, a source term \sum_dB_dj_d is a further specified reduction of this one-field energy. Each map includes spatial identifications, measures, and polarization contractions. Its range is a real space \mathcal H of response profiles of the same field. Nonlinear bilinear currents require the corresponding expansion and variations; they are not automatically identical to the linear coordinates above. Assume a fixed positive self-adjoint stiffness L\ge\ell_0 I>0 on \mathcal H and sources for which L^{-1/2}B_dj_d exist. Work in a finite region with stated boundary conditions, or on a domain where these operator assumptions hold. An operator with zero modes requires a separate constraint, boundary, or limiting treatment. For this conditional response reduction, write E[X,j]=E_{\rm direct}[j]+\frac12\langle X,LX\rangle -\left\langle X,\sum_dB_dj_d\right\rangle. \tag{1} The currents and all maps use a specified common unit convention. Field normalization acts on every leg of a current as explained in Canonical coupling normalization. Exact elimination and reciprocity Set S=\sum_dB_dj_d. Completing the square gives E=E_{\rm direct} +\frac12\|L^{1/2}(X-L^{-1}S)\|^2 -\frac12\langle S,L^{-1}S\rangle. At fixed sources the unique minimizing response is X_*=L^{-1}S. The eliminated energy and its blocks are therefore E_{\rm eff}=E_{\rm direct}-\frac12\sum_{a,b} \langle j_a,G_{ab}j_b\rangle,\qquad G_{ab}=B_a^*L^{-1}B_b,\qquad G_{ba}=G_{ab}^*. \tag{2} The induced source potential is -\sum_bG_{ab}j_b, including the sign from (1). In the quadratic case the complete retained Hessian is H_{\rm eff}=H_{\rm rr}-B^*L^{-1}B. The Gram expression is a response correction, not the entire direct interaction. The full energy must still control stability as sources vary; positivity of the response stiffness alone does not do that. Different physical interaction channels can have different signs, constraints, derivative vertices, and tensor contractions. Equations (1)–(2) give every pair in this correction from the same field-response operator and source maps. There is no independently adjustable coefficient for each pair in the correction once B_d and L have been specified. There can still be sector parameters inside B_d: a reduction in pairwise freedom is not their derivation. Rank measures independent response profiles Collect B=(B_1,\ldots,B_N) and define C=L^{-1/2}B. Then G=C^*C,\qquad \langle j,Gj\rangle=\|Cj\|^2\ge0,\qquad \ker G=\ker C. \tag{3} On a finite retained source space, \operatorname{rank}G=\operatorname{rank}C. It is bounded by the number of independent response modes of the field to which the retained sources couple. One field has many spatial modes, so one field does not force this rank to be one. For one fixed, normalized source profile f_d in each sector, let b_d=B_df_d and v_d=L^{-1/2}b_d. The pair numbers are g_{ab}=\langle v_a,v_b\rangle,\qquad |g_{ab}|^2\le g_{aa}g_{bb}. \tag{4} This is Cauchy–Schwarz in the response metric. If g_{aa}=0, then v_a=0 and g_{ab}=0 for every b in this channel. Vanishing coupling to one particular other source only establishes orthogonality to that source's response, not absence from the whole channel. When g_{aa},g_{bb}>0, equality in (4) holds precisely when v_a,v_b are proportional. The complete nonzero matrix has rank one precisely when all nonzero response profiles lie on one common line: v_d=\alpha_d v,\qquad g_{ab}=\alpha_a\alpha_b\|v\|^2. \tag{5} For complex channel amplitudes, transpose becomes Hermitian adjoint, and the last product is \overline{\alpha_a}\alpha_b\|v\|^2. The rank and inequality statements are unchanged. Thus a factorization B_d=\alpha_d\widetilde B_d of bare coefficients is insufficient for (5); the \widetilde B_df_d must generate the same spatial response up to scale. This is the exact additional condition needed by a common-anchor response. That note's subsequent conversion of source potentials to occupied mass poles still needs its kinetic and reference-count factors. Its displayed positive current-current energy also differs in sign from the negative term induced by (1). The shared rank criterion does not identify the two actions: an application must derive the interaction sign and the physical mass branch as well as the profile factorization. These positivity and rank statements concern the static scalar response in (1). They are not universal inequalities for the sum of all gauge, gravitational, and matter interaction coefficients. A direct matter term can change the total quadratic form. Spatial example across all depths Choose a shared spatial chart \mathbb R^s, s\le d, and normalized sector densities \rho_d(x,y)=p_{\sigma_d}(x)f_d(y),\quad \int f_d\,dy=1,\quad p_\sigma(x)=\frac{e^{-|x|^2/(2\sigma^2)}}{(2\pi\sigma^2)^{s/2}}. Take source image b_d=h_d p_{\sigma_d} and the local stiffness L=\kappa I, \kappa>0. This is a declared static contact benchmark, not a derived electromagnetic or weak response law. The exact overlap is g_{ab}=\frac{h_ah_b}{\kappa} \frac{1}{[2\pi(\sigma_a^2+\sigma_b^2)]^{s/2}}, \qquad g_{aa}=\frac{h_a^2}{\kappa(4\pi\sigma_a^2)^{s/2}}. \tag{6} For nonzero h_a,h_b, the magnitude of the normalized correlation is \frac{|g_{ab}|}{\sqrt{g_{aa}g_{bb}}} =\left(\frac{2\sigma_a\sigma_b}{\sigma_a^2+\sigma_b^2}\right)^{s/2}. \tag{7} The Gaussian integral can be evaluated one coordinate at a time. The inequality 2\sigma_a\sigma_b\le\sigma_a^2+\sigma_b^2 proves (4) explicitly, with equality exactly at equal widths. Displaced centers multiply (7) by \exp[-|x_a-x_b|^2/(2(\sigma_a^2+\sigma_b^2))]. Shared preparation Coupling consequence Equal marginal, any normalized containing fibre No multiplicative dependence on the containing depth Same center and width \lvert g_{ab}\rvert/\sqrt{g_{aa}g_{bb}}=1 \sigma_b=2\sigma_a, s=3 \lvert g_{ab}\rvert/\sqrt{g_{aa}g_{bb}}=(4/5)^{3/2} h_a=0 in this channel g_{ab}=0 for every b in this channel For finitely many distinct positive widths, these centered Gaussians are linearly independent: along a radial line their exponentials have distinct decay rates, and the slowest-decaying term in any putative vanishing linear combination must have zero coefficient; repeat. Their Gram matrix is therefore strictly positive definite. A single scalar response component of the field can produce full rank among these preparations. Equal widths with differing containing depths instead give (5), including for the assigned depths 3,4,5,6,10 whenever the same shared marginal and vertex are chosen. Depth five is not singled out by this geometric contact model. A neutral sector's suppression has to enter through its derived channel map, not an arbitrary factor of five. Retarded response and a controlled static limit For linearized equations of the same field, let D(\omega) be their operator in retained and remaining coordinates. Wherever the retarded inverse of D_{\rm ss} exists, eliminating the remaining coordinates gives the exact block expression D_{\rm eff}(\omega)=D_{\rm rr}(\omega) -D_{\rm rs}(\omega)D_{\rm ss}^{-1}(\omega)D_{\rm sr}(\omega). The inverse is a response kernel for field evolution. This step assumes no exchanged particles. Both the blocks and their causal boundary conditions come from the original equations. If that reduction yields harmonic response coordinates with positive inertia M, their equation is M\ddot X+LX=S(t). With Fourier convention e^{-i\omega t} and retarded boundary conditions, G_{ab}^{R}(\omega) =B_a^*\left[L-(\omega+i0)^2M\right]^{-1}B_b. \tag{8} For real reciprocal coefficients its transpose reverses source indices at the same frequency. Above accessible resonances it need not be a positive static Gram matrix. An instantaneous interaction is the low-frequency approximation to this specified response, not proof of instantaneous physical signalling. In a finite-mode model put A=L^{-1/2}ML^{-1/2} and C=L^{-1/2}B. For \epsilon=\omega^2\|A\|<1, the Neumann series gives G(\omega)=C^*(I-\omega^2A)^{-1}C,\qquad \|G(\omega)-G(0)\| \le \|C\|^2\frac{\epsilon}{1-\epsilon}. \tag{9} This states when one static coupling matrix approximates the dynamic response. The field stiffness, inertia, and source maps must be derived before treating the resulting frequency dependence as a particle prediction. Related and verification Generalized sector coupling — combines spatial reciprocity, normalization, and channel tests. Neutrino channel control — distinguishes a vanishing interaction term from suppressed field response. Cross-sector moment kernel — an existing example in which coordinate tensors obstruct automatic factorization. Gaussian contact profiles — derives the more general covariance and displacement overlap. generalized_coupling_checks.py independently minimizes response energies, checks source gradients and response ranks, integrates the Gaussian profiles, and tests (9) against the full frequency-dependent inverse.

title: Complete spatial polarization data
summary: Complete spatial Clifford tensors retain the amplitudes and phases of a polarized field, exposing information that a circulation tensor captures at six dimensions but can omit at ten.
text: Summary: Complete spatial Clifford tensors retain the amplitudes and phases of a polarized field, exposing information that a circulation tensor captures at six dimensions but can omit at ten. Begin with the full oscillating field For a monochromatic vector with complex amplitude a+ib, where a,b are real spatial vectors, E(t)=\operatorname{Re}[(a+ib)e^{-i\omega t}] =a\cos\omega t+b\sin\omega t. \tag{1} Its trajectory lies in \operatorname{span}_{\mathbb R}\{a,b\}, even when the containing physical space has many dimensions. The squared ellipse axes are the eigenvalues of \begin{pmatrix}|a|^2&a\cdot b\\a\cdot b&|b|^2\end{pmatrix}. \tag{2} Parallel a,b give linear polarization; orthogonal equal-length a,b give circular polarization. More spatial dimensions permit more plane orientations. A field with several modes, spatially varying amplitudes or different frequencies has further structure which (1) does not describe. The Dirac polarization waves give an exact multimode example with a shared scalar source and changing spatial currents. For a particle field, the allowed components must come from its actual spatial equation. In a fixed degenerate spatial multiplet, write \Psi_z(x,t)=e^{-iMt}W(x)z,\qquad \int W^\dagger W\,dx=I_N,\qquad z^\dagger z=1. \tag{3} The spatial Dirac construction supplies examples where W(x) includes both radial components and all bound coordinates. The coefficients z describe the polarization of this field. Their number is not the number of physical spatial dimensions. All x coordinates are ordinary macroscopic directions in the one nested manifold. Equation (3) is a fixed-multiplet description. It does not assert that every physical particle has that profile, or that its other spatial modes can be discarded. Retain amplitudes and relative phases without selecting one tensor The matrix \varrho=zz^\dagger,\qquad \varrho^\dagger=\varrho,\quad \varrho^2=\varrho,\quad \operatorname{tr}\varrho=1 \tag{4} retains every relative amplitude and phase in z. It removes only the common constant phase. For any operator O on the multiplet, \langle O\rangle=\operatorname{tr}(\varrho O). \tag{5} A common phase relative to another coherent field must still be retained in the combined field and its transition terms. Likewise, replacing z by a position-dependent phase cannot be justified by (4); its derivatives enter the spatial equation, as shown in Spatial polarization textures. To express (4) as spatial tensors, choose Hermitian Euclidean Clifford matrices \gamma_i, satisfying \{\gamma_i,\gamma_j\}=2\delta_{ij}I. They describe how the field transforms under rotations of its actual spatial coordinates. For even depth use one specified chiral representation; for odd depth use the stated irreducible spin representation. Define the Hermitian spatial operators B_{ij}=-i\gamma_i\gamma_j,\qquad C_{ijkl}=\gamma_i\gamma_j\gamma_k\gamma_l, \qquad i<j<k<l. \tag{6} Restriction to the selected chiral space is understood. Their expectation values are the two-form J_{ij}=\operatorname{tr}(\varrho B_{ij}) and four-form K_{ijkl}=\operatorname{tr}(\varrho C_{ijkl}). Count and verify a complete operator basis At the depths below, the listed operators \Gamma_A form a complete Hermitian basis on the indicated polarization multiplet: physical spatial depth complex components N complete operator grades number of operators 3 2 scalar and two-form 1+3=4 5 4 scalar, two-form and four-form 1+10+5=16 6, one chirality 4 scalar and two-form 1+15=16 10, one chirality 16 scalar, two-form and four-form 1+45+210=256 In five dimensions a four-form is dual to a vector in those same five spatial directions. The table counts descriptions of fields, not additional spatial coordinates or independent particles. The Clifford trace identities give \operatorname{tr}(\Gamma_A\Gamma_B)=N\delta_{AB}. \tag{7} To see why the stated grades suffice, products of distinct Clifford generators are trace-orthogonal unless their index sets agree or are related by the top-dimensional duality. In an irreducible odd-dimensional module, the top product is scalar; on an even-dimensional chiral module it is fixed by chirality. The table selects one representative of each dual pair. Its N^2 orthogonal operators span the entire N\times N matrix algebra. Consequently \boxed{\varrho=\frac1N\sum_A \operatorname{tr}(\varrho\Gamma_A)\Gamma_A.} \tag{8} The scalar coefficient is one. For a single normalized coherent polarization, purity also gives \sum_{A\ne0}\operatorname{tr}(\varrho\Gamma_A)^2=N-1. \tag{9} The coefficients are constrained by the full equation \varrho^2=\varrho; (9) alone is insufficient. Mixtures obey (8) too, but must satisfy positivity and have \operatorname{tr}\varrho^2\le1. At six dimensions, J therefore determines the entire polarization matrix within the selected four-component multiplet: \boxed{\varrho_6=\frac14\left(I+\sum_{i<j}J_{ij}B_{ij}\right).} \tag{10} For a pure ray, its J satisfies J^2=-I_6. One way to establish this for every ray is to note that the fifteen traceless B_{ij} span the Hermitian generators of SU(4). Their spin representation acts transitively on the rays, and rotates J as a physical two-form. A reference ray has three unit orthogonal planes; rotating it preserves J^2=-I_6. Arbitrary complex coefficients in this fixed chiral multiplet already include all its constant polarizations. Additional six-dimensional complexity must also consider other spatial modes and textures. At ten dimensions the complete expression is instead \boxed{\varrho_{10}=\frac1{16} \left(I+\sum_{i<j}J_{ij}B_{ij} +\sum_{i<j<k<l}K_{ijkl}C_{ijkl}\right).} \tag{11} The circulation tensor alone can lose relative-phase information. An explicit ten-dimensional coherent family Construct five fermionic matrix pairs a_j=(\gamma_{2j-1}+i\gamma_{2j})/2. Let |0\rangle be their common vacuum and |1234\rangle=a_1^\dagger a_2^\dagger a_3^\dagger a_4^\dagger|0\rangle, with its phase fixed so that \langle0|C_{1357}|1234\rangle=1. These are basis labels for components of one spatial field, not constituent particles or extra coordinates. The normalized same-chirality family \boxed{z_{\eta,\theta} =\cos\eta\,|0\rangle+e^{i\theta}\sin\eta\,|1234\rangle} \tag{12} has \boxed{J=\operatorname{diag} (\lambda J_2,\lambda J_2,\lambda J_2,\lambda J_2,J_2), \quad \lambda=\cos2\eta,\quad J_2=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{pmatrix}.} \tag{13} Every off-diagonal occupation transition in a two-form changes at most two matrix occupations, so it cannot connect the two components in (12). The diagonal two-forms are 1-2a_j^\dagger a_j, giving (13). The four-form does connect them: \boxed{K_{1357}=\sin2\eta\cos\theta.} \tag{14} Thus \theta can change the field polarization without changing any component of J. At \eta=\pi/4, the fields with \theta=0,\pi are orthogonal, yet have exactly the same J. Every vector in (12) is a pure coherent state in the sense of (4). The term Cartan-pure spinor imposes a separate algebraic condition: the complex spatial vectors v satisfying \gamma(v)z=0 span a maximal five-dimensional complex annihilator. The vacuum has that property; for 0<\eta\le\pi/4, (12) has only a one-dimensional complex annihilator. Indeed, write a general complex Clifford vector as \sum_j(u_j a_j+v_j a_j^\dagger). Acting on (12), its one-occupation terms force every v_j=0, while its three-occupation terms force u_1=\cdots=u_4=0. Both coefficients in (12) are nonzero in this range, and the distinct occupation grades cannot cancel each other. Only a_5 remains. On the vacuum, all five a_j annihilate the field coefficient. This complex algebraic test concerns combinations of the existing spatial directions. It does not remove real physical directions from the particle. The Clifford construction and distinction between pure and general spinors provide a mathematical comparison; (7)–(14) are checked directly here. Even a two-form interaction can read the additional information Let a specified complex spatial rotation pattern act through O_f=\sum_A f_A B_A, where A labels coordinate planes. For a pure polarization, its component orthogonal to the initial mode has squared norm \boxed{\|(I-\varrho)O_fz\|^2=f^\dagger\mathcal V f,\qquad \mathcal V_{AB}=z^\dagger B_AB_Bz-J_AJ_B.} \tag{15} This is a positive response matrix. It retains relative phases in the incoming pattern f as well as the occupied field z. For disjoint ordered planes, B_{ij}B_{kl}=-C_{ijkl}. Shared indices instead reduce to a two-form, and identical planes give the identity. Consequently the response to a two-form probe can depend on four-form polarization data even though its mean source depends only on J. No additional four-form interaction term is required for this distinction. Equal-current spatial polarizations constructs the full bound fields and a reciprocal six-inside-ten example. The periodic polarization test supplies the corresponding approach when complete field resolvents and sidebands are needed. Neither an instantaneous response norm nor this operator classification is a physical scattering rate. Verification spatial_polarization_structure_checks.py constructs all the actual matrices and verifies their full trace Gram matrices, reconstruction of arbitrary complex rays and mixtures, the ten-dimensional phase family and its Clifford annihilators. Independent operator products check the response in (15). Reports are timestamped and checks remain active under Python optimization.

title: Conserved spatial charge
summary: A local charge generator must preserve the complete spatial Dirac kinetics, distinguishing a conserved electric-charge candidate from a rotation-neutral polarization of one probe.
text: Summary: A local charge generator must preserve the complete spatial Dirac kinetics, distinguishing a conserved electric-charge candidate from a rotation-neutral polarization of one probe. A neutral pattern must remain neutral under its field equation A spatial polarization can be annihilated by a particular rotation operator. That supplies an exact compatibility condition for that probe. An electric-charge assignment requires more: its density and current must obey continuity under the complete spatial dynamics. This matters for the conditional current used in Soft spatial current response. Its leading charged-particle response cannot be suppressed by simply freezing an unfavorable orientation. A proposed geometric origin of neutrality must specify the physical generator and preserve its kernel. All derivatives below act on ordinary macroscopic spatial coordinates in the one nested manifold. A matrix acting on field components does not introduce further spatial dimensions. Compute the full local continuity equation Take i\partial_t\Psi =-i\alpha_i\partial_i\Psi+V[\Psi]\Psi, \qquad V^\dagger=V, \tag{1} with constant Hermitian spatial Dirac matrices \alpha_i. For a Hermitian, possibly position-dependent matrix Q(x,t), define n_Q=\Psi^\dagger Q\Psi,\qquad j_{Q,i}=\frac12\Psi^\dagger\{Q,\alpha_i\}\Psi. \tag{2} These are candidate charge density and current, not an electric identification by definition. Differentiating (2) using (1) gives \boxed{ \begin{aligned} \partial_t n_Q+\partial_i j_{Q,i} ={}&\Psi^\dagger \left[\partial_tQ+\frac12\{\alpha_i,\partial_iQ\} +i[V,Q]\right]\Psi\\ &+\frac12\left[ (\partial_i\Psi^\dagger)[Q,\alpha_i]\Psi -\Psi^\dagger[Q,\alpha_i]\partial_i\Psi \right]. \end{aligned}} \tag{3} For example, the two derivative terms in \partial_t n_Q are -(\partial_i\Psi^\dagger)\alpha_iQ\Psi -\Psi^\dagger Q\alpha_i\partial_i\Psi. Combining them with \partial_i j_{Q,i} gives exactly the second line. The potential contributes i\Psi^\dagger[V,Q]\Psi. This proof includes arbitrary complex field values and derivatives. For a constant Q and a scalar Dirac potential V=\beta\mathfrak m[\Psi], conservation for arbitrary local field data requires \boxed{[Q,\alpha_i]=0\quad\hbox{for every retained direction}, \qquad [Q,\beta]=0.} \tag{4} The second condition applies where the scalar potential is nonzero. The first follows because the first spatial derivatives at a point can be varied independently. It cannot be replaced by vanishing expectation of the second line for one stationary field. Apply the complete kinetic representation If \alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_d,\beta act irreducibly on the full complex field module, their common commutant consists of scalar matrices. One proof uses the associative matrix algebra they generate: irreducibility makes this the full matrix algebra, whose commuting matrices are qI. Consequently (4) gives Q=qI. \tag{5} This does not derive q. It says that a constant local phase-type charge on one such complete module is the same for all its spatial polarizations. The canonical normalization preserves that supplied charge. Several equivalent copies instead permit Q=I_{\rm Dirac}\otimes q_{\rm copies}, provided the remaining dynamics preserves it. Inequivalent invariant blocks may also have different scalar charges. Assigning and occupying those blocks requires a physical derivation. Their labels are field components, not additional spatial dimensions. Every retained propagation direction matters. For example, a containing representation of six bound coordinates and one existing normal coordinate has \Xi=\beta i^3\alpha_1\cdots\alpha_6,\qquad [\Xi,\alpha_i]=[\Xi,\beta]=0,\qquad \{\Xi,\alpha_y\}=0. \tag{6} The bound operator alone permits separate constants on the two \Xi blocks. Its normal kinetic term connects them and removes that freedom as a conserved local charge of the complete equation. Normal Dirac propagation explicitly retains this normal partner. The example concerns the stated representation; it does not forbid distinct invariant particle families in a larger derived master field. Test the balanced five-dimensional rotation The rotation-neutral construction uses Q_{\rm rot}=\frac12(B_{12}+B_{34}),\qquad B_{ij}=-i\alpha_i\alpha_j,\qquad P_0=I-Q_{\rm rot}^2. \tag{7} On the positive-\beta rest polarization module, P_0 has rank two. Every w in that doublet satisfies Q_{\rm rot}w=0. However, [Q_{\rm rot},\alpha_1]=i\alpha_2,\qquad [Q_{\rm rot},\alpha_5]=0. \tag{8} Thus this spin-only rotation generator does not satisfy (4). The same issue appears as a missing transverse kinetic complement in Neutral doublet transport. An exact spatial plane-wave evolution makes the distinction explicit. Choose normalized \beta w=w, Q_{\rm rot}w=0, and initial field e^{ipx_1}w. Under the full free Dirac operator, \Psi(t,x)=e^{ipx_1} \left[\cos(Et)-i\frac{p\alpha_1+m\beta}{E}\sin(Et)\right]w, \qquad E=\sqrt{p^2+m^2}. \tag{9} Applying (8) gives \boxed{ \|Q_{\rm rot}\Psi\|^2 =\frac{p^2}{p^2+m^2}\sin^2(Et).} \tag{10} The mean is \Psi^\dagger Q_{\rm rot}\Psi=-\|Q_{\rm rot}\Psi\|^2 w^\dagger B_{12}w. It remains zero for an equal-weight preparation of the two opposite B_{12} eigenpolarizations, despite the nonzero response norm. General complex preparations can change both the mean and the norm. Propagation along x_5 instead preserves the kernel because the second commutator in (8) vanishes. A favorable propagation direction is therefore a conditional geometric property, not a conserved electric-neutral particle assignment. Equation (9) is a full spatial Dirac initial-value example, not an identified neutrino mode. It tests the proposed matrix generator on allowed spatial data. Full spatial rotations have an orbital term The actual rotation generator is \mathcal L_{ij} =-i(x_i\partial_j-x_j\partial_i) -\frac i2\alpha_i\alpha_j. \tag{11} For a radial scalar source, [\mathcal L_{ij},H_b]=0. The orbital commutator cancels the spin commutator with the spatial kinetic operator. This is why the full rotation-neutral Dirac field can remain neutral under a chosen total rotation while its spin components alone do not satisfy (4). That conserved quantity is an angular momentum of the actual spatial field. It is a first-order differential generator, so it lies outside the constant zero-order phase-charge hypothesis of (4)–(5). Promoting such a spatial rotation to a local coupling requires its coordinate and derivative terms too. Formally replacing a derivative by \partial_\mu+iA_\mu\mathcal L changes the principal spatial operator through the orbital part of \mathcal L. The action must then derive the corresponding frame dynamics, connection source, conservation law and photon modes. Retaining only its spin matrix would discard the very term which conserved the rotation charge. The useful distinction is therefore between a specified probe's geometric nullspace and a conserved physical source. Both can be geometrical. Their identification must follow from the complete same-field action and its occupied spatial solutions. Particle and antiparticle identification remains open V2 has not yet supplied a physical account of antiparticles or specified what changes in a particle's spatial pattern to produce its antiparticle. The conserved-generator conditions above constrain a candidate charge assignment; they do not identify that physical transformation. Assigning opposite charge labels or using opposite-frequency solutions still requires a derivation connecting those mathematical descriptions to the occupied particle and antiparticle fields. Verification spatial_charge_generator_checks.py checks (3) against direct field time derivatives for arbitrary complex spatial data. Independent commutant calculations include all Dirac matrices through depth ten and verify the effect of the normal derivative. Exact matrix evolution checks (9)–(10) for arbitrary complex doublet polarizations, momenta and masses. Direct spatial polynomial derivatives verify the orbital-plus-spin kinetic cancellation in (11). All checks remain active under Python optimization and reports use timestamped filenames.

title: Reciprocal scalar envelopes

The scalar envelope reduction determines how one profile responds when its amplitude changes. The two envelope amplitudes describe orthogonal projected channels of \Psi_\infty with the kinetic measures specified in the nested-pair construction; they are not independent interaction particles or further physical dimensions. Keep the two centers and rest polarizations fixed in this scalar envelope reduction. The scalar stationary profiles retain that polarization degeneracy; changing spatial shapes and orientations has the additional responses in Dynamical shape opening. Their product satisfies the reciprocal identity (5), which can also be checked by recomputing the profiles at independently varied s_a,s_b. There is also a symmetric form which makes the source dependence explicit. Put c=(A,B)^T, R=\operatorname{diag}(p,q)/g_0, and collect the two frequency gradients in F=(

A soft relative response can therefore arise when the two amplitudes change nearly the same common source. Check the complete normal fluctuation problem For a common normal Fourier wavenumber k, the full ordinary/conjugate matrix of the two-envelope model is \mathcal B(k)=  egin{pmatrix} \mathcal A&kI&\mathcal A&0\ kI&-2D&0&0\ -\mathcal A&0&-\mathcal A&kI\ 0&0&kI&2D \end{pmatrix}. 	ag{15} Eliminating the other components gives the Hermitian quadratic pencil for \lambda=\omega^2:  oxed{\left[(\lambda-k^2)^2I-4\lambda D^2 +4k^2D^{1/2}\mathcal A D^{1/2}ight]r=0.} 	ag{16} This also supplies a useful stability condition for any number of envelopes. Suppose 0\preceq\mathcal A\preceq D, with D>0. For a normalized possibly complex vector r, put a=r^\dagger D^2r>0 and b=r^\dagger D^{1/2}\mathcal A D^{1/2}r, so 0\le b\le a. Multiplying (16) by r^\dagger gives \lambda^2-2(k^2+2a)\lambda+k^4+4k^2b=0. 	ag{17} Its discriminant is 16[a^2+k^2(a-b)]\geq0, and its roots are nonnegative. Hence the reduced normal frequencies are real. The tested pairs satisfy the stronger bound 0\prec\mathcal A\preceq D/5. Negative scalar compressibility or excessive curvature need not satisfy this result; the diagnostic retains growing modes in both corresponding controls. This is a condition excluding exponential growth in the reduced linear spectrum. At k=0, the upper-amplitude block \left( egin{smallmatrix}\mathcal A&\mathcal A\-\mathcal A&-\mathcal A\end{smallmatrix}ight) squares to zero. When \mathcal A
e0, its generalized zero directions describe phase drift caused by changing the conserved background densities. Real frequencies alone do not exclude that linear-in-time drift; a bounded orbital-stability statement must fix the appropriate densities and account for phase symmetry. The scalar bound profiles can also have the separate radial instabilities documented elsewhere. Fixed centers and polarizations omit further collective motions. The calculation provides a reciprocal amplitude interaction and its reduced spectral criterion; full spatial particle stability requires the other response channels too. Verification coupled_scalar_envelope_checks.py solves the actual nested profiles at increased radial resolution and computes their constrained source derivatives. Independent changes of each scalar density verify the frequencies, full spatial energy and coupling matrix. Unequal densities and changed common coefficients test the homogeneity relations without fitting each pair separately. The complete eight-component fluctuation matrix is checked against its long-wave limits and the independent pencil (16). Direct complex field variations recompute both spatial profiles at every perturbed scalar density and reproduce the ordinary/conjugate source matrix. Conditions remain active with Python optimization enabled. Related Self-consistent nested Dirac pair — supplies the spatial equations and both readjusting profiles. Scalar envelope of a bound Dirac field — supplies the normalized normal-coordinate action and scalar density convention. Dynamical opening of spatial shape channels — retains the additional polarization and spatial shape responses.

title: Equal-current spatial polarizations
summary: Complete ten-dimensional fields can share density and circulation yet respond differently to the same six-dimensional partner, because reciprocal rotation dynamics retains polarization information beyond the current tensor.
text:
Summary: Complete ten-dimensional fields can share density and circulation yet respond differently to the same six-dimensional partner, because reciprocal rotation dynamics retains polarization information beyond the current tensor. Put the additional polarization into an actual spatial field The complete polarization tensors identify information absent from a ten-dimensional circulation tensor. That information can be carried by full spatial solutions, rather than only by vectors with no specified spatial profile. Use the declared flat scalar Dirac moment model on ordinary macroscopic bound coordinates x\in\mathbb R^d. All sectors belong to the one nested physical manifold. With spatial Clifford matrices \gamma_i, define \alpha_i=\sigma_1\otimes\gamma_i,\qquad  eta=\sigma_3\otimes I,\qquad H_b=-i\alpha_i\partial_i+ eta A r^2. 	ag{1} For w=(z,0)^T and a real normalized radial solution F,G,  oxed{\Phi_z(x)=  rac{F(r)w+iG(r)\alpha(\widehat x)w}{\sqrt{\Omega_{d-1}}}, \qquad H_b\Phi_z=M\Phi_z.} 	ag{2} The radial source obeys A=g_0T_\sigma/d, with T_\sigma=\int r^2\Phi_z^\dagger eta\Phi_z\,dx. On the ordinary spatial axis x=r e_9,  oxed{\Phi_\pm^\dagger \alpha_1\alpha_3\alpha_5\alpha_7\Phi_\pm=\pmho(r).} 	ag{6} The operator in (6) commutes with \alpha_9, so both radial components carry the same sign there. The field still occupies all ten bound coordinates through (2). One nonzero current plane does not reduce its physical spatial dimensionality. Complete spatial rotations distinguish the fields The total generator of a rotation in the ij coordinate plane is \mathscr J_{ij}=-i(x_i\partial_j-x_j\partial_i) - rac i2\alpha_i\alpha_j. 	ag{7} It contains the orbital derivative and the field's spin action, as derived for complete spatial rotations. For a common physical rotation R and its spin lift S(R), S(R)\Phi_z(R^Tx)=\Phi_{S_{m rest}(R)z}(x),\qquad \mathscr J_{ij}\Phi_z=\Phi_{B_{ij}z/2}. 	ag{8} This is a rotation of the spatial field. Obtain the rotation from a polarized lower partner A reciprocal example uses the existing bilateral rotation-moment energy. Specify normalized field channels on Q_6\subset Q_{10}, with a fixed local spatial inclusion I:\mathbb R^6	o\mathbb R^{10}, and energy  oxed{U_{m rot}= rac{\kappa}{2} \langle I J_a I^T,J_bangle,\qquad \langle A,Bangle=\sum_{i<j}A_{ij}B_{ij}.} 	ag{12} The coefficient \kappa is one specified interaction parameter for this benchmark. It is not an electromagnetic coupling derived from particle data. The channel projection and rotational moment term are assumptions of the declared reduced action for modes of the same field. Give both full spatial channels their ordinary first-order kinetic terms. To define (12) away from the radial family, take J_{ij}=2\langle\Phi,\mathscr J_{ij}\Phiangle as its integrated rotation-moment observable. Equation (8) makes this equal to the rest two-form on that family. Variation of this specified full-field energy gives the source operators  oxed{ \delta H_a=\kappa\sum_{\mu<

Each channel may have its own radial carrier; it is factored out in (14). Choose the six shared directions as (e_1,e_3,e_5,e_7,e_9,e_{10}) and a lower polarization whose embedded tensor has unit planes 13, 57 and 9\,10. This is a particular relative orientation in the nested space. It makes no direction intrinsically different to either particle. With either z_b=z_+ or z_b=z_-, the higher tensor has only its 9\,10 plane. The lower source is therefore its local 56 rotation. Choose the lower unit state z_{a0} with all three local plane weights +1. The exact pair solution is  oxed{ z_a(t)=e^{-i\kappa t/2}z_{a0},\qquad z_b(t)=e^{-i\kappa t/2}e^{-i\kappa tG}z_b(0).} 	ag{15} The lower tensor remains fixed. The higher J_b also remains fixed: the rotation generated by G acts in directions where that tensor is zero and commutes with its 9\,10 plane. Substitution into (14) therefore reproduces the same generators at every time, proving reciprocal closure. Both norms and U_{m rot}=\kappa/2 are conserved. higher initial polarization mean current tensor during the interaction overlap with its initial full spatial mode z_+ unchanged 1 z_- the same unchanged tensor \cos^2(\kappa t) The second field has nontrivial spatial polarization motion that a model following only J_a,J_b misses. Even an energy expressed entirely in their two-forms requires the larger polarization dynamics to recover that motion. Scope of the spatial solution Multiplying (15) by the complete profiles and radial carrier phases gives solutions of the declared nonlinear spatial channel equations including (13). Rotations preserve the radial scalar density, so their original self-binding sources remain valid. The derivative part of (13) also adds the corresponding rotational advection to the local conserved number current. That drift is the same in the two compared preparations; (3) names the Dirac current rather than silently including this extra term. The example uses two individual spatial field channels. It compares all pointwise number currents, the four-form in (6), and actual orbital-plus-spin rotations. title: Descending photon source
summary: A higher-sector field sources a photon mode by projection over its bound coordinates while retaining normal propagation, with reciprocal feedback fixed by the same action.
text: Summary: A higher-sector field sources a photon mode by projection over its bound coordinates while retaining normal propagation, with reciprocal feedback fixed by the same action. Start with the higher-dimensional field pattern There is one infinite physical manifold and one nested chain of ordinary macroscopic spatial submanifolds. A higher-sector particle may determine an interaction through its complete spatial field pattern. A photon response is then a particular projection of that interaction. This construction does not assume that the lower particle's bound depth sets the strength of the source. All retained amplitudes below belong to the single field \Psi_\infty. There are no mediator particles. A separation into target and photon amplitudes is a mode decomposition to be derived and normalized, not a postulate of independent physical fields. The photon geometry separates two bound spatial coordinates from the perpendicular phase directions. In a fixed product chart of a containing depth b\geq3, write x=(u,y),\qquad u\in E\simeq\mathbb R^2, \qquad y\in N\simeq\mathbb R^{b-2}. \tag{1} This is a relation to the photon plane. It does not divide the higher particle's dimensions into different physical kinds. A product chart, fixed frame, and product measure are assumptions for the formulas below; curved or moving frames require their Jacobians and connection terms. Project the bound mode and retain the propagation coordinates Let \chi_0(u) be a normalized bound profile, \int_E|\chi_0|^2du=1. Let S_\gamma:\mathbb C^2\to\mathcal F_x be an isometric map from the two photon amplitudes to the relevant field components in this chart. The bundle \mathcal F is the field's amplitude bundle over physical space. Deriving S_\gamma from the master field is part of the sector construction; its two columns are not extra spatial coordinates. For a vector-wave diagnostic they can be the two spatial polarization vectors in E. Define an isometric inclusion and its Hilbert-space adjoint by (I_\gamma a)(u,y)=\chi_0(u)S_\gamma a(y), \qquad (P_\gamma\Psi)(y)=\int_E\overline{\chi_0(u)} S_\gamma^\dagger\Psi(u,y)\,du. \tag{2} For square-integrable packets, P_\gamma I_\gamma=I and \|I_\gamma a\|_{L^2(E\times N)}=\|a\|_{L^2(N)}. Set Q=I-I_\gamma P_\gamma. Every field in the domain decomposes as \Psi=I_\gamma a+h,\qquad P_\gamma h=0. \tag{3} The complement h is not automatically one particle sector. A proposed higher-particle family must be embedded into it, or a nonorthogonal family must use the full kinetic Gram normalization. The photon amplitude a(y,t) retains its propagation phase, for example e^{i(k\cdot y-\omega t)}. Integrating over y would erase this dependence or select a particular Fourier component. It is not the projection in (2). The source marginal in nested sector reciprocity serves a different purpose and must not be substituted for a propagating-mode projection. Exact projected field equation Write the specified field equation as L\Psi+\mathcal N[\Psi]=0, where L contains the selected linear spatial and temporal operators and \mathcal N contains the remaining terms. All operator products below require a common valid domain. With fixed I_\gamma, define D_\gamma=P_\gamma L I_\gamma. Substitution of (3) gives the exact row \boxed{D_\gamma a =-P_\gamma Lh-P_\gamma\mathcal N[I_\gamma a+h].} \tag{4} If the linear operator preserves the photon mode and its orthogonal complement, P_\gamma Lh=0. That is an intertwining property to check; bound-depth assignment alone does not establish it. Even then, the nonlinear projected term need not close on a. The initial photon-sector forcing of a prescribed higher field h is s_\gamma[h]=-P_\gamma\big(Lh+\mathcal N[h]\big). \tag{5} Thus the source is first computed from the higher-dimensional pattern and its field equations. Photon polarization and the bound profile then select which parts enter the output. Its strength need not be a function of the number two. A configuration with s_\gamma[h]\ne0 is not a complete stationary solution with a=0. Its lower-sector background response must be solved before a stability or small-scattering calculation is made. A nonzero static source also does not by itself imply radiation: outgoing waves depend on the source frequency and the propagating spectrum of D_\gamma. One action determines the reverse response Let \mathcal E[\Psi] be a twice differentiable real energy on a real Hilbert space of field variations. Complex fields may be treated as their real and imaginary components. Around a valid background \Psi_0, let H=D^2\mathcal E[\Psi_0] be the self-adjoint Hessian. For fixed isometric target and photon inclusions I_b,I_\gamma, the quadratic cross term is \mathcal E_{\rm cross}(a,q)=\langle a,Bq\rangle, \qquad B=I_\gamma^*H I_b. \tag{6} Variation gives the photon force Bq and target force B^*a: \boxed{B_{\gamma b}=I_\gamma^*H I_b, \qquad B_{b\gamma}=I_b^*H I_\gamma=B_{\gamma b}^*.} \tag{7} This reciprocal pairing permits a source-led, downward calculation. It does not require equal responses to unequal preparations, occupations, or incident fluxes. A genuinely time-dependent background can exchange energy with perturbations and requires its time-dependent variational equations. Reciprocity of the real Hessian is not automatically a time-reversal symmetry of a scattering experiment. When coordinates depend on the field, vary the inclusions, frame, and kinetic terms too. Holding an action-dependent projector fixed can omit part of the source. When a selected higher solution already contains photon components, expand around that complete solution rather than counting those components twice. A direct finite projection check For a normalized bound vector \chi and discrete normal-coordinate vector f, I_\gamma f=\chi\otimes f and P_\gamma(\chi\otimes f)=f. A nonconstant phase sequence in f therefore survives exactly. A bound profile \eta\perp\chi obeys P_\gamma(\eta\otimes f)=0, independently of that phase. For a separated linear operator L=L_E\otimes I+I\otimes L_N with L_E\chi=\lambda_0\chi, the projected operator is D_\gamma=\lambda_0I+L_N. An off-diagonal term connecting \eta to \chi supplies a nonzero P_\gamma Lh, as retained explicitly in (4). These finite identities check the projection; they do not prescribe the physical photon dispersion. Verification polarization_coupling_checks.py checks the displayed identities with independent spatial quadrature, energy variations, or full finite-system evolution as appropriate. These checks verify the declared mathematics and benchmarks, not empirical couplings. Related Nested sector reciprocity — distinguishes full source marginalization from propagation-preserving mode selection. Photon plane coupling — gives the conditional two-form selection at a specified output wavevector. Canonical coupling normalization — handles nonorthogonal mode families and physical vertex normalization. Generalized sector coupling — organizes the source and response calculation across all sectors. Dirac source linearization computes the source and its reciprocal response explicitly for the written scalar self-interaction. Spatial source complementarity gives exact bounds on which vector and rotation descriptors survive a lower projection. Bilateral polarization coupling retains both objects' polarization and response. A zero static source overlap does not by itself make the mixed response derivative vanish.

title: Spatial Dirac polarization waves
summary: The full spatial Dirac field supports exact linear polarization waves and nonlinear polarized plane superpositions whose scalar binding source stays fixed while their spatial currents change.
text: Summary: The full spatial Dirac field supports exact linear polarization waves and nonlinear polarized plane superpositions whose scalar binding source stays fixed while their spatial currents change. Restore the polarizations omitted by a single-amplitude envelope The scalar envelope fixes a rest polarization while following changes of the bound profile. The scalar spatial source itself leaves a family of rest polarizations degenerate. Their normal propagation can be derived from the full spatial Dirac equation, without assuming that those motions are frozen or gapped. All fields below occupy the same ordinary bound spatial coordinates x\in\mathbb R^d and an existing normal coordinate y in a containing sector. The polarization amplitudes specify spatial field patterns on that manifold. Their component labels do not add physical dimensions. Choose an orthonormal set of allowed rest spinors collected in a matrix V, with V^\dagger V=I_N and \beta V=V. Every column belongs to the containing spatial Clifford representation. A further selected chirality can be imposed when it defines the intended radial family, but scalar binding alone does not select that chirality or the occupied polarization. A full spatial frame for the polarization amplitudes For a normalized real radial profile f,g, define F(x)=\frac{[f(r)I+i g(r)\alpha(\widehat x)]V} {\sqrt{\Omega_{d-1}}},\qquad W(x)=\big(F(x),\alpha_yF(x)\big). \tag{1} The bound equation and its normal partner satisfy H_bF=MF,\qquad H_b\alpha_yF=-M\alpha_yF, \quad H_b=-i\alpha_i\partial_i+\beta\mathfrak m(x), \tag{2} with M>0. Thus, after integration over the actual bound coordinates, W^\dagger W=I_{2N},\qquad \alpha_yW=W(\sigma_1\otimes I_N),\qquad H_bW=W(M\sigma_3\otimes I_N). \tag{3} The normalized spinor amplitudes therefore retain the normal kinetic operator. They have not been obtained by dropping its negative-frequency partner. The scalar identity is stronger: it holds pointwise, \boxed{W(x)^\dagger\beta W(x) =\sigma_0(x)(\sigma_3\otimes I_N),\qquad \sigma_0(x)=\frac{f(r)^2-g(r)^2}{\Omega_{d-1}}.} \tag{4} To check it, the diagonal blocks follow from \beta V=V and anticommutation with \alpha(\widehat x). The mixed block vanishes: F^\dagger\beta\alpha_yF=0. Its radial cross terms cancel because \beta\alpha_y commutes with \alpha(\widehat x), and the remaining terms connect opposite \beta eigenspaces. For any complex amplitude \chi\in\mathbb C^{2N}, the reconstructed field has \Psi=W\chi,\qquad \overline\Psi\Psi=\sigma_0(x)s, \qquad s=\chi^\dagger(\sigma_3\otimes I_N)\chi. \tag{5} Its scalar source depends on the total proper scalar density, while its full spatial current can distinguish the polarizations and their phases. Linear polarization waves are full-field modes Let the rest background be \chi_0=\sqrt{s_0}(z,0)^Te^{-iMt}, with z^\dagger z=1. Readjust the radial profile to its scalar density s_0 as usual. Take a perturbation in any rest polarization z_\perp orthogonal to z. Equation (4) gives \delta(\overline\Psi\Psi)=0 \tag{6} at every bound spatial point, for either component of its normal partner. The scalar center and all scalar moments consequently have zero first variation too. The linearized full field equation in this direction has no additional source-feedback term. In the frame rotating at the background phase frequency, the two normal amplitudes \eta obey \boxed{i\partial_t\eta =\big[-i\sigma_1\partial_y+M\sigma_3-MI_2\big]\eta.} \tag{7} These are exact linearized modes of the specified full spatial source model. Their physical normal wavenumber k gives \boxed{\omega_\pm(k)=-M\pm\sqrt{M^2+k^2}.} \tag{8} In particular, \omega_+(k)=\frac{k^2}{2M}+O(k^4/M^3). \tag{9} There is no positive gap isolating one chosen rest polarization from its orthogonal neighbors. At k=0, this branch is the tangent to the stationary polarization family. Its long-wave frequency is quadratic, which must be retained if these modes are included in a coupling reduction. It is not a derived photon dispersion relation. The radial source can have separate unstable modes; (8) does not establish stability of the entire background. It identifies a specific set of polarization motions that a fixed-polarization envelope omits. Exact finite polarized waves can share one unchanged source The same pointwise identity also gives nonlinear solutions beyond first order. Choose mutually orthonormal rest polarizations z_j and positive proper densities s_j with \sum_j s_j=s_0. Solve the radial source once at s_0, obtaining M. For arbitrary normal momenta k_j, put E_j=\sqrt{M^2+k_j^2},\qquad u_j=\begin{pmatrix} \sqrt{(E_j+M)/(2E_j)}\\ k_j/\sqrt{2E_j(E_j+M)} \end{pmatrix}. \tag{10} The amplitude field \boxed{\chi(t,y)= \sum_j\sqrt{\frac{s_jE_j}{M}}\, (u_j\otimes z_j)e^{i(k_jy-E_jt)}} \tag{11} has constant scalar density s_0. Indeed, u_j^\dagger\sigma_3u_j=M/E_j, and every cross term in (5) vanishes by z_i^\dagger z_j=0 for i\ne j. Each term solves the same frozen normal Dirac equation, and their sum preserves precisely the scalar source which made that operator self-consistent. Therefore \Psi=W\chi solves the full nonlinear scalar source equation exactly. The laboratory number density and normal current, integrated over the bound coordinates, are \boxed{n=\sum_j\frac{s_jE_j}{M},\qquad j_y=\sum_j\frac{s_jk_j}{M}.} \tag{12} The relativistic normalization factors in (11) are needed for both the source and the current. Replacing them by unit laboratory amplitudes would generally change the scalar source and require another profile. These uniform waves are modes of the same field sharing one bound profile. This construction does not replace the distinct-depth, mutually deformed pair problem with two independently assigned particles. Scalar density does not describe the complete spatial motion Orthogonal polarizations remove the scalar cross terms in (5). They need not remove cross terms in \Psi^\dagger\alpha_i\Psi. Distinct E_j,k_j can therefore produce a changing bound spatial current even while every scalar binding moment remains constant. The diagnostic uses s_1=0.7, s_2=0.3, k_1=0.4M and k_2=-0.7M with two complex orthogonal spatial polarizations. At depths three, five and six, it verifies the unchanged scalar source and an explicitly changing local bound current. Both full spatial polarizations are needed to describe that solution; the scalar density alone loses the motion. For a varying total s(t,y), the bound profile also varies. Replacing W by W_s restores the profile-derivative residual calculated in the scalar-envelope note, now with \sigma_1\otimes I_N. Constant s makes that residual vanish, including (11). General wavepackets require the actual radial, shape and center response as well. This gives a precise coupling limit: scalar self-binding permits and transports different polarizations, but does not choose the occupied one. A physical neutrality mechanism must supply that selection and the current sampled by an incoming field; it cannot infer them from the unchanged scalar source alone. Reflection symmetry of scalar Dirac sources shows why this degeneracy can persist with unequal scalar confinement axes. It also checks the nonlinear moment source before treating a frozen eigenspace as a degenerate family of self-consistent fields. Two-frequency spatial Dirac currents uses opposite-frequency components of this same frame to construct an exact current oscillating at twice the bound frequency. Its unit-norm family separates a slow clock from a small current or a small source response. Complete spatial polarization data identifies which tensors retain all constant amplitudes and phases in the chosen multiplet. Spatial polarization textures derives the additional kinetic terms when those amplitudes vary across the bound coordinates, including the component outside the retained frame. The source-preserving normal waves above and bound-coordinate textures therefore require their respective complete spatial equations. Verification dirac_polarization_wave_checks.py constructs the full containing Clifford fields, checks (4) at spatial points for arbitrary complex amplitudes, and integrates the canonical norm over the bound coordinates. Independent source integrals and finite spatial derivatives verify the linear polarization modes. For the finite two-wave solutions it recomputes the scalar moment and checks the complete nonlinear equation using independent finite derivatives in time, the normal coordinate and every bound coordinate. It also checks both normalization factors, the normal current and the changing bound current. Conditions remain active under Python optimization. Related Normal propagation of spatial Dirac modes — supplies the full normal partner and boost convention. Scalar envelope of a bound Dirac field — supplies the profile response when total scalar density changes. Rotation-neutral Dirac fields — supplies the complete polarized bound field and its currents. Polarized Dirac shape response — supplies additional spatial shape motions beyond this radial polarization family. Self-consistent scalar Dirac moment modes — supplies the source equation and separate radial stability limits.

title: Reflection symmetry of scalar Dirac sources
summary: Spatial reflection symmetries force degenerate Dirac polarization multiplets even for unequal scalar confinement axes, and identify when those families also preserve the nonlinear moment source.
text: Summary: Spatial reflection symmetries force degenerate Dirac polarization multiplets even for unequal scalar confinement axes, and identify when those families also preserve the nonlinear moment source. Anisotropic scalar confinement can retain polarization degeneracy The spatial polarization waves use the rest-polarization family of a radial Dirac profile. A stronger statement applies to scalar potentials which are even in each principal spatial coordinate: unequal confinement strengths do not by themselves remove the entire degeneracy. Work in the stated flat-coordinate spatial model, with a self-adjoint operator and a domain preserved by the reflections below. The bound coordinates are ordinary macroscopic directions of the physical sector. A curved global sector or different boundary conditions require their own symmetry check; a coordinate expression alone does not establish these global symmetries there. Let H_0=-i\sum_{i=1}^d\alpha_i\partial_i+\beta M(x), \qquad M(x_1,\ldots,-x_i,\ldots,x_d)=M(x). \tag{1} The matrices are Hermitian and satisfy \{\alpha_i,\alpha_j\}=2\delta_{ij}I, \{\alpha_i,\beta\}=0, and \beta^2=I. A scalar quadratic source with a real symmetric coefficient matrix can be written in this form after choosing its principal axes. Combine each actual coordinate reflection with its Clifford matrix Define \mathcal P_i\Psi(x)=\Psi(R_ix), where R_i reverses the ith coordinate, and put \boxed{C_i=\alpha_i\mathcal P_i.} \tag{2} These are unitary Hermitian operators on the spatial field. The coordinate reflections commute with the constant Clifford matrices, so C_i^2=I,\qquad C_iC_j=-C_jC_i\quad(i\ne j). \tag{3} Conjugating the kinetic operator by C_i reverses every term: the coordinate reflection reverses the ith derivative, while \alpha_i reverses the other Clifford matrices. The even scalar mass changes sign because \alpha_i\beta\alpha_i=-\beta. Hence \boxed{C_iH_0C_i=-H_0,\qquad [H_0,C_iC_j]=0.} \tag{4} Every even product preserves the same energy eigenspace. These operators act on actual spatial coordinates and field components; their labels do not describe another physical space. An identity potential V_0(x)I which is also even in every coordinate commutes with each C_i. It therefore preserves the second identity in (4) for H=H_0+V_0I, although the first identity then need not hold. The multiplicity argument only needs the even products to commute with H. Derive the minimum multiplicity without an assumed particle label For m=\lfloor d/2\rfloor, define commuting Hermitian involutions W_j=-iC_{2j-1}C_{2j},\qquad j=1,\ldots,m. \tag{5} Each commutes with H. In a finite isolated energy eigenspace, choose a joint eigenvector with signs w_j=\pm1. For odd d=2m+1, the energy-preserving operator C_{2j}C_d flips w_j and leaves every other sign unchanged. Its unitarity keeps the result nonzero. Applying these operators produces all 2^m sign patterns at the same energy. Different sign patterns are orthogonal. For even d=2m, use C_{2j}C_{2m} for j<m. It flips w_j and w_m together, producing 2^{m-1} orthogonal patterns with fixed total sign product. Therefore every such eigenspace contains a multiplet of size at least \boxed{N_d=2^{\lfloor(d-1)/2\rfloor}.} \tag{6} Repeated multiplets can make the degeneracy larger. The minimum sizes at the working depths are: spatial depth minimum scalar-source multiplet 3 2 5 4 6 4 10 16 The proof permits unequal strengths along every axis. It requires the reflection symmetries and operator domain, rather than spherical symmetry. These numbers count degenerate field modes, not additional spatial coordinates or a physical particle census. For the central five-dimensional family, the balanced total spatial rotation has two neutral members within its four-mode family, as derived in Rotation-neutral Dirac fields. Scalar confinement with the symmetries above cannot create an isolated two-mode energy band by splitting a four-mode multiplet. Occupation may depend on formation and other source terms, which require their own derivation. Check the nonlinear source before declaring a degenerate solution family A degeneracy of a frozen operator alone is insufficient for a nonlinear field equation. Different eigenvectors could change the source which was used to construct that operator. For the centered quadratic moment kernel, the relevant source data can be checked explicitly. Suppose a finite eigenspace consists of exactly one minimal multiplet. For any operator commuting with all the even reflection transformations, its compression onto that multiplet is scalar. This follows directly from the sign proof: commuting with the W_j makes it diagonal in the distinct sign states, and commuting with their flips makes all diagonal entries equal. Every diagonal scalar moment operator \beta x_i^2 commutes with the even transformations. Its expectation is therefore independent of the chosen normalized polarization in that eigenspace. For a pure scalar quadratic source M(x)=m+\sum_i a_ix_i^2, \tag{7} assume the a_i are distinct. The full ordinary spatial rotation generator J_{ij}=-i(x_i\partial_j-x_j\partial_i) -\frac i2\alpha_i\alpha_j \tag{8} obeys \boxed{[J_{ij},H_0] =2i(a_i-a_j)\beta x_ix_j.} \tag{9} The orbital and spin commutators cancel in the kinetic term. Between any two vectors at the same energy, the left side has zero matrix element. Thus the mixed scalar moment operator has zero compression onto that whole eigenspace. The parity operator \Pi=\beta\mathcal P_1\cdots\mathcal P_d also commutes with H_0 and the even transformations. A minimal multiplet has one parity sign. Its scalar density is even under x\mapsto-x, so its scalar first moment vanishes. Provided the total scalar integral is nonzero, its scalar center is the origin. Consequently every normalized member has the same centered scalar moment matrix. If one solves the nonlinear quadratic moment source equation, all members of that minimal multiplet solve the same source equation. This statement concerns a kernel determined by those moments; another nonlinearity depending on further local density data needs another check. When some axis coefficients coincide, (9) alone does not determine the corresponding mixed moments. The explicit central and two-block fields in Scalar Dirac modes and Nested Dirac pair separately verify their polarization-independent scalar sources. Implication for coupling calculations The scalar model can bind spatial profiles, deform a nested pair and produce polarization-dependent dynamical shape response. Its persistent polarization families explain why those results do not yet select an occupied neutral mode. Increasing axis anisotropy while preserving the same scalar reflection symmetries does not supply that missing energy splitting. The full shape response can still distinguish prepared polarizations through its angular spectrum and source matrix. The required physical calculation must retain that response and determine which polarization is occupied and which current the incoming field samples. A source symmetry and a transition selection rule are separate parts of that calculation. Verification dirac_reflection_symmetry_checks.py checks (4) by differentiating complete spatial fields at coordinate points, including an even nonquadratic scalar potential. An independent Cartesian Hermite regulator with unequal axis coefficients preserves the reflections and reproduces the predicted multiplet sizes at depths three, five, six and ten. These spectra verify multiplicity, not converged physical masses.
