The diagnostic checks each sign-flipping operation, the complete orbital-plus-spin commutator, scalar moment compression and parity within one minimal eigenspace. It also verifies that the multiplicity requirement is conditional on the source symmetry. All conditions remain active under Python optimization. Related Spatial Dirac polarization waves — derives normal propagation of the degenerate polarization family. Rotation-neutral Dirac fields — supplies the total spatial generator and the central neutral subspace. Self-consistent scalar Dirac moment modes — supplies the nonlinear moment source and its stability limits. Self-consistent nested Dirac pair — verifies the source for the two-block spatial profile. Polarized Dirac shape response — retains polarization-dependent response despite stationary degeneracy.

title: Polarized Dirac shape response
summary: Full spatial Dirac quadrupole sources split into two calculable angular families whose polarization weights, radial spectra and reciprocal source feedback determine the allowed shape response.
text: Summary: Full spatial Dirac quadrupole sources split into two calculable angular families whose polarization weights, radial spectra and reciprocal source feedback determine the allowed shape response. Calculate the shapes the field can actually change into The transition-density interaction compares both objects' changing spatial patterns. A complete calculation also needs the motions those patterns can undergo. Here those motions are calculated from the full first-order Dirac operator and the same scalar moment source which determines the stationary profile. This is a conditional model on ordinary spatial coordinates x\in\mathbb R^d within the one nested physical manifold. Field components, angular basis functions and shape coefficients are descriptions of this field, not further physical dimensions. The radial profile is the stated scalar model's solution; it does not replace the actual electron orbit. Use Hermitian Clifford matrices \alpha_i,\beta and a unit rest polarization w with \beta w=w. Write the normalized stationary field as \Phi(x)=\frac{f(r)w+i g(r)\alpha(\widehat x)w} {\sqrt{\Omega_{d-1}}},\qquad \int_0^\infty(f^2+g^2)r^{d-1}dr=1. \tag{1} Its self-consistent central operator is H_0=-i\alpha\cdot\nabla+\beta(m+ar^2),\qquad H_0\Phi=E\Phi. \tag{2} Scalar Dirac moment modes derives a=g_0T/d, where T=\int r^2(f^2-g^2)r^{d-1}dr. The common coefficient g_0 also fixes the feedback below. A quadrupole has two different Dirac angular responses Let A be a real symmetric traceless spatial matrix. Its source vertex is V_A(x)=\beta(x^TAx),\qquad v_A=V_A\Phi. \tag{3} Both signs in \beta matter. In particular the source acts on the lower radial component as well as the upper one. For any x, define spinor-valued homogeneous polynomials \begin{aligned} p_A(x)&=(x^TAx)w,\\ N_A(x)&=\frac{2}{d+2}\alpha(Ax)w,\\ M_A(x)&=p_A(x)-\alpha(x)N_A(x). \end{aligned} \tag{4} They obey \boxed{\alpha\cdot\partial\,M_A=0,\qquad \alpha\cdot\partial\,N_A=0,\qquad p_A=M_A+\alpha(x)N_A.} \tag{5} A polynomial annihilated by \alpha\cdot\partial is called monogenic. Here (5) follows directly: \alpha\cdot\partial p_A=2\alpha(Ax)w, \alpha\cdot\partial N_A=2\operatorname{tr}A\,w/(d+2)=0, and \alpha\cdot\partial(\alpha(x)N_A)=(d+2)N_A. Thus the two functions are derived from the actual source. On the unit sphere, equation (3) becomes \sqrt{\Omega_{d-1}}\,v_A =r^2\left[fM_A-i g\alpha(\widehat x)M_A\right] +r^2\left[f\alpha(\widehat x)N_A-i gN_A\right]. \tag{6} The first family has upper angular degree two and lower degree three. The second has upper degree two and lower degree one. Both retain the original d spatial coordinates. Their different radial Dirac operators give different spectra even though they arise from the same quadrupole. The target's polarization fixes the angular weights Choose a real orthonormal basis A_r of traceless symmetric matrices, \operatorname{tr}(A_rA_s)=\delta_{rs}, and define J_{ij}=w^\dagger(-i\alpha_i\alpha_j)w\quad(i<j), \qquad J_{ji}=-J_{ij}. \tag{7} J is the ordinary spatial circulation tensor of the prepared field. Its action on the shape basis is the real skew matrix \mathcal K_{rs} =\sum_{i<j}J_{ij}[A_r,A_s]_{ij} =\frac12\operatorname{tr}\left(A_r[J,A_s]\right). \tag{8} Use the normalized spherical average \langle1\rangle_S=1 and set c_0=2/[d(d+2)], c_1=4/[d(d+2)^2]. Direct second and fourth spherical moments give \boxed{G_N=\big[\langle N_r^\dagger N_s\rangle_S\big] =c_1(I+i\mathcal K),\qquad G_M=\big[\langle M_r^\dagger M_s\rangle_S\big] =c_0I-G_N.} \tag{9} The cross average \langle M_r^\dagger\alpha(\widehat x)N_s\rangle_S vanishes. For example, the first identity follows by averaging \alpha(A_r\widehat x)\alpha(A_s\widehat x) and retaining both its scalar part \operatorname{tr}(A_rA_s) and its bivector part in (8). Both Gram matrices are positive semidefinite because they are actual spatial inner products. For a complex incident shape c_rA_r, the two source strengths are c^\dagger G_Mc and c^\dagger G_Nc, with their radial factors restored below. Thus the target polarization J and the incident shape and phase c enter together. A common physical rotation of J and every A_r leaves the prediction unchanged. For pure rest polarizations at depths five and six, diagonalizing i\mathcal K gives: spatial depth shape helicity \lambda and multiplicity \operatorname{rank}G_M \operatorname{rank}G_N 5 -1:3,\;-\frac12:2,\;0:4,\;\frac12:2,\;1:3 14 11 6 -1:6,\;0:8,\;1:6 20 14 Here helicity labels a complex rotating spatial quadrupole relative to J. It is not an independently assigned particle charge. The five-dimensional null direction supplies the half-helicity channels. At \lambda=-1, the N family has zero source weight, but the M family remains available. A zero in one family is therefore not a zero of the whole interaction. Derive the radial operators without removing angular components For a monogenic polynomial of degree \ell, the ordinary angular Dirac pair has radial equations \begin{aligned} (E-M)F&=G'+\frac{d+\ell-1}{r}G,\\ (E+M)G&=-F'+\frac\ell rF. \end{aligned} \tag{10} Writing F=r^\ell f_\ell, G=r^\ell g_\ell converts the radial integration weight to r^{d+2\ell-1}dr. Its matrix is the previously derived radial matrix evaluated at the numerical parameter d+2\ell. This parameter accounts for powers of the same radius; it introduces no additional spatial directions. Let H_D denote that radial matrix with the unchanged scalar coefficients m,a. For the two families in (6), H_M=H_{d+4},\qquad H_N=-XH_{d+2}X,\qquad X=\begin{pmatrix}0&I\\I&0\end{pmatrix}. \tag{11} The second formula follows by exchanging the upper and lower radial angular roles. Its signs can also be checked directly with \alpha\cdot\partial(F\alpha(\widehat x)N) =(F'+(d+\ell-1)F/r)N. Project the two radial source pairs (r^2f,-r^2g) onto their respective orthonormal physical radial bases, obtaining real vectors u_M,u_N. Their complete-basis norms satisfy \|u_M\|^2=\|u_N\|^2 =\int_0^\infty r^4(f^2+g^2)r^{d-1}dr. \tag{12} In particular the total source norm has the isotropic value c_0\int r^4(f^2+g^2)r^{d-1}dr for every unit complex shape. The polarization dependence enters how that strength is divided between families with different dynamics, not a depth-specific zero inserted in the total norm. Keep both ordinary and conjugate feedback Put L=\operatorname{diag}(H_M-E,H_N-E) and define u_\lambda= \begin{pmatrix} \sqrt{c_0-c_1(1+\lambda)}\,u_M\\ \sqrt{c_1(1+\lambda)}\,u_N \end{pmatrix}. \tag{13} A real spatial source pairs helicities \lambda and -\lambda. The full ordinary/conjugate fluctuation block is \boxed{\mathcal B_\lambda= \begin{pmatrix} L+g_0u_\lambda u_\lambda^T&g_0u_\lambda u_{-\lambda}^T\\ -g_0u_{-\lambda}u_\lambda^T&-L-g_0u_{-\lambda}u_{-\lambda}^T \end{pmatrix}.} \tag{14} Its coefficient is the same g_0 as in the stationary source. Multiplication by \operatorname{diag}(I,-I) gives a Hermitian energy Hessian. The matrix itself need not be Hermitian or have a positive energy, because the full Dirac fluctuation problem retains both signs of the spectrum. For z away from the indicated poles define the bare shape response \chi_\lambda(z)= u_\lambda^T(z-L)^{-1}u_\lambda +u_{-\lambda}^T(-z-L)^{-1}u_{-\lambda}. \tag{15} Eliminating the responding field from (14) gives \boxed{\chi^{\rm full}_\lambda(z) =\frac{\chi_\lambda(z)}{1-g_0\chi_\lambda(z)}.} \tag{16} This is the response to an additional specified scalar shape source. It is also a building block for a reciprocal pair calculation: each object's induced shape becomes part of the other's source. A scattering probability still requires the physical incoming/outgoing mode map, appropriate boundary conditions and flux normalization. A spectral example from the self-consistent profiles At a=1, m=0.5, the first positive frequencies of the finite quadrupole block converge as follows: depth \lambda first positive frequency second positive frequency 5 0 1.311394217 1.758838889 5 \frac12 1.283179965 1.844170152 5 1 1.261523857 1.924425431 6 0 1.263961888 1.674646832 6 1 1.216595363 1.821722236 These are model fluctuation frequencies, not fitted particle masses or weak-interaction rates. The table fixes a, so the self-consistent g_0 differs between depths. Both geometries retain nonzero shape responses. Their differing helicity spectra provide a calculable distinction without establishing anomalously weak five-dimensional coupling. No growing quadrupole modes were found in these finite calculations or in the corresponding m=0 examples. The latter backgrounds nevertheless have the radial instability documented in the profile note. Stability of one angular response does not remove an instability elsewhere. Dynamical opening of spatial shape channels uses this complete response to calculate how a higher shape with zero static restriction can drive a lower polarized field at nonzero frequency. Incoming spatial shape modes compares these active modes at depths five and six using one common interaction coefficient, checks their moment restrictions and distinguishes their incident amplitudes from forces which first create a higher-sector response. Verification angular_dirac_response_checks.py constructs full Clifford fields, differentiates their spatial polynomials, and independently integrates their angular Gram matrices with a positive spherical rule. It tests both radial operators against differentiated physical radial functions, source completeness, low-frequency convergence, and the full matrix resolvent against (16). The centered full-field energy is separately varied by finite differences. Conditions remain active with Python optimization enabled. Related Rotation-neutral Dirac fields — supplies the full spatial field and its circulation tensor. Self-consistent scalar Dirac moment modes — supplies the stationary profiles and their radial stability test. Translational Dirac response — applies the same method to center motion and its exact zero mode.

title: Dirac source linearization
summary: The written scalar Dirac self-interaction gives an explicit real-linear response with ordinary and conjugate mode couplings determined by the higher spatial field.
text: Summary: The written scalar Dirac self-interaction gives an explicit real-linear response with ordinary and conjugate mode couplings determined by the higher spatial field. The existing nonlinear term Use the scalar self-interaction present in the projected Dirac action. In units \hbar=1, its Hamiltonian form is i\partial_t\Psi=H_0\Psi+\mathcal N[\Psi], \qquad \mathcal N[\Psi]=\kappa(\Psi^\dagger\beta\Psi)\beta\Psi. \tag{1} Here \beta=\beta^\dagger, \beta^2=I, \kappa is real, and H_0 is the specified self-adjoint spatial Dirac operator including whichever fixed background terms have actually been adopted. Its domain and the spatial measure must make the following pairings valid. The energy is \mathcal E[\Psi] =\langle\Psi,H_0\Psi\rangle +\frac\kappa2\int(\Psi^\dagger\beta\Psi)^2d\mu. \tag{2} This is one field on the nested macroscopic spatial manifold. Spinor components describe amplitudes over that space, not independent spatial dimensions. Equation (1) is a specified contribution to V2 dynamics, not the completed master action or a derivation of occupied particle geometries. No mediator particle is introduced. Nonlinear Dirac equations with this scalar structure and linearization about solitary waves are treated in Boussaïd and Comech. The sign convention here is fixed directly by (2). Differentiate the complete source At a spatial field \phi, set s=\phi^\dagger\beta\phi\in\mathbb R, \qquad v=\beta\phi. For a variation \eta, the scalar changes by \delta s=v^\dagger\eta+\eta^\dagger v. Therefore D\mathcal N[\phi]\eta =\kappa\left[s\beta\eta +v(v^\dagger\eta+\eta^\dagger v)\right]. \tag{3} Equivalently, \boxed{ D\mathcal N[\phi]\eta=A_N\eta+B_N\overline\eta, \qquad A_N=\kappa(s\beta+vv^\dagger), \qquad B_N=\kappa vv^T.} \tag{4} The s\beta term is the variation of the final field factor. The two rank-one terms come from changing the source scalar itself. Retaining only s\beta\eta would freeze the higher particle's source while it is being perturbed. The complete derivative is real-linear; generally D\mathcal N[i\eta]\ne iD\mathcal N[\eta]. The matrices obey A_N=A_N^\dagger and B_N=B_N^T. Spatial variation of s(x) and v(x) retains the target's local shape and polarization. Replacing them by spatial averages is an additional approximation. Linearized dynamics about a stationary profile Suppose \Psi_0=e^{-i\mu t}\phi is an actual solution of (1), so (H_0+\kappa s\beta)\phi=\mu\phi. \tag{5} In the same rotating frame put \Psi=e^{-i\mu t}(\phi+\eta). The linearized equation is i\partial_t\eta=A\eta+B\overline\eta, \qquad A=H_0-\mu+A_N, \qquad B=B_N. \tag{6} Its doubled representation is i\partial_t \begin{pmatrix}\eta\\\overline\eta\end{pmatrix} =\mathcal L \begin{pmatrix}\eta\\\overline\eta\end{pmatrix}, \qquad \mathcal L= \begin{pmatrix}A&B\\-\overline B&-\overline A\end{pmatrix}. \tag{7} The second row is the conjugate of the first; it does not add another physical field or another set of spatial dimensions. With \Sigma_3=\operatorname{diag}(I,-I), \mathcal H=\Sigma_3\mathcal L =\begin{pmatrix}A&B\\\overline B&\overline A\end{pmatrix} =\mathcal H^\dagger. \tag{8} This is the quadratic-energy structure. \mathcal L itself need not be Hermitian or have a real spectrum. Stability cannot be inferred merely from the Hermiticity of H_0. The global phase tangent supplies the consistency identity \mathcal L \begin{pmatrix}i\phi\\-i\overline\phi\end{pmatrix}=0, \tag{9} which follows immediately from (5). A moving orbit or a background with several temporal frequencies instead requires time-dependent coefficients; a stationary spectral analysis cannot silently replace that motion. Spatial coupling between mode families Let f_a(x) be photon-sector test modes and u_\lambda(x) target variation modes, normalized by the action's kinetic metric. The ordinary and conjugate matrix elements of the interaction derivative are K_{a\lambda}=\int f_a^\dagger A_Nu_\lambda\,d\mu, \qquad C_{a\lambda}=\int f_a^\dagger B_N\overline{u_\lambda}\,d\mu. \tag{10} Thus a target amplitude vector q produces the linearized source Kq+C\overline q. The spatial integrals include polarization, relative phase, and all of the higher-dimensional profile present in (4). Any cross-family kinetic matrix element of H_0 must also be retained. Interchanging target and photon mode labels gives Hermitian reciprocity for K and transpose symmetry for C: K_{\lambda a}=\overline{K_{a\lambda}}, \qquad C_{\lambda a}=C_{a\lambda}. \tag{11} For the second equality, use B_N^T=B_N and transpose the scalar pairing. In the doubled mode space these are precisely the symmetries of the real quadratic energy. They do not require treating the conjugate variation as an independent particle. A zero of one matrix element excludes that particular linear response. It is not a zero of the complete interaction unless all relevant ordinary, conjugate, and kinetic blocks vanish. The criterion must be applied to the actual nonlinear source, not to the parity of a bare field alone; angular kernel parity gives an explicit example of this distinction. Which temporal frequencies the source contains For a finite prescribed field h(x,t)=\sum_j c_j\phi_j(x)e^{-i\Omega_jt}, equation (1) gives \mathcal N[h] =\kappa\sum_{j,\ell,m} \overline c_jc_\ell c_m (\phi_j^\dagger\beta\phi_\ell)\beta\phi_m e^{-i(\Omega_\ell+\Omega_m-\Omega_j)t}. \tag{12} Projection onto an output mode f_a uses the full cubic spatial overlap T_{a;j\ell m} =\kappa\int f_a^\dagger\beta\phi_m (\phi_j^\dagger\beta\phi_\ell)\,d\mu. \tag{13} The frequency combination and spatial compatibility follow from the same written term. Frequency matching alone does not make (13) nonzero. Several triples reaching the same output frequency interfere coherently. Equations (10)–(13) assume a linear output-mode inclusion in the master field. If a photon is instead realized as a nonlinear collective observable of that field, derive its tangent map and induced equations. For example a bilinear observable contains frequency differences, whereas the cubic field source in (12) contains the displayed three-term combinations. Their different frequency rules cannot be interchanged without deriving that output map. Scope of the concrete calculation Complete scalar response determines the full pointwise rank, singular values and inverse of (3). At nonzero scalar density the complete source derivative is invertible; at scalar nullity it retains one real response direction. Those facts concern the full source before a spatial channel projection and before adding H_0-\mu. Transition-density coupling derives the corresponding nonlocal source derivative and full quartic mode tensor for the projected bilocal density interaction, with both patterns retained. The operator D\mathcal N[\phi] is now explicit for this term. The remaining physical inputs are the actual higher-sector solution, the photon embedding or collective map, all additional action terms, and the boundary conditions selecting incoming and outgoing modes. The matrix formulas apply at any depth supporting the specified Dirac structure and do not themselves single out depth five. Local scalar contact normalization adds the spatial virial and an exact normalized massive profile for the same local source convention. It makes explicit why a scalar vertex coefficient does not by itself determine a stationary particle frequency. Verification Local polarized pulse coupling retains the exact cross-current of two traveling components of this same field. Its complete local equations give source zeros and both reciprocal weak-scattering maps without first postulating a bilocal spatial kernel. Causal scalar response solves this complete derivative about a specified uniform spatial background, including every scalar angular mode, both signed propagation channels and the conserved zero mode. The background is a control, not an identified particle. polarization_coupling_checks.py checks the displayed identities with independent spatial quadrature, energy variations, or full finite-system evolution as appropriate. These checks verify the declared mathematics and benchmarks, not empirical couplings. Source frequencies in spatial coupling tracks the distinct temporal frequencies in the bilinear density, complete cubic field source and perturbations relative to the stationary carrier. Related Descending photon source — retains normal propagation when projecting the higher-field source. Projected Dirac current — supplies the written scalar interaction and its action conventions. Canonical coupling normalization — fixes the mode metrics used in (10). Angular kernel parity — distinguishes source selection from parity of the underlying field.

title: Dressed spatial source vertices
summary: Eliminating spatial modes dresses both the interaction vertex and its kinetic normalization, with exact finite-frequency conservation identities and nonzero responses that a bare projection can miss.
text: Summary: Eliminating spatial modes dresses both the interaction vertex and its kinetic normalization, with exact finite-frequency conservation identities and nonzero responses that a bare projection can miss. Carry the source through the same reduction as the dynamics The projected Dirac current shows why a current can lose required terms under direct mode compression. This note calculates those terms by eliminating the omitted modes of the same field. It supplies the physical normalization and the complete source matrix for a specified linear Hermitian problem. All modes describe \Psi_\infty on the one nested manifold of ordinary macroscopic spatial dimensions. Retained and omitted components are a mathematical decomposition of that field. They are not extra dimensions, independent interaction fields or mediator particles. Let a fixed orthogonal mode projector define a block decomposition H=\begin{pmatrix}A&B\\B^\dagger&C\end{pmatrix}, \qquad H=H^\dagger. \tag{1} The formulas apply to a finite regulator or to operators with compatible domains and the stated inverses. Work at a real spectral parameter E outside the spectrum of C. A continuum or a resonance requires the appropriate boundary-value resolvent and flux normalization; the positive norm identities below concern this Hermitian, real-energy setting. The full real-linear Dirac fluctuation problem may also require its ordinary and conjugate blocks before this reduction is applicable. Exact reconstruction and the norm of a reduced amplitude The omitted row of (H-E)\Psi=0 gives R(E)=(E-C)^{-1},\qquad \Psi=\Omega(E)u,\qquad \Omega(E)=\begin{pmatrix}I\\R(E)B^\dagger\end{pmatrix}. \tag{2} The retained equation and its inverse operator are H_{\rm eff}(E)=A+BR(E)B^\dagger, \qquad K(E)=EI-H_{\rm eff}(E),\qquad K(E)u=0. \tag{3} This is the effective-operator construction explained in Compression and effective dynamics. It obeys the useful exact identity (E-H)\Omega(E)=\begin{pmatrix}K(E)\\0\end{pmatrix}. \tag{4} The full field norm is not generally u^\dagger u. Since \partial_E R=-R^2, \boxed{Z(E)=\Omega^\dagger\Omega =I+BR(E)^2B^\dagger =I-\partial_EH_{\rm eff}(E),\qquad \|\Psi\|^2=u^\dagger Z(E)u.} \tag{5} Z is positive and at least I in this setting. For a selected energy, b=Z^{1/2}u gives a normalized physical amplitude and \widehat\Omega=\Omega Z^{-1/2} is an isometry. Energy dependence makes this a mode normalization; replacing Z(E) by one constant over an entire broad spectrum is an extra approximation. Differentiate the entire effective operator Let H(a)=H+aV+O(a^2), where a is a specified source perturbation amplitude and V=V^\dagger is its full spatial vertex. The same-field interpretation requires that amplitude and vertex to be obtained from the adopted action. This calculation does not identify a with a physical photon in advance. At fixed E and fixed mode projector, direct differentiation gives \begin{aligned} \partial_aH_{\rm eff}={}&V_{PP} +V_{PQ}RB^\dagger+BRV_{QP} +BRV_{QQ}RB^\dagger\\ ={}&\Omega^\dagger V\Omega. \end{aligned} \tag{6} The final term follows from differentiating the inverse: \partial_aR=RV_{QQ}R. The middle terms retain the probe's effect on the coupling to the omitted modes. Their signs and coefficients are fixed by the same full operator. Consequently the normalized static source vertex is \boxed{\widehat V(E)=Z(E)^{-1/2}\Omega(E)^\dagger V\Omega(E)Z(E)^{-1/2}.} \tag{7} For an isolated eigenvalue E(a) and reduced eigenvector u, differentiating K(E(a),a)u=0 yields \frac{dE}{da} =\frac{u^\dagger(\partial_aH_{\rm eff})u}{u^\dagger Zu}. \tag{8} This equals the full-field expectation of V in the normalized eigenstate. Both the source and its normalization are therefore required to predict an energy shift. A probe-dependent projector adds its own variation terms; (6) is explicitly the fixed-projector formula. For a transition between two retained spatial modes, the corresponding vertex is \Gamma_{fi}=\Omega_f^\dagger V_{fi}\Omega_i, \qquad \widehat\Gamma_{fi}=Z_f^{-1/2}\Gamma_{fi}Z_i^{-1/2}. \tag{9} The two lifts include both mode preparations. If the full vertex satisfies V_{if}=V_{fi}^\dagger, then \widehat\Gamma_{if}=\widehat\Gamma_{fi}^\dagger. Polarization and shape enter through both full spatial states and the source operator; this relation does not replace either preparation by an isotropic average. Charge normalization and a finite-frequency identity If the adopted action already supplies one conserved generator qI on the full mode family, its normalized equal-energy density vertex is exactly Z^{-1/2}\Omega^\dagger(qI)\Omega Z^{-1/2}=qI. \tag{10} A small retained fraction cannot turn this supplied charge into a neutral particle. This preserves a given charge; it does not assign q to any sector or identify the physical electromagnetic symmetry. For two different energies at the same spatial momentum, the resolvent identity gives R(E_f)-R(E_i)=-(E_f-E_i)R(E_f)R(E_i). Hence the complete density vertex obeys \boxed{\Omega_f^\dagger\Omega_i =I-\frac{H_{\rm eff}(E_f)-H_{\rm eff}(E_i)}{E_f-E_i}.} \tag{11} Its coincident limit is (5). Equation (11) ties the energy dependence of the dynamics to the finite-frequency density response, so they cannot be chosen independently. The full spatial current retains continuity For an affine spatial symbol H(p)=M+\sum_a\alpha_a p_a, \qquad M=M^\dagger,\quad\alpha_a=\alpha_a^\dagger, \tag{12} use the same fixed retained projector at incoming and outgoing momenta. The minimally varied density and spatial-current matrices, without their common supplied charge factor, are \Gamma^0_{fi}=\Omega_f^\dagger\Omega_i, \qquad \Gamma^a_{fi}=\Omega_f^\dagger\alpha_a\Omega_i. \tag{13} Apply (4) on the left and right of the exact full-operator difference. Writing \omega=E_f-E_i and k=p_f-p_i gives \boxed{\omega\Gamma^0_{fi}-k_a\Gamma^a_{fi} =K(E_f,p_f)-K(E_i,p_i).} \tag{14} Between actual incoming and outgoing solutions, the right side has zero matrix element. This is the reduced continuity identity. It remains valid when M and the velocities mix the retained and omitted modes strongly, as long as the stated reconstruction exists. For a nonlinear spatial symbol, the finite-momentum current must instead be obtained by varying its actual coupling to the probe. Replacing that vertex by a derivative at one momentum need not satisfy the finite-difference identity. A transverse photon would contract the correctly derived spatial vertex with its physical polarization; continuity fixes the longitudinal relation but does not supply the transverse interaction by itself. A bare zero can miss a real source Consider the completely specified two-mode model H=\begin{pmatrix}0&t\\t&\Delta\end{pmatrix}, \qquad V=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}, \qquad \Delta>0. \tag{15} Retain the first component. Its bare vertex is V_{PP}=0, but H_{\rm eff}=t^2/(E-\Delta) and \partial_aH_{\rm eff}=2t/(E-\Delta) when the probe changes t to t+a. The full lower eigenvalue gives \frac{dE_-}{da}\bigg|_{a=0} =-\frac{2t}{\sqrt{\Delta^2+4t^2}}. \tag{16} At t=0.4, \Delta=2, the physical vertex is about -0.37139. Equation (7) reproduces it exactly. This is a source through the components of the same field which the bare projection omitted. Even a truly invariant retained space at zero probe can retain a nonlinear response. Set t=0 in (15). The first derivative vanishes, but E_-(a)=\frac{\Delta-\sqrt{\Delta^2+4a^2}}2 =-\frac{a^2}{\Delta}+O(a^4),\qquad E_-''(0)=-\frac2\Delta. \tag{17} The induced source is linear in a small applied amplitude even though the unperturbed source expectation is zero. Thus a neutral charge, a vanishing linear transition vertex, and absence of polarizability are separate tests. The geometric response examples require this same distinction. Application to the neutral spatial modes Spatial transport of a neutral doublet shows that a fixed spinor projection can remove the first-order Dirac action of perpendicular spatial momenta. Equations (2)–(14) provide a way to retain that contribution in both the dynamics and the source before identifying a physical coupling. They also prevent a missing projected current from being mistaken for derived electromagnetic neutrality. The required next inputs are the full spatial particle solution, the actual photon inclusion or collective map, and the action which defines V. The descending photon source specifies the propagation-preserving output projection; its complete current must be carried through the same reduction. Verification dressed_coupling_checks.py compares the source derivative with independent finite differences of the full effective operator, reconstructs full eigenstates, and checks their energy shifts against direct diagonalization. Independent incoming and outgoing momenta test (14), including on-shell matrix elements. The two-mode examples verify both the nonzero dressed source and quadratic response. All conditions remain active under Python optimization. Related Canonical coupling normalization — establishes the kinetic-metric normalization extended here to eliminated modes. Projected Dirac current — supplies the current and projection-defect problem addressed by the full vertex.

title: Dynamical opening of spatial shape channels
summary: The full Dirac response can rotate a statically inaccessible higher-dimensional shape into a lower-sector source, producing a derived low-frequency barrier with both objects' polarizations retained.
text: Summary: The full Dirac response can rotate a statically inaccessible higher-dimensional shape into a lower-sector source, producing a derived low-frequency barrier with both objects' polarizations retained. A shape can fail to match statically and still respond dynamically For the spatial moment interaction, a source in a higher sector acts on a lower one through its restricted shape tensor. A mixed shape with one direction perpendicular to the lower sector has zero restriction. The full field can nevertheless move that pattern into another spatial shape which does have a nonzero restriction. This note calculates that process using the self-consistent Dirac profiles and complete quadrupole response in Dirac shape response. All coordinates belong to the same nested manifold of literal macroscopic spatial dimensions. The tensors label actual spatial patterns; their component counts do not introduce other physical dimensions. The result is a conditional spatial coupling mechanism. It does not assign the chosen quadrupole to a photon, or identify its suppression with a measured neutrino rate. Two radial functions determine the entire polarized shape response Let L_M,L_N be the two radial Dirac fluctuation operators, with normalized radial source vectors u_M,u_N. Define R_M(z)=u_M^T(z-L_M)^{-1}u_M,\qquad R_N(z)=u_N^T(z-L_N)^{-1}u_N. \tag{1} The spectral parameter z has the same time convention as the Dirac equation; a retarded boundary value requires the appropriate prescription at the real spectrum. The derivation uses values away from poles. For a real orthonormal traceless shape basis A_r, the target's spatial circulation tensor J acts by \mathcal K_{rs}=\frac12\operatorname{tr}(A_r[J,A_s]). \tag{2} Put c_0=2/[d(d+2)] and c_1=4/[d(d+2)^2]. The angular Gram matrices derived from the full Clifford field give the exact bare matrix response \boxed{\chi_0(z,J)=A(z)I+B(z)i\mathcal K,} \tag{3} where \begin{aligned} A(z)&=(c_0-c_1)[R_M(z)+R_M(-z)] +c_1[R_N(z)+R_N(-z)],\\ B(z)&=c_1[R_N(z)-R_M(z)-R_N(-z)+R_M(-z)]. \end{aligned} \tag{4} A is even in frequency and B is odd. Thus the static response is isotropic in the shape basis, while the rotating part of the response retains the prepared spatial polarization J. The source's own feedback supplies the complete response \boxed{\chi(z,J)=\big[I-g_0\chi_0(z,J)\big]^{-1}\chi_0(z,J),} \tag{5} with the same scalar coefficient g_0 as in the stationary profile. Equations (3)–(5) contain all the shape helicities and both ordinary and conjugate Dirac fluctuations. They do not replace the latter by a positive scalar oscillator. Both target preparation and source shape are essential. If the source has complex shape coefficients c, its response is \chi(z,J)c. Reversing the prepared circulation gives the transpose identity \chi(z,J)^T=\chi(z,-J),\qquad \chi(-\bar z,J)=\overline{\chi(z,J)}. \tag{6} A fixed polarized preparation need not have a symmetric response matrix. These relations retain the underlying real energy and its reciprocal variation without assuming that reversing a process leaves its preparations unchanged. Restriction can change the type of spatial shape For an isometric inclusion I:\mathbb R^p\to\mathbb R^d, the moment source restricts as \mathcal R(C)=I^TCI. \tag{7} A traceless shape in d dimensions need not remain traceless after restriction. Its lower trace is a breathing source and must be retained when calculating the complete interaction. With Hilbert–Schmidt-normalized tensor bases, the map from higher traceless shapes to all lower symmetric shapes has singular values \underbrace{1,\ldots,1}_{p(p+1)/2-1}, \qquad \sqrt{\frac{d-p}{d}}. \tag{8} To derive the last value, apply the adjoint map to the normalized lower breathing shape I_p/\sqrt p and remove its higher trace. The squared norm is 1-p/d. Lower traceless shapes already embed as higher traceless shapes with the same norm, giving the unit values. For five dimensions inside six, fourteen lower quadrupoles have unit restriction singular value and the lower breathing channel has value 1/\sqrt6. Five independent higher mixed shapes have zero static restriction. This is a statement about this spatial tensor kernel, not about the entire physical coupling of a particle species. The higher field's rotation opens the mixed shapes Take a six-dimensional orthogonal circulation tensor J, with J^2=-I, and let the lower five-plane be n^\perp. Put u=Jn, so u lies in that plane and has unit norm. Relative to this particular inclusion, J=\begin{pmatrix}J_5&u\\-u^T&0\end{pmatrix}. \tag{9} The block notation describes the relation between the two objects. It does not make any of the six spatial directions inherently different. Every traceless symmetric C with zero full restriction has the form C=\begin{pmatrix}0&v\\v^T&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad v\in\mathbb R^5. \tag{10} Its spatial rotation satisfies \boxed{\mathcal R\left(\frac12[J,C]\right) =\frac12(uv^T+vu^T).} \tag{11} For unit u, the right side is zero only when v=0. For example, multiplying by u gives v+(u\cdot v)u=0, whose component along u then gives u\cdot v=0 and hence v=0. Thus none of the five nonzero statically hidden mixed quadrupoles remains hidden after this first spatial rotation. In matrix form, \ker\mathcal R\cap\ker(\mathcal R\mathcal K)=\{0\}. This retains the mixed part of the higher geometry instead of discarding it during restriction. There are still input combinations with zero output at an individual frequency, because the output has fewer components. The result concerns a fixed spatial pattern being invisible throughout the response, which is a stronger condition than a zero at one selected frequency. A derived low-frequency matching barrier Away from a static collective pole, equations (3)–(5) give \chi(z,J)=\frac{A(0)}{1-g_0A(0)}I +\frac{B'(0)}{[1-g_0A(0)]^2}z\,i\mathcal K+O(z^2). \tag{12} The coefficient is fixed by the actual radial modes: B'(0)=2c_1\left( \|L_M^{-1}u_M\|^2-\|L_N^{-1}u_N\|^2\right). \tag{13} For a source c with \mathcal Rc=0, \boxed{\mathcal R\chi(z,J)c =\frac{iB'(0)}{[1-g_0A(0)]^2}z\, \mathcal R\mathcal Kc+O(z^2).} \tag{14} The original static mismatch is exact, but a nonzero-frequency field motion opens the channel. The resulting mode amplitude is linear in small frequency when the coefficient in (13) is nonzero. Its squared amplitude is then quadratic; a physical transition rate also requires the relevant mode map, state density and incident flux. This is an explicit version of a spatial matching barrier produced by the field's own dynamics. It does not require assigning a special small coupling coefficient to the five-dimensional particle. Include the lower object's response as well Let \chi_a,\chi_b be the two objects' own complete shape responses. For a weak cross term with coefficient \epsilon multiplying their moment pairing, the leading response of the lower shape to a higher applied source h_b is \boxed{\delta M_a(z) =\epsilon\,\chi_a(z,J_a)\mathcal R\chi_b(z,J_b)h_b(z) +O(\epsilon^2).} \tag{15} Both polarizations and both spatial spectra enter. The reverse response uses \mathcal R^T, obtained from the same real pair energy. Common physical rotations transform both circulation tensors, both shape bases and the inclusion together, leaving the physical prediction unchanged. The coefficient \epsilon here controls a perturbative contact expansion; it is not an independently fitted constant for each particle pair. At leading order one may use the isolated self-consistent profiles. Their static deformation changes (15) at the next order. A finite interaction requires the corresponding complete pair background, as illustrated by Self-consistent nested Dirac pair. For a specified quadratic fluctuation energy, both responses can be solved exactly from \begin{aligned} \delta M_a&=\chi_a(h_a+\epsilon\mathcal R\delta M_b),\\ \delta M_b&=\chi_b(h_b+\epsilon\mathcal R^T\delta M_a). \end{aligned} \tag{16} This gives reciprocal feedback and collective poles. Applying that finite quadratic model to a nonlinear physical pair requires its Hessian at the correct background; it is not supplied just by combining two isolated profiles at an arbitrary large contact coefficient. A normalized example Choose J_6 with unit rotations in planes 12,34,56, and the lower five-plane spanned by axes 1 through 5. Apply the unit complex shape C=\frac12(e_3e_6^T+e_6e_3^T) +\frac i2(e_4e_6^T+e_6e_4^T). \tag{17} Its static restriction vanishes. Its entire response lies in a spatial subspace whose lower projection is traceless, so the lower breathing channel is not needed for this particular example. Take m=0.5 and one common interaction coefficient g_0=6.5. Self-consistency determines the isolated source strengths a_5=1.031769686 and a_6=0.998746098; they are not separately fitted interaction coefficients. Retain both profiles' complete source feedback. For the lower circulation with unit rotations in 12 and 34, the norm of the transfer coefficient \chi_5\mathcal R\chi_6C is: frequency lower response norm per unit weak-contact coefficient 0 0 0.1 9.40182\times10^{-6} 0.05 4.70316\times10^{-6} 0.025 2.35182\times10^{-6} 0.0125 1.17593\times10^{-6} The amplitude divided by frequency tends to approximately 9.40742\times10^{-5} in these model units, as calculated directly from the zero-frequency radial derivative. Reversing the lower target's 34 circulation while keeping the higher preparation fixed changes the finite-frequency response. The static zero is therefore compatible with both genuine dynamical access and a dependence on both polarizations. The incoming quadrupole in (17) is a specified spatial source, not a derived photon inclusion. This example supplies a mechanism to test against that physical inclusion; it does not establish universal five-dimensional suppression. Persistent spatial shape barriers extends this calculation across the hierarchy. It classifies shapes with a permanent zero and those whose first opening is quadratic in frequency, retaining the lower breathing response when needed. Verification spatial_shape_transfer_checks.py compares (3)–(5) with the full complex ordinary/conjugate source matrix, including every shape direction. It checks restriction singular values, the rank statement following (11), low-frequency scaling, both target preparations, covariance of the whole nested geometry, and reverse transfer. It also checks the controlled weak-contact expansion against exact finite quadratic feedback. As a separate completeness test, the equal norms of u_M,u_N cancel the would-be 1/z rotating response at large frequency. The response begins with A=O(z^{-2}), B=O(z^{-3}). Omitting an angular family can spoil that cancellation as well as the low-frequency result. Related Polarized Dirac shape response — derives the angular families and their complete feedback. Transition-density coupling — derives the moment pairing which supplies the spatial restriction. Reciprocal scattering of spatial modes — distinguishes a geometric source zero from a zero caused by spectral interference.

title: Generalized sector coupling
summary: A common interaction on arbitrary nested sectors yields reciprocal responses, normalized vertices, and testable coupling relations, with neutrinos as a channel-specific control.
text: Summary: A common interaction on arbitrary nested sectors yields reciprocal responses, normalized vertices, and testable coupling relations, with neutrinos as a channel-specific control. Physical scope There is one infinite physical manifold with one nested chain of ordinary macroscopic spatial submanifolds. Particles at different depths are structures of \Psi_\infty on that chain. All directions belonging to a given particle are of the same spatial kind. A decomposition relative to another particle's submanifold describes their relation; it does not give either particle an inherent division into different kinds of space. The following construction applies to arbitrary finite collections of sectors, including the working depths 2,3,4,5,6,10. It assumes specified spatial maps, measures, mode subspaces, and an interaction channel. It does not require accepting a particular list of global sphere or projective topologies. Actual embeddings and their domain conditions must be supplied wherever a proposed topology is used. IDWT has no mediator particles. The source profiles, response modes, and representation indices below describe the one field on this physical space. Coupling starts with its direct interaction terms. Eliminating some of its modes is a conditional reduction of those equations, not a particle-exchange mechanism. The working coupling hypothesis includes a changing geometric match: each particle can drive the other's spatial pattern toward greater compatibility or toward incompatibility during an encounter. Bilateral polarization coupling separates that physical target from a restricted orientation benchmark whose relative overlap remains constant. Both the change in compatibility and its effect on subsequent interaction must follow from the same dynamics. The concrete shape calculation is developed in Transition-density coupling, followed by Reciprocal scattering of spatial modes. The complementary route through rotation-neutral modes and their spatial transport tests how one geometric operation can be blocked while another remains active. The constructions below provide their common spatial maps and normalization. Localized spatial fields and reciprocal feedback Positive-frequency scalar vertices retain complete incoming bands and the off-diagonal spatial interference that builds the local source. A fixed normalized incoming polarization has massless inclusive squared strength \sin^2(\theta/2); a count of output components supplies no further multiplier. Available channels and the actual coherent contraction are separate parts of the calculation. Axial spatial Dirac packets give an exact angular family with transverse localization and complete complex polarization vectors in odd-dimensional space. A full Cartesian calculation independently checks its three-dimensional head-on response. Localized scalar encounters also evolve four incoming packets in two chiral patterns, retaining the generated spatial modes beyond the resonant quartet. At the stated three-dimensional benchmark, opposite relative phases reverse an approximately 1.77\% classical chiral-norm transfer, with conserved total norm and a continuum reflection law. Changing spatial compatibility compares the incoming and outgoing full patterns through the same prescribed free encounter, after removing their known free evolution. At fixed five-dimensional preparation rules and one coefficient, different complex phases give either increased or decreased contact. The effects are small and survive positive unit normalization of each outgoing pattern. Time ordering of the source derives the first nonzero contact coefficient from the complete local equation. Its independent coupling variations retain both partners' spatial response; no steering toward alignment is added. Scalar Born frequency accounting supplies a further constraint. Complete scalar vertices remove the negative-output resonant Born channel for positive incoming scattering data, while a finite-time positive preparation can still have a nonresonant signed response. Those spectral signs have no assigned particle-antiparticle interpretation here. These are conditional controls of the specified local scalar dynamics on ordinary spatial fields. Selecting stable occupied particle patterns, projecting one physically normalized interaction across distinct depths, and identifying observed electric and weak channels remain necessary. The calculations do not determine the global geometry of the observed three-dimensional space or an observed neutrino interaction rate. Spatial current, propagation and measurable response Local polarized Dirac pulses retain the actual scalar cross term of two traveling parts of the same field. They give exact spatial mismatch conditions and reciprocal weak-scattering maps with both complex-linear and conjugate terms. The full nonlinear collision changes normalized spatial compatibility in either direction under the same local equation. These are transversely unbound flat pulse controls, not identified particles or a completed distinct-depth coupling law. Causal local Dirac response derives two retarded scalar channels from the written local term at a specified uniform background. The instantaneous moment causality test exhibits an immediate remote influence in the candidate nonlocal equation. Its spatial harmonic comparison shows that matching one screened denominator does not derive that candidate: the higher spatial modes, response sign and direct contact all matter. Collective translation waves derives \mathcal I=M+T/d from the complete scalar Dirac field. The two displacement polarizations at depth two propagate at half the underlying Dirac speed on the zero-bare-mass branch. Their count alone does not identify photons. With an explicitly supplied minimal connection of the same field, Soft spatial current response derives the Thomson current, magnetic moment and uniform polarization correction. Soft polarized scattering retains the photon phase and every target polarization transition. At photon speed one, the forward spin coefficient is (g_{\rm mag}-2)^2/(8\mathcal I^2). Canonical spatial spin response independently relates the electric spin-orbit coefficient to that same magnetic moment: c_S=g_{\rm mag}-1. These relations constrain one common current. The conditional six-dimensional scalar ground profile predicts g_{\rm mag}=2.07691916, which differs from the measured electron value 2.00231930436; changing the common scale does not repair this ratio. Conserved spatial charge derives the continuity identity for a proposed charge operator with every spatial derivative retained. A neutral rotation eigenspace by itself is not a conserved local electric-charge sector. A rotation-based source must retain its actual orbital and frame terms. No depth-five neutrality or surviving weak rate has yet followed from the same physical interaction. A separate declared stationary component action supports exact null spatial pulses, with two normalizable spatial displacements and finite pulse energy. Its spatial displacement action derives the common quartic interaction by completing the full profile. The retarded spatial response then supplies a positive frequency-dependent kernel, a derived soft logarithm and outgoing radiation of the same field. This construction provides a calculable interaction mechanism with both polarizations. Its component action, background and coupling to occupied particle fields must still be derived from the master action before comparison with physical photon or neutrino rates. Polarized pulse collisions gives exact reciprocal energy-dependent delays within the local displacement action. Polarized spatial radiation separately retains its full spatial continuum: opposite circular senses can cancel the leading outgoing channel while the conservative interaction survives. The same spectral measure fixes the long-pulse emitted-energy coefficient. Complete polarization before choosing a coupling shape Complete spatial polarization data retains every amplitude and relative phase in a specified spatial multiplet. Its circulation tensor is complete for one six-dimensional chiral multiplet, while a ten-dimensional field can require four-form information as well. These are field descriptors on the actual spatial manifold. Equal-current spatial polarizations constructs two complete ten-dimensional bound fields with identical density and Dirac current but different responses to the same polarized lower partner. One reciprocal six-inside-ten rotation-moment energy gives an exact pair solution: both mean tensors stay fixed while one higher field's full polarization changes. The stated interaction is a conditional benchmark; its coefficient and occupied modes are not identified physical couplings. Spatial polarization textures then allows amplitudes and phases to vary across the actual bound coordinates. It derives both the retained equation and its required Dirac complement. Preserving a scalar source does not by itself make a texture a spatial solution. This supplies the kinetic test needed before treating a richer pattern as a particle's allowed polarization. Parts of the calculation Nested sector reciprocity derives the upper-to-lower marginal and its reciprocal cylindrical response. Compatible maps compose along the chain without introducing a new coupling factor for every intermediate sector. Canonical coupling normalization derives physical mode vertices from the kinetic metric and shows which charge and transition identities survive projection. Common field response eliminates specified stable response modes of the same field. It derives the resulting correction to direct pair interactions and determines exactly when that correction has rank one. Neutrino channel control tests the same construction against electric neutrality, colour singlet structure, surviving weak vertices, and low-energy response suppression. Nested moment coupling applies the existing dot-square kernel to all distinct working depths. It gives an exact minimum-depth matrix, its full rank, and the trace projection required for a scalar rank-one response. Results that do not require a parameter for every pair For a real scalar interaction on Q_a\subset Q_b, the reciprocal source responses are V_a=gK R_{ba}j_b,\qquad V_b=gR_{ba}^{*}K^{*}j_a. The same coefficient appears in the action. Differences between the two response maps come from their domains, measures, and transpose relation. For compatible projections through Q_c, the source map satisfies R_{ca}=R_{ba}R_{cb}. After canonical matter normalization, a coherent vertex becomes Z_a^{-1/2}K_{ab}Z_b^{-1/2}. This removes arbitrary choices of mode amplitude convention. A common conserved generator acting as q on each retained family becomes qI in every normalized family, even when their depths and profiles differ. This preserves a supplied universal charge; the physical charge assignment still has to be derived. Eliminating a positive response block of the same field gives the correction G_{ab}=B_a^{*}L^{-1}B_b. For fixed source preparations this implies G_{ba}=G_{ab}^{*},\qquad |g_{ab}|^2\le g_{aa}g_{bb}. Rank one occurs exactly when all nonzero profiles L^{-1/2}B_df_d are proportional. The same field can have many independent spatial responses, producing a higher-rank correction. Its direct coupling block remains part of the complete interaction. The inequality is limited to the positive static channel specified in the derivation; it does not automatically govern every physical force. Consequences for the particle hierarchy The generalized calculation separates three effects that can coexist: Equal charge across unequal depths. Consistent normalization preserves a common charge generator. Large differences in mode count need not produce differences in charge. Unequal response within one interaction. Spatial profile differences and field dynamics change finite-momentum vertices and contact strengths without changing the conserved zero-momentum charge. Absence from a particular channel. A derived generator or source map can annihilate a sector while other channel maps remain nonzero. Active neutrinos are an essential test of this distinction. The explicit Gaussian benchmark couples equal shared marginals equally at every containing depth. Different widths produce a strict deficit from rank-one saturation. Consequently spatial nesting alone neither suppresses depth five nor guarantees a common rank-one response. These are exact results for the declared model, not a fitted particle coupling table. The rank-one common-anchor proposal can now be tested at the operator level: derive whether the actual normalized source images are proportional in the field-response metric. Even if they are, converting that response to mass poles requires the reference-band factors and kinetic normalization retained in that proposal. Result for the existing moment kernel For centered isotropic profiles on nested flat spatial subspaces, the dot-square kernel gives G_{de}=u_du_e\min(d,e), with u_d containing the one-sector coefficient and second-moment scale. The matrix across (2,3,4,5,6,10) has rank six when every u_d is nonzero. Its normalized pair correlations are \sqrt{\min(d,e)/\max(d,e)}, independent of those scales. In particular, depth five has ordinary nonzero entries. This is a result for the specified scalar interaction, not an electric or weak coupling prediction. Selecting only the trace of the spatial moment tensor would instead give the rank-one geometric factor de/D in a containing depth D. The complete kernel also includes a nonzero traceless response. This identifies a definite physical projection to derive if a scalar common response is to follow from this kernel. Physical inputs still needed for numerical predictions The common construction fixes relations after its operators are specified. To predict particle couplings, V2 must supply the actual spatial and polarization maps B_d, the field's linearized evolution operator, the mode kinetic metrics, and the occupied preparations from its field equations. Depth-dependent parameters hidden inside those maps remain parameters. The electric, weak, and colour identifications also require the correct generators and representations on every sector. For the photon this includes its protected zero mode and transverse propagating field. The positive scalar confinement model developed below has no localized zero bound frequency; its massive normal branch cannot by itself supply that photon mode. This statement concerns the frozen bound eigenproblem. Collective fluctuations also vary the source and can have zero modes; their propagation requires the full fluctuation operator. The next useful physical calculation is to derive a channel's source maps and evaluate their response Gram matrix across several particle sectors. This would test common-source factorization, channel zeros, and coupling ratios together. The present work supplies the equations and independently checked benchmarks needed to assess that calculation. Verification generalized_coupling_checks.py uses weighted spatial marginals, finite differences of reciprocal energies, conservative time evolution, nonorthogonal mode changes, independent response minimization, Gaussian quadrature, and explicit charge and weak-transition matrices. These verify the stated conditional results; they do not assign empirical coupling constants. Interaction operator tools — supplies the projected variational and spatial-profile prerequisites. Coupling between two polarized spatial patterns Both interacting objects carry spatial polarization. Their relative shapes, orientations, phases, and allowed responses must remain in the calculation. The higher-dimensional field may determine the source that drives a lower response; the lower bound depth need not set its strength. This possibility and photon-led probing are assessed through variations of the same action. The new calculation proceeds through the following connected steps: Descending photon source selects the photon bound mode while retaining normal propagation coordinates and phase. It distinguishes a higher source from a complete stationary solution. Dirac source linearization differentiates the written nonlinear scalar term, retaining both ordinary and conjugate variations and the cubic spatial/frequency overlap. Bilateral polarization coupling varies both objects. A zero static overlap can coexist with a nonzero mixed response; a solved reciprocal orientation benchmark conserves relative overlap while both objects precess. Coherent spatial overlap retains both shapes and phases in exact Gaussian integrals and a normalized opposing-lobe source whose long-wavelength contribution cancels. Polarized response spectrum combines normalized spatial vertices with the allowed target motions and finite exposure. It separates a protected dark input from a spectral or truncation zero. Three finite geometric controls make the spatial assumptions testable. Photon plane coupling restricts a specified magnetic two-form term to the actual two photon amplitudes. Isotropic polarization comparison proves identical five- and six-dimensional overlap distributions for the stated uniform tensor ensemble. Spatial source complementarity derives which higher vector and rotational descriptors survive on a lower subspace, including the conditional depth-five joint-source lower bound. These results supply explicit response operators and shape integrals, rather than a particle coupling table. Predicting distinctive five-dimensional suppression still requires the actual selected spatial solution, its allowed variations, and the physical source/output map. A chosen zero projection, an averaged density, or one missing response in a truncated basis does not replace that derivation. polarization_coupling_checks.py checks the geometric projectors and distributions, full nonlinear source derivatives, reciprocal evolution, spectral response, and complex spatial integrals by independent methods. From spatial shape to an actual response Transition-density coupling derives the complete first and second variations of the nonlocal projected-density energy. Both changing spatial patterns enter its coherent quartic vertex; the frozen-background potential is retained alongside the product of source variations. For normalized quadrupole modes, the dot-square kernel yields T_{0A;0C}=\frac{g}{2\omega_a\omega_b} \operatorname{tr}(A B C B^T). Here A and C describe both shapes and B their specified geometric comparison. Two traceless planar quadrupoles with relative angle \theta have an amplitude proportional to \cos2\theta. At 45^\circ their coupling vanishes; at 90^\circ its sign reverses. A breathing mode and a traceless shape have a different exact selection rule. These are derived higher-order polarization examples on actual spatial profiles, with no particle-specific zero imposed. Reciprocal scattering of spatial modes then solves incoming propagation and the target's response together in a conservative model of the same field. Orthogonal polarized inputs leave the target unexcited. Matched inputs reflect according to the frequency response, and a direct spatial wavepacket reproduces the result. A small nonzero vertex can still reflect fully at an isolated narrow resonance; a rare interaction rate requires the spectrum and incoming flux, not just a small static overlap. The target's complete allowed variations also matter for photons. Polarized photon transition strength derives the full two-polarization response matrix for the specified simple spatial Pauli term. One incident polarization can be dark, but its summed response has a positive bound at every tested depth. This particular probe therefore supplies no automatic five-dimensional suppression. A higher-source route to distinct channels A more specific mechanism candidate starts with a six-dimensional spatial complex structure. Its compression to any five-dimensional hyperplane has two equal rotation planes and one null axis. In the spatial spin action, rotation-neutral modes then satisfy Q_5=\frac{H_1+H_2}{2},\qquad P_0=\frac{I-H_1H_2}{2},\qquad Q_5P_0=0. Three equal planes in six dimensions and five in ten have no zero spin weight. The cancellation is an operator identity for the specified probe, not merely zero mean source. The five-dimensional particle still has five ordinary spatial dimensions. Nonneutral polarizations also exist there, and the full higher source has a mixed term that acts on the neutral modes. A physical photon projection must determine which terms it samples. The equal-rate guarantee is specific to the six-to-five compression; direct ten-to-five examples can have unequal rates and no neutral vector. Spatial transport of the neutral doublet provides a constructive second channel. The neutral projector is P_0=(I-n\cdot\gamma)/2, where n is the actual spatial null-axis direction. As this direction varies over physical positions, the projected kinetic energy acquires a nonzero \mathfrak{su}(2) curvature and the fixed positive term |\nabla n|^2|b|^2/4. Its determinant curvature is zero. Thus neutrality under the balanced rotation can coexist with response to changing spatial geometry, all within the one field. This does not yet identify electromagnetic and weak interactions. Selection of the occupied neutral band, the complete physical current, reciprocal source motion and its normalization remain essential. Scalar self-binding alone leaves neutral and nonneutral constant polarizations degenerate. The neutral projection also does not close the first-order spatial Dirac symbol: perpendicular momenta still act through the omitted modes, whose contribution must be retained in deriving an effective kinetic term. Rotations of nested sectors further shows that the equal-plane rotations move some members of a fixed chain. They can preserve the entire nesting by transporting it together, but the moving-embedding and omitted-mode terms must then be included. The decisive next calculation is the same-field source projection on a selected spatial particle solution: retain both partners' variations, identify the physical photon current, and check whether it annihilates the five-dimensional mode while another derived response remains. The current notes supply explicit shape vertices, a concrete neutral candidate and its geometric transport, together with the equations needed to test that identification. spatial_coupling_mechanism_checks.py verifies these results with full Clifford representations, nonlocal finite differences, spatial quadrature, exact moving-mode derivatives, conservative scattering, direct wavepacket evolution, and independent projector transport. Full spatial Dirac sources and reciprocal deformation Rotation-neutral Dirac fields retains the full ordinary spatial field, including its angular lower components. The total rotation is orbital plus spin: a five-dimensional neutral field can occupy all five spatial directions even when its lower components are not neutral under the spin operator alone. Its local spatial current need not vanish. The scalar moment branch solves a complete first-order spatial Dirac equation with its own scalar source. Its bound frequencies, dilation law and radial fluctuations are computed together. This is a conditional source model. Several massless-background branches have growing radial modes, and the scalar source leaves rest polarizations degenerate. It does not supply the actual Coulomb-plus-precession electron orbit or a selection of the occupied five-dimensional neutral mode. Dressed source vertices reconstruct the eliminated spatial components and their kinetic norm. If \Omega lifts a retained amplitude into the full field, a source V has canonical vertex V_{\rm can}=Z^{-1/2}\Omega^\dagger V\Omega Z^{-1/2}, \qquad Z=\Omega^\dagger\Omega. A zero bare projection can hide a nonzero full response. Conversely, a supplied universal charge qI remains qI after consistent normalization; discarding part of the norm cannot derive neutrality. The polarized shape response differentiates the actual spatial profiles in every quadrupole direction and retains both ordinary and conjugate fluctuations. The translation response includes the scalar center variation, recovers the zero translation mode and derives its inertial pole. A separately centered shape pairing alone has no separation-dependent force; that requires the pair's spatial contact or propagation dependence. Dynamical shape opening then gives a concrete matching barrier. A higher shape can have zero static restriction into the lower sector, yet the higher field's polarized response rotates it into an accessible shape. Its leading low-frequency transfer retains both objects: \delta M_a=\epsilon\, \chi_a(z,J_a)\mathcal R\chi_b(z,J_b)h_b+O(\epsilon^2). The calculated opening amplitude can be linear in frequency without a special small coefficient assigned to one depth. A rate additionally requires the physical incident mode, occupied target and flux. The self-consistent nested pair goes beyond fixed isolated profiles. One common scalar energy deforms both partners, with the same source coefficient in their shared directions. Their reciprocal scalar envelopes consequently have a symmetric coupling matrix G_{ij}=\partial^2U/\partial s_i\partial s_j. Its entries obey Gs=M/5 in the massless-background model; they cannot be fitted independently for each pair. Several nested depths have a common amplitude mode and a softer relative-amplitude mode, derived from their solved profiles with the same interaction coefficient. Normal Dirac propagation retains the partner which carries motion through an ordinary containing direction. Exact uniform boosts preserve the scalar binding source. The full moment-response equation also retains source variation, spatial center motion and both ordinary and conjugate normal fluctuations. It provides a route to collective dispersion without fixing the bound profiles inside a small envelope ansatz. The scalar envelope derives the accompanying density-dependent profile response and also gives its explicit full-field residual when the density varies. Stability of those restricted envelope equations does not establish stability of the spatial bound profiles or decoupling of their center and polarization motions. These results supply actual spatial source and response calculations for the proposed matching mechanism. The remaining physical identification is the occupied particle geometry and its photon current, followed by the surviving interaction channels and their rates. No neutral projector, shape label or relative-amplitude eigenvalue by itself completes that step. Persistent spatial shape barriers classifies the complete geometric kernel across nested depths for an orthogonal higher circulation. Three restriction maps determine whether a higher pattern has direct access, opens linearly or quadratically in frequency, or stays invisible to the specified interaction. The visible ranks change with the higher circulation relative to the actual lower inclusion. A common-coefficient ten-to-five Dirac example verifies the quadratic opening with both responses and the lower breathing mode. The classification holds a specified source pattern fixed as frequency changes. A free spatial mode must also satisfy its own eigenproblem; a pure shape helicity with zero restriction remains inaccessible. Spatial Dirac polarization waves restores the rest polarizations omitted by a single scalar envelope. Full linear polarization waves are gapless, and exact finite polarized planes can change the bound spatial current while preserving the scalar source. This shows directly why scalar binding alone does not select an occupied polarization or identify neutrality. Reflection symmetry of scalar Dirac sources extends that boundary beyond radial confinement. Reflection-preserving scalar sources retain at least four-mode multiplets at depths five and six, even with unequal axis strengths. Their spatial shape response can depend on polarization while the source still lacks an isolated selected neutral doublet. Bound frequency and the actual coupling source Source frequencies in spatial coupling distinguishes the stationary carrier, spatial transition frequencies and complete nonlinear source. Small inter-mode clocks can survive large normal momentum, but the source matrix elements and response scale must accompany them. A common dilation of the scalar bound profile leaves its dimensionless shape response unchanged at a fixed frequency ratio. Two-frequency spatial Dirac currents gives an exact current oscillating at twice the bound frequency, with fixed canonical norm and one common interaction coefficient. A slower member is broader and can retain a substantial moving current. Its small mean scalar moment does not eliminate relative-component response, and its full linearization has periodic coefficients. Incoming spatial shape modes shows that an already specified incoming moment enters the reciprocal pair equation without another application of its own susceptibility. Individual shape helicities retain a nonzero hyperplane restriction. Low-frequency opening of a blocked applied force instead arises from changing cancellation between several components. Applying this mechanism to neutrinos therefore requires the selected occupied spatial mode and photon source map, followed by the normalized response of both partners. Periodic fields, geometry and the full pair Periodic spatial source response now derives the complete ordinary/conjugate field equation and its frequency sidebands, including scalar-center motion. A scalar rest cancellation can coexist with an oscillating spatial current response. Radial dynamics of two-frequency fields separates the number norm from the kinetic weight and transfers an existing radial instability into the full periodic field. Two-frequency fields in a readjusted nested pair keeps both deformed profiles and their occupied polarizations. A containing field can maintain a finite lower frequency as the lower mean scalar balance approaches zero. The reciprocal frequency derivative remains finite, while the scalar-center curvature becomes singular. The exactly zero-balance center is undefined, so that endpoint is a limit of positive-balance fields, not an already established nonlinear evolution at zero scalar normalization. The slow shape poles have frequencies and residues that decrease together, but the tested positive-frequency member has negative canonical spectral weight. The total scalar response remains finite. This calculation does not identify a stable weakly coupled particle from a soft pole alone. Reciprocal response with two spatial clocks retains both backgrounds and the curvature of their common energy. Deformation can open a shape–center sideband which cancels in a central radial example. Normal propagation can also generate responses involving both clocks. The complete polarization test calculates exactly which second occupied polarizations cancel a selected sideband and how that kernel changes with the incoming lower spatial pattern. For one explicit lower traceless pattern, every finite spectral residue cancels at rest; normal momentum opens its amplitude linearly and its squared response quadratically. Common rotation of the fields and incoming pattern preserves the result. These are source-channel identities with the same coefficient across depths, not a depth-five interaction zero or an interaction rate. A global antilinear reduction has separate matrix, scalar-interference and nested-projection requirements. It cannot be supplied by assuming that a two-component envelope symmetry acts on every higher-dimensional spatial perturbation. The full response equations remain available when that shortcut does not apply. The physical photon current, selected particle geometry and stability must still connect these conditional mechanisms to observed coupling. A common spatial pair with changing compatibility The projective moment action specifies one scalar kernel across a nested chain without separate pair coefficients. Its complete complex spatial pair evolves both profiles within an exact symmetry class and resolves increasing and decreasing interaction overlap. Relative phase and the higher two-form response remain in the spatial equations. This is a conditional example on the specified projective geometry; an instantaneous spatial kernel still needs a controlled causal reduction from the master field and physical channel identification. Mode counts and a finite response Spectral weights in oscillator response shows why exact Hockey-Stick source counts still need the response spectrum. For the stated cylindrical scalar-source map, stiffness growing as the paired normal level to power s gives a finite infinite-band response precisely when s>q/2. An affine spectrum in four normal directions leaves shared-mode-dependent logarithmic growth after its common linear growth cancels. The result constrains that source and spectrum; it is not a depth-five suppression or an observed coupling law. Radial polarization at even depths Complete radial polarization fields provides an exact spherical family in every dimension from two onward, including six and ten, with independent complex radial polarization vectors. Its full Cartesian current can have tangential components despite a radial density, and its complete integrated polarization matrix is conserved. The radial fields share one center; this supplies an even-depth spatial control while general separated-center encounters remain open.

title: Incoming spatial shape modes
summary: A specified incoming spatial moment and an applied force have different response maps; individual shape helicities obey exact hyperplane restriction bounds which clarify the frequency-dependent cancellation mechanism.
text: Summary: A specified incoming spatial moment and an applied force have different response maps; individual shape helicities obey exact hyperplane restriction bounds which clarify the frequency-dependent cancellation mechanism. Distinguish an incoming pattern from a force that creates it Dynamical shape opening follows a fixed force applied to a higher spatial field. The higher response converts that force into a changing moment, which then drives the lower partner. A freely propagating particle must also satisfy its own field equation, so its actual moment cannot automatically be identified with that forcing vector. The two objects occupy nested submanifolds of the same ordinary macroscopic spatial manifold. Both polarizations, the actual spatial inclusion and the response of each object remain in the following equations. Moment and helicity labels describe spatial patterns; they are not additional spatial dimensions or physical particle assignments. Retain both responses without processing the incident mode twice Let \mathcal R(C)=I^TCI restrict a higher spatial moment into the lower sector. Its adjoint uses the full Frobenius moment norm, including lower breathing. Let \chi_a,\chi_b be the corresponding complete response operators at a specified frequency and normal momentum, and let \epsilon denote the common contact coefficient. For a prescribed unperturbed incoming moment b_{\rm in}, the coupled linear response equations are a=\epsilon\chi_a\mathcal R b,\qquad b=b_{\rm in}+\epsilon\chi_b\mathcal R^\dagger a. \tag{1} They give, wherever the indicated inverse exists, \boxed{a= [I-\epsilon^2\chi_a\mathcal R\chi_b\mathcal R^\dagger]^{-1} \epsilon\chi_a\mathcal R b_{\rm in}.} \tag{2} Both objects readjust, and the denominator retains repeated feedback. If the incident moment is instead produced by an applied force f_b, then b_{\rm in}=\chi_bf_b. Substituting it into (2) recovers the previous leading response \epsilon\chi_a\mathcal R\chi_b f_b. An actual incoming moment is already the result of its own spatial dynamics; applying \chi_b to it again would change the physical input. Consequently \mathcal R b_{\rm in}=0 gives zero lower response in this specified channel, while \mathcal R f_b=0 need not. The latter force can produce \mathcal R\chi_bf_b\ne0. For a scattering problem the incoming field and outgoing response use their specified propagation boundary conditions. At a discrete pole or resonance, use the full coupled operator or its appropriate limiting resolvent. A finite pair of free bound oscillators has hybridized mode frequencies; an inverse evaluated directly at an uncoupled pole does not replace that eigenproblem. At finite nonlinear contact, the background must also be the readjusted nested pair. Individual rotating shapes preserve their geometric restriction Take an even-dimensional higher sector with orthogonal circulation J^T=-J, J^2=-I. On complex symmetric traceless spatial tensors define \mathcal K(C)=\frac12[J,C],\qquad T=i\mathcal K. \tag{3} The eigenvalues of T are 0,\pm1. A shape helicity is an eigenvector Tc=\lambda c; it labels rotation of the actual spatial pattern relative to J. For the full radial Dirac response, \chi(z)c=\chi_\lambda(z)c, \qquad \chi_\lambda(z)= \frac{A(z)+\lambda B(z)}{1-g_0[A(z)+\lambda B(z)]}. \tag{4} Therefore \boxed{\mathcal R\chi(z)c=\chi_\lambda(z)\mathcal Rc.} \tag{5} Changing frequency changes the amplitude of an individual helicity, while its relative spatial restriction stays the same. Degenerate modes can be combined within a helicity; (5) holds for that whole subspace. Combinations of different helicities can instead acquire different relative responses. A hyperplane retains a fixed fraction of every pure helicity Let the containing sector have d=2m, with m\ge2, and let the lower sector be any hyperplane of dimension d-1. Choose coordinates in which J rotates the planes 12,34,\ldots and the omitted normal is axis d. This is a common change of coordinates for the geometry and inclusion, not a preferred division of the higher particle's spatial dimensions. The singular values of the restriction map on each normalized helicity subspace are: helicity singular value multiplicity +1 or -1 1 m(m-1)/2 +1 or -1 1/\sqrt2 m-1 +1 or -1 1/2 1 0 1 (m-1)^2-1 0 \sqrt{(m+1)/(2m)} 1 0 1/\sqrt2 2(m-1) To derive the nonzero-helicity rows, take the orthonormal complex spatial vectors v_j=(e_{2j-1}+ie_{2j})/\sqrt2. Their symmetric squares and products span one helicity, with the conjugates spanning the other. Restriction preserves v_j for j<m and gives I^Tv_m=e_{d-1}/\sqrt2 at the vector level. A square of v_m therefore loses a factor 1/2 in tensor norm; a normalized mixed product loses 1/\sqrt2; the remaining products retain norm one. For helicity zero, represent the commuting real tensors by Hermitian m\times m matrices. Write their final row and column as a vector v and scalar a, with upper block H_0 and \operatorname{tr}H_0=-a.
