The full and restricted squared spatial norms are respectively 2\|H_0\|^2+4\|v\|^2+2|a|^2, \qquad 2\|H_0\|^2+2\|v\|^2+|a|^2. \tag{6} Split H_0 into its traceless part and -aI/(m-1). These orthogonal parts give the final three rows. Complexification preserves the same singular values for complex forcing amplitudes. In particular, for six dimensions restricted to five, \boxed{\|\mathcal Rc\|\ge\frac12\|c\| \quad\text{on each nonzero helicity subspace},} \tag{7} and the zero-helicity lower bound is 1/\sqrt2. Every individual helicity therefore retains a nonzero full five-dimensional moment. This is a geometric norm bound, not a lower bound on a physical neutrino interaction probability. The mode's radial source magnitude, the target's allowed preparations, its output map and flux normalization remain essential. In particular, the output here is all symmetric five-dimensional moments, not the physical photon channel. The full Dirac modes realize these helicities The spatial Dirac shape calculation gives radial source vectors u_\lambda,u_{-\lambda} and the complete ordinary/conjugate fluctuation matrix \mathcal B_\lambda= \begin{pmatrix} L+g_0u_\lambda u_\lambda^T&g_0u_\lambda u_{-\lambda}^T\\ -g_0u_{-\lambda}u_\lambda^T&-L-g_0u_{-\lambda}u_{-\lambda}^T \end{pmatrix}. \tag{8} An eigenvector (p,q) has moment amplitude h=u_\lambda^Tp+u_{-\lambda}^Tq. When h\ne0, its moment pattern has helicity \lambda. Independently, its frequency obeys 1-g_0\chi_{0,\lambda}(\omega)=0, \quad \chi_{0,\lambda}(z) =u_\lambda^T(z-L)^{-1}u_\lambda +u_{-\lambda}^T(-z-L)^{-1}u_{-\lambda}. \tag{9} The diagnostic solves (8) and checks (9), retaining both signs of the radial Dirac spectrum. With one common g_0=6.5 and bare scalar coefficient m_0=0.5, the first active six-dimensional shape frequencies are approximately: helicity first active frequency second active frequency -1 1.414313 2.402246 0 1.263426 1.673915 +1 1.216080 1.820918 The bound background frequency is 3.091416 in these model units. Radial refinement and the independent resolvent condition agree. These are shape excitations of the declared scalar model, not observed particle masses or a complete stability calculation. The analogous five-dimensional calculation uses the same g_0 and retains its additional half-helicities. The slow applied frequencies used in the earlier opening example are below these active shape frequencies. They should not be assigned to a free particle merely because the applied response is well defined there. Frequency opening describes cancellation between visible components Decompose a specified force as f=\sum_\lambda f_\lambda. Then \mathcal R\chi(z)f =\sum_\lambda\chi_\lambda(z)\mathcal Rf_\lambda. \tag{10} At z=0, the odd function B vanishes, so all \chi_\lambda(0) are equal. A force with \sum_\lambda\mathcal Rf_\lambda=0 is therefore statically hidden even though its individual components remain visible. As frequency changes, their different responses can spoil that cancellation. This is the mechanism behind linear or quadratic opening in Persistent spatial shape barriers. An actual occupied particle could realize a coherent combination or a frequency-dependent spatial mode, but its field equation must establish that preparation. A low bound frequency alone does not choose the cancelling combination. Source frequencies also explains why the frequency driving that combination must be derived from its actual spatial source. Verification incoming_shape_mode_checks.py compares singular values with independent coordinate tensors, including explicit tensors attaining the lower bounds at depths four, six and ten. Common rotations transform the circulation and inclusion together. Full ordinary/conjugate Dirac eigenvectors and independent radial resolvents verify the active modes at two radial resolutions and a common interaction coefficient. Independent coupled block equations check (2) with both objects responding, and explicitly distinguish an incident moment from an applied force. All checks remain active under Python optimization. Related Dynamical opening of spatial shape channels — supplies the forced response which (2) specializes. Persistent spatial shape barriers — supplies the complete fixed-force frequency classification. Polarized Dirac shape response — supplies the actual spatial fluctuation operators and their polarization weights. Source frequencies in spatial coupling — supplies the temporal interpretation needed for a particle application.

title: Isotropic polarization comparison
summary: Uniform five-dimensional null-axis and six-dimensional complex-structure tensors have identical photon-plane overlap distributions under an explicitly isotropic preparation.
text: Summary: Uniform five-dimensional null-axis and six-dimensional complex-structure tensors have identical photon-plane overlap distributions under an explicitly isotropic preparation. The preparation is part of the model Use the two-plane diagnostic from photon plane coupling: C_d=\|P_EJ_dk\|^2, \qquad |k|=1,\qquad E\subset k^\perp,\qquad \dim E=2. \tag{1} The real skew tensors are the fixed, normalized candidates already used in the dimensional magnetic kernel: J_6^2=-I_6, \qquad J_5^2=-I_5+nn^T,\qquad |n|=1. \tag{2} Choose k uniformly on the sphere in each containing spatial space. Conditional on k, choose E uniformly among two-planes in k^\perp. This is a mathematical ensemble of relative preparations. It does not follow from nesting, transversality, or the particle's depth. An actual observer, binding geometry, or preparation may restrict this ensemble. Both objects are polarized in each preparation. Fixing J_d chooses the target's frame; it does not replace its polarization by an average. Independent isotropic rotations of both objects give the same relative ensemble. Correlations between their polarizations would change it. All coordinates remain ordinary spatial directions of one manifold. Equation (2) describes a specified uniform rotational response tensor; it does not establish the full shape or field solution of either particle. Six dimensions For every k, J_6k is a unit vector perpendicular to k. The space k^\perp has dimension five. Its squared projection onto a uniformly oriented two-plane has the beta law \boxed{C_6\sim\operatorname{Beta}\left(1,\frac32\right).} \tag{3} To obtain this law, rotate the plane to the first two axes and express a uniform direction as a vector of five independent standard Gaussians divided by its norm. The numerator is the sum of two squared Gaussians; the remaining three supply the complementary denominator. The gamma ratio derivation and normalization are given in full in isotropic projection fractions. Five dimensions First put A=|J_5k|^2=1-(n\cdot k)^2. The four directions perpendicular to n give A\sim\operatorname{Beta}(2,1/2). Conditional on k, the normalized direction J_5k/|J_5k| lies in a four-dimensional k^\perp. Its squared projection onto a uniform two-plane is B\sim\operatorname{Beta}(1,1),\qquad C_5=AB. \tag{4} The conditional law of B is the same for every non-null k, so A and B are independent. The exactly null directions have sphere measure zero and do not change this distribution. The density of A is f_A(a)=\frac34\,a(1-a)^{-1/2},\qquad 0<a<1. Since B is uniform, the product density is f_{C_5}(c) =\int_c^1\frac{f_A(a)}{a}\,da =\frac32\sqrt{1-c}. \tag{5} This is precisely the density in (3). Consequently \boxed{C_5\overset{\rm law}=C_6 \sim\operatorname{Beta}\left(1,\frac32\right).} \tag{6} The five-dimensional tensor's null axis lowers |J_5k|, while projection into the photon plane takes place in a smaller transverse space. Under this ensemble the two effects give the same complete distribution. Exact moments and small-overlap fraction For either depth, \mathbb E[C]=\frac25, \qquad \operatorname{Var}(C)=\frac{12}{175}, \qquad \Pr(C\leq t)=1-(1-t)^{3/2},\quad 0\leq t\leq1. \tag{7} More generally, \mathbb E[C^r]=(1)_r/(5/2)_r for r>-1. Near zero the fraction is 3t/2+O(t^2). For example, about 1.50\% of this ensemble has C\leq0.01, at both depths. This threshold refers to a normalized angular overlap, not a scattering probability. Quantity Depth five Depth six Mean full-transverse strength \mathbb E|J_dk|^2 \frac45 1 Mean fraction retained by the photon plane, conditional on k \frac12 \frac25 Mean sum over two photon polarizations \mathbb E C_d \frac25 \frac25 Mean unpolarized angular overlap \frac15 \frac15 The normalization in (2) fixes each nonzero rotational singular value to one. It does not fix the Frobenius norm to be equal: \|J_5\|^2=2 and \|J_6\|^2=3. Renormalizing the tensors or using action-derived physical coefficients changes the scale and must be declared. No physical charge or coupling coefficient is inferred from this comparison. A general adjacent-dimension identity Let J_{2m} be an orthogonal complex structure and let J_{2m-1} have one unit null axis and unit rotational singular values on its complement. Choose a p-plane E\subset k^\perp by the same ensemble, with 1\leq p\leq2m-2. Then both depths give \boxed{\|P_EJ_dk\|^2 \sim\operatorname{Beta}\left(\frac p2, \frac{2m-1-p}{2}\right),\qquad d=2m-1,2m.} \tag{8} For the odd depth the factors have beta parameters (m-1,1/2) and (p/2,m-1-p/2). To prove the product rule, take independent unit-scale gamma variables X,Y,Z with shapes p/2,m-1-p/2,1/2. The ratios X/(X+Y) and (X+Y)/(X+Y+Z) are independent; their product is X/(X+Y+Z), with exactly the beta parameters in (8). If the middle shape is zero, the first ratio is the constant one and the result follows directly. These tensor assumptions are not asserted for every spinor or every physical particle at the indicated depths. A definite photon polarization Let h=(\varepsilon_1^TJ_dk,\varepsilon_2^TJ_dk) in an orthonormal frame of the photon plane. The relative ensemble is invariant under rotating that frame, so h has a uniform angular direction conditional on |h|^2=C_d. Equation (6) therefore gives the same complete real two-component distribution of h at depths five and six. For any fixed normalized complex polarization c\in\mathbb C^2, the intensity I_c=|c^\dagger h|^2 consequently has the same distribution at both depths. This statement includes each object's definite polarization; it does not require averaging the photon over its two states. Its first two moments are \boxed{\mathbb E[I_c]=\frac15, \qquad \operatorname{Var}(I_c) =\frac{3+5|c^Tc|^2}{175}.} \tag{9} To derive the second moment, write I_c=h^TR_ch with R_c=\operatorname{Re}(cc^\dagger). The radial law and uniform angle give \mathbb E[h_i h_j]=\delta_{ij}/5 and \mathbb E[h_i h_j h_k h_l] =\frac{\delta_{ij}\delta_{kl}+\delta_{ik}\delta_{jl} +\delta_{il}\delta_{jk}}{35}. Since \operatorname{tr}R_c=1 and \operatorname{tr}(R_c^2)=(1+|c^Tc|^2)/2, equation (9) follows. For linear polarization, I_c\sim\operatorname{Beta}(1/2,2) and \Pr(I_c\leq t)=3\sqrt t/2-t^{3/2}/2. For circular polarization, I_c=C_d/2. Ellipticity changes the intensity distribution while preserving the equality between the two specified dimensional models. Interpretation This exact equality identifies which information a uniform isotropic tensor model retains. To obtain a distinctive five-dimensional response, the calculation needs additional derived spatial information: a restricted relative preparation, spatially varying response patterns, the allowed transition spectrum, or other terms of the same field's action. Those structures can be tested before any orientation average is taken. Verification polarization_coupling_checks.py checks beta product densities by independent quadrature, moments and CDFs, and separately samples orthonormal spatial frames. The probability law follows from the derivation; finite samples are a supplementary check. Related Photon plane coupling — defines the rank-two diagnostic and distinguishes a sum from an unpolarized average. Isotropic projection fractions — derives the underlying probability law from spatial Gaussian coordinates. Dimensional magnetic kernel — supplies the specific uniform five- and six-dimensional tensors.

title: Self-consistent nested Dirac pair
summary: A common scalar moment interaction determines both nested Dirac profiles and their relative deformation, with reciprocal source variation and no independent coupling coefficient for the pair.
text: Summary: A common scalar moment interaction determines both nested Dirac profiles and their relative deformation, with reciprocal source variation and no independent coupling coefficient for the pair. Let both spatial profiles respond to one interaction The single-profile calculation derives a scalar confining source from the full spatial Dirac field. Here the same interaction determines two profiles on nested spatial sectors. The higher field changes the lower source and the lower field changes the higher source; neither profile is held fixed during self-consistency. Take Q_p\subset Q_{p+q} and local flat coordinates x\in\mathbb R^p, y\in\mathbb R^q in the containing sector. The distinction between x and y is relative to this particular lower partner. All p+q directions are ordinary, equivalent kinds of macroscopic spatial direction. For a six-dimensional field with a five-dimensional partner, this is a description of their nesting, not an inherent division of the six-dimensional particle's space. Adopt orthogonal projected channels of the same field \Psi_\infty, with the appropriate tangential Dirac kinetic terms, specified spatial measures and separately fixed unit norms. These are explicit assumptions of a projected scalar model. Nested reciprocity describes the required measures and inclusion maps; a probability-normalized extension over an infinite fiber cannot silently be replaced by a constant of unit amplitude. No additional interaction particle is introduced. Specify the interaction below as a function of the projected channel densities. A coherent unprojected superposition also requires the transition-density terms of its full source. Integrated kinetic orthogonality alone does not remove those pointwise scalar cross terms. Connecting the projected model to that coherent field requires the corresponding source projection. The calculation establishes stationary solutions of this projected model. It does not identify them as the actual electron orbit, a neutrino profile, or a stable two-particle bound state. The common energy fixes both source matrices Let M_p and M_{p+q} be separately centered scalar moments \int \xi\xi^T\Phi^\dagger\beta\Phi on their respective sectors. Use the isometric spatial inclusion I:\mathbb R^p\to\mathbb R^{p+q} and define the containing-space source matrix S=IM_pI^T+M_{p+q}. \tag{1} The common scalar moment energy is \boxed{\mathcal E =T_p+T_{p+q}+m_pQ_p+m_{p+q}Q_{p+q} +\frac{g_0}{2}\operatorname{tr}S^2,\qquad g_0>0.} \tag{2} Here T_d=\langle\Phi_d,-i\alpha\cdot\nabla\Phi_d\rangle and Q_d=\int\Phi_d^\dagger\beta\Phi_d is a scalar integral, not an electric charge. Expanding (2) gives both self terms and g_0\operatorname{tr}(M_pI^TM_{p+q}I) as the cross term. There is one coefficient g_0 for all three terms. The projected bilocal variation then gives scalar source matrices A_p=g_0I^TSI,\qquad A_{p+q}=g_0S. \tag{3} The higher-to-lower source is the restriction of the common matrix. The lower-to-higher source is its reciprocal inclusion. The spatial matrices and both field profiles must be varied together. A closed stationary symmetry class Consider real profiles whose scalar moments have the form M_p=t_pI_p,\qquad M_{p+q}=\begin{pmatrix}t_xI_p&0\\0&t_yI_q\end{pmatrix}. \tag{4} Equations (1)–(3) imply \boxed{a=g_0(t_p+t_x),\qquad b=g_0t_y.} \tag{5} The lower Dirac operator has scalar mass m_p+a|x|^2; the higher one has scalar mass m_{p+q}+a|x|^2+b|y|^2. In particular, the coefficient along every shared spatial direction is the same for both fields. The higher field may acquire a different spatial width relative to its lower partner without assigning its directions different physical kinds. This is a stationary symmetry class. Arbitrary complex perturbations can generate additional mixed spatial moments, so a stability calculation must include those responses rather than assuming that (4) closes all time-dependent motions. Two-frequency fields in a readjusted nested pair extends the real stationary profiles to exact opposite-frequency components in both channels. Their currents can oscillate with independent clocks while both scalar sources retain the same self-consistency equations. Keep the full anisotropic Dirac field The higher profile requires more than the two radial functions of a central field. Let r=|x|, s=|y|, choose a unit rest polarization w with \beta w=w, and put C_x=\alpha(\widehat x), C_y=\alpha(\widehat y). They obey C_x^2=C_y^2=I and C_xC_y=-C_yC_x. An angularly normalized full spatial field is \boxed{\Phi_{p+q}(x,y)= \frac{F_{00}w+iF_{10}C_xw+iF_{01}C_yw+F_{11}C_xC_yw} {\sqrt{\Omega_{p-1}\Omega_{q-1}}},} \tag{6} with real functions F_{ab}(r,s). For q=1, the second angular integration is the two signs of the one existing spatial coordinate. It does not create a further space. The 00 and 11 components have positive \beta sign; the 10 and 01 components have negative sign. The scalar density is therefore \sigma=\frac{F_{00}^2+F_{11}^2-F_{10}^2-F_{01}^2} {\Omega_{p-1}\Omega_{q-1}}. \tag{7} This identity holds pointwise for every normalized w. Cross terms with opposite \beta signs vanish, and the remaining cross Clifford product C_xC_y is anti-Hermitian, so its expectation contributes no real scalar term for these real profiles. The norm has the same expression with all four squares positive. Consequently pt_x=\int r^2\sigma\,dx\,dy,\qquad qt_y=\int s^2\sigma\,dx\,dy. \tag{8} This stationary scalar source remains degenerate in the rest polarization w. Both objects can be polarized, but this term by itself does not prefer a particular neutral rotation weight. Their response to a non-isotropic spatial source still retains polarization, as in Dirac shape response. A reproducible product radial operator For each radial coordinate use the normalized even and odd-angular Laguerre functions in the single-profile note. Let K_p,K_q represent the corresponding upper-to-lower radial derivatives, and let R_p^{(0)},R_p^{(1)},R_q^{(0)},R_q^{(1)} represent multiplication by the squared radii in those bases. The product basis is ordered 00,10,01,11. Define X=K_p\otimes I,\qquad Y=I\otimes K_q, D_{ab}=(-1)^{a+b} \left[mI+a_{\rm s}R_p^{(a)}\otimes I +b_{\rm s}I\otimes R_q^{(b)}\right], \tag{9} where a_{\rm s},b_{\rm s} denote the physical coefficients called a,b in (5), to distinguish them from the component indices. Direct spatial differentiation of (6) gives \boxed{H= \begin{pmatrix} D_{00}&X^T&Y^T&0\\ X&D_{10}&0&Y^T\\ Y&0&D_{01}&-X^T\\ 0&Y&-X&D_{11} \end{pmatrix}.} \tag{10} The minus signs follow from anticommuting C_x and C_y. Removing F_{11} changes the anisotropic Dirac equation. In the isotropic limit a=b, the central positive branch has F_{11}=0 and reproduces the ordinary radial solution in p+q dimensions. Away from that limit the mixed upper component is generally nonzero. A dimensionless self-consistency equation For m_p=m_{p+q}=0, write \rho=b/a. At shared scale a=1, compute the lower per-axis scalar moment t_p and the higher moments t_x(\rho),t_y(\rho) from their full Dirac profiles. Equations (5) reduce to \boxed{\rho=\frac{t_y(\rho)}{t_p+t_x(\rho)},\qquad a=\left[g_0\big(t_p+t_x(\rho)\big)\right]^{3/5}.} \tag{11} The first equation determines the relative deformation without a pair coefficient. The second determines the common spatial scale for any specified g_0. Both frequencies scale as a^{1/3} and all scalar second moments as a^{-2/3}. For p=5, q=1, the converged branch at a=1 gives quantity value lower frequency E_5 2.444444940 higher frequency E_6 2.710963578 relative source coefficient b/a 0.628369372 common g_0 at a=1 3.139333022 lower total scalar moment 5t_p 0.814814980 higher shared scalar moment 5t_x 0.777880017 higher remaining scalar moment t_y 0.200160151 For example g_0(0.814814980+0.777880017)/5=1 and g_0(0.200160151)=0.628369372, checking both source equations with the same coefficient. The higher mixed upper component has norm fraction about 7.25694\times10^{-5} and is retained throughout the calculation. These numbers describe the declared stationary scalar model. They are not a particle mass fit or an empirical neutrino coupling prediction. Energy and reciprocal variation provide independent checks For each massless partner, a norm-preserving spatial dilation gives its kinetic expectation as twice its scalar source expectation. Summing the stationary equations yields E_p+E_{p+q}=6\mathcal E_{\rm int},\qquad \boxed{\mathcal E=\frac56(E_p+E_{p+q}).} \tag{12} The total energy at the displayed scale is approximately 4.296173765. The full Dirac energy is not globally bounded below, so this identity does not establish a global ground state or nonlinear stability. For independent variations of both partner fields, their cross Hessian is \delta_p\delta_{p+q}\mathcal E =g_0\operatorname{tr} \left(I\delta M_pI^T\delta M_{p+q}\right). \tag{13} The same bilinear is obtained by differentiating either source in (3). It is the explicit reciprocal response of the two solved profiles. The general tensor form remains valid when their orientations and shape perturbations are restored; the stationary table uses the symmetry (4). Normal propagation retains the deformed scalar source The higher field's four real profiles also supply the normal frame needed by Reciprocal scalar envelopes. Choose an ordinary free coordinate in a sector containing the whole pair, with Clifford matrix \alpha_z anticommuting with the bound matrices and \beta. It is an existing direction of the same physical manifold. Write the matrix in the numerator of (6) as P=F_{00}I+iF_{10}C_x+iF_{01}C_y+F_{11}C_xC_y. The two anticommuting spatial matrices give the exact quaternion identity \boxed{P^\dagger P= (F_{00}^2+F_{10}^2+F_{01}^2+F_{11}^2)I.} \tag{14} Since \beta\alpha_z commutes with both C_x and C_y, the mixed scalar normal-partner block vanishes. For an orthonormal rest-polarization matrix V with \beta V=V, put F=PV/\sqrt{\Omega_{p-1}\Omega_{q-1}} and W=(F,\alpha_zF). Then \boxed{W(x,y)^\dagger\beta W(x,y) =\sigma(x,y)(\sigma_3\otimes I),} \tag{15} where \sigma is (7). This identity holds for arbitrary complex normal amplitudes and every selected rest polarization. Thus their scalar density multiplies the same deformed spatial source, rather than introducing unaccounted interference terms. Angular integration removes the mixed normal current. The two partner families have the canonical spatial norm. When any real profile parameter s varies, the angular average of the projected derivative contains only the radial norm derivative: \int W^\dagger\partial_sW\,dx\,dy=0 \tag{16} for a normalized profile family. This justifies the first-order kinetic normalization used in the two-envelope reduction. An exact uniform normal boost preserves the scalar density pointwise, as in Normal Dirac propagation. Boosting the deformed partner therefore leaves both reciprocal scalar source matrices unchanged for a uniform pair. Varying envelope densities can still drive omitted spatial profiles through the residual described in the scalar envelope calculation; (16) does not establish full dynamical closure. Several specified values of the one common coefficient test the scaling in (11). Reports have timestamped filenames and all conditions remain active under Python optimization. title: Nested moment coupling
summary: The dot-square kernel on centered isotropic nested subspaces gives a minimum-depth Gram matrix of full rank, despite factorized bare coefficients.
text: Summary: The dot-square kernel on centered isotropic nested subspaces gives a minimum-depth Gram matrix of full rank, despite factorized bare coefficients. Applying the specified quadratic kernel This calculation applies the existing cross-sector moment kernel to an arbitrary finite nested chain. It is a flat spatial benchmark, or a tangent-chart calculation with the flat kernel explicitly adopted. It does not replace the actual curved sector geometry or derive its global interaction law. Use a finite containing spatial space \mathbb R^D, with isometric embeddings E_d:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^D whose images are nested. Set P_d=E_dE_d^{\mathsf T}. All these directions are ordinary spatial directions in the same containing manifold; the projectors express relations between subspaces, not an inherent split in any particle. Embedding a sector's moment tensor in this way is a coordinate identification inside the kernel. It does not assign a delta-sheet density to the particle or remove the lower-sector field's specified cylindrical continuation through the containing directions. Let \rho_d be a centered, normalized density with finite second moment M_d=\int xx^{\mathsf T}\rho_d(x)\,dx. Use the real positive bare factorization g_{de}=v_dv_e, v_d>0, and the kernel K_{de}(x,y)=v_dv_e\left(x^{\mathsf T}E_d^{\mathsf T}E_e y\right)^2. The common origin, embeddings, and profiles are fixed in this calculation. Allowing their motion requires the corresponding variations. Pairwise integration, using (u^{\mathsf T}w)^2=\operatorname{tr}(uu^{\mathsf T}ww^{\mathsf T}), gives U_{de}=v_dv_e\operatorname{tr} \left(E_dM_dE_d^{\mathsf T}E_eM_eE_e^{\mathsf T}\right). \tag{1} This result depends only on the second moments, so it holds for every centered profile satisfying the stated moment condition. Isotropic sectors give a minimum-depth matrix Suppose each sector is isotropic in its own ordinary spatial directions: M_d=s_dI_d, s_d>0. Write u_d=v_ds_d. Nesting implies P_dP_e=P_{\min(d,e)},\qquad \operatorname{tr}(P_dP_e)=\min(d,e). Consequently \boxed{U_{de}=u_du_e\,A_{de},\qquad A_{de}=\min(d,e).} \tag{2} For amplitudes J_d multiplying these fixed density profiles, the positive quadratic energy is U(J)=\frac12\sum_{d,e}J_d u_d A_{de}u_e J_e =\frac12\left\|\sum_d u_dJ_dP_d\right\|_{\rm F}^2. \tag{3} It has symmetric Hessian G_{de}=u_du_e\min(d,e) and source response \Sigma_d=u_d\sum_e u_e\min(d,e)J_e. \tag{4} The sum in (4) retains the external depth d. In general it cannot be replaced by one common scalar C in \Sigma_d=u_dC. This is a concrete operator-level test of factorization in the written kernel. It does not infer masses from its Hessian. Exact rank, determinant, and pair correlation Order distinct depths 0<d_1<\cdots<d_N\le D, set d_0=0, and define \Delta_i=d_i-d_{i-1}>0. For the lower triangular matrix T_{ij}=1 if j\le i, and zero otherwise, A=T\,\operatorname{diag}(\Delta_1,\ldots,\Delta_N)\,T^{\mathsf T}. \tag{5} Indeed, the (i,j) entry is the sum of the increments through \min(i,j), namely \min(d_i,d_j). Since T is invertible, A>0,\qquad \operatorname{rank}A=N,\qquad \det A=\prod_{i=1}^N\Delta_i. \tag{6} For the working distinct depths (2,3,4,5,6,10), the rank is six and the determinant is 2\cdot1\cdot1\cdot1\cdot1\cdot4=8. The corresponding G is also full rank when all u_d\ne0. Several profiles with the same depth and identical isotropic moments produce proportional columns instead; the theorem counts distinct projectors, not automatically distinct particles. All the unknown positive u_d cancel from the pair correlation: \boxed{ \frac{G_{de}}{\sqrt{G_{dd}G_{ee}}} =\frac{\min(d,e)}{\sqrt{de}} =\sqrt{\frac{\min(d,e)}{\max(d,e)}}.} \tag{7} Depth pair Normalized correlation 3,4 \sqrt{3/4} 3,5 \sqrt{3/5} 4,5 \sqrt{4/5} 5,6 \sqrt{5/6} 6,10 \sqrt{3/5} Thus distinct depths do not saturate a rank-one response even when their bare coefficients satisfy g_{de}^2=g_{dd}g_{ee}. The squared correlation for depths three and four is 3/4, not one, in this full moment model. These correlations describe the specified scalar kernel; they are not electric-charge ratios, scattering probabilities, or measured coupling constants. Depth five has a nonzero row and no exceptional decoupling. Electric neutrality and low weak-interaction rates therefore cannot be obtained from this positive scalar moment matrix alone. The appropriate neutrino control needs derived channel maps. Which projection would give rank one The decomposition into the trace and traceless part in the containing space is P_d=\frac{d}{D}I_D+\widetilde P_d,\qquad \operatorname{tr}\widetilde P_d=0. Orthogonality in the Frobenius inner product gives A_{de}=\frac{de}{D} +\operatorname{tr}(\widetilde P_d\widetilde P_e),\qquad \operatorname{tr}(\widetilde P_d\widetilde P_e)=\min(d,e)-\frac{de}{D}. \tag{8} The first term has rank one. The second is a positive semidefinite Gram matrix and is generally nonzero. If the largest retained depth is D, its last row is zero and it has rank N-1: the remaining traceless projectors are independent, as follows from their successive spatial shells. Keeping only the trace response would produce G^{\rm trace}_{de}=u_du_e de/D, with one common response. This is a definite additional projection of the interaction. It is not implied by each profile being isotropic on its own sector, because P_d is not isotropic on the entire containing space when d<D. Equation (8) identifies the extra physical condition a scalar common-anchor mechanism would need in this model: the actual interaction must select the trace channel, or otherwise make the normalized response profiles proportional. It must also explain what happens to the traceless response, preserve the kinetic normalization, and establish the relation to the complete occupied mass operator. Verification and related generalized_coupling_checks.py computes the double profile integral by exact second-moment cubature after arbitrary common spatial rotations, checks the Hessian by finite differences, verifies (5)–(8), and compares all six depth rows. No empirical parameters are fitted. Generalized sector coupling — the complete coupling construction and its physical scope. Common field response — gives the general Gram and proportional-profile criterion; its eliminated scalar energy has a different sign from (3). Rank-one common anchor — the source-cancellation proposal to which this moment calculation supplies an explicit test.

title: Two-frequency fields in a readjusted nested pair

text:
Summary: Both deformed nested Dirac profiles admit exact opposite-frequency components with independent polarizations, and the containing field can keep the lower field confined at finite frequency when its own mean scalar source vanishes. Use the source of both occupied fields The readjusted nested pair describes two projected channels of the one field on Q_p\subset Q_D, with D=p+q. Those shared directions are equivalent in physical kind to its other q directions; their grouping is relative to this pair. Its spatial algebra is stronger than a radial-density approximation, because it retains all four components of the anisotropic higher field. Use the projected channel source and kinetic measures of the nested-pair model. With separately centered signed scalar moments, its common energy contains \mathcal E_{m int}= rac{g_0}{2}\operatorname{tr}S^2, \qquad S=IM_aI^T+M_b,\qquad A_a=g_0I^TSI,\quad A_b=g_0S. 	ag{1} Here I is the physical spatial inclusion. The fields and the normal partner used below introduce no additional physical manifold or interaction particle. The Clifford relations give  oxed{P^\dagger P=\left(\sum_{a,b}F_{ab}^2ight)I, \qquad [P, eta Y]=0.} 	ag{3} To check the first identity, terms linear in C_x,C_z,C_xC_z cancel between the two products because the functions are real and C_xC_z=-C_zC_x. The diagonal scalar density is the same for every normalized w: \sigma_0= rac{F_{00}^2+F_{11}^2-F_{10}^2-F_{01}^2} {\Omega_{p-1}\Omega_{q-1}}. 	ag{5} These are pointwise spatial identities. A central lower field has the corresponding two-component identities. They require the stated real stationary profile class; arbitrary complex axial motion is not being assumed to stay within it. Define  oxed{\Psi_i(t)=u_i\phi_{i1}e^{-iM_it} +v_iY\phi_{i2}e^{iM_it},\qquad |u_i|^2+|v_i|^2=1, \quad s_i=|u_i|^2-|v_i|^2.} 	ag{6} Because \{H_i,Y\}=0, the normal partner has eigenfrequency -M_i. Its scalar density has the opposite sign, and (4) removes its interference with the positive component. Therefore \Psi_i^\dagger eta\Psi_i=s_i\sigma_{i0}, \qquad \int\Psi_i^\dagger\Psi_i=1. 	ag{7} Solve both profiles using these same weights. If t_a is the lower scalar second moment per axis, and t_x,t_z are the higher per-axis moments, their common source is  oxed{A=g_0(s_at_a+s_bt_x),\qquad B=g_0s_bt_z.} 	ag{8} Each field in (6) solves its complete nonlinear projected channel equation with the unchanging source (8), uniformly in the selected normal coordinate. Its number currents can still oscillate. In particular, \int j_{Y,i}\,dx_i =2\operatorname{Re}\left[  ar u_i v_i\langle w_{i1},w_{i2}angle e^{2iM_it}ight]. 	ag{9} Both occupied polarizations and their relative phase remain visible in this output. Equation (9) is a number current of the specified field; its physical photon projection is not assigned here. In general M_a
e M_b. The full linearized pair has frequencies 2M_a and 2M_b in its coefficients, so it need not have a single period. The complete source response must then retain both frequency indices and the reciprocal cross curvature. The exact background construction alone does not establish stability. Reciprocal response with two spatial clocks derives the full pair equation, including deformation-induced scalar-center sidebands and both independent background frequencies. The containing source changes the low-frequency limit Set both bare scalar coefficients to zero and keep g_0 fixed. Write \epsilon_d and T_d for the frequency and total signed second moment of the unit-normalized central profile with quadratic coefficient one. Spatial dilation gives M_d(A)=\epsilon_d A^{1/3},\qquad T_d(A)=T_d A^{-2/3},\qquad T_d= rac{\epsilon_d}{3}. 	ag{10} For an isolated lower field, self-consistency gives M_a\propto s_a^{1/5} as s_a	o0. In the pair, hold s_b>0 and instead let s_a	o0. The higher source becomes isotropic over all its D directions, and (8) has the endpoint  oxed{A_0=B_0= \left( rac{g_0s_bT_D}{D}ight)^{3/5}>0.} 	ag{11} The lower channel still feels this higher source. Its limiting frequency and that of the containing field are  oxed{M_{a,0}=\epsilon_p A_0^{1/3}>0,\qquad M_{b,0}=\epsilon_D A_0^{1/3}.} 	ag{12} As s_a\downarrow0, the positive- and negative-frequency weights become equal. The lower mean scalar density tends to zero while its total number norm stays one. The limiting profile remains localized in the containing potential and retains the finite clock in (12). e0 to define X_a=\int x\sigma_a/Q_a. At exactly zero balance that center is undefined. A limiting profile in a prescribed centered potential therefore does not by itself define a differentiable nonlinear field equation at s_a=0. No such endpoint evolution is asserted here. Independent solves at one common g_0=6.5 and s_b=0.3 give: nested depths p\subset D M_a at s_a=0.03 M_a at s_a=0.003 limiting M_{a,0} limiting M_{b,0} 3\subset4 1.400622 1.374623 1.371607 1.683475 5\subset6 1.961723 1.926351 1.922253 2.182830 5\subset10 1.907913 1.866965 1.862173 3.006941 6\subset10 2.163510 2.119713 2.114605 3.006941 These are frequencies of the declared model, not measured particle masses. They show why an isolated-field frequency scaling cannot be applied unchanged after the containing field has supplied part of the confinement. If both balances scale together, the common dilation law still gives M_i\mapsto c^{1/5}M_i. A vanishing mean source retains reciprocal derivative coupling On the stationary family, the full energy and its derivatives are U= rac56(s_aM_a+s_bM_b),\qquad \partial_{s_i}U=M_i,\qquad G_{ij}=\partial_{s_j}M_i=G_{ji}. 	ag{13} The readjusted scalar response derives these identities by varying both complete profiles. title: Rotations of nested spatial sectors
summary: A rotation preserving every fixed member of the nested spatial chain has a restricted block structure, while rotating the whole chain requires the moving embeddings in the projected dynamics.
text: Summary: A rotation preserving every fixed member of the nested spatial chain has a restricted block structure, while rotating the whole chain requires the moving embeddings in the projected dynamics. The same spatial chain must support the interaction Local geometric coupling operators have to fit together on the one nested manifold. Consider a common point with a nested chain of tangent spaces V_{d_1}\subset V_{d_2}\subset\cdots\subset V_{d_N}, \qquad d_1<\cdots<d_N=D. \tag{1} All directions are ordinary macroscopic spatial directions. The orthogonal differences between these spaces record their relation to other sectors; they give no particle an inherent division into different kinds of space. The following theorem concerns rotations of this finite tangent flag. It does not classify all interactions, differential operators, curved global embeddings, or dynamical sector projectors of the master field. Rotations preserving every fixed member Let P_r be the orthogonal projector onto V_{d_r} and K^T=-K a real spatial rotation generator. Preservation of V_{d_r} is equivalent to (I-P_r)KP_r=0. Skew symmetry also annihilates its transpose block, so equivalently [K,P_r]=0. \tag{2} Set P_0=0 and E_r=P_r-P_{r-1}. Nesting makes these mutually orthogonal projectors. If (2) holds for every r, K commutes with every E_r and hence has precisely the form \boxed{K=\bigoplus_{r=1}^N K_r,\qquad K_r\in\mathfrak{so}(d_r-d_{r-1}).} \tag{3} Conversely every such block diagonal generator preserves the flag. Therefore the Lie algebra dimension is \sum_{r=1}^N\frac{(d_r-d_{r-1})(d_r-d_{r-1}-1)}2. \tag{4} For the working depths (2,3,4,5,6,10), the increments are (2,1,1,1,1,4). The algebra is \mathfrak{so}(2)\oplus\mathfrak{so}(4), \qquad \dim=1+6=7. \tag{5} At depths three through six, its only possible nonzero tangential rotation is the shared two-plane. The four-dimensional final block acts in directions outside V_6. This result depends on requiring all listed sectors to stay fixed under the same infinitesimal rotation. Consequence for a rotation-neutral construction Rotation-neutral spatial modes uses two equal rotation planes at depth five and three at depth six. In an adapted six-dimensional frame these are generated by K_5=J_{12}+J_{34},\qquad K_6=J_{12}+J_{34}+J_{56}, \tag{6} where J_{ab}=e_ae_b^T-e_be_a^T. The first generator moves the fixed three-dimensional member; the second also moves the five-dimensional one. For the complete equal-plane generator in an even containing depth, \|[K,P_r]\|_F^2= \begin{cases}0,&r\text{ even},\\2,&r\text{ odd},\end{cases} \tag{7} for the coordinate flag with the last incomplete plane crossing its boundary. The crossing term cannot be discarded while calling (6) the restriction of a rotation that fixes every member of the chain. Indeed, under the fixed-flag assumption a nonzero five-dimensional spin generator has only one plane: Q_5=\kappa H_{12}/2. Since H_{12}^2=I, it has no neutral spinor subspace. Including the ordinary single-valued orbital functions does not produce a neutral mode of this one-plane rotation: the orbital weights are integers and the spin weights are half integers. Twists or further field structure change that premise. This locates a definite requirement for the two-plane cancellation: it must come from dynamics that move the nested embeddings, a derived effective operator, or other specified geometric structure beyond (3). Moving the entire chain preserves nesting Let R(t) be an orthogonal spatial motion with \dot R=K(t)R, and transport every sector together: P_r(t)=R(t)P_r(0)R(t)^T, \qquad \dot P_r=[K,P_r]. \tag{8} Then P_r(t)P_s(t)=P_r(t) for r\leq s, and every rank is unchanged. Thus the full chain can rotate while remaining nested. Preserving the nesting does not require preserving each member's original position. For u(t)\in\operatorname{ran}P_r(t), differentiate P_ru=u: (I-P_r)\dot u=\dot P_ru=(I-P_r)Ku. \tag{9} This normal component describes motion of the embedding in the same physical space. It is not an additional spatial dimension or a separate interaction particle. Omitting it freezes part of the proposed geometry. The induced mode equation retains the moving basis Spatial tangent projectors and projectors on field amplitudes are different objects. Once a physical field-mode inclusion has been derived, write it as an isometry I(t) with I^\dagger I=I_{\rm amp}, where I_{\rm amp} is the amplitude-space identity. Decompose the one field into \Psi=I(t)a+h,\qquad I^\dagger h=0, \qquad i\dot\Psi=H(t)\Psi. Differentiating a=I^\dagger\Psi gives the exact projected row \boxed{i\dot a= \left(I^\dagger HI-iI^\dagger\dot I\right)a +I^\dagger Hh+i\dot I^\dagger h.} \tag{10} The connection term -iI^\dagger\dot I is Hermitian. The last term records motion relative to the omitted modes. Neither can be suppressed solely because h was initially zero. The complement equation must preserve that condition, or its response must be retained or eliminated consistently. For a complete unitary basis U(t), the corresponding generator is U^\dagger HU-iU^\dagger\dot U. A change of description transforms probes as well; it does not create a new physical motion or coupling by itself. Use in generalized coupling The fixed-chain result provides a precise check on proposed common rotation generators. The moving-chain result supplies a constructive alternative when the higher spatial pattern rotates the nested geometry. Equation (10) then identifies the additional terms that a downward source calculation must include. Neither result derives a preferred embedding motion, electromagnetic charge, or the occupied five-dimensional neutral states. They keep the proposed cancellation compatible with the single nested chain of spatial submanifolds while making its next dynamical calculation explicit. Verification spatial_coupling_mechanism_checks.py solves all fixed-flag commutator constraints as a linear system, obtains the seven-dimensional stabilizer, checks its restrictions at every depth, and tests moving-projector ranks and derivatives. The projected field equation is also checked against direct evolution and basis differentiation. Related Rotation-neutral spatial modes — supplies the equal-plane cancellation whose compatibility is tested here. Descending photon source — gives the fixed-mode projected row extended by (10). Nested sector dynamics — states the spatial lift and intertwining conditions needed for a closed reduced evolution.

title: Nested sector reciprocity
summary: Compatible spatial marginals and their dual pullbacks give reciprocal coupling equations on arbitrary nested sectors, with exact composition along a chain.
text:
Summary: Compatible spatial marginals and their dual pullbacks give reciprocal coupling equations on arbitrary nested sectors, with exact composition along a chain. Spatial maps and measures All sectors are ordinary macroscopic spatial submanifolds in one nested chain within the infinite physical manifold. The calculation uses any finite pair Q_a\subset Q_b, not a particular particle. Inclusion alone supplies neither a global product nor a retraction. Assume a specified map r_{ba}:Q_b	o Q_a that agrees with the inclusion where required, or work in a product neighborhood on which such a map exists. Specify measures through a disintegration d\mu_b(x,y)=d\mu_a(x)\,d
u_x(y). The fibre measure d
u_x includes the geometric Jacobian. It is not automatically a probability measure. For integrable real scalar sources j_b, define the marginal and the pullback of a scalar test field f_a: (R_{ba}j_b)(x)=\int_{r_{ba}^{-1}(x)}j_b(x,y)\,d
u_x(y), \qquad (R_{ba}^{*}f_a)(x,y)=f_a(x). Fubini's theorem gives the duality identity \int_{Q_a}f_a R_{ba}j_b\,d\mu_a =\int_{Q_b}(R_{ba}^{*}f_a)j_b\,d\mu_b. 	ag{1} Here the star denotes the dual map in this integral pairing. On an infinite fibre, the pullback of a nonzero function need not be in L^2(Q_b). Equation (1) remains valid for an L^1 source and bounded test field; calling it a bounded Hilbert-space adjoint requires additional domain assumptions. On finite fibres with uniformly bounded volume, the corresponding L^2 maps are bounded. For spinor or tensor sources, first specify how their indices are transported to a common bundle and contracted. A bare integral of components in unrelated frames is not a covariant marginal. Those linear transport and polarization maps must be retained in R and its dual. One interaction, two reciprocal responses Let K_a be a fixed real spatial kernel on the shared sector: (K_a u)(x)=\int_{Q_a}K_a(x,x')u(x')\,d\mu_a(x'). Its transpose in the measure pairing has kernel K_a(x',x). Choose the sign and coefficient by writing the interaction energy U_{ab}=g\langle j_a,K_a R_{ba}j_bangle_a, \qquad S_{m int}=-\int U_{ab}\,dt. Vary the two sources independently while keeping the geometry and kernel fixed. The result is V_a= rac{\delta U_{ab}}{\delta j_a}=gK_a R_{ba}j_b, \qquad V_b= rac{\delta U_{ab}}{\delta j_b} =gR_{ba}^{*}K_a^{*}j_a. 	ag{2} Thus the upper-to-lower response is a marginal followed by the kernel. The reverse response is the transpose kernel followed by a cylindrical pullback. These maps generally have different domains and different matrix entries; reciprocity is their dual relation: \langle \delta j_a,gK_aR_{ba}\delta j_bangle_a =\langle gR_{ba}^{*}K_a^{*}\delta j_a,\delta j_bangle_b. 	ag{3} If a specified positive scalar model has j_d=|\psi_d|^2 and canonical time derivative, varying \psi_d^* gives i\partial_t\psi_a=(H_a+V_a)\psi_a,\qquad i\partial_t\psi_b=(H_b+V_b)\psi_b. Real V_d and self-adjoint H_d preserve each norm. For static geometry and kernels, the complete two-field Hamiltonian preserves total energy. This density coupling can exchange energy while preserving the number in each mode family. Particle-changing vertices are additional interaction structures. A Dirac scalar source  ar\psi\psi instead requires its own adjoint and projector variation, as derived in Projected bilocal variation. Composition through intermediate sectors For Q_a\subset Q_b\subset Q_c, assume compatible projections r_{ca}=r_{ba}\circ r_{cb} and their corresponding disintegrations. Iterated integration proves R_{ca}=R_{ba}R_{cb},\qquad R_{ca}^{*}=R_{cb}^{*}R_{ba}^{*}. 	ag{4} This is an exact consistency requirement for direct and staged spatial reduction. Polarization maps obey the same composition only if they intertwine compatibly; projecting out an intermediate component can discard a coupling that a direct map retains. Equation (4) does not multiply two interaction constants together. Reducing a source through an intermediate sector is not the same physical process as propagating through an intermediate dynamical mode. The latter includes that mode's propagator and allowed vertices. title: Spatial transport of a neutral doublet
summary: The two neutral polarizations of a balanced five-dimensional rotation carry a nonzero traceless geometric curvature when its physical null axis varies, with an exact spatial kinetic-energy decomposition.
text:
Summary: The two neutral polarizations of a balanced five-dimensional rotation carry a nonzero traceless geometric curvature when its physical null axis varies, with an exact spatial kinetic-energy decomposition. A neutral mode can respond to changing spatial geometry Rotation-neutral spatial modes identifies a two-component neutral subspace for the sum of two equal spatial rotation planes. This note derives how those modes respond when the rotation's physical null axis changes. Their geometric response is nonzero even though the balanced tangential rotation annihilates them. The axis is an ordinary spatial direction in a five-dimensional tangent space of the one infinite manifold. Its orientation is described by a unit vector n\in S^4. This sphere is a set of possible directions, not an additional physical space. When n=n(x), its variation occurs over actual spatial positions x; all derivatives below are pulled back to those positions. The two complex amplitudes describe polarization of the same field \Psi_\infty, not two extra spatial dimensions or mediator particles. The explicit kinetic calculations use a flat Euclidean spatial chart and ordinary derivatives. A curved sector requires its metric and spin connection in the same projection. This is a conditional projected-kinetic mechanism. It does not identify the resulting connection with the observed weak interaction or its trace with electric charge. The physical mode selection and electromagnetic current remain to be derived. The neutral projector is fixed by the physical null axis Use the five Hermitian Clifford matrices \gamma=(\sigma_1\otimes I,\sigma_2\otimes I, \sigma_3\otimes\sigma_1,\sigma_3\otimes\sigma_2, \sigma_3\otimes\sigma_3),\qquad \{\gamma_a,\gamma_b\}=2\delta_{ab}I_4. 	ag{1} For a pure normalized source polarization z, put n_a=z^\dagger\gamma_a z,\quad J_{ab}=z^\dagger(-i\gamma_a\gamma_b)z\ (a<b),\quad S=\sum_{a<b}J_{ab}(-i\gamma_a\gamma_b). 	ag{2} The five-dimensional source identities give |n|=1, J^2=-I+nn^T, S+n\cdot\gamma=4zz^\dagger-I, and \operatorname{spec}S=(2,0,0,-2). Relation to the first-order spatial Dirac operator Equation (12) starts from a positive spatial gradient energy. The master Dirac kinetic term is first order, so its projection requires a separate calculation. Rotation-neutral Dirac fields in physical space provides a complementary full-field construction. Its position-dependent lower component retains the omitted spin weights while orbital motion keeps the total spatial rotation exactly neutral. A controlled finite-gap spatial motion A solvable full four-component evolution tests the projection against its omitted modes. u tG},\qquad H(t)=\Delta R(t)S_0R(t)^\dagger,\qquad \Delta>0. 	ag{13a} The eigenvalues are (-2\Delta,0,0,2\Delta); this calculation assumes an initially occupied neutral band. u|, the moving spin frame returns as R(T)=-I, and the slow-limit neutral transport has holonomy -I. Virtual transitions also shift the accumulated neutral phases at finite speed; a small leakage probability alone does not bound that phase error. The circle illustrates that a curve can have nontrivial holonomy even though the pullback of a curvature two-form to a single curve vanishes. A global check on the neutral bundle For the convention (1), \gamma_1\gamma_2\gamma_3\gamma_4\gamma_5=-I. Expanding (3) gives the coordinate-free trace identity \operatorname{tr}(\mathcal F\wedge\mathcal F) =\operatorname{tr} ig(P(dP)^4 ig) = rac18\epsilon_{eabcd}n_e\, dn_a\wedge dn_b\wedge dn_c\wedge dn_d =3\,\mathrm{vol}_{S^4}. 	ag{14} Here the outward orientation is used, so \mathrm{vol}_{S^4}=\epsilon_{eabcd}n_e\,dn_a\wedge dn_b\wedge dn_c\wedge dn_d/4!. Since \operatorname{vol}(S^4)=8\pi^2/3, the anti-Hermitian Chern–Weil convention c_2=[\operatorname{tr}(\mathcal F\wedge\mathcal F) -\operatorname{tr}\mathcal F\wedge\operatorname{tr}\mathcal F]/(8\pi^2) yields \int_{S^4}c_2=1,\qquad \operatorname{tr}\mathcal F=0. 	ag{15} Reversing orientation or taking the complementary doublet changes the second Chern number's sign. Its nonzero magnitude confirms that the curvature cannot be removed by choosing another polarization basis. It does not require a physical orientation texture to cover the whole sphere. This Clifford-projector bundle is the mathematical structure commonly called a Yang monopole. An independent experimental realization in a controlled parameter space is described by Sugawa and colleagues. That realization supports the mathematical comparison; it is not evidence that the IDWT particle assignment or spatial coupling proposed here occurs in nature. The present interpretation uses orientations of an actual spatial axis, with the derivation supplied explicitly above. Dressed spatial source vertices derives the complete source and its normalization after eliminating those omitted components, including exact finite-frequency continuity identities. What this supplies to the coupling problem The same higher geometric source can now support two precise statements: its balanced tangential rotation annihilates the doublet, while spatial changes of its null axis induce nonzero, noncommuting transport within it. This provides an explicit example of neutrality in one geometric operation coexisting with another response, without inserting an arbitrary second matrix to manufacture that distinction. There are still essential physical selection questions. The zero doublet is the middle eigenspace of S, not its unique ground state. The scalar self-binding model admits neutral and nonneutral polarizations at the same energy. A physical constraint, isolated populated band or dynamical selection must therefore be derived before (12) closes the actual field problem. At finite gaps, omitted modes contribute corrections and possible transitions. The moving-mode equation retains their exact terms. Furthermore, the full six-dimensional source contains a mixed contribution acting nontrivially on this doublet. Its absence from a photon response cannot be assumed. The descending source projection must identify the physical current. Zero determinant curvature in (8) is not a proof of zero electric charge, and nonzero \mathfrak{su}(2) curvature is not a calculation of weak chirality, coupling strength or scattering rate. Those identifications require the same field action and the occupied spatial particle solutions. title: Neutrino channel control

Physical target The assigned neutrino sector has five ordinary spatial dimensions within the same nested physical manifold as the other sectors. Its rare interactions in ordinary matter provide an important control on a generalized coupling rule. IDWT uses direct dynamics of \Psi_\infty and has no mediator particles. That rule must retain the weak interactions through which active neutrinos are detected. The discovery of neutrino neutral-current scattering is a direct example: CERN's account of weak neutral currents. The target is channel-dependent: zero ordinary electric charge and no colour charge, with allowed weak interactions. Rare scattering is not equivalent to a vanishing weak vertex, and a small mass does not itself specify an interaction strength. The following matrix example is a benchmark for the projected rule, not a derivation of the physical electroweak representation from spatial depth. The neutrino's electric neutrality does not annihilate these other generators. These are the standard lepton representation matrices; the physical vertices also carry weak coupling constants, chirality, and the appropriate Lorentz structure. See PDG, Electroweak Model, §10.1. Spatial spin chirality in a higher-dimensional sector must not be silently identified with the observed spacetime weak chirality. The value y=-1/2 was selected here by the neutrality condition; it has not been predicted. A V2 application must derive the generator and occupied projector independently, then evaluate (1). The anomaly-free charge family shows explicitly why anomaly cancellation alone leaves additional freedom. For colour, a singlet requires every colour generator to annihilate the state, equivalently zero positive total quadratic Casimir. A zero mean colour vector is insufficient. See the colour singlet criterion. Likewise \langle Qangle=0 alone can describe a charged superposition; the stronger QP_
u=0 identifies a retained neutral subspace. This is a test of the ordinary electric-charge vertex. Neutrality alone does not exclude every higher-order electromagnetic response operator, such as a permitted transition moment. Such terms need a separate action and symmetry analysis. Suppression by a field-response scale A second distinction is between an absent interaction term and a small response of the same field. Suppose a specified reduction of its static linearized equations yields a positive spatial operator -\Delta+\Lambda^2, with \Lambda>0 an inverse-length response scale. For fixed source coefficients h_a,h_b, its Fourier inverse is \mathcal K_\Lambda(k)= rac{h_ah_b}{|k|^2+\Lambda^2}. This is a conditional field-response benchmark. The scale \Lambda is not identified with the mass of an exchanged particle. A physical application must derive this operator and the source coefficients from \Psi_\infty; spatial depth alone supplies neither. For 0<|k|\ll\Lambda, \mathcal K_\Lambda(k)= rac{h_ah_b}{\Lambda^2} \left[1- rac{|k|^2}{\Lambda^2} +O\!\left( rac{|k|^4}{\Lambda^4}ight)ight]. 	ag{2} Compared with the zero-scale response at the same nonzero momentum and the same source coefficients,  rac{\mathcal K_\Lambda(k)}{\mathcal K_0(k)} = rac{|k|^2}{|k|^2+\Lambda^2}. 	ag{3} The interaction term can remain nonzero while the low-momentum response is suppressed. No statement about particle exchange is needed to derive (2)–(3). Their use in neutrino physics would require the actual weak current structure, field evolution, and measurement response. They do not already calculate a neutrino scattering rate. A general V2 rule should derive the direct interaction and any reduced response kernel from the same field equations. Putting a zero into the neutrino's entire coupling row would remove both terms in (1). Assigning it an arbitrary tiny common coefficient would also fail to explain the different channel behavior. Spatial source barriers and the low-frequency proposal The full periodic polarization calculation now tests actual spatial source operators rather than a depth-only weight. For a specified lower traceless pattern, every finite spectral residue of one scalar rest sideband cancels. Its amplitude opens linearly in normal momentum, and its source-conditioned Gram opens quadratically. Both occupied polarizations, the incoming spatial pattern and common physical rotations are retained. This supplies a concrete geometric momentum barrier in the specified source channel. The same calculations also show why that result is not yet the neutrino rule. The complete set of scalar inputs has no cancelling second polarization in the tested deformed five-dimensional preparation, while a particular incoming pattern can have a cancelling subspace. Other current readouts and source feedback need not share that zero. The actual photon source must determine which of these spatial operators it samples. The readjusted periodic pair further shows that reducing a lower object's mean scalar balance does not necessarily make its clock arbitrarily slow: the containing field can maintain its confinement and a finite limiting frequency. The exactly zero signed normalization has an undefined scalar center. Separately, slow collective shape poles retain a canonical spectral sign that prevents identifying their small residues alone with stable weak absorption. The neutrino simplex spectrum constrains its three assigned mass levels and a common normalization. It does not yet supply the occupied spatial wavefunctions or the photon current needed by these source tests. The scalar diagnostic profiles must therefore remain distinct from those physically assigned neutrino modes until that mapping is derived. The target remains a neutral electromagnetic channel with surviving, normalized weak response from the same field dynamics. Application to the spatial hierarchy Complete local scalar response adds a pointwise constraint: a small or zero background scalar does not suppress every source-response direction. Its full derivative and its projected vertex have different nullspaces, and the actual kinetics must preserve any proposed cancellation. This does not identify the ordinary electric generator or the surviving weak channel. The kinetic scalar-null classes give exact source-free spatial preparations in the minimal module at every odd depth. This includes five but does not distinguish it from three, seven or nine. Their kinetic involution is not a conserved electric generator for arbitrary scalar-coupled fields, and the scalar term supplies no self-binding inside a single class. For each derived neutrino preparation the calculation should determine: Whether the electric generator annihilates the retained subspace. Whether the colour representation is a singlet. Which normalized charged and neutral weak vertices survive. What the derived field evolution and kinematics imply for response rates at the energy being compared. None of these results follows from d=5 by itself. In the scalar common-marginal example, depth five couples exactly as other containing depths do. That is the appropriate geometric control: any physical distinction must be traced to a derived channel or dynamical structure. The existing neutrino mass spectrum fixes neither the generator nor the weak response map. Related and verification Generalized sector coupling — states the sector-independent construction being tested. Canonical coupling normalization — preserves generator identities through nonorthogonal mode bases. Common field response — distinguishes channel null spaces from frequency-dependent response. generalized_coupling_checks.py checks the generator algebra, neutrality versus weak transitions in nonorthogonal bases, and the controlled limit of the field-response scale.

title: Normal propagation of spatial Dirac modes
summary: Retaining the normal Dirac partner gives exact free-direction propagation, source-preserving boosts and a full moment-response equation for collective fluctuations.
text: Summary: Retaining the normal Dirac partner gives exact free-direction propagation, source-preserving boosts and a full moment-response equation for collective fluctuations. A bound sector can propagate through a containing spatial direction Choose bound coordinates x\in\mathbb R^d and one perpendicular coordinate y in a containing sector of the same nested physical manifold. The coordinate y is another ordinary macroscopic spatial direction. For the lower field it is a free direction relative to its bound spatial profile; it is not an internal or auxiliary dimension. Use a Clifford representation appropriate to that containing space, with Hermitian \alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_d,\alpha_y,\beta. The containing representation may include several copies of a lower representation. Its field components and the mode decompositions below do not add further physical coordinates. Let a normalized full spatial bound mode obey H_b\phi=M\phi,\qquad H_b=-i\alpha_i\partial_i+\beta\mathfrak m(x), \qquad M>0,\qquad\int\phi^\dagger\phi\,dx=1. \tag{1} M is this model's positive bound frequency. Its use as a rest parameter in the calculation does not identify it with a measured particle mass or replace the actual electron orbit. The full bound field, including its lower radial components, is the one derived in Rotation-neutral Dirac fields. The omitted partner carries the normal propagation Because \alpha_y anticommutes with every \alpha_i and with \beta, \{H_b,\alpha_y\}=0,\qquad H_b(\alpha_y\phi)=-M\alpha_y\phi. \tag{2} The two normalized fields \phi,\alpha_y\phi are orthogonal. For a free normal momentum k, the full operator H_b+k\alpha_y acts on their span as \begin{pmatrix}M&k\\k&-M\end{pmatrix}. \tag{3} Consequently its positive frequency and normalized spatial mode are \boxed{E=\sqrt{M^2+k^2},\qquad \phi_k=\sqrt{\frac{E+M}{2E}}\,\phi +\frac{k}{\sqrt{2E(E+M)}}\alpha_y\phi.} \tag{4} The normal velocity is \langle\phi_k,\alpha_y\phi_k\rangle=k/E. A projection onto \phi alone would instead give the constant operator M, losing this propagation. Exact elimination gives H_{\rm eff}(E,k)=M+\frac{k^2}{E+M},\qquad Z(E,k)=1+\frac{k^2}{(E+M)^2}. \tag{5} The physical velocity reconstructed with this norm is [2k/(E+M)]/Z=k/E. This is a direct spatial example of the dressed-source construction. The negative-frequency partner here is a component of the same field's Dirac dynamics, not an additional interaction particle. The scalar source also gives an exact zero-mode condition. Since \{H_b,\beta\}=2\mathfrak m(x)I, a normalized bound eigenfield obeys \boxed{M\langle\beta\rangle =\int\mathfrak m(x)\,\phi^\dagger\phi\,dx.} \tag{5a} For the present nonnegative quadratic scalar profiles, the right side is strictly positive for every nonzero square-integrable field. There is therefore no localized zero-frequency bound mode in this source class. The positive branch has \langle\beta\rangle>0 and its normal dispersion in (4) remains massive. The massless zero mode required by the photon construction needs its own source dynamics. Transverse localization and preservation of normal propagation alone do not establish that zero mode. Equation (5a) concerns the bound eigenproblem (1). The full real-linear fluctuation operator also varies the source and can have collective zero modes, including the translation mode. Their normal dispersion and any identification with a photon require that complete fluctuation calculation. A normal boost preserves the scalar binding source To retain self-consistency, specify the source's spatial dependence. Use the scalar moment interaction locally in the free coordinate: \mathcal E_{\rm int} =\frac{g_0}{2}\int dy\,\operatorname{tr}M_\sigma(y)^2, \qquad M_\sigma(y)=\int (x-X(y))(x-X(y))^T \Psi^\dagger\beta\Psi\,dx. \tag{6} The interaction is nonlocal in the stated bound coordinates and local in (t,y). Its action is invariant under boosts in the (t,y) plane: those boosts leave x unchanged, while \overline\Psi\Psi is a scalar. This is an explicit assumption about the kernel in the free directions, not a claim of a completed Lorentz-covariant action in every spatial plane. For rapidity \eta, put S_\eta=e^{\eta\alpha_y/2},\qquad E=M\cosh\eta,\qquad k=M\sinh\eta. The exact uniformly propagating field is \boxed{\Psi_\eta(t,x,y) =e^{i(ky-Et)}S_\eta\phi(x).} \tag{7} Since S_\eta^\dagger\beta S_\eta=\beta, \Psi_\eta^\dagger\beta\Psi_\eta=\phi^\dagger\beta\phi \tag{8} pointwise. Its scalar center and every bound scalar moment remain unchanged. Thus if the rest profile solves the scalar source equation, the same source binds (7) with the same coefficient g_0. No confining potential has to be retuned for this boost. Equations (4) and (7) use different density conventions. The canonical mode in (4) has unit norm per chosen normal normalization interval. The boosted field in (7) has the Lorentz-transformed density. Dividing (7) by \sqrt{\cosh\eta} restores unit laboratory density and also divides its scalar source by \cosh\eta. A nonlinear source then has to be solved at that changed scalar density. The distinction is developed in Scalar envelope of a bound Dirac field. Retain the local current when transforming the density Write \rho=\phi^\dagger\phi and j_y=\phi^\dagger\alpha_y\phi. The exact pointwise transformations are \boxed{\rho_\eta=\cosh\eta\,\rho+\sinh\eta\,j_y, \qquad (j_y)_\eta=\sinh\eta\,\rho+\cosh\eta\,j_y.} \tag{9} The unboosted mode can have a nonzero local normal current even when its integrated normal current vanishes. For a central radial profile \phi=\frac{f(r)w+i g(r)\alpha(\widehat x)w}{\sqrt{\Omega_{d-1}}}, \qquad\beta w=w, define J_{iy}=w^\dagger(-i\alpha_i\alpha_y)w. Direct Clifford multiplication gives j_y(x)=\frac{2f(r)g(r)}{\Omega_{d-1}} \sum_iJ_{iy}\widehat x_i,\qquad \int j_y\,dx=0. \tag{10} This is an ordinary spatial current of the field. Calling it an electric current would require the physical charge generator from the action. Its first spatial moment is \int x_i j_y\,dx=F_0J_{iy},\qquad F_0=\frac2d\int_0^\infty r^d f(r)g(r)\,dr. \tag{11} The full Dirac equation supplies an independent identity. Since \{H_b,x_i\alpha_y\}=-i\alpha_i\alpha_y, \boxed{F_0=\frac{1-2G/d}{2M},\qquad G=\int_0^\infty g(r)^2r^{d-1}dr.} \tag{12} One can also derive it by integrating the two radial Dirac equations: \int r^d(M+\mathfrak m)fg=d(1-G)/2 and \int r^d(M-\mathfrak m)fg=(d-2)G/2. For v=\tanh\eta, the centroid of the boosted number density is therefore \boxed{(X_\rho)_i=vF_0J_{iy}.} \tag{13} The scalar source center stays fixed by (8). The number-density centroid can shift because the boost mixes density with the spatially varying current. The effect depends on the actual field polarization and containing Clifford representation; it cannot be inferred from the bound depth alone. For example a selected even-dimensional rest chirality makes the mixed J_{iy} vanish, while the tested pure odd-dimensional rest preparations have nonzero mixed circulation. Collective propagation requires variation of the full source The normal partner solves the frozen bound eigenproblem exactly. A collective fluctuation also changes the binding source. For a finite moment interaction this additional response can be retained without restricting the field to two normal amplitudes. Let b_A(x) be the full spatial source vectors at a stationary profile, and let \kappa be the real symmetric curvature matrix of its moments. Write the extra, real-linear source derivative as \delta N_{\rm extra}[\eta] =\sum_{A,B}b_A\kappa_{AB}h_B, \qquad h_A=2\operatorname{Re}\langle b_A,\eta\rangle. \tag{14} The frozen operator H_b\eta is retained in addition to (14). For the centered isotropic scalar moment model, take a Frobenius-orthonormal basis A of all symmetric spatial tensors and include b_A=\beta(x^TAx)\phi,\qquad b_i=\beta x_i\phi. \tag{15} The shape block of \kappa is g_0I; its dipole block is -2aI/Q_\sigma, where \mathfrak m=m+a|x|^2 and Q_\sigma=\langle\phi,\beta\phi\rangle\ne0. The second block is fixed by varying the scalar center. It must be included along with the breathing and traceless shapes. This is the full centered source variation derived in Translation response. The finite list of moments describes spatial patterns in the existing sector, not additional physical coordinates. Let C denote the column operator with columns b_A, and set L_q=H_b+q\alpha_y-M. With the ordinary and conjugate perturbation convention \delta\Psi=e^{-iMt} \left(u(x)e^{i(qy-\omega t)} +v(x)^*e^{-i(qy-\omega^*t)}\right), the full Fourier equation is \boxed{ \omega\begin{pmatrix}u\\v\end{pmatrix} =\left[\mathcal B_0(q)+\mathsf S\kappa\mathsf T\right] \begin{pmatrix}u\\v\end{pmatrix}, \quad \mathcal B_0(q)=\begin{pmatrix}L_q&0\\0&-L_{-q}^*\end{pmatrix}, \quad \mathsf S=\begin{pmatrix}C\\-C^*\end{pmatrix}, \quad\mathsf T=(C^\dagger,C^T).} \tag{16} Here the star on a matrix denotes entrywise conjugation. In particular, the conjugate block keeps the opposite normal momentum. The moment amplitude is h=\mathsf T(u,v)^T. Away from the frozen resolvent poles, eliminate the full spatial field, retaining all its components. Its moment response is \boxed{\Pi(\omega,q) =C^\dagger(\omega-L_q)^{-1}C -C^T(\omega+L_{-q}^*)^{-1}C^*.} \tag{17} An imposed source coefficient f then gives \boxed{h=[I-\Pi(\omega,q)\kappa]^{-1}\Pi(\omega,q)f.} \tag{18} This small matrix contains the full bound-field response through its resolvents. It is not the response obtained by freezing the radial profiles inside an envelope ansatz. Both ordinary and conjugate fluctuations, scalar-center motion and shape response remain present. The normal anticommutation identity gives a useful exact evaluation: \begin{aligned} (\omega-L_q)^{-1} &=[\omega+M+H_b+q\alpha_y] [(\omega+M)^2-H_b^2-q^2]^{-1},\\ (\omega+L_{-q}^*)^{-1} &=[\omega-M-H_b^*+q\alpha_y^*] [(\omega-M)^2-(H_b^*)^2-q^2]^{-1}. \end{aligned} \tag{19} All scalar terms multiply the identity. This expresses normal momentum dependence in terms of the actual squared bound operator; it introduces no independent interaction field. A homogeneous source-carrying mode away from frozen poles satisfies \det(I-\Pi\kappa)=0. Modes in the source kernel must also be kept. For any finite spatial regulator, the full characteristic identity is \det[\omega-\mathcal B(q)] =\det[\omega-\mathcal B_0(q)]\det[I-\Pi(\omega,q)\kappa]. \tag{20} At a frozen pole, the factors can cancel singularities; the complete operator or their continued product determines the spectrum. Dropping the frozen factor would lose source-free modes. For example, phase symmetry gives the collective zero direction (i\phi,-i\phi^*) at q=0 even when M>0. Equations (16)–(20) supply a full-source route to the normal dispersion of collective modes. Identifying a transverse massless photon still requires solving that spectrum for the appropriate spatial solution. A zero frequency at q=0 alone does not establish a linear lightlike branch or its physical polarization. The same construction applies to the nested pair under its specified projected-channel assumptions. Use both full spatial perturbation spaces and the curvature of their common energy. For the second-moment shapes, its block is \kappa_{\rm shape}=g_0 \begin{pmatrix}I&\mathcal R\\\mathcal R^\dagger&I\end{pmatrix}, \qquad \mathcal R(C)=I_{ab}^TCI_{ab}, \tag{21} where I_{ab} is the actual lower-to-higher spatial inclusion and \mathcal R^\dagger uses the Frobenius moment norm. Center variations supply the additional dipole blocks. The source column operator is block diagonal over the two projected channels; the off-diagonal curvature in (21) carries their mutual response. Equations (17)–(18) consequently retain both objects' full spatial variations and repeated source feedback. For finite pair coupling the background must be the jointly readjusted pair, so these equations cannot use two unchanged isolated profiles. Two-frequency spatial Dirac currents combines both normal partners into an exact nonlinear field with a changing spatial current and a constant scalar source. It retains the complete boost phase and the response of its periodic background. Periodic spatial source response extends these full resolvents to a two-frequency background, retaining the frequency sidebands of its source and both ordinary and conjugate field variations. Collective translation waves solves the source-carrying dipole branch for selected even-dimensional chiral fields. The complete source and normal partners give exact inertia and stiffness; at bound depth two the two displacement polarizations have low-frequency speed one-half in Dirac units. A collective zero alone therefore does not identify a photon in this scalar model. Verification normal_dirac_transport_checks.py constructs the containing Clifford representation and directly differentiates the boosted spatial field at depths three, five and six. It checks the complete bound-plus-normal Dirac equation, the pointwise scalar source, the same self-consistent moment coefficient, density/current transformation, and the polarization-dependent centroid. Independent radial integration checks (12), and reconstruction checks (4)–(5). Independent Cartesian Hermite regulators at depths three and five verify the full centered nonlinear source derivative, both normal resolvents, the driven response (18) and the complete characteristic identity (20). The projected squared-coordinate operators retain their full-basis matrix elements. These are finite-regulator algebra checks, not converged collective particle spectra; the full phase zero mode is retained. The exact uniform boost does not cure a bound-profile instability. The radial stability limits of the scalar branch remain those in the profile note, and spatially varying envelopes require the additional response terms described in the envelope reduction. Related Self-consistent scalar Dirac moment modes — supplies the full bound profiles and their source equation. Dressed spatial source vertices — explains the reconstruction and kinetic norm in (5). Scalar envelope of a bound Dirac field — derives the response when the normal amplitude and scalar density change.

title: Null spatial pulses
summary: A specified stationary spatial field supports two normalizable displacement modes, exact finite pulses at the underlying wave speed, and circular polarization with a massless-vector angular-momentum ratio.
text: Summary: A specified stationary spatial field supports two normalizable displacement modes, exact finite pulses at the underlying wave speed, and circular polarization with a massless-vector angular-momentum ratio. A constructive propagation test The scalar Dirac translation branch has two displacement polarizations at bound depth two, but its finite carrier frequency changes the relation between inertia and normal stiffness. A stationary background with identical time and propagation normalizations provides another mechanism to examine. Specify the following component action as a mathematical benchmark: S[n]=\frac Z2\int dt\,dy\,d^2x\, \left[ |\partial_t n|^2-|\partial_y n|^2 -|\partial_1 n|^2-|\partial_2 n|^2 \right],\qquad n\cdot n=1,\quad Z>0. \tag{1} The two x coordinates are ordinary bound-plane spatial directions; y is an existing perpendicular propagation direction in the same containing manifold. The three real components of n are field values. Their unit-vector constraint adds no physical spatial dimensions. Equation (1) is not already derived from the master action for \Psi_\infty. It tests whether a stationary retained field pattern could supply the missing propagation structure. Any physical use would have to derive this component action, its background and its couplings as parts of that one field. No mediator particle is introduced. Its complete constrained field equation is \Box n+(\partial_\mu n\cdot\partial^\mu n)n=0, \qquad \Box=\partial_t^2-\partial_y^2-\partial_1^2-\partial_2^2. \tag{2} An explicit spatially localized background For any \lambda>0, take n_0(x)= \frac{(2\lambda x_1,\ 2\lambda x_2,\ |x|^2-\lambda^2)} {|x|^2+\lambda^2}. \tag{3} Direct differentiation gives n_0^2=1,\qquad \partial_i n_0\cdot\partial_j n_0 =\frac{4\lambda^2}{(|x|^2+\lambda^2)^2}\delta_{ij}, \tag{4} and \Delta_x n_0+|\nabla_x n_0|^2n_0=0. \tag{5} Thus (3) solves the full static equation, with finite energy per unit propagation length \mathcal T=\frac Z2\int|\nabla_x n_0|^2d^2x=4\pi Z. \tag{6} This is the familiar unit-winding two-dimensional sigma-model profile. Its mathematical context is the finite-energy spatial construction of Belavin and Polyakov. Equations (3)–(6) give the profile and verification here without requiring that reference. The background approaches a constant field value at spatial infinity. Its gradient energy is localized; the background itself is not a normalized one-particle wavefunction. The displacement perturbations below do have finite canonical norm. Exactly two finite-norm position modes in this family Translations produce tangents -\partial_i n_0. Their kinetic Gram matrix is \boxed{Z\int\partial_i n_0\cdot\partial_j n_0\,d^2x =\mathcal T\delta_{ij}.} \tag{7} Both time and y derivatives in (1) use this same matrix. The two linear displacement modes therefore obey \partial_t^2X_i-\partial_y^2X_i=0,\qquad \omega^2=k^2. \tag{8} The size and axial field-phase parameters of (3) are also static moduli, but their infinite-plane kinetic norms diverge logarithmically. For a disk of radius R, the size norm divided by Z is \int_{|x|<R}|\partial_\lambda n_0|^2d^2x =4\pi\left[ \log\left(1+\frac{R^2}{\lambda^2}\right) -\frac{R^2}{R^2+\lambda^2} \right]. \tag{9} The axial-phase norm is \lambda^2 times (9). By comparison, each translation norm divided by Z is 4\pi R^2/(R^2+\lambda^2) and tends to a finite limit. Thus only the two position moduli in this four-parameter, fixed-boundary family give normalizable waves on the infinite transverse plane. This statement does not classify every fluctuation of the sigma model. Retain the complete finite-amplitude field Let u=t-y and choose any twice differentiable real two-vector X(u). Then \boxed{n(t,x,y)=n_0(x-X(t-y))} \tag{10} is an exact solution of (2), at arbitrary displacement amplitude.
