Indeed, \partial_t n=-X_i'\partial_i n_0,\qquad \partial_y n=+X_i'\partial_i n_0, \tag{11} so \partial_t^2n=\partial_y^2n and |\partial_t n|^2=|\partial_y n|^2 pointwise. Every acceleration and nonlinear derivative term cancels between t and y, leaving exactly (5). Replacing t-y by t+y gives the opposite direction. More existing normal coordinates may be retained: use u=t-\widehat k\cdot y with |\widehat k|=1. The two bound displacement directions remain perpendicular to propagation. This is the same general null-coordinate mechanism behind arbitrary traveling field deformations discussed by Vachaspati and Vachaspati. The explicit proof above concerns only the stated action. For X' square-integrable, the excess energy and normal momentum over the stationary background are finite: \boxed{ E_{\rm pulse}=\mathcal T\int|X'(u)|^2du,\qquad P_y=E_{\rm pulse}} \tag{12} for propagation toward +y, and P_y=-E_{\rm pulse} in the opposite direction. This is a null excess energy-momentum relation, not a claim that the underlying extended background has zero energy. Linear, elliptical and circular polarization A monochromatic displacement has X(u)=a\cos(\omega u)+b\sin(\omega u),\qquad a,b\in\mathbb R^2. \tag{13} Parallel a,b give a line; independent a,b give an ellipse; orthogonal equal-length vectors give a circle. Both real amplitudes, their relative phase and the actual spatial orientation are retained. The orbital angular momentum about the propagation axis follows directly from the spatial stress tensor. The centered profile's angular integral vanishes, leaving L_{12}=\mathcal T\int (X_1\dot X_2-X_2\dot X_1)\,dy. \tag{14} For a circular mode X=A(\cos\omega u,\pm\sin\omega u), averaging per unit propagation length gives \langle E\rangle=\mathcal T A^2\omega^2,\qquad \langle L_{12}\rangle=\pm\mathcal T A^2\omega,\qquad \frac{\langle L_{12}\rangle}{\langle E\rangle} =\pm\frac1\omega. \tag{15} This is the angular-momentum ratio also associated with circular massless vector modes. Here it comes from actual circular displacement of the spatial profile. The ratio alone does not identify the photon's helicity representation or a single-quantum spin. Those require the physical asymptotic state, rotation action and quantization. The profile is also equivariant under simultaneous coordinate rotation and rotation of its first two field components. That combined symmetry acts pointwise as rotation of X. Its component contribution integrates to zero for these translated profiles, consistent with the orbital calculation above. Coupling still needs the full complementary field The two normalizable modes, exact speed and handedness are useful propagation data. They do not by themselves give a Maxwell current, electric charges, a Coulomb law, or neutrino selectivity. Two opposite pulses generally require a further spatial deformation. Spatial displacement action derives that residual and the exact action of uniformly tilted and moving profiles. As with general polarization textures, an equation for selected coordinates alone must not replace the full spatial field equation. Verification null_spatial_wave_checks.py checks the complete static field, canonical norms, winding integral and finite-radius tails. Independent spacetime differences verify finite linear, elliptical and circular pulses in both propagation directions. The combined coordinate-plus-component symmetry is checked pointwise, with energy and angular momentum integrated separately. The same diagnostic tests the complementary response needed for opposite pulses.

title: Reciprocal response with two spatial clocks
summary: The full response of a readjusted nested pair retains two background frequencies, reciprocal shape coupling and both scalar centers, while spatial parity identifies which deformation-induced sidebands can survive.
text: Summary: The full response of a readjusted nested pair retains two background frequencies, reciprocal shape coupling and both scalar centers, while spatial parity identifies which deformation-induced sidebands can survive. Start from both nonlinear spatial fields The two-frequency nested fields solve their common scalar source while their spatial currents carry independent clocks. The next variation must keep both full field perturbations. It cannot replace one object's geometry by a prescribed force and then infer the response of the whole pair. Use the projected channel action and spatial measures of the nested Dirac pair. Its coordinates describe Q_p\subset Q_D in the one nested manifold of ordinary macroscopic spatial dimensions. A common normal coordinate y belongs to an existing containing sector. The two channel labels and the frequency indices below are descriptions of the same field; they introduce no additional physical space or interaction particle. For i=a,b, write \Psi_{i0}=\psi_{i+}e^{-iM_it}+\psi_{i-}e^{iM_it},\qquad \psi_{i+}=u_i\phi_{i1},\quad \psi_{i-}=v_iY_i\phi_{i2},\qquad H_i\phi_{ij}=M_i\phi_{ij}. \tag{1} The stationary profiles and their deformations must solve the source of both occupied channels. Each channel retains its two rest polarizations. The common energy fixes the complete moment curvature Let A_i be the self-consistent quadratic source matrix in channel i, and Q_i=\int\Psi_{i0}^\dagger\beta_i\Psi_{i0}\ne0. Define source operators for all symmetric second moments and scalar dipoles: O_{iA}=\beta_i(x_i^TAx_i),\qquad O_{i\mu}=\beta_i x_i^\mu. \tag{2} Use Frobenius-orthonormal symmetric tensor bases including breathing. If I:\mathbb R^p\to\mathbb R^D is the spatial inclusion, the higher-to-lower restriction matrix is R_{AB}=\operatorname{tr}(A I^TB I). \tag{3} For the common energy g_0\operatorname{tr}(IM_aI^T+M_b)^2/2, its second-moment curvature is \boxed{\kappa_{\rm shape}=g_0 \begin{pmatrix}I&R\\R^T&I\end{pmatrix}.} \tag{4} Separately centering each scalar density also gives \boxed{\kappa_{{\rm dip},i}=-\frac{2A_i}{Q_i}.} \tag{5} For an anisotropic field this is a spatial matrix, not a single radial coefficient. At the centered background there is no mixed first-order shape–dipole block or cross-channel dipole block in this particular energy. Both statements follow by differentiating M_i=M_{i,\rm raw}-d_id_i^T/Q_i at d_i=0. The scalar-center derivation explains why (5) must remain even when the background center does not move. The full field equation keeps both clocks Let C_i(t) have columns O_{iA}\Psi_{i0}(t), including the dipoles, and put S_i(t)=\begin{pmatrix}C_i(t)\\-C_i(t)^*\end{pmatrix},\qquad T_i(t)=(C_i(t)^\dagger,C_i(t)^T),\qquad B_{i0}(q)=\operatorname{diag}(H_i+qY_i,-(H_i-qY_i)^*). \tag{6} Assemble these as channel block diagonal matrices S,T,B_0. For Z=(\eta_a,\eta_a^*,\eta_b,\eta_b^*)^T, the complete response is \boxed{i\partial_tZ=[B_0+S(t)\kappa T(t)]Z+S(t)f, \qquad h=T(t)Z.} \tag{7} Here \kappa contains (4)–(5), so source motion in either channel feeds back through the same energy. Independent complex variations of both nonlinear field equations reproduce (7), including both centers. The cross-channel field blocks contain mixed carrier frequencies \pm M_a\pm M_b, in addition to the self-block frequencies 0,\pm2M_i. The moment lattice below organizes these terms using each channel's own carrier; it does not omit the mixed field harmonics. The canonical identity is \Sigma B=(\Sigma B)^\dagger, with one ordinary/conjugate signature pair for each channel. This retains the real action; it does not assert positive energy or stability. A frequency lattice replaces a single assumed period The single-field periodic response gives bare moment kernels \Pi_{i,\Delta}(\omega,q) at shifts \Delta=0,\pm2. Put \mathbf M=(M_a,M_b) and label common source frequencies by \omega_{\mathbf n}=\omega+2\mathbf n\cdot\mathbf M, \qquad \mathbf n\in\mathbb Z^2. \tag{8} Define a bare channel and frequency operator by \boxed{\mathbb P_{i\mathbf n,j\mathbf m}= \begin{cases} \Pi_{i,2(n_i-m_i)}(\omega_{\mathbf m},q), &i=j,\ n_k=m_k\ (k\ne i),\ |n_i-m_i|\le1,\\ 0,&\text{otherwise}, \end{cases}} \tag{9} and \mathbb K_{i\mathbf n,j\mathbf m} =\delta_{\mathbf n\mathbf m}\kappa_{ij}. The common source equation is \boxed{h=\mathbb P(f+\mathbb K h),\qquad h=(I-\mathbb P\mathbb K)^{-1}\mathbb P f.} \tag{10} Each bare propagation changes only its own clock index. Cross-channel feedback then permits a sequence involving both, producing frequencies such as \omega+2M_a+2M_b. If M_a/M_b is irrational, no single background period exists. If it is rational, coincident physical frequencies must be combined consistently; two labels need not be independent physical harmonics in that case. A matched finite check retains -N\le n_a,n_b\le N for moments. For fields in channel i, retain -N\le n_i<N, with the other index unchanged. Their frequencies are \omega_{\mathbf n}+M_i. Matching the positive and negative background columns gives \boxed{\mathbb P_N=T_FD_F^{-1}S_F,\qquad Z_F=(D_F-S_F\mathbb K_NT_F)^{-1}S_Ff.} \tag{11} Equation (10) with this same cutoff gives exactly h=T_FZ_F. This is a finite identity; convergence of a physical pole or response as the spatial and frequency cutoffs increase remains an additional test. Spatial parity specifies which rest sidebands can survive For a centered even scalar potential, the combined spatial parity \tau_i=\beta_i\mathcal P_x commutes with H_i and anticommutes with Y_i. Choose positive profiles in the \tau_i=+1 sector. Then \psi_{i\sigma} has parity \sigma. A scalar second moment has operator parity \epsilon=+1 and a scalar dipole has \epsilon=-1. At q=0, each frozen resolvent preserves parity. A source column O_A\psi_\sigma has parity \epsilon_A\sigma, so its overlap with a readout column can survive only when \epsilon_A\sigma=\epsilon_B\rho. Therefore \boxed{\begin{array}{c|cc} &\text{same operator parity}&\text{opposite operator parity}\\\hline \Delta=0&\text{allowed}&0\\ \Delta=\pm2&0&\text{allowed} \end{array}} \tag{12} “Allowed” means parity supplies no zero, not that the amplitude must be nonzero. The central radial examples have a stronger cancellation of the opposite-parity rest sidebands. Deformation can remove that stronger cancellation while preserving (12). Full self-consistent Cartesian examples at common g_0=6.5 and balances (s_a,s_b)=(0.3,0.55) give: nested pair lower mixed shape–dipole sideband higher mixed shape–dipole sideband 2\subset3 zero nonzero 3\subset5 zero nonzero 5\subset6, selected higher chirality zero zero These are responses of the declared finite spatial preparations. The six-dimensional result retains its selected chirality, while the five-dimensional result demonstrates an open channel rather than an inserted neutrino suppression. A quadrupole-only calculation would omit the center response which carries the allowed odd-dimensional sideband. At nonzero normal momentum, qY_i exchanges combined parity. The equal-parity sidebands can then open too. The complete calculation in (7)–(11) retains this normal propagation and both clocks. Polarization selection of a periodic spatial source calculates the entire cancelling polarization subspace and the normal-momentum opening for a specified lower spatial pattern. Read each current only after the pair responds The spatial current readout applies to the solved pair field. For each channel, its integrated density and normal current satisfy at an interior retained harmonic \boxed{\omega_{\mathbf n}\,\delta N_{i,\mathbf n} =q\,\delta J_{i,y,\mathbf n}.} \tag{13} Each projected channel's number remains conserved because its scalar source is Hermitian. The cross response changes its geometry and current without violating that continuity equation. No identification with a physical photon source or an interaction rate is assumed by this readout. Verification paired_periodic_response_checks.py solves both Cartesian source profiles at one common coefficient and checks their nonlinear equations at independent carrier phases. Full complex finite variations verify the reciprocal curvature and both scalar-center blocks. The parity selection is checked in complete spatial resolvents. Matched two-index field and moment equations independently reproduce the full induced response at two harmonic cutoffs, including an output involving both clocks. Current measurements check (13) after feedback. Reports use timestamped filenames and all conditions remain active under Python optimization. The regulated frequencies are not particle mass predictions.

title: Spatial current response of a two-frequency field
summary: The spatial number current retains polarization-dependent frequency sidebands that can cancel in the scalar binding source, with an exact continuity identity and the full source feedback preserved.
text: Summary: The spatial number current retains polarization-dependent frequency sidebands that can cancel in the scalar binding source, with an exact continuity identity and the full source feedback preserved. The source and the measured current are different bilinears The periodic source equation follows the complete spatial Dirac perturbation through its scalar binding moments. The same perturbation also changes the spatial number current. A cancellation in one readout does not automatically cancel the other. All spatial coordinates belong to the one nested manifold of ordinary macroscopic dimensions. Let x span the d bound directions and y be the existing containing direction used for the normal partner. For i\partial_t\Psi= [-i\alpha_i\partial_i-i\alpha_y\partial_y+\beta\mathfrak m]\Psi, \qquad \mathfrak m\in\mathbb R, \tag{1} direct differentiation gives \boxed{\partial_t\rho+\partial_i j_i+\partial_y j_y=0, \qquad \rho=\Psi^\dagger\Psi,\quad j_\mu=\Psi^\dagger\alpha_\mu\Psi.} \tag{2} The scalar potential cancels pointwise because it is Hermitian and multiplies the field at that point. Its coefficient may depend on the field's spatial moments without changing this identity. These are the number density and Noether current of the specified field action. Identifying their physical photon projection requires the additional current map discussed in source frequencies. Derive each current harmonic from the full field Use the two-frequency background \Psi_0=\psi_+e^{-iMt}+\psi_-e^{iMt},\qquad \psi_+=a\phi_1,\quad\psi_-=b\alpha_y\phi_2, \quad H_b\phi_j=M\phi_j. \tag{3} The profiles have the same radial scalar source and may have different rest polarizations. For scalar input operators O_A and Hermitian output operators J_\ell, form columns C_\sigma=(O_A\psi_\sigma)_A,\qquad D_\sigma=(J_\ell\psi_\sigma)_\ell. \tag{4} An integrated number measurement uses J=I, and an integrated normal current uses J=\alpha_y. A resolved bound-current measurement uses the position-evaluation quadratic form with \alpha_i; its finite Galerkin representation is a Hermitian matrix. Solving the ordinary and conjugate field equations gives the bare output at frequency \omega+\Delta M, where \Delta=0,\pm2: \boxed{\begin{aligned} \Gamma_\Delta(\omega,q) ={}&\sum_{\sigma-\rho=\Delta} D_\rho^\dagger(\omega+\sigma M-H_q)^{-1}C_\sigma\\ &-\sum_{\rho-\sigma=\Delta} D_\rho^T(\omega-\sigma M+H_{-q}^*)^{-1}C_\sigma^*, \qquad H_q=H_b+q\alpha_y. \end{aligned}} \tag{5} Thus the current readout changes the left columns of the scalar response, while the spatial propagation and input source remain the same. The star means entrywise conjugation, and the conjugate block has opposite normal momentum. A real perturbation also includes its conjugate Fourier component. After integration over the decaying bound profile, (2) requires \boxed{(\omega+\Delta M)\Gamma_{N,\Delta} =q\Gamma_{y,\Delta}.} \tag{6} This identity holds for every source column and output harmonic. At rest the total number has no response at a nonzero output frequency. The normal current is not constrained to vanish by that statement. Rest current sidebands measure both occupied polarizations Define the transition scalar moment \mu_{21,A}=\langle\phi_2,O_A\phi_1\rangle. \tag{7} For the radial background and the centered scalar second moments and dipoles, the integrated normal current has \boxed{\Gamma_{y,+2}=\frac{2a\bar b}{\omega}\mu_{21},\qquad \Gamma_{y,-2}=-\frac{2\bar a b}{\omega}\mu_{21}^*,\qquad \Gamma_{y,0}=0\quad(q=0).} \tag{8} For example, the ordinary positive-sideband term in (5) is a\bar b\langle\phi_2,(\omega+M-H_b)^{-1}O_A\phi_1\rangle =a\bar b\mu_{21,A}/\omega. Normal anticommutation and \alpha_yO_A\alpha_y=-O_A give the same contribution from the conjugate term. Their sum yields the first expression in (8). The negative sideband retains the conjugate transition moment and opposite sign. The 1/\omega factor describes the phase change of an existing 2M clock under a sustained scalar forcing. It is a linear phase response, not a divergent finite-amplitude current. The readjusted radial clock distinguishes the frozen matrix element from a stationary frequency derivative after the profile changes. For these radial scalar moments, \mu_{21} is proportional to \langle w_2,w_1\rangle. Both rest polarizations therefore enter (8). Orthogonal polarizations cancel the integrated oscillating current. That cancellation does not make all local current matrix elements zero. Complete Cartesian field calculations at depths three, five and six give the following comparison for orthogonal occupied polarizations: measured response at rest depth 3 depth 5 depth 6, selected bound chirality integrated normal current at \omega\pm2M zero zero zero sampled local bound current at \omega nonzero nonzero nonzero sampled local bound current at \omega\pm2M nonzero nonzero zero The local statements concern the declared spatial preparations, source columns and finite regulators. The six-dimensional sideband cancellation uses its selected chirality; it is not a general theorem about every six-dimensional field. The five-dimensional field is treated with the same operators and coefficient as the other depths. No neutrino zero is inserted. Preserve source feedback before reading the current Let h_j and f_j be scalar moment and force amplitudes at \omega+2jM, and let \mathbb P,\mathbb K be the complete moment response and curvature from the periodic source equation. Define \mathbb\Gamma_{jk}=\Gamma_{2(j-k)}(\omega+2kM,q) for |j-k|\le1, with the other bare blocks zero. Then \boxed{h=\mathbb P(f+\mathbb K h),\qquad j=\mathbb\Gamma(f+\mathbb K h) =\mathbb\Gamma(I-\mathbb K\mathbb P)^{-1}f.} \tag{9} The output retains every induced source harmonic. A matched full-field frequency cutoff gives an independent implementation: solve the complete ordinary/conjugate field matrix, then apply the current readout directly. Interior harmonics satisfy (6) after feedback. Cutoff boundaries must use the same retained field harmonics in both calculations. For two interacting objects, their common action supplies the cross curvature and both responses. Equation (9) describes how to read an output from that solved field; it does not replace the partner's response with a fixed detector or introduce an additional interaction particle. Verification periodic_current_checks.py uses the actual centered Cartesian Dirac fields, independent occupied polarizations and one common interaction coefficient. It checks the full normal continuity relation, the analytic rest-current residues and the distinction between integrated and resolved spatial outputs. A complete ordinary/conjugate harmonic solve independently verifies the current after source feedback. Direct time-dependent spatial bilinears and their Fourier transform reproduce the output sidebands. Reports have timestamped filenames and verification remains active under Python optimization. These results identify geometric selection within the stated model; the physical photon map and normalized interaction rates remain open.

title: Polarization selection of a periodic spatial source
summary: A positive matrix calculated from full spatial source operators identifies exactly which occupied polarizations cancel a selected frequency sideband, while retaining the incoming object's spatial pattern and common-rotation covariance.
text: Summary: A positive matrix calculated from full spatial source operators identifies exactly which occupied polarizations cancel a selected frequency sideband, while retaining the incoming object's spatial pattern and common-rotation covariance. Turn a proposed polarization barrier into a complete calculation The reciprocal periodic field equation retains the source of both deformed objects. Its bare spatial response also permits an exact question: for a given occupied positive-frequency profile, which second polarizations cancel a specified source sideband? The answer depends on the spatial source operators, the complete bound Dirac resolvents, normal propagation and the incoming pattern. It can be calculated without selecting a special zero for one particle depth. All fields live over ordinary macroscopic spatial directions in the one nested manifold. Polarization coefficients label field components over those directions; they are not additional physical dimensions. Let W be an isometric frame of the occupied positive-frequency spatial multiplet: H_bW=MW,\qquad W^\dagger W=I_k,\qquad \phi_1=Wz_1,\quad\phi_2=Wz_2,\quad\|z_1\|=\|z_2\|=1. \tag{1} The dagger in (1) includes integration over the full bound spatial field. The frame contains both upper and lower Dirac components, not merely their rest spinors. In the tested multiplets every unit z preserves the same self-consistent binding moments. This property is checked before their polarizations are varied. The background is \Psi_0=aWz_1e^{-iMt}+bYWz_2e^{iMt}, where Y is its existing normal Clifford matrix. Keep the actual source operators O_A, including all scalar second moments and dipoles, and define U_A=O_AW,\qquad V_A=O_AYW,\qquad H_q=H_b+qY. \tag{2} Here q labels the perturbation's Fourier dependence e^{iqy} about the rest background, along the existing containing coordinate y. Keep the full polarization matrix of every source channel For the positive shifted output at \omega+2M, the full ordinary and conjugate response gives a k\times k matrix for each input–output pair: \boxed{F_{AB}(\omega,q)= V_A^\dagger(\omega+M-H_q)^{-1}U_B -V_B^\dagger(\omega+M+H_{-q})^{-1}U_A.} \tag{3} The second term follows by transposing the conjugate propagation term. It retains H_{-q}; it must not be replaced by the first resolvent or assigned its sign by analogy. The actual scalar sideband is \boxed{\Pi_{+2,AB}=a\bar b\,z_2^\dagger F_{AB}z_1.} \tag{4} Equation (4) keeps both occupied polarizations rather than replacing their relation by a depth-dependent coefficient. Its cancellation concerns this particular frequency sideband. Same-frequency scalar responses and the spatial current outputs are separate readouts of the full perturbed field. A positive Gram matrix describes the entire cancelling subspace For fixed z_1, define \boxed{G(z_1)=\sum_{A,B} (F_{AB}z_1)(F_{AB}z_1)^\dagger\succeq0.} \tag{5} Then \boxed{\sum_{A,B}|\Pi_{+2,AB}|^2 =|ab|^2z_2^\dagger G(z_1)z_2.} \tag{6} For ab\ne0, all selected input–output sideband amplitudes vanish exactly when z_2\in\ker G. The smallest eigenvalue gives the minimum summed response over unit second polarizations. A full-rank G rules out a cancelling second polarization at that tested frequency and for that complete channel set. The equivalence is immediate from the sum of nonnegative squared amplitudes in (6). Strictly positive weights on the channel terms can change the numerical eigenvalues but cannot change the common kernel. Thus the nullspace criterion does not require adding dimensional quantities with an assumed physical metric. Comparing strengths or rates does require the appropriate source units, kinetic weights and flux normalization, as in canonical coupling normalization. Retain the actual incoming object's shape The all-channel condition in (5) is stronger than the condition for one incoming source. For a specified complex spatial force pattern f_B, define F_A(f)=\sum_BF_{AB}f_B,\qquad \boxed{G_f(z_1)=\sum_A(F_A(f)z_1)(F_A(f)z_1)^\dagger.} \tag{7} This matrix tests that particular pattern and its phase. It can have a larger kernel than (5), even when (5) has full rank. If the lower object's moment is a tensor C on its own p directions, the containing source uses its actual inclusion ICI^T to construct f. The lower pattern must be derived or specified; it is not determined solely by p. In a solved interaction, the appropriate force is the effective force after both objects' response, including self-feedback. A zero in (7) for the initially applied pattern does not prove that the readjusted force stays in that kernel. The full pair equation supplies that additional calculation. Results from the same operator rule at several depths The following comparison uses complete readjusted Cartesian profiles, one common g_0=6.5, balances (0.3,0.55), and the complex test frequency \omega/M=0.17+0.19i. The matrix ranks agree at total Cartesian degrees one and two. These are regulated source-resolvent tests, not measured particle preparations or interaction probabilities. containing profile and lower partner occupied frame dimension k \dim\ker G at q=0 \dim\ker G at q=0.2M depth 3 in 2\subset3 2 1 0 depth 5 in 3\subset5 4 0 0 selected depth-6 chirality in 5\subset6 4 4 0 For the deformed five-dimensional example, no second polarization cancels all these source sidebands at the tested rest frequency. This is not a derived neutrino suppression. For the selected six-dimensional chirality, the rest sideband cancels throughout that occupied frame, while normal propagation opens it. The three-dimensional cancelling line agrees with the correlated polarization supplied by the bound-space antilinear symmetry. That symmetry does not extend to its retained normal derivative. The five-dimensional matrix conditions differ, so orthogonality of the two polarizations alone supplies no corresponding cancellation theorem. For an incoming lower traceless tensor C=\operatorname{diag}(1,-1,0,\ldots)/\sqrt2, the source-conditioned G_f in (7) instead vanishes at rest in all three sampled geometries. Their complete all-channel matrices are nevertheless different, as the table shows. At the sampled nonzero normal momentum, each G_f is full rank. These results make both the spatial pattern and its propagation essential to the claimed barrier. Verify a rest cancellation at every pole and derive its opening A few sampled frequencies cannot prove a frequency-independent barrier. Let P_E be each complete spectral projector of the finite bound operator, and put U_f=\sum_Bf_BU_B and V_{\bar f}=\sum_B\bar f_BV_B. Expansion of (3) in its full spectrum shows that the selected source vanishes identically at rest precisely when \boxed{V_A^\dagger P_EU_f =V_{\bar f}^\dagger P_{-E}U_A \quad\text{for every }A,E.} \tag{7a} The diagnostic verifies these matrix residues for the embedded lower traceless tensor above, at both spatial resolutions and all three depths. This establishes a complete finite spectral identity, not merely a zero at the displayed test frequency. A continuum statement would require the corresponding spectral-measure identity and operator domains. Normal anticommutation gives the resolvents through \mathcal D=(\zeta^2-H_b^2-q^2)^{-1}, with \zeta=\omega+M. Grouping the positive and negative bound eigenvalues in (7a) cancels the entire part even in q. The remaining selected output is exactly \boxed{F_A(f;\omega,q) =q\left[V_A^\dagger Y\mathcal D U_f -V_{\bar f}^\dagger Y\mathcal D U_A\right].} \tag{7b} It is odd in normal momentum, away from its poles. Its leading coefficient is obtained by setting q=0 only inside \mathcal D, so \boxed{G_f(q)=q^2G_{f,\rm lead}+O(q^4).} \tag{7c} The checked leading matrices are positive definite on each selected occupied frame. Thus every second polarization in those frames acquires this particular bare response when a small nonzero normal momentum is introduced, with an amplitude linear in q. Independent full resolvents verify both the sign reversal under q\mapsto-q and (7c). This is a derived momentum barrier for a stated spatial source. It does not equate the normal wavenumber with the particle's bound clock, and it does not remove the partner's feedback or the normalization needed for an interaction rate. The result is independent of a coordinate or polarization-frame choice Under an occupied-frame change W\mapsto WV, with V unitary, F_{AB}\mapsto V^\dagger F_{AB}V,\qquad z_j\mapsto V^\dagger z_j,\qquad G\mapsto V^\dagger GV. \tag{8} A common physical rotation of the spatial field, incoming shape and inclusion acts on the source channels through an orthogonal matrix D: the symmetric tensors rotate as tensors and the dipoles as vectors. The complete spatial field rotation includes its orbital and spin parts. Its response satisfies \boxed{F'_{AB}=\sum_{C,E}D_{AC}D_{BE}F_{CE}, \qquad f'=Df.} \tag{9} Consequently the complete G is unchanged in the correspondingly rotated occupied frame, and G_{f'}'=G_f. A common rotation cannot create or remove the polarization barrier. A relative rotation of the objects can change f and their compatibility, which is the geometric question being tested. Verification periodic_polarization_checks.py constructs an isometric frame from the full solved spatial eigenspace and checks its binding moments for independent occupied polarizations. Independent ordinary/conjugate resolvents verify every entry of (4), while extremal Gram eigenvectors reproduce the full measured sideband norm. Both Cartesian degrees, both normal momenta, strictly positive channel weights and the explicitly embedded lower tensor are checked. Every complete spectral residue verifies the rest cancellation; independent small-momentum resolvents verify its linear amplitude and quadratic Gram. Actual orbital-plus-spin field rotations verify (9), including rotation of the incoming pattern. Reports use timestamped filenames and checks remain active under Python optimization. The physical photon map, the occupied neutrino geometry and normalized rates still require their own derivation.

title: Periodic spatial source response
summary: The full response of a two-frequency spatial Dirac field reduces to a frequency-indexed moment equation that retains scalar-center motion, normal propagation and the conditions for source-sideband cancellation.
text: Summary: The full response of a two-frequency spatial Dirac field reduces to a frequency-indexed moment equation that retains scalar-center motion, normal propagation and the conditions for source-sideband cancellation. Follow the complete periodic background The two-frequency spatial field has an unchanging scalar binding source and a changing number-current pattern. Its linearized field equation nevertheless has periodic coefficients. The response can be derived without assigning its bound frequency to an external forcing frequency or discarding one of its two components. All coordinates describe ordinary macroscopic spatial directions of the one nested manifold. The bound coordinates are x\in\mathbb R^d and y is one existing containing direction. The field-component indices, source moments and temporal harmonics below are mathematical descriptions of that same field; they add no physical spatial dimensions or particles. The present normal momentum is along the direction used to construct the opposite-frequency partner. Let H_b=-i\alpha_i\partial_i+\beta(m_0+a_{\rm source}|x|^2) be the self-consistent bound operator, with \{H_b,\alpha_y\}=0. Choose normalized radial fields with possibly different rest polarizations, H_b\phi_1=M\phi_1,\qquad H_b\phi_2=M\phi_2,\qquad \Psi_0(t)=a\phi_1e^{-iMt}+b\alpha_y\phi_2e^{iMt}. \tag{1} Their complete radial frame has the pointwise scalar identities \phi_j^\dagger\beta\phi_j=\sigma_0 and \phi_1^\dagger\beta\alpha_y\phi_2=0. Thus the binding density is s\sigma_0, where s=|a|^2-|b|^2>0. Both profiles must be solved at that scalar weight and the same interaction coefficient. Set |a|^2+|b|^2=1 for the unit canonical norm used in the examples. Retain shape and scalar-center variation Use Hermitian spatial source operators O_A=\beta(x^TAx),\qquad O_i=\beta x_i, \tag{2} where A runs over a Frobenius-orthonormal basis of all symmetric spatial tensors, including breathing. Define C_\sigma as the column operator whose columns are O_A\psi_\sigma, with \psi_+=a\phi_1 and \psi_-=b\alpha_y\phi_2. Then C(t)=\sum_{\sigma=\pm1}C_\sigma e^{-i\sigma Mt}. \tag{3} The real symmetric moment curvature is constant on this background. Its shape block is g_0I, and its dipole block is -2a_{\rm source}I/Q_\sigma, with Q_\sigma=\int\Psi_0^\dagger\beta\Psi_0\,dx\ne0. Translational response derives that second block by varying the scalar center. An unchanged background center does not justify omitting its perturbations. For the complexified ordinary and conjugate perturbation Z=(\eta,\eta^*)^T, the full equation at normal momentum q is \boxed{ i\partial_tZ=\left[\mathcal B_0(q)+S(t)\kappa T(t)\right]Z +S(t)f(t),} \tag{4} with \begin{gathered} H_q=H_b+q\alpha_y,\qquad \mathcal B_0(q)=\begin{pmatrix}H_q&0\\0&-H_{-q}^*\end{pmatrix},\\ S(t)=\begin{pmatrix}C(t)\\-C(t)^*\end{pmatrix},\qquad T(t)=(C(t)^\dagger,C(t)^T),\qquad h=T(t)Z. \end{gathered} \tag{5} The star means entrywise conjugation; the conjugate block retains the opposite normal momentum. These are laboratory field frequencies, with no stationary carrier subtracted from H_q. The additional source coefficients are f, while h contains the induced moments. A physical real perturbation includes the conjugate Fourier component at (-\omega,-q). Equation (4) follows by the complete real-linear differentiation in Dirac source linearization. Its energy Hessian obeys \Sigma\mathcal B=(\Sigma\mathcal B)^\dagger, where \Sigma=\operatorname{diag}(I,-I). This action identity does not make the energy positive. The field coefficients contain frequencies 0,\pm2M and have period \pi/M. A monochromatic source produces three bare moment frequencies First remove the feedback term \kappa h and impose f e^{i(qy-\omega t)}. Multiplication by (3) drives ordinary fields at \omega+\sigma M and conjugate fields at \omega-\sigma M. Reading those fields through T(t) gives moment outputs at \omega+\Delta M, for \Delta=0,\pm2: \boxed{ \begin{aligned} \Pi_\Delta(\omega,q) ={}&\sum_{\sigma-\rho=\Delta} C_\rho^\dagger(\omega+\sigma M-H_q)^{-1}C_\sigma\\ &-\sum_{\rho-\sigma=\Delta} C_\rho^T(\omega-\sigma M+H_{-q}^*)^{-1}C_\sigma^*. \end{aligned}} \tag{6} The first sum has ordinary propagation; the second has the conjugate response with its required sign. For example: moment output ordinary contribution conjugate contribution \omega+2M C_-^\dagger(\omega+M-H_q)^{-1}C_+ -C_+^T(\omega+M+H_{-q}^*)^{-1}C_-^* \omega-2M C_+^\dagger(\omega-M-H_q)^{-1}C_- -C_-^T(\omega-M+H_{-q}^*)^{-1}C_+^* Normal propagation can be evaluated with the full squared bound operator: \begin{aligned} (\zeta-H_q)^{-1} &=(\zeta+H_b+q\alpha_y)(\zeta^2-H_b^2-q^2)^{-1},\\ (\zeta+H_{-q}^*)^{-1} &=(\zeta-H_b^*+q\alpha_y^*) (\zeta^2-(H_b^*)^2-q^2)^{-1}. \end{aligned} \tag{7} The domain and pole qualifications are those of the full normal response. No radial or angular field components have been eliminated by simply neglecting them. Repeated feedback couples the frequency sidebands Let h_j and f_j denote moment amplitudes at \omega+2jM. Define an operator on their frequency-indexed sequence by \mathbb P_{jk}(\omega,q)= \begin{cases} \Pi_{2(j-k)}(\omega+2kM,q),&|j-k|\le1,\\ 0,&|j-k|>1. \end{cases} \tag{8} The complete source equation is \boxed{h=\mathbb P(f+\mathbb K h),\qquad h=(I-\mathbb P\mathbb K)^{-1}\mathbb P f,\qquad \mathbb K_{jk}=\delta_{jk}\kappa.} \tag{9} Its repeated feedback can populate more frequencies than the three in (6). A finite harmonic cutoff is an approximation to this sequence; convergence of a physical response or pole must be checked as that cutoff increases. At singular frequencies use the complete field operator or the appropriate limiting resolvent. There is also an exact finite-cutoff identity useful for verification. Keep field frequencies \omega+(2n+1)M, -N\le n<N, and moment frequencies \omega+2jM, -N\le j\le N. Let D be the block diagonal frozen field resolvent denominator, and construct S_F,T_F by matching the harmonics in (3)–(5). Then \boxed{\mathbb P_N=T_FD^{-1}S_F,\qquad \det(D-S_F\mathbb K_NT_F) =\det D\,\det(I-\mathbb P_N\mathbb K_N).} \tag{10} The frozen determinant factor retains source-free field modes and pole cancellations. A truncated moment equation and a differently truncated field equation need not agree at their frequency boundaries. Matching both cutoffs gives (10) exactly. A periodic field can have a simpler scalar readout at rest Periodic field coefficients do not guarantee a nonzero sideband in every observable. At q=0, let P_E be the complete spectral projector of H_b at eigenvalue E in a finite spatial regulator. Since \alpha_yP_E\alpha_y=P_{-E}, the positive sideband in (6) vanishes identically away from the poles if and only if every residue satisfies \boxed{C_-^\dagger P_EC_+ =\left(C_-^\dagger P_{-E}C_+\right)^T.} \tag{11} The negative sideband has the corresponding conjugate relation. This criterion follows by expanding both resolvents in spectral projectors. It checks an identity at every pole rather than inferring cancellation from a few sampled frequencies. A continuum statement would require the corresponding equality of spectral measures and valid operator domains. For the centered Cartesian radial examples at depths three, five and six, all complete projectors satisfy (11) for the scalar second moments and dipoles. The direct source response has no \omega\pm2M scalar output at rest, even though its field perturbation contains both carriers and its full field operator is periodic. This is a verified property of the declared regulators; it is not an assumption about an arbitrary source, an arbitrary nonlocal probe or a physical photon current. For identical rest polarizations, write C for the unit-profile source columns and \chi_1 for their bare single-frequency response. Since C_+=aC and C_-=-b\alpha_yC, the diagonal harmonic obeys the exact normal-partner identity \boxed{\Pi_0(\omega,q) =|a|^2\chi_1(\omega,q)-|b|^2\chi_1(\omega,q)^T.} \tag{12} This identity follows directly from (7), including the opposite normal momentum. Different occupied rest polarizations require their respective single-frequency responses. Equation (12) concerns the diagonal harmonic; at nonzero q it does not remove the other blocks of (9). In particular, if a shape channel has \chi_1=A(\omega)I+B(\omega)T, with T^T=-T, then \boxed{\Pi_0=sA(\omega)I+nB(\omega)T, \qquad n=|a|^2+|b|^2.} \tag{13} The signed scalar balance and canonical norm multiply different parts of the response. Replacing both by a single small scalar source would lose its polarization-dependent dynamics. Check growth in the full periodic field When (11) removes the rest scalar sidebands, there is an autonomous source realization with four full spatial blocks: \begin{gathered} L_4=\operatorname{diag}(H_b-M,H_b+M,-H_b^*+M,-H_b^*-M),\\ T_4=(C_+^\dagger,C_-^\dagger,C_+^T,C_-^T),\qquad S_4=\Sigma_4T_4^\dagger,\qquad \Sigma_4=\operatorname{diag}(I,I,-I,-I),\\ \boxed{\mathcal A_4=L_4+S_4\kappa T_4.} \end{gathered} \tag{14} Its resolvent gives exactly \Pi_0. For a mode (u_+,u_-,v_+,v_-) of frequency \omega, reconstruct the physical ordinary and conjugate fields as \boxed{Z(t)=e^{-i\omega t} \begin{pmatrix} e^{-iMt}u_++e^{iMt}u_-\\ e^{iMt}v_++e^{-iMt}v_- \end{pmatrix}.} \tag{15} For a nonreal source-carrying pole, (11) makes its unwanted scalar sidebands vanish, so (15) solves (4) at q=0. Source-free modes of L_4 have real frequencies and cannot create exponential growth. Conversely, the closed rest moment equation separates the harmonics of a growing Floquet solution into poles of this same source resolvent. This is a finite-dimensional rest-response reduction under (11), not a claim of a global symmetry for arbitrary fields or propagating modes. The period is P=\pi/M. The vector multiplying e^{-i\omega t} in (15) changes sign after P, so its full evolution multiplier is -e^{-i\omega P}. Independent integration of (4) over a full period checks this multiplier and the growth rate \operatorname{Im}\omega. The evolution preserves the indefinite canonical form even when a mode grows; conservation of that form is not positive-energy stability. At unit number norm, scalar balance s=0.3, one common g_0=6.5 and zero bare mass, the total-degree-one Cartesian regulators give: depth bound frequency M largest source-pole growth rate full time-evolution growth rate 3 1.757394 1.067734 1.067734 5 2.792114 0.988712 0.988712 6 3.301631 0.967062 0.967062 These values verify the reduction in the declared spatial regulators. They are not converged particle frequencies. In these examples the periodic field is unstable, so a small residue of one slow response pole cannot be interpreted as a stable weakly coupled particle. Slow shape poles and their signed response derives the slow frequency and residue together and verifies their canonical sign. Propagation and the second object's response remain essential In the same spatial calculations, normal momentum makes the scalar shape sidebands nonzero. Their first small-q term is linear in q; the positive and negative normal momenta give opposite sideband amplitudes for the tested preparation. Thus the rest cancellation does not authorize using a stationary scalar susceptibility for the whole propagating periodic field. A reciprocal nested interaction uses the curvature of the common energy, including its off-diagonal shape restriction and scalar-center terms. The readjusted nested pair supplies the stationary source requirement. If two periodic backgrounds have different bound frequencies, their common response generally needs both frequency indices; a single period cannot be assumed for an irrational frequency ratio. Both objects' spatial polarizations and their feedback must be retained. The source-frequency analysis explains why an actual photon output map is still necessary. A scalar moment cancellation is a statement about that readout, while a photon could sample a different spatial current with different surviving sidebands. Spatial current response derives those output columns from the same field and verifies the normal continuity identity before and after source feedback. Verification periodic_dirac_response_checks.py constructs complete centered Cartesian field sources with one common interaction coefficient. Complex finite variations verify (4), including all center, breathing and shape terms. An independent temporal Fourier transform reconstructs the full periodic field operator. Complete spectral projectors check (11). Dense normal Dirac resolvents independently check (6)–(7). Explicit time-dependent forced fields retain both spatial polarizations; their temporal Fourier transforms recover the predicted moment sidebands. Matched full-field and moment harmonic cutoffs check (9)–(10), retaining ordinary and conjugate fluctuations. Full-period evolution independently verifies the reconstructed growing modes, their Floquet multipliers and preservation of the canonical form. Reports use timestamped filenames and checks remain active under Python optimization. These calculations establish the stated algebra and regulated response; they do not identify physical particle masses or interaction rates. Related Two-frequency spatial Dirac currents — supplies the exact nonlinear background and its changing current. Source frequencies in spatial coupling — distinguishes the carrier from the spatial clock sampled in an interaction. Normal propagation of spatial Dirac modes — supplies full normal resolvents and the centered source conventions. Translational Dirac response — derives the scalar-center curvature retained throughout this calculation.

title: Photon plane coupling
summary: Restricting a magnetic two-form overlap to the photon's actual two-plane gives a rank-two projector and an explicit polarization-dependent coupling diagnostic.
text: Summary: Restricting a magnetic two-form overlap to the photon's actual two-plane gives a rank-two projector and an explicit polarization-dependent coupling diagnostic. Spatial setting and conditional interaction All directions below are ordinary macroscopic spatial directions in one nested physical manifold. Work in a flat tangent chart of a containing sector, with real Euclidean space V of dimension d\geq3. The photon has an oriented physical two-plane E\subset V and unit phase direction k\in E^\perp. Its complex polarization belongs to E\otimes\mathbb C. This is the geometry in photon transversality. The calculation adopts the spatial two-form pairing of the dimensional magnetic kernel. It is one specified interaction term of the single field \Psi_\infty. It does not introduce mediator particles or establish that this term is the whole electromagnetic response. Electric, orbital, and additional spatial response terms must be retained when the action supplies them. For skew matrices use the Hermitian pairing and norm \langle A,B\rangle=\frac12\operatorname{tr}(A^\dagger B), \qquad \|A\|^2=\langle A,A\rangle. For real vectors define u\wedge v=uv^T-vu^T. A unit linear polarization \varepsilon\in E gives the normalized wave two-form B(\varepsilon)=\varepsilon\wedge k, \qquad \|B(\varepsilon)\|^2=1. \tag{1} Its two-form plane includes k; that is a description of the wave's spatial curvature. The photon's bound oscillation plane remains E. Restrict the field projector to the photon plane Choose real orthonormal \varepsilon_1,\varepsilon_2 spanning E, write P_E=\sum_a\varepsilon_a\varepsilon_a^T, and set B_a=\varepsilon_a\wedge k. The two matrices B_a are orthonormal. For any complex skew matrix M, \langle B_a,M\rangle=\varepsilon_a^T M k. The orthogonal projector onto these two admissible wave amplitudes is \boxed{ \mathcal Q_{E,k}M =\sum_{a=1}^2 B_a\langle B_a,M\rangle =w\wedge k,\qquad w=P_E M k.} \tag{2} Because w\perp k, applying \mathcal Q_{E,k} again leaves it unchanged. The orthonormal expansion also proves self-adjointness, positivity, and rank two. In particular, \boxed{\|\mathcal Q_{E,k}M\|^2=\|P_E M k\|^2.} \tag{3} The earlier closed-field projector is \mathcal P_kM=P_kM+MP_k, \qquad P_k=kk^T. It admits every polarization in k^\perp and has rank d-1. Our photon has only the two amplitudes selected by E. Consequently \mathcal Q_{E,k}\mathcal P_k =\mathcal P_k\mathcal Q_{E,k}=\mathcal Q_{E,k}, \qquad 0\leq\mathcal Q_{E,k}\leq\mathcal P_k. \tag{4} These projectors coincide at depth three, where E=k^\perp. At larger depths a sum over all d-1 transverse amplitudes is a different diagnostic from a sum over this photon's two polarizations. Definite polarization and the sum over two polarizations For one real spatial rotation tensor J, define h_a=\varepsilon_a^T Jk,\qquad C(E,k;J)=h^\dagger h=\|P_EJk\|^2. \tag{5} A normalized complex polarization c\in\mathbb C^2 has wave two-form B(c)=\sum_a c_aB_a. The squared overlap is |\langle B(c),J\rangle|^2 =|c^\dagger h|^2 =c^\dagger hh^\dagger c. \tag{6} Thus the maximum over photon polarizations is C. When h\ne0, one orthogonal complex polarization has zero overlap with this one tensor. For real J, the two circular polarizations each give C/2. An unpolarized ensemble, described by I_2/2, also gives C/2; the sum over the two orthonormal input polarizations is C, not that average. Preparation or operation Squared angular overlap Specified polarization c |c^\dagger h|^2 Best matched polarization C Either circular polarization for real J \frac{C}{2} Unpolarized average \frac{C}{2} Sum over two orthonormal polarizations C The overlap vanishes for every photon polarization in this plane exactly when P_EJk=0. Shared spatial directions alone do not decide that equation. For a normalized complex structure J^2=-I, |Jk|=1 still permits P_EJk=0 when the containing geometry allows E perpendicular to Jk. The earlier full-transverse value one therefore does not imply that every photon preparation has nonzero overlap. Several target responses If target response \lambda has tensor M_\lambda, use h_{\lambda a}=\langle B_a,M_\lambda\rangle. For independently distinguishable output responses with nonnegative weights w_\lambda, the input-polarization matrix is W=\sum_\lambda w_\lambda h_\lambda h_\lambda^\dagger, \qquad c^\dagger Wc\geq0. \tag{7} A dark input must be orthogonal to every response with positive weight. Two independent response vectors can make W positive definite, removing the dark polarization present for a single tensor. Contributions to the same coherent output must instead be added as amplitudes before squaring. Equations (1)–(7) are angular and algebraic results. A physical transition amplitude additionally integrates spatial profiles and phases and uses the action's mode normalization. A probability or rate requires temporal dynamics, final-state availability, and incident-flux normalization. Verification and related Polarized photon transition strength extends the frozen source calculation to every target polarization tangent in the adopted spin module, including helicity-sensitive response zeros. polarization_coupling_checks.py checks the projector by an independently assembled orthonormal two-form basis, tests complex inputs, and compares direct matrix pairings with polarization amplitudes in rotated spatial frames. Dimensional magnetic kernel — supplies the assumed two-form term and full-transverse projector. Generalized sector coupling — places the overlap within reciprocal, normalized dynamics of the same field. Bilateral polarization coupling retains both objects' polarization and response. A zero static source overlap does not by itself make the mixed response derivative vanish.

title: Polarized photon transition strength
summary: Summing all spinor response directions gives an exact two-polarization transition matrix for a simple spatial Pauli probe, including helicity-sensitive zeros and a nonzero total-strength bound at every tested depth.
text: Summary: Summing all spinor response directions gives an exact two-polarization transition matrix for a simple spatial Pauli probe, including helicity-sensitive zeros and a nonzero total-strength bound at every tested depth. Include the target's allowed polarization changes The photon-plane calculation compares a fixed target source with a specified photon. An incident wave also perturbs the target. This note computes that response for a particular spatial Pauli term, keeping all polarization variations in the adopted spin module. Work in a finite Euclidean spatial chart of the one nested macroscopic manifold. Let k,e_1,e_2 be orthonormal ordinary spatial vectors, with e_1,e_2 the photon plane and k a propagation direction perpendicular to it. At higher depth these are three selected directions within the containing space, not a separate three-dimensional compartment. Let z be a normalized target spinor. In even dimensions use a selected half-spin representation; the following bivector operators preserve it. Their components describe the spatial field's polarization and do not add physical dimensions. This is a frozen-envelope Pauli benchmark, not the complete electromagnetic current or a derived neutrino coupling. The two spatial probe operators With \gamma(v)=v^a\gamma_a and Euclidean Clifford relations, define T_a=-i\gamma(e_a)\gamma(k),\quad a=1,2, \qquad T_0=-i\gamma(e_1)\gamma(e_2). \tag{1} All three are Hermitian and square to the identity. Direct multiplication using the three orthogonal vectors gives T_1T_2=iT_0,\qquad T_2T_1=-iT_0. \tag{2} A definite complex photon polarization c=(c_1,c_2)^T, c^\dagger c=1, acts through T(c)=c_1T_1+c_2T_2. The actual coupling prefactor, spatial integral and time dependence must still be obtained from the action. Define the three real target polarization components h_a=z^\dagger T_a z,\qquad s=z^\dagger T_0z, \qquad C=h_1^2+h_2^2. \tag{3} For an orthonormal basis u_\lambda of the complete complement z^\perp, the transition amplitudes are u_\lambda^\dagger T(c)z. The source expectation and the orthogonal response are different quantities. Exact transition matrix Completeness of the response basis gives G_{ab}=\sum_\lambda \big(u_\lambda^\dagger T_a z\big)^* \big(u_\lambda^\dagger T_b z\big) =z^\dagger T_a(I-zz^\dagger)T_bz. \tag{4} Using (2), this becomes \boxed{G= \begin{pmatrix} 1-h_1^2&-h_1h_2+is\\ -h_1h_2-is&1-h_2^2 \end{pmatrix}.} \tag{5} Thus the complete squared response in these normalized amplitude units is \sum_\lambda|u_\lambda^\dagger T(c)z|^2=c^\dagger Gc. \tag{6} Its trace, determinant and eigenvalues are \operatorname{tr}G=2-C,\qquad \det G=1-C-s^2, \qquad g_\pm=1-\frac C2\pm\sqrt{s^2+\frac{C^2}{4}}. \tag{7} Positivity implies C+s^2\leq1. Equivalently, these are the three expectations of a Pauli algebra and form a Bloch vector of length at most one. A complex input polarization is dark precisely when it lies in \ker G. Such a kernel exists exactly when C+s^2=1. For a real linear polarization c, the imaginary antisymmetric part drops out and (6) is 1-(c^Th)^2. For circular polarizations, c_\pm=\frac{(1,\pm i)^T}{\sqrt2},\qquad \boxed{c_\pm^\dagger Gc_\pm=1\mp s-\frac C2.} \tag{8} The target's polarization therefore distinguishes the two helicity responses. Averaging the two incident polarizations yields 1-C/2; it is not the squared unperturbed source expectation C/2. A full response cannot be dark to both polarizations Since C\leq1, equation (7) gives the dimension-independent bound \boxed{\operatorname{tr}G\geq1.} \tag{9} Consequently this nonzero simple Pauli coupling cannot annihilate the complete two-polarization response on any normalized pure target spinor. One circular or linear polarization may be blocked; both cannot be blocked simultaneously in the complete module. If h_1=h_2=0, the unperturbed source vanishes but the total transition strength is instead two. For a real polarization operator T with T^2=I, a finite pulse gives an independent exact check: e^{-i\theta T}z=(\cos\theta)z-i(\sin\theta)Tz, \qquad 1-|z^\dagger e^{-i\theta T}z|^2 =\sin^2\theta\big[1-(z^\dagger Tz)^2\big]. \tag{10} This measures departure from the original ray. A nonzero source expectation can still produce an elastic phase response, so (9)–(10) are statements about the orthogonal transition component, not a partition of every possible scattering effect. Five- and six-dimensional isotropic comparison Spin(5) and either Spin(6) half-spin module have four complex components. On both, the subgroup generated by the three operators in (1) consists of two equivalent spin-one-half copies. One can identify the module for this calculation with \mathbb C^2\otimes\mathbb C^2 so that these probes act on the first factor. This tensor notation is a representation decomposition, not a new physical spatial factorization. Uniform spatial rotations of a fixed pure ray give the same invariant probability distribution on \mathbb{CP}^3 in both cases. Spin(5) is transitive there, and its invariant distribution agrees with the Fubini–Study distribution, which is also invariant under Spin(6). The prior isotropic comparison provides the underlying spatial ensemble and its assumptions. Therefore the entire joint distribution of (h_1,h_2,s), and consequently of G, is identical under this specified ensemble. In particular \mathbb E\,h_a^2=\frac15,\qquad \mathbb E\,G=\frac45I_2, \qquad \mathbb E\,(c^\dagger Gc)=\frac45 \tag{11} for any fixed normalized complex photon polarization. The moment follows directly from the normalized pure-state identity \mathbb E(zz^\dagger)^{\otimes2}=(I+\mathrm{Swap})/[4\cdot5]: unitary invariance makes the average proportional to the symmetric projector, whose trace is ten; normalization fixes the coefficient. Each T_a is traceless with \operatorname{tr}T_a^2=4. Correlated spatial preparations and actual mode frequencies must be calculated rather than averaged away. What can still distinguish physical couplings Equation (6) sums unweighted polarization transitions in a fixed profile. It does not impose the energy of the incident photon, include all spatial profile variations, or normalize the incident flux. The action can supply different spatial form factors, kinetic coefficients and accessible frequency spectra. The polarized response spectrum retains those frequency and exposure restrictions. A coupling generated by a higher spatial operation need not reduce to the simple bivectors in (1). For example, rotation-neutral modes cancel a sum of two spatial rotation generators as an operator; (9) does not apply to that sum. Identifying the actual higher-sector source is therefore substantive. The photon having two bound spatial dimensions does not alone select (1) as the complete interaction law. Verification spatial_coupling_mechanism_checks.py constructs independent Clifford representations at depths three, four, five, six and ten. It sums the full response complement, checks (5)–(9) for complex polarized targets, and compares (10) with matrix-exponential evolution. These test the conditional operator calculation, not physical particle rates. Related Photon plane coupling — specifies the two transverse spatial bivectors and the unperturbed source overlap. Isotropic polarization comparison — proves the fixed-source distribution used as the starting comparison. Bilateral polarization coupling — explains why target variations must accompany the incident polarization.

title: Polarized pulse collisions
summary: The derived local displacement action gives exact reciprocal pulse delays while retaining both vector waveforms, and its causal cubic equation identifies where the full spatial response enters.
text: Summary: The derived local displacement action gives exact reciprocal pulse delays while retaining both vector waveforms, and its causal cubic equation identifies where the full spatial response enters. Keep the scope of the effective collision equation The spatial displacement action integrates a specified stationary component field over its two actual bound coordinates. For a displacement X(t,y)\in\mathbb R^2 it gives \mathscr L=-\mathcal T\sqrt{D},\qquad D=(1-|\dot X|^2)(1+|X_y|^2)+(\dot X\cdot X_y)^2. \tag{1} The coefficient \mathcal T is the same spatial integral that normalizes the wave energy. The coordinate y is an existing propagation direction, and X is an actual position of the bound profile. Equation (1) is exact for constant gradients of the completed spatial field. Treating it as a local action for varying gradients defines its leading derivative description. The finite collisions solved below are exact solutions of that local action. They are not asserted to solve the complete finite-width component field: the retarded spatial response supplies its frequency-dependent deformation and outgoing modes. Write reciprocal evolution without a fitted collision rule Let v=\dot X, w=X_y and p=\mathcal T^{-1}\partial\mathscr L/\partial v. The dimensionless Hamiltonian density is h=\sqrt{1+|w|^2+|p|^2+(p\cdot w)^2}. \tag{2} The complete local evolution is \boxed{ \dot X=\frac{p+(p\cdot w)w}{h},\qquad \dot p=\partial_y\frac{w+(p\cdot w)p}{h},\qquad w=X_y.} \tag{3} Its energy and normal momentum above the resting background are E=\mathcal T\int(h-1)\,dy and P_y=-\mathcal T\int p\cdot w\,dy. Both vector polarizations, including their relative phases, remain in (3). Solve a collision by actual spacetime coordinates Take two arbitrary smooth real vector waveforms A(u),B(v) with square-integrable derivatives. Define a=A',\quad b=B',\qquad I_A(u)=\int_{-\infty}^{u}|a(s)|^2ds,\qquad I_B(v)=\int_{-\infty}^{v}|b(s)|^2ds. \tag{4} An exact parametrized solution of (1) is \boxed{ \begin{aligned} t&=\frac{u+v+I_A(u)+I_B(v)}2,\\ y&=\frac{v-u+I_A(u)-I_B(v)}2,\\ X&=A(u)+B(v). \end{aligned}} \tag{5} The two tangent vectors of this sheet in the containing spacetime are Y_u=\left(\frac{1+|a|^2}2,\frac{-1+|a|^2}2,a\right), \qquad Y_v=\left(\frac{1+|b|^2}2,\frac{1-|b|^2}2,b\right). \tag{6} Both are null for the metric dt^2-dy^2-dX^2, and \partial_u\partial_vY=0. Moreover, 2Y_u\cdot Y_v=1-2a\cdot b+|a|^2|b|^2. These identities are the conformal-coordinate minimal-area equation and constraints, proving (5). A sufficient regularity condition is |a(u)|^2|b(v)|^2<1 everywhere. Indeed, the physical null-coordinate map is t-y=u+I_B(v),\qquad t+y=v+I_A(u), \tag{7} with Jacobian 1-|a|^2|b|^2>0. It therefore describes a regular graph in (t,y) for sufficiently small bounded slopes. The formula does not promise a single graph after that condition fails. Extract the two outgoing delays Before overlap, each pulse has its original free waveform. After the opposite pulse has passed, (7) gives \boxed{ X_A^{\rm out}=A(t-y-\Delta_A),\quad \Delta_A=\frac{E_B}{\mathcal T}; \qquad X_B^{\rm out}=B(t+y-\Delta_B),\quad \Delta_B=\frac{E_A}{\mathcal T}.} \tag{8} Here E_A=\mathcal T\int|A'|^2du and E_B=\mathcal T\int|B'|^2dv are the incoming pulse energies. Positive shifts in the arguments' arrival times are delays. Every spatial component and phase of each waveform is retained. These delays are reciprocal and involve the same tension. They hold for linear, elliptical and circular patterns within (1). For this isotropic local action, rotating one linear polarization does not change the delay at fixed pulse energy. That is a derived property of the specified geometry, rather than an imposed compatibility factor. For example, A(u)=\epsilon L e^{-u^2/(2L^2)}e_1 has E_A/\mathcal T=\epsilon^2L\sqrt{\pi}/2. A second Gaussian pulse, in any real unit direction, gives the corresponding delay from its own energy. Restore the causal spatial response at cubic order For a weak displacement, define its trace-free source matrix S=\dot X\dot X^T-X_yX_y^T -\frac12\left(|\dot X|^2-|X_y|^2\right)I_2. \tag{9} Let \mathcal F_{\rm ret} act on each matrix component by the Fourier multiplier F(\lambda\sqrt{(\Omega+i0)^2-q^2}) derived from the full spatial Hessian. With no independent incoming complementary deformation, its eliminated field gives the cubic response equation \boxed{ \Box X_i+ \partial_\mu\!\left[ (\mathcal F_{\rm ret}S)_{ij}\partial^\mu X_j \right]=0 \quad\hbox{through cubic order in the weak field}.} \tag{10} Here \mu runs over t,y. To see its normalization, write the two real quadrupole components as S_1=S_{11} and S_2=S_{12}. The full deformation has radial variables h_A, source fS_A and quadratic kinetic factor \mathcal T\lambda^2/4. Solving their retarded equations gives \tfrac12\langle f,h_A\rangle_w=\mathcal F_{\rm ret}S_A. Variation of their original coupling to S_A(X) produces \mathcal T(\mathcal F_{\rm ret}S)_{ij}\partial^\mu X_j. An independent full-profile check uses \eta_h=\tfrac12(Sx)_i\partial_i n_0\,h(r) and gives Z\int\left[ \partial_i n_0\cdot\partial_j\eta_h+ \partial_j n_0\cdot\partial_i\eta_h \right]d^2x =\mathcal T F_h S_{ij},\qquad F_h=4\int_0^\infty\frac{r^3h(r)}{(1+r^2)^3}\,dr, \tag{10a} where the radius in F_h is scaled by \lambda. This is the change in the actual translation kinetic matrix. Substituting each retarded radial response yields the same force coefficient. This derives (10) from the retained and complementary field equations; one does not vary a dissipative retarded kernel as an ordinary real energy. Setting F=1 gives the cubic expansion of (3). For X=A(t-y)+B(t+y), its leading correction is \delta X=-A'(u)I_B(v)-B'(v)I_A(u), \tag{11} which is exactly the first correction obtained by inverting (7). The full F adds finite-width dispersion and radiation. Polarized spatial radiation calculates that outgoing energy from the same spatial source. The component action and its identification with the master field remain conditional. Neither the exact local delays nor the causal cubic equation assign electric charges or measured elementary-particle interaction rates. Verification polarized_pulse_collision_checks.py checks the actual spacetime tangents and mixed derivatives of (5). A separate normalized variation of the full spatial profile checks (10a). A separate Fourier-space time evolution of the nonlinear Hamiltonian equations (3) checks outgoing vector profiles, both delays, energy and normal momentum for parallel, perpendicular and elliptical inputs. Spatial and time refinement distinguish integration error from a polarization effect. Reports use timestamps and checks survive Python optimization.

title: Polarized response spectrum
summary: A normalized two-sided mode coupling gives an exact finite-time polarization response matrix whose dark inputs depend on both spatial overlap and the target spectrum.
text: Summary: A normalized two-sided mode coupling gives an exact finite-time polarization response matrix whose dark inputs depend on both spatial overlap and the target spectrum. Both preparations and their mode spaces Choose normalized perturbation modes of two objects in the same field \Psi_\infty. Let p\in\mathbb C^m and q\in\mathbb C^n be their amplitudes, with spatial mode inclusions I_a,I_b. The mode counts m,n are not physical spatial dimensions. Both families describe polarized spatial patterns on their actual nested submanifolds. Assume for this benchmark that the retained perturbation equation has a self-adjoint canonical generator i\frac{d}{dt}\begin{pmatrix}p\\q\end{pmatrix} =\begin{pmatrix}H_a&B^\dagger\\B&H_b\end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix}p\\q\end{pmatrix}. \tag{1} The block B is obtained from the spatial variational operator, not chosen solely from the two mode counts. Nonorthogonal families require the full kinetic Gram normalization. Equation (1) preserves \|p\|^2+\|q\|^2 and includes reciprocal response of both objects. These are modes of one field, with no mediator particles. This self-adjoint normal-mode form is an assumption. A general nonlinear Dirac linearization has the ordinary and conjugate blocks derived in Dirac source linearization. It must be analyzed in that full space or reduced to (1) by a justified stable-mode construction; simply discarding its conjugate block is not valid. Coupling between two definite polarizations For normalized source and target directions c\in\mathbb C^m and f\in\mathbb C^n, the specified channel amplitude is \mathcal A(f,c)=f^\dagger Bc. \tag{2} Both polarizations occur explicitly. Reversing these matched channels uses c^\dagger B^\dagger f=\overline{\mathcal A(f,c)}. A zero for one f does not imply Bc=0: another target response may be available. Under unitary changes of either mode basis, B transforms as B\mapsto U_b^\dagger BU_a. Its singular values are invariant and are the same for B and B^\dagger. Thus a reciprocal linear vertex has the same nonzero channel strengths in either direction, even though the actual source may be prepared in the higher sector. For uniform unit-vector preparations in the two mode spaces, \mathbb E_c\|Bc\|^2=\frac{\operatorname{tr}(B^\dagger B)}m, \qquad \mathbb E_f\|B^\dagger f\|^2 =\frac{\operatorname{tr}(B^\dagger B)}n. \tag{3} These different averages describe different preparations. Replacing m,n by spatial depth or by an oscillator count would require a derived identification and occupation rule. Resolve the target's temporal response For a weak prescribed input p(t)=ce^{-i\omega t} and q(0)=0, the target equation in (1) has the exact forced solution q(T)=-i\int_0^T e^{-iH_b(T-t)}Bc\,e^{-i\omega t}dt. \tag{4} This is exact for the driven row. Treating p as unchanged is the leading approximation to the reciprocal system when its depletion is small. It does not remove the B^\dagger q term from the underlying action. Let H_bu_\lambda=\Omega_\lambda u_\lambda in an orthonormal target basis and write b_\lambda=u_\lambda^\dagger B. Integration gives |u_\lambda^\dagger q(T)|^2 =F_T(\Omega_\lambda-\omega)|b_\lambda c|^2, \qquad F_T(\Delta)=T^2\operatorname{sinc}^2\left(\frac{\Delta T}{2}\right), \tag{5} where \operatorname{sinc}(x)=\sin(x)/x and \operatorname{sinc}(0)=1. Summing distinguishable orthogonal output modes yields \boxed{\|q(T)\|^2=c^\dagger W_T(\omega)c, \qquad W_T(\omega)=B^\dagger F_T(H_b-\omega)B\geq0.} \tag{6} The matrix W_T combines the spatial compatibility in B with the target's allowed motions and their frequencies. Its eigenvectors give the input polarizations with greatest and least response during the specified exposure. For one photon plane m=2, its two eigenvalues need not be equal, and neither is set by the number two. Source zeros, spectral zeros, and robust dark inputs Because every term in (6) is nonnegative, c\in\ker W_T(\omega) \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad b_\lambda c=0\ \text{for every }\lambda \text{ with }F_T(\Omega_\lambda-\omega)>0. \tag{7} A finite-time zero can also occur at a zero of the sinc factor. It is not protected against changing the exposure time or frequency. In contrast Bc=0 gives zero driven response for every T and \omega. Conversely, since q(T)=-iTBc+O(T^2), zero response for every sufficiently small T implies Bc=0. If W is positive definite and an omitted perturbation changes it by a Hermitian \delta W, then \lambda_{\min}(W+\delta W) \geq\lambda_{\min}(W)-\|\delta W\|. \tag{8} A positive response bounded above the uncertainty cannot become exactly dark under that perturbation. For a candidate dark unit vector c with Bc=0 and a corrected coupling B+\delta B, \|q(T)\|^2\leq T^2\|\delta B\|^2 \tag{9} in the forced model, because F_T\leq T^2. This gives a quantitative way to distinguish an exact selection rule from a small response caused by an explicitly bounded correction. Coherence and incomplete output spaces For a coherent detector direction f, the measured amplitude is f^\dagger q(T), so contributions from several target modes can interfere. It is not generally the sum of their separate intensities. If the target already has an initial polarization amplitude q_0, its solution includes e^{-iH_bT}q_0 and interference with the driven term. The initial phases of both objects therefore remain relevant. If only a target subspace P is retained, PBc=0 does not establish Bc=0 when (I-P)Bc\ne0. Moreover, P must be invariant under H_b to use PH_bP as a closed generator without a complement response. The projected-current calculation gives a concrete example where omitted modes carry the response. For a finite discrete spectrum, (5) describes reversible excitation and interference; it does not supply an irreversible long-time rate. A continuum with a sufficiently regular spectral density permits the distributional limit F_T(\Delta)/T\to2\pi\delta(\Delta). Applying that limit requires the continuum and weak-depletion assumptions, as discussed in continuum mode memory. Interpreting the resulting norm or flux as an observed cross section still requires the physical incident and detector normalization. Verification polarization_coupling_checks.py checks the displayed identities with independent spatial quadrature, energy variations, or full finite-system evolution as appropriate. These checks verify the declared mathematics and benchmarks, not empirical couplings. Related Reciprocal scattering of spatial modes — includes the wave's backreaction and derives conserved reflection and transmission from the same spatial vertex. Bilateral polarization coupling — distinguishes a background source from the mixed response of two polarized objects. Dirac source linearization — supplies explicit ordinary and conjugate spatial matrix elements from the written nonlinear term. Canonical coupling normalization — fixes the mode metrics before interpreting singular values. Continuum mode memory — states when finite-mode response can be approximated by an irreversible continuum law. Projected Dirac current — shows why a truncated dark subspace need not imply zero full response.

title: Polarized spatial radiation
summary: Both complex pulse polarizations determine an exact outgoing quadrupole source, whose full spatial spectral measure fixes radiated energy and a low-frequency suppression law.
text: Summary: Both complex pulse polarizations determine an exact outgoing quadrupole source, whose full spatial spectral measure fixes radiated energy and a low-frequency suppression law. A response channel of the same spatial field The spatial displacement action uses a declared stationary component field with two ordinary bound coordinates, an existing propagation coordinate y, size \lambda and tension \mathcal T. Two weak incoming displacement pulses are X=A(u)+B(v), where u=t-y, v=t+y. Their derivatives a=A' and b=B' have independent real spatial waveforms and complex Fourier polarizations. The local collision calculation gives conservative reciprocal delays. The full spatial field can also carry energy away in its complementary quadrupole modes. This note calculates that channel to leading order in the weak incoming slopes. It assumes no independent incoming complementary excitation. These modes belong to the same component field; no mediator particle is added. Its identification with the physical master field remains conditional. Keep both complex frequency polarizations The real trace-free source has components S_1=2(a_1b_1-a_2b_2),\qquad S_2=2(a_1b_2+a_2b_1). \tag{1} Use Fourier conventions \widetilde S(\Omega,q)= \int dt\,dy\,e^{i\Omega t-iqy}S(t,y),\qquad \widetilde a(\alpha)=\int du\,e^{i\alpha u}a(u). \tag{2} Since dt\,dy=\tfrac12du\,dv, the product source is exactly \boxed{ \widetilde S(\Omega,q) =C\!\left( \widetilde a\!\left(\frac{\Omega+q}{2}\right), \widetilde b\!\left(\frac{\Omega-q}{2}\right) \right),\qquad C(A,B)= \begin{pmatrix} A_1B_1-A_2B_2\\ A_1B_2+A_2B_1 \end{pmatrix}.} \tag{3} The pairing is complex bilinear; inserting a conjugate would describe a different frequency combination. For an outgoing propagating quadrupole, \Omega>0 and \Omega^2-q^2>0. Thus both arguments \alpha=(\Omega+q)/2 and \beta=(\Omega-q)/2 are positive. The emitted mode samples the sum of two incoming positive frequencies. For arbitrary complex vectors, define the signed circular component h(A)=2\operatorname{Im}(A_1^*A_2). Direct expansion gives \boxed{\|C(A,B)\|^2 =\|A\|^2\|B\|^2+h(A)h(B).} \tag{4} Every amplitude and relative phase of both objects is present. Exchanging the pulses leaves C unchanged. A common rotation through \theta in their actual bound plane rotates C through 2\theta, as required for a quadrupole. Distinguish a radiation zero from no interaction For unit positive-frequency circular vectors in fixed bound-plane axes, e_+=\frac{(1,i)}{\sqrt2},\qquad e_-=\frac{(1,-i)}{\sqrt2}, \tag{5} equation (3) gives the following strengths: Positive-frequency inputs \|C\|^2 Two real unit linear vectors, at any relative angle 1 e_+,e_+ or e_-,e_- 2 e_+,e_- or e_-,e_+ 0 These signs label rotation senses relative to the same physical axes, not an already-established photon-helicity assignment. Because the pulses propagate oppositely, a helicity convention tied to each propagation direction would require a separate sign conversion. If the positive-frequency spectra have these fixed circular vectors, opposite senses cancel the entire leading timelike quadrupole source. Real waveforms retain the conjugate negative-frequency components. Their difference-frequency source can remain nonzero and spacelike. Consequently the conservative interaction and its delay can survive while this outgoing radiation channel vanishes. An exactly one-sided polarization statement concerns the full Fourier spectrum. A Gaussian envelope times a real circular carrier generally has a small opposite-frequency tail; its cancellation is correspondingly approximate. Narrow-band intuition must not silently remove that tail. Derive the emitted energy from the actual kinetic norm The retarded response defines a positive dimensionless radial spectral measure by F(z)=\int_0^\infty\frac{d\mu(\ell)}{\ell-z^2}, \qquad \int\frac{d\mu(\ell)}{\ell}=1. \tag{6} Its radial operator is the full spatial quadrupole Hessian, with f(r)=8/(1+r^2) and d\mu=\tfrac12d\langle f,P_\ell f\rangle_w. No radiation weight is fitted. In a normalized spatial eigenmode with eigenvalue \ell, the amplitude h_\ell(t,q) obeys \ddot h_\ell+\left(q^2+\frac{\ell}{\lambda^2}\right)h_\ell =\frac{f_\ell}{\lambda^2}S(t,q). \tag{7} Its full-field kinetic energy has coefficient \mathcal T\lambda^2/4 for each real quadrupole component. Solving (7) with zero incoming data and evaluating its outgoing energy therefore gives \boxed{ E_{\rm out} =\frac{\mathcal T}{2\lambda^2} \int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{dq}{2\pi} \int_0^\infty d\mu(\ell)\, \left\| \widetilde S\!\left( \sqrt{q^2+\ell/\lambda^2},q \right) \right\|^2.} \tag{8} This is the leading emitted energy, fourth order in the incoming weak slopes. The integral is positive and symmetric under exchanging the two pulses, which sends q to -q. It includes the full radial continuum and both quadrupole polarizations. For a real forced oscillator, the same normalization follows directly: after the source has ceased, |\dot h|^2+\omega^2|h|^2=|\widetilde f(\omega)|^2. Combining the q and -q components gives (8) for real spatial fields. This also fixes the factors of two from Fourier and kinetic conventions. Retain the energy lost by each incoming pulse Write dE_{\rm out}(\ell,q) for the positive measure in (8), including both quadrupole components, and put \Omega=\sqrt{q^2+\ell/\lambda^2}. The outgoing normal momentum is P_{\rm out}=\int(q/\Omega)\,dE_{\rm out}. The same source coupling fixes the two leading pulse energy losses: \boxed{ \Delta E_A=\int\frac{\Omega+q}{2\Omega}\,dE_{\rm out}, \qquad \Delta E_B=\int\frac{\Omega-q}{2\Omega}\,dE_{\rm out}.} \tag{8a} Both are nonnegative. Their sum is E_{\rm out}, while their difference is P_{\rm out}, as required by the opposite incoming propagation directions. Equivalently, their weights are \alpha/(\alpha+\beta) and \beta/(\alpha+\beta). This partition can be checked directly from the full coupling. In dimensionless radial coordinates its term is \tfrac{\mathcal T}{2}\sum_{c=1}^2\langle h_c,fS_c\rangle_w. Varying the first incoming waveform by its time translation gives \partial_uS_c; varying the second gives \partial_vS_c. Thus the integrated work removed from the first pulse is -\tfrac{\mathcal T}{2}\sum_{c=1}^2\int dt\,dy\, \langle h_c,f\partial_uS_c\rangle_w, and similarly for the second. Their sum integrates by parts to the work on the complementary field. Using its retarded solution supplies exactly (8a). There is no independently assigned absorption coefficient for either pulse. The losses refer to the outgoing complement at leading fourth order in weak slopes, with the retained right- and left-moving wave energies computed from their reciprocal response. The local conservative delays are part of the same expansion, but the local action alone omits these finite-width losses. Obtain the long-pulse law The outgoing low-frequency response derived from the complete spatial Hessian is \operatorname{Im}F(\omega+i0)=\pi\omega^2/4+o(\omega^2). Thus the continuum density near threshold is d\mu/d\ell=\ell/4+o(\ell). For pulses concentrated at frequencies small compared with 1/\lambda, substitute this into (8) and change variables to \alpha=(\Omega+q)/2, \beta=(\Omega-q)/2: \boxed{ \frac{E_{\rm out}}{\mathcal T} =\frac{\lambda^2}{\pi} \int_0^\infty d\alpha\int_0^\infty d\beta\, \alpha\beta(\alpha+\beta) \|C(\widetilde a(\alpha),\widetilde b(\beta))\|^2 +\hbox{higher-frequency corrections}.} \tag{9} The Jacobian is d(\Omega^2-q^2)\,dq=4(\alpha+\beta)\,d\alpha\,d\beta. The powers in (9) follow from the spatial spectral density and source derivatives, rather than a presumed frequency filter.
