For equal Gaussian displacement pulses in real unit directions, A(u)=\epsilon L e^{-u^2/(2L^2)}e_a,\qquad B(v)=\epsilon L e^{-v^2/(2L^2)}e_b,\qquad L\gg\lambda, \tag{10} the derivative spectrum satisfies |\widetilde a(\alpha)|^2= 2\pi\epsilon^2L^4\alpha^2e^{-L^2\alpha^2}. The elementary Gaussian moments in (9) give \boxed{ \frac{E_{\rm out}}{\mathcal T} =\frac{3\pi^{3/2}}2\, \frac{\epsilon^4\lambda^2}{L} +o\!\left(\frac{\epsilon^4\lambda^2}{L}\right),\qquad \frac{E_{\rm out}}{E_A+E_B} =\frac{3\pi}{2}\epsilon^2 \left(\frac{\lambda}{L}\right)^2 +o\!\left(\epsilon^2\frac{\lambda^2}{L^2}\right).} \tag{11} The small-frequency limit here is L/\lambda\to\infty at fixed weak slope, within the leading weak-field radiation calculation. Higher orders in the slope are separate corrections. The incoming pair energy is E_A+E_B=\mathcal T\epsilon^2L\sqrt\pi. For unequal widths L_A,L_B and weak slopes \epsilon_A,\epsilon_B in real unit directions, the corresponding leading individual losses are \boxed{ \frac{\Delta E_A}{\mathcal T} =\frac{3\pi^{3/2}}4 \frac{\lambda^2\epsilon_A^2\epsilon_B^2}{L_A}, \qquad \frac{\Delta E_B}{\mathcal T} =\frac{3\pi^{3/2}}4 \frac{\lambda^2\epsilon_A^2\epsilon_B^2}{L_B}.} \tag{12} The shorter pulse contributes more emitted energy at fixed slopes. Swapping the complete incoming profiles swaps the two results. For \lambda=1, the complete radial spectral calculation gives E_{\rm out}/E_{\rm soft} approximately 0.99717, 0.99986 and 0.999992 at L=5,10,20, with agreement under radial refinement. No coefficient is changed between these comparisons. This establishes a concrete frequency-dependent suppression and a two-polarization cancellation for one specified outgoing channel. Its frequency is the actual incoming spatial waveform frequency, as distinguished in Source frequencies in spatial coupling. The calculation does not assign a neutrino mode, an electric charge, or a measured electromagnetic or weak rate. Verification polarized_pulse_collision_checks.py checks the complex source identity, exchange symmetry, common spatial rotation and both circular senses. Independent Fourier transforms of real multi-frequency waveforms retain all conjugate components and check the timelike cancellation alongside its nonzero spacelike source. Direct forced-mode time integration checks the emitted-energy normalization against an independent temporal Fourier integral. Unequal-width pulses additionally test both direct source-work integrals against (8a) and the actual outgoing mode energy. A separate full radial eigensystem and source measure evaluate (8), with radial resolution and outer-domain refinement, and recover (11). The companion nonlinear evolution tests the conservative pulse delays. Reports have timestamps and checks survive Python optimization.

title: Radial dynamics of two-frequency fields
summary: An exact map from complex radial motion to the full two-frequency spatial field separates number norm from kinetic weight and transfers radial dynamics, source response and instability without a dimension-specific symmetry assumption.
text: Summary: An exact map from complex radial motion to the full two-frequency spatial field separates number norm from kinetic weight and transfers radial dynamics, source response and instability without a dimension-specific symmetry assumption. Extend the stationary construction to radial motion The two-frequency current construction uses two stationary components of one spatial field. Its radial dynamics can also be derived exactly when the profile changes with time. The map below is defined on actual radial functions over d ordinary macroscopic spatial directions, with one existing containing normal direction used for the partner matrix \alpha_y. All sectors remain submanifolds of the one nested physical manifold. Choose fixed unit rest polarizations w_1,w_2 satisfying \beta w_j=w_j. They need not coincide. For arbitrary complex radial functions u=(F,G), define \Phi_w[u]\,(x)=\frac{F(r)w+iG(r)\alpha(\widehat x)w} {\sqrt{\Omega_{d-1}}},\qquad \|u\|_r^2=\int_0^\infty(|F|^2+|G|^2)r^{d-1}dr. \tag{1} Here \Omega_{d-1} is the area of the unit sphere. The functions obey regularity at the origin and the decay needed for the stated integrals and integrations by parts. For constants a,b, put \boxed{\Psi[u]=a\Phi_{w_1}[u]+b\alpha_y\Phi_{w_2}[u^*], \quad n=|a|^2+|b|^2,\quad s=|a|^2-|b|^2>0.} \tag{2} Conjugation in u^* acts on the radial functions F,G. It does not conjugate the fixed spatial Clifford matrices or the chosen rest polarization. Equation (2) defines a real-linear map into the full field. It does not assume a global antilinear symmetry on arbitrary spatial fields. When a two-frequency spatial symmetry exists derives the separate matrix and scalar-interference requirements for such a global map, including its compatibility with normal propagation. The scalar source remains radial pointwise The Clifford relations give \Phi_{w_1}[u]^\dagger\beta\alpha_y\Phi_{w_2}[u^*]=0. \tag{3} The diagonal terms connect opposite \beta eigenspaces and vanish. The two radial cross terms cancel because their coefficient is F^*G^*-G^*F^*=0 and \beta\alpha_y commutes with \alpha(\widehat x). This holds for complex F,G and both independent rest polarizations. Consequently \boxed{\Psi^\dagger\beta\Psi =\frac{s}{\Omega_{d-1}}(|F|^2-|G|^2).} \tag{4} The scalar center stays at the origin whenever its defining scalar normalization is nonzero. Its second-moment tensor is M_\sigma=(sT/d)I_d, where T[u]=\int_0^\infty r^2(|F|^2-|G|^2)r^{d-1}dr. \tag{5} Thus the common scalar moment interaction g_0 gives \mathfrak m(r)=m_0+(g_0s/d)T[u]r^2. A nonlinear radial equation generates the full spatial solution The real radial Dirac differential operator is H_r[u]= \begin{pmatrix} \mathfrak m(r)&\partial_r+(d-1)/r\\ -\partial_r&-\mathfrak m(r) \end{pmatrix}. \tag{6} It is self-adjoint on the appropriate radial domain with measure r^{d-1}dr. Suppose \boxed{i\partial_tu=H_r[u]u.} \tag{7} The field \Phi_w[u] then satisfies the complete bound-coordinate Dirac equation. Since (6) has real coefficients, the conjugate radial functions satisfy i\partial_tu^*=-H_r[u]u^*. Anticommutation of the full bound operator with \alpha_y supplies that same negative sign for the second term of (2). Both terms therefore solve the full spatial equation with precisely the scalar source in (4). This proves an exact invariant radial family, uniform in the normal coordinate y. A varying y-dependent amplitude or an angular shape perturbation requires the additional spatial dynamics. The complete periodic response retains those possibilities rather than assuming this radial family exhausts the field. For a stationary real profile u_0, u(t)=u_0e^{-iMt} makes (2) the original two-frequency solution. Time-dependent complex profiles in (7) also give full nonlinear spatial solutions; the construction is not confined to harmonic motion. Number norm and kinetic normalization have different weights The positive and normal-partner radial frames are orthogonal after integration over the actual bound spatial directions. For variations \delta u,\delta v, equation (2) gives \boxed{ \begin{aligned} \|\Psi[u]\|^2&=n\|u\|_r^2,\\ \operatorname{Re}\langle\delta\Psi[u],\delta\Psi[v]\rangle &=n\operatorname{Re}\langle\delta u,\delta v\rangle_r,\\ \operatorname{Im}\langle\delta\Psi[u],\delta\Psi[v]\rangle &=s\operatorname{Im}\langle\delta u,\delta v\rangle_r. \end{aligned}} \tag{8} The second component is conjugated, so it reverses the imaginary part of the radial inner product. At n=1, the map preserves the real perturbation norm exactly. Its symplectic form, and hence the first-order kinetic term, instead has weight s. Let H_{r,0} be (6) with the bare scalar coefficient m_0 and no self-interaction. The full energy restricted to (2) is \boxed{\mathcal E_{\rm full} =s\langle u,H_{r,0}u\rangle_r+ \frac{g_0s^2}{2d}T[u]^2 =s\,\mathcal E_{r,g_0s}[u].} \tag{9} The kinetic term has the same overall factor s. Therefore the complete restricted action is s times the radial action with coefficient g_0s, and variation gives (7) for fixed a,b. The amplitudes and their relative polarizations remain additional possible variations outside this restricted calculation. For a radial scalar moment, a tangent source variation has the form \delta(sT)=2s\operatorname{Re}\langle u,Q\delta u\rangle_r, where Q is the signed radial second-moment operator. In the canonical coordinate \xi=\sqrt{s}\,\delta u, this becomes \boxed{\delta(sT)=2\sqrt{s}\operatorname{Re}\langle u,Q\xi\rangle_r.} \tag{10} Both the changing profile and its kinetic weight must enter the normalized coupling vertex. Unit total number norm alone does not determine the normalization of every collective coordinate. Radial instability is inherited Let u_0e^{-iMt} be a radial stationary solution at coefficient g_0s. A growing perturbation of its radial equation maps through (2) into a perturbation of the full two-frequency field. At n=1, equation (8) preserves its norm at every time. A radial exponential growth rate is therefore preserved by the map, including an oscillating growing mode. The negative-frequency component cannot remove that instability. This statement is conditional on the radial instability being present. It does not assert that every scalar Dirac source is unstable. The zero-bare-mass moment branches already have such modes. Direct nonlinear evolution of the five- and six-dimensional radial equations confirms their transfer through (2), while both the full number norm and energy remain conserved. A phase rotation of the stationary background should be removed when comparing a nonlinear perturbation with a tangent mode. If its real linearization has eigenvalue \lambda with nonzero imaginary part, the physical radial tangent evolves as \operatorname{Re}(e^{\lambda t}v) in real coordinates. Retaining only e^{\operatorname{Re}\lambda t}\operatorname{Re}v would miss its oscillation and give an incorrect verification. The current retains both polarizations and the radial phase Integrating the normal number current gives \boxed{\int j_y\,dx =2\operatorname{Re}\left[ \bar a b\,\langle w_1,w_2\rangle \int_0^\infty(F^{*2}+G^{*2})r^{d-1}dr\right].} \tag{11} For a real unit stationary profile this reduces to a 2M oscillation, with an additional factor from the overlap of the two rest polarizations. Orthogonal rest polarizations can remove this integrated normal-current oscillation. That is a statement about one integrated current; local bound-direction currents and other response channels still need to be calculated. The current in (11) is the spatial number current of the single Dirac field. Identifying its projection with a physical photon source remains a separate dynamical step. A readjusted stationary current clock The frequency of a nearby stationary branch changes when its scalar source changes. Add an isotropic coefficient f_{\rm ext} multiplying r^2/\sqrt d. On the zero-bare-mass branch, write the total quadratic coefficient as A to distinguish it from the amplitude a in (2). Self-consistency and spatial scaling give A=\frac{f_{\rm ext}}{\sqrt d}+\frac{g_0s}{d}T(A),\qquad T(A)=\frac{M(A)}{3A},\qquad M(A)\propto A^{1/3}. \tag{12} At zero external coefficient, \boxed{\frac{dA}{df_{\rm ext}}=\frac{3}{5\sqrt d},\qquad \frac{dM}{df_{\rm ext}}=\frac{M}{5A\sqrt d}.} \tag{13} The frozen-profile scalar matrix element is T/\sqrt d=M/(3A\sqrt d). Profile readjustment reduces that derivative by a factor 3/5 in this specific homogeneous source model. Independent stationary solves verify (13). Following the derivative as an actual slow dynamical evolution would also require stability; a stationary branch derivative does not supply it. Verification radial_bifrequency_checks.py uses arbitrary complex radial profiles and independent rest polarizations. Full spatial quadrature checks the scalar density, center, moments, number current, tangent metric and kinetic form. Independent finite derivatives in every bound coordinate verify (7) as an actual spatial field equation. A nonlinear radial trajectory and its reconstructed two-component field check the source equation, conserved norm and energy, and the complete oscillating growth mode. Separate stationary profile solves check the current-clock derivative. Reports preserve previous runs with timestamped filenames and all checks remain active under Python optimization. Related Two-frequency spatial Dirac currents — supplies the stationary family extended here. Periodic spatial source response — retains normal propagation and angular motions outside the radial family. Self-consistent scalar Dirac moment modes — supplies the radial equation, scaling and stability calculation. Canonical coupling normalization — explains why a source coefficient must be combined with its kinetic normalization. Complete radial polarization fields allows independent complex vector profiles in both radial components. That separate family closes under the local scalar equation in even and odd dimensions and retains the full tangential current. It does not assume the two components share one scalar radial profile or require a partner normal matrix.

title: Reciprocal scattering of spatial modes
summary: A solved conservative wave model turns a two-sided spatial overlap into reflection and transmission, separating protected polarization mismatch from narrow resonances and coherent transparency.
text: Summary: A solved conservative wave model turns a two-sided spatial overlap into reflection and transmission, separating protected polarization mismatch from narrow resonances and coherent transparency. From an allowed overlap to an actual encounter A nonzero geometric vertex does not specify how much of an incident wave scatters. The target responds, and that response changes the wave which drives it. This note solves that reciprocal problem in a conservative mode benchmark, including both incident polarizations and all retained target shape modes. The variables are modes of the one field on the nested macroscopic spatial manifold. The propagating modes represent a chosen physical propagation direction, with their bound transverse profiles already included in their normalization. The target variables represent localized spatial changes of the same field. They are not additional mediator particles or additional physical spatial dimensions. The model is conditional on a self-adjoint first-order mode reduction. A general Dirac linearization retains the ordinary and conjugate blocks in Dirac source linearization; reducing it to the form below requires justification. The lattice dispersion below is an exact solvable benchmark, not a proposed photon dispersion law. One reciprocal quadratic energy Let a_n\in\mathbb C^p, n\in\mathbb Z, describe p propagating polarization amplitudes on a line, and let b\in\mathbb C^m describe the target response modes. Take E=-J\sum_n\left(a_n^\dagger a_{n+1}+a_{n+1}^\dagger a_n\right) +b^\dagger H_b b+b^\dagger Va_0+a_0^\dagger V^\dagger b, \tag{1} with J>0, H_b=H_b^\dagger and an m\times p spatial vertex V. The two preparations enter through the target profiles which determine V and through the incident polarization. Their canonical normalization must come from the field action. A shared frequency offset can be added to all modes if positive absolute frequencies are required; the calculation uses frequencies relative to that offset and sets \hbar=1. Variation yields i\dot a_n=-J(a_{n-1}+a_{n+1})+\delta_{n0}V^\dagger b, \qquad i\dot b=H_bb+Va_0. \tag{2} The conserved mode norm is \sum_n\|a_n\|^2+\|b\|^2. Both appearances of V in (2) are fixed by the same energy. No independently chosen one-way response coefficient is allowed. The scalar version belongs to the exactly solvable family of discrete wave resonance models studied by Miroshnichenko and Kivshar. The following matrix formulas are derived directly from (2). Solve the incoming and outgoing wave equations Choose 0<k<\pi. A free wave has relative frequency and positive group velocity \varepsilon=-2J\cos k,\qquad v=2J\sin k. \tag{3} For an incident polarization c, use the stationary amplitudes a_n=e^{ikn}c+e^{-ikn}r\quad(n\leq0), \qquad a_n=e^{ikn}t\quad(n\geq0). \tag{4} The value at the shared site gives t=c+r. Substitution into its original difference equation gives iv r=V^\dagger b. Combining that equation with the target equation gives D(\varepsilon)=\varepsilon I-H_b+\frac{i}{v}VV^\dagger, \qquad \boxed{b=D^{-1}Vc,\quad r=\mathsf r c=-\frac{i}{v}V^\dagger D^{-1}Vc,\quad t=\mathsf t c=(I+\mathsf r)c.} \tag{5} The inverse is evaluated with outgoing boundary conditions. If an exact decoupled target eigenmode makes it singular, use the limiting resolvent on the coupled subspace; an unexcited dark bound mode does not spoil the scattering solution. The term iVV^\dagger/v is the response into the propagating modes of the same field. Its size and sign have been derived from the spatial junction equation, not inserted as a phenomenological loss rate. Exact flux conservation Because D-D^\dagger=2iVV^\dagger/v, the inverse identity gives D^{-1}-D^{-\dagger} =-\frac{2i}{v}D^{-\dagger}VV^\dagger D^{-1}. Consequently \mathsf r+\mathsf r^\dagger=-2\mathsf r^\dagger\mathsf r, \qquad \boxed{\mathsf r^\dagger\mathsf r+\mathsf t^\dagger\mathsf t=I.} \tag{6} The two-port scattering matrix and its second unitarity identity are S=\begin{pmatrix}\mathsf r&\mathsf t\\\mathsf t&\mathsf r\end{pmatrix}, \qquad \mathsf r^\dagger\mathsf t+\mathsf t^\dagger\mathsf r=0, \qquad S^\dagger S=I. \tag{7} All propagating polarizations here have the same group velocity. If their dispersions differ, the flux metric must be included. Complex polarized targets need not give S=S^T while that preparation is held fixed: time reversal transforms the target and probe preparations as well. Adjoint terms in one energy establish conservative mutual coupling; they do not erase those polarization conditions. One shape channel: exact mismatch and a narrow resonance Let there be one target mode of frequency \Omega, and write V=gq^\dagger, where q^\dagger q=1 is the normalized spatial coupling direction in the two incident polarizations. Then P=q q^\dagger,\qquad \delta=\varepsilon-\Omega, \qquad \Gamma(\varepsilon)=\frac{g^2}{v(\varepsilon)}, \qquad \mathsf r=-\frac{i\Gamma}{\delta+i\Gamma}P. \tag{8} For c^\dagger c=1, the reflected fraction is \boxed{\mathcal R(\varepsilon,c) =\frac{\Gamma^2}{\delta^2+\Gamma^2}|q^\dagger c|^2.} \tag{9} This separates two effects with different physical meanings: If q^\dagger c=0, the target is never driven: b=0, r=0, t=c. This is a geometric polarization mismatch for the specified channel. For the matched polarization c=q, any nonzero g gives complete reflection at \delta=0. A small coupling makes the resonance narrow; it does not make its peak small. Away from a band edge and at weak coupling, v varies little across the resonance. Its full width at half maximum is approximately 2\Gamma, and its integrated reflected spectral weight is approximately \pi\Gamma. The exact expression remains (9) with its energy-dependent velocity. A broad incident spectrum can therefore scatter weakly even when a finely tuned monochromatic wave scatters strongly. For a quadrupole channel with g=g_0\cos(2\theta) from transition-density coupling, the width scales as \cos^2(2\theta). At exactly zero overlap the channel closes. For arbitrarily small nonzero overlap its ideal resonant peak can remain large. The limits of zero coupling and exact resonant frequency do not commute. Real finite-time preparations must be evaluated with their actual bandwidth. Coherent transparency can retain target motion Take one incident polarization and two target modes, H_b=\begin{pmatrix}-\Omega&0\\0&\Omega\end{pmatrix}, \qquad V=\begin{pmatrix}g\\g\end{pmatrix},\qquad\Omega\ne0. At the central relative frequency \varepsilon=0, (5) has b=\frac g\Omega\begin{pmatrix}1\\-1\end{pmatrix}c, \qquad V^\dagger b=0,\qquad r=0,\qquad t=c. \tag{10} The two target responses cancel in the outgoing source while both are nonzero. This is a frequency-specific transparency, unlike the invariant input nullspace \ker V. It illustrates why observing transmission alone does not establish that the incoming pattern never engaged the target. Independent spatial wavepacket check The diagnostic evolves (2) directly on 501 sites with two polarizations and one target mode. Before evaluating it, the benchmark fixes J=1, g=0.6, \Omega=0, carrier k=\pi/2, an incident Gaussian intensity width 12 centred at site -80, and final time 100. The boundaries are at \pm250, outside the relevant encounter and outgoing packets. The target direction is q=(\cos0.43,e^{0.71i}\sin0.43)^T; its complex polarization is retained. Integration of (9) over the incoming packet spectrum predicts matched reflection 0.8590726693. Direct evolution gives: incident polarization reflected norm transmitted norm q 0.859071525 0.140926211 c_\perp, q^\dagger c_\perp=0 below 10^{-27} 1.000000000 (q+c_\perp)/\sqrt2 0.429535762 0.570463105 Reflected and transmitted packets are counted outside 25 sites from the target. Their values agree with the integrated stationary prediction to within 1.2\times10^{-6}; a small remainder is still near the target at the finite stopping time. The full evolving norm and energy are conserved. The dark input leaves the target unexcited throughout the sampled evolution. These are model units and mode norms. They are not measured particle cross sections or an assignment of a lattice to physical space. Consequence for the coupling mechanism Shape and polarization enter the spatial vertex. Reciprocal field dynamics then determine its resonant enhancement, interference and outgoing flux. An exact rotation-neutral source can close a specified vertex entirely. A small but nonzero overlap instead requires a bandwidth and spectrum calculation before it can explain rare scattering. To apply this result across the particle hierarchy, derive V, H_b, the continuum dispersion and the background preparation from the same field action. The higher spatial geometry may determine the full vertex; the two photon polarizations specify the incident channel on which it acts. Verification and related spatial_coupling_mechanism_checks.py checks the unreduced spatial equations, multichannel unitarity, a protected dark input, resonant reflection, coherent transparency and full wavepacket evolution. The propagating lattice is solved directly for the final check; the scattering formula is not used to evolve it. Transition-density coupling — supplies spatial vertices with both shape preparations retained. Polarized response spectrum — gives finite-exposure response before completing the reciprocal scattering problem. Coherent spatial overlap — includes spatial phase and interference in the input source profiles.

title: Retarded displacement response
summary: The full spatial quadrupole Hessian gives a positive frequency-dependent interaction kernel, with a derived logarithmic soft correction and outgoing radiation into modes of the same field.
text: Summary: The full spatial quadrupole Hessian gives a positive frequency-dependent interaction kernel, with a derived logarithmic soft correction and outgoing radiation into modes of the same field. Keep the deformation sourced by both waves The spatial displacement calculation uses the declared component action S=\tfrac Z2\int\partial_\mu n\cdot\partial^\mu n, n^2=1, with profile n_0(x)=\frac{(2\lambda x_1,2\lambda x_2,|x|^2-\lambda^2)} {|x|^2+\lambda^2},\qquad \mathcal T=4\pi Z. \tag{1} The x coordinates are the two ordinary bound spatial directions. The existing normal coordinate y carries propagation. The coefficients of n add no physical spatial dimensions, and this component action remains to be derived from the master field before identifying its waves as photons. Opposite pulses have displacement X=A(t-y)+B(t+y) and derivatives a=A',b=B'. Their trace-free spatial source is S=2(ab^T+ba^T-a\cdot b\,I_2),\qquad \mathcal R=S_{ij}\left[ \partial_i\partial_jn_0+ (\partial_i n_0\cdot\partial_jn_0)n_0 \right]. \tag{2} The complete static Hessian \mathcal J gives the response \eta_0=\tfrac12(Sx)_i\partial_i n_0 with \mathcal J\eta_0=-\mathcal R. Its static energy norm is finite, while its canonical L^2 norm diverges logarithmically. A frequency-independent elimination therefore needs to be replaced by the actual retarded spatial inverse. The exact one-way waves remain those of Null spatial pulses. Reduce the full spatial Hessian without discarding its norm Write a radial quadrupole variation as \eta_h(x)=\frac12(Sx)_i\partial_i n_0(x)\,h(r). \tag{3} The constrained Hessian acts exactly as \boxed{ \mathcal J\eta_h=\eta_{\mathcal H_\lambda h},\qquad \mathcal H_\lambda h =-h''+\left(-\frac3r+\frac{4r}{r^2+\lambda^2}\right)h' +\frac8{r^2+\lambda^2}h.} \tag{4} This follows by differentiating (3) in the full three-component field equation, including the constraint terms. The radial kinetic measure is w_\lambda(r)\,dr=\frac{r^3}{(r^2+\lambda^2)^2}\,dr. \tag{5} Consequently \mathcal H_\lambda =-\frac1{w_\lambda}\frac d{dr} \left(w_\lambda\frac d{dr}\right) +\frac8{r^2+\lambda^2}. \tag{6} Its quadratic form is positive. Regularity is imposed at r=0. At nonzero frequency the boundary condition is outgoing at infinity, or decaying for an imaginary frequency. These conditions belong to the same physical spatial field as the incoming modes. Let s=S_{11}+iS_{12}, so |s|^2=4|a|^2|b|^2. Direct spatial integration supplies the complete normalization: Z\|\eta_h\|^2 =2\pi Z\lambda^2|s|^2 \int_0^\infty w_\lambda(r)|h(r)|^2dr. \tag{7} The complex number s records the two real quadrupole components. It does not replace either wave's complex frequency amplitudes. Define the common frequency-dependent interaction Scale r by \lambda and use dimensionless frequency z. In this paragraph \lambda=1 inside the radial operator. Define (\mathcal H_1-z^2)h_z=\frac8{1+r^2}, \qquad \boxed{F(z)=4\int_0^\infty \frac{r^3}{(1+r^2)^3}h_z(r)\,dr.} \tag{8} For \operatorname{Im}z>0, this is the retarded inverse. For a Fourier component e^{-i\Omega t+iqy}, its argument is z=\lambda\sqrt{(\Omega+i0)^2-q^2}, with the outgoing branch. In particular, two opposite positive-frequency waves have \Omega^2-q^2=4\omega_A\omega_B. Equation (8) is one radial response for both quadrupole polarizations. It gives, with the source amplitude factored as in (3), \boxed{ Z\langle\mathcal R, (\mathcal J-(\Omega+i0)^2+q^2)^{-1}\mathcal R\rangle =\mathcal T|s|^2F(z).} \tag{9} The static solution is h_0=1, hence F(0)=1. It is a finite-energy form limit, not an L^2(w_1\,dr) eigenvector; the constant radial function has a logarithmically divergent kinetic norm. The conservative static quartic term is therefore \tfrac12\mathcal T|s|^2=2\mathcal T|a|^2|b|^2, as independently derived from the exact moving profile. At finite frequency, (9) supplies the response and its delay. A retarded inverse describes causal response; its dissipative part must not be varied as if it were an ordinary real instantaneous energy. The full field action remains the conservative system. Eliminating its outgoing modes has the same meaning as Continuum mode memory. There are no added mediator particles. Positivity and spectral normalization On the positive radial domain, F(z)=\int_0^\infty\frac{d\mu(\ell)}{\ell-z^2}, \qquad d\mu\ge0. \tag{10} The source and kinetic measure in (8), not a fitted weight, determine \mu. Direct radial integrals give \boxed{ \int\frac{d\mu(\ell)}{\ell}=1,\qquad \int d\mu(\ell)=\frac83,\qquad \int\ell\,d\mu(\ell)=\frac{64}{5}.} \tag{11} For example, the last two are \tfrac12\langle f,f\rangle_w and \tfrac12\langle f,\mathcal H_1f\rangle_w, with f=8/(1+r^2). They reduce to convergent rational integrals. Thus 0<F(i\xi)<1 for \xi>0, and it decreases with \xi. The same positive measure gives \frac8{3\xi^2}-\frac{64}{5\xi^4} \le F(i\xi)\le\frac8{3\xi^2}. \tag{12} The lower bound is useful at large \xi. It follows from (\ell+\xi^2)^{-1} =\xi^{-2}-\ell\xi^{-4} +\ell^2/[\xi^4(\ell+\xi^2)]. Derive the logarithmic low-frequency correction For z=i\xi, \xi>0, the inner radial expansion starts with h_{i\xi}(r)=1-\frac{\xi^2}{8}(r^2+2)+\cdots, \qquad \mathcal H_1\left(\frac{r^2+2}{8}\right)=1. \tag{13} It ceases to be uniform when r approaches 1/\xi. In the outer coordinate t=\xi r, the leading equation is -h_{\rm out}''+\frac1t h_{\rm out}' +\left(1+\frac8{t^2}\right)h_{\rm out} =\frac8{t^2}. \tag{14} The decaying solution which matches (13) is h_{\rm out}(t)=\frac8{t^2}-tK_3(t) =1-\frac{t^2}{8}+O(t^4|\log t|). \tag{15} Choose 1\ll R\ll1/\xi. Substitution into (8) gives the inner contribution to 1-F as \xi^2(\tfrac12\log R-\tfrac18)+o(\xi^2). The outer contribution is evaluated by \begin{aligned} 4\int_\epsilon^\infty \frac{1-8/t^2+tK_3(t)}{t^3}\,dt &=\frac2{\epsilon^2}-\frac8{\epsilon^4} +\frac{4K_2(\epsilon)}{\epsilon^2}\\ &=\frac12\log\frac1\epsilon +\frac{\log2-\gamma_{\!E}}2+\frac38+o(1). \end{aligned} \tag{16} The derivative identity d(K_2(t)/t^2)/dt=-K_3(t)/t^2 proves the first line. The integer-order expansions are recorded in NIST DLMF §10.31. With \epsilon=\xi R, the arbitrary matching radius cancels: \boxed{ F(i\xi)=1-\xi^2\left[ \frac12\log\frac1\xi+c_0 \right]+o(\xi^2),\qquad c_0=\frac14+\frac{\log2-\gamma_{\!E}}2.} \tag{17} Control the approximation with the positive spatial form A composite trial field is \widetilde h=(1-\xi^2/4)h_{\rm out}(\xi r). It matches both terms of the inner expansion at fixed r. Put A_\xi=\mathcal H_1+\xi^2 and d=A_\xi\widetilde h-f. The exact variational identity gives F_{\rm trial} =\langle f,\widetilde h\rangle_w -\frac12\langle\widetilde h,A_\xi\widetilde h\rangle_w, \qquad 0\le F(i\xi)-F_{\rm trial} =\frac12\langle d,A_\xi^{-1}d\rangle_w. \tag{18} Since A_\xi\ge 8/(1+r^2)+\xi^2 in quadratic-form order, \boxed{ 0\le F(i\xi)-F_{\rm trial} \le\frac12\int_0^\infty \frac{w_1(r)|d(r)|^2}{8/(1+r^2)+\xi^2}\,dr.} \tag{19} This provides an explicit error control, rather than an assumed gap. For H=h_{\rm out}(\xi r), its residual is d=\left(1-\frac{\xi^2}{4}\right) \left[-\frac{4H'}{r(1+r^2)} +\frac{8(1-H)}{r^2(1+r^2)}\right] -\frac{2\xi^2}{1+r^2}. \tag{20} The leading order-\xi^2 terms cancel. The small-argument Bessel expansion and its large-argument decay bound the integral in (19) by O(\xi^6(1+|\log\xi|)^2), splitting the radial domain at r=1 and r=1/\xi. The same split in the trial functional gives (17). Numerical quadrature evaluates (18)–(19) independently of the radial resolvent; its integration errors are recorded separately. Retain outgoing radiation in the interaction The corresponding outgoing expansion in the upper half-frequency plane is \boxed{ F(z)=1+z^2\left[-\frac14\log(-z^2)+c_0\right]+o(z^2).} \tag{21} It follows by using K_3(-izr) in the outgoing outer solution and the same inner matching. The logarithm is continued from imaginary frequency. At a positive real frequency, \boxed{ \operatorname{Im}F(\omega+i0) =\frac{\pi}{4}\omega^2+o(\omega^2).} \tag{22} The positive sign is fixed by the positive spectral measure in (10). It represents energy entering outgoing transverse modes of this same field. It is not an inserted damping constant. Check the threshold coefficient with spatial scattering states There is an independent spatial route to the coefficient in (22). The regular zero-energy homogeneous solution is exactly h_{\rm reg}(r)=r^4+3r^2+3,\qquad \mathcal H_1h_{\rm reg}=0. \tag{23} It grows at infinity. The other independent zero-energy solution is singular at the origin, so a regular decaying zero mode does not intervene in the threshold matching. Set u=rh/(1+r^2). This is an isometry from the radial measure w_1\,dr to r\,dr. The homogeneous scattering equation becomes \left[-\frac{d^2}{dr^2}-\frac1r\frac d{dr} +\frac{9r^4+2r^2+1}{r^2(1+r^2)^2}\right]u=k^2u. \tag{24} Its potential approaches 9/r^2+O(r^{-4}). Matching the regular solution (23) to the outer region kr fixed gives the leading, delta-in-k normalized field h_k\sim\sqrt{k}\,rJ_3(kr). The regular matching removes a leading singular Y_3 contribution. The source overlap is controlled by its actual large-radius tail: \begin{aligned} \langle f,h_k\rangle_w &=8k^{3/2}\int_0^\infty\frac{J_3(t)}{t^2}\,dt +o(k^{3/2})\\ &=k^{3/2}+o(k^{3/2}). \end{aligned} \tag{25} The integral equals 1/8 because d[J_2(t)/t^2]/dt=-J_3(t)/t^2, J_2(t)/t^2\to1/8 at the origin, and it vanishes at infinity. The derivative identity is given by NIST DLMF §10.6. Consequently d\mu=\frac12|\langle f,h_k\rangle_w|^2dk =\frac{\ell}{4}[1+o(1)]\,d\ell,\qquad \ell=k^2. \tag{26} This recovers (22) from spatial continuum normalization. Direct integration of the full homogeneous equation, followed by a large-radius J_3,Y_3 fit and the source integral, independently checks (25) at finite small k. The asymptotic Bessel tail is included in that source integral. The component action therefore supplies a definite common interaction kernel, including both spatial polarizations, finite kinetic normalization and its outgoing response. Its scale is \mathcal T=4\pi Z, with frequency dependence set by the profile size \lambda. Neither Z, \lambda, a physical electric charge, nor the occupied electron and neutrino modes have been derived from V2's master action. No measured electromagnetic or weak-interaction rate is claimed. Polarized spatial radiation uses this full spectral measure to calculate outgoing pulse energy and the cancellation condition involving both complex input polarizations. Verification retarded_displacement_checks.py compares (4) with finite differences of the full constrained spatial Hessian. It independently checks the spectral moments, source equation, positive Euclidean response and high-frequency bounds. Three radial resolutions, continuum trial-function integrals and outgoing upper-half-plane solves check (17)–(22). An independent regular scattering-state integration checks (23)–(26). The stable Bessel series avoids subtracting two large nearly equal terms near the origin. Reports retain quadrature errors and use timestamped filenames; checks remain active under Python optimization.

title: Rotation-neutral spatial modes
summary: A common rotation of two spatial planes has an exact neutral spinor subspace, while three equal planes have none; full spatial motion and dynamical selection determine whether this can become a particle coupling rule.
text:
Summary: A common rotation of two spatial planes has an exact neutral spinor subspace, while three equal planes have none; full spatial motion and dynamical selection determine whether this can become a particle coupling rule. A concrete cancellation between spatial polarizations An interaction can vanish because a spatial pattern is unchanged by the particular geometric operation to which it couples. This is stronger than zero overlap of two unperturbed sources. The calculation below gives an explicit example involving two oppositely polarized rotation planes. All coordinates are ordinary macroscopic spatial coordinates in the one nested manifold. Spinor components describe fields on those coordinates. The calculation uses a flat spatial chart and a specified rotation probe; it does not identify a spinor parameter space with the particle's spatial submanifold. Nor does it identify the probe with electromagnetism in advance. The construction first works separately at each containing depth. Combining these probes into one action on the entire nested chain requires compatible embeddings and their variations. A common formula for several local probes is not by itself one globally defined conserved charge. Rotations of nested spatial sectors derives the fixed-chain constraint and the moving-embedding terms required to pursue this candidate through the whole hierarchy. Spin action of the specified spatial rotation In d Euclidean spatial directions let the Hermitian Clifford matrices obey \{\gamma_a,\gamma_b\}=2\delta_{ab}I. Choose m=\lfloor d/2floor mutually orthogonal, oriented spatial planes (e_1,e_2),\ldots,(e_{2m-1},e_{2m}), and define H_j=-i\gamma_{2j-1}\gamma_{2j},\qquad H_j^2=I,\qquad [H_j,H_k]=0. 	ag{1} These are spatial rotation generators, not independent interaction fields. The spin action of rotation by the same angle in every chosen plane is U_{m spin}(	heta)=e^{-i	heta Q_d}, \qquad Q_d= rac12\sum_{j=1}^mH_j. 	ag{2} The factor one-half is the spin lift: a 2\pi rotation in one plane acts as -I. This convention can also be constructed with exterior creation and annihilation operators; see Woit's spinor representation notes. It is not an electromagnetic normalization. In a simultaneous eigenbasis write H_jz_s=s_jz_s, s_j\in\{+1,-1\}. Then the weights are exactly Q_dz_s=q_s z_s,\qquad q_s= rac12\sum_js_j. 	ag{3} For the full spin module all sign choices occur. At even depth a chosen half-spin module restricts their product \prod_js_j to one sign. The choice of half-spin module is an additional physical input. depth number of rotation planes full spin weights, with repetitions 3 1 - rac12, rac12 4 2 -1,0,0,1 5 2 -1,0,0,1 6 3 - rac32,- rac12,- rac12,- rac12, rac12, rac12, rac12, rac32 10 5  rac12(5-2r) with multiplicity  inom5r, 0\leq r\leq5 The table counts field components, not extra spatial dimensions. Zero is possible when m is even; the full neutral multiplicity is then  inom m{m/2}. In a half-spin module the neutral weights all have the same chirality (-1)^{m/2}, so the other half-spin module has none. Thus this is a plane-parity rule, not a unique characterization of depth five. Five-dimensional cancellation as an operator identity For d=5, equation (2) is Q_5=(H_1+H_2)/2. Its neutral projector follows from the Clifford algebra:  oxed{P_0= rac{I-H_1H_2}{2},\qquad P_0^2=P_0,\qquad \operatorname{rank}P_0=2,\qquad Q_5P_0=0.} 	ag{4} The two planes have opposite spin rotation weights on this subspace. Either weight can be nonzero, and each plane separately acts nontrivially. Their sum annihilates the complete state. Consequently e^{-i	heta Q_5}P_0=P_0 \quad	ext{for every real }	heta. 	ag{5} For example use \gamma=(\sigma_1\otimes I,\sigma_2\otimes I, \sigma_3\otimes\sigma_1,\sigma_3\otimes\sigma_2, \sigma_3\otimes\sigma_3). Then H_1=\sigma_3\otimes I, H_2=I\otimes\sigma_3, and z=(0,1,0,0)^T has weights (+1,-1). Both rotations are ordinary spatial rotations. The fifth spatial direction is still present in the field's profile; it is the null direction of this particular skew probe. No direction is reclassified as a different kind of space. In six dimensions, the sum of three signs is odd. Therefore, on either half-spin module and on the full module,  oxed{\|Q_6z\|\geq rac12\|z\|.} 	ag{6} The same bound holds for the five-plane operator at depth ten. This supplies an explicit geometric distinction between these chosen probes without setting a five-dimensional coupling coefficient to zero. A geometric origin for the two equal plane rates The equal rates can arise from a higher spatial complex structure. Let J^2=-I on six ordinary spatial directions and choose a unit normal n to a five-dimensional hyperplane V. With P=I-nn^T, put B=(PJP)|_V and u=Jn\in V. For v\in V, direct multiplication gives  oxed{B^2=-I_V+uu^T,\qquad Bu=0,\qquad |u|=1.} 	ag{6a} Thus the tangential compression of any orthogonal six-dimensional complex structure has two equal unit rotation planes and one null direction. It supplies precisely the equal-rate operator type used in (4), without adjusting the two rates independently. The hyperplane is an observer-relative or partner-relative subspace of the same physical space. Compression has also removed a nonzero mixed term. With the ordered decomposition V\oplus\operatorname{span}(n), J= egin{pmatrix}B&u\-u^T&0\end{pmatrix}. 	ag{6b} Take J to be the pure-ray moment in the chosen four-component Spin(6) half-spin module, as in the existing chiral source construction. Denote the tangential bivector action by S_5 and the mixed action by R, so the full unscaled spin action is S_6=S_5+R. In an adapted pure-ray basis one has S_5=\operatorname{diag}(2,0,0,-2),\qquad R=\operatorname{diag}(1,-1,-1,1),\qquad S_6=\operatorname{diag}(3,-1,-1,-1). 	ag{6c} These spectra and simultaneous relations are unchanged under the corresponding spatial spin rotations. The neutral projector of the tangential action obeys P_0=I- rac{S_5^2}{4},\qquad S_5P_0=0,\qquad RP_0=-P_0,\qquad S_6P_0=-P_0. 	ag{6d} The full spin generator is S_6/2. Consequently the tangential neutral mode still has a nonzero response to the mixed part of this higher source. This is useful for a mechanism with distinct geometric channels, but it requires the physical lower-channel projection to be derived. Simply dropping the mixed part would create a neutral coupling by omission. The equal-plane source and its surviving complement are both fixed by the same six-dimensional geometry. Which component the photon current samples, and whether the mixed component acts directly or through other spatial modes, remain dynamical questions. Spatial transport of a neutral doublet derives another response directly from this projector: variation of its physical null axis produces a nonzero traceless geometric curvature and a fixed positive contribution to the spatial kinetic energy. Which higher depths guarantee this cancellation The equal-rate guarantee in (6a) uses a codimension-one hyperplane. For a lower spatial subspace of general codimension, write an orthogonal complex structure on the containing space as J= egin{pmatrix}B&C\-C^T&D\end{pmatrix},\qquad  oxed{B^2=-I+CC^T.} 	ag{6e} There can now be several independent mixed directions, and the nonzero rotation rates of B need not agree. In particular, a direct ten-dimensional source compressed to five dimensions does not automatically inherit the two equal rates of the six-to-five case. This can be checked by an explicit family with every containing direction still equivalent in kind. Let J_2=\left( egin{smallmatrix}0&1\-1&0\end{smallmatrix}ight), B=\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1J_2,\lambda_2J_2,0), and 0\leq\lambda_2\leq\lambda_1\leq1. Then C=(I+B^2)^{1/2},\qquad J_{10}= egin{pmatrix}B&C\-C&-B\end{pmatrix} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad J_{10}^2=-I_{10},\quad J_{10}^T=-J_{10}. 	ag{6f} The blocks describe the relation to a chosen five-dimensional partner, not an inherent division of a ten-dimensional particle. They can be rotated together with the entire nested chain. The compressed spin action has the four weights q= rac{\pm\lambda_1\pm\lambda_2}{2},\qquad \min_{\|z\|=1}\|Q_5z\|= rac{|\lambda_1-\lambda_2|}{2}. 	ag{6g} For example, (\lambda_1,\lambda_2)=(0.9,0.4) gives weights \pm0.65,\pm0.25 and no neutral vector. Equal rates do give the neutral doublet, with the completely zero source as a separate degenerate case. Thus extending the mechanism through the whole hierarchy requires the actual source map and compatible geometric preparations. A higher depth alone is not sufficient. Direct ten-to-five response and a projection through an independently selected six-dimensional complex structure are different physical assumptions and must follow from the same field action. Spatial motion must be included A field transforms through its position dependence as well as its spinor components. Define the ordinary orbital operators L_j=-i\left(x_{2j-1}\partial_{2j}-x_{2j}\partial_{2j-1}ight), \qquad \mathscr Q_d=\sum_jL_j+Q_d. 	ag{7} For a radial envelope f(|x|), every L_jf=0. Hence \Phi(x)=f(|x|)z, z\in\operatorname{ran}P_0, is an actual five-dimensional spatial field satisfying \mathscr Q_5\Phi=0. Its density can have nonzero extent in all five coordinates. This is a neutral spatial mode of the specified rotation, not a particle collapsed onto fewer dimensions. More general angular profiles carry integer weights under the simultaneous orbital rotation and must be tested with (7). With the usual single-valued spatial functions, an odd number of equal planes gives e^{-2\pi i\mathscr Q_d}=(-1)^mI=-I. 	ag{8} A nonzero vector annihilated by \mathscr Q_d would instead be fixed by this finite rotation. Thus there is no such vector for odd m. Additional bundle twists, gauge phases, boundaries, or a different rotation action can change this premise and require their own calculation. When neutrality survives dynamics Let \mathcal F[\Phi] be the full evolution vector field of the one master field. Suppose solutions are unique on the adopted domain and it is equivariant under this rotation: \mathcal F[U(	heta)\Phi]=U(	heta)\mathcal F[\Phi]. 	ag{9} If U(	heta)\Phi_0=\Phi_0 for all 	heta, both the evolved solution and its rotation solve the same initial-value problem. Uniqueness therefore preserves the neutral subspace. For linear dynamics this reduces to [H,\mathscr Q_d]=0 with compatible operator domains. A reciprocal mode interaction a\langle\Phi,\mathscr Q_d\Phiangle then has both its source and its matter variation zero on a neutral field: \partial_aE_{m int}=\langle\Phi,\mathscr Q_d\Phiangle=0, \qquad  rac{\delta E_{m int}}{\delta\Phi^*}=a\mathscr Q_d\Phi=0. 	ag{10} Here a is a specified perturbation amplitude of that same field. A full spatially varying connection requires a local covariant action and its complete current, not just the uniform-mode expression (10). Zero expectation alone would not suffice. The normalized spinor (1,0,0,1)^T/\sqrt2 has \langle Q_5angle=0 but \|Q_5z\|=1: it combines two charged weights and responds to (2). Other couplings and imperfect cancellation An operator R=-i\gamma_1\gamma_5 acts nontrivially on the neutral example above: \|Rz\|=1 and Q_5Rz
e0. Thus neutrality under Q_5 is compatible with transitions under another spatial operation. This is the kind of channel distinction needed in a neutrino calculation; it does not identify R with an observed weak vertex or calculate a scattering rate. Equal plane rates matter. If Q_5(\epsilon)= rac12 ig[(1+\epsilon)H_1+(1-\epsilon)H_2 ig], then Q_5(\epsilon)z=\epsilon z for the (+1,-1) example. The squared coupling action is \epsilon^2. A dynamical symmetry selecting equal rates could protect the cancellation; choosing them by hand leaves it conditional. Under a common physical rotation of the probe and the field, the annihilation condition is unchanged. Rotating just one changes their relative preparation and must be evaluated afresh. What a physical mechanism still has to select There is an exact self-bound spatial example in the existing positive scalar moment model, extended to a multicomponent field with ho=\Phi^\dagger\Phi. In units with kinetic coefficient one, take E[\Phi]=\int\|
abla\Phi\|^2dx+ rac g2\operatorname{tr}M^2, \qquad M=\int(x-X)(x-X)^Tho(x)dx,\qquad \intho=1. 	ag{11} The centre X=\int xho is varied with the field, as in centroid-relative self-binding. For any constant normalized spinor z, \Phi_z(x,t)=e^{-id\omega t} \left( rac\omega\piight)^{d/4}e^{-\omega|x-X|^2/2}z, \qquad \omega^3= rac g2 	ag{12} is an exact resting solution. Its moment is M=I/(2\omega), so the nonlinear potential g(x-X)^TM(x-X) is \omega^2|x-X|^2 and cancels the quadratic part of the Gaussian Laplacian. These profiles minimize (11) at fixed norm. Indeed, integration by parts in the square \int\|
abla\Phi+	frac12M^{-1}(x-X)\Phi\|^2dx\geq0 gives E[\Phi]\geq rac14\operatorname{tr}M^{-1} + rac g2\operatorname{tr}M^2\geq rac{3d\omega}{4}. 	ag{13} For each positive eigenvalue s of M, the minimized expression is 1/(4s)+gs^2/2, whose minimum has gs^3=1/4. Equality in the first square requires a Gaussian times a constant spinor, and equality in the eigenvalue bound requires all s=1/(2\omega). Taking d=5 and z\in\operatorname{ran}P_0 therefore supplies a normalized neutral spatial solution with nonzero extent in all five directions. But (12) also supplies equally minimal solutions in the two nonzero rotation-weight subspaces. Their energy and shape width are identical. The scalar density kernel has no preference between them. This is an auxiliary spatial field solution, not the actual electron orbit or a derived Dirac particle solution. The derivation supplies actual neutral modes and a definite six-dimensional comparison. It does not force a five-dimensional excitation to occupy the neutral subspace: its two nonzero weights also exist. A spin-independent radial self-binding energy gives the same energy to all constant normalized spinors, as the full spatial example now demonstrates. An initial constant spinor polarization is preserved by this scalar evolution, but there is no attraction of an arbitrary polarization toward the neutral subspace. Applying this result to electromagnetic neutrality requires deriving the probe from the one field's action, including the orbital contribution, photon current, kinetic normalization, physical boundary conditions, and the selected particle solutions. Consistency along the nested spatial chain is part of that derivation. The existence of a neutral eigenspace is a concrete mechanism candidate, not a completed charge assignment. Verification spatial_coupling_mechanism_checks.py constructs Clifford matrices independently of the sign-counting formula, checks the full spectra, the neutral projector, finite rotations, a surviving other channel, the unequal-rate leakage law, and explicit ten-to-five compressions with both equal and unequal rates. Spatial Gaussian quadrature also checks the self-bound solution, its energy and the neutral/nonneutral degeneracy in (11)–(13). Related Bilateral polarization coupling — distinguishes a static source zero from the vanishing reciprocal variation in (10). Neutrino channel control — requires neutral and surviving channels to follow from the same geometry and action. Five-dimensional CP3 selection and spectral discrimination — supplies the explicit five-dimensional spinor and distinguishes a selected source from a physical spatial base.

title: Scalar envelope of a bound Dirac field
summary: Readjusting the scalar bound profile gives a normalized Dirac envelope potential with a derived density power, exact uniform moving branches and a specified reciprocal fluctuation spectrum.
text: Summary: Readjusting the scalar bound profile gives a normalized Dirac envelope potential with a derived density power, exact uniform moving branches and a specified reciprocal fluctuation spectrum. Derive the envelope interaction from the spatial source Consider the scalar bound profile and one free normal spatial coordinate in Normal propagation of spatial Dirac modes. The envelope describes amplitudes of the same field on that existing coordinate. It is not another physical space or a mediator particle. Use a fixed rest polarization and center, and let the real bound radial profile adjust to a positive scalar envelope density s. The construction below is a variational reduction to that profile family. Uniform fields give exact solutions of the stated scalar model. Varying envelopes can also drive omitted shape, center and polarization modes; the reduction does not establish their decoupling or the stability of the full field. Let \chi(t,y) be the two amplitudes of the bound mode and its normal Dirac partner. In their normalized basis, \alpha_{\rm eff}=\sigma_1,\qquad \beta_{\rm eff}=\sigma_3,\qquad s=\chi^\dagger\beta_{\rm eff}\chi>0. \tag{1} The microscopic scalar density is s\,\phi_s(x)^\dagger\beta\phi_s(x), where \int\phi_s^\dagger\phi_s=1. These component matrices arise from the full normal partner; they do not replace the bound spatial coordinates. The massless-background profile fixes the density power Set the bare scalar coefficient m=0 in the bound-profile calculation. For a quadratic source of strength a, its positive frequency and unit-profile scalar moment are M(a)=\epsilon_d a^{1/3},\qquad T(a)=\frac{M(a)}{3a}. \tag{2} The envelope density changes the self-consistency equation to a=\frac{g_0sT(a)}d. \tag{3} Solving it gives \boxed{M(s)=M_*s^{1/5},\qquad M_*=\epsilon_d\left(\frac{g_0\epsilon_d}{3d}\right)^{1/5}.} \tag{4} The power follows from the first-order bound kinetic term and the quadratic scalar moment. It is not an independently chosen envelope nonlinearity. The depth enters the profile coefficient \epsilon_d and the common scalar coefficient in (4). This branch is defined about positive scalar density. Its spatial size scales as s^{-1/5} and its bound frequency as s^{1/5}. As s tends to zero the profile spreads and its bound frequency vanishes. A reduction assuming a fixed isolated bound profile cannot be extended to that zero-density limit without checking the full spatial response. The bound kinetic contribution is 2sM(s)/3 and the interaction energy is sM(s)/6. Thus their complete reduced potential is \boxed{U(s)=\frac56M_*s^{6/5},\qquad U'(s)=M(s).} \tag{5} The derivative includes the response of the spatial profile. Keeping its width fixed while differentiating would give a different interaction. The normalized variational equation For the chosen real normalized profile family, the projected connection from varying s vanishes: its diagonal inner product is the derivative of the unit norm and its off-diagonal normal-partner inner product vanishes by angular integration. The restricted first-order action is \boxed{L_{\rm eff} =\int dy\left[ i\chi^\dagger\partial_t\chi -\chi^\dagger(-i\alpha_{\rm eff}\partial_y)\chi -U(\chi^\dagger\beta_{\rm eff}\chi)\right].} \tag{6} It gives i\partial_t\chi =\left[-i\alpha_{\rm eff}\partial_y +\beta_{\rm eff}M(s)\right]\chi. \tag{7} The fixed-center and fixed-polarization restrictions in this action must remain explicit. The full spatial equation can have components outside this profile family when s varies. Eliminating those components requires their actual response and the corresponding dressed vertices; the absence of a projected connection is not a proof that the complement is dynamically inactive. The omitted term can be calculated explicitly. Let W_s=(\phi_s,\alpha_y\phi_s), with spatial inner products understood. Massless profile scaling gives \phi_s(x)=s^{d/10}\phi_1(s^{1/5}x),\qquad \partial_s\phi_s=\frac1{5s} \left(\frac d2+x\cdot\nabla_x\right)\phi_s. \tag{7a} Angular integration and real radial normalization give W_s^\dagger W_s=I and W_s^\dagger\partial_sW_s=0. Nevertheless, (\partial_sW_s)^\dagger(\partial_sW_s)=g_{ss}I,\qquad g_{ss}=\|\partial_s\phi_s\|^2>0. \tag{7b} For a solution of (7), reconstruct \Psi=W_s\chi in the full spatial equation. Since \alpha_yW_s=W_s\sigma_1, its residual is \boxed{\mathcal R =(i\partial_t+i\alpha_y\partial_y-H_b)\Psi =i(\partial_sW_s) \big[(\partial_ts)I+(\partial_ys)\sigma_1\big]\chi.} \tag{7c} It obeys W_s^\dagger\mathcal R=0,\qquad \|\mathcal R\|^2 =g_{ss}\left\|\big[(\partial_ts)I +(\partial_ys)\sigma_1\big]\chi\right\|^2. \tag{7d} Thus the envelope equation can hold exactly while a nonzero residual drives the omitted spatial profile. Constant scalar density makes this residual vanish, including the uniform moving solutions below. Small density gradients make the explicit source small, but a controlled elimination still needs the complement's spectrum and response. Its unstable or gapless modes cannot be declared harmless from the vanishing projected connection alone. Uniform propagation with laboratory density held fixed For a positive-frequency plane wave with normal momentum k, write n=\chi^\dagger\chi. Its normalized spinor gives E^2=M(s)^2+k^2,\qquad s=\frac{nM(s)}E. \tag{8} Using (4), these relations are equivalent to \boxed{M^4E=M_*^5n,\qquad E(E^2-k^2)^2=M_*^5n,\qquad E>|k|.} \tag{9} There is one positive solution: the left side increases from zero for E>|k|. At fixed laboratory density, changing momentum changes the scalar density and therefore the bound profile. This is consistent with the normal boost calculation, where holding the proper scalar density fixed instead gives a constant M and a laboratory density n=sE/M. The total energy density is \boxed{\mathcal H(n,k)=nE-\frac{nM^2}{6E}.} \tag{10} The subtracted term is the interaction counted twice in density times the nonlinear phase frequency. Independent variation gives \frac{\partial\mathcal H}{\partial n}=E,\qquad \frac{\partial\mathcal H}{\partial k}=\frac{nk}{E}=j_y. \tag{11} Thus the action fixes the frequency, current and scalar source together. For a nonlinear plane family, the derivative of its phase frequency at fixed density is not a substitute for the energy derivative in (11). The normal stress has a consistent Lorentz transformation At fixed proper scalar density s, define the rest energy density and pressure of this uniform reduced field by \varepsilon_0=U(s)=\frac56sM, \qquad P=sU'(s)-U(s)=\frac16sM. \tag{12} For \gamma=E/M the transformed energy is \gamma^2(\varepsilon_0+P)-P =nE-\frac{nM^2}{6E}, \tag{13} exactly (10). The field has a pressure as well as an energy density. It is not the kinematics of one noninteracting point particle with a fixed energy per unit laboratory length. These are properties of the specified normal envelope model, with no electric charge assigned. A complete fluctuation check within the envelope model At rest take \chi_0=\sqrt n\,(1,0)^T e^{-iMt}, with M=M_*n^{1/5}. The scalar source derivative is a=nM'(n)=M/5. For a normal Fourier wavenumber q, the ordinary and conjugate fluctuation matrix is \mathcal B(q)= \begin{pmatrix} a&q&a&0\\ q&-2M&0&0\\ -a&0&-a&q\\ 0&0&q&2M \end{pmatrix}. \tag{14} The conjugate row contains the opposite Fourier momentum before complex conjugation; its displayed kinetic signs retain that operation. Direct evaluation of the characteristic polynomial gives \boxed{\omega_\pm^2(q) =q^2+2M^2\pm2M\sqrt{M^2+\frac45q^2}.} \tag{15} Both values are nonnegative. Their product is q^4+(4/5)M^2q^2 and their sum is positive. The low branch satisfies \omega_-^2=q^2/5+O(q^4/M^2), agreeing with dP/d\varepsilon_0=1/5 from (12). This verifies normal fluctuations of the declared reduced action. It does not establish stability of the bound field: the m=0 radial branches at several working depths have the separate growing modes already documented in the bound-profile note. Those degrees of freedom, together with changing centers and polarizations, remain part of a full coupling calculation. Reciprocal scalar envelopes readjusts two nested spatial profiles together and derives their full scalar coupling matrix from one common interaction coefficient. Spatial Dirac polarization waves restores the other rest polarizations. Their linear normal waves have a quadratic gapless branch, and certain finite polarized superpositions preserve the scalar source exactly while their bound spatial current changes. Verification normal_dirac_transport_checks.py solves (9) at several densities and momenta, independently reconstructs the adjusted bound profiles and checks their scalar source equations. Finite differences of the full energy verify both derivatives in (11). The normal Lorentz stress is checked against that same energy, and the complete ordinary/conjugate matrix spectrum is compared with (15). Independent finite differences of the full spatial field verify (7c)–(7d) for complex envelope amplitudes, including the nonzero residual norm and its zero projection onto the retained amplitudes. All conditions remain active under Python optimization. Related Normal propagation of spatial Dirac modes — provides the full spatial boost and the density convention needed here. Self-consistent scalar Dirac moment modes — derives the profile scaling and its full radial stability limits. Dressed spatial source vertices — supplies the reconstruction required if omitted modes are eliminated.

title: Self-consistent scalar Dirac moment modes
summary: The scalar moment kernel admits self-consistent radial Dirac modes with a calculable source and virial law, while the complete conjugate response detects an instability in several massless-background branches.
text:
Summary: The scalar moment kernel admits self-consistent radial Dirac modes with a calculable source and virial law, while the complete conjugate response detects an instability in several massless-background branches. A spatial profile derived from the existing source term A coupling vertex needs actual spatial field profiles. This note applies the nonlocal scalar moment interaction to a full first-order Dirac field, retaining both radial components and the change in its own source. The model is a conditional flat spatial calculation on \mathbb R^d within the one nested macroscopic manifold. It does not replace a particle's proposed global spatial geometry or the actual Coulomb-plus-precession electron orbit. The computed modes are stationary solutions of the stated model; their existence alone does not establish stable physical particles. Use Hermitian Dirac matrices \alpha_i, eta, \hbar=c=1, and a bare scalar coefficient m\geq0. Define \sigma(x)=\Psi(x)^\dagger eta\Psi(x),\qquad Q_\sigma=\int\sigma(x)dx,\qquad X= rac{\int x\sigma(x)dx}{Q_\sigma}, on a domain where Q_\sigma
e0, and let M_\sigma=\int(x-X)(x-X)^T\sigma(x)dx. 	ag{1} The scalar density need not be positive. The field norm is separately \int\Psi^\dagger\Psi=1. Adopt the energy  oxed{\mathcal E[\Psi] =\langle\Psi,(-i\alpha\cdot
abla+m eta)\Psiangle + rac{g_0}{2}\operatorname{tr}M_\sigma^2, \qquad g_0>0.} 	ag{2} This is the scalar channel of the transition-density interaction with the centered dot-square kernel. Centering has the variational role derived in centroid-relative self-binding. Because the first central scalar moment is zero, variations of X cancel in the first variation of (1). The exact field equation is i\partial_t\Psi= \left[-i\alpha\cdot
abla+  eta\left(m+g_0(x-X)^TM_\sigma(x-X)ight)ight]\Psi. 	ag{3} All coefficients in the response come from the same field. Equation (3) has no additional interaction particle or externally supplied confining potential. Its full energy is not bounded below over arbitrary Dirac fields, so a lowest positive-frequency branch is not a global energy minimum. The radial self-consistency equation Use the angularly normalized radial field in Rotation-neutral Dirac fields, with upper radial function f and lower function ig\alpha(\widehat x). The scalar moment is isotropic: M_\sigma= rac{T}{d}I, \qquad T=\int_0^\infty r^2(f^2-g^2)r^{d-1}dr. 	ag{4} Writing a= rac{g_0T}{d}, 	ag{5} the stationary radial equations become  oxed{(E-m-ar^2)f=g'+ rac{d-1}{r}g, \qquad(E+m+ar^2)g=-f'.} 	ag{6} Thus a pure scalar quadratic mass profile is generated by the same moment whose spatial mode it confines. Given a normalized positive-frequency solution of (6) with T>0, equation (5) determines the coefficient required for self-consistency. Alternatively one can fix g_0 and solve for a. The latter form is needed to compare sectors under one common interaction. These radial modes retain all d position coordinates. Their rest spinor polarization can carry different rotation weights while sharing the same radial source. The scalar interaction therefore does not select the neutral weights over the other polarizations. Scaling and the total energy Under the norm-preserving dilation \Psi_\lambda(x)=\lambda^{d/2}\Psi(\lambda x), the Dirac kinetic expectation scales as \lambda and the moment energy as \lambda^{-4}. The bare mass expectation is unchanged. Stationarity consequently requires  oxed{T_D=4\mathcal E_{m int}=2aT,} \qquad T_D=\langle\Psi,-i\alpha\cdot
abla\Psiangle. 	ag{7} Multiplying the stationary field equation by \Psi^\dagger and integrating then gives E=3aT+m\langle etaangle, \qquad \mathcal E=E- rac{aT}{2}. 	ag{8} The spectral frequency and the total nonlinear energy are different. For m=0, rescaling the radial coordinate gives E(a)=\epsilon_d a^{1/3},\qquad T= rac{E}{3a},\qquad  oxed{a=\left( rac{g_0\epsilon_d}{3d}ight)^{3/5}, \quad E=\epsilon_d\left( rac{g_0\epsilon_d}{3d}ight)^{1/5}, \quad\mathcal E= rac56E.} 	ag{9} Here \epsilon_d is the lowest positive radial frequency at a=1, m=0. The powers in (9) follow from the first-order kinetic term and the quadratic spatial moment; they are not the scaling of a scalar Schrödinger oscillator. No particle mass or occupied mass-formula index has been assigned to this radial frequency. A reproducible radial representation Put x=wr^2 and \alpha=d/2-1. Use normalized upper and lower bases f_n(r)=N_n^{(f)}e^{-x/2}L_n^\alpha(x),\qquad g_n(r)=N_n^{(g)}r e^{-x/2}L_n^{\alpha+1}(x), 	ag{10} with (N_n^{(f)})^2= rac{2w^{\alpha+1}n!}{\Gamma(n+\alpha+1)}, \qquad (N_n^{(g)})^2= rac{2w^{\alpha+2}n!}{\Gamma(n+\alpha+2)}. 	ag{11} The derivative identity is -f_n'=\sqrt{w(n+d/2)}\,g_n+\sqrt{wn}\,g_{n-1}. 	ag{12} Let K be this upper-to-lower matrix. Multiplication by r^2 gives tridiagonal matrices R_f,R_g with diagonal entries (2n+d/2)/w and (2n+d/2+1)/w. Their upper off-diagonals are respectively -\sqrt{(n+1)(n+d/2)}/w and -\sqrt{(n+1)(n+d/2+1)}/w. The finite radial Hamiltonian is H_a= egin{pmatrix}mI+aR_f&K^T\K&-mI-aR_g\end{pmatrix}. 	ag{13} The basis width w is a numerical parameter, not a physical source coefficient. Changing it and increasing the number of functions provides independent convergence controls. At a=1, m=0, the converged positive branch gives: spatial depth d frequency \epsilon_d scalar moment T self-consistent g_0=d/T 3 1.702365726 0.567455242 5.286760574 4 2.089440608 0.696480203 5.743163961 5 2.444444940 0.814814980 6.136362393 6 2.775809151 0.925269717 6.484595670 10 3.947163845 1.315721282 7.600393897 The table fixes the source scale a to display the dimensionless profiles. It does not use a common g_0 across its rows. Equation (9) performs that common-coefficient comparison without independently fitting each depth. The complete radial fluctuation problem The source changes when the spatial field changes. In the finite radial representation set B=\operatorname{diag}(R_f,-R_g) and let \phi be a real normalized stationary coefficient vector. Then T=\phi^TB\phi, a=g_0T/d, and v=B\phi. Writing a perturbation as \eta=x+iy in the rotating frame gives  oxed{ rac{d}{dt} egin{pmatrix}x\y\end{pmatrix} = egin{pmatrix}0&L_-\-L_+&0\end{pmatrix}  egin{pmatrix}x\y\end{pmatrix},} 	ag{14} where L_-=H_a-EI,\qquad L_+=L_-+ rac{2g_0}{d}vv^T. 	ag{15} This retains the ordinary and conjugate source variations in Dirac source linearization. The phase mode has L_-\phi=0. On the fixed-norm tangent space, \phi^Tx=0; quotienting the phase direction removes the associated zero-mode numerical ambiguity. It does not remove growing physical radial perturbations. For the m=0, a=1 branch, converged radial growth rates include 1.028404447 at depth three, 1.027065172 at four, 0.954281303 at five, and 0.816171505 at six, in the model's time units. These are finite nonzero rates, not small numerical real parts of a phase zero mode. Direct nonlinear evolution of the depth-five field reproduces the growing linearized perturbation, with the remainder decreasing when the initial perturbation is reduced. Norm and the full nonlinear energy remain conserved during that growth. Consequently these massless-background branches cannot be identified as stable particles on the strength of their stationary profiles. They remain well-defined source and response calculations for the stated model. A radial calculation alone also does not establish stability against every spatial angular perturbation, even where it detects no radial growth. Polarized Dirac shape response calculates the quadrupole motions of these same profiles. Translational Dirac response retains their moving center and derives its zero mode and inertial response. Self-consistent nested Dirac pair lets both a lower and a containing spatial field determine their profiles through one common scalar coefficient. Radial dynamics of two-frequency fields embeds this entire radial equation into the full opposite-frequency spatial family, retaining its source, kinetic weight and any radial instability. Verification spatial_dirac_mode_checks.py checks the basis and kinetic matrices by independent Gauss–Laguerre quadrature, compares positive frequencies at several basis sizes and widths, and substitutes the reconstructed functions directly into both equations (6). It checks self-consistency, the dilation identity, the distinction between total energy and frequency, and nonlinear perturbation evolution. As an independent spectral control, the same radial method is tested with equal scalar and vector quadratic backgrounds. Eliminating the lower component there gives the analytic equation (E-m)^2(E+m)=2a(4n+d)^2 for radial level n. This control belongs to the solvable class described by Ginocchio; it tests the discretization and is not substituted for the scalar source in (3). Related Rotation-neutral Dirac fields in physical space — gives the full angular field and its conserved total rotation. Transition-density coupling — supplies the nonlocal scalar source and full variations. Centroid-relative self-binding — explains the translation-preserving center variation.

title: Slow shape poles and their signed response
summary: The two-frequency scalar shape response has poles whose frequency and residue decrease together, but their canonical sign and finite total response prevent identifying them from softness alone as stable weakly coupled particles.
text:
Summary: The two-frequency scalar shape response has poles whose frequency and residue decrease together, but their canonical sign and finite total response prevent identifying them from softness alone as stable weakly coupled particles. Solve for the collective frequency instead of supplying it The complete periodic response distinguishes the bound field's carrier from its collective source poles. In the radial rest examples, scalar quadrupole sidebands cancel and the remaining frequency equation can be solved directly. This gives a concrete test of whether a slow source also has a weak response. Use the zero-bare-mass scalar model with one fixed g_0, unit number norm and scalar balance s=|a|^2-|b|^2>0. The bound profile dilates by \ell=s^{1/5}. Let A(z) and B(z) be the even and odd scalar functions of the full single-frequency spatial shape response, calculated at s=1. For a tensor eigenvector of the circulation action T with eigenvalue h, the two-frequency bare response is  oxed{\Pi_h(\omega;s)=A(z)+ rac{h}{s}B(z),\qquad z= rac{\omega}{\ell},\qquad \chi_h= rac{\Pi_h}{1-g_0\Pi_h}.} 	ag{1} The tensor labels describe spatial shape patterns over the existing macroscopic dimensions. They are not new physical directions. The 1/s factor comes from retaining both frequency components and their different scalar and canonical weights; it is not a chosen weak-coupling coefficient. Derive the slow pole and its residue Suppose the frozen source resolvents are analytic near z=0, and put A(z)=A_0+O(z^2),\qquad B(z)=B_1z+O(z^3), \qquad D_0=1-g_0A_0. 	ag{2} For hB_1
e0 and D_0
e0, set z=s\zeta in the denominator of (1). The implicit-function theorem gives the simple root  oxed{\omega_h(s) =s^{6/5} rac{D_0}{g_0hB_1} \left[1+O(s^2)ight].} 	ag{3} The source residue R_h is defined by \chi_h(\omega)=R_h/(\omega-\omega_h)+O(1). At the pole \Pi_h=1/g_0, so  oxed{R_h=- rac{1}{g_0^2\partial_\omega\Pi_h(\omega_h)} =- rac{s^{6/5}}{g_0^2hB_1}\left[1+O(s^2)ight].} 	ag{4} Thus both the pole frequency and its source weight become small. Their signs also matter. The checked profiles have A_0<0, B_1<0 and D_0>0. The h=+1 member has negative frequency and positive residue; its conjugate h=-1 member has positive frequency and negative residue. At one common g_0=6.5 and s=0.001, full radial response calculations give: spatial depth positive slow frequency, h=-1 its signed residue static full response 3 0.004989695 -0.000487181 -0.056209060 5 0.005806261 -0.000575196 -0.054789326 6 0.006199339 -0.000616903 -0.054348207 The same calculation supplies the slow poles at all three depths. It does not select a uniquely five-dimensional particle or an occupied mode. Check the sign with the full canonical field realization The scalar functions in (1) arise from both angular radial families and both signs of the Dirac spectrum. Let L be their complete reference radial operator with its bound carrier subtracted, and let v_h,v_{-h} be the respective spatial source vectors. The four-block realization is  egin{gathered} L_4=\operatorname{diag}(\ell L,-\ell L,-\ell L,\ell L),\qquad \Sigma_4=\operatorname{diag}(I,I,-I,-I),\ t=\ell^{-2}(a v_h,-b v_h,a v_{-h},-b v_{-h})^T,\  oxed{\mathcal B_4=L_4+g_0\Sigma_4tt^\dagger,\qquad \chi_h=t^\dagger(\omega-\mathcal B_4)^{-1}\Sigma_4t.} \end{gathered} 	ag{5} The amplitudes may be taken real in this single-helicity realization, with a^2=(1+s)/2 and b^2=(1-s)/2. The \ell^{-2} factors are the dilated quadratic source moments. Expanding the four frozen blocks recovers (1), including its 1/s term. The matrix obeys \Sigma_4\mathcal B_4= (\Sigma_4\mathcal B_4)^\dagger. For a simple real mode \mathcal B_4v=\omega_hv with v^\dagger\Sigma_4v
e0, its resolvent residue is  oxed{R_h= rac{|t^\dagger v|^2}{v^\dagger\Sigma_4v}.} 	ag{6} This independent normalization reproduces (4). Replacing the denominator by the positive Euclidean norm would erase the sign of the physical canonical form. A small source residue must be assessed with that form. Interpret the work sign with the stability qualification For a real source term H_{m ext}=f(t)O, let f(t)=\operatorname{Re}(f_0e^{-i\omega t}) and let a bounded particular output have amplitude \chi f_0. The mean supplied power is  oxed{\langle\dot f\,\delta Oangle =- rac{\omega|f_0|^2}{2}\operatorname{Im}\chi.} 	ag{7} A simple real pole continued as R/(\omega-\omega_0+i0) has positive absorptive weight at positive \omega_0 when R>0 and the opposite work sign when R<0. Equation (6) identifies this signed contribution without assigning an absolute physical energy to a Floquet frequency, which can be shifted by the background frequency. An unstable full background has no generic settled periodic response. For it, (1) is a meromorphic source resolvent, and its individual real-pole weight does not establish stable absorption. The radial dynamics already transfer existing radial instabilities to these two-frequency fields. Stability and selection of the occupied field must therefore precede any particle interpretation. A real canonical two-mode example checks the effect of opposite signs: H= rac12(p_a^2+\omega_a^2q_a^2) - rac12(p_b^2+\omega_b^2q_b^2)+\varepsilon q_aq_b. 	ag{8} Both reciprocal equations follow from this same energy. Their frequencies satisfy  oxed{(\omega^2-\omega_a^2)(\omega^2-\omega_b^2) +\varepsilon^2=0.} 	ag{9} At equal uncoupled frequencies a nonzero coupling gives growth, while the indefinite total energy remains conserved. This illustrates the normalization issue; it is not an added interaction field or a derived physical two-particle model. A small pole weight does not make the full response small At zero forcing frequency, B(0)=0, so  oxed{\chi_h(0;s)= rac{A_0}{1-g_0A_0},} 	ag{10} independent of s. At fixed nonzero z=\omega/\ell with hB(z)
e0, the 1/s term instead becomes large. Source feedback then gives  oxed{\chi_h(\ell z;s)\longrightarrow- rac1{g_0}.} 	ag{11} Neither limit is a weak total scalar response. The frequency of an incoming field, its selected spatial pattern, the pole residue and the full output map are separate parts of a coupling calculation, as explained in source frequencies. Verification slow_shape_pole_checks.py compares full four-block field resolvents with (1), locates the slow poles independently, and checks their residues using both source derivatives and the complete canonical eigenvectors. Increasing radial resolution verifies the quoted frequencies and signed residues. Both source components, both angular radial families and both signs of the Dirac spectrum are retained. Direct real-time work verifies the convention in (7), and the complete canonical pair checks (9) and energy conservation during growth. Reports use timestamped filenames and verification remains active under Python optimization. The results establish the stated source spectrum and its limits, without a stable weak-particle identification.

title: Soft polarized scattering
summary: Retaining the photon spatial phase and the target's complete polarization multiplet gives the low-frequency forward spin response in the conditionally gauged scalar Dirac model.
text: Summary: Retaining the photon spatial phase and the target's complete polarization multiplet gives the low-frequency forward spin response in the conditionally gauged scalar Dirac model. Keep the incoming wave's spatial structure Use the normalized full spatial profile and conditional current coupling derived in Soft spatial current response. The particle occupies its stated d ordinary spatial directions in the one nested manifold. Choose propagation along x_3 and transverse polarizations along x_1,x_2. This selects three measurement directions; it does not split the particle's space into different kinds of dimension. The incident photon amplitude is a complex transverse vector \varepsilon=(\varepsilon_1,\varepsilon_2), with \varepsilon^\dagger\varepsilon=1. Its source operator includes \alpha_i e^{ikx_3} =V_i^{(0)}+ikV_i^{(1)} -\frac{k^2}{2}V_i^{(2)}+O(k^3), \qquad V_i^{(n)}=x_3^n\alpha_i,\quad i=1,2. \tag{1} The current readout includes the opposite spatial phase. Thus a uniform electric-field calculation cannot simply be called the real-photon amplitude. Set k=\omega for the conditional case where photon speed equals the underlying Dirac speed, both set to one. The target also retains its complete complex polarization z in \phi_z(x)=W(x)z,\qquad \int W^\dagger W\,dx=I_N,\qquad z^\dagger z=1. \tag{2} These coefficients describe the field's spatial pattern. The complete tensor description explains which relative amplitudes and phases a single circulation tensor can omit. The complete zero-frequency multiplet contributes Let P project on the full resting multiplet (2), and let B_{ij} denote -i\alpha_i\alpha_j restricted to its constant upper polarization frame. Spatial parity and direct radial integration give PV_i^{(0)}P=0,\qquad PV_i^{(1)}P=-F_0B_{i3}. \tag{3} The coefficient F_0=(1-2G/d)/(2M) is the full field's current moment, including its lower radial component. A polarization variation within W orthogonal to the occupied ray changes neither scalar density nor scalar source at first order. These are exact degenerate stationary directions, as in Dirac polarization waves. The ordinary and conjugate zero-frequency resolvents therefore give \begin{aligned} \Pi^{(11)}_{ij}(\omega) &=\frac1\omega z^\dagger[PV_i^{(1)}P,PV_j^{(1)}P]z+O(1)\\ &=\frac{2iF_0^2}{\omega}J_{ij}+O(1). \end{aligned} \tag{4} Here J_{ij}=z^\dagger B_{ij}z. The commutator identity [B_{i3},B_{j3}]=2iB_{ij} gives the second line. Projection only onto the occupied ray would miss this term. The global phase direction cancels between the two signed responses; the full multiplet commutator retains the physical polarization changes. The phase coefficients in the incoming and outgoing vertices make (4) contribute +k^2\Pi^{(11)}. At k=\omega, this is an order-\omega spin response, despite being second order in spatial phase. Include the other spatial-phase terms and shape feedback For Hermitian source labels A,B, use \Pi_{AB}= \langle A\phi,(\omega-H_b+M)^{-1}B\phi\rangle +\langle B\phi,(-\omega-H_b+M)^{-1}A\phi\rangle. \tag{5} Let C contain all scalar first moments and all scalar second moments, including breathing. With their curvature matrix \mathcal K, the complete source response is \chi_{VV} =\Pi_{VV} +\Pi_{VC}\mathcal K (I-\Pi_{CC}\mathcal K)^{-1}\Pi_{CV}. \tag{6} This is the actual scalar source variation, not a fixed-target prescription. The connection is sourced reciprocally by that same current in the conditional action.
