A physical scattering rate additionally needs its derived radiation operator and incident/outgoing flux normalization. Parity separates V^{(0)},V^{(2)} from V^{(1)}. It removes the single phase cross term even with all shape feedback retained. The V^{(0)}–V^{(2)} response must also be checked: multiplied by k^2, a spurious inverse-frequency pole could contaminate the soft limit. The complete angular calculation below retains that cross response. In the tested radial branches and transverse preparations it remains bounded, so it cannot change the order-\omega term. The only singular even-source contribution needed at that order is (4). Higher phase terms are suppressed by additional powers of k, with odd cross terms removed by parity. This expansion assumes an isolated stationary multiplet and translation sector, with no additional zero-frequency shape instability. The angular construction uses the complete monogenic families of degrees zero, one and two and their opposite radial partners. For example, a harmonic spinor polynomial p_\ell(x)w decomposes as p_\ell(x)w=M_\ell(x)+\alpha(x)N_{\ell-1}(x),\qquad N_{\ell-1}=\frac{\alpha_i\partial_i(p_\ell w)} {d+2\ell-2}. \tag{7} Both M_\ell and N_{\ell-1} are monogenic. Their radial Dirac operators retain the full upper and lower profile functions. Formal radial dimension shifts account for the radial weight; they add no physical spatial directions. The unused cubic angular family is orthogonal to every V^{(0)} and scalar dipole source, so it does not enter the V^{(0)}–V^{(2)} cross term. Combine the two spin contributions The spatially uniform current kernel has the independently derived term \chi^{(00)}_{ij} =\frac{\delta_{ij}}{\mathcal I} +i\omega\left(\frac1{2\mathcal I^2} -\frac{2F_0}{\mathcal I}\right)J_{ij} +O(\omega^2). \tag{8} Adding (4) on shell gives \boxed{ \chi^{\rm forward}_{ij} =\frac{\delta_{ij}}{\mathcal I} +i\omega\,\frac{(g_{\rm mag}-2)^2}{8\mathcal I^2}J_{ij} +O(\omega^2),\qquad g_{\rm mag}=4\mathcal I F_0.} \tag{9} The cancellation is \frac1{2\mathcal I^2}-\frac{2F_0}{\mathcal I}+2F_0^2 =2\left(F_0-\frac1{2\mathcal I}\right)^2. \tag{10} For an outgoing polarization \varepsilon', the coherent response is \varepsilon'^\dagger\chi^{\rm forward}\varepsilon. Both photon phases and both complex polarization components remain present, together with the target's spatial circulation. Compare the form with the low-energy scattering theorem For the conventional normalized electromagnetic radiation equation, a forward amplitude has factor -q^2/(4\pi) times the current kernel used here. Put \kappa_{\rm mag}=(g_{\rm mag}-2)/2. Equations (9)–(10) then give the spin-amplitude coefficient -\frac{q^2\kappa_{\rm mag}^2}{8\pi\mathcal I^2}\,\omega. \tag{11} This is the anomalous-moment-squared structure of the electromagnetic low-energy theorem. Equation (4) of Gorchtein and Zhang states the corresponding forward expansion with their explicit electromagnetic normalization. Here it is a comparison of response formulas; their separate weak-current analysis is not a V2 interaction mechanism. For arbitrary outgoing direction \widehat n', the same leading uniform current would give, with that radiation normalization, \frac{d\sigma_{\varepsilon'\varepsilon}}{d\Omega} =r_q^2|\varepsilon'^\dagger\varepsilon|^2,\qquad r_q=\frac{q^2}{4\pi\mathcal I}, \tag{12} at sufficiently low energy and negligible recoil. Summing the two outgoing transverse polarizations gives r_q^2(1-|\widehat n'\cdot\varepsilon|^2). For a normalized incident polarization the angular integral is 8\pi r_q^2/3. Consequently a chosen polarization can eliminate a particular output channel without making a freely moving charged target transparent to every output. This complements the complete target-transition test. Equations (11)–(12) require a correctly normalized physical photon action. The present calculation derives the target current kernel under the declared coupling hypothesis; it does not derive that radiation action. The six-dimensional scalar profile's magnetic moment also disagrees with the single-electron benchmark, as quantified in the companion note. Matching the structural identity (11) is therefore a useful consistency test, not a completed observational interaction law. The photon speed matters as well. If its speed in the same units is c_\gamma, then k=\omega/c_\gamma and the two terms combine as \frac1{2\mathcal I^2}-\frac{2F_0}{\mathcal I} +\frac{2F_0^2}{c_\gamma^2}. \tag{13} The cancellation in (10) requires c_\gamma=1 in the stated model. The depth-two scalar translation wave has c_{\rm tr}=1/2 in these Dirac units. Identifying it as the photon would therefore require a different, fully consistent completion of its propagation and coupling. Verification soft_photon_response_checks.py constructs the angular source functions directly on the actual spatial sphere, orthonormalizes their complete monogenic spans, and integrates their radial profiles independently of the soft formula. It retains every scalar first and second moment in (6), both frequency signs, and all three displayed phase vertices. Checks compare the low-frequency coefficients for aligned and arbitrary complex target polarizations and tilted incident planes at depths 3, 5 and 6, with two radial resolutions. Direct full-spatial integrals and separate radial circular-channel resolvents check the ingredients of (8) up to depth 10. The executable reports the conditional electron magnetic-moment discrepancy rather than treating the benchmark as fitted.

title: Soft spatial current response
summary: The full spatial translation and velocity tangents determine the low-frequency electric current, its polarization correction, and the magnetic moment of a conditionally gauged scalar Dirac profile.
text: Summary: The full spatial translation and velocity tangents determine the low-frequency electric current, its polarization correction, and the magnetic moment of a conditionally gauged scalar Dirac profile. Specify the physical current being tested Let a normalized localized field on d ordinary spatial coordinates obey H_b\phi=M\phi,\qquad H_b=\alpha_i(-i\partial_i)+\beta(m+a|x|^2),\qquad \int\phi^\dagger\phi\,dx=1. \tag{1} Its quadratic scalar source is varied with its own centered moment functional. The coordinates belong to the one nested macroscopic spatial manifold. The field components describe its spatial polarization. For this calculation, make an explicit additional hypothesis: a retained connection amplitude of the same field enters the equation as H[A,\Phi]=\alpha_i(-i\partial_i-qA_i) +\beta\mathfrak m[\Psi]+q\Phi. \tag{2} The connection, charge generator qI, and its eventual radiation normalization must be derived from the master action to identify this with a physical interaction. Equation (2) is a conditional test of the resulting particle response. It introduces no mediator particle. Varying this same action gives the reciprocal connection source \rho_{\rm em}=q\Psi^\dagger\Psi,\qquad j_{{\rm em},i}=q\Psi^\dagger\alpha_i\Psi. \tag{3} The scalar binding functional is invariant under local common phase changes, so it preserves the corresponding number continuity equation. Keeping the full spatial field also keeps the kinetic normalization required by Dressed source vertices. Keep the field's displacement and velocity Write the normalized radial field as \phi(x)=\frac{f(r)w+i g(r)\alpha(\widehat x)w} {\sqrt{\Omega_{d-1}}},\qquad \beta w=w,\quad w^\dagger w=1. \tag{4} The constant vector w may have arbitrary complex polarization in the selected complete spatial multiplet. Define J_{ij}=w^\dagger(-i\alpha_i\alpha_j)w,\qquad G=\int_0^\infty g(r)^2r^{d-1}dr, \qquad F_0=\frac2d\int_0^\infty r^d f(r)g(r)\,dr. \tag{5} The radial Dirac equations imply F_0=\frac{1-2G/d}{2M}. \tag{6} This current-moment identity is derived in Normal propagation of spatial Dirac modes. The total spatial angular momentum includes the orbital contribution and satisfies \langle\mathcal L_{ij}\rangle=J_{ij}/2 on (4). The complete translation calculation supplies the two tangent fields \eta_i=-\partial_i\phi,\qquad \zeta_i=iMx_i\phi+\frac12\alpha_i\phi, \qquad \Psi=e^{-iMt}[\phi+X_i\eta_i+v_i\zeta_i+\cdots]. \tag{7} Here X is the scalar center and v its generalized velocity coordinate. The first variation of every scalar binding source under v_i\zeta_i vanishes pointwise. The profile's inertial coefficient is \mathcal I=M+\frac{T}{d},\qquad T=\langle\phi,\alpha_i(-i\partial_i)\phi\rangle. \tag{8} The stationary frequency M and translation inertia \mathcal I must not be interchanged. For the zero-bare-mass quadratic scalar branch, \mathcal I=M(1+2/(3d)). Derive the spatial symplectic coefficients The original field action has kinetic term \tfrac i2\int(\Psi^\dagger\dot\Psi-\dot\Psi^\dagger\Psi)\,dx. Direct spatial integration gives \boxed{ \begin{aligned} 2\operatorname{Im}\langle\eta_i,\eta_j\rangle&=0,\\ 2\operatorname{Im}\langle\eta_i,\zeta_j\rangle &=\mathcal I\delta_{ij},\\ 2\operatorname{Im}\langle\zeta_i,\zeta_j\rangle &=-\frac12J_{ij}. \end{aligned}} \tag{9} The first identity follows from commuting translation generators. The second includes the full Dirac velocity partner in (7). For the third, put \chi_i=Mx_i\phi-i\alpha_i\phi/2, so \zeta_i=i\chi_i. Its cross terms give -MF_0J_{ij} to the imaginary overlap, while the Dirac spin term gives \frac14\langle\phi,-i\alpha_i\alpha_j\phi\rangle =\frac14\left(1-\frac{4G}{d}\right)J_{ij}. \tag{10} Equation (6) makes their sum -J_{ij}/4, proving the last line of (9). The orbital and lower radial components are essential to these identities. The number-density centroid differs from the scalar center. Since 2\operatorname{Re}(\phi^\dagger\zeta_j)=\phi^\dagger\alpha_j\phi, \boxed{R_{\rho,i}=X_i+F_0J_{ij}v_j.} \tag{11} Indeed, \int x_i\phi^\dagger\alpha_j\phi\,dx=F_0J_{ij}. Number continuity then identifies the integrated number current with \dot R_\rho. All quantities in (9)–(11) are integrals of fields and derivatives on the actual spatial coordinates. Apply a slowly varying uniform electric field To the required order, use energy \mathcal I|v|^2/2-qE\cdot R_\rho. The symplectic matrix from the stated field-action convention is \begin{pmatrix} 0&-\mathcal I I_d\\ \mathcal I I_d&J/2 \end{pmatrix} \tag{12} in coordinates (X,v). Its equations give \mathcal I\dot v=qE,\qquad \mathcal I\dot X+\frac12J\dot v =\mathcal I v+qF_0JE. \tag{13} Keeping J at its unperturbed value suffices at linear order in this uniform electric perturbation. Therefore \dot R_\rho =v+q\left(\frac{2F_0}{\mathcal I} -\frac1{2\mathcal I^2}\right)JE. \tag{14} For time dependence e^{-i\omega t} and E=i\omega A, the induced current is \boxed{ \delta j_{\rm em} =-q^2\left[ \frac1{\mathcal I}I_d +i\omega\left(\frac1{2\mathcal I^2} -\frac{2F_0}{\mathcal I}\right)J +O(\omega^2)\right]A.} \tag{15} The leading coefficient is independent of target polarization. It gives the usual Thomson current structure if \mathcal I is the physical inertial mass and (2) is the physical normalized connection coupling. Those identifications are additional to the derivation. Check against the complete source response There is an independent route which keeps the entire radial spectrum. Let c_i=\beta x_i\phi and u_i=\alpha_i\phi be the scalar-center and current source columns. For any Hermitian source labels A,B, define \Pi_{AB}(\omega)= \langle A\phi,(\omega-H_b+M)^{-1}B\phi\rangle +\langle B\phi,(-\omega-H_b+M)^{-1}A\phi\rangle. \tag{16} Both signed frequency terms are required. The center curvature is \kappa=-2a/Q_\sigma, where Q_\sigma=\int\phi^\dagger\beta\phi\,dx. Its feedback gives \boxed{\chi_{uu}=\Pi_{uu} +\Pi_{uc}\kappa(I-\Pi_{cc}\kappa)^{-1}\Pi_{cu}.} \tag{17} All coordinate indices are retained. Parity separates these odd source columns from the even scalar shape sources at zero spatial wavenumber. The current columns can also be generated without a current ansatz: u_i=i(H_b-M)(x_i\phi). \tag{18} Complete angular radial families in (16)–(18) reproduce every coefficient of (15). The frozen-profile response \Pi_{uu} tends to zero; the moving center supplies the finite leading term. This distinguishes a vanishing frozen overlap from a vanishing physical response. Relate the current moment to a measured particle property The actual antisymmetric magnetic moment tensor from (3) is \mu_{ij}=\frac12\int(x_i j_{{\rm em},j} -x_j j_{{\rm em},i})\,dx=qF_0J_{ij}. \tag{19} Using S_{ij}=J_{ij}/2 and defining the gyromagnetic factor by \mu_{ij}=g_{\rm mag}qS_{ij}/(2\mathcal I) gives \boxed{g_{\rm mag}=4\mathcal I F_0,\qquad \chi_{uu}(\omega,0) =\frac1{\mathcal I}I_d +i\omega\frac{1-g_{\rm mag}}{2\mathcal I^2}J+O(\omega^2).} \tag{20} For a selected three-dimensional observation plane this is the ordinary magnetic-moment convention. Selecting that plane distinguishes a measurement geometry; it introduces no inherent split in an electron's six spatial directions. The zero-bare-mass scalar ground profiles give: bound spatial depth conditional g_{\rm mag} 3 2.14608436 5 2.09132914 6 2.07691916 A single-electron measurement in 2023 found g/2=1.00115965218059(13), hence g=2.00231930436118(26). This is the benchmark reported by Fan, Myers, Sukra and Gabrielse, not an atomic-system calculation. Thus the stated six-dimensional scalar profile, with the current (3), does not reproduce the electron magnetic moment. Changing the common coupling rescales the zero-bare-mass profile and leaves this dimensionless factor unchanged. A different occupied field or a derived modification of the physical current would have to supply its own prediction. The spatially uniform kernel (20) is not yet the on-shell photon amplitude. The photon phase and the complete degenerate target polarizations supply another term, calculated in Soft polarized scattering. Conserved spatial charge gives the full kinetic conditions a proposed geometric charge generator must satisfy. Canonical spatial spin response uses the full moving polarization frame to derive the canonical center and the electric spin-orbit coefficient from this same current moment. Verification soft_photon_response_checks.py checks (9)–(11) by direct radial and angular integration of the full spatial fields, including arbitrary complex polarizations. A separate angular radial resolvent calculation verifies (15) and (20) at depths 3, 5, 6 and 10, with zero and positive bare scalar mass. The companion scattering check retains the photon phase and all scalar shape feedback. Reports have timestamped names and checks remain active under Python optimization. These checks establish the stated conditional mathematics; the connection, charge assignment, stable occupied particles and empirical interaction law remain to be derived.

title: Source frequencies in spatial coupling
summary: The full field source, spatial observables and changing mode patterns carry different temporal frequencies, whose relation to normalized response determines whether a slow bound oscillation weakens coupling.
text: Summary: The full field source, spatial observables and changing mode patterns carry different temporal frequencies, whose relation to normalized response determines whether a slow bound oscillation weakens coupling. Identify the clock carried by the interacting spatial pattern A low bound oscillation frequency can affect coupling only through the source actually sampled by the other object. In particular, the frequency in a spatial susceptibility need not equal the phase frequency of the unperturbed bound field. The distinction can be established directly from the written source, without assigning a weak coefficient to depth five. All fields below live on the one nested manifold of ordinary macroscopic spatial dimensions. Mode indices and amplitude components describe fields over that space. They introduce neither further spatial directions nor interaction particles. A finite expansion illustrates the source algebra; it is an exact solution of the nonlinear field equation only when its profiles and amplitudes also satisfy that equation. Bilinear sources carry transition frequencies For normalized spatial modes, write \Psi(t,x,y)=\sum_j c_j\Phi_j(x) e^{i(k_jy-E_jt)}. \tag{1} The normal coordinate y is an existing containing spatial direction. For any time-independent Hermitian source matrix A(x), \boxed{\rho_A=\Psi^\dagger A\Psi =\sum_{i,j}\bar c_i c_j\Phi_i^\dagger A\Phi_j e^{i[(k_j-k_i)y-(E_j-E_i)t]}.} \tag{2} The transition density includes both spatial polarizations, their relative phase and the overlap required by the adopted nested inclusion. Integrating it against a spatial kernel preserves its temporal frequency. Its contribution can vanish geometrically even when that frequency is allowed. The complete spatial vertex is derived in Transition-density coupling. For a single stationary field e^{-iMt}\phi(x), every such bilinear is stationary. This applies to its scalar density and ordinary Dirac current. For a superposition, off-diagonal terms can describe actual moving spatial patterns. Their frequencies are differences, rather than a common phase. A pure occupied mode can still have nonzero transition matrix elements to other modes. The absence of a pre-existing off-diagonal mean density is not the absence of a response to an applied source. The complete nonlinear field source retains a carrier A bilinear density is only one factor in the scalar Dirac source. For \mathcal N[\Psi]=(K\rho_\beta)\beta\Psi, the complete term has \boxed{\Omega_{i;j\ell}=E_j+E_\ell-E_i, \qquad q_{i;j\ell}=k_j+k_\ell-k_i.} \tag{3} Here K is a time-local spatial kernel; a specified kernel with temporal memory would add its own response. The source coefficient includes the full cubic spatial overlap, as derived in Dirac source linearization. For a single frequency, \mathcal N[e^{-iMt}\phi]=e^{-iMt}\mathcal N[\phi]. \tag{4} Thus cancellation of the phase from \Psi^\dagger\beta\Psi does not make the full nonlinear field source time independent. A linear output-mode projection of \Psi samples (3); a photon realized as a bilinear collective observable samples (2) and its tangent response. The physical output map must decide which construction applies. They cannot be identified solely because each contains a small frequency. The principal clocks can be recorded without conflating them: object being followed temporal frequency stationary field component M bilinear spatial transition E_j-E_i cubic field source E_j+E_\ell-E_i perturbation about e^{-iMt}\phi frequency relative to the background carrier opposite-frequency spatial-current beat 2M in its rest description The last row is an exact nonlinear construction in Two-frequency spatial Dirac currents. It supplies a real spatial clock tied to the bound frequency; its amplitude and coupling still need to be calculated. Slow inter-mode clocks can survive large normal momentum For the normal Dirac branch, let E_i(k)=\sqrt{M_i^2+k^2} in units \hbar=c=1. At the same normal momentum, \boxed{E_j(k)-E_i(k) =\frac{M_j^2-M_i^2}{E_j(k)+E_i(k)}.} \tag{5} It equals M_j-M_i at rest and approaches (M_j^2-M_i^2)/(2|k|) at large |k|. Therefore a hierarchy of small bound frequencies can provide slow transition clocks even for energetic propagation. The frequency relation alone does not supply the required spatial transition matrix element or a physical neutrino assignment. Other transitions have different clocks. Within one branch, E(k+q)-E(k) =\frac{2kq+q^2}{E(k+q)+E(k)}. \tag{6} At fixed nonzero forward momentum transfer, this need not vanish as M tends to zero. The complete interaction must retain such channels when its source permits them. The already derived polarization wave has \omega(k)=\sqrt{M^2+k^2}-M. Consequently \frac{\partial\omega}{\partial M}\bigg|_k =\frac{M}{\sqrt{M^2+k^2}}-1<0\quad(k\ne0). \tag{7} Reducing the bound frequency at fixed normal wavelength increases this particular fluctuation frequency. Scaling the wavelength together with M is a different comparison. The scalar moment source of these orthogonal polarization waves has zero first variation at every depth where the stated construction applies. A source phase \Omega t-qy sampled by a target moving with speed v in that direction has proper-time frequency \gamma_v(\Omega-vq). Both the temporal and spatial phase are needed when comparing clocks in different preparations. Include the response scale and normalization The frequency barriers are expansions about zero forcing frequency with fixed profiles and regular response functions. An amplitude proportional to \omega or \omega^2 is small relative to the corresponding spectral and source scales. Those coefficients can change when the particle's bound scale changes. The zero-bare-mass scalar moment branch gives an exact control. Let D_\lambda\phi(x)=\lambda^{d/2}\phi(\lambda x). For unit spatial norm, dilating a complete bound solution gives \phi_\lambda=D_\lambda\phi, \quad M_\lambda=\lambda M, \quad a_\lambda=\lambda^3a, \quad g_\lambda=\lambda^5g. \tag{8} The scalar second moment scales as \lambda^{-2}. A quadrupole source column b_A=\beta(x^TAx)\phi therefore scales as \lambda^{-2}D_\lambda b_A, while the full fluctuation operator scales as \lambda D_\lambda L D_\lambda^\dagger. Both ordinary and conjugate resolvents yield \boxed{\chi_\lambda(\omega) =\lambda^{-5}\chi_1(\omega/\lambda), \qquad g_\lambda\chi_\lambda(\lambda z)=g\chi_1(z).} \tag{9} This holds for the complete self-consistent shape response, not just a bare overlap. A common change of bound scale does not suppress this dimensionless response at a fixed frequency ratio. There is a corresponding fixed-g statement for the single-frequency family of proper density s=\lambda^5. Its field has the additional factor \sqrt{s}. Each source column gains \sqrt{s}, cancelling the \lambda^{-5} factor in the susceptibility. At fixed g, \chi_s(\omega)=\chi_1(\omega/\lambda). \tag{10} This is a density-family identity, not permission to vary an isolated particle's norm to fit its mass. A two-frequency background has additional periodic response coefficients and must be treated separately. Different physical particle scales could still provide a small frequency ratio; their selected profiles and normalization must establish it. Conditions for the proposed neutrino mechanism The proposed five-dimensional application requires a selected spatial mode whose actual source has no unsuppressed static contribution, followed by a derived slow source clock in the frame of its interaction partner. The full response must include both polarizations and all accessible ordinary, conjugate and spatial channels. An incoming mode also has to satisfy its own field equation; Incoming spatial shape modes checks that distinction explicitly. A physical photon additionally has a massless propagating branch. Its outgoing Green function can have poles where a regular static susceptibility does not. The low-frequency power of a gapped shape response cannot by itself determine the normalized photon amplitude or its emitted or scattered flux. V2's neutrino spectrum provides proposed mass indices and a conditional scale reconstruction. The projected mass-operator construction still leaves the depth-five normalization to be derived. Neither the frequency rules nor a chosen small normalization complete that task. Verification source_frequency_checks.py compares full complex spatial bilinears and a nonlocal cubic source with independent temporal Fourier transforms. It checks normal transition clocks, observer phases and complete scalar matrix elements. Independent spatial radial solves and both signs of the fluctuation resolvent verify (8)–(10). Reports preserve previous runs with timestamped filenames; all conditions remain active under Python optimization. Related Dirac source linearization — fixes the complete field-source and rotating-background conventions. Transition-density coupling — supplies the two-sided spatial vertices accompanying the clocks. Two-frequency spatial Dirac currents — gives an exact changing current with a bound-frequency clock. Incoming spatial shape modes — distinguishes a free pattern from a forcing coefficient.

title: Rotation-neutral Dirac fields in physical space
summary: A full radial Dirac field can preserve an exactly neutral total spatial rotation through compensating orbital and spin motion, even though a projector on neutral spin components discards part of the field.
text: Summary: A full radial Dirac field can preserve an exactly neutral total spatial rotation through compensating orbital and spin motion, even though a projector on neutral spin components discards part of the field. Keep the position dependence of the polarization The neutral-doublet calculation shows that projecting the first-order spatial Dirac operator onto neutral spin components removes some momentum responses. Full spatial modes provide a constructive way to retain those components. The conserved rotation acts on position and spin together. Work on a flat d-dimensional spatial model of a sector in the one nested macroscopic manifold. All d directions are ordinary spatial dimensions. The finite spinor components below describe the same field on those coordinates. Choosing rotation planes specifies a probe or a physical preparation; it does not divide a particle's dimensions into different kinds. This note derives neutrality under that specified spatial rotation. Its identification with an electromagnetic interaction remains a separate current calculation. No mediator particle or additional physical dimension is introduced. The full Dirac representation Let Hermitian matrices satisfy \{\alpha_i,\alpha_j\}=2\delta_{ij}I, \qquad \{\alpha_i,\beta\}=0, \qquad\beta^2=I. \tag{1} Let V be an isometric basis of the positive rest eigenspace, \beta V=V, V^\dagger V=I. The map \alpha(v)V lies in the opposite \beta eigenspace for every spatial vector v. The two eigenspaces are field components, not parts of physical space. The full central spatial Hamiltonian is H=-i\alpha_i\partial_i+\beta M(r)+V_0(r)I, \qquad r=|x|. \tag{2} Its radial coefficients may be specified backgrounds or come from a self-consistent source. A derivation must say which applies and keep their response when they are dynamical. For z^\dagger z=1, consider the spatial field \boxed{\Psi(x)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{\Omega_{d-1}}} \left[f(r)Vz+i g(r)\alpha(\widehat x)Vz\right],} \qquad \widehat x=x/r, \tag{3} where \Omega_{d-1} is the area of the unit (d-1)-sphere and f,g are real radial functions. Regularity requires g(r)=O(r) at the origin. The norm and scalar source are \|\Psi\|^2=\int_0^\infty(f^2+g^2)r^{d-1}dr, \qquad \overline\Psi\Psi=\frac{f^2-g^2}{\Omega_{d-1}}. \tag{4} The lower component has a direction-dependent polarization. Removing it would change both the field equation and the scalar source. Substitution into H\Psi=E\Psi gives the full radial equations \boxed{(E-M-V_0)f=g'+\frac{d-1}{r}g, \qquad (E+M-V_0)g=-f'.} \tag{5} They follow from \alpha(\widehat x)^2=I and \alpha_i\partial_i\alpha(\widehat x)=(d-1)I/r. No nonrelativistic approximation has been made. Self-consistent scalar Dirac moment modes solves these radial equations with the potential generated by the existing nonlocal scalar source, and checks its complete radial response. Orbital motion preserves the same total rotation weight Choose m=\lfloor d/2\rfloor ordinary orthogonal rotation planes and set S=-\frac i2\sum_{j=1}^{m}\alpha_{2j-1}\alpha_{2j}, \qquad L=-i\sum_{j=1}^{m} \left(x_{2j-1}\partial_{2j}-x_{2j}\partial_{2j-1}\right), \qquad\mathscr Q=L+S. \tag{6} The Dirac matrices rotate with their spatial arguments. Explicitly, [S,\alpha(x)]=-L\alpha(x),\qquad [\mathscr Q,\alpha(\widehat x)]=0. \tag{7} Every radial function is annihilated by L. If the rest polarization has S Vz=qVz, equation (3) therefore obeys \boxed{\mathscr Q\Psi=q\Psi.} \tag{8} This is an operator identity for the entire position-dependent field. For a physical rotation R(\theta) in the chosen planes, its finite version is e^{-i\theta S}\Psi\big(R(\theta)^{-1}x\big) =e^{-iq\theta}\Psi(x). \tag{9} The kinetic operator and both central terms in (2) commute with \mathscr Q. A rotation-equivariant nonlinear scalar source also preserves an initially fixed rotation sector, subject to the adopted domains and uniqueness of evolution. Retaining the lower component is fully consistent with that conservation. The five-dimensional neutral modes remain available The rest weights are the spin lifts of the chosen spatial rotations. At depth five the four-component rest module has weights (-1,0,0,1), so two independent choices in (3) give \mathscr Q\Psi=0. Those fields can have nonzero density throughout all five spatial coordinates. At depth six the rest module is a selected four-component half-spin representation. Three equal rotation planes give half-integer weights with no zero. The five-plane depth-ten construction likewise has no zero weight. With ordinary single-valued spatial wavefunctions, the full 2\pi rotation acts as -I when the number of planes is odd; orbital integer weights cannot turn it into a zero eigenvalue. The rotation-weight note gives the representation assumptions and the other depths, including the even-plane cases which also admit zero weights. The comparison concerns the same type of geometric operation. It is not a proof that this operation is the photon current or that all five-dimensional particles occupy its neutral modes. Neutral and nonneutral radial polarizations in (3) have the same scalar density and radial equations. Their occupation still requires a dynamical explanation. What a spin-only projection would discard Let F=\int f^2r^{d-1}dr,\qquad G=\int g^2r^{d-1}dr, \qquad F+G=1. Spherical averaging and the Clifford identity \sum_i\alpha_iS\alpha_i=(d-4)S give \langle S\rangle=q\left(1-\frac{4G}{d}\right), \qquad \langle L\rangle=\frac{4Gq}{d}, \qquad\langle\mathscr Q\rangle=q. \tag{10} For a five-dimensional zero-weight state, the lower component also obeys \boxed{\langle S^2\rangle=\langle L^2\rangle=\frac45G, \qquad\mathscr Q\Psi=0.} \tag{11} The spin and orbital actions cancel on the full field, although each can have a nonzero norm. One way to obtain (11) is to use S^2=I/2+ a Clifford grade-four term and \sum_i\alpha_iT_4\alpha_i=(d-8)T_4. On a rest state with S^2Vz=0, the lower angular average gives 4/5. A projector onto \ker S alone discards a fraction 4G/5 of the complete field norm: the lower component in four of the five spatial directions has nonzero spin weight, compensated by its orbital dependence. That discarded norm is not a violation of the conserved total neutrality in (8). Equations (7)–(11) specify the distinction exactly. A neutral total rotation does not imply zero local current Define the rest polarization bivector by J_{ij}=z^\dagger V^\dagger(-i\alpha_i\alpha_j)Vz, \quad i<j, \qquad J_{ji}=-J_{ij}. \tag{12} Direct substitution of (3) into the Dirac velocity current yields \boxed{j_i(x)=\Psi^\dagger\alpha_i\Psi =-\frac{2f(r)g(r)}{\Omega_{d-1}}J_{ij}\widehat x_j.} \tag{13} The current is tangent to the radial spheres. Its divergence vanishes: J is skew, x^TJx=0, and \operatorname{tr}J=0. These are literal spatial circulation planes of the field. The unpaired direction of a five-dimensional rotation can be a null direction of its current tensor while remaining a direction in which the field has spatial extent. For a specified charged minimal action, the electric current would include its supplied charge factor. Equation (13) itself is the velocity current; zero weight under \mathscr Q does not make this current vanish. The physical source must be obtained from the same action and the appropriate photon projection. Dressed source vertices shows how to retain the required current if modes are subsequently eliminated. Compatibility with the entire nested geometry The rotation used here can move lower members of a nested chain. Rotations of nested sectors distinguishes preserving each fixed member from transporting the whole chain while preserving its nesting. A physical application must include those embedding motions and both interacting objects' polarizations. Equations (8)–(13) retain full spatial motion but do not select a universal embedding or assign a charge generator to every particle. Normal propagation of spatial Dirac modes retains the containing-space Dirac partner and derives exact free-direction boosts of this full spatial field, including its scalar source and current. Verification spatial_dirac_mode_checks.py builds full Clifford matrices independently at depths three, five, six and ten. It tests finite rotations of position-dependent fields, spatial finite differences of L, the complete current, and positive spherical cubature for the spin variance and discarded fraction. title: Spatial displacement action
summary: Full spatial deformation gives the exact constant-gradient action and a common leading interaction between two polarized displacement waves, with the complementary field retained explicitly.
text:
Summary: Full spatial deformation gives the exact constant-gradient action and a common leading interaction between two polarized displacement waves, with the complementary field retained explicitly. Retain both incoming spatial polarizations Use the declared unit-vector field action of Null spatial pulses: S= rac Z2\int dt\,dy\,d^2x\, \partial_\mu n\cdot\partial^\mu n,\qquad n^2=1. 	ag{1} Its static profile is n_0(x)= rac{(2\lambda x_1,2\lambda x_2,|x|^2-\lambda^2)} {|x|^2+\lambda^2},\qquad \mathcal T=4\pi Z. 	ag{2} The coordinates are ordinary spatial directions in one containing manifold; n has three constrained field components. Equation (1) remains a conditional component action to be derived from the master field before any physical photon identification. Each one-way pulse n_0(x-X(t\mp y)) solves the complete field equation. To examine an interaction, retain both real vector profiles: X(t,y)=A(t-y)+B(t+y),\qquad a=A'(t-y),\quad b=B'(t+y). 	ag{3} Both a and b have their own two-dimensional spatial polarization. A relative angle is physical data; replacing either vector by its norm before varying the field would discard it. Compute the omitted spatial deformation Let n_i=\partial_i n_0 and define the tangent second derivative \mathcal H_{ij}=\partial_i\partial_jn_0 +(n_i\cdot n_j)n_0. 	ag{4} The static field equation gives \mathcal H_{11}+\mathcal H_{22}=0. Substituting the rigidly shifted profile into the complete field equation leaves \mathcal R= (\dot X_i\dot X_j-X_{y,i}X_{y,j})\mathcal H_{ij} =S_{ij}\mathcal H_{ij}, 	ag{5} because \Box_{t,y}X=0, with  oxed{ S=2\left(ab^T+ba^T-(a\cdot b)I_2ight).} 	ag{6} The trace has dropped out using (4). The residual is tangent to the field-value constraint and represents an actual change of the spatial profile. In two bound directions,  oxed{S^2=4|a|^2|b|^2I_2,\qquad \operatorname{tr}S^2=8|a|^2|b|^2.} 	ag{7} Thus a nonzero pair of opposite pulses always has a nonzero quadrupole source. Perpendicular polarizations have a\cdot b=0 but still S
e0. For example, a=e_1,b=e_2 gives S=2 egin{pmatrix}0&1\1&0\end{pmatrix}; a=b=e_1 gives S=2\operatorname{diag}(1,-1). The source orientation changes while its norm stays the same. This is a full-field example of the distinction between a vanishing overlap and a vanishing reciprocal response in Bilateral polarization coupling. For (2), direct differentiation sharpens (5): \mathcal R =- rac4{|x|^2+\lambda^2}(Sx)_i n_i, \qquad  oxed{\int|\mathcal R|^2d^2x = rac{128\pi}{3\lambda^2}|a|^2|b|^2.} 	ag{8} Its projection onto each translation tangent vanishes by spatial parity: \int n_i\cdot\mathcal R\,d^2x=0. A calculation retaining only X would therefore miss this entire complementary source, just as a projected polarization texture can miss its full field residual. Complete a uniformly moving and tilted plane exactly For constant velocity v and slope w, put C=I_2+ww^T-vv^T,\qquad C>0,\qquad L=C^{-1/2}. 	ag{9} The full profile  oxed{n(t,x,y)=n_0\!\left(L(x-vt-wy)ight)} 	ag{10} solves the nonlinear field equation. In fact, LCL^T=I_2, so the derivatives of its two spatial arguments have exactly the static orthonormal contraction. The positive-definiteness condition states that their normal plane is spacelike. This construction includes the required rotation and contraction of the spatial profile. It does not hold that profile rigid while changing its motion. Integrating the original action over the actual x plane gives  oxed{\mathscr L(v,w) =-\mathcal T\sqrt{\det(I_2+ww^T-vv^T)}.} 	ag{11} The factor is the Jacobian 1/\det L. Equivalently, \det C=(1-|v|^2)(1+|w|^2)+(v\cdot w)^2. 	ag{12} Equation (11) is the induced-area action, often called the Nambu–Goto form, here obtained by integrating the explicit full spatial solution. No independent interaction coefficient is assigned to each polarization. Derive the common quartic term in two ways Expanding (11) about a straight resting background gives  egin{aligned} \mathscr L ={}&-\mathcal T+ rac{\mathcal T}{2}(|v|^2-|w|^2)\ &+ rac{\mathcal T}{8}(|v|^2-|w|^2)^2 + rac{\mathcal T}{2} \left[|v|^2|w|^2-(v\cdot w)^2ight] +O((v,w)^6). \end{aligned} 	ag{13} Using v=a+b,w=-a+b, its quartic part is  oxed{\mathscr L_4=2\mathcal T|a|^2|b|^2 = rac2{\mathcal T} |\partial_{u_-}\varphi|^2|\partial_{u_+}\varphi|^2,\qquad \varphi=\sqrt{\mathcal T}\,X,} 	ag{14} where u_-=t-y and u_+=t+y. Here \varphi is the canonically normalized displacement field. The same \mathcal T fixes propagation normalization and the interaction coefficient. There is an independent spatial-response derivation of (14). Let \mathcal J be the constrained static energy Hessian divided by Z, on tangents perpendicular to n_0. Its quadratic form is \langle\eta,\mathcal J\etaangle =\int\left[|
abla\eta|^2-|
abla n_0|^2|\eta|^2ight]d^2x. 	ag{15} The trace-free part of the completed profile's second-order change is \eta= rac12(Sx)_i n_i,\qquad \mathcal J\eta=-\mathcal R. 	ag{16} The trace part is a static size variation and has zero Hessian at this order. Direct integration gives  oxed{ Z\langle\eta,\mathcal Rangle=-4\mathcal T|a|^2|b|^2,\qquad Z\langle\eta,\mathcal J\etaangle=4\mathcal T|a|^2|b|^2.} 	ag{17} Substituting this response into -Z\langle\eta,\mathcal Rangle -	frac Z2\langle\eta,\mathcal J\etaangle gives 2\mathcal T|a|^2|b|^2, precisely (14). The complementary spatial field supplies the interaction that the rigid translation projection misses. Domain of the interaction result Equation (11) is exact for constant gradients. Equation (14) is its leading local term with four first derivatives, with its coefficient also fixed by the static response calculation. It is not the complete scattering law of arbitrary finite pulses. The correction (16) has a 1/r tail. Its static quadratic-form energy is finite, but its L^2 norm grows logarithmically with transverse cutoff. The original sigma model also has a gapless transverse continuum. An arbitrary time-dependent elimination consequently needs boundary conditions and a retarded spatial response; a gapped-mode approximation cannot simply be assumed. A finite collision must retain the additional profile deformation and any emitted field. The equal-strength result in (7) and (14) is specific to this two-dimensional profile and this component action. It establishes a coherent geometrical interaction calculation with both wave polarizations, but neither a measured electromagnetic coefficient nor an interaction with the occupied electron or neutrino geometry has been derived. Retarded displacement response constructs that causal spatial inverse and derives its low-frequency logarithm, positive spectral normalization and outgoing radiation. Polarized pulse collisions solves the local induced-area equations with both full vector waveforms and derives their reciprocal energy-dependent delays. Verification null_spatial_wave_checks.py checks the complete finite pulses and moving planes using independent spacetime differences. Physical-space quadrature verifies (11); separate derivative, source and Hessian integrals verify (8) and (15)–(17). Both parallel and perpendicular polarizations are retained. The executable also checks the constant-gradient expansion and its canonical coefficient. Reports have timestamped names and all checks remain active under Python optimization.

title: Spatial polarization textures
summary: Allowing polarization to vary across a bound particle can preserve its scalar density while creating a full spatial kinetic residual, whose omitted components must be solved before the texture is a physical mode.
text: Summary: Allowing polarization to vary across a bound particle can preserve its scalar density while creating a full spatial kinetic residual, whose omitted components must be solved before the texture is a physical mode. Allow the polarization to vary over the actual bound coordinates A constant vector of complex amplitudes describes one part of a particle's polarization; Complete spatial polarization data identifies its full tensor description. Its phase and orientation can also vary across its spatial profile. That possibility must be tested in the field equation rather than accepted because it preserves a selected density. Use the complete stationary radial frame of Equal-current spatial polarizations: H_bW=MW,\qquad W^\dagger W=\rho(x)I,\qquad W^\dagger\beta W=\sigma(x)I. \tag{1} The bound coordinates x are ordinary macroscopic directions in the particle's submanifold. There is only the one infinite nested physical manifold. The frame's column labels describe field components over it. Consider \boxed{\Psi(x,t)=e^{-iMt}W(x)z(x,t),\qquad z^\dagger z=1.} \tag{2} At every point, the number and scalar densities remain \rho and \sigma. For a scalar self-binding source depending only on the latter density's centered moments, its coefficient is unchanged. This statement holds regardless of how rapidly z varies. It establishes the source value, not the full spatial equation. The spatial derivative supplies an additional response With H_b=-i\alpha_i\partial_i+\beta m_{\rm eff}(x), direct application of the product rule gives \boxed{ H_b(Wz)=MWz-i\sum_i\alpha_iW\,\partial_i z.} \tag{3} Consequently the remaining field equation after removing the carrier is \boxed{iW\partial_tz=-i\sum_i\alpha_iW\,\partial_i z.} \tag{4} The right side need not lie in the image of W(x). Where \rho(x)>0, define the actual local projector and compressed current matrices \boxed{ P_W=\frac{WW^\dagger}{\rho},\qquad A_i=\frac{W^\dagger\alpha_iW}{\rho}.} \tag{5} Equation (4) is equivalent to the projected equation together with its complementary condition: \boxed{ i\partial_tz=-i\sum_i A_i\partial_i z,\qquad 0=-i\sum_i(I-P_W)\alpha_iW\,\partial_i z.} \tag{6} The second equality is essential. Solving only the first can manufacture an apparent polarization mode while omitting a nonzero spatial response. For a real evolving field, additional profile components can be excited, and its source must then be recomputed. The radial frame gives the full matrix identity \boxed{W^\dagger\alpha_iW =-\frac{2FG}{\Omega_{d-1}} \sum_j B_{ij}\widehat x_j,} \tag{7} where B_{ji}=-B_{ij} and B_{ii}=0. The diagonal bilinear of (7) recovers the ordinary Dirac current. Its entire matrix is needed for the varying amplitudes in (6). The first equation also carries the number continuity condition. Because \partial_i(\rho A_i)=0 for this fixed radial frame, \partial_t(\rho\,z^\dagger z) +\partial_i(\rho\,z^\dagger A_i z)=0 \tag{8} follows from it. Maintaining the pointwise constraint z^\dagger z=1 requires the resulting current to have zero divergence. An arbitrary initial texture need not preserve that constraint under its dynamics. A concrete texture lies outside the retained equation Take a normalized constant z_0 and a Hermitian spatial rotation matrix B with B^2=I, and set z(x)=e^{ikx_1B}z_0. \tag{9} Only \partial_1z=ikBz is nonzero, so its stationary kinetic remainder is \boxed{\mathcal R=k\alpha_1WBz,\qquad \|\mathcal R(x)\|^2=k^2\rho(x).} \tag{10} On the physical axis x=r e_1, equation (7) gives A_1=0. Thus \boxed{P_W\mathcal R=0,\qquad \|(I-P_W)\mathcal R\|^2=k^2\rho.} \tag{11} At that point the entire nonzero response is missed by the projected polarization equation. The example identifies precisely which part of the full spatial equation must be retained; it does not claim that the imposed texture is a stationary particle. Even a common spatial phase can conceal the missing motion Let \Phi be a unit-normalized stationary field of the same model. For a smooth real function \theta(x), put \widetilde\Phi(x)=e^{i\theta(x)}\Phi(x). \tag{12} Every local nondifferential bilinear is unchanged: \widetilde\Phi^\dagger O\widetilde\Phi=\Phi^\dagger O\Phi \tag{13} for a local component operator O. This includes the number density, the scalar source and every local Dirac current component. The spatial equation nevertheless gives \boxed{ (H_b-M)\widetilde\Phi =e^{i\theta}\alpha(\nabla\theta)\Phi,\qquad \|(H_b-M)\widetilde\Phi\|_{L^2}^2 =\int\rho\,|\nabla\theta|^2\,dx.} \tag{14} The last equality uses the full Clifford identity \alpha(v)^\dagger\alpha(v)=|v|^2I for real v. For \theta=kx_1, the residual norm is exactly |k| for a normalized field. This is a physical spatial phase gradient, despite all the unchanged bilinears in (13). The original scalar Dirac equation has a global phase symmetry. A local phase with its connection held fixed changes the field dynamics. If a gauge connection is part of a different specified action, transform that connection too before declaring two configurations gauge-equivalent. What a complete polarization calculation must add The constant polarization waves supply exact solutions with their own normal partner and unchanged scalar source. The scalar envelope derives a separate remainder when the bound profile changes with its amplitude. Equations (3)–(14) add the bound-coordinate texture response. A proposed richer particle pattern must therefore supply its spatial amplitudes and phases, satisfy the complete kinetic equation, and retain the profile components and source changes generated by that equation. The neutral-doublet transport provides another example where a projected derivative omits a necessary Dirac complement. Neither a density plot nor the number of polarization parameters is sufficient to establish a physical mode. Verification spatial_polarization_structure_checks.py uses complete self-consistent spatial fields at depths three, five, six and ten. It tests their local metrics and projectors, then differentiates the textured fields in every actual bound coordinate. Independent full Dirac evaluations verify (3), the projected and complementary terms in (6), the wholly omitted response in (11), and the spatial-phase norm in (14). The scalar source and every Dirac current are recomputed rather than inferred from a plotted profile. Reports are timestamped and all checks remain active under Python optimization.

title: Spatial source complementarity
summary: Projecting a normalized odd-dimensional rotation tensor and its null-axis vector onto a lower spatial subspace gives an exact complementarity identity and conditional source-strength bound.
text: Summary: Projecting a normalized odd-dimensional rotation tensor and its null-axis vector onto a lower spatial subspace gives an exact complementarity identity and conditional source-strength bound. A source determined by the higher geometry This calculation starts with a higher-dimensional spatial source and asks which of its components survive on a chosen lower subspace. All spaces are ordinary macroscopic spatial directions in one nested manifold. The split is relative to that lower subspace; it is not an inherent division of the higher particle. Use the normalized skew tensor and unit null vector from the dimensional magnetic kernel: J^T=-J,\qquad J^2=-I+nn^T,\qquad |n|=1 \tag{1} in dimension d=2m+1. These imply Jn=0 and unit rotational singular values on n^\perp. At depth five, the specified pure spatial spinor model supplies both J and n. For other odd dimensions, (1) defines a conditional tensor family rather than a claim about all spinors or physical particles. Let W be an r-dimensional lower spatial subspace and let Z=W^\perp, of dimension s=d-r. In adapted orthonormal frames, J=\begin{pmatrix}A&Q\\-Q^T&C\end{pmatrix}, \qquad n=\begin{pmatrix}n_W\\n_Z\end{pmatrix}. \tag{2} A is the restriction of the rotational two-form to W, while n_W is the projected vector. Use \|A\|^2=-\operatorname{tr}(A^2)/2 for skew matrices and the ordinary Euclidean norm for vectors. Exact projection identity The diagonal blocks of (1) are A^2-QQ^T=-I_r+n_Wn_W^T, \qquad C^2-Q^TQ=-I_s+n_Zn_Z^T. Writing t=|n_W|^2 and using |n_Z|^2=1-t, their traces give 2\|A\|^2+\|Q\|_F^2=r-t, \qquad 2\|C\|^2+\|Q\|_F^2=s-1+t. Subtracting eliminates every mixed component and yields \boxed{\|A\|^2+|n_W|^2-\|C\|^2=r-m.} \tag{3} Consequently \|A\|^2+|n_W|^2\geq r-m. \tag{4} The lower bound is useful when r>m. It is a statement about projected source descriptors, before identifying an interaction channel or rate. Five-dimensional source viewed in three dimensions For d=5 and r=3, equation (3) reads \boxed{\|A\|^2+|n_W|^2=1+\|C\|^2\geq1.} \tag{5} Every real three-dimensional skew matrix has one rotational singular value a\geq0, with \|A\|^2=a^2. Since A is a compression of a norm-one operator, a\leq1. These bounds sharpen two endpoint cases: If n_W=0, then \|A\|^2=1 and C=0. If A=0, then |n_W|=1 and C=0. Both cases are attainable. In an orthonormal basis of \mathbb R^5, take J=e_1\wedge e_2+e_3\wedge e_4 and n=e_5. The first case is W=\operatorname{span}(e_1,e_2,e_3); the second is W=\operatorname{span}(e_1,e_3,e_5). Thus orientation alone cannot make both projected descriptors small in this normalized family. If a response reads these as orthogonal, distinguishable channels with positive weights g_B,g_V, then g_B\|A\|^2+g_V|n_W|^2\geq\min(g_B,g_V). \tag{6} This bound requires both channels to be present with the stated positive metric. A physical map might omit one channel, assign different derived normalizations, or coherently combine contributions. In those cases the actual map must be evaluated; (6) does not replace it. In particular, the five-dimensional vector supplied by the scalar-exchange benchmark has not been identified as an electromagnetic source by this identity. Relation to photon observations in a shared three-plane Let k\in W be a unit propagation direction and take the observer's photon plane E=W\cap k^\perp. Because k^TJk=0, P_EJk=Ak. \tag{7} Write Av=b\times v in an oriented frame on W; this three-dimensional axial-vector notation is only a way of describing the restricted two-form. Then |b|^2=\|A\|^2 and C(E,k;J)=|b|^2-(b\cdot k)^2. \tag{8} For a uniform propagation direction within this fixed W, \mathbb E_{k\in S(W)}C=\frac23\|A\|^2. \tag{9} This is the sum over two photon polarizations. An unpolarized average has the additional factor 1/2. If A=0, every such photon direction has zero magnetic overlap, even though the higher tensor J is nonzero. For the five-dimensional model, (5) then requires a fully projected vector n_W. Its physical coupling must be evaluated separately. The preparation in (9) fixes the observer subspace and target tensor. It differs from the full isotropic relative-preparation ensemble in isotropic polarization comparison. Even-dimensional comparison For a normalized even-dimensional tensor J^2=-I in d=2m, the same trace calculation gives \boxed{\|A\|^2-\|C\|^2=r-m.} \tag{10} At d=6,r=3, the two restricted norms are equal and both may vanish. For example J=e_1\wedge e_2+e_3\wedge e_4+e_5\wedge e_6 and W=\operatorname{span}(e_1,e_3,e_5) give A=C=0, while the mixed block carries the complete rotation. This is a relation to a chosen observer three-plane; the electron's six spatial dimensions remain equivalent and have no inherent split. The odd/even identities provide exact tests of a proposed descending source map. They do not determine a particle's global spatial topology, prepare the required orientations, or assign empirical coupling strengths. Verification polarization_coupling_checks.py checks the displayed identities with independent spatial quadrature, energy variations, or full finite-system evolution as appropriate. These checks verify the declared mathematics and benchmarks, not empirical couplings. Related Dimensional magnetic kernel — derives the particular five-dimensional vector and rotational tensor and distinguishes candidate interaction terms. Descending photon source — derives the higher-field source before selecting its lower response. Photon plane coupling — supplies the overlap used in (7)–(9). Isotropic polarization comparison — evaluates a different, explicitly averaged ensemble.

title: Transition-density coupling
summary: The complete derivative of a bilocal density interaction pairs both objects' transition densities, giving reciprocal mode vertices and an exact signed quadrupole matching law from the existing spatial kernel.
text: Summary: The complete derivative of a bilocal density interaction pairs both objects' transition densities, giving reciprocal mode vertices and an exact signed quadrupole matching law from the existing spatial kernel. The spatial patterns which must match A coupling calculation compares the changes that two spatial patterns can undergo. For a density interaction the relevant objects are their transition densities, which can have signs and complex phases even when each original density is positive. Their pairing provides a precise version of shape matching with both objects polarized. Use one field \Psi(t,x) on a specified finite containing spatial region of the nested macroscopic manifold. The labels x,y below are two points in that same physical space. Let A_\alpha(x) be fixed Hermitian matrices on its field components, and define real scalar bilinears \rho_\alpha(x)=\Psi(x)^\dagger A_\alpha(x)\Psi(x). \tag{1} For a compatible Dirac scalar channel one may take A_\alpha=\beta P_\alpha when \beta P_\alpha is Hermitian. Positivity of the bilinear is not assumed. The channel labels do not supply spatial embeddings; the appropriate nested maps, transport and measures must be included in the kernel used for a physical application. The same energy fixes both responses Take a real exchange-symmetric spatial kernel K_{\alpha\beta}(x,y)=K_{\beta\alpha}(y,x) and the energy term E_{\rm int}[\Psi]=\frac12\sum_{\alpha,\beta} \iint\rho_\alpha(x)K_{\alpha\beta}(x,y)\rho_\beta(y) d\mu_xd\mu_y. \tag{2} Define U=K\rho with the indicated integrals. Its field source is \big(\mathcal N[\Psi]\big)(x)=\sum_\alpha U_\alpha(x)A_\alpha(x)\Psi(x). \tag{3} This is the Hamiltonian convention \delta E=2\operatorname{Re}\langle\delta\Psi,\mathcal N\rangle. The bilocal variation derives (3) directly from the two density factors in (2). At a specified background \phi, let (D\eta)_\alpha(x)=2\operatorname{Re} \big[\phi(x)^\dagger A_\alpha(x)\eta(x)\big], \qquad V_\phi=\sum_\alpha(K\rho[\phi])_\alpha A_\alpha. \tag{4} D\eta is the change in the source density. Differentiating the whole source, including that change, gives \boxed{D\mathcal N[\phi]\eta =V_\phi\eta+\sum_\alpha A_\alpha\phi\,(KD\eta)_\alpha.} \tag{5} The first term is multiplication by the existing potential. The second term is the response of the potential to the changing pattern. It is generally real-linear and depends on \eta and its conjugate. For two independent field variations, the complete mixed second derivative is \boxed{\big(E_{\rm int}''[\phi]\big)(\eta,\zeta) =2\operatorname{Re}\langle\eta,V_\phi\zeta\rangle +\langle D\eta,KD\zeta\rangle_{\rm real}.} \tag{6} Exchange symmetry of K makes (6) symmetric in the two variations. This is reciprocity before any mode truncation or amplitude convention. With the real field pairing \operatorname{Re}\langle\eta,\zeta\rangle, the density-map adjoint satisfies D^*f=2\sum_\alpha A_\alpha\phi f_\alpha; thus (5) is also V_\phi+\tfrac12D^*KD. A response with D\eta=0 has no density-feedback term, but it can still respond through V_\phi, kinetic cross terms or other action terms. In particular D(i\phi)=0 while D\mathcal N[\phi]\,(i\phi)=i\mathcal N[\phi]. The full phase zero mode requires an actual stationary solution and the kinetic part of its equation. The complete coherent mode vertex Let \Phi_i(x) be modes normalized in the derived kinetic metric. If they are not orthonormal, apply the canonical normalization before interpreting amplitude magnitudes. Define transition densities r_{ij}^{\alpha}(x)=\Phi_i(x)^\dagger A_\alpha(x)\Phi_j(x). \tag{7} For \Psi=\sum_i c_i\Phi_i the exact quartic term is E_{\rm int}=\frac12\sum_{i,j,k,l} \bar c_i c_j\bar c_kc_l\,T_{ij;kl}, \qquad T_{ij;kl}=\sum_{\alpha,\beta}\iint r_{ij}^{\alpha}(x)K_{\alpha\beta}(x,y)r_{kl}^{\beta}(y) d\mu_xd\mu_y. \tag{8} Both pairs of modes enter. Reversing a transition changes its density to its complex conjugate, giving T_{ij;kl}=T_{kl;ij},\qquad \overline{T_{ij;kl}}=T_{ji;lk}. \tag{9} This retains the spatial shapes and relative phases required by the one field. The diagonal densities alone do not determine (8). Likewise, frequency matching does not guarantee a nonzero spatial vertex. A rotating wave approximation can select resonant terms only after this full tensor and the temporal frequencies have been calculated. Exact factorization for the spatial dot-square kernel For two prescribed spatial charts and their rectangular identification B:\mathbb R^e\to\mathbb R^d, adopt the scalar term K(x,y)=g(x^TBy)^2. Define complex transition moments M_{ij}^{(a)}=\int xx^T\bar\Phi_i^{(a)}\Phi_j^{(a)}\,dx, \qquad M_{kl}^{(b)}=\int yy^T\bar\Phi_k^{(b)}\Phi_l^{(b)}\,dy. Expansion of the two dot products gives \boxed{T_{ij;kl}=g\operatorname{tr} \left(M_{ij}^{(a)}B M_{kl}^{(b)}B^T\right).} \tag{10} There is no extra complex conjugate in this bilinear expression; the reversal identities are already in (9). The geometric action supplies the identification B, and common physical rotations transform all three tensor factors consistently. Centre motion or a position-dependent contact factor must also be varied when they belong to the adopted energy. The source channel has at most d(d+1)/2 independent symmetric moment components at fixed depth. These are descriptions of spatial shape, not additional spatial axes. Higher spatial structure can enter other terms of the action even when it is absent from this particular kernel. A normalized shape-matching example Use ordinary flat Gaussian modes with width parameter \omega>0, \phi_0(x)=\left(\frac\omega\pi\right)^{d/4} e^{-\omega|x|^2/2}. For a real symmetric matrix A with \operatorname{tr}A^2=1, define the polarized quadratic shape mode \phi_A(x)=\sqrt2\,\omega \left(x^TAx-\frac{\operatorname{tr}A}{2\omega}\right)\phi_0(x). \tag{11} Gaussian second and fourth moments give \langle\phi_0,\phi_A\rangle=0,\qquad \|\phi_A\|=1,\qquad \int xx^T\phi_0\phi_A\,dx=\frac{A}{\sqrt2\,\omega}. \tag{12} For example the covariance of x^TAx under |\phi_0|^2 is \operatorname{tr}A^2/(2\omega^2), establishing the normalization. The covariance of xx^T with x^TAx is A/(2\omega^2), establishing the transition moment. Two such patterns, with shape tensors A,C and widths \omega_a,\omega_b, therefore have the exact vertex T_{0A;0C}=\frac{g}{2\omega_a\omega_b} \operatorname{tr}(A B C B^T). \tag{13} For two real fluctuation amplitudes q_a,q_b about the respective backgrounds, the mixed second derivative of the cross energy is four times (13): each density variation contributes a factor two. Equation (13) itself is the normalized quartic mode vertex, not that Hessian. In a shared two-plane take B=I and A=\frac1{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}, \qquad C=R(\theta)A R(\theta)^T. Then \boxed{T_{0A;0C}=\frac{g}{2\omega_a\omega_b}\cos(2\theta).} \tag{14} The patterns have the same nonzero spatial support and norm, yet this transition is exactly blocked at \theta=\pi/4. At \theta=\pi/2 the amplitude reverses sign. Rotating both objects by the same angle changes neither result. Squaring the amplitude gives a \cos^2(2\theta) angular factor for an otherwise specified transition probability. There is also an orientation-independent mismatch: a traceless shape A has zero pairing with the breathing shape C=I/\sqrt d for every relative rotation in this isotropic kernel. Other compatible shape transitions can remain nonzero. These are explicit geometric selection rules obtained from the existing interaction, without assigning a separate zero to a selected particle species. Scope of the selection rule For harmonic-oscillator basis functions, multiplication by x_ix_j changes total oscillator number by 0 or \pm2. Thus (10) connects only the corresponding mode pairs on each side. This is a rule for the transition density and its moment; it is not a claim that an odd spatial field has zero self-energy. The distinction is derived in angular kernel parity. Equations (11)–(14) are a conditional flat-profile example. They do not replace the actual Coulomb-plus-precession electron orbit or specify a neutrino profile. Their role is to demonstrate, using an explicit kernel, how polarization becomes a higher-order spatial shape selection rule. The occupied particle solutions, photon map, accessible target motions, kinetic scales and scattering boundary conditions remain to be derived. Verification spatial_coupling_mechanism_checks.py compares (5)–(6) with finite differences of the full nonlocal complex-field energy using unequal spatial weights, indefinite bilinears and both positive and indefinite kernels. It reconstructs the complete quartic energy from (8), checks reciprocity, and independently evaluates (12)–(14) by Gaussian double quadrature with both shape orientations varied. Related Projected bilocal variation — supplies the action and first variation extended here. Dirac source linearization — gives the local scalar analogue, including conjugate response blocks. Cross-sector moment kernel — derives the tensor identification and its covariance. Bilateral polarization coupling — motivates varying both spatial patterns.

title: Translational Dirac response
summary: Varying the scalar center restores the exact translation zero mode and yields a calculable inertial response of the full self-bound spatial Dirac field.
text: Summary: Varying the scalar center restores the exact translation zero mode and yields a calculable inertial response of the full self-bound spatial Dirac field. A self-bound field must be able to move The centered scalar interaction determines its own spatial profile and center. Holding that center fixed while varying the field would replace part of its dynamics by an external constraint. This note retains the center and derives its response from the same energy as the scalar Dirac moment modes. All coordinates are ordinary spatial coordinates in a sector of the one nested physical manifold. Translation moves the field within those coordinates. Response coefficients and angular functions add no physical dimensions or interaction particles. Use \sigma=\Phi^\dagger\beta\Phi, Q_\sigma=\int\sigma\ne0, P_\sigma=\int x\sigma, X=P_\sigma/Q_\sigma, and M_\sigma=\int(x-X)(x-X)^T\sigma\,dx, \qquad \mathcal E_{\rm int}=\frac{g_0}{2}\operatorname{tr}M_\sigma^2. \tag{1} Q_\sigma is a scalar bilinear integral, not an electric charge. It need not equal the separately normalized field norm. The center contributes a required dipole feedback At a centered radial background, M_\sigma=(T/d)I and a=g_0T/d. For an arbitrary field variation let \delta\sigma=2\operatorname{Re}(\Phi^\dagger\beta\eta),\qquad \delta P=\int x\,\delta\sigma\,dx,\qquad \delta C=\int xx^T\delta\sigma\,dx. The first variation of the central moment is \delta M=\delta C, but the source also depends on x-X. Differentiating the entire scalar potential gives \boxed{\delta U(x)=g_0x^T\delta Cx -\frac{2a}{Q_\sigma}x\cdot\delta P.} \tag{2} The second term supplies the center's dipole response. Its coefficient \kappa=-2a/Q_\sigma follows from the same centered energy, including its sign; it is not an independently chosen interaction strength. For two variations the full interaction Hessian is \begin{aligned} \mathcal E_{\rm int}''(\eta,\zeta) ={}&2\operatorname{Re}\langle\eta,\beta ar^2\zeta\rangle +g_0\operatorname{tr}(\delta C_\eta\delta C_\zeta)\\ &-\frac{2a}{Q_\sigma}\delta P_\eta\cdot\delta P_\zeta. \end{aligned} \tag{3} This is symmetric in both variations, as required for reciprocal dynamics. The negative center term is consistent with translation invariance: a shift of the entire field does not cost binding energy. The dipole source has a full spatial Dirac decomposition With the rest polarization w and Clifford matrices of the profile note, a dipole source in direction b is v_b=\beta(b\cdot x)\Phi. Its angular polynomial splits as \begin{aligned} p_b(x)&=(b\cdot x)w=M_b(x)+\alpha(x)N_b,\\ N_b&=\frac1d\alpha(b)w,\qquad M_b(x)=(b\cdot x)w-\frac1d\alpha(x)\alpha(b)w. \end{aligned} \tag{4} Both M_b and N_b are annihilated by \alpha\cdot\partial. The radial operators and source norms follow by the same direct method as Polarized Dirac shape response, now with degrees one and zero. For the circulation tensor J_{ij}=w^\dagger(-i\alpha_i\alpha_j)w their angular Gram matrices are G_N=\frac{I+iJ}{d^2},\qquad G_M=\frac Id-G_N. \tag{5} The two radial operators are H_{d+2} and -XH_dX, with the same physical scalar coefficients m,a. The larger numerical radial parameter again accounts only for powers of the existing radius. Let L contain these two operators minus the stationary frequency. For helicity \lambda of iJ, let u_\lambda,u_{-\lambda} be the normalized radial source vectors with squared angular weights 1/d-(1+\lambda)/d^2 and (1+\lambda)/d^2. Their bare response is \chi_\lambda(z)=u_\lambda^T(z-L)^{-1}u_\lambda +u_{-\lambda}^T(-z-L)^{-1}u_{-\lambda}. \tag{6} The complete dipole response is \chi_\lambda/(1-\kappa\chi_\lambda), with the center coefficient from (2). The ordinary and conjugate blocks are both retained. Translation gives an exact response identity For a translated stationary field \Phi(x-\epsilon b), the tangent is \eta_b=-b\cdot\nabla\Phi. Translation leaves the central moment unchanged and gives \delta P=Q_\sigma b. Differentiating the stationary equation therefore gives \boxed{\kappa\chi_\lambda(0)=1.} \tag{7} This places a zero-frequency collective mode in the complete response, even though the frozen confining Dirac operator has finite excitation gaps. The identity holds in all physical translation directions. Commuting translations also have zero mutual symplectic pairing. In the radial representation this is \|L^{-1}u_\lambda\|^2=\|L^{-1}u_{-\lambda}\|^2, \qquad \chi_\lambda'(0)=0. \tag{8} The first identity follows equivalently from the spatial integral of the commutator of momentum generators. It is a useful independent check of the angular decomposition and both Dirac radial branches. At finite numerical resolution the translation zero and its conjugate momentum direction can produce small spurious growth rates. Fixing total momentum and quotienting the translation direction removes that pair. This operation preserves the remaining fluctuation frequencies; it does not remove a nonzero physical instability. The inertial coefficient follows from the low-frequency response Apply a specified slowly varying scalar source h(t)\cdot x\,\beta. Its contribution to the energy is h\cdot P_\sigma and the force on the translated field is -Q_\sigma h to first order. Expanding (6) at zero frequency and using (7)–(8) gives \chi^{\rm full}_\lambda(z) =-\frac{2}{\kappa^2\chi_\lambda''(0)z^2}+O(z^{-1}). \tag{9} Comparing \delta X=\delta P/Q_\sigma with the force response defines the inertial coefficient \boxed{\mathcal M_{\mathrm{tr}} =-\frac{\kappa^2Q_\sigma^2}{2}\chi_\lambda''(0) =-2a^2\chi_\lambda''(0).} \tag{10} The second derivative involves the sum of opposite helicities, so this leading inertia is isotropic for the radial background. Higher-frequency response can still depend on J. In the present examples it is positive. At a=1, m=0, the numerical values are approximately 2.080669220 at depth three, 2.770370932 at five, 3.084232390 at six, and 4.210308101 at ten. These are coefficients in the specified model's translation dynamics. The instantaneous nonlocal energy does not supply a Lorentz-covariant completion, so equality to the stationary frequency or total binding energy is not presumed. At depths with a separate radial instability, this translation response does not make the whole background stable. Relation to a force between two patterns This calculation supplies a field's response when a reciprocal pair interaction exerts a force. The force itself must come from differentiating that pair energy with respect to its two positions. A moment pairing which depends only on separately centered shapes and a fixed identification matrix has no dependence on their relative translation. Its orientation and shape responses remain meaningful, while a separation-dependent force requires the corresponding spatial contact or propagation kernel. They must not be used as a replacement for the existing orbit-shape derivation. See Actual orbit research correction. 1. Position moments do not exhaust orbital data The positive scalar ground-state result remains intact. The following is an excited-state construction, not another ground-state minimum. It shows why isotropic second moments do not imply vanishing orbital current. Use a flat six-dimensional oscillator H_omega=p^2+omega^2 r^2, with unit norm, and split its real basis into O=(e1,e2,e3) and H=(e4,e5,e6). Define orthonormal circular modes z_a=(e_a-i e_(a+3))/sqrt(2), a=1,2,3. In the oscillator shell of total degree N>=2 take \phi_N=\frac1{\sqrt3}\sum_{a=1}^3|N\hbox{ quanta in }z_a\rangle. This is a pure superposition, not a mixture. The coordinate polynomials (x_a-i x_(a+3))^N are harmonic, so the state lies in ell=N as well as shell N. Its one-body cross matrix elements vanish because a one-body operator cannot transfer all N>=2 quanta between two orthogonal modes. With rho the trace-N one-body density matrix, \rho=\frac N3 P_-,\qquad P_-=\frac12(I+iJ_0),\qquad J_0=\begin{pmatrix}0&I_3\\-I_3&0\end{pmatrix}. Thus Re rho=N I/6, while Im rho=N J_0/6 is nonzero. For a fixed shell, the anomalous expectations of two creation or two annihilation operators vanish, giving M=\langle xx^T\rangle=\frac{N+3}{6\omega}I_6, \qquad \langle L\rangle=-2\operatorname{Im}\rho=-\frac N3J_0. The position covariance is isotropic and the circulation has full rank six. The density itself need not be isotropic: the quadratic scalar kernel sees only its second moments, not its higher angular moments. 2. These are scalar self-consistent stationary solutions For the single-sector functional E=T+(g/2)tr M^2 with g>0, variation gives the mean-field potential g x^T M x. It equals omega^2 r^2 precisely when \omega_N^3=\frac{g(N+3)}6. At that width, phi_N is an exact stationary scalar Hartree solution, with phase eigenvalue mu=(2N+6)omega_N. Its energy is E=(3/2)(N+3)omega_N, not mu. For N=2, choosing omega=1 gives g=6/5, M=5I/6, and mu=10. The scalar problem supplies an entire symmetry-related family, not a chosen absolute J_0 or a particle-index selector. The state is above the unconstrained scalar ground state. Its linear stability is a separate calculation. 3. Conditional spin source and the circulation sign If this orbital is used in the local vector-potential Dirac reduction of the spin-orbit audit, its angular expectation produces \mathcal S=-\frac N3\sum_{a=1}^3\Sigma_{a,a+3}. In the stated chiral convention this has eigenvalues {-N,N/3,N/3,N/3}. For a positive spin-orbit coefficient the unique lowest ray lies in the locked orbit, with complex structure J_0. Reversing the orbital circulation negates the matrix and gives a triply degenerate lowest eigenvalue instead. Thus the current sign relative to chirality and the interaction coefficient must be retained; a magnitude-only source calculation misses the distinction. The scalar Hartree functional does not prove that its potential is the time-component vector potential of the Dirac model. Nor does a projected spin matrix identify the spatial Dirac-section fibre with the homogeneous CP3 base coordinate. These bridges remain open. 4. A shared-well normalization constraint With fixed g and unit norm, these isolated self-bound solutions have N-dependent omega_N. They cannot all be treated as excitations of one fixed harmonic well while each is simultaneously taken to source that well alone. For charge Q the relation becomes omega_N^3=g Q(N+3)/6. Keeping omega fixed would require Q proportional to 1/(N+3), or a separate dominant background that fixes the well. Neither is supplied by the one-quantum normalization. This does not disprove a fixed-background cumulative-band construction. It specifies what must distinguish that construction from isolated self-binding. N here is a flat oscillator degree, not an independently derived assignment to an electron, a chemistry orbital, or a V2 projective band. Then \boxed{ E_L=A_OJ_2A_H^T. } If x_O\not\parallel p_O and x_H\not\parallel p_H, both A_O and A_H have column rank two and J_2 is invertible. It is already fixed, up to sign, by the oriented normals of the two rank-two planes. 99.2 Rank-two 3\times3 tensors have a unique SO(3) Procrustes maximizer Let a real rank-two tensor have singular-value decomposition E=U \begin{pmatrix} \sigma_1&0&0\\ 0&\sigma_2&0\\ 0&0&0 \end{pmatrix} V^T, \qquad \sigma_1,\sigma_2>0. Because the third singular vectors correspond to zero singular value, their signs may be chosen so that U,V\in SO(3). Consider the orientation-preserving Procrustes problem \max_{Q\in SO(3)}\operatorname{tr}(Q^TE). Write Q=URV^T, \qquad R\in SO(3). Then \operatorname{tr}(Q^TE) = \sigma_1R_{11}+\sigma_2R_{22}. Since every diagonal entry of an orthogonal matrix is at most one, \operatorname{tr}(Q^TE) \le \sigma_1+\sigma_2. Equality requires R_{11}=R_{22}=1. Orthogonality then forces the first two rows and columns to be the first two coordinate basis vectors, and the condition \det R=1 forces R_{33}=1. Hence R=I_3 is the unique maximizer. Therefore \boxed{ Q_E=UV^T } is a uniquely selected element of SO(3) even though \det E=0. So full matrix rank is not required for full orientation selection in three dimensions. 99.3 Canonical exact example For E= \begin{pmatrix} 0&a&0\\ -b&0&0\\ 0&0&0 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad a,b>0, one has E=Q_0 \operatorname{diag}(b,a,0), with \boxed{ Q_0= \begin{pmatrix} 0&1&0\\ -1&0&0\\ 0&0&1 \end{pmatrix} \in SO(3). } For any Q=Q_0R, \qquad R\in SO(3), the trace objective is \operatorname{tr}(Q^TE) =bR_{11}+aR_{22} \le a+b, with equality only for R=I. title: CP5 tangent splitting obstruction
summary: The complex tangent bundle of CP5 admits no global rank-three plus rank-two splitting, even without imposing determinant one.
text: Physical premise (IDWT): There is one infinite-dimensional physical manifold. All sectors form one nested chain of submanifolds within it. See spatial meaning and mathematical scope. Summary: The complex tangent bundle of CP5 admits no global rank-three plus rank-two splitting, even without imposing determinant one. Why this matters Gauge selection §15 already excludes determinant-one tangent holonomy because c1(T CP5)=6H. The obstruction is stronger: a global complex 3+2 tangent splitting itself is impossible. Keeping the determinant connection does not cure that failure. 1. Exhaust the possible Chern factors Let E=T^(1,0) CP5. The Euler sequence gives c(E)=1+6H+15H^2+20H^3+15H^4+6H^5, \qquad H^*(\mathbb{CP}^5;\mathbb Z)=\mathbb Z[H]/(H^6). Suppose E=A_3 direct-sum B_2. The Whitney product formula says c(E)=c(A)c(B). Since both factors have degree at most their ranks, their product has degree at most five. Equality modulo H^6 is therefore an exact polynomial equality. The top coefficient is nonzero, so the degrees must be exactly three and two. Over the rationals the polynomial factors as c(E)=(1+2H)(1+H+H^2)(1+3H+3H^2). The two quadratics are irreducible (discriminant -3), and the linear factor occurs only once. Normalizing constant terms to one, the only possible rank-two Chern factors are c(B)=1+H+H^2\quad\hbox{or}\quad c(B)=1+3H+3H^2. 2. Both factors fail a necessary bundle condition Restrict B to a linear CP3 inside CP5. A complex rank-two bundle on CP3 with c1=aH and c2=bH^2 must satisfy ab=0 modulo 2. This is the classical Atiyah–Rees/Schwarzenberger condition; see Opie, Theorem 1.2 and Remark 1.3. The two candidates have (a,b)=(1,1) and (3,3), hence ab odd in both cases. Neither is the Chern class of such a bundle. The supposed splitting cannot exist. An independent check uses K(CP3)=Z[t]/(t^4), t=[O(1)]-1, and ch(t)=exp(H)-1. The rank-two candidate characters are \operatorname{ch}(B)=2+aH+\frac{a^2-2b}{2}H^2 +\frac{a^3-3ab}{6}H^3. Their coefficients in the integral K-theory basis (1,t,t^2,t^3) would be (2,1,-1,1/2) and (2,3,0,-1/2), respectively. Half-integral final coefficients are impossible. The K-theory basis is established in Hatcher, Vector Bundles and K-Theory, §2.2. 3. Precise consequence for V2 No unitary connection on T^(1,0) CP5 can have its full holonomy contained in a conjugate U(3) times U(2): such a reduction would produce the excluded rank-three and rank-two subbundles. This conclusion does not assume the connection is Levi–Civita, holomorphic, or determinant one. Tensoring the tangent bundle by a line bundle cannot help with the splitting: a split of E tensor L would untwist to a split of E. Separately its first Chern class would be (6+5k)H for L=O(k), never zero for integer k. The pointwise exterior-algebra branching, charge normalization, and local stabilizer calculations remain valid. What fails is promoting that local split to the literal global tangent bundle. An auxiliary gauge bundle, a different effective carrier, or a properly specified non-global construction is required. This theorem does not forbid the Standard Model group on CP5 or every possible V2 gauge completion. The normal-spinor calculation provides a compatible distinction: the tangent/normal splitting along an embedded CP3 exists and has an explicit induced connection. It is not a rank-three plus rank-two splitting over the entire CP5 base.
