title: Projected Dirac current
summary: Varying a minimally gauged diagnostic action fixes the current form and normalization identities, while projection exposes missing-mode contributions.
text: Physical premise (IDWT): There is one infinite-dimensional physical manifold. All sectors form one nested chain of submanifolds within it. Particle depth counts ordinary, literal macroscopic spatial dimensions. “Observed” and “unobserved” describe an observer's access to those dimensions, not different kinds of physical dimension. See spatial meaning and mathematical scope. Summary: Varying a minimally gauged diagnostic action fixes the current form and normalization identities, while projection exposes missing-mode contributions. What the written action permits The six-dimensional electron module, section 8, supplies a diagnostic Dirac action with unspecified physical connections and nuclear interaction. The scalar self-contact term is algebraic in ψ̄ψ. It does not itself determine an electromagnetic connection. Conditional on a charged U(1) connection a, take ℏ = c = 1 and D_A=\nabla_A+iq a_A,\qquad \mathcal L_m=\bar\psi(i\gamma^AD_A-m-V_N)\psi -\frac\kappa2(\bar\psi\psi)^2. Here q is signed charge, A is a spacetime/sector index, and V_N is the scalar term in that diagnostic action, not an already-derived Coulomb field. Under ψ → e^{-iqχ}ψ and a → a+dχ the action is invariant. Variation gives J^A=-\frac{\delta S_m}{\delta a_A}=q\bar\psi\gamma^A\psi. The field equations and their adjoints give ∇_A J^A = 0. Algebraic neutral scalar interactions contribute no additional derivative with respect to a. Derivative interactions, a-dependent projectors, or added orbit-driving terms must instead be varied too. This is the usual minimal-coupling construction; see Tong's QED section. It derives a current from an assumed charged action, not electric charge or the physical U(1) identification from the master theory. The coefficient Z in −ZF²/4 also matters: canonical normalization of the photon gives coupling q/√Z. A current formula alone does not predict the fine-structure constant. Projection and total charge For fixed admissible mode sections s_a with ψ = Σ_a c_a s_a, define the Gram matrix G_ab = ∫s_a†s_b dμ. The kinetic action is ∫dt [iℏ c†G ċ − c†h c]. The local charge matrix is R_ab(u) = q s_a(u)†s_b(u), and therefore \int R(u)d\mu=qG. In orthonormal coordinates b = G^{1/2}c, total charge is q b†b. Multiplicity of modes does not multiply a normalized particle's electric charge. A moving orthonormal basis S(t) adds −iℏ S†Ṡ to the energy Hamiltonian; its response to a probe cannot be omitted if the basis depends on that probe. After a specified conserved pushforward to observer space, the dipole and integrated current matrices satisfy D_i=\int x_iR(x)d^3x,\qquad I_i=\int j_i(x)d^3x=\frac{i}{\hbar}[h,D_i] for time-independent matrices, no boundary flux, and a closed projected subspace. This is a consistency condition, not a way to determine D_i from h alone. Choosing D_i arbitrarily and defining I_i by this equation does not derive the physical charge distribution. Exact truncation defect Let P be an orthogonal projector and Q = 1−P. Suppose the full local operator identity is (i/ℏ)[h,R]+div j = 0. Direct compression gives \frac{i}{\hbar}[PhP,PRP]+P(\operatorname{div}j)P =-\frac{i}{\hbar}PhQRP+\frac{i}{\hbar}PRQhP. All operators here act on the retained space where appropriate. The right side vanishes if h preserves that space. Merely preserving charge globally is weaker than satisfying local conservation after projection. Even if QhP = 0 without a probe, a dipole D can have QDP ≠ 0. Then the unforced orbit is exactly retained but its weak-field response need not be. Projecting D to PDP before calculating response discards intermediate Q modes. Integrating those modes out consistently produces additional, generally frequency-dependent response terms. For a linear probe with QhP = 0 at zero field, these include terms quadratic in the applied field in the effective action; their variation contributes to linear response. One cannot infer their absence from PDP = 0. The geometric example below demonstrates this explicitly without fitting a spectrum. Charge versus degree The degree L of O(L) is not automatically the electric charge of a particle in that section space. If every connection is the Lth tensor power of one physical fluctuating connection, its infinitesimal coupling scales with L. That is not a universal electron charge across orbit families. A model can instead specify different background fluxes and a universally normalized electromagnetic perturbation, or distinguish a geometric twist from the electromagnetic bundle. Which interpretation V2 uses must be stated in the action. Representation degree alone does not settle it. Reproduction and boundary projected_current_checks.py checks the projection-defect identity, its disappearance for an invariant subspace, and charge normalization with a nonorthogonal Gram metric. The selected-line and geometric-probe notes apply this framework to actual orbit evolution. The remaining physical inputs are the master-selected bundle, orbit-driving term, electromagnetic observer map, nuclear contribution, and normalization. Related Orbit current projection — conserved pushforward and distinction from the exposure image. Selected spinor line current — a global candidate lift and the current required by its orbit drive. Geometric probe selection — exact mode integrals and an explicit missed response under four-mode truncation. Research status — current proof boundaries and correction routes.

title: Common-anchor action audit
summary: Action and kinetic-normalization tests locate the unresolved fixed-reference bridge.
text: Physical premise (IDWT): There is one infinite-dimensional physical manifold. All sectors form one nested chain of submanifolds within it. Particle depth counts ordinary, literal macroscopic spatial dimensions. “Observed” and “unobserved” describe an observer's access to those dimensions, not different kinds of physical dimension. See spatial meaning and mathematical scope. Summary: Action and kinetic-normalization tests locate the unresolved fixed-reference bridge. NOT A PHYSICS MODULE. This note records the action-level attempt to derive or falsify the V2 common-anchor law as it proceeds. 1. Target The relation under test is \frac{(M_d^\star)^2}{g_{dd}}=\frac{m_e^2}{g_{66}}, or, in frequency language, \frac{\omega_d^\star}{\omega_e}=\sqrt{\frac{g_{dd}}{g_{66}}}. The task is to determine whether this follows from the written V2 projected dynamics rather than being an additional scale ansatz. 2. First source-level result The self-contact module explicitly starts from a sector-diagonal scalar interaction \mathcal L_{\rm sc}=-\frac{\kappa_d}{2}J_d^2 and derives the projected scalar coefficient \mu_d=\kappa_dR_dB_d. The finite-band contact theorem then gives M_{n,d}=\mu_dS(n,d). Therefore the written operator ordering is \boxed{\mu_d\;\longrightarrow\;\mu_dS(n,d)}. The sector coefficient is formed first; the simplex/contact eigenvalue multiplies it afterward. Section 9.1 of the self-contact module introduces the common-anchor equation separately as a projected fixed-point condition and explicitly states that the master equation of motion must supply that equation. No equation in the inspected self-contact passage identifies \kappa_dR_dB_d with g_{dd} or \sqrt{g_{dd}}. 3. Cross-depth source audit The bound/free module writes reciprocal cross-depth interactions schematically as S_{ab}=g_{ab}\int dt\,I_{ab}, whose variations give g_{ab} times the other sector's marginal/contact density. The higher-dimensional-polarization module writes a schematic current/gauge interaction S_{\rm int}=g_{ab}\int_{Q_a}\langle A_a,(\pi_{ba})_*J_b\rangle. These establish incidence, reciprocity, representation filtering, and the existence of coupling coefficients. In the inspected passages they do not identify the scalar self-contact coefficient \kappa_d, the projected scalar coefficient \mu_d, or an occupied reference frequency with g_{dd} or \sqrt{g_{dd}}. The polarization source in fact says that a nonzero invariant vertex leaves its coupling coefficient to the projected dynamics. 4. Exact placement test for the rank-one proposal Let v_d=\sqrt{g_{dd}},\qquad G=vv^T, and for the proposed depth-3, depth-4, and electron reference bands define D_\star=\operatorname{diag}(1,15,18564). If the rank-one response acts on primitive pre-contact coefficients, \sigma=GJ=v(v^TJ), then the written contact projection gives M^\star=D_\star\sigma=(D_\star v)(v^TJ). Hence \boxed{ \frac{M_d^\star}{M_6^\star} =\frac{D_d^\star\sqrt{g_{dd}}}{D_6^\star\sqrt{g_{66}}} }. This is Case B, not the desired common-anchor law. If instead a deeper master equation acts directly on the already-projected occupied reference coefficients, M^\star=vC, then \boxed{ \frac{M_d^\star}{M_6^\star}=\sqrt{\frac{g_{dd}}{g_{66}}} }. This is Case A. The algebraic way to begin before contact multiplication and still end in Case A is to use \widetilde G=D_\star^{-1}vv^TD_\star^{-1}, so that D_\star\widetilde GJ lies along v. But this changes the primitive diagonal couplings to \widetilde g_{dd}=\frac{g_{dd}}{(D_d^\star)^2}. That is not a harmless relabeling of the quoted V2 couplings unless an independent projection or kinetic-normalization theorem derives exactly this weighting. 5. Interim verdict The naive rank-one source-to-self-energy mechanism does not derive the common-anchor law when attached directly to the scalar coefficient already written in V2. With the explicit self-contact ordering it produces Case B. Case A remains possible only if the deeper projected master dynamics supplies additional structure, for example: a rank-one equation acting directly on occupied reference frequencies; an independently derived two-sided reference-count weighting before contact projection; sector-dependent projected overlap or kinetic factors that cancel the reference counts exactly; or a nonlinear fixed-point equation in which the reference-band factors enter before the final ratio is formed. None of those mechanisms has yet been found in the inspected source passages. The identity g_{34}^2=g_{33}g_{44} is therefore insufficient by itself. It establishes rank one for a coupling-coefficient matrix, but does not determine the operator layer on which that matrix acts. Since D_\star v is not proportional to v, the simplex projection and the proposed rank-one image do not commute in the way required by the anchor law. The remaining problem is an operator-ordering and normalization problem, not an unknown-amplitude problem. 6. Next proof obligation Trace the actual derivation and mathematical role of g_{33}=8\sqrt7,\qquad g_{44}=12/\sqrt7,\qquad g_{34}=4\sqrt6,\qquad g_{66}=1/4. For each value, determine whether it is defined as a scalar self-interaction coefficient, a polarization/gauge normalization, a stiffness, a kernel eigenvalue, or another object. Only then can the use of these same numbers in the scalar reference-frequency fixed-point equation be classified as derived, merely compatible, or category-invalid. No V1 material is used as evidence here. 7. Historical V2 action supplies a real candidate mechanism - but not yet a current-V2 derivation The git history contains an earlier V2, not V1, formulation from August 28, 2026. It is useful provenance because it shows what the common-anchor statement was intended to mean before the present projective-contact modules were written. That historical V2 wrote one quartic master interaction S_{\rm int} =\frac12\sum_{d,e}g_{de} \int K_{de}(\xi_d,\xi_e)\,\rho_d\rho_e, with g_{de}=v_dv_e, \qquad g_{dd}=v_d^2. For the displayed kernel, K_{de}=(\xi_d\cdot\xi_e)^2. The same historical text then states the lightest-mode fixed point \frac{(M_d^\star)^2}{g_{dd}} =\frac{m_e^2}{g_{66}}, which is exactly the present common-anchor condition. This matters because the rank-one-response idea was not invented during the present audit: an earlier V2 master action already contained a rank-one coupling matrix and explicitly described one collective interaction channel. 7.1 Exact variation of the historical rank-one action Let \rho_d=\bar\Psi P_d\Psi. For a symmetric kernel and symmetric coupling matrix, variation of the quadratic density functional with respect to \rho_d gives \Sigma_d =\sum_e g_{de}K_{de}\rho_e. Using g_{de}=v_dv_e, \boxed{ \Sigma_d =v_d\sum_e v_eK_{de}\rho_e. } This is an important refinement of the simpler toy calculation \Sigma=v(v^TJ). Rank one of the coefficient matrix alone does not yet imply \Sigma_d=v_dC with one sector-independent scalar C, because the geometric kernel still carries the external sector label d through K_{de}. The required additional condition is \boxed{ \sum_e v_eK_{de}\rho_e=C \quad\text{independent of }d } on the relevant fixed-point branch, or an equivalent projector/normalization theorem that reduces the full kernel to a common scalar functional. The historical prose asserts precisely such a common condensate, but the displayed action by itself does not prove that the K_{de} dependence collapses this way. 7.2 Why this still does not automatically solve the present projective-contact problem The historical V2 and current V2 place the spectral count at different conceptual stages. The current self-contact theorem derives M_d^\star=D_d^\star\mu_d, where \mu_d is the sector-normalized scalar contact coefficient before multiplication by the occupied-band dimension. Therefore, if the historical rank-one response \Sigma_d is identified with the current primitive coefficient \mu_d, then M_d^\star =D_d^\star v_dC, which is Case B: \frac{M_d^\star}{M_6^\star} =\frac{D_d^\star v_d}{D_6^\star v_6}. To recover Case A in the current architecture, one must establish one of two precise identifications: post-projection response: the historical \Sigma_d corresponds directly to the occupied reference eigenvalue M_d^\star, not to \mu_d; or count-compensated primitive response: projection of the historical kernel produces \mu_d\propto\frac{v_d}{D_d^\star}, so that the subsequent contact multiplier restores M_d^\star\propto v_d. The historical source does not perform the present finite-band projective-contact calculation, so it cannot decide between these two identifications. 7.3 A second incompatibility that must be resolved The historical V2 derives a self-consistent harmonic stiffness \lambda_d=\left(\frac{g_{dd}}2\right)^{2/3} from the quartic kernel, and then separately states that the physical mass spectrum is m(n,d)=m_{{\rm scale},d}S(n,d). But the ordinary isotropic harmonic-oscillator eigenvalues scale linearly with excitation number and with \sqrt{\lambda_d}; their degeneracy count is S(n,d) only after cumulative counting. The historical source does not derive why the eigenfrequency itself equals the cumulative degeneracy rather than the usual oscillator eigenvalue. The current projective-contact theorem was written precisely to supply a genuine operator whose occupied eigenvalue is S(n,d). Consequently, importing the historical harmonic-well fixed point wholesale would mix two distinct spectral mechanisms. 7.4 Result of the historical-source test Survives as provenance and a candidate mechanism: V2 originally intended g_{de} to be one rank-one quartic self-interaction matrix; V2 originally intended the electron-relative scale law to be a kernel-vacuum fixed point; the square-root coupling ratios therefore have a coherent action-level motivation, not merely a numerical coincidence. Does not yet survive as a derivation in the current V2 operator architecture: rank one of g_{de} does not by itself remove the sector dependence of the geometric kernel K_{de}; the historical action does not derive the inverse reference-count factor required if its response is pre-contact; the historical harmonic-well spectrum and the current projective-contact spectrum are not the same operator construction. The common anchor is therefore better motivated than the current files alone made visible, but still unproved in present V2. 8. Sharpened next calculation The next decisive calculation is now concrete. Project the historical-style rank-one master kernel through the current finite-band projectors and ask whether its occupied-line matrix element has the form \langle z_d;N_d|P_d\mathcal K_\infty P_d|z_d;N_d\rangle =C\sqrt{g_{dd}} or =C\sqrt{g_{dd}}\,D_d^\star, or instead acquires a compensating factor 1/D_d^\star before the contact eigenvalue is applied. Equivalently, define the projected source functional F_d[\rho] =\sum_e v_e\,\langle z_d;N_d|P_dK_{de}[\rho_e]P_d|z_d;N_d\rangle. Case A requires D_d^\star F_d[\rho] \propto \text{constant in }d, when the primitive scalar coefficient is used, whereas a direct post-projection formulation requires simply F_d[\rho]\propto\text{constant in }d. This is now the exact normalization theorem to prove or falsify. 9. Fixed reference normalization is compatible with band blindness The current self-contact theorem states that, for the ordinary family law, M_{n,d}=\mu_dS(n,d), with all explicit band dependence carried by the reproducing-kernel diagonal S(n,d). Its action-level domain explicitly requires the scalar contact strength \mu_d to be band-blind. This sharpens the Case A/Case B fork. Suppose the historical rank-one master response is attached to the current primitive scalar coefficient: \mu_d=v_dC, \qquad v_d=\sqrt{g_{dd}}. Then the present contact theorem gives M_d^\star=D_d^\star v_dC, and therefore Case B. The only primitive-level algebraic rescue previously identified was \mu_d\propto\frac{v_d}{D_d^\star}. Here D_d^\star is fixed once per sector. Dependence on that fixed reference does not imply dependence on the varying occupied band n or N=n-1. Thus \mu_d=Cv_d/D_d^\star is band-blind and gives M_{n,d}=Cv_dD_{n,d}/D_d^\star, with M_d^\star=Cv_d. The earlier claim that band blindness alone excludes this normalization is withdrawn. Replacing D_d^\star by the running D_{n,d} would violate band blindness, but that is a different prescription. Therefore: \boxed{ \mu_d=Cv_d\text{ forces Case B; fixed }\mu_d=Cv_d/D_d^\star\text{ gives Case A.} } A fixed inverse-reference normalization changes the primitive-response identification, not the band-blind contact theorem. Its physical origin remains unproved; it cannot be silently inserted as a result of the historical kernel. This rules out only the simultaneous unweighted primitive response \mu_d=Cv_d and the desired reference ratios with unequal reference counts. Case A can follow from a post-contact / occupied-reference fixed point, or from a derived fixed sector normalization at the primitive layer. Neither route has been derived from the current master action. 10. Current V2 explicitly records the missing coordinate-kernel to phase-ray bridge Section 8.6 of the present self-contact module distinguishes two operators: P_{N,d}|q|^2P_{N,d} from the coordinate harmonic kernel, and D_N|z;N\rangle\langle z;N| from phase-ray point contact. It then states that their relation still requires either: a master interaction written locally on the homogenized phase-ray bundle; or a derivation showing that the coordinate-space nonlinear kernel transforms into occupied-ray contact after oscillator and sector projection. This is exactly the missing bridge between the historical V2 master kernel (\xi_d\cdot\xi_e)^2 and the present projective-contact mass operator. So the source audit now yields a stronger documentary conclusion: \boxed{ \text{the current V2 source itself identifies the historical-to-current operator bridge as unfinished.} } Consequently, the historical statement that the kernel vacuum supplies the common anchor cannot presently be imported as a completed derivation. It points to the right location in the dynamics, but the required projection theorem has not yet been written. 11. Revised status after the bridge audit Established in current V2: occupied phase-ray point contact gives the exact simplex eigenvalue D_N=S(n,d); the ordinary family law has a band-blind primitive coefficient \mu_d; therefore a primitive response proportional to \sqrt{g_{dd}} produces Case B. Established as historical V2 provenance: an earlier V2 master action used a rank-one coupling matrix g_{de}=v_dv_e; it intended one collective self-interaction channel; it stated the electron-relative common-anchor law as a kernel-vacuum fixed point. Still missing: the projection of that coordinate-space rank-one kernel into the current occupied phase-ray scalar-contact operator; a proof that the resulting complete occupied reference eigenvalue, rather than the primitive coefficient, lies along v_d; or any other current-V2 equation that yields M_d^\star\propto\sqrt{g_{dd}} with a derived fixed sector normalization or occupied-reference fixed point. The common-anchor law is not disproved. The unweighted primitive identification is excluded; a fixed inverse-reference normalization remains algebraically allowed but physically underived. 12. Kinetic-normalization audit: no present rescue of the primitive rank-one anchor The remaining obvious place for a compensating factor was canonical or kinetic normalization. The current V2 mass module does not provide one. Its operator ordering is explicit: the spatial Dirac/Laplace operator constructs the mode eigenspace; the localized contact operator maps the rank of that eigenspace to the rest-energy eigenvalue; the sector coefficient is \mu_d=\kappa_dR_dB_d, and is independent of the band label under the ordinary mass theorem. No reference-band wavefunction renormalization or kinetic factor proportional to \frac1{D_d^\star} appears in that derivation. A separate gauge/polarization module does say that propagation laws and kinetic normalizations of the projected gauge connection remain to be obtained from the master action. But that statement concerns projected connection components and cross-sector propagation; no current source identifies such a normalization with the scalar rest-energy contact coefficient, and no formula supplies the reference-band dependence required here. The cross-depth contact theorem also preserves complete normalized marginal weight: \int \bar\rho_{b\to a}=1. Thus full marginalization does not furnish an inverse simplex factor either. Combining these facts gives the following present-V2 no-go statement. 12.1 Primitive-rank-one incompatibility theorem Assume simultaneously: the ordinary current V2 contact law M_{n,d}=\mu_dD_{n,d}, \qquad D_{n,d}=S(n,d); band blindness of the primitive scalar contact coefficient \mu_d; normalized cross-depth marginalization with no band-dependent loss of weight; identification of the historical rank-one response with that primitive coefficient, \mu_d=C\sqrt{g_{dd}} for one sector-independent C. Then for any chosen reference bands, \boxed{ \frac{M_d^\star}{M_6^\star} = \frac{D_d^\star}{D_6^\star} \sqrt{\frac{g_{dd}}{g_{66}}} } and not \sqrt{\frac{g_{dd}}{g_{66}}} unless accidentally D_d^\star=D_6^\star. For the adopted references, D_3^\star=S(1,3)=1, \qquad D_4^\star=S(3,4)=15, \qquad D_6^\star=S(13,6)=18564, so the accidental-equality condition fails drastically. Therefore the four assumptions above are mutually incompatible with the common-anchor law. At least one must change. Since assumptions 1--3 are explicit parts of the current V2 contact construction, the natural conclusion is: \boxed{ \text{the desired anchor is incompatible with the unweighted identification }\mu_d=Cv_d. } It can instead act on the complete occupied reference eigenvalues, or arise from a derived fixed sector weighting such as \mu_d=Cv_d/D_d^\star. The latter preserves assumptions 1--3 but replaces assumption 4; it is not excluded merely because it acts at the primitive layer. 12.2 Numerical size of the contradiction The difference is not perturbative. The desired Case A factors relative to the electron reference are \sqrt{g_{33}/g_{66}}\approx 9.2013065, \qquad \sqrt{g_{44}/g_{66}}\approx 4.2593773. A primitive rank-one response followed by the present contact theorem instead gives \frac{1}{18564}\sqrt{g_{33}/g_{66}} \approx 4.9565\times10^{-4}, and \frac{15}{18564}\sqrt{g_{44}/g_{66}} \approx 3.4416\times10^{-3}. These differ from the required reference-frequency ratios by factors exactly equal to the missing count ratios. This cannot be repaired by unit conventions. 13. Status of the common-anchor attack The first attempted action-level derivation has therefore failed in a precise way. It did not fail because rank-one coupling is useless. Historical V2 shows why rank one is a serious clue. It failed because the current exact simplex theorem fixes where the count enters, and a primitive rank-one response then places that count on the wrong side of the proposed fixed point. The surviving proof target is now narrower: Derive a fixed-point equation for the complete occupied reference eigenvalue M_d^\star, or derive the fixed sector normalization of the primitive coefficient (for example 1/D_d^\star) from the master projection. Any future derivation that merely writes \mu_d\propto\sqrt{g_{dd}} has already been ruled out for the present V2 mass operator. Related Research status — current proof boundaries and correction guidance.

title: Rank-one common anchor
summary: A conditional source-cancellation mechanism fixes output ratios but not their physical identification.
text: Physical premise (IDWT): There is one infinite-dimensional physical manifold. All sectors form one nested chain of submanifolds within it. Particle depth counts ordinary, literal macroscopic spatial dimensions. “Observed” and “unobserved” describe an observer's access to those dimensions, not different kinds of physical dimension. See spatial meaning and mathematical scope. Summary: A conditional source-cancellation mechanism fixes output ratios but not their physical identification. NOT A PHYSICS MODULE OR COMPLETED SCALE DERIVATION. The source-cancellation calculation below is exact for a specified rank-one response. Its identification with the actual V2 projected reference-frequency dynamics remains unproved. 1. The constructive possibility The earlier work treated a coupling matrix as though it had to act directly on wave-mode coefficients, then diagonalized it or took its square root. A different role is possible: the matrix can map scalar source currents to scalar Dirac self-energies. In that role, its rank-one image fixes ratios of output coefficients without determining the source magnitudes. This provides a concrete sufficient mechanism for the square-root coupling ratios. It does not require an oscillator frequency-squared matrix, and it does not require an amplitude measurement. The remaining physical identification is substantial and is kept explicit below. 2. Exact source elimination Consider a finite, compatibly normalized common source space. The test interaction is \mathcal L_{\rm int}=-\frac12\mathbf J^TG\mathbf J, \qquad G=vv^T, \qquad v_d=\sqrt{g_{dd}}>0. This is an algebraic candidate after choosing common units and integration conventions. Any common dimensional prefactor is suppressed here and can be absorbed in the common response scalar. A physical cross-depth action must establish the compatible measures and maps; the displayed finite expression does not do that automatically. Writing U=(1/2)\mathbf J^TG\mathbf J, its scalar self-energy coefficients are \Sigma_d=\frac{\partial U}{\partial J_d} =\sum_eG_{de}J_e =v_dC, \qquad C=\sum_ev_eJ_e. For arbitrary symbolic source entries, the row relations give \boxed{v_6\Sigma_d-v_d\Sigma_6=0.} On a nonzero electron-reference branch, \boxed{\frac{\Sigma_d}{\Sigma_6}=\frac{v_d}{v_6} =\sqrt{\frac{g_{dd}}{g_{66}}}.} No J_d has been assigned a measured value, fitted, or solved for. The source vector and any common multiplier cancel. This is elimination of an unneeded source, not an amplitude-domain reconstruction. The positive choice of v specifies the adopted sign convention. Relating these scalar coefficients to positive rest frequencies still requires the appropriate common mass-sign branch. A zero response cannot serve as the electron anchor. 3. Coefficient ratios are not automatically pole ratios The exact result above concerns \Sigma_d. To conclude \frac{\omega_d^\star}{\omega_e}=\sqrt{\frac{g_{dd}}{g_{66}}}, one must establish that \Sigma_d is the relevant complete occupied scalar rest-frequency coefficient after canonical kinetic normalization and the prescribed mode projection. Different kinetic factors, additional mass terms, noncommuting operator pieces, spatially varying backgrounds, or frequency-dependent self-energies can prevent this coefficient ratio from being the ratio of physical poles. A common local scalar function is not automatically a common constant in every sector's eigenvalue problem. The self-contact source, Section 9.1, currently introduces the common-anchor relation conditionally and says the master equation must supply it. The present calculation offers a sufficient response mechanism to test against that obligation. It does not change that documentary status into a completed theorem. 4. The decisive reference-band versus primitive-unit test Use the specified references (n_3^\star,n_4^\star,n_6^\star)=(1,3,13), whose contact multipliers are (D_3^\star,D_4^\star,D_6^\star)=(1,15,18564). The ordinary contact law gives \omega_d^\star=D_d^\star\varpi_d. There are two inequivalent ways to place the rank-one response relative to this multiplication. Case A: response already gives the occupied reference frequencies If \Sigma_d=Cv_d already denotes \omega_d^\star, then \frac{\omega_d^\star}{\omega_e}=\frac{v_d}{v_6}, \qquad \boxed{\frac{\varpi_d}{\omega_e} =\frac{v_d}{D_d^\star v_6}.} For the adopted g_{33}=8\sqrt7, g_{44}=12/\sqrt7, g_{66}=1/4, this gives: Depth Occupied reference frequency divided by \omega_e Primitive unit \varpi_d/\omega_e 3 9.201306535164823 9.201306535164823 4 4.259377267212064 0.28395848448080424 6 1 1/18564\approx0.0000538677009265245 This reproduces the proposed anchor architecture, conditional on the Case A identification. The calculation does not independently derive the adopted coupling values. Case B: response gives the coefficient before contact multiplication If instead \varpi_d=Cv_d is the pre-contact unit, the occupied reference frequencies obey \boxed{\frac{\omega_d^\star}{\omega_e} =\frac{D_d^\star v_d}{D_6^\star v_6}.} The same numerical couplings now give: Depth Occupied reference frequency divided by \omega_e 3 0.0004956532285695337 4 0.0034416429114512473 6 1 The discrepancy is not a rounding error or a choice of MeV units. Case A divided by Case B is exactly 18564 at depth three and 18564/15 at depth four. The response and the simplex multiplier cannot be composed in an unspecified order. This distinction is directly motivated by self-contact Sections 6.4 and 9: the source first defines the projected coefficient \mu_d, then multiplies it by S(n,d). Its separate common-anchor statement concerns M_d^\star=\mu_dS(n_d^\star,d). A rank-one law for the former is not automatically a rank-one law for the latter with the same vector. 5. What two-sided reference-count weighting would do Let D_\star=\operatorname{diag}(1,15,18564). A symmetric primitive response matrix \widetilde G=D_\star^{-1}GD_\star^{-1} =\widetilde v\widetilde v^T, \qquad \widetilde v=D_\star^{-1}v, has diagonal entries \boxed{\widetilde g_{dd}=g_{dd}/(D_d^\star)^2.} If this were the primitive response, multiplying its outputs by D_d^\star would give a vector proportional to v, recovering the Case A reference ratios. This is a correct algebraic construction and retains rank one. It is not a derived V2 normalization. The primitive matrix is no longer the original G with the original diagonal entries. Dividing only one side would also change the action's symmetric response interpretation. Calling the two-sided transformation a harmless field redefinition would require transforming the kinetic form, currents, measures, and the meaning of the quoted couplings consistently. No such projection/kinetic-normalization theorem was established in the inspected passages. The reference counts must not be inserted solely because they recover the desired numbers. 6. Why cross-depth geometry is still an obstruction to automatic factorization The reciprocity source, Section 5, writes the two variations of the same cross-depth interaction as a lower-depth response to the higher-depth marginal and a higher-depth response to the lower-depth field extended across the additional fibre. The polarization-coupling source, Section 6, separately assigns pushforward to contact, invariant brackets to polarization selection, and the coupling coefficient and field equations to dynamics. These are valuable geometric and variational structures. They do not automatically make every sector's full response proportional to the same source functional after projection. Even when the numerical coefficients factor as g_{de}=v_dv_e, the full operator can contain sector-dependent kernels, fibre maps, spinor contractions, and kinetic normalizations. Factorization of the coefficient matrix is not yet factorization of all those maps together. The common-source cancellation is therefore sufficient when the projected response has the proved finite form. Checking that premise in the actual source geometry is indispensable. The reported bounded searches did not establish an independent full projected reference-response action; that search result is not a universal absence theorem. 7. Proof obligations before promoting the mechanism The immediate task is an identification calculation, not a source-amplitude solve. It must show that the projected scalar interaction has the needed common response after the cross-depth measures and kernels are included; track every D_d^\star through projection and variation; put the kinetic term into the same normalization used for the frequency extraction; and connect the resulting scalar coefficient to the complete reference pole on the appropriate branch. If those steps establish Case A, the reference ratios follow without determining C. If the action instead establishes Case B, the different ratios are a real consequence of that prescription and must not be hidden by relabeling \Sigma_d. If additional kernels destroy the common response, their frequency effects have to be calculated rather than silently absorbed into a universal source. Closing the reference law would still not solve the baryon problem by itself. A composite operator, its color-singlet constraint, and any induced frequency-dependent interactions remain to be derived. The signed color-pair coefficient and exact block reduction in the review note are tools for that next stage, not missing mass factors that can simply be multiplied together. 8. Reproducible status The regression script differentiates the symbolic quadratic interaction, proves the row annihilator identities for arbitrary sources, calculates both reference prescriptions, and verifies the two-sided count weighting. The independent checks are packaged for repetition. Established: a rank-one scalar response can give the desired square-root coefficient ratios with complete cancellation of unmeasured source magnitudes. Not established: that the written V2 master action realizes this response for canonically normalized occupied reference frequencies, that the reference-count weighting is dynamically selected, that the self-consistent branch exists and is stable, or that a nucleon pole has been predicted. This is the principal constructive lead from the latest calculations. Its conditional status is part of the finding, not a reason to discard it or to claim more than has been shown. Related Research status — current proof boundaries and correction guidance. Common field response — derives the full response-profile criterion for rank one and its static coupling bound.

title: Angular kernel parity
summary: The dot-square angular integral has an exact finite spectrum, while its density-sourced Hartree potential acts by multiplication and preserves parity.
text: The valid integral-operator statement On the ordinary spatial unit sphere S^{d-1}, d\geq2, use probability-normalized measure d\sigma and define (Tf)(x)=\int_{S^{d-1}}(x\cdot y)^2 f(y)\,d\sigma(y). If f(-y)=-f(y), changing y to -y proves Tf=0. In fact the complete nonzero spectrum consists of T1=\frac1d,\qquad T(y^TAy)(x)=\frac{2}{d(d+2)}x^TAx \quad(A=A^T,\ \operatorname{tr}A=0). This follows from rotational invariance and \int y_iy_jy_ky_l\,d\sigma =\frac{\delta_{ij}\delta_{kl}+\delta_{ik}\delta_{jl} +\delta_{il}\delta_{jk}}{d(d+2)}. Rotational invariance and index symmetry force the numerator's three delta pairings to have one common coefficient. Contracting i=j and k=l gives \int|y|^4d\sigma=1, fixing that coefficient to 1/[d(d+2)]. Contracting with the traceless matrix A gives the quadratic eigenvalue. The range contains only constants and traceless quadratics. The corresponding eigenvalues have multiplicities 1 and (d-1)(d+2)/2; all other spherical harmonics, including even degrees four and higher, lie in the kernel. The trace is 1/d+[(d-1)(d+2)/2],2/[d(d+2)]=1. Why a density interaction is different In a quartic density interaction, the mean-field operation is U_\rho(x)=g(T\rho)(x),\qquad \psi(x)\longmapsto U_\rho(x)\psi(x), rather than \psi\mapsto gT\psi. Squaring an odd wave function produces an even density, which can source U_\rho. For an exact example take \psi(x)=\sqrt d\,x_1, so \int|\psi|^2d\sigma=1. Then \rho=d x_1^2,\qquad U_\rho(x)=\frac{g}{d+2}(1+2x_1^2),\qquad \langle\psi|U_\rho|\psi\rangle =\frac{g(d+8)}{(d+2)^2}>0 \quad(g>0). Thus an even kernel gives a nonzero mean-field shift to an odd state in this explicit scalar model. An even multiplication operator preserves parity; it need not annihilate the odd subspace. Application to projected fields Using this angular nullspace for a projected field requires an explicit identification of that field with the scalar angular functions. Physical spin-one polarization has its own representation. A mass-protection argument using the nullspace must establish that the full projected action and its corrections preserve the same structure. The photon module instead keeps P_\gamma\mathcal M P_\gamma=0 as the condition on the full mass operator. The n=0 counting label alone does not prove it. Gauge invariance supplies a different constraint. For a consistently gauged, anomaly-free quantum theory with a symmetry-preserving prescription, q_\mu\Pi^{\mu\nu}=0 permits nonzero transverse vacuum polarization. It does not require \Pi^{\mu\nu}=0 or a constant measured coupling. A regular transverse coefficient leaves the usual massless pole; singular terms or symmetry-breaking backgrounds require additional analysis. See Wingate's QED lectures, §6.2 for an explicit nonzero vacuum-polarization calculation. In a simultaneous matter-and-connection gauge transformation the covariant kinetic term is invariant: the matter phase variation and connection variation cancel. On-shell current conservation and the quantum Ward identities require their respective field and measure assumptions. Verification and related interaction_operator_checks.py checks the sphere spectrum and the odd-state mean-field example by independent circle and sphere quadratures, plus the nonzero transverse tensor. Interaction operator tools — summarizes the angular result and its application. Projected bilocal variation — derives the actual mean-field operation from a density action.

title: Anomaly-free charge family
summary: The one-family anomaly equations admit a hypercharge and B-minus-L family when a right-handed neutrino is included; selecting observed charges needs additional conditions.
text:
What is being checked This note gives a conditional consistency test for a complete specified charge table. It concerns representations of observed four-dimensional chiral fields, not additional physical spatial dimensions, and does not derive those fields from the nested spatial sectors. Use only left-handed Weyl fields, conjugating right-handed fields: Field SU(3)	imes SU(2) Abelian charge Q (\mathbf3,\mathbf2) q u^c (\overline{\mathbf3},\mathbf1) u d^c (\overline{\mathbf3},\mathbf1) d L (\mathbf1,\mathbf2) l e^c (\mathbf1,\mathbf1) e 
u^c (\mathbf1,\mathbf1) n The mixed non-Abelian, mixed gravitational, and cubic Abelian conditions are 2q+u+d=0,\qquad 3q+l=0, 6q+3u+3d+2l+e+n=0, \qquad 6q^3+3u^3+3d^3+2l^3+e^3+n^3=0. The cubic SU(3) anomaly cancels between two fundamentals and two antifundamentals. There are four weak doublets counting colours, satisfying the usual even-doublet condition. These checks assume precisely this field content and chirality assignment. A family of exact solutions For one scalar doublet H of charge h, invariance of the ordinary Yukawa terms QHu^c, QH^\dagger d^c, LH^\dagger e^c, and LH
u^c requires, respectively, q+h+u=0,\quad q-h+d=0,\quad l-h+e=0,\quad l+h+n=0. The weak-index contractions use the invariant alternating tensor where needed; these equations display the Abelian charge sums. Combining them with l=-3q gives the family (q,u,d,l,e,n)=(q,-q-h,-q+h,-3q,3q+h,3q-h). Every displayed anomaly vanishes for arbitrary q,h. In particular, the cubic sum reduces to 6q^3+3(-q-h)^3+3(-q+h)^3+2(-3q)^3 +(3q+h)^3+(3q-h)^3=0. In the field order (Q,u^c,d^c,L,e^c,
u^c), define the conventional vectors Y=\left( rac16,- rac23, rac13,- rac12,1,0ight), \qquad B-L=\left( rac13,- rac13,- rac13,-1,1,1ight). Then the general displayed family is X=aY+b(B-L), with a=2h, b=3q-h, by direct substitution in each entry. The two-parameter freedom and its relation to the neutrino charge are also described in Allanach, Davighi and Melville, §3.1. The calculation here is an explicit sufficient family, not a classification of every spectrum or of every solution without the Yukawa assumptions. For a compact global U(1), compatible charge lattices impose further integrality conditions; rational examples already demonstrate nonuniqueness. Imposing n=0 removes b in this family. Choosing h=1/2 then yields (q,u,d,l,e,n)=\left( rac16,- rac23, rac13,- rac12,1,0ight). Conjugation restores the usual right-handed charges. Neutrino neutrality and the normalization are extra conditions, or must follow from an independently derived geometric charge map. They do not follow solely from having three colours. Conversely, dropping 
u^c while calling the neutrino Dirac would omit a field from this anomaly calculation. V2's existing determinant-trivial gauge carrier gives a particular charge assignment by a separate construction. The freedom here neither changes that assignment nor inserts a new gauge field into V2. It specifies what anomaly cancellation alone can establish, leaving the physical carrier, chirality, and occupied-mode bridge to be derived. Verification and related interaction_operator_checks.py checks the polynomial identities symbolically, mixed Y/B-L sums, the neutral-neutrino specialization, and nonstandard rational solutions. title: Bounded spectral perturbations
summary: A bounded self-adjoint perturbation preserves compact resolvent, bounds every ordered eigenvalue shift, and preserves isolated spectral-cluster rank under an explicit gap condition.
text: Hypotheses Let H be self-adjoint, bounded below, with compact resolvent. Let V be bounded and self-adjoint, with v=\|V\|. Then H+V is self-adjoint on the same operator domain D(H) and is bounded below by \inf\sigma(H)-v. For a nonreal z with |\operatorname{Im}z|>v, (H+V-z)^{-1}=(H-z)^{-1} \left[I+V(H-z)^{-1}\right]^{-1}. The bracket is invertible by its Neumann series. The first factor is compact, so the perturbed resolvent is compact. The resolvent identity extends compactness to every point of the perturbed resolvent set. Eigenvalue displacement Order eigenvalues increasingly, counting multiplicity, as E_j(H). For every unit u in the common domain, \langle u,Hu\rangle-v \leq\langle u,(H+V)u\rangle \leq\langle u,Hu\rangle+v. Taking the maximum over a j-dimensional trial space and then the infimum over such spaces gives \boxed{|E_j(H+V)-E_j(H)|\leq v.} The variational characterization used here is stated in Nam, Functional Analysis II, §2.3. It includes repeated eigenvalues. A perturbation may split a degeneracy while respecting every bound. An isolated cluster Suppose a finite group of eigenvalues is separated from the rest by a positive minimum gap g. If 2v<g, the perturbed cluster and the perturbed neighboring eigenvalues remain separated by at least g-2v. It has the same number of eigenvalues counting multiplicity. The associated subspace can rotate. To express its continuity, take a closed counterclockwise contour \mathcal C enclosing only the cluster and satisfying \operatorname{dist}(z,\sigma(H))\geq\delta>v along the contour. For H_t=H+tV, 0\leq t\leq1, define P_t=\frac{1}{2\pi i}\oint_{\mathcal C}(z-H_t)^{-1}\,dz. Neumann inversion holds on the whole contour, so these orthogonal spectral projectors vary continuously in norm. Their finite integer rank is constant. The resolvent identity also gives the explicit estimate \|P_t-P_0\| \leq\frac{\operatorname{length}(\mathcal C)}{2\pi} \frac{tv}{\delta(\delta-tv)}. The contour condition supplies this bound directly; it is separate from the eigenvalue-count statement. Oscillator example For the confining oscillator, write w=\sqrt\lambda. Its distinct levels are E_N=(2N+d)w, separated by 2w. Every level defines a cluster of \binom{N+d-1}{d-1} eigenvalues. Any bounded self-adjoint V with \|V\|<w preserves these separated cluster counts along H+tV. Their eigenvalues need not remain equal or equally spaced. For example, a twofold level E with perturbation \begin{pmatrix}0&\epsilon\\\epsilon&0\end{pmatrix} splits into E\pm\epsilon. The level count survives and the two frequencies change. A physical interaction must supply its actual operator norm and domain before this bound can establish robustness of a sector calculation. Unbounded interactions require an appropriate relative-bound argument. Verification and related spectral_analysis_checks.py tests ordered shifts, cluster counts, subspace rotations, the contour bound, and explicit degeneracy splitting on independently constructed Hermitian matrices. The infinite-dimensional domain and compactness statements are proved above. Spectral analysis tools — navigation and scope.

title: Centroid-relative self-binding
summary: Centering the auxiliary scalar moment functional yields an explicit translation-covariant self-binding model with zero net self-force.
text:
Scope and reason for this addition Binding a particle's structure about its own centre differs from trapping its centre at an external origin. This distinction fits the V2 spatial premise: an electron has six ordinary macroscopic spatial dimensions, treated alike by its self-binding. Its shared directions with a lower-depth observer acquire no preferred status. The existing self-consistent functional explicitly leaves a correctly varied centroid prescription open. Here is that prescription for its flat scalar model. The calculation below is a checked completion of this auxiliary model; it is not a recovered derivation of the master Dirac dynamics, a global construction on physical CP3, or the actual Coulomb-plus-precession orbit. Define the centre inside the functional Let x\in\mathbb R^d be ordinary spatial coordinates and assume a decaying field with finite kinetic energy and second moment. Write ho=|\psi|^2,\qquad Q=\intho\,dx>0,\qquad R= rac{1}{Q}\int xho(x)\,dx,\qquad z=x-R, M=\int zz^{\mathsf T}ho(x)\,dx. M is the unnormalized central second moment. For g>0, define E[\psi]= rac{\hbar^2}{2m}\int|
abla\psi|^2\,dx+U[ho], \qquad U= rac g2\operatorname{tr}(M^2). Equivalently, U= rac g2\iint  ig[(x-R)\cdot(y-R) ig]^2ho(x)ho(y)\,dx\,dy. The same density-dependent R is used throughout. Translation of the whole field translates R and leaves M and E unchanged. Under a spatial rotation O, M becomes OMO^{\mathsf T} and \operatorname{tr}(M^2) is unchanged. No subset of the d directions is selected. Variation and self-force One must vary R as well as the explicit density factors. Its variation cancels because \int zho\,dx=0: \delta M =\int zz^{\mathsf T}\deltaho\,dx -\delta R\left(\int zho\,dxight)^{\mathsf T} -\left(\int zho\,dxight)\delta R^{\mathsf T} =\int zz^{\mathsf T}\deltaho\,dx. Therefore  rac{\delta U}{\deltaho(x)}=g z^{\mathsf T}Mz, \qquad i\hbar\partial_t\psi =\left[- rac{\hbar^2}{2m}\Delta+g z^{\mathsf T}Mzight]\psi for the usual scalar Schrödinger variational dynamics. At each fixed time, R and M are spatially constant coefficients in this potential. Its total self-force is -\intho\,

abla)\psi\,dx,\qquad \dot P=0,\qquad \dot R= rac{P}{mQ}. Thus the centre moves freely while the self-potential acts on the shape. In the rest frame R=0, choosing \hbar^2/(2m)=1 recovers the existing isotropic stationary calculation. Translating that solution gives a family of equally energetic resting centres. title: Chiral pseudoscalar mass term
summary: A specified leading chiral action makes pseudoscalar mass squared proportional to light-quark masses, with the response scale left as matched input.
text: Conditional symmetry protection The V2 hadronic problem needs a mechanism for light pseudoscalar masses. A useful adjacent benchmark is a leading chiral effective action. Assume spontaneous SU(3)_L\times SU(3)_R\to SU(3)_V breaking, positive light quark masses, and momenta and masses within its low-energy expansion. In natural units define \mathcal L_2=\frac{F^2}{4}\operatorname{Tr}(\partial_\mu U\partial^\mu U^\dagger) +\frac{F^2}{4}\operatorname{Tr}(\chi U^\dagger+U\chi^\dagger), \qquad \chi=2B_0 M, where M=\operatorname{diag}(m_u,m_d,m_s), U=\exp(i\Phi/F), \Phi=\sum_{a=1}^8\lambda_a\pi_a, and \operatorname{Tr}(\lambda_a\lambda_b)=2\delta_{ab}. Here F>0 has mass units and B_0>0 also has mass units. The flavour components are fields on physical space, not extra spatial dimensions. Both constants require matching to the underlying dynamics. Expansion with normalization explicit Expanding U to quadratic order gives \mathcal L_2=\frac12\sum_a\partial_\mu\pi_a\partial^\mu\pi_a +F^2B_0\operatorname{Tr}M -\frac{B_0}{2}\operatorname{Tr}(M\Phi^2)+O(\pi^4). The real-field mass matrix is therefore (\mathsf M^2)_{ab}=\frac{B_0}{2} \operatorname{Tr}\left(M\{\lambda_a,\lambda_b\}\right). For example \lambda_1 has unit entries at (1,2),(2,1), so \operatorname{Tr}M\lambda_1^2=m_u+m_d. The charged fields \pi^\pm=(\pi_1\mp i\pi_2)/\sqrt2 have m_{\pi^\pm}^2=B_0(m_u+m_d). The same calculation for the other flavour pairs gives Field Leading squared mass \pi^\pm B_0(m_u+m_d) K^\pm B_0(m_u+m_s) K^0,\bar K^0 B_0(m_d+m_s) \eta_8, with m_u=m_d \frac{B_0}{3}(m_u+m_d+4m_s) For unequal m_u,m_d, the neutral (\pi_3,\pi_8) block additionally has off-diagonal entry B_0(m_u-m_d)/\sqrt3 and must be diagonalized. In the isospin limit, 4m_K^2-m_\pi^2=3m_{\eta_8}^2 at this order. The quadratic mass vanishes with M. This is the explicit cancellation pattern supplied by chiral symmetry in this action. In the two-flavour restriction it gives F^2m_\pi^2=-(m_u+m_d)\langle\bar q q\rangle_0 with the per-flavour convention \langle\bar q q\rangle_0=-F^2B_0. This condensate relation uses chiral-limit parameters and holds to leading order in the light masses. The leading mass relations and their scale limitation are reviewed in PDG, Quark Masses, §60.5.2. The scheme dependence of B_0 compensates that of the quark masses. Electromagnetic effects and higher orders require additional terms. This benchmark identifies what a V2 pseudoscalar mechanism must reproduce if it realizes these chiral premises; it does not determine F or B_0. Anomaly-free charge family — complementary flavour and chiral-charge bookkeeping. Hadronic pseudoscalar requirement — locates the V2 application. title: Colour singlet criterion
summary: Vanishing mean colour charge is weaker than the singlet condition; the positive total quadratic Casimir distinguishes them exactly.
text: Convention This singlet diagnostic supports V2's hadronic contact calculations by distinguishing mean charge, charge variance, and invariant states. The matrices below represent field amplitudes on the physical manifold; their sizes introduce no physical spatial dimensions. Use Hermitian fundamental generators of SU(N) with \operatorname{tr}(T_aT_b)=\delta_{ab}/2. Their completeness relation is \sum_a(T_a)_{ij}(T_a)_{kl} =\frac12\left(\delta_{il}\delta_{jk}-\frac1N\delta_{ij}\delta_{kl}\right). It is the orthogonal projector onto traceless matrices in this normalization. Contracting with two density matrices gives the purity relation below; contracting the middle indices gives the fundamental Casimir. For a density matrix \rho of trace one, write n_a=\operatorname{tr}(\rho T_a). Completeness gives \rho=\frac{I}{N}+2\sum_a n_aT_a, \qquad \sum_a n_a^2=\frac12\left(\operatorname{tr}\rho^2-\frac1N\right). For a pure fundamental state this norm is (N-1)/(2N). In contrast, \sum_a T_a^2=C_FI,\qquad C_F=\frac{N^2-1}{2N}. For SU(3) with T_a=\lambda_a/2, the pure mean-charge norm squared is 1/3, while the quadratic Casimir is 4/3. Changing generator normalization changes both consistently; it does not equate these two quantities. Exact singlet test On a specified tensor product of particle representations, let Q_a=\sum_iT_a^{(i)}, using -T_a^* for an antifundamental factor. Then C_{\rm tot}=\sum_aQ_a^2\geq0, \qquad \langle\psi|C_{\rm tot}|\psi\rangle =\sum_a\|Q_a\psi\|^2. Consequently \langle C_{\rm tot}\rangle=0 exactly when every generator annihilates \psi, equivalently when \psi is an SU(N) singlet. For a positive density matrix, zero expectation means that its support lies wholly in the singlet subspace. Merely having \langle Q_a\rangle=0 leaves the sum of variances uncontrolled: \langle C_{\rm tot}\rangle =\sum_a\langle Q_a\rangle^2+\sum_a\operatorname{Var}(Q_a). Explicit SU(3) witnesses are: State Mean total charge \langle C_{\rm tot}\rangle Single fundamental \rho=I/3 Zero 4/3 Product |r\bar r\rangle Zero 2 Meson singlet (|r\bar r\rangle+|g\bar g\rangle+|b\bar b\rangle)/\sqrt3 Zero 0 Ordered product |rgb\rangle Zero 3 Normalized antisymmetric three-quark determinant Zero 0 Here r,g,b form an orthonormal basis labelled 1,2,3. The last state is |\epsilon\rangle=\frac1{\sqrt6} \sum_{i,j,k=1}^3\epsilon_{ijk}|ijk\rangle. For the meson, the generator action is proportional to the vectorized matrix T_a-T_a=0. For the determinant, a simultaneous basis change multiplies the state by \det U=1. Both states are therefore singlets. The ordered product states instead retain nonzero total charge variance. The distinction agrees with the determinant projection and pair-generator calculation in the hadronic ledger, §§74–76. Limits of a Casimir penalty An assumed term \kappa C_{\rm tot} with \kappa>0 has zero energy exactly on available singlets. This is a useful conditional selection operator. It does not derive that term from the master kernel, set \kappa, or prove spatial confinement, a growing separation energy, or nuclear depth three. If other coloured fields participate, the constraint concerns their total charge too; a valence-only projection requires justification. Verification and related interaction_operator_checks.py constructs all eight generators, the two- and three-particle charge operators, and the states in the table. It checks both mean charges and charge variances. Interaction operator tools — summarizes the singlet diagnostic and its verification.

title: Confining oscillator domain
summary: The harmonic spatial operator has a closed energy form, compact resolvent, and an explicit eigenbasis whose Gaussian tails justify specified boundary limits.
text: Operator and energy domain On a flat model of d ordinary spatial directions within the one nested physical manifold, consider H=-\Delta+\lambda|x|^2,\qquad \lambda>0,\qquad \mathcal H=L^2(\mathbb R^d,d^dx). This is a specified scalar confinement operator. Its use for a particular sector requires the corresponding kinetic and binding dynamics. Define its energy through the positive quadratic form q[u]=\int\left(|\nabla u|^2+\lambda|x|^2|u|^2\right)d^dx, \qquad \mathcal Q=H^1(\mathbb R^d)\cap\{u:|x|u\in L^2\}. Here H^1 requires square-integrable weak first derivatives. The form norm is (\|u\|_2^2+q[u])^{1/2}. It is complete: a Cauchy sequence converges in H^1 and its products |x|u converge in L^2; local convergence identifies the latter limit with |x| times the former. The densely defined closed form therefore defines the positive self-adjoint Friedrichs operator H. Compact resolvent Suppose a sequence is bounded in this form norm by a common constant. For every R>0, \int_{|x|>R}|u(x)|^2\,d^dx \leq \frac{q[u]}{\lambda R^2}. On each finite ball, the Rellich compactness theorem supplies an L^2-convergent subsequence of the H^1-bounded restrictions. Choose a diagonal subsequence over increasing balls. The uniform tail estimate makes this subsequence Cauchy on all of \mathbb R^d: first make both tails small, then use convergence on the chosen ball. Thus \mathcal Q\hookrightarrow L^2 is compact. The resolvent (H+1)^{-1} maps bounded L^2 sets to bounded form-norm sets. Composing with that compact inclusion proves compactness of the resolvent. The spectrum consists of isolated eigenvalues of finite multiplicity tending to infinity, with a complete orthonormal eigenbasis. This is the confining-potential case of the spectral theorem discussed in Phan Thành Nam, Functional Analysis II, §2.5. Explicit basis and general states Set w=\sqrt{\lambda}. For a multi-index \alpha=(\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_d) of nonnegative integers, write |\alpha|=\sum_j\alpha_j=N and \alpha!=\prod_j\alpha_j!. The physicists' Hermite polynomials give \phi_\alpha(x)= \frac{(w/\pi)^{d/4}}{\sqrt{2^N\alpha!}} \prod_{j=1}^d H_{\alpha_j}(\sqrt w\,x_j) e^{-w|x|^2/2}, \qquad H\phi_\alpha=(2N+d)w\,\phi_\alpha. The one-dimensional Hermite differential equation proves the eigenvalue, and Hermite orthogonality proves normalization. Counting multi-indices with sum N gives \binom{N+d-1}{d-1} states at that energy. The spherical basis and radial overlaps are given in Normalized oscillator modes. Every normalizable state has an L^2-convergent expansion u=\sum_\alpha c_\alpha\phi_\alpha with \sum_\alpha|c_\alpha|^2<\infty. Writing E_\alpha=(2|\alpha|+d)w, \begin{aligned} u\in\mathcal Q&\iff\sum_\alpha E_\alpha|c_\alpha|^2<\infty,\\ u\in D(H)&\iff\sum_\alpha E_\alpha^2|c_\alpha|^2<\infty. \end{aligned} In the corresponding scaled time, unitary evolution is u(t)=\sum_\alpha c_\alpha e^{-iE_\alpha t}\phi_\alpha. It preserves the norm for every L^2 state, including superpositions. For example (\phi_0+\phi_{(1,0,\ldots,0)})/\sqrt2 has two energy components with relative phase e^{-2iwt}. Gaussian tails and boundary terms A fixed eigenfunction is a polynomial of degree at most N times e^{-w|x|^2/2}. For r\geq1 its polynomial obeys a bound Cr^N. Using \Omega_{d-1}=2\pi^{d/2}/\Gamma(d/2) gives, for R\geq1, \begin{aligned} \int_{|x|>R}|\phi_\alpha|^2\,d^dx &\leq C^2\Omega_{d-1}\int_R^\infty r^{2N+d-1}e^{-wr^2}\,dr\\ &=\frac{C^2\Omega_{d-1}}{2w^{N+d/2}} \Gamma(N+d/2,wR^2). \end{aligned} Here \Gamma(s,z)=\int_z^\infty t^{s-1}e^{-t}\,dt is the upper incomplete gamma function. Polynomial derivatives have the same Gaussian envelope. Surface integrals of finite products of these eigenfunctions and their derivatives, with polynomially bounded coefficients, therefore tend to zero at infinity. This supplies explicit boundary control for finite oscillator-mode calculations. For general energy-domain states, the form tail bound above still applies. Pointwise Gaussian decay or a particular boundary flux requires additional regularity and decay assumptions. The fibre-integrated stress calculation states the flux condition for a conserved source. At level N, every normalized eigenstate has \langle |x|^2\rangle=\frac{N+d/2}{w}, \qquad L=w^{-1/2}=\lambda^{-1/4}. The diagonal one-coordinate identity \langle x_j^2\rangle=(\alpha_j+1/2)/w proves this for the Cartesian basis; the terms in |x|^2 that change total level have zero matrix elements within a fixed eigenspace, proving the general case. The coefficient \lambda has units of inverse length to the fourth in this scaled operator. Matching L to a physical length requires the physical coefficients of the action. Verification and related spatial_profile_checks.py checks normalized Hermite modes, differential residuals, moments, superposition evolution, and independent tail quadratures. The compactness argument is analytic; finite numerical checks test its explicit examples. Gaussian contact profiles — uses the ground-state covariance in an overlap calculation. title: Continuum mode memory
summary: Eliminating a coupled continuum produces an exact memory kernel, with exponential decay available only under additional weak-coupling and spectral assumptions.

title: Coulomb exponential profiles
summary: Normalized exponential profiles give exact Coulomb integrals, a two-particle variational bound, and finite-range contact estimates.
text: A specified spatial benchmark Use atomic units, \hbar=m_e=e^2/(4\pi\epsilon_0)=1, and ordinary three-dimensional coordinates. The auxiliary Coulomb Hamiltonian is H_Z=\sum_{i=1}^2\left(-\frac12\Delta_i-\frac Z{r_i}\right) +\frac1{|x_1-x_2|}. The two position labels describe two particles in the same spatial region. This benchmark supplies integration and variational tools. Applying it to V2's six-dimensional electron and actual Coulomb-plus-precession orbit requires a separately justified reduction and interaction law. For \zeta>0, choose \chi_\zeta(x)=\left(\frac{\zeta^3}{\pi}\right)^{1/2}e^{-\zeta r}, \qquad p_\zeta(r)=4\zeta^3r^2e^{-2\zeta r}. The identity \int_0^\infty r^ke^{-ar}\,dr=k!/a^{k+1} gives \int p_\zeta=1, \langle r^{-1}\rangle=\zeta, and, from |\nabla\chi_\zeta|^2=\zeta^2|\chi_\zeta|^2, kinetic energy \zeta^2/2 per particle. Pair repulsion and optimized scale The angular average of 1/|x-y| for radii r,s is 1/\max(r,s): integrating (r^2+s^2-2rsu)^{-1/2}/2 over u\in[-1,1] proves the assertion. Hence \begin{aligned} J_\zeta &=\int_0^\infty\!\int_0^\infty \frac{p_\zeta(r)p_\zeta(s)}{\max(r,s)}\,dr\,ds\\ &=32\zeta^6\int_0^\infty r e^{-2\zeta r} \left(\int_0^r s^2e^{-2\zeta s}\,ds\right)dr =\frac{5\zeta}{8}. \end{aligned} For example, substituting \int_0^r s^2e^{-as}ds=[2-e^{-ar}(a^2r^2+2ar+2)]/a^3 reduces the last integral to elementary factorial integrals. The spatial product \chi_\zeta(x_1)\chi_\zeta(x_2), multiplied by a normalized antisymmetric spin singlet, is an admissible fermion trial state for this Hamiltonian. Its energy is E_Z(\zeta)=\zeta^2-2Z\zeta+\frac{5\zeta}{8} =\left(\zeta-Z+\frac5{16}\right)^2 -\left(Z-\frac5{16}\right)^2. For Z>5/16, its minimum occurs at \zeta=Z-5/16. The variational principle gives \inf\sigma(H_Z)\le -(Z-5/16)^2 Hartree. For Z=2 the trial value is -729/256. This is an upper bound on the ground energy, with both the Hamiltonian and trial family specified. A finite-range interaction bound If a multiplication potential vanishes for r>L and satisfies |V(x)|\le V_0, then |\langle V\rangle|\le V_0\,\Pr(r\le L),\qquad \Pr(r\le L)=1-e^{-2\zeta L} [1+2\zeta L+2(\zeta L)^2] =\frac43(\zeta L)^3+O((\zeta L)^4). This bounds a contact effect once its strength and range are supplied. More generally, a regular partial wave behaving as r^\ell near zero has radial weight O(r^{2\ell+2}), so its probability within L is O(L^{2\ell+3}). The exponent follows from the spatial measure; its coefficient depends on the normalized state. Gaussian contact profiles — complementary exact profile integrals. Actual orbit research correction — identifies the physical orbit target to which a reduction must connect. title: Counting mode tools
summary: Exact counting and spectral tools with explicit operator, normalization, and occupation assumptions.
text: Exact counting and spectral tools with explicit operator, normalization, and occupation assumptions. All physical coordinates belong to one nested chain of ordinary macroscopic spatial submanifolds. The scalar models and coefficient spaces here are mathematical tools whose physical application requires a specified operator. Simplex band level moments — derives exact mean and variance for a uniform cumulative band. Weighted mode evaluation — states the necessary and sufficient point-evaluation bound. Simplex heat trace — bounds a specified positive spectral tower and its truncation error. Round sphere dirac counts — keeps eigenvalues and dimension-dependent spinor multiplicities explicit. Normalized oscillator modes — supplies normalized functions, shell convolutions, and weighted overlaps. Several frequencies from one field A governing operator determines available frequencies; source coupling and nonlinear dynamics determine which excitations become occupied and persist. The motivating open question is how several frequencies that are not direct harmonics of one another arise within \Psi_\infty. Parallel multi-delay comb filters were an exploratory guess. Other resonance mechanisms remain possible within the field's dynamics. For example, the conservative amplitude equation \ddot q+\begin{pmatrix}2&-1\\-1&2\end{pmatrix}q=0 has squared frequencies 1,3, with normalized eigenvectors (1,1)/\sqrt2 and (1,-1)/\sqrt2. Its frequencies are 1,\sqrt3 in the chosen units. Such amplitudes describe modes of a field; they add no physical spatial dimensions. Connecting a resonance model to the occupied particle spectrum still requires the source, interaction, and state.

title: Cyclic resonance spectrum
summary: A nearest-neighbour amplitude ring has exact Fourier resonances, paired levels, and a calculable response to alternating couplings.
text: Several resonances from a finite coupling operator For N\ge3 field amplitudes a_j with j taken modulo N, specify i\dot a_j=\alpha a_j-\beta(a_{j-1}+a_{j+1}),\qquad \beta>0. Here \alpha,\beta have frequency units. A common sufficiently large \alpha makes all frequencies positive if required by the application. The Fourier vectors u_k(j)=e^{2\pi ikj/N}/\sqrt N diagonalize the operator, since each shifted component multiplies by e^{\pm2\pi ik/N}: \omega_k=\alpha-2\beta\cos\frac{2\pi k}{N},\qquad k=0,\ldots,N-1. Norm and the Hermitian quadratic energy are conserved. These resonances arise from the couplings themselves. They need not be direct harmonics of a common frequency. The amplitudes describe field components on the one physical manifold. Degeneracy and a conditional filling rule The modes k and N-k have equal frequency. The bottom mode k=0 is a singleton; for even N, the top mode k=N/2 is another singleton. With an independently specified twofold spin multiplicity and fermion occupation, filling the bottom singleton and q complete pairs uses 2+4q particles. The rule applies before the top singleton is reached; filling that last singleton changes the count by two. Cyclic symmetry is C_N; the pair labels are not three-dimensional SO(3) shells. In units \hbar=1, examples at half filling are: Ring Relative levels \omega-\alpha Filled relative energy N=6 -2\beta,-\beta,-\beta,\beta,\beta,2\beta -8\beta for six particles N=4 -2\beta,0,0,2\beta -4\beta for four particles The four-ring has a partly occupied degenerate middle pair in the noninteracting description. These energies concern the specified model; chemical stability also depends on geometry, interactions, and occupation. Alternating coupling in the four-ring Set alternating edges to t_1=\beta+\delta, t_2=\beta-\delta, |\delta|<\beta. Separating the two sublattices gives off-diagonal block -\left(\begin{smallmatrix}t_1&t_2\\t_2&t_1\end{smallmatrix}\right). Its singular values are 2\beta,2|\delta|, hence the full relative spectrum is \{-2\beta,-2|\delta|,2|\delta|,2\beta\}. The four-particle relative energy is E_{\rm fill}(\delta)=-4\beta-4|\delta|. A distortion therefore lowers this electronic contribution. If the specified structural cost is C\delta^2/2, C>0, the total has minima at |\delta|=4/C when this lies within |\delta|<\beta. A physical bond displacement needs its own map to \delta and elastic coefficient. Counting mode tools — states the open frequency-selection question. Spectral survival recurrence — describes finite-mode return and recurrence. title: Cylindrical barrier separation
summary: A barrier continued cylindrically has no route around it through the added coordinates; a separated Hamiltonian reduces each transverse mode to a longitudinal crossing problem.
text: Why the barrier argument belongs in V2 A barrier independent of the additional spatial coordinates cannot be evaded merely by moving through those coordinates. This is a useful consequence of the bound-within/free-without premise. The result concerns cylindrical continuation of the interaction potential. It does not require a uniform, normalizable particle wavefunction. Use a product region with coordinates (x,y), where x is the supported crossing coordinate and y denotes the additional ordinary macroscopic spatial directions within the containing sector. These are coordinates of one physical space. Their grouping is relative to the barrier, not an inherent division of the electron's six dimensions. Suppose V(x,y)=V_0(x). If the barrier occupies the interval I in x, its support in this region is I\times F, where F is the full available space of y. A continuous path from one side of I to the other must pass through I in its x coordinate, whatever its y coordinate does. There is no geometric detour in F. This does not prohibit quantum transmission through the barrier, or a path around an actual edge in the supported coordinates of a finite physical barrier. Exact separation under a specified Hamiltonian For a flat scalar diagnostic with no mixed kinetic or interaction terms, take H=-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}(\partial_x^2+\Delta_y)+V_0(x) =H_x+H_y. Fourier transformation in y gives, for each transverse momentum k, \Psi(x,y)=\phi_k(x)e^{ik\cdot y},\qquad H_x\phi_k= \left(E-\frac{\hbar^2|k|^2}{2m}\right)\phi_k. The transmission problem is therefore the ordinary longitudinal one at energy E_x=E-\hbar^2|k|^2/(2m). At fixed E_x, adding the separated coordinates does not change its transmission coefficient. At fixed total E, changing the transverse momentum changes E_x, so transmission need not stay the same. For a wave packet, apply the mode decomposition and combine the outgoing fluxes for the prepared incident state. This is an exact statement for the specified separated operator, not a derivation of the full electron–barrier Hamiltonian. Curvature, mixed kinetic terms, additional coordinate-dependent interactions, or a moving barrier can invalidate this reduction. Any claim about a measured tunnelling time also requires a defined time observable and preparation. Verification The spatial structure checks verify the separated differential-operator identity and show explicitly that a mixed potential destroys it. Related Nested sector dynamics — states the operator conditions needed in addition to coordinate nesting. Nested spatial tools — companion tools for spatial evolution and normalization.

title: Dipole dispersion response
summary: Second-order dipole coupling yields an attractive inverse-sixth-power energy with a coefficient fixed by the specified excitation response.
text: Model and range Use atomic units and two separated systems A,B in an ordinary spatial three-plane, with nondegenerate ground states, positive excitation gaps \Delta_a,\Delta_b, and zero permanent dipoles. Assume separation R large compared with their sizes, negligible exchange, and propagation delay short compared with the relevant response times. The leading instantaneous interaction is V=R^{-3}d_A^i T_{ij}d_B^j,\qquad T_{ij}=\delta_{ij}-3\hat R_i\hat R_j. This is a conditional ground-state response calculation. A classical field application must supply its fluctuation state and normalization; zero-point excitation weight is not implicit in the geometry. Spectral sum First order vanishes. The second-order ground energy is \Delta E^{(2)}=-\frac{C_6}{R^6},\qquad C_6=\sum_{a,b}\frac{ |\langle0_A|d_A^i|a\rangle T_{ij} \langle0_B|d_B^j|b\rangle|^2}{\Delta_a+\Delta_b}\ge0. All denominators are positive, fixing the attractive sign. Sums include complete excited multiplets and, where necessary, continuum integrals; convergence is an assumption on the response. For isotropic systems each spectral tensor is proportional to \delta_{ij} and \operatorname{Tr}T^2=6. Writing D_a=\sum_i|\langle0|d^i|a\rangle|^2 with degenerate states grouped gives C_6=\frac23\sum_{a,b}\frac{D_aD_b}{\Delta_a+\Delta_b}. The sign and power have a direct second-order oscillator derivation in the van der Waals teaching article. Imaginary-frequency form Define isotropic polarizability at imaginary frequency iu by \alpha(iu)=\frac23\sum_a\frac{\Delta_aD_a}{\Delta_a^2+u^2}. Partial fractions, including the continuous equal-gap limit, give \int_0^\infty\frac{ab\,du}{(a^2+u^2)(b^2+u^2)} =\frac{\pi}{2(a+b)},\qquad a,b>0. Substitution into the spectral sum therefore proves \boxed{C_6=\frac3\pi\int_0^\infty\alpha_A(iu)\alpha_B(iu)\,du.} For a single-resonance response \alpha_X(iu)=\alpha_X(0)\Omega_X^2/(\Omega_X^2+u^2), C_6=\frac32\alpha_A(0)\alpha_B(0) \frac{\Omega_A\Omega_B}{\Omega_A+\Omega_B}. For equal resonances this is 3\alpha_A(0)\alpha_B(0)\Omega/4. Replacing the resonance by an ionization scale is an additional approximation. These equations give a target for a V2 response calculation once its actual modes, dipole vertex, and state have been determined. Continuum mode memory — retains exact response before taking a decay approximation. Gaussian contact profiles — supplies short-range spatial overlaps for comparison with this long-range expansion. title: Fixed-null calibration
summary: A specified null model permits exact combination of independent match probabilities, explicit treatment of probability floors, and honest finite-simulation uncertainty.
text: Define what is random before scoring a match A numerical coincidence acquires a tail probability only after specifying a null distribution and a complete scoring procedure. For a statistic T whose larger values mean a closer match, the null tail is p(t)=\Pr_{H_0}(T\geq t). Under a continuous null distribution, the probability integral transform makes p(T) uniform on [0,1]. Discrete tails defined with inclusive ties are conservative: \Pr(p(T)\leq\alpha)\leq\alpha. As a simple conditional example, suppose the offset R from a fixed lattice target is uniform on [-\Delta/2,\Delta/2]. A match at least as close as the observed offset has p=\frac{2|R|}{\Delta}. For a multiplicative ladder with ratio r>1, a corresponding log-uniform cell has R=\log(x/x_*) and \Delta=\log r. This is an exact statement about that chosen cell distribution. A nonuniform ladder, measurement-error distribution, fitted anchor, or search across several targets must be included in its actual null model. Combining independent continuous tails Let U_1,\ldots,U_k be independent uniform null probabilities. Then Y_i=-\log U_i obeys \Pr(Y_i>y)=e^{-y} for y\geq0. Convolution, or multiplication of the Laplace transforms \mathbb E[e^{-sY_i}]=(1+s)^{-1}, gives X=\sum_iY_i\sim\operatorname{Gamma}(k,1),\qquad f_X(x)=\frac{x^{k-1}e^{-x}}{(k-1)!}. For observed x=-\sum_i\log p_i, repeated integration by parts yields \boxed{p_{\rm combined}=\Pr(X\geq x) =e^{-x}\sum_{j=0}^{k-1}\frac{x^j}{j!}.} Equivalently 2X has a chi-square distribution with 2k degrees of freedom. Independence is essential. Several ratios using one measured anchor, or several quantities derived from one fit, generally have a joint null that must be retained. Probability floors have atoms Suppose a scoring rule caps the evidential contribution of each match by using \widehat U_i=\max(U_i,f_i) with a fixed 0<f_i<1. Write a_i=-\log f_i. Then \widehat Y_i=-\log\widehat U_i=\min(Y_i,a_i). Its probability measure consists of density e^{-y} on 0\leq y<a_i and an atom of mass f_i=e^{-a_i} at a_i. Its Laplace transform is \mathbb E[e^{-s\widehat Y_i}] =\frac{1+s e^{-(1+s)a_i}}{1+s}, with a removable value at s=-1. In particular \mathbb E[\widehat Y_i]=1-f_i. The exact distribution of the sum is the convolution of these mixed measures; retaining the atoms matters at an inclusive tail threshold. For two contributions, let Q_a(t)=\Pr(\min(Y,a)\geq t)= \begin{cases} 1&t\leq0,\\e^{-t}&0<t\leq a,\\0&t>a. \end{cases} Then the exact inclusive tail is \Pr(\widehat Y_1+\widehat Y_2\geq x) =\int_0^{a_1}e^{-y}Q_{a_2}(x-y)\,dy +e^{-a_1}Q_{a_2}(x-a_1). At x=a_1+a_2 this equals f_1f_2, the mass of the joint atom. For any number of terms, \widehat X\leq X for the same underlying uniform variables, so the ordinary gamma tail evaluated at an observed \widehat x is a conservative upper bound on its capped null tail. A floor chosen after inspecting the result must itself be part of the selection procedure to retain such calibration. Repeat the whole procedure in simulation If a numerical analysis searches over depths, index assignments, formulas, anchors, tolerances, or subsets, apply that same search to each simulated null dataset. For example, if the reported statistic is the best score T=\max_{m\in\mathcal M}T_m, the null simulation must recompute that maximum. The null model should reproduce shared errors and fitted parameters with the same fitting procedure. This defines the object being calibrated. A selected formula cannot be treated as independently fixed merely because it can later be written without adjustable parameters. A fresh independent dataset can instead test a formula fixed before those data are examined. Two finite-simulation quantities For a fixed observed threshold, let K of N independent null simulations meet or exceed it. Conditional on that threshold, K\sim\operatorname{Binomial}(N,p). If K=0, solving \Pr_p(K=0)=(1-p)^N=\alpha gives the one-sided confidence upper limit \boxed{p_{\rm upper}=1-\alpha^{1/N} \simeq\frac{-\log\alpha}{N}.} At 95% confidence the leading numerator is about 2.996. Zero observed exceedances therefore provide a resolution bound, not a zero tail probability. For numerical stability evaluate the exact expression as -\operatorname{expm1}(\log\alpha/N). A different question is a valid Monte Carlo hypothesis test. If the observed dataset and N null datasets produce exchangeable statistics, the rank of the observed one is uniform among N+1 distinct ranks. Its valid inclusive upper-tail Monte Carlo p-value is p_{\rm MC}=\frac{K+1}{N+1}. Inclusive ties make it conservative. The rank argument and distinction from estimating a fixed tail are discussed by Phipson and Smyth, §§2 and 4. This p-value is not the confidence upper bound above. Exchangeability must be justified; simulating from a fitted model without reproducing the fitting process does not automatically supply it.
