title: Gaussian mode geometry
summary: Normalized positive Gaussian profiles have an exact parameter-space metric determined by their mean and covariance, with zero Berry curvature for this real family.
text: Profiles on ordinary spatial coordinates On \mathbb R^d let a normalized density have mean X and positive definite covariance \Sigma: \rho(x)=\frac{\exp[-(x-X)^T\Sigma^{-1}(x-X)/2]} {(2\pi)^{d/2}\sqrt{\det\Sigma}}, \qquad \psi(x)=\sqrt{\rho(x)}. The coordinates x describe ordinary spatial directions of a sector in the nested physical manifold. X and \Sigma label field profiles on that space. Geometry on these parameters measures changes of profiles; it does not supply additional physical spatial dimensions or identify their parameter space with the electron's physical \mathbb{CP}^3. For parameters \theta^i, define the projected derivative tensor Q_{ij}=\langle\partial_i\psi, (I-|\psi\rangle\langle\psi|)\partial_j\psi\rangle, \qquad g_{ij}=\operatorname{Re}Q_{ij}. This convention measures the leading loss of squared overlap: 1-|\langle\psi(\theta),\psi(\theta+d\theta)\rangle|^2 =g_{ij}d\theta^i d\theta^j+o(|d\theta|^2). Derivation from Gaussian moments Put y=x-X and A=\Sigma^{-1}. Logarithmic differentiation gives d\log\psi= \frac12 dX^TAy +\frac14\left[y^TA(d\Sigma)Ay-\operatorname{tr}(A\,d\Sigma)\right]. Its expectation against \rho is zero. Normalization and reality also give \langle\psi,d\psi\rangle=0, so the projector subtraction vanishes. The linear and centered quadratic terms have zero cross moment by odd Gaussian parity. For symmetric B,C, Gaussian fourth moments imply \mathbb E[(y^TBy-\operatorname{tr}(B\Sigma)) (y^TCy-\operatorname{tr}(C\Sigma))] =2\operatorname{tr}(B\Sigma C\Sigma). One proof writes y=\Sigma^{1/2}z and uses independent standard normal coordinates, whose fourth moment is \mathbb E[z_i z_j z_k z_l]= \delta_{ij}\delta_{kl}+\delta_{ik}\delta_{jl}+\delta_{il}\delta_{jk}. The resulting line element is \boxed{ds^2=\frac14dX^T\Sigma^{-1}dX +\frac18\operatorname{tr} (\Sigma^{-1}d\Sigma\,\Sigma^{-1}d\Sigma).} Because d\log\psi=\tfrac12d\log\rho, this is one quarter of the classical Fisher information metric of the Gaussian density family. The mean/covariance form of that statistical metric is also given in Lawson et al., §2. Berry connection and oscillator width With convention \mathcal A=-i\langle\psi,d\psi\rangle, the connection vanishes throughout this globally positive real family. Consequently its Berry curvature d\mathcal A is zero. The metric is nonzero because neighboring normalized profiles differ even when their relative phase is fixed. Multiplying every profile by a smooth parameter-dependent common phase changes the connection by an exact differential and leaves both metric and curvature unchanged. For the ground state of H=-\Delta+\lambda|x|^2, \Sigma=I/(2\sqrt\lambda). At fixed center, \Sigma^{-1}d\Sigma=-\frac{d\lambda}{2\lambda}I, \qquad g_{\lambda\lambda}=\frac{d}{32\lambda^2}. If a specified self-consistency model imposes \lambda=(g/2)^{2/3} with g>0, the chain rule gives g_{gg}=\frac{d}{72g^2}=\frac{d}{288\lambda^3}. This is a metric on the chosen family of normalized profiles. A kinetic term for time-dependent width or a physical response coefficient must be derived from the action and its other modes. title: Green function marginal
summary: Full flat-fibre integration of a normalized Laplace Green function gives the lower-dimensional Green function, while restriction to a slice does not.
text: Physical scope This static operator benchmark specifies the source normalization and distinguishes integration from restriction. Its physical use requires a specified electromagnetic action and observer response. All coordinates here are ordinary macroscopic spatial coordinates in a flat model at finite depth within the one nested physical manifold. Writing \mathbb R^d=\mathbb R^m\oplus\mathbb R^{d-m} chooses coordinates relative to the smaller submanifold; it gives the containing particle no inherent division into different kinds of dimensions. Normalized identity For integers d>m>2, set p=d-m, r=|x|>0, and G_d(z)=\frac{\Gamma(d/2-1)}{4\pi^{d/2}}|z|^{2-d}, \qquad -\Delta_dG_d=\delta_d. The coefficient follows from unit source flux. For G_d(r)=c_dr^{2-d}, integrating -\Delta_dG_d over a ball gives -\Omega_{d-1}r^{d-1}G_d'(r)=c_d(d-2)\Omega_{d-1}=1. Using the unit-sphere area below and \Gamma(d/2)=(d/2-1)\Gamma(d/2-1) gives the displayed c_d. Then, with the full Euclidean fibre measure, \boxed{\int_{\mathbb R^p}G_d(x,y)\,d^py=G_m(x).} Indeed, polar coordinates and u=s^2/r^2 give \begin{aligned} I_{d,m}(r) &=\Omega_{p-1}\int_0^\infty s^{p-1}(r^2+s^2)^{-(d-2)/2}\,ds\\ &=\pi^{p/2}\frac{\Gamma((m-2)/2)}{\Gamma((d-2)/2)}r^{2-m}, \qquad \Omega_{p-1}=\frac{2\pi^{p/2}}{\Gamma(p/2)}. \end{aligned} The integral uses Euler's beta integral, DLMF §5.12. Multiplying by the coefficient in G_d proves the boxed identity. For d=m there is no fibre integration and the assertion is immediate. The equality also holds as locally integrable distributions in x; it does not assign a finite value to the point-source singularity at x=0. At m=3, the unnormalized integral is C_d/r, with C_d=\frac{\pi^{(d-2)/2}}{\Gamma((d-2)/2)}, \qquad (C_3,C_4,C_5,C_6,C_{10}) =\left(1,\pi,2\pi,\pi^2,\frac{\pi^4}{6}\right). The normalized marginal is always 1/(4\pi r). Physical charges additionally depend on source couplings and kinetic normalization. The 1/r quantity is a potential; its radial derivative gives a 1/r^2 force. What changes the conclusion Operation Result for the stated flat kernel Full unweighted integration over \mathbb R^{d-3} 1/(4\pi r) Restriction to y=0 \Gamma(d/2-1)r^{2-d}/(4\pi^{d/2}) Integration with an integrable finite-aperture weight Generally depends on the weight; at distances large relative to its support it retains the r^{2-d} leading power For a normalized finite box weight, the weighted integral tends to zero as the box grows at fixed r; it is not the unweighted marginal. No probability normalization factor may be silently cancelled. The radial integrand at large s scales as s^{1-m}. For m=2 the potential integral diverges logarithmically, and for m<2 it diverges more strongly. A two-dimensional Green function requires its own additive-constant or reference prescription. The photon's bound depth two is not automatically the dimension of its static propagator. Curved metrics, finite boundaries, fibre weights, and dynamical currents require a new calculation. In particular, observer inaccessibility alone does not specify which operation in the table is physically realized. The theorem permits the full marginal of the ordinary flat kernel to pass the static Coulomb test; it neither selects that kernel nor proves the complete field theory. title: Isotropic projection fractions
summary: An isotropically prepared spatial direction has a beta-distributed squared projection onto a fixed subspace, with explicit moments and observer-relative momentum bookkeeping.
text: Geometric preparation Let v be a uniformly distributed unit vector in a D-dimensional Euclidean spatial space, and P the orthogonal projector onto a fixed q-dimensional subspace, 0<q<D. The squared projected fraction is F=\|Pv\|^2\in[0,1]. Uniformity is a preparation assumption. In a scattering application the interaction, incoming state, and detector acceptance determine whether that assumption is justified. The subspaces here are ordinary spatial directions within the single nested physical manifold. Distribution and moments Take independent standard real Gaussian coordinates z_1,\ldots,z_D. Their joint density is rotation invariant, so v=z/\|z\| is uniform on the unit sphere. In a basis adapted to P, put X=\sum_{j=1}^q z_j^2,\qquad Y=\sum_{j=q+1}^D z_j^2,\qquad F=\frac{X}{X+Y}. X and Y are independent gamma variables of common scale 2 and shapes a=q/2, b=(D-q)/2. Change variables to F and S=X+Y, whose Jacobian is S. Their density factors into a gamma density for S and \boxed{f_F(t)=\frac{t^{a-1}(1-t)^{b-1}}{B(a,b)}, \quad 0<t<1,\quad B(a,b)=\frac{\Gamma(a)\Gamma(b)}{\Gamma(a+b)}.} Integration gives \mathbb E[F^k]=\frac{(q/2)_k}{(D/2)_k},\qquad \mathbb E[F]=\frac qD,\qquad \operatorname{Var}(F)=\frac{2q(D-q)}{D^2(D+2)}. Here (a)_k=a(a+1)\cdots(a+k-1). The beta-integral formula also holds for real k>-q/2. Thus a magnitude fraction has \mathbb E[\sqrt F]=B(a+1/2,b)/B(a,b), which generally differs from \sqrt{q/D}. The endpoint cases q=0,D are deterministic. Beam-relative example in six ordinary spatial dimensions Suppose a beam direction lies within the observer's three-dimensional spatial subspace of an electron's six dimensions. Its orthogonal spatial complement has D=5 dimensions. Two of them lie in the observer's transverse plane and three are perpendicular to the observer's subspace. If the transverse direction is isotropic in that five-dimensional space, the fraction perpendicular to the observer's subspace has F\sim\operatorname{Beta}(3/2,1),\qquad \mathbb E[F]=\frac35,\qquad \operatorname{Var}(F)=\frac{12}{175},\qquad \Pr(F\leq t)=t^{3/2}. The electron has six equivalent ordinary spatial dimensions. The grouping above is relative to the beam and observer, with no inherent electron split. The 3/5 result concerns squared transverse momentum under the specified preparation. It supplies neither a scattering rate nor an energy threshold. Opposing momentum components can balance within a multi-particle event even when each has a nonzero perpendicular component. Projected mass shell If a particle satisfies the relativistic mass shell in the containing spatial sector, decompose its momentum relative to the observer as p=p_{\parallel}+p_{\perp}. Orthogonality gives E^2=c^2(|p_{\parallel}|^2+|p_{\perp}|^2)+m^2c^4. An observer reconstruction using the full particle energy E and only p_{\parallel} would therefore assign M_{\rm app}^2=\frac{E^2}{c^4}-\frac{|p_{\parallel}|^2}{c^2} =m^2+\frac{|p_{\perp}|^2}{c^2}. The qualification that E is the full particle energy matters: a partial energy deposit has its own detector model. This equation is kinematic; whether a process populates p_{\perp} requires its interaction. title: Nested sector dynamics
summary: Cylindrical function lifts require a projection, and exact inheritance of dynamics additionally requires an invariant domain and an intertwining operator relation.
text: What nesting supplies All spatial sectors in V2 belong to one nested chain in the same infinite physical manifold. Their dimensions are ordinary macroscopic spatial directions. Describing their relationship through functions needs two steps: defining the lift of a function and checking the lift of its dynamics. For an inclusion i:Q_a\hookrightarrow Q_b, the canonical function map is restriction, in the opposite direction: i^*:C^\infty(Q_b)\longrightarrow C^\infty(Q_a),\qquad i^*F=F\circ i. To lift functions from Q_a to Q_b cylindrically, specify a smooth projection \pi:Q_b\to Q_a with \pi\circ i=\mathrm{id}. Then J=\pi^*,\qquad Jf=f\circ\pi,\qquad i^*Jf=f is an injective algebra map. In a product chart (x,y), this is simply Jf(x,y)=f(x). Nested inclusions alone do not supply a global \pi. The sector geometry audit already identifies this geometric limitation. When a lower-sector equation is preserved For a time-independent lift J, an exact evolution lift requires H_bJf=JH_af on a domain preserved by the relevant evolutions. For unbounded operators, domain compatibility is part of the assertion; a symbolic differential identity alone is not a complete operator theorem. A direct differential example is H_a=-\Delta_x+V_a(x),\qquad H_b=-\Delta_x-\Delta_y+V_a(x). Since \Delta_yJf=0, the displayed intertwining identity holds on smooth cylindrical fields. If instead H_b contains \kappa xy in a two-coordinate example, then H_bJf-JH_af=\kappa xyf(x), which depends on y and leaves the cylindrical class. Coordinate nesting survives, but this exact autonomous lower-sector evolution does not. A constant extension is not square-integrable over a noncompact fibre of infinite volume. In that case the preceding calculation is a statement about fields or generalized modes, not a normalized Hilbert-space embedding. For a Hilbert-space version one can instead specify a normalized transverse eigenfunction \chi and use J_\chi f=f\chi; a separated Hamiltonian then gives H_bJ_\chi f=J_\chi(H_a+\epsilon)f,\qquad H_y\chi=\epsilon\chi. Such an eigenfunction and its boundary conditions must actually exist. They are extra model data, not a derivation of cylindrical continuation. Consequence for interactions Nesting allows a shared-coordinate description; it does not guarantee that every interacting sector retains its isolated spectrum. A nonzero coupling can introduce backreaction, mix states, or shift energies. Use the explicit intertwining condition when exact inheritance is needed, and an effective reduction when it fails. The spatial structure checks verify the separated and mixed differential examples. title: Oscillator rotation branching
summary: Harmonic-polynomial decomposition gives exact angular multiplicities for a flat oscillator shell and its restriction to an observer-selected spatial three-plane.
text: Shells under ordinary spatial rotations For an isotropic scalar oscillator on \mathbb R^d, d\ge3, the creation operators transform as a spatial vector. Shell N therefore has the representation \operatorname{Sym}^N(\mathbb C^d). Its polynomial representation decomposes as \operatorname{Sym}^N(\mathbb C^d) =\bigoplus_{k=0}^{\lfloor N/2\rfloor}r^{2k}\mathcal H_{N-2k}^{(d)}, \qquad h_d(\ell)=\dim\mathcal H_\ell^{(d)} =\binom{\ell+d-1}{d-1}-\binom{\ell+d-3}{d-1}. Here \mathcal H_\ell^{(d)} denotes homogeneous harmonic polynomials; binomial coefficients with top smaller than bottom are zero. To see the decomposition, subtract successive traces (Laplacians) of a homogeneous polynomial. The identity \Delta(r^{2k}h_\ell)=2k(2\ell+2k+d-2)r^{2k-2}h_\ell has a nonzero coefficient for k>0, permitting recursive removal of each trace. Dimensions then telescope to \binom{N+d-1}{d-1}. For the cumulative band 0\le N<n, the multiplicity of \mathcal H_\ell^{(d)} is \left\lfloor\frac{n-1-\ell}{2}\right\rfloor+1 \quad(0\le\ell<n). In particular the rotational scalar occurs once in each even shell, and \lceil n/2\rceil times in the cumulative band. A shell's parity condition and a cumulative band's scalar content are different counts. Restriction to a selected three-plane For d>3 choose a spatial three-plane O and perpendicular complement O^\perp within the same d directions. Under rotations of O that fix O^\perp, the shell representation decomposes into a sum over N_O+N_\perp=N. A three-dimensional oscillator shell N_O contains angular momenta \ell=N_O,N_O-2,\ldots, each once. The complementary shell contributes scalar multiplicity g_{d-3}(N_\perp)=\binom{N_\perp+d-4}{d-4}. Thus m_d(\ell,N)=\sum_{j=0}^{\lfloor(N-\ell)/2\rfloor} \binom{N-\ell-2j+d-4}{d-4}, \qquad \sum_{\ell=0}^N(2\ell+1)m_d(\ell,N)=\binom{N+d-1}{d-1}. Summing m_d over N<n gives the cumulative multiplicity. At d=6,n=13, its values for \ell=0,\ldots,12 are (1036,784,581,420,295,200,130,80,46,24,11,4,1), and their (2\ell+1)-weighted sum is 18564=S(13,6). This is an exact restriction of the flat oscillator representation to a specified subgroup. Matching a dimension does not identify a unique group embedding. title: Projected bilocal variation
summary: Varying an exchange-symmetric interaction between projected densities retains the channel projector and one kernel convolution in each mean-field term.
text: Scope Work in a specified finite containing spatial region Q, with one field \Psi(t,x), fixed measure, and fixed channel projectors P_a(x). The labels x,y are two positions in the same physical space, not additional physical dimensions. Channel indices do not replace the required nested spatial embeddings; those maps must be supplied when applying this local model. Let \rho_a=\bar\Psi P_a\Psi be real, Grassmann-even scalar bilinears. Use projectors compatible with the chosen adjoint; in a Lorentzian Dirac convention this means P_a^\dagger\gamma^0=\gamma^0P_a. No positivity of \bar\Psi P_a\Psi is assumed. Vary \Psi and \bar\Psi independently. Variation Absorb coupling coefficients and coordinate identifications into a real kernel with exchange symmetry K_{ab}(x,y)=K_{ba}(y,x). Write \mathcal D=i\Gamma^A\nabla_A for the kinetic Dirac operator, where A ranges over the one time coordinate and the spatial directions in Q, and \nabla_A includes the chosen spin connection. Choose the interaction sign explicitly: S=\int dt\int_Q\bar\Psi\,\mathcal D\Psi\,d\mu -\frac12\int dt\sum_{a,b}\iint_{Q\times Q} \rho_a(x)K_{ab}(x,y)\rho_b(y)\,d\mu_xd\mu_y. At fixed projectors, kernel, and metric, U_a(x)=\sum_b\int_Q K_{ab}(x,y)\rho_b(y)\,d\mu_y, \qquad \frac{\delta S_{\rm int}}{\delta\bar\Psi(x)} =-\sum_a U_a(x)P_a(x)\Psi(x). To see the cancellation of the half, vary each density in the double integral and exchange (a,x) with (b,y) in the second contribution. The two contributions are identical. Thus the field equation is \boxed{\left(\mathcal D-\sum_a U_aP_a\right)\Psi=0.} With a plus interaction in the action the corresponding sign is plus. The projector remains attached to the varied field. The kernel occurs once inside U_a. If the kernel is not exchange-symmetric, only its symmetrized part contributes to the scalar-density functional. At density level, \frac{\delta U_a(x)}{\delta\rho_b(y)}=K_{ab}(x,y). This is the reciprocal response. It does not require equal response coefficients after changing field normalizations or identifying different coordinate spaces. Remaining physical requirements The kinetic symbol includes the appropriate geometric connection; replacing covariant derivatives by partial derivatives on a curved sector needs a justified local approximation. Dynamical projectors, metric-dependent measures, and kernels produce additional variations, including contributions to stress-energy. They are held fixed only for the variation above. For a local phase with generator \hat Q, the displayed scalar densities are invariant if [P_a,\hat Q]=0 and the adjoint transforms compatibly. More general charged bilocal factors need appropriate transport or invariant contractions. Gauge covariance is not implied by the double-integral notation. The equation is a Dirac mean-field equation. Its reduction to a positive scalar Schrödinger density, the sign of self-binding, a causal completion of the instantaneous spatial kernel, and the physical mass operator remain separate obligations. In particular, the flat scalar oscillator closure cannot be obtained merely by relabelling \bar\Psi\Psi as |\Psi|^2. Verification and related interaction_operator_checks.py compares the analytic variation with finite differences using complex fields, nontrivial projectors, unequal integration weights, and nonsymmetric kernels. title: Radial confinement bounds
summary: The radial spatial measure fixes the centrifugal term, while a Hardy bound gives an explicit sufficient condition excluding levels below a saturating threshold.
text:

For a normalized spherical harmonic with angular eigenvalue \ell(\ell+d-2), write \psi(x)=R(r)Y_\ell(\hat x) and u(r)=r^{(d-1)/2}R(r). This transformation sends the radial norm to \int_0^\infty|u|^2dr. Differentiating R=r^{-(d-1)/2}u yields H_\ell u=-u''+ \left[V(r)+ rac{(\ell+(d-2)/2)^2-1/4}{r^2}ight]u. The term (d-1)(d-3)/(4r^2) is contributed by the radial measure. Use the Friedrichs realization inherited from the full spatial quadratic form. In particular the regular branch has u\sim r^{\ell+(d-1)/2}; the critical d=2,\ell=0 endpoint selects the regular, nonlogarithmic branch. An arbitrary half-line boundary condition describes a different operator. A form bound on attraction For d\ge3, integration by parts for smooth compactly supported \psi gives 0\le\int\left|
abla\psi+a rac{x}{r^2}\psiight|^2dx =\int|

abla\psi|^2dx\ge  rac{(d-2)^2}{4}\int rac{|\psi|^2}{r^2}dx.} This is Hardy's inequality; see Nonnenmacher, Proposition 3.2.7. For the dimensionless operator H_{m sat}=-\Delta+\lambda rac{r^2}{1+r^2},\qquad \lambda>0, subtract its limiting potential \lambda. title: Resonant quartet dynamics
summary: A conservative quartic amplitude interaction has exact action invariants and a detuning-controlled exchange law under specified pump preparation.
text: Four distinct field modes In frequency units with canonical equation i\dot a_j=\partial H/\partial a_j^*, choose H=\sum_{j=1}^4\omega_j|a_j|^2+ \kappa a_1^*a_2^*a_3a_4+kappa^*a_1a_2a_3^*a_4^*. For example i\dot a_1=\omega_1a_1+\kappa a_2^*a_3a_4 and i\dot a_3=\omega_3a_3+\kappa^*a_1a_2a_4^*; exchange 1\leftrightarrow2 and 3\leftrightarrow4 for the other two equations. The positions of the complex conjugates are essential to reciprocity. Let I_j=|a_j|^2 and Z=\kappa a_1^*a_2^*a_3a_4. Direct differentiation gives \dot I_1=\dot I_2=2\operatorname{Im}Z, \qquad \dot I_3=\dot I_4=-2\operatorname{Im}Z. Every charge Q_c=\sum c_jI_j with c_1+c_2=c_3+c_4 is conserved. These include total norm, I_1-I_2, and I_3-I_4. The Hamiltonian itself is conserved and total norm bounds every amplitude, giving global solutions for finite initial data. Mode amplitudes add no physical spatial dimensions. Frequency matching Writing a_j=b_je^{-i\omega_jt} makes the first interaction proportional to e^{i\Delta t} with \Delta=\omega_1+\omega_2-\omega_3-\omega_4. A label equality n_1+n_2=n_3+n_4 implies \Delta=0 when all four frequencies follow the same affine law \omega_j=An_j+B. It need not do so under a nonlinear count law or unequal sector scales. For example 1+4=2+3, while S(1,2)+S(4,2)=11 and S(2,2)+S(3,2)=9. In a first-order calculation that freezes the other three rotating amplitudes, the forced change is proportional to \int_0^t e^{i\Delta s}ds and is bounded by 2/|\Delta| times that fixed forcing strength. This bound belongs to that approximation. Exact exchange with undepleted pumps For independently maintained pumps b_2,b_4, the 1,3 subsystem obeys i\dot b_1=g e^{i\Delta t}b_3,\qquad i\dot b_3=g^*e^{-i\Delta t}b_1,\qquad g=\kappa b_2^*b_4. Set b_1=c_1e^{i\Delta t/2} and b_3=c_3e^{-i\Delta t/2}. Then i\frac d{dt}\begin{pmatrix}c_1\\c_3\end{pmatrix} =\begin{pmatrix}\Delta/2&g\\g^*&-\Delta/2\end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix}c_1\\c_3\end{pmatrix}. The matrix square is (|g|^2+\Delta^2/4)I. Starting with (c_1,c_3)=(0,1), |c_1(t)|^2=\frac{4|g|^2}{\Delta^2+4|g|^2} \sin^2\left(\frac{\sqrt{\Delta^2+4|g|^2}}2t\right). This derives resonance-enhanced transfer and its finite detuning width. title: Round-sphere Dirac counts
summary: The round-sphere Dirac spectrum has a dimension-dependent spinor multiplicity, giving two times the simplex count on S3 and four times it on S5.
text: The operator and its multiplicity For the untwisted complex spinor Dirac operator on a round sphere S^d of radius R, d\ge2, the eigenvalues and multiplicities for each sign are \lambda_k^\pm=\pm\frac{k+d/2}{R},\qquad m_d(k)=2^{\lfloor d/2\rfloor}\binom{k+d-1}{d-1}, \qquad k=0,1,\ldots. The unit-radius result is Bär, The Dirac operator on space forms of positive curvature, Theorem 1; rescaling the metric supplies the displayed factor 1/R. Summing the positive branch through level k=n-1 gives N_+(n)=\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}m_d(k) =2^{\lfloor d/2\rfloor}S(n,d). This is a cumulative eigenstate count with multiplicity, not an individual Dirac eigenvalue. Including both signs doubles this count. Low-dimensional examples Sphere Spinor factor Positive cumulative count S^3 2 2S(n,3) S^5 4 4S(n,5) At the V2 neutrino indices 10,15,22, the round S^5 operator gives 8008,46512,263120 positive-branch states. Restricting to fewer components would need a specified invariant projection and its own spectrum. At radius one on S^3, the eigenvalue 7/2 belongs to k=2 and has multiplicity 12. Multiplicity 20 belongs to k=3, whose eigenvalue is 9/2. The coincidence m_3(3)=S(4,3)=20 does not equate a shell count with a cumulative count. Use in V2 These formulas provide a checked benchmark for the candidate sphere operators. The spinor factor counts field components; it introduces no additional physical spatial directions. They do not select a sphere as the actual sector geometry, construct its nesting, or derive the law m=\mu S(n,d). The mass law and the individual sphere Dirac eigenvalues remain different quantities. Existing particle depths and the neutrino mass ratios use a separately specified contact mass operator. The mode counting checks verify the cumulative sums and the explicit S^3 and S^5 examples. They check applications of the cited spectrum, not a numerical construction of the sphere Dirac operator. title: Shared time coordinate
summary: All nested spatial sectors use one time coordinate; this premise neither equates proper times nor supplies a metric or causal theorem.
text: The premise already used by V2 The time variable in the V2 evolution equations is shared across sectors. The photon module already uses shared time. There is one infinite physical manifold, with one temporal direction and one nested chain of spatial submanifolds. A sector's depth counts only its spatial dimensions. Thus a six-dimensional electron has six ordinary macroscopic spatial directions and uses the same time coordinate as three-dimensional matter and a ten-dimensional tau. Its six spatial directions are six of the tau's ten. Sharing three with an observer does not make those three different in kind, and no sector acquires a separate time dimension. At a finite depth, a local evolution chart can be written (t,q_d),\qquad q_d\in Q_d,\qquad Q_a\subset Q_b\quad(a<b). The same t appears in both charts. This notation records the framework's temporal premise; it does not construct an infinite-dimensional metric or Dirac operator. A global product with a time axis is a stronger geometric choice than merely using such local charts. Shared coordinate time and elapsed time One coordinate t does not imply that every physical clock accumulates the same proper time. For example, in the finite-dimensional flat Lorentzian metric ds^2=-c^2dt^2+\sum_{j=1}^{d}(dq^j)^2, \qquad d\tau=dt\sqrt{1-\frac{\lVert\dot q\rVert^2}{c^2}}, timelike paths with different speeds have different elapsed proper times. This is a compatibility example using the usual metric definition of proper time, not a derivation of the V2 metric. See Carroll, General Relativity notes, §1, equation 1.97. Likewise, one timelike direction alone does not forbid boosts along any particular spatial direction or prove the absence of closed timelike curves. Those questions need the actual metric, global causal assumptions, and a specification of physically accessible operations. Finally, a block-diagonal metric need not be an exact product metric: ds^2=-c^2dt^2+a(t)^2\sum_j(dq^j)^2 has no time–space cross terms, yet its spatial block depends on time. Consequently, neither exact operator separation nor ordinary observer Lorentz dynamics follows just from the common time coordinate. title: Simplex band level moments
summary: Uniform counting over a cumulative oscillator band gives exact mean and variance of the excitation level, without selecting a physical occupation or mass correction.
text: Uniform cumulative-band counting The mean excitation level d(n-1)/(d+1) is an exact identity for uniform counting across a cumulative oscillator band. Set N=n-1 and give equal weight to each Cartesian oscillator state (a_1,\ldots,a_d) with nonnegative integer entries and K=\sum_i a_i\le N. The shell degeneracy and band size are g_d(k)=\binom{k+d-1}{d-1},\qquad B=\sum_{k=0}^{N}g_d(k)=S(n,d). Thus the probability of a shell under this specified counting measure is g_d(k)/B, not 1/(N+1). Exact first and second moments The factorial-moment identities k g_d(k)=d\binom{k+d-1}{d},\qquad k(k-1)g_d(k)=d(d+1)\binom{k+d-1}{d+1} and the hockey-stick sum give \mathbb E[K]=\frac{dN}{d+1},\qquad \mathbb E[K(K-1)]=\frac{dN(N-1)}{d+2}, \operatorname{Var}(K)= \frac{dN(N+d+1)}{(d+1)^2(d+2)}. Equivalently, append a slack coordinate a_0=N-K. The uniform set of weak compositions \sum_{i=0}^{d}a_i=N is symmetric in all d+1 entries, so each has mean N/(d+1). The slack is counting notation, not an additional physical spatial direction. For an affine diagnostic f(K)=A+BK, its counting average is therefore A+BdN/(d+1). A quadratic diagnostic additionally uses the second moment. This gives exact finite-band benchmarks before any physical occupation weights are introduced. Physical scope The coordinates being counted describe d equivalent ordinary spatial oscillator directions in an auxiliary flat model. Equal weighting of all states in the cumulative band is explicit model data. A single occupied shell, a coherent state, and a nonuniform mixture generally have different moments. Applying these moments to a physical energy correction requires the perturbing operator and the relevant physical state. The counting mixture is a mathematical benchmark for those calculations. The mode counting checks compare these expressions with direct rational shell sums and explicit weak-composition enumeration. title: Simplex heat trace
summary: The tower with one eigenvalue per simplex index has an explicit heat-trace bound and convergence domain, distinct from the spatial dimension of a sector operator.
text: Specify the tower being summed Let a positive diagonal operator A_d have one eigenvalue \lambda_n=\mu S(n,d),\qquad n\ge1,\qquad \mu>0, for each index, with no extra degeneracy. Define K_d(t)=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}e^{-t\mu S(n,d)},\qquad t>0. Here t is a heat parameter in inverse-eigenvalue units, not the shared physical time coordinate. This is an analytic diagnostic for the proposed count sequence; it does not identify A_d with the spatial Dirac operator. A bound that proves the asymptotic For integer d\ge1, \frac{n^d}{d!}\le S(n,d)\le\frac{(n+d-1)^d}{d!}. Put a=\mu t/d! and f(x)=e^{-ax^d}. Its integral is I_d(t)=\int_0^\infty f(x)\,dx =\Gamma\!\left(1+\frac1d\right) \left(\frac{d!}{\mu t}\right)^{1/d}. Since f decreases, its positive-integer sum lies between I_d-1 and I_d. The shifted sum beginning at integer d differs by at most d-1. Sandwiching K_d between these two sums gives \max(0,I_d(t)-d)\le K_d(t)\le I_d(t). In particular, K_d(t)= \Gamma\!\left(1+\frac1d\right) \left(\frac{d!}{\mu t}\right)^{1/d}+O(1) \quad(t\downarrow0). For a numerical cutoff L, the omitted positive tail obeys 0\le K_d(t)-\sum_{n=1}^{L}e^{-t\mu S(n,d)} \le\int_L^\infty e^{-ax^d}\,dx =\frac{\Gamma(1/d,aL^d)}{d\,a^{1/d}}, where the final expression uses the upper incomplete gamma function. Thus both the leading approximation and finite numerical sum have explicit error bounds. Different generating functions count different things The ordinary index generating function is also exact: \sum_{n\ge1}S(n,d)z^n=\frac{z}{(1-z)^{d+1}}, \qquad |z|<1. It weights the index by the count; the heat trace instead places the count in an exponential. Their singular exponents need not agree. Likewise, comparison with n^{-ds} shows that \sum_n S(n,d)^{-s} converges absolutely exactly when \operatorname{Re}s>1/d. The heat exponent 1/d is therefore a property of this one-eigenvalue-per-index tower. It is not evidence that the corresponding spatial dimension equals d. For example, the actual round-sphere Dirac spectrum has eigenvalues linear in its level and nontrivial multiplicities, as detailed in round-sphere Dirac counts. V2's physical depth is the number of ordinary macroscopic spatial directions in its principal-symbol construction. This diagnostic does not replace that construction or change any depth. What this does not regularize The bounds establish the displayed trace and convergence region. They do not establish analytic continuation at s=0 or finiteness of all interaction sums. Even if an operator zeta function is regular there, its regularized determinant changes under rescaling: \log\det\nolimits_\zeta(\alpha A) =\log\det\nolimits_\zeta A+\zeta_A(0)\log\alpha. This follows by differentiating \zeta_{\alpha A}(s)=\alpha^{-s}\zeta_A(s). A finite value at zero alone neither determines its derivative nor removes normalization-scale dependence. The mode counting checks check direct heat sums against both bounds and verify the index generating-function coefficients. Related Simplex reciprocal sum — gives the exact s=1 value for d>1. title: Simplex reciprocal sum
summary: Reciprocal simplex counts have an exact telescoping sum and truncation remainder, providing a conditional trace check for the V2 count spectrum.
text: A useful identity adjacent to the mass spectrum The identity below concerns the count S(n,d)=\binom{n+d-1}{d} used by the V2 mass module. It supplies a closed-form check and an exact truncation error for sums of inverse counts. No new geometry or particle assignment is needed. For positive integer n and integer d>1, \frac{1}{S(n,d)} =\frac{d}{d-1} \left[\frac{1}{S(n,d-1)}-\frac{1}{S(n+1,d-1)}\right]. To verify this, factor (d-1)!/[n(n+1)\cdots(n+d-2)] from the difference in brackets. The remaining factor is (d-1)/(n+d-1), giving d!/[n(n+1)\cdots(n+d-1)] after multiplication by d/(d-1). Summing the difference gives \sum_{n=1}^{N}\frac{1}{S(n,d)} =\frac{d}{d-1} \left[1-\frac{1}{S(N+1,d-1)}\right], and hence \sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{S(n,d)}=\frac{d}{d-1}, \qquad \sum_{n=N+1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{S(n,d)} =\frac{d}{(d-1)S(N+1,d-1)}. The remainder tends to zero for every d>1. For d=1, S(n,1)=n, so the corresponding harmonic series diverges. Adjacent-depth recursion The factorial definition also gives the multiplicative recursion \frac{S(n,d)}{S(n,d+1)}=\frac{d+1}{n+d},\qquad S(n,d+1)=\frac{n+d}{d+1}S(n,d). At fixed n>1, S(n,d) strictly increases with d; for n=1 all counts equal one. At fixed d, the ratio decreases with n. These are count identities for any positive indices, usable alongside the additive Pascal recursion without assigning physical occupation weights. What the trace interpretation requires If a specified positive operator has exactly one eigenvalue \mu_d S(n,d) per positive integer n, with no additional degeneracy, then its inverse trace is \operatorname{Tr}(A_d^{-1})=\frac{d}{(d-1)\mu_d}. This is conditional on that operator and counting measure. The formula does not establish that the master Dirac operator has this spectrum or that all these bands are occupied particles. Restricting to the occupied particle indices gives a different finite sum; including a massless zero mode makes an ordinary inverse undefined. If each band is instead assigned multiplicity S(n,d), each band's contribution to the inverse trace is 1/\mu_d, and the infinite trace diverges. This simple example is why multiplicities must be stated. Oscillator excitation energies and cumulative counts also remain distinct, as in the existing mass analysis. Verification and related work The spatial structure checks compare direct rational finite sums with the telescoping expression across several depths and truncations. The all-N proof is the algebra above, rather than numerical extrapolation. Nested spatial tools — companion tools for spatial evolution and normalization.

title: Simplex spectral zeta
summary: Explicit analytic continuation of the one-eigenvalue-per-index simplex tower gives its value and derivative at zero, including the normalization dependence of its zeta determinant.
text:
Specify the positive spectrum For integer d\geq2, consider one eigenvalue per positive integer index, with no additional multiplicity: P_d(n)=S(n,d)= inom{n+d-1}{d} = rac{n(n+1)\cdots(n+d-1)}{d!}, \qquad Z_d(s)=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}P_d(n)^{-s}. Comparison with n^{-ds} proves absolute convergence for \operatorname{Re}s>1/d. All eigenvalues in this definition are dimensionless. The integer d labels the polynomial sequence; interpreting an actual spatial operator requires its eigenvalues and multiplicities. The associated positive heat sum is developed in Simplex heat trace. Continuation by subtracting the large-index terms Set A_d= rac{d(d-1)}2, \qquad b_n=\prod_{j=0}^{d-1}\left(1+ rac jnight). Uniformly for s in a compact set, b_n^{-s}=1-sA_d/n+O(n^{-2}). Therefore R_d(s)=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} n^{-ds} \left[b_n^{-s}-1+ rac{sA_d}{n}ight] converges locally uniformly and defines a holomorphic function for \operatorname{Re}s>-1/d. Initially in the convergent half-plane, then by continuation,  oxed{Z_d(s)=(d!)^s \left[\zeta(ds)-sA_d\zeta(ds+1)+R_d(s)ight].} Here \zeta is the Riemann zeta function. The remainder bound follows by expanding \log b_n=A_d/n+O(n^{-2}) and its exponential; the tail is O(n^{-d\operatorname{Re}s-2}). This also justifies local termwise differentiation. In this half-plane, the pole at s=1/d has residue (d!)^{1/d}/d. At s=0, the apparent pole in the second term cancels against its factor s. Value and derivative at zero Use \zeta(0)=-1/2 and \zeta(1+ds)=1/(ds)+\gamma+O(s), where \gamma is Euler's constant. Since R_d(0)=0,  oxed{Z_d(0)=- rac12- rac{A_d}{d}=- rac d2.} The derivative of the remainder is an ordinarily convergent series: R_d'(0)=\sum_{n\geq1} \left[-\log b_n+ rac{A_d}{n}ight] =\sum_{j=0}^{d-1}\log\Gamma(1+j)+\gamma A_d. To obtain the last equality, take the logarithm of the gamma-function product: \log\Gamma(1+j)=-\gamma j+ \sum_{n\geq1}\left[ rac jn-\log\left(1+ rac jnight)ight]. Only finitely many j are summed. Differentiating the continuation formula then cancels the \gamma A_d terms and gives  egin{aligned} Z_d'(0) &=- rac d2\log(d!)+d\zeta'(0) +\sum_{j=0}^{d-1}\log(j!)\ &= oxed{- rac d2\log(2\pi d!) +\sum_{j=0}^{d-1}\log(j!)}. \end{aligned} The Riemann values used here, including \zeta'(0)=-	frac12\log(2\pi), are recorded in DLMF §25.6. Regularized product and scale Define the zeta determinant by \det_\zeta P_d=\exp[-Z_d'(0)]. The result is  oxed{\det
olimits_\zeta P_d = rac{(2\pi d!)^{d/2}}{\prod_{j=0}^{d-1}j!}.} This regularized product has the following simple benchmarks: Spectrum, one eigenvalue per n\geq1 Value at zero Zeta determinant n -	frac12 \sqrt{2\pi} n(n+1)/2 -1 4\pi n(n+1)(n+2)/6 -	frac32 (12\pi)^{3/2}/2 The first row follows directly from Z_1=\zeta. If the physical eigenvalue is \mu P_d(n), choose a fixed comparison unit E_* and set r=\mu/E_*>0. Then Z_{rP_d}(s)=r^{-s}Z_d(s) and \log\det
olimits_\zeta(rP_d) =\log\det
olimits_\zeta P_d- rac d2\log r. Thus the normalization convention remains explicit. Z_d(0) is an analytically continued spectral quantity, not a count of spatial directions. A gravitational or vacuum-energy use additionally needs a specified physical operator, action, regularization prescription, and scale matching. title: Spectral survival recurrence
summary: Pure-point spectral evolution has a positive mean return weight and arbitrarily accurate recurrences, while an integrable continuous spectral density permits decay of the return amplitude.
text: A specified evolution and preparation Let H be a self-adjoint frequency operator and u a normalized field profile. Time evolution is u(t)=e^{-itH}u; for an energy operator replace H by H/\hbar. The return amplitude and weight are a(t)=\langle u,e^{-itH}u\rangle, \qquad P(t)=|a(t)|^2. These are Hilbert-space diagnostics of the selected linear evolution. They apply to classical complex mode amplitudes as well as quantum states. Their interpretation as an observed survival probability requires a measurement prescription. Mode amplitudes describe fields on the one physical manifold and introduce no further spatial dimensions. For a preparation supported on the pure-point spectrum, combine each degenerate eigenspace into one orthogonal projector P_j, with distinct frequencies \omega_j. Put p_j=\|P_ju\|^2. Then p_j\geq0,\quad \sum_jp_j=1, \qquad a(t)=\sum_j p_j e^{-i\omega_jt}. The series converges absolutely and uniformly in time, because its omitted tail is bounded by the omitted sum of p_j. Time average For a finite spectral sum, integrate each pair of phases: \frac1T\int_0^T e^{-i(\omega_j-\omega_k)t}\,dt \longrightarrow \begin{cases}1&j=k,\\0&j\ne k.\end{cases} Uniform tail control extends this calculation to a countable sum. Hence \boxed{\lim_{T\to\infty}\frac1T\int_0^T P(t)\,dt =\sum_jp_j^2>0.} Degeneracies must be grouped before squaring their weights. The average of a(t) itself retains only a zero-frequency component, so it is a different quantity. A small mean return weight can coexist with eventual recurrence. For two equally weighted frequencies, a(t)=e^{-i(\omega_1+\omega_2)t/2} \cos\!\left(\frac{\omega_2-\omega_1}{2}t\right), \qquad P(t)=\cos^2\!\left(\frac{\omega_2-\omega_1}{2}t\right). The recurrence of the ray occurs every 2\pi/|\omega_2-\omega_1|. The difference of frequencies controls the beating. Approximate recurrence without commensurability Choose a finite set of occupied frequencies and a reference \omega_1. For any time unit \tau>0, consider the phase vectors k\tau(\omega_j-\omega_1)/(2\pi) modulo one, for integers k. Partition this finite-dimensional unit cube into boxes of side 1/Q. Among one more points than boxes, two share a box. Subtracting their integer times gives a positive t at which every selected relative phase is within 2\pi/Q of an integer multiple of 2\pi. For a countable spectrum choose the finite set with omitted weight \eta. If the selected phase errors have absolute value at most \epsilon, \|e^{-itH}u-e^{-i\omega_1t}u\|^2 =\sum_jp_j|e^{-i(\omega_j-\omega_1)t}-1|^2 \leq\epsilon^2+4\eta. Both terms can be made arbitrarily small. Such times are unbounded: if the approximating integer times remained bounded as the tolerance shrank, one of them would be an exact common period, whose multiples are unbounded. For any fixed tail cutoff the same argument supplies arbitrarily late returns. Exact ray recurrence requires all occupied frequency differences times t to lie in 2\pi\mathbb Z; approximate recurrence needs no such commensurability. This is the spectral recurrence setting discussed by Campos Venuti, §I. An absolutely continuous preparation The spectral theorem more generally gives a probability measure \mu_u: a(t)=\int e^{-i\omega t}\,d\mu_u(\omega). If d\mu_u=f(\omega)d\omega with f\in L^1, the Riemann–Lebesgue lemma gives a(t)\to0. For a uniform density on [\omega_0-B,\omega_0+B], B>0, a(t)=e^{-i\omega_0t}\frac{\sin Bt}{Bt}. This decay describes dephasing of the return amplitude while the full evolution remains unitary. Singular continuous spectral measures require their own analysis; absolute continuity is the sufficient hypothesis used here. Selecting a physical persistent mode additionally requires its coupling and dynamics, beyond a recurrence identity. Verification and related spectral_analysis_checks.py checks exact finite time averages, commensurate and incommensurate examples, and continuous-density Fourier integrals. title: Weighted mode evaluation
summary: A weighted coefficient norm bounds point evaluation exactly when the corresponding inverse-weighted evaluation sum is finite; counts alone do not establish that condition.
text: Why the basis values matter Inverse simplex counts can control mode expansions when the basis values satisfy the evaluation criterion below. The reciprocal-sum identity supplies a useful bound. For a specified scalar readout of the mode functions, write initially for finitely supported coefficients f_c(x)=\sum_{n\ge1}c_n\phi_n(x),\qquad \|c\|_w^2=\sum_{n\ge1}w_n|c_n|^2,\qquad w_n>0. This is a norm on coefficient sequences. Calling it a spatial L^2 norm would require an additional basis and measure identification. Its use for classical fields does not introduce any extra physical spatial dimensions. Necessary and sufficient condition At a fixed evaluation point, define B(x)=\sum_{n\ge1}\frac{|\phi_n(x)|^2}{w_n}. Cauchy–Schwarz gives |f_c(x)|\le \|c\|_w\sqrt{B(x)}. Conversely, for a finite cutoff L with B_L(x)>0, choose c_n=\frac{\overline{\phi_n(x)}}{w_n\sqrt{B_L(x)}} \quad(1\le n\le L). These coefficients have norm one and evaluation \sqrt{B_L(x)}. Thus evaluation extends boundedly to the completed coefficient space if and only if B(x)<\infty, and its norm is exactly \sqrt{B(x)}. This proof also identifies the missing assumption in an argument based only on \sum_n1/w_n. Applying the simplex weights For one scalar mode per n, take w_n=S(n,d) with d>1. If |\phi_n(x)|\le C uniformly in both n and x on the region of interest, then B(x)\le C^2\frac{d}{d-1}. The exact reciprocal-count remainder gives a uniform tail bound: \left|\sum_{n>L}c_n\phi_n(x)\right| \le C\left(\sum_{n>L}S(n,d)|c_n|^2\right)^{1/2} \left[\frac{d}{(d-1)S(L+1,d-1)}\right]^{1/2}. This establishes uniform convergence for finite weighted norm under the stated uniform mode bound. It is a usable truncation estimate, not a general claim about every sector basis. If band n has several components, the actual criterion becomes B(x)=\sum_{n,\alpha}\frac{|\phi_{n,\alpha}(x)|^2}{w_n}. For example, give band n multiplicity g_d(n-1)=\binom{n+d-2}{d-1}. There exist orthonormal families with all components having unit magnitude at a point: distinct Fourier modes on a circle with normalized measure provide a mathematical example. Then B(0)=\sum_{n\ge1}\frac{g_d(n-1)}{S(n,d)} =\sum_{n\ge1}\frac{d}{n+d-1}=\infty. The one-mode reciprocal sum converges while this evaluation is unbounded. This counterexample tests the inference from weights alone; the circle is not a replacement geometry for an IDWT particle. Limits for contact calculations V2's finite-band contact theorem uses a specified finite reproducing kernel. Passing to an infinite field requires controlling the corresponding evaluation sum and occupation weights. Derivative readouts need the sums of squared derivative values; interaction energies and determinants need their own estimates. Finite inverse-count weight alone is not a proof of universal ultraviolet control. Evaluation on a homogeneous spatial space Let a compact homogeneous space X have invariant volume \operatorname{Vol}X. Take a rank-N orthogonal projector onto smooth scalar functions or bundle sections, invariant under a transitive unitary symmetry action. For an orthonormal basis \phi_j of its range the evaluation kernel is K(x,y)=\sum_{j=1}^N\phi_j(x)\phi_j(y)^\dagger. Equivariance conjugates K(x,x) by the fibre symmetry. Its trace is therefore constant on the transitive orbit. Integrating that trace gives N, so \operatorname{tr}K(x,x)=\frac{N}{\operatorname{Vol}X}. For scalar functions this is the squared norm of point evaluation, and |f(x)|^2\le N\|f\|^2/\operatorname{Vol}X in the projected space. For a spherical-harmonic shell on the unit S^2, it gives K_\ell(x,x)=(2\ell+1)/(4\pi); summing shells 0\le\ell<n gives n^2/(4\pi). The identity fixes the summed evaluation weight. Individual basis values can vanish at a point. For bundle sections, a chosen source direction v probes v^\dagger K(x,x)v, while summing an orthonormal set of fibre polarizations gives the trace. Scalar proportionality on the fibre requires an additional isotropy representation condition. The compact homogeneous hypotheses must hold for this bound to replace a direct evaluation sum. The mode counting checks test saturation of the finite bound, generic complex coefficients, and the multiplicity counterexample. Related Simplex reciprocal sum — supplies the exact tail used above. title: Zonal hybrid geometry
summary: Spherical-harmonic addition gives exact directed-state overlaps and conditional trigonal, tetrahedral, and octahedral orthogonality.
text: Directed angular functions On the unit sphere of a chosen ordinary spatial three-plane, let Y_{\ell m} be orthonormal with area measure. Define a normalized angular coefficient vector for unit direction v by |\ell,v\rangle=\sqrt{\frac{4\pi}{2\ell+1}} \sum_{m=-\ell}^{\ell}\overline{Y_{\ell m}(v)}|\ell,m\rangle. The spherical-harmonic addition theorem gives \langle\ell,v|\ell,w\rangle=P_\ell(v\cdot w), \qquad \|\,|\ell,v\rangle\|=1. The normalization and addition formula are specified in DLMF 14.30.8–9. Different \ell blocks are orthogonal. Thus a directed function |h_v\rangle=\sum_\ell c_\ell|\ell,v\rangle, with the same coefficients for each direction and \sum|c_\ell|^2=1, has overlap \boxed{\langle h_v|h_w\rangle=\sum_\ell|c_\ell|^2P_\ell(v\cdot w).} These are angular functions, not trajectories or additional physical spatial dimensions. The three-plane is selected relative to the system being described; the electron's six spatial directions remain equivalent. The scalar-plus-vector case Let |h_i\rangle=a|s\rangle+b|p_{v_i}\rangle, with a,b>0, a^2+b^2=1. Suppose the n functions are orthonormal and their span contains |s\rangle. Completeness within that span implies 1=\sum_{i=1}^n|\langle h_i|s\rangle|^2=na^2. Consequently a^2=1/n, b^2=(n-1)/n, and off-diagonal orthogonality requires v_i\cdot v_j=-\frac1{n-1}\quad(i\ne j). Their direction Gram matrix has one zero eigenvalue and n-1 eigenvalues n/(n-1), so it can be realized in a three-plane only if n\le4. The sum of the directions is zero. This gives the regular simplex cases: n Scalar share a^2 Pair cosine Geometry 2 \frac12 -1 Opposite directions 3 \frac13 -\frac12 Trigonal directions 4 \frac14 -\frac13 Tetrahedral directions The simultaneous directed form, equal coefficients, orthonormality, and span condition are assumptions. Orthogonalizing arbitrary directed functions generally changes their form; it does not establish these assumptions or select nuclear equilibrium angles. A six-direction construction With squared shares (|c_0|^2,|c_1|^2,|c_2|^2)=(1/6,1/2,1/3), \frac16+\frac12x+\frac13P_2(x)=\frac{x(x+1)}2. The six directions \{\pm e_1,\pm e_2,\pm e_3\} have distinct pair cosines 0 or -1, so their six directed functions are orthonormal. This proves an octahedral construction for the displayed shares. Selecting those shares or an actual molecular geometry requires dynamics. Multicentre orbit axes — obtains related direction geometry from an actual prescribed route. Cylindrical molecular shape stability — tests full ligand forces beyond kinematic axes. title: Accurate cylindrical correction
summary: Accuracy-controlled fixed-Casimir shooting revisits the rejected cylindrical candidates with analytic derivatives and independent endpoint checks.
text: Physical premise (IDWT): There is one infinite-dimensional physical manifold. All sectors form one nested chain of submanifolds within it. Particle depth counts ordinary, literal macroscopic spatial dimensions. “Observed” and “unobserved” describe an observer's access to those dimensions, not different kinds of physical dimension. See spatial meaning and mathematical scope. Summary: Accuracy-controlled fixed-Casimir shooting revisits the rejected cylindrical candidates with analytic derivatives and independent endpoint checks. Timed investigation This calculation tests orbit existence and stability through numerical continuation and independent closure checks. The numerical search is not an interval existence proof. Initial finding At h=0.0128, the archived state has refined recurrence error 5.3145\times10^{-6}. A new analytic variational corrector, using the same fixed-Casimir chart, reduced the independently integrated trial residual to 2.0765\times10^{-10} in one correction of norm 3.702\times10^{-6}. This is evidence of a nearby accurately recurrent solution rather than an obstruction at this homotopy value. Final refinement and further continuation are recorded below as they complete. The analytic local derivative agrees with the independent complex-step implementation to 4.55\times10^{-13} over random states on both smooth sides of the nuclear-profile boundary. The analytic chart derivative agrees with centered differences to 1.67\times10^{-10}. No claim of a two-sided Jacobian at the nonsmooth profile join is made. Independent closure and first stability result Explicitly splitting integration at each finite-profile boundary gives a corrected h=0.0128 period T=20.48965735631915. The original independent state-only DOP853 routine returns a refined closure error 5.28\times10^{-12}; its last endpoint refinement is 9.01\times10^{-11}. A separate full-six-coordinate Radau integration closes to 1.67\times10^{-11}. Source Casimirs remain fixed by the chart. The full 27-variable state (six positions, six momenta, fifteen source components) has largest Floquet multiplier modulus 1.138471302788. Refining the full monodromy changes its largest matrix entry by only 4.41\times10^{-10} and leaves the growth exponent 0.0063293591391 per model-time unit unchanged at the displayed precision. This is a resolved linear instability, not neutral-mode rounding. The nonlinear perturbation check and mode localization below confirm it. This result restores numerical existence near the old candidate while rejecting its stability in the full fixed-centre model. It does not establish or exclude another stable branch or a moving-nucleus molecular solution. The growing mode lies outside the four-coordinate invariant plane: its squared projection into that plane is 1.72\times10^{-25}. Direct nonlinear integrations, with the source perturbed by conjugation so its Casimirs remain fixed, reproduce the predicted three-period amplification 1.475591904. Continuation beyond the original endpoint The corrected branch reaches h=0.100, not the purely cylindrical endpoint h=1. Ten candidates pass fresh, boundary-segmented DOP853 and Radau integrations: both closure errors below 10^{-8}, endpoint difference below 10^{-9}, initial source-Casimir error below 2\times10^{-12}, and section error below 10^{-8}. These tests recompute acceptance rather than trust saved solver labels. The complete, uniform results are in cross-method-verification.json. The h=0.100 and turning-point h=0.0096 solver reports retain a failed legacy refinement gate: their medium-accuracy unsegmented integrations were not sufficiently converged. The fresh segmented cross-method test supersedes that numerical rejection without weakening its thresholds. At h=0.016 and 0.0256, three-turn nonlinear perturbations also reproduce the Floquet growth, while preserving source Casimirs. These tested points are unstable, despite their accurately closed orbits. The h=0.040 and 0.070 nonlinear probes also reproduce the predicted growth. The h=0.100 result is a Floquet diagnostic only. At h=0.0064 and 0.0096, the transverse blocks have no resolved exponentially growing multiplier. Full matrices have small splittings near unit neutral multipliers, of order 10^{-6} to 10^{-5}, which are not a demonstration of physical instability or of nonlinear stability. Orbit-size and family-selection controls The optional affine two-row slice (--gauge) chooses a local member of an underdetermined family. Its two residual null directions have not both been proved to be pure coordinate gauge. Also, setting q_0=1,q_1=0 does not itself set the orbit's maximum visible radius. An alternative --physical-section imposes \dot q_0=0 and the second active unobserved momentum equal to zero, in addition to the original section. At h=0.0096 this gives period 20.558807735241658, closure errors 4.73\times10^{-13} (segmented DOP853) and 4.71\times10^{-12} (segmented Radau), and sampled maximum visible radius 1.0000000000000833. The radial second derivative at the section is -0.8029593, confirming a local maximum. Its full-coordinate Floquet calculation likewise finds no resolved transverse exponential mode; near-unit splitting changes with refinement and does not establish nonlinear stability. The continued paths retain six radial maxima per full period, with raised radial minima: the turning-point h=0.0096 path has minimum visible radius 0.0129064, while the h=0.100 path spans approximately [0.14022,1.02787]. They are petal-like recurrent paths, not exact visible centre crossings. The affine-sliced samples are not a fixed-maximum-radius stability scan. Why the reduced stability test misses a mode Let A be the active four-coordinate space with two visible and two unobserved coordinates. Linearization about q,p\in A and C\in\mathfrak{so}(A) splits the full 27-variable system into blocks of sizes 27=14+6+6+1. The 14-block is the original active orbit. Each remaining spatial coordinate contributes its position, momentum, and four mixed source components. The last component rotates the two inactive directions and is constant to linear order. The blocks decouple exactly because the potential depends only on the full and visible squared radii and all inactive base coordinates vanish. Random-state checks give exactly zero off-block entries and active-block agreement to 2.23\times10^{-16}. At h=0.0128, the growing mode belongs to the third visible direction and its source components, not the third unobserved direction. Its six-block has the reciprocal real pair 1.1384713,0.87837084, one unit-circle pair, and two unit multipliers. The unobserved-side six-block has only unit-modulus multipliers within numerical accuracy. Omitting the third visible perturbation therefore removes a physically relevant instability from this diagnostic. title: Chiral CP3 selection
summary: A normalized six-dimensional chiral spinor coupled to an unconstrained bivector selects a CP3 minimum family with a Berry term and nonlinear energy confinement, conditional on its master-field derivation and identification with physical spatial coordinates.
text: Physical premise (IDWT): There is one infinite-dimensional physical manifold. All sectors form one nested chain of submanifolds within it. Particle depth counts ordinary, literal macroscopic spatial dimensions. “Observed” and “unobserved” describe an observer's access to those dimensions, not different kinds of physical dimension. See spatial meaning and mathematical scope. Summary: A normalized six-dimensional chiral spinor coupled to an unconstrained bivector selects a CP3 minimum family with a Berry term and nonlinear energy confinement, conditional on its master-field derivation and identification with physical spatial coordinates. Fixed-depth route using chiral polarization Electron depth six is fixed by the mass-formula assignment in this model. Instead of requiring the filled twelve-state response band of the preceding candidate model, consider one normalized chiral Spin(6) polarization z in C4 and an unconstrained real skew 6x6 bivector B. A six-dimensional Dirac spinor has chiral halves of this size; selecting one half and representing the relevant polarization by a pure normalized vector are additional premises, not consequences of dimension alone. The Pauli bilinear map already checked in the geometric-response note gives J(z)=J(zz dagger), with J squared=−I and <J,J>=3. It is linear in the density matrix. We do not impose B squared=−rho² I. The purpose of the coupling is to determine whether that condition follows for B. The chiral spinor here is a polarization variable. It must not silently be identified with a global spatial Dirac field on an already assumed CP3 base. The earlier spinor-bundle obstruction remains in force. Linear bivector coupling and exact energy minimum Let mu>0, g>0, and <A,B>=−tr(AB)/2. Define the Hermitian chiral operator h(B) by the expectation identity z^\dagger h(B)z=-g\langle B,J(z)\rangle. It is the bivector representation on the chosen chiral spinor. In the explicit traceless two-Pauli basis P_A, its checked matrix is h(B)=−(g/4) sum_A <B,J(P_A)> P_A. The total joint energy is E(B,z)=\mu\langle B,B\rangle-g\langle B,J(z)\rangle =\mu\|B-\rho J(z)\|^2-\frac{3g^2}{4\mu},\qquad \rho=\frac{g}{2\mu}. This is an exact completed square for every B and normalized z. Therefore the global minima have B=rho J(z), and B squared=−rho² I follows. The family of minima modulo the common spinor phase is CP3. The positive quadratic cost and the bilinear chiral coupling are the effective interaction assumptions; their presence and normalization remain to be derived from the master theory. For a chosen chirality and the stated signs, the map selects one component of the orthogonal-complex structures. If both chiralities are admitted symmetrically, the opposite component returns with the same energy. Thus the construction does not derive a physical chirality selection. At a minimum the source operator has the especially simple form h(\rho J(z))=-g\rho(4zz^\dagger-I_4). Its occupied ray has eigenvalue −3g rho and the other three eigenvalues are +g rho. The gap is 4g rho=2g²/mu. Unlike the preceding real-band model, there is no separately assumed twelve-state filling or externally supplied gap Delta; the gap follows from the self-consistent bivector amplitude. Normal variations in matrix space and conservative confinement The auxiliary skew 6x6 matrix B has 15 independent rotation-plane components. Six parameter variations stay tangent to the CP3 minimum family; the other nine are "normal variations in matrix space," meaning deviations away from that family. These are not nine additional spatial directions. The electron's assigned spatial depth remains six. Eliminating the spinor into the lowest eigenstate of h(B) gives E_eff(B)=mu||B||²+lambda_min(h(B)). Near a selected minimum the source ground ray is nondegenerate. The full fifteen-parameter matrix-space Hessian has six zero tangent eigenvalues and nine positive eigenvalues 2mu. These are checked through finite differences of the Hellmann–Feynman gradient 2mu B−gJ(z_ground(B)). An explicit joint action is L=i\hbar z^\dagger\dot z+\frac{M}{2}\langle\dot B,\dot B\rangle-E(B,z), \qquad z^\dagger z=1, with the phase multiplier understood. It gives the reciprocal equations M\ddot B=-2\mu B+gJ(z),\qquad i\hbar\dot z=h(B)z. Both spinor norm and the total energy are conserved. The exact square gives \mu\|B-\rho J(z)\|^2+\frac{\|\Pi\|^2}{2M} =E_{\rm total}-E_{\min}. This controls distance to the entire minimum family and the momentum for small excess energy, not merely an eigenvalue test at one point. Direct coupled evolution verifies conservation and the bound. It is conservative stability of the family, not attraction to one orientation, and not a proof of stability for an electron orbit after adding the nuclear interaction. Phase dynamics now survive For the rank-one projector P=zz dagger and horizontal variations u,v, i\operatorname{tr}\bigl(P[\delta_uP,\delta_vP]\bigr) =-2\operatorname{Im}(u^\dagger v). This is nonzero in general and is checked against an explicit canonical pair. It supplies the projective Berry/symplectic term missing from the filled real-band candidate. Direct differentiation of J under the spinor equation gives \dot J=-\frac{2g}{\hbar}[B,J], matching the existing geometric commutator convention with I_e=hbar/2. At an isolated minimum B=rho J this commutator vanishes, as it should: the self-coupling creates the geometry and gap, not a preferred moving orientation. Nuclear orientation energy is still needed to drive precession. Reduction to the earlier CP3 dynamics In the algebraic M=0 limit, B=rho J(z) exactly. The self-energy becomes a constant, leaving the Berry term and any added nuclear energy V_N(J). The latter then produces the previously checked first-order CP3 precession. Thus a consistent effective route to the earlier action exists within this model; a real-band source with zero Berry curvature could not do this. For small nonzero M, substituting the leading B=rho J into the kinetic term gives 4M rho² ds_FS²/dt², using <dJ,dJ>=8 ds_FS². This is the leading derivative expansion, not an exact constraint at finite frequency. Frequency scales must be small relative to the eliminated amplitude dynamics before discarding its corrections. Source and kinetic parameters are not fitted to an observed electron frequency here. What has and has not been selected The construction supplies a CP3 collective minimum family, positive stiffness for normal variations in matrix space, a self-generated polarization gap, and the projective phase term, without assuming the defining constraint on B or a filled real source band. It does assume a pure chiral polarization, a quadratic bivector cost, and their coupling. The pure chiral ray already carries CP3 polarization geometry; the nontrivial selection result is that an initially unrestricted B locks to it and acquires controlled normal variations in matrix space. This is not a derivation of CP3 without any spinorial premises. Most importantly, a CP3 polarization/collective space is not automatically the electron's spatial base. If z is a spinor fibre variable at a point of an independent Q6, this result describes that fibre and its response. A master-field reduction must show why the collective variables are the actual six configuration coordinates, without duplicating spatial degrees of freedom or ignoring the spatial spinor-bundle obstruction. The normalization used here is for a finite collective spinor. If z is instead a local field with variable density, global charge conservation does not fix its pointwise norm. Eliminating B then produces an attractive density-quartic contribution, and density stabilization must be supplied and checked separately. The finite normalized calculation is not a proof of spatial localization or absence of field collapse. The remaining physical identification concerns z and B, the chiral sector and its coupling, and the configuration reduction—not another particle-depth comparison. No geometry is ruled out merely because it differs from the V1 assignments. There is a useful algebraic route to examine at that next step. For an unnormalized pure chiral amplitude w, let n=w dagger w. The bilinear identity becomes ||J(ww dagger)||²=3n². Algebraically eliminating B therefore gives the local term −3g² n²/(4mu). An attractive density quartic can thus admit this auxiliary-bivector representation at the classical commuting-amplitude level. This observation does not supply an independent B kinetic term or establish an operator identity for anticommuting quantum fields. The written master-current construction uses bar(Psi)Psi, not automatically w dagger w for a single chiral amplitude. Their projection and normalization must be evaluated before claiming this auxiliary channel is already derived from the master scalar interaction. summary: The reciprocal tensor-response model admits uniformly precessing electron–response solutions whose rate obeys a cubic, with distinct branches and stability that must be checked rather than assumed.

Summary: The reciprocal tensor-response model admits uniformly precessing electron–response solutions whose rate obeys a cubic, with distinct branches and stability that must be checked rather than assumed. Exact collective solution This result uses the effective response channel in the linked note; it is not a derived microscopic nuclear current or a replacement for the actual-orbit target. Let K generate a planar rotation in O, put a in (0,1), q=sqrt(1−a²), and use the following time-dependent mixed blocks: A=aK,\quad C=-aK,\quad Q(t)=\operatorname{diag}\big(qR(\omega t),1\big), \qquad R(\theta)=e^{\theta K_2}. Take a response rotating at the same rate, X(t)=\operatorname{diag}\big(xR(\omega t),z\big),\qquad Y=M_X\dot X. The oscillator equation and electron equation independently require z=\chi g,\qquad x=\frac{\chi gq}{1-\omega^2/\Omega_X^2},\qquad \omega q=\frac{2ga}{\mathcal I_e}x. With kappa=chi g², the common rate must therefore obey \boxed{ \omega\left(1-\frac{\omega^2}{\Omega_X^2}\right) =\frac{2\kappa a}{\mathcal I_e}. } Unlike assigning X(t) as an external drive, this ansatz solves both reciprocal equations if the cubic holds. It constructs a family of self-consistent motions, not attraction from arbitrary initial conditions. The response has its own stored energy and momentum. The endpoint cases, zero coupling, and the response pole omega=plus/minus Omega_X are excluded from this nonzero-q derivation and require separate treatment. Branch structure Define omega_ad=2 kappa a/I_e > 0. For \omega_{\rm ad}<\frac{2\Omega_X}{3\sqrt3} there are two positive sub-resonant roots and one negative root below −Omega_X. The two positive branches merge at Omega_X/sqrt(3). Beyond that threshold only the negative real branch remains. The negative branch has an out-of-phase planar response, not a negative susceptibility parameter. This root count follows from the extrema of the cubic. For a fixed positive a and increasingly fast response, the low positive branch approaches omega_ad. This is the finite-response continuation of the static precession result. The relation determines the rate given (kappa,I_e,Omega_X,a); it does not determine those physical inputs or select an integer petal count. Full tangent stability The rotating-frame linearization includes all six CP3 tangent directions plus nine X and nine Y variables, not only the planar ansatz. Choose the dimensionless example chi=I_e=1, Omega_X=2, a=3/5, kappa=25/64. Its three self-consistent roots are \omega_- =\frac{-1-\sqrt{61}}4,\qquad \omega_{\rm low}=\frac12,\qquad \omega_{\rm high}=\frac{-1+\sqrt{61}}4. For reproducible rational algebra use U=gX and Z=gY. In the frame rotating only the O plane at rate omega, the equations are \dot J=-[B_U,J]-[\operatorname{diag}(\omega K,0),J],\qquad \dot U=Z/M_X-\omega KU,\qquad \dot Z=-U+\kappa Q-\omega KZ. At the low root, Q=diag(4/5,4/5,1), U=diag(1/3,1/3,25/64), and Z=K/24. The exact 24-dimensional characteristic polynomial, up to its positive leading normalization, factors as \lambda^4(\lambda^2+4)(4\lambda^2+1)(4\lambda^2+9) (4\lambda^2+25)(144\lambda^4+1324\lambda^2+1825)\,p_8(\lambda), where p_8(\lambda)=5435817984\lambda^8+96096780288\lambda^6 +601412116420\lambda^4+1573811889137\lambda^2+1436009168896. Exact real-root counting after setting t=lambda² shows that every nonzero factor has strictly negative real t roots. Thus the nonzero linear eigenvalues are imaginary for this example, without a numerical tolerance being used as the proof. Zero has algebraic multiplicity four, nullity three, and squared-matrix nullity four: one size-two Jordan block remains. The result is absence of exponential linear growth, not bounded linear evolution or nonlinear orbital stability. The high positive branch has no numerically resolved exponential mode in the same full tangent test. This is a numerical result only; it is not covered by the exact low-branch polynomial proof. The negative branch has a positive growth rate approximately .665240. A small constraint-preserving perturbation grows in an independent nonlinear rotating-frame integration. At amplitudes 1e-5 and 5e-6, the differences from linear evolution at time 3 are approximately 1.31e-10 and 3.56e-11. Thus this branch supplies a genuine unstable counterexample to treating every self-consistent rotation as stable. Verification and boundaries collective_precession_checks.py checks the three branches at the same coupling, the full equilibrium equations, tangent-space closure, nonlinear perturbations, exact characteristic factors and root counts, and the neutral Jordan structure. Its normal run completes 32 evaluations across 13 runtime conditions. No autonomous capture into one branch, integer L selection, Coulomb orbital clock, physical current normalization, or petal readout has been derived. What is new is an explicit reciprocal model with self-consistent precession and a nontrivial tested stability distinction between branches. Related Research status — current boundaries and results. title: Cylindrical molecular shape stability
summary: The prescribed three-petal route gives a strict trigonal ligand minimum, while the nominal tetrahedral quarter-turn rays carry transverse force and relax to a strict disphenoidal minimum.
text: Physical premise (IDWT): There is one infinite-dimensional physical manifold. All sectors form one nested chain of submanifolds within it. Summary: The prescribed three-petal route gives a strict trigonal ligand minimum, while the nominal tetrahedral quarter-turn rays carry transverse force and relax to a strict disphenoidal minimum. Question beyond radial balance The finite cylindrical profile calculation found restoring roots when every ligand was constrained to share one radius. That only tests the breathing coordinate. A molecular candidate can be restoring in that coordinate and still buckle or shear. This check holds the central nucleus and prescribed 6D electron route fixed, but varies every supported-space coordinate of every ligand independently. For ligand centres R_a\in\mathbb R^3, it evaluates U(R_1,\ldots,R_n)=Z_L\left\langle \sum_a V_{r_N}(|q_{\rm vis}(t)-R_a|)\right\rangle_t +\sum_a\frac{Z_0Z_L}{|R_a|} +\sum_{a<b}\frac{Z_L^2}{|R_a-R_b|}, using the finite uniform-ball cylindrical profile V_{r_N} and the same diagnostic values as the radial calculation. The gradient is analytic; the Cartesian Hessian is a centered difference of that gradient and is checked against an independent second energy difference. Three-petal trigonal result At nuclear profile radius r_N=0.3, (Z_0,Z_L)=(1,0.1), and R=0.937604839, the three petal-axis centres are stationary to 3.97\times10^{-14}. The nine Cartesian ligand Hessian eigenvalues are (0.548468,0.557117,0.557117,0.585964,0.585964,0.598115, 0.652028,0.652028,0.659033). They are all positive. Thus the frozen-route energy diagnostic gives a strict trigonal local minimum against arbitrary independent ligand displacement, not merely a restoring common radius. The same conclusion holds at r_N=0.1 and 0.6: the minimum pair angle remains exactly 120^\circ, and the smallest Hessian eigenvalues are 3.17715, 0.548468, and 0.0588992 respectively. The declining stiffness with profile width is quantitative, but no shape mode changes sign. Four-centre correction The four quarter-turn rays of the (1,2) route have the Gram matrix of a regular tetrahedron. That kinematic fact does not make the regular tetrahedron a force equilibrium after the entire route is time averaged. At the radial root R=0.901811770, the largest Cartesian energy-gradient component is 2.996\times10^{-2} and is transverse to the assigned ray. Unconstrained relaxation of all twelve ligand coordinates converges to \begin{aligned} &(\phantom{-}0.771577,0,\phantom{-}0.462280), &&(0,\phantom{-}0.771577,-0.462280),\\ &(-0.771577,0,\phantom{-}0.462280), &&(0,-0.771577,-0.462280). \end{aligned} This is a disphenoid rather than a regular tetrahedron: four pair angles are 105.31619^\circ and two are 118.14528^\circ. Its final gradient is below 10^{-10}, and all twelve Hessian eigenvalues are positive, ranging from 0.183516 to 0.608247. The route therefore supports a strict nearby 3D four-centre minimum, but its present time weighting predicts a distortion away from the regular tetrahedral angles. Boundary of the result This remains a prescribed-route diagnostic with a fixed central nucleus and fixed nuclear support planes. The electron route has not been solved or relaxed as a function of the ligand coordinates, so this is not a derived Born--Oppenheimer energy surface. It establishes a local ligand minimum only for that restricted energy. It does not establish recurrence or Floquet stability of the reciprocal system, where the electron route, angular source, nuclear motion, and plane rotors all respond together. Conversely, the regular-tetrahedron correction should not be erased by calling the calculation incomplete: within the stated approximation, the transverse force is nonzero and the stable minimum is the reported disphenoid. The displacement is robust but profile-dependent: r_N four repeated angles two repeated angles minimum Hessian eigenvalue 0.1 108.69956^\circ 111.02582^\circ 0.456196 0.3 105.31619^\circ 118.14528^\circ 0.183516 0.6 99.06970^\circ 133.21424^\circ 0.0500167 The r_N=0.6 row retains point-centre nuclear repulsion even though some uniform-ball nuclear profiles overlap. It is therefore a hybrid diagnostic, not the result for consistent finite-density pair interactions. The r_N=0.3 reported minima have no such profile overlap. Listed Hessian digits are numerical output, not an error-certified continuum precision. Angle data could constrain profile width only after the electron route, charges, nuclear interaction, and averaging law are independently fixed. Angles alone do not identify a unique nuclear density. Reproduction cylindrical_molecular_shape_checks.py checks stationarity, full Cartesian Hessians, independent energy curvature, the regular-tetrahedron transverse residual, and relaxed four-centre stability. Multicentre orbit axes — supplies the exact axes; the present result distinguishes kinematic axes from force-balanced geometry. Reciprocal cylindrical molecule — supplies the conservative dynamical system required for the next periodic-orbit test.

title: Cylindrical petal continuation
